## ¶ The order of books contained in this volume.

¶ A work on the **fourfold life**, namely on the **healthy life**, the **long life**, the life **to be acquired from heaven**, and the **super-celestial life**. <note>This refers to Champier's *De quadruplici vita*, which blends medical advice with Neoplatonic and Hermetic philosophy regarding the soul's health.</note>
The **Theology of Asclepius**, disciple of Hermes, addressed to King Ammon: with commentaries by the same Master Symphorien on the same.
**Medicinal Forests** <note>original: "Silue medicinales". In Renaissance literature, a 'silva' (forest) refers to a collection of diverse writings or raw materials.</note> by the same Master Symphorien, pertaining to the completion of the books on the healthy and long life.
**Introductions** by the same into the **practice of medicine**.
Certain matters on the **practice of medicine** excerpted from **Pliny the Younger**. <note>During this era, a medical manual known as *Medicina Plinii* was widely circulated and incorrectly attributed to Pliny the Younger; Champier is utilizing this popular source.</note>

The **Trophy of the Gauls** <note>A celebratory history of France, which Champier connects to the ancient Gauls to bolster national prestige.</note> by the same Master Symphorien, divided into four partial booklets.
The **first** is on the division of Gaul: their origins and their victories against other nations. On the illustrious deeds of **Charles VIII** and **Louis XII**, Kings of the Franks. On the entry of the same **Louis XII**, King of the Franks, into the city of Genoa. On the praise of the Gauls from the testimonies of authors of other nations. On the second expedition against the Genoese. On the genealogy of the Kings of the Franks.
The **second book** is on the antiquity <gloss>and</gloss> praise of the city of Lyon. On the illustrious men of the same city.
The **third book** is on the famous **Gallic writers** who flourished in Gaul.
The **fourth book** is on the **supreme pontiffs** <note>Popes</note> who were Gauls.
A **defense** <term>apologia|a formal written defense of a person or a cause</term> against a slanderer of Gaul.
A **defense** of Brother Angelo de’ Ducci, an Italian from Brescia, of the Carmelite order.
Various **letters** to the same Master Symphorien.

<meta>This page continues the introductory front matter of Symphorien Champier’s volume. Following the table of contents, we find a formal dedicatory letter (Epistola) addressed to the author by his colleague Sebastian Coppin. This was a common Renaissance practice to establish the author's credibility and intellectual lineage.</meta>

# Epistle

->¶ Sebastian Coppin of Montluçon grants much health to Symphorien<-
->Champier of Lyon, most sagacious interpreter of the Paeonian art.<-
<note>original: "peonie artis". Paean was the physician of the Greek gods; the "Paeonian art" is a poetic term for medicine.</note>

---

<margin>Cato of Utica.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring figures in an architectural interior setting, likely representing an academic or classical scene.</image-desc>
You have recently finished calling back to harbor your labors produced by your own prowess: <note>original: "proprio marte lucubrationes". Literally "studies by your own Mars," meaning works produced through one's own intense personal effort and "night-oil."</note> they were most welcome. Thinking it far better to spend one’s life in the vigorous play of literature than to let the mind grow old in idleness and neglect, you seem to have perfectly emulated the divine opinion of Cato of Utica, <note>Cato the Younger (95–46 BCE), a Roman statesman known for his rigid morality.</note> who said that human life is very much like iron: for if it is exercised, it is worn away indeed, but with brilliance; if not, it is consumed by foul rust. By Hercules, sloth makes the body effeminate and the mind sluggish; and like a vapor flowing from the river Lethe, <note>In Greek mythology, the river of forgetfulness.</note> it brings about oblivion. This was expressed in these most elegant verses by a notable poet among the moderns: <margin>Baptista Mantuanus.</margin> "But the Father, <note>Referring to God or Jupiter as the creator.</note> who tempers all things with useful cares, intends to strengthen our might and powers through constant struggle; and for us, for whom he prepares the citadel of heaven, he denies sloth and sleep—lest, indeed, the mind, weakened by sweet years and sluggish rest, should languish, and torpor should make the slow limbs effeminate. For torpor is a vapor rising from the blind whirlpool of sleep-bearing Lethe, and it spreads a dark cloud over human senses." Listen also to Maro: <note>Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note> <margin>Baptista Mantuanus.</margin> "The Father himself willed that the way of cultivation should not be easy, and he first stirred the fields through art, sharpening mortal hearts with cares, nor did he allow his realms to grow sluggish with heavy lethargy." <margin>Virgil.</margin> Thus, as a follower of Plato, you were born not for yourself alone, but consulting the common utility of all. Just as you are an object of admiration while living, so when deceased (which mortals strive for with greatest effort) you desire to deserve the immortality of your name, led by the precept of Sallust: <margin>Sallust.</margin> "It becomes all men who study to excel other living creatures to strive with the greatest power lest they pass their lives in silence." <margin>Sallust.</margin>

Wherefore, I follow you with the highest praises, as you are devoted to literary leisure <note>original: "litterario ocio". In the Renaissance, 'otium' (leisure) was not laziness, but the time set aside for scholarly study.</note> through which you untie riddles very much like Gordian knots, while also performing the duty of curing health. For according to the opinion of Cato, <margin>The reasoning for leisure and business.</margin> there ought to be an account of the leisure and business of famous men no less than their work, which is esteemed not without cause. Thus Publius Scipio, called by the surname Africanus, was said to never be less idle than when he was at leisure, nor less alone than when he was alone. Nor did I think it worthy to pass over in silence Julius Caesar and Octavius Augustus, one of whom, while setting out with his army, used to read very much, and if there was any moment of time in the camps, he was accustomed to write books most accurately. <margin>The diligence of Julius and Octavius Caesar.</margin> The other, having undertaken so great a task in the Mutinine war, was always accustomed either to read, or write, or declaim daily. The monuments of letters make much of Hercules, the son of Jupiter and Alcmena, who emerged into such great strength and glory that he is seen both placed among the gods and as having deservedly attained that name; and of Hector, son of Priam, the bravest of the Trojans, who by his strength overcame Patroclus, who was joined to Achilles by the greatest bond; and of Achilles, most sung in Maeonian <note>Homeric</note> songs, who is said to have dragged the corpse of Hector tied to his horse around Troy. Why should I mention the Carthaginian Hannibal, who was seen to excel other leaders in prudence as much as the Roman people surpassed all nations in fortitude? And unless he had been weakened by the envy of his own citizens, he might have been seen to overcome the Romans. This man, made general at twenty-five years of age, <margin>Hannibal broke the Alps.</margin> opened the Alpine mountains with vinegar and fire, so that a loaded elephant could go where previously one unarmed man could scarcely crawl. When the Romans held wide dominion over affairs, they were accustomed to gift their leaders with triumphal honors, among whom Gnaeus Pompey the Great is found to have been most outstanding. <margin>Triumph.</margin> Truly, the triumph was the greatest honor shown to Roman leaders. For they were carried by white horses, in which Camillus was the first of all to be carried in a gilded chariot, his head crowned with laurel; before the triumphing man, the conquered enemy was led with his neck weighed down by chains, and with the Senate going before, he ascended the Capitol to the temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest, where, having sacrificed a white bull, he then returned to his own home. But if we extol with the highest praises those supported by bodily strength who became famous in war and arms, do not those deserve much more who excel by the strength of their intellect? Among whom you by no means hold the lowest part. There are many works extant from your workshop proving this. I will mention first those "Aquitanian Vigils" which are titled the *Ship of Princes and Ladies*. <note>Refers to Champier's *La Nef des princes et des batailles de la noblesse* (1502).</note> In those, very many of the innermost secrets of almost all disciplines are open. There exists a concise work published by you commonly called the *Door of Dialectics*, in which...

<sig>a ij</sig>

<summary>A formal commendatory letter from Sebastian Coppin to the polymath Symphorien Champier, praising his tireless intellectual productivity and comparing his dedication to classical heroes and scholars like Caesar and Scipio.</summary>
<keywords>Symphorien Champier, Sebastian Coppin, medicine, humanism, Cato the Younger, Virgil, Hannibal, Ship of Princes and Ladies, classical antiquity, diligence</keywords>

--- Page 22 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory letter from Sebastian Coppin to Symphorien Champier. The previous page ended with a quote from Baptista Mantuanus about the necessity of hard work to avoid the "rust" of idleness. Here, Coppin lists Champier's specific academic achievements and compares his fame to that of the Roman historian Livy.</meta>

you seem to have restored Cippean logic. <note>original: "sippeam dialecticen". This refers to the *Logica Cippea*, a specific pedagogical method of logic named after the "Cippus" (boundary stone) which Champier promoted.</note> I am silent regarding your other works, such as your "Gate to Physics," or your treatises on the heavens and the world, on generation and corruption, and on the soul and its immortality. I pass over your little book against magicians and enchanters, your "Additions" to the surgeon Guy de Chauliac, <note>Guy de Chauliac (c. 1300–1368) was the most famous surgical authority of the Middle Ages; Champier edited and updated his works.</note> and your "Introductions" to the kingdom of Galen. <note>Claudius Galen (129–c. 216 CE), the Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> Indeed, these works are so widely known that, as the saying goes, 
<margin>Juvenal.</margin>
"No one knows their own home better." <note>A quote from Juvenal's Satires (1.7), implying these books are household names among scholars.</note> Now, a new work embraces the ancient inventors of both the Apolline art <note>The "Apolline art" refers to medicine, as Apollo was the god of healing.</note> and of divine laws. In your hands is that memorable work titled "On the Fourfold Life." You are also completing the "Trophy of the Gauls," which comprises a fourfold history of that people, along with several other small works, as the matter itself indicates. From these, one can easily discern how much you excel in both natural genius and learned doctrine. Consequently, no one can read and re-read them without great pleasure of mind. They are composed with such ornament, such grace, and finally such success that they are of use both to me and to everyone.

I have noticed, moreover, that you have so joined gravity of character and honesty of life with the best literary studies that I could easily conclude you would shortly emerge as a most excellent and distinguished man—a fact which the outcome of events will surely prove. For at present, the city of Lyon, most fertile in outstanding talents, has no one better or more learned than you. I believe that those who know you through your books will readily travel there so that they may also see you in person, just as Jerome says to Paulinus regarding Titus Livy: <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 CE) wrote a famous letter to Paulinus of Nola describing how people traveled from the ends of the earth just to see the great historian Livy.</note> "We read that certain nobles came from the farthest reaches of Spain and the Gauls to Titus Livy, who flows from a milky fountain of eloquence; and those whom Rome had not drawn to contemplate its own sights, the fame of one man brought there." 

For I know, I truly know, O most excellent of men, where virtue has long since destined you, where grace accompanies you, and where your merits lead. I know, I say, by what steps you ascend: namely, by wise eloquence, by human courtesy, by manifest virtue, and by the incomparable brilliance of your life, you have long since been ascending by the straight path into the heavens. 

<margin>Virgil</margin>
"Flourish in your new-found virtue, O fighter; thus one journeys to the stars." <note>original: "Macte nova virtute... sic itur ad astra". A famous line from Virgil’s Aeneid (9.641) encouraging heroic effort.</note> Thus the ancient glory of the fathers comes through merit. Farewell.

# To the most deserving doctor in the most health-giving faculty of medicine, Lord Symphorien Champier of Lyon. Brother Guichard de Lessard of the Lyon convent of the Hermit Brothers of Saint Augustine, humble professor in the nurturing faculty of theology at Paris, Bishop of Hieropolis, and official of the Lord of Lyon, sends many greetings.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'M' showing two figures in robes, possibly scholars or physicians, in conversation within a landscape.</image-desc>Our ancestors, the most expert of physicians (as you well know), took no small amount of labor upon themselves to acquire good literature and to teach it to posterity. Jesus Sirach <note>Also known as Ben Sira, the author of the biblical book of Ecclesiasticus.</note> judged these men most worthy of praise in his forty-fourth chapter <note>The original text cites chapter 43, but the quote comes from chapter 44 of Ecclesiasticus.</note> saying: *Let us praise famous men, our fathers in their generation.* Shortly after it follows: *People will tell of their wisdom and the church will declare their praise.* Nor were there only those among the Hebrews (by whom God was known) who sought wisdom with the most studious affection; even the Gentiles <note>Non-Jewish, classical Greeks and Romans.</note> who ignored God, having spurned the pleasures of the world and cast down riches and honors, sweated with all their strength (as they say) over both human and divine sciences. This is clearer than light in the books recently and most elegantly composed by you and published through the work of printers. Among these was that Gentile, Ptolemy Philadelphus, King of the Egyptians, who, so that the Law which they call "Divine" might become known to him and he might share it with the wise men of his kingdom, called for seventy interpreters after his pursuit of other sciences. <note>Ptolemy Philadelphus (3rd century BCE) is traditionally credited with commissioning the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> This is attested by our father Aurelius Augustine in *The City of God*, book 18, chapter 42, and in *On Christian Doctrine*, book 2, chapter 4. 

But alas, in these times there is an abundance of those whom Paul, the "vessel of election" to the Gentiles, foresaw long ago by the inspiration of the divine spirit: men who are lovers of themselves, greedy, arrogant, always learning but never reaching the knowledge of the truth. Most learned man, you most clearly refuse to imitate their habits through your own actions. For while others sleep, you watch, and you spend no small part of the night sleepless. You cultivate the field <note>A pun on the name Champier, which is derived from the Latin "campus," meaning field.</note> so excellently, Champier, and sow it with such fruitful seed, that from it spring fragrant flowers with fruit. If I wished to recount them all, to use Virgil's words: *The evening would close Olympus before the day was done.* <note>original: "Ante diem clauso componeret vesper olimpo." A classical trope used to say a list is too long to finish in one day.</note> I would not be sufficient for each one, much less for all of them. Nor am I able to sufficiently praise these outstanding things which, through the erudition of your genius, you have fashioned with laborious night-work not many days ago for the benefit of students. 

I cannot easily say with what joy and with what pleasure of mind I have read them. Nor have I found anything worthy of blame, unless I am mistaken. Indeed, you have discussed *The Healthy Life* most sharply and prudently; *The Long Life*; *The Life to be Prepared Heavily* [Celestial] in a heavenly manner; and *The Super-celestial Life* faithfully. Therefore, I pray to the Most High that He may grant you a sound mind in a sound body <note>A reference to the Roman poet Juvenal's famous phrase "mens sana in corpore sano."</note> for years as long as Nestor's, <note>Nestor was a legendary Greek hero known for his great age and wisdom.</note> and the grace to contemplate the life from heaven, so that by your demanding merits you may deserve to reach eternal life. Farewell, my most delightful Symphorien, and continue your love for me constantly. Farewell again. From Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' featuring scrolling floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>During the times of the Goths, Vandals, and Huns, not only did illustrious nations like Gaul, Italy, and Greece suffer fires, slaughters, robberies, and other such destructions, but (what is much worse) the finest literature, which was in its greatest bloom before those calamitous centuries, suffered an execrable and almost irreparable disaster. For those ignorant of the good arts pursue scholars with capital hatred and relentlessly harass them as enemies. It is no wonder that the Goths and the rest of the Scythian peoples, having never experienced the sweetness of the Muses, held the disciplines of Pallas [Athena] <note>Pallas Athena was the Greek goddess of wisdom and the arts; "Palladian disciplines" refers to academic and artistic study.</note> as hated and most hostile. Nor was the noble metropolis of Lyon exempt from that wasting plague, even though it was the ancient parent and teacher of the most learned men—such as the teacher of Plancus, that follower of Cicero from whom all studies of humanity flow like great rivers from the most abundant springs. 

At last you have arrived as the liberator of this lamented city and the father of your country, Symphorien Champier; you are worthy of the greatest praise because you have shaped the city's ruined morals—for it is more excellent to build the souls of citizens than their walls. Indeed, Lycurgus of the Spartans and Solon of the Athenians, who gave them laws, are considered founders. And it was more greatly profitable for Rome when the religion of Pompilius...

and learning for laying the foundations of an empire than the buildings of Romulus <note>The legendary founder of Rome; the author suggests Champier's intellectual work is more foundational than physical architecture.</note>. Therefore, we ought to rightfully congratulate you, eagle of physicians and philosophers, who have published so many immortal monuments for our instruction and that of posterity: namely, the books on the **fourfold life**—**healthy**, **long**, **to be acquired from heaven**, and **super-heavenly** <note>original: "de vita quadruplici. sana: longa: celitus comparanda: et supercelesti." This refers to the structure of the book, which expands on Marsilio Ficino’s famous "Three Books on Life" by adding a fourth spiritual dimension.</note>—with which we can be content as a complete doctrine. You provide frequent victories for the Gauls <note>The French people.</note> against foreign nations and eternal incitements to virtue. You have forged many other things with the hammer of your lofty genius to last for eternal days. It is pious to believe, therefore, that the spirits of our ancestors applaud; the blessed orator, and Photinus and Irenaeus <note>Saint Photinus and Saint Irenaeus were the first bishops of Lyon, emphasizing Champier's connection to his home city's Christian history.</note>, the bishops, exult greatly, as they hear that one of their own descendants from their city has driven out that **Gothic barbarism** <note>A common Renaissance term for the "Middle Ages" or uncultured style, which humanists like Champier sought to replace with classical Roman elegance.</note> and restored the city's ancient face. 

Nor was it enough for you, even if you satisfied all our countrymen, to fatten the souls of the citizens with your sweetest, sumptuous feasts of knowledge, unless you also looked after the goods of the body, which are considered second in importance among the most excellent philosophers. Indeed, you are so expertly skilled in medicine—the prince of the noble arts and, as the wise man says, especially necessary <note>A reference to the Biblical Book of Sirach 38:1: "Honor the physician for the need thou hast of him."</note>—that you are regarded by everyone as a storehouse and almost a sanctuary of all literature. Nor do you pursue the theories of Hippocratic doctrine for profit, as many do; rather, you help and assist the poor and the wealthy equally and without distinction. 

Therefore, you deserve to enjoy the privileges and favors of those ancient physicians who, because of their singular virtue and health-giving industry, were granted honors by the most munificent emperors, since you take their place. By your auspices, you have made that most holy age—long buried—live again in our **golden** and almost **Saturnian** time <note>A "Saturnian age" refers to a mythical Golden Age of peace and plenty.</note>. Yet the laws state that a famous physician, with his wife, children, and household, can by no means be forced into any civil duties or functions. And for no crime should he be subjected to questioning, nor called to court against his will. Nor should they suffer any loss from merchants or epidemics. Truly, by imperial decree, it is provided that any soldier or courtier be expelled from the threshold of a famous physician’s house so that he may not be taken in for lodging, even if a prince or army is passing by. We find the learned medical academy decorated with so many other indulgences and immunities that we could not list them individually in an entire day. Thus, no one of good character will think you should be deprived of these, as you are the most consummate physician not only of bodies (which are frail and fleeting) but also of immortal souls. Continue, therefore, as you have begun, treasurer of the literary hoard, as we know for certain you will do, to deserve more and more from our republic every day. Farewell. Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507.

### ->Gonzalo de Toledo to Lord Symphorien<-
### ->Champier, doctor of arts and medicine, his most<-
### ->honorable friend. Many greetings.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring white leafy and floral scrollwork on a dark background within a square frame. In the center of the 'E', there is a circular floral motif.</image-desc>

Although many men of excellent genius, my dearest Symphorien, have written with wonderful zeal and diligence about the **threefold life**—namely, the **healthy**, the **long**, and the **heavenly to be acquired**—such as the most illustrious author **Marsilio Ficino** <note>An Italian scholar and priest who was one of the most influential humanist philosophers of the early Renaissance.</note>, **Arnaldus de Villa Nova** <note>A 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>, and many other physicians; nevertheless, none of them followed this order which you have in this book on the **fourfold life**, condensed by you with great care and singular eloquence into a brief summary. In this matter, you have observed the Horatian precept <note>A rule from the Roman poet Horace's "Art of Poetry."</note> like an oracle, which is: *Whatever you teach, be brief, so that docile minds may quickly perceive what is said and faithful ones may retain it.* 

I would judge such a noble gift to be most suitable not only for me, a very small man, but even for these kings and princes, who ought to protect their bodies with good health so that they may guard the rudders of the world in tranquil peace. However, I joyfully behold your holy and friendly spirit toward me. And I vehemently congratulate myself and the other physicians of our time, who are about to receive the fruit—and indeed a most abundant one—of your labor and industry. For the book is "juicy," fertile, and seasoned with the most edible seasonings of diverse doctrine, so structured that it appeals to both the palate and the stomach <note>A metaphor for the book being both pleasant to read and easy to intellectually digest.</note>. Therefore, in return for this most beautiful gift of yours, since I cannot currently repay you with anything greater, I have decided to take diligent care that from that one volume which you wrote with your learned hand and gave to me, many copies may be spread and diffused among posterity through the service of the printing press. This I will do, both because of the bond of a grateful soul and especially because of this plan: so that you...

### Letter

...I might free you entirely from all thought or care of visiting your sick, and exempt you from the concerns of your household. In the meantime, continue as you have begun, my dear Champier, most esteemed among the physicians of Lyon, and apply yourself vigilantly to the study of letters. Try to make scholars daily more enriched in the fine arts by your writing and reading, and you will crush the biting teeth of the envious with your excellent reputation. For I judge that no one is so negligent or inexperienced in human affairs that—if they speak the truth—they would not accept this work with a cheerful face. Farewell. From Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507.

-> ¶ Philippe Laurent, physician to the most serene Queen of the French, <-
-> to Master Symphorien Champier of Lyon, well-deserving professor <-
-> of the Apolline art <note>original: "apollinee artis," referring to Apollo, the Greek god of healing and music; a humanist way of saying "medicine."</note>. Hearty greetings. <-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial L, featuring intricate foliate patterns and scrolling vines within a double-lined square border.</image-desc>

Praise is given—and indeed not undeservedly—to that most sagacious leader of the Greeks, Ulysses, who, after the ten-year Trojan War was finished, chose to risk his path by land and sea while the other Greeks (overcome by love of country and an immense desire for praise) returned home more quickly. He approached diverse peoples and nations as if he were likely to find there something that would contribute not a little to the establishment of the best way of life. Hence Homer sang of him: *Tell me, Muse, of the man who, after the fall of Troy, saw the customs and cities of many men* <note>original: "Dic mihi musa virum capte post tempora Troie: Qui mores hoim multorū vidit ⁊ vrbes." A quote from the opening of the Odyssey.</note>. But in my opinion, I should judge that even greater praise is due to you, my most charming Symphorien, for you have surveyed most diligently not the nations of diverse peoples, but the arts and disciplines of diverse authors, turning over many of their volumes. 

From these studies, in addition to the books you published in previous years for the instruction of a good life, you have in these days sent out to the public—through the industry of the printers <note>original: "chalcographorū," literally "brass-writers," a Renaissance term for printers using metal type.</note>—booklets on the **fourfold life**, on the **trophies of the Gauls**, on the **antiquity of the city of Lyon**, on its **illustrious men**, and on the **renowned writers** of all Gaul (Cisalpine, I mean). Therefore, it is only right that those lovers of knowledge who toil to acquire disciplines should admit they are deeply indebted to you, for you have driven the densest fog of ignorance from their minds. Who, I ask, is more diligent than you alone in the harmonious style of speaking? Who in sophisticated charm? Who, I say, in investigating the knowledge of physical matters? No one, by Hercules, no one! For you are so gifted, learned, and erudite that you nourish and feed all people with the richness of your talent and the abundance of all sciences. 

All can therefore admire you, but very few can imitate you; likewise, no one can reproach you unless they are out of their mind. And I conceive of one thing in you that is most rare, or perhaps never before found—something divine and worthy of admiration: namely, the highest eloquence joined with the study of philosophy. By this, you seem to me not only to equal but even to surpass the Italians, who spend a good part of their time attaining eloquence while neglecting the study of most chaste philosophy. 

But see, I pray, my most pleasant Symphorien, what madness occupies the minds of certain men! When they have learned how to bring forth two or three propositions of any science, they boast and show themselves off just as if they had washed their lips in the **horse-spring** <note>original: "fonte... caballino," referring to Hippocrene, the spring on Mt. Helicon created by the hoof of Pegasus, said to bring poetic inspiration.</note> or dreamed on the heights of Parnassus. They are like those "Greeks" and "empirics" <note>Laurent is mocking uneducated practitioners who rely on experience alone without theoretical knowledge.</note> who, when they have learned how to prepare a single **enema** <note>original: "clisteriū."</note> or write out one **medical recipe**, walk about so haughtily and pompously as if Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine.</note> had revealed to them every secret of the healing art. Hence, like certain "naked wise men" <note>original: "gymnoshophiste," referring to the Gymnosophists of India, here used as a metaphor for those who think they are self-taught sages.</note> imbued with the learning of all disciplines, they "enlarge their fringes" and "love the first places at feasts" <note>A biblical allusion to the Pharisees in Matthew 23:5-6.</note>. For this reason, they are not afraid to place themselves above the greatest philosophers. "We do not want your philosophy," they say, "shaggy and hairy, lumpy, barbaric, and tangled." 

These are the sort of people who, according to the whim of their own will, profess to be able to turn black into white and vice versa. They want to amplify and raise up whatever they wish, and to diminish and depress others, transforming them into whatever face or habit they desire—so that things appear not as they are by their own nature, but as those people want them to be seen. But who would not condemn and detest curls and rouge on a dishonest maiden? Is it not the duty of a sophist or a sycophant to lie, deceive, circumvent, and play tricks? It is certainly not the duty of a philosopher, whose entire study stands centered around the investigation of truth—which Cicero asserts is proper to man. 

<margin>Into the mouths of many.</margin>
For a man of integrity does not use these kinds of vices, paintings, or disguises unless necessity requires it.

<margin>Flourished.</margin>
Because if Pythagoras had been able to live without food, he would have even spared the vegetables. In the same way, if he could have explained the concept of the mind or the affection of the soul with less effort than speech requires, he would have used perpetual silence. # Letter

...and erudition for laying the foundations of empire through the buildings of Romulus <note>The author compares Champier's intellectual work to the legendary founding of Rome by Romulus.</note>. We rightfully owe congratulations to you, O eagle among physicians and philosophers, who has published so many immortal monuments for our instruction and that of posterity. I speak specifically of your books on the fourfold life: the healthy, the long, the heavenly-attained, and the super-heavenly, with which we can be well-satisfied for every doctrine. Your works record the frequent victories of the French against foreign nations as eternal incentives to virtue. Many other works you have forged with the hammer of your sublime genius, destined to endure for eternal days. It is right, therefore, to believe that the spirits of our ancestors—the orator Plautus Faustus, and the bishops Photinus and Irenaeus <note>Photinus and Irenaeus were early Christian martyrs and bishops of Lyon; the author suggests they are proud of their city’s modern son.</note>—rejoice greatly because they hear that one of their descendants has driven out that Gothic barbarism <note>original: "gothicam illam barbariem"; a common Renaissance term for the supposedly "uncivilized" medieval style of Latin and philosophy</note> from their city and restored its ancient face to the town.

Nor was it enough for you—even if you had satisfied all our countrymen—to nourish the souls of the citizens with your most sweet and sumptuously prepared "side-dishes" of knowledge, unless you also looked after the goods of the body, which are considered abundant among the most distinguished philosophers. Indeed, you are so expertly skilled in medicine—the prince of the noble arts and, as the wise man says, primary and necessary—and you cultivate it in no small measure, so that you are everywhere judged by all to be the storehouse and almost the sanctuary of all literature. Nor do you pursue the theories of Hippocratic doctrine for profit, as many are accustomed to do, but you come to the aid of the poor and the wealthy equally and without distinction, following your habit of being helpful. 

Therefore, not without reason should you enjoy the prerogatives and favors of those ancient physicians who, because of their singular virtue and life-saving industry, were granted exemptions by the most munificent Emperors. For you take their place, and by your efforts, you have made that most holy age—buried for so very long—live again in our golden and nearly Saturnian time <note>The "Saturnian" age refers to the mythical Golden Age of peace and plenty.</note>. Furthermore, the laws concerning these prerogatives state that a famous physician, along with his wife, children, and household, can in no way be forced into any civil duties or public functions. He is never to be subjected to interrogation for a crime, nor summoned to court against his will. Nor should they suffer any loss from merchants or epidemics. Indeed, it is provided by imperial decree that any soldier or courtier be expelled from the threshold of a famous physician’s house rather than being taken in as a guest, even if a prince or an army is passing through. We find the learned medical academy decorated with so many other indulgences and immunities that we could not enumerate them individually in an entire day. Thus, no one of good character will think you should be defrauded of these honors, as you exist as a most perfect physician—not only of bodies, which are frail and fleeting, but also of immortal souls. Continue, therefore, as you have begun, O treasurer of the literary storehouse, for we know for certain you will deserve more and more from our republic every day. Farewell. Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507.

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory letter from Philippe Laurent to the physician Symphorien Champier. Laurent is defending the plain, direct style of scientific and philosophical writing against critics who prefer "flowery" or sophisticated rhetoric. He frames Champier’s work as part of a noble tradition that values substance over style.</meta>

->Letter<-

**Hippocrates of Cos**, **Avicenna**, **Rhazes**, and almost countless others wrote without ostentation or any flowery rhetoric, since they understood that it was the actual fruits, and not the flowers of speech, that were useful to us. Therefore, those who strive only for rhetorical embellishments—prioritizing the flower over the fruit, as it were—should not blame such learned men as if they had left out anything relevant to their profession through silence. 

In my opinion, those critics are far from the mark. Just as a house made of marble does not require painting or artificial coloring, so too philosophy <note>In this context, "philosophy" refers broadly to the study of nature and science, including medicine.</note> does not need these kinds of verbal ornaments. Yet, I frankly admit that among various nations there have been many who wrote eloquently, elegantly, and brilliantly in theology, medicine, and other disciplines. I am not speaking of those poets whom the divine **Plato** judged should be expelled from a well-ordered city; I truly wish their eloquence had never reached us.

<margin>James 3</margin>
But enough about them. Continue, I pray you, my Symphorien, as you have begun; do not fear the barking of an evil-speaking tongue. For every nature (as you well know) of beasts, birds, serpents, and other creatures is tamed and has been tamed by human nature, but no man can tame the tongue. <note>original: "linguam autem nullus hominum domare potest." A direct quote from the Bible, James 3:8.</note> It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison. For once the slanderer—who is "chatterier than a turtledove" <note>A common Renaissance adage used to describe someone who talks incessantly.</note>—has vomited out his venom, he will grow quiet. For even the envious, the wrathful, the lazy, the drunkard, and the lover—no one is so wild that they cannot be tamed. 

<margin>Horace, likewise in his Epistles.</margin>
I would have you persuade yourself that I am the one most devoted to you out of our entire order. For just as the night seems long to those whose lover has deceived them, and the day seems long to those who owe labor, and the year feels slow to orphans oppressed by the harsh guardianship of mothers, so the time flows slowly and unpleasantly for me while it delays the hope and the plan of acting diligently—that which would be pleasing and welcome to you, who have deserved so well from us. This is because you have brought into the light a work which "benefits the poor and the rich alike, but which, if neglected, would equally harm the young and the old." <note>Laurent is quoting Horace’s *Epistles* (1.1.20–26) to describe his eager anticipation for Champier’s medical publication.</note>

Farewell, and continue to love me as you do.

Lyon, in the year of our salvation 1507, the 4th Kalends of July. <note>June 28, 1507.</note>

# Letter

**Hippocrates of Cos**; **Avicenna**; **Rhazes**; <note>Hippocrates (Greek), Avicenna (Persian), and Rhazes (Persian) were the foundational authorities of medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note> and almost countless others wrote without pomp or any flowery speech, since they understood that it was not the flowers of speech but the actual fruits that are useful to us. But in my opinion, those people are wandering far from the truth. For just as a house made of marble does not admit painting or artificial coloring, so too philosophy does not need verbal ornaments of that kind. Nevertheless, I frankly admit that there have been many among various nations who have written eloquently, ornately, and splendidly both in theology and in medicine, as well as in other disciplines. I am not speaking of that certain class of poets whom the divine **Plato** judged should be expelled from a well-ordered city. And would that their eloquence had never reached us!

<margin>James 3</margin>
But enough of these matters. Continue, I beg you, my **Symphorian**, as you have begun; do not fear the slanderous barking of the tongue. For every nature <note>original: "Omnis natura," referencing James 3:7-8 regarding the inability of man to tame the tongue.</note> of beasts and birds and serpents and the rest are tamed and have been tamed by human nature, but no man can tame the tongue. For whether one is envious, or wrathful, or lazy, or a wine-bibber, or a lover: "No one is so savage that he cannot be tamed." <note>A quote from Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.39.</note> I would wish you to

<margin>Horace</margin>

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring stylized foliage and circular patterns within a double-lined square border.</image-desc>

Writers of history have recorded, O most noble prelate, that priests have been held in the greatest honor and always of admirable reputation among all nations, both because of their eminence in learning <margin>Priests</margin> and because of the holiness of their lives. Hence, while other nations were shrouded in silence, as the history of Genesis relates: when an intolerable famine oppressed all of Egypt, and everyone, pressed by the magnitude of the hunger, was forced to sell their possessions because their money was spent, the priests alone retained their lands and possessions for themselves, as they were provided with fixed rations from the public granaries. <margin>Gen. 47</margin> Likewise, as Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE.</note> testifies: the Egyptians judge them worthy of such great honor that they choose their kings only from their college of priests. No one is promoted to this peak of the priesthood unless they are from the assembly of philosophers, who <margin>Diodorus Siculus book 2</margin> instruct their sons in the letters which are called "sacred" and in others that pertain to common learning. For the common people were led by a certain opinion that a degree of divinity was communicated to them from the gods in heaven, which was not granted to others; and therefore a certain necessity intervened, whereby it was believed that through their favorable sacrifices, all things would succeed prosperously for them. Nor did they believe the anger of the gods was so ready or immediate for vengeance. As a certain poet <note>The Roman poet Ovid, in his work *Tristia*.</note> said: "If Jupiter should send his lightning bolts every time men sin, in a short time there will be no one left." Certainly, the priests of false gods are by no means to be compared to the priests of the true God, since there is as great a difference between them as between the body and the spirit, or between the animal and the spiritual. For in many places in Holy Scripture, the priests of the Most High God are called "angels" <note>The Latin *angelus* and Greek *angelos* literally mean "messenger."</note> because of the excellence of their dignity. The prophet <margin>The prophet Malachi</margin> Malachi testifies to this, saying: "The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, for he is the messenger <margin>Malachi ch. 2</margin> of the Lord of hosts."

You, O most sacred of prelates, so far surpass these men (if it were permitted to compare great things with small) as much as your metropolitan city <note>Lyon</note> surpasses other cities; to use Virgilian <margin>Virgil</margin> words: "But she has lifted her head among other cities as high as cypresses are wont to do among the bending osiers." <note>A quote from Virgil’s *Eclogues* 1.24-25, comparing the greatness of Rome to other towns.</note> For you have attained the primacy in the Gallican Church; you are appointed, as the Apostle says: "A high priest taken from among men in those things which pertain to God, that you may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins." <margin>Hebrews</margin>

But with what honors should we pursue the height of your dignity for such benefits? Or with what facility of mind shall we deserve your kindness toward us? No one, even gifted with no small eloquence, could easily achieve this in words. So great is the magnitude of your benefits toward us that our strengths are by no means sufficient to give thanks, let alone to repay the favor. For to confess the truth frankly, our health depends on you, to whose will we devote both ourselves primarily and all our things. To whom also I offer this monument of my love toward your humanity: this small work I have forged "On the Fourfold Life," <note>original: *De quadruplici vita*. This is the title of the work this preface introduces.</note> no small part of our late-night labors <note>original: *lucubrationes*, a term for scholarly works composed by lamplight at night.</note>. # Introductory letter to the following work.

¶ To the most noble and in every way most learned and especially most observant lord: Lord François de Rohan, Bishop of Angers, then Archbishop of Lyon and Primate of the Gauls: Symphorien Champier, physician of Lyon, wishes the greatest health.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial M, containing an archway with two figures, possibly saints or church authorities. This ornamental block starts the word "Maximo".</image-desc>
**M**ost noble of leaders, writers of history have recorded that priests were held in the highest honor and were always of admirable esteem <margin>Priests</margin> among all nations, both due to their eminence in learning and the sanctity of their lives. Whence, while other nations are shrouded in silence, as the history of Genesis relates: when an intolerable famine oppressed all Egypt, and all others—having spent their money—were compelled by the magnitude of the famine to sell their <margin>Genesis 47</margin> possessions: only the priests retained their lands and possessions for themselves, and they were even provided fixed food portions from the public granaries. Likewise, as Diodorus Siculus <margin>Diodorus</margin> is witness: the Egyptians deem them worthy of such great honor that they choose their kings only from that college of priests. Nor is anyone promoted to the peak of the priesthood unless from the assembly of philosophers, who instruct <margin>Book 2</margin> their children in the letters which are called "sacred," and in others which pertain to common learning. For the ignoble commoners were led by some opinion or other: that some share of divinity was communicated to the priests from the lords of heaven, a gift denied to others; and because of this, a certain necessity intervened, whereby they believed that everything would succeed prosperously for them if the Lord was propitiated by the sacrifices of these same men. Nor did they think the anger of the gods was so ready or present for vengeance. Whence, as a certain man said: <margin>Ovid</margin> "If Jupiter were to send his lightning bolts as often as men sin, in a short time there will be no one left." <note>Original: "Si quotiens peccant homines sua fulmina mittat Juppiter: exiguo tempore nullus erit." A quote from Ovid's Tristia, emphasizing divine patience.</note> Truly, the priests of false gods are not at all to be compared to the priests of the true God, since there is as much difference between them as between the body and the spirit, or between the animal and the spiritual. For in many places of the Sacred Page <note>A traditional term for the Bible.</note> the priests of the Most High God are called "angels" because of the excellence of their dignity; which the prophet Malachi <margin>Malachi ch. 2</margin> testifies, saying: "The lips of the priest shall keep knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts." <note>Malachi 2:7. The Hebrew word for messenger, 'malakh', is translated as 'angelus' in Latin.</note> Whom (if it were permitted to compare great things to small) <margin>Virgil</margin> you, most sacred of prelates, exceed as much as your metropolis <note>Lyon</note> exceeds other cities; which, to use Virgilian words, "has raised its head among other cities as much as cypresses are wont to do among bending shrubs." <note>A reference to Virgil’s Eclogues, comparing the height and dignity of a great city to a tree among bushes.</note> For you, having obtained the primacy in the Gallican Church, have been appointed—as the Apostle says—<margin>Hebrews 5</margin> a "high priest for men in those things which pertain to God, that you may offer gifts and sacrifices for sins." 

But with what honors shall we <insert>pursue</insert> pursue the highness of your dignity for such benefits? Or by what means shall we merit the kindness of your mind toward us? Indeed, no one, even if endowed with no mediocre eloquence, could easily achieve this in words. For so great is the magnitude of your benefits toward us, that our powers are by no means sufficient for giving thanks, much less for repaying the favor. For from you, to confess the truth frankly, our health depends; to whose will we devote both ourselves especially and all our things. To whom also I offer this monument of my love toward your humanity: this little work fashioned regarding the ***fourfold life***, no small part of our late-night labors. But lest any troublesome carping critic should object to us that **Marsilio Ficino**—a man distinguished in every kind of discipline, as well as skilled in both the Greek and Latin tongues—has done almost the same thing and published a work of admirable doctrine regarding the ***triple life***...

### Introductory letter to the following work.

...small treatise: and that we either value his teaching as nothing, or have converted a not insignificant part of his labor into our own work, and wish to snatch glory for ourselves from another's toil. I do not deny this; on the contrary, I frankly confess: Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a celebrated Italian scholar and priest who led the revival of Neoplatonism in the Renaissance.</note> was a man of admirable erudition, whom I have always valued as highly as anyone from the college of scholars. Indeed, I freely confess that I have profited greatly from reading him. For I have set him before me as a leader in this business, and I have followed him. 

But since, as the poet says: <margin>Virgil in the Eclogues</margin> "We cannot all do everything." <note>original: "Non omnia possumus omnes." A famous line from Virgil's Eclogue 8.</note> And as Horace <margin>Horace in the Art of Poetry</margin> bears witness: "Sometimes even good Homer nods." <note>A classic idiom suggesting that even the greatest authors occasionally make mistakes or have lapses.</note> I have added several things; and from the volumes of both Catholic theologians and the most ancient philosophers, we have gathered this small book concerning the celestial life. 

I ask you to receive, most worthy of prelates <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop.</note>, this small work divided into four books concerning the fourfold life, in the spirit with which it is offered. Of these, the first is titled *On a Healthy Life*. For it is not enough to live, unless we also live healthily; for as the author of Ecclesiasticus <margin>Ecclesiasticus 30</margin> testifies: "There is no wealth above the wealth of the health of the body." 

And because men desire, furthermore, not only to be well at times, but also to live a long time while being healthy, I added a small book *On a Long Life*. And since they sometimes distrust earthly medicines and remedies—and celestial bodies influence these lower things—I added a small book *On Obtaining a Life both Healthy and Long from Heaven*. And because this aspires to an even more worthy life, namely the celestial and spiritual, I have joined a fourth small book, in which the opinions of both Christian theologians and ancient philosophers regarding the happiness of the soul are recounted. 

This, most excellent of prelates, is the medley of our book, which, relying on your patronage, will go forth securely into public and will undergo the judgment of others without fear; nor will it dread the empty talk of the malicious or the envious. Farewell, lover of letters. From Lyon. In the year of our Lord 1507. June 8th <note>original: "vi. Idus Junij" or the sixth day before the Ides of June.</note>.

# Books on a Healthy Life, Chapter One

### The Book on a Healthy Life by Lord Symphorien Champier, physician of Lyon, begins

<margin>What man is according to Mercury.</margin>
Hermes of Egypt, whom they call Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus ("Thrice-Great Hermes") was a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric writing known as the Hermetica, which Renaissance scholars like Champier and Ficino believed contained ancient, divine wisdom.</note>, says that man is nearly the greatest of the gods after the first God. For he says elsewhere: "Man is a great miracle." <note>This is one of the most famous quotes from the "Asclepius," a Latin dialogue attributed to Hermes. It became a cornerstone of Renaissance Humanism's focus on human dignity.</note> The wise man is the greatest miracle of all: he who is content with himself for living well, who is situated above fortune, living like the clear sky, undisturbed and purified; no storm clouds his serenity. Because virtue reconciles him with God,
<margin>Man's kinship. All things were made.</margin>
he shares a kinship with Him. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, known for walking while they taught.</note> and the Stoics affirm that for his sake, all things that move beneath the sphere of the moon are created and set in motion. Moreover, the Arabs, Hebrews, and Christian theologians assert that the world itself was established for the sake of man. As the most celebrated authors say: man is a kind of mortal god. And since rarity itself stirs admiration for things, it happens that one sees a wise man so rarely that the orator from Arpinum <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), born in Arpinum.</note> judged that nature had more often failed to produce one than that a wise man had truly existed. Antiquity indeed speaks of many who excelled in long life and many virtues. For our theologians say that our first parent <note>Adam.</note> imbued his sons and grandsons with such disciplines that each one knew for himself what was useful and what was harmful to life. We cannot, therefore, live well unless we simply live. Nor is it easy to deserve much from men or God unless we live long, sober lives and remain in good health. This little book of ours contains every such faculty within itself.

### The ten leaders for scholars. Chapter 1.

<margin>Concerning God according to the ancients.</margin>
Whoever attempts to enter that narrow, difficult, and long path—which indeed leads finally to the sublime temple of wisdom through continuous labor—seems to stand in total need of ten leaders for this journey. The first of these is truly outside heaven, in heaven, and everywhere. The following three are in heaven. Three are in the soul. The last three lead us on earth. In the beginning, there is God everywhere, who is eternal: that is, He who holds the name of true essence without an 

<column-break/>

origin. Concerning God, Virgil—who, although he was far from the truth <note>Meaning he was a "pagan" poet, though Renaissance Christians often looked for divine truths hidden in his poetry.</note>, nevertheless was seen to have sung thus in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, guided by nature:
<margin>Virgil: Aeneid book 6.</margin>
"In the beginning, the spirit within nourishes the heaven and the earth, the watery plains, the glowing orb of the moon, and the Titan stars; and Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the entire mass and mingles with the great body." <note>original: "Principio celum ac terras..." This famous passage was often interpreted by Renaissance philosophers as a poetic description of the World Soul (Anima Mundi).</note> And Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher.</note> judged God to be 
<margin>Anaxagoras.</margin>
an infinite mind that moves by itself. The Stoics call Him the Word, the Mind, or Jove. Pythagoras calls Him the Monad <note>The "Unit" or "One."</note>. Anaxagoras calls Him the Divine Soul. Diogenes calls Him Divine Reason. Archilaus calls Him the Mind. Others call Him the First Cause. Others, the First Intelligence. Aristotle, however, calls Him the Prince, the First Mover, and the Governor of all. Besides these, there were many others whose positions we pass over in silence as being more obscure. God, therefore, exists as the first leader and governor for scholars. For all wisdom and perfection are from God. For it is He who assigned bile to Horace, phlegm to Heraclitus, blood to Socrates, and melancholy to Orestes <note>This refers to the theory of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile/melancholy, and yellow bile), which were thought to determine a person's temperament and health.</note>. And just as the soul is in the whole body, so God, always working in the whole world, has added strength to natural things like a sharp edge and ordained them to act. He is able, if He wills—and sometimes He does will, though it rarely happens in practice—to both do certain things outside the order of nature and to hinder them at His own discretion. 

Mercury follows, so that we may enter upon the path of the Muses by investigating; he either impels or exhorts us. Indeed (as our Ficino witnesses), the duty of all investigation is attributed to Mercury. And as Alchabitius <note>Al-Qabisi, a 10th-century Arab astrologer and mathematician.</note> says, Mercury signifies rhetorical preaching, business, estimations, geometry, the disposition of things, philosophy, auguries, the work of numbers, and all doctrine. Then Phoebus <note>The Sun.</note> himself illuminates both the seeking souls and the things sought with such abundant splendor that what was being sought by us is clearly found. For the sun is the great spirit of heaven, and with him all the signs [of the Zodiac] are given life. Most gracious Venus approaches, who so seasons and adorns every matter with her rays that whatever (by Ficino’s authority) was sought at the instigation of Mercury and had already been found when Phoebus showed it, always delights and profits us, being surrounded by a certain miraculous and healthy beauty of Venus. 

The three leaders of this journey in the soul follow: namely, an ardent and stable will; sharpness of intellect; and a tenacious memory. The last three are on earth: a most prudent head of the household; a most proven teacher; and a most skilled physician. Without these ten leaders, no one has been or will ever be able to reach philosophy itself, which is the study of wisdom. As for the other leaders—to use Ficino’s words—from...

# Book on a Healthy Life, Chapter 1

### Leaf 3

In the beginning, the Almighty God and Nature granted us many things, but our own diligence must provide the final three <note>Champier refers to a traditional division of life's requirements: those given by God, those provided by nature, and those achieved through human effort.</note>. Many wise men of antiquity have treated the duties and offices pertaining to the head of a household and to the teacher regarding the study of letters—most notably Plato in his books *The Republic* and *The Laws*, followed by Aristotle, and excellently by Isocrates, Quintilian, and Plutarch. Yet, until now, only the physician has been missing for the devoted student of letters: someone to extend a hand to those on their journey and assist with healthful advice and medicines those whom neither heaven, nor mind, nor father, nor teacher has abandoned.

<margin>Cornelius Celsus.</margin>
For as Cornelius Celsus <note>original: "Cornelius celsus. lib. i. cap. ij." A first-century Roman medical writer whose work was rediscovered during the Renaissance.</note> says in his first book, chapter two: "For those with a weak stomach—a group that includes a large portion of city-dwellers and nearly all those eager for letters—greater care is necessary, so that what the condition of the body, the location, or the intensity of study takes away, medical care may restore." Arise now, young men and heroes, eager under God’s guidance! Approach the physician gladly, who, with God showing the way and favoring the work, will bestow healthful counsel and remedies.

->The eight principal enemies of scholars<-
Bad air; Excessive rest; Phlegm <note>original: "Pituita," one of the four humors, associated with coldness and moisture</note>; Black bile <note>original: "Atra bilis," the humor associated with melancholy and deep thought</note>; Sexual intercourse; Overindulgence; Afflictions of the soul <note>original: "Accidētia anime," referring to intense emotions like grief, anger, or anxiety that affect physical health</note>; Morning sleep. Chapter 2.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a scholar seated at a desk with an open book in a library setting.</image-desc>
Since we have been led to mention the natural defects of our bodies, let us follow through with what we have begun. Let us describe the enemies of scholars with a curiosity that is not without use. By enumerating these, you will understand that it is nearly impossible for a wise man to live without a physician. For the health of the body and the mind have this in common: health in both is attained in only one way. The virtue of the mind and the health of the body are situated in a certain balance <note>original: "temperie," the proper mixing of qualities</note>; the latter consists of the humors, the former of the passions. Balance is a kind of middle point, and the middle is reached in only one way—just as a line is made straight in only one way, but bent in many; and a target is hit by an archer in only one way, but missed in many. Therefore, the body is well in one state of balance, but unwell in almost infinite ways. Indeed, the number of diseases increases daily so much that even the most learned and skilled physicians are uncertain in distinguishing them, often accepting the false for the true. Therefore, pitying the most laborious lot of scholars—who travel a difficult path that diminishes the strength <note>original: "nervos," literally "nerves" or "sinews"</note> of Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and weaving; Champier uses her name here to represent the intellectual life.</note>—I stand by those who study as their physician, with a skill as complete as my will is ready. Whoever

<column-break/>

therefore (to use the words of Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Florentine philosopher and physician whose "Three Books on Life" is the primary source for this text.</note>) embarks upon this journey, as a certain poet might say: they are often endangered by land and sea. For whether they sail the sea, they are continually tossed among the waves between Scylla and Charybdis <note>The famous mythical sea monsters of the Strait of Messina, representing a choice between two evils.</note>; or whether they travel by land (if I may put it so), eight monsters immediately present themselves. The first is bad air, which nourishes them. The second is excessive rest. The third is phlegm. The fourth is black bile. The fifth is terrestrial Venus and Priapus <note>Metaphors for sexual lust and physical indulgence.</note>. The sixth is Bacchus and Ceres <note>Metaphors for wine and food/gluttony.</note>. The seventh is the afflictions of the soul. The eighth is Hecate <note>A goddess of the night and crossroads, here representing the dangers of excessive nocturnal sleep or dark dreams.</note>, who frequently opposes them.

->On the first monster: Air. Chapter 3.<-

<margin>Air's healthfulness.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a bird and floral patterns.</image-desc>
Air, as the Stoics argue and imagine, being placed between the sea and the heavens, is consecrated under the name of Juno <note>In ancient allegory, Juno was often associated with the air (aer), while her husband Jupiter (Jove) was associated with the higher ether or fire.</note>, who is the sister and consort of Jove, because there is a similarity to the ether and a great union with it. They made this element feminine and gave it the name of Juno because nothing is softer than it. Finally, in the regimen of health, Air has five rules. First, it should be clear and bright. Second, it should be dry. Third, it should not be windy, but especially one should avoid the East and North winds. Fourth, the air of the room should be purified so that it is in no way foul; the windows should be opened, and bundles of fragrant things should be burned, such as laurel, juniper, oregano, and sage. Fifth, it should be fumigated with frankincense or myrrh, or other fragrant aromatics. Therefore, the physician must consider the dispositions of the air, as Galen <note>The most influential Greek physician of antiquity (c. 129–216 AD).</note> says in book two of *On the Art of Health*, chapter eight: "In the cure of diseases, the composition <note>original: "complexio," the specific qualities of the local air</note> of the air must be investigated, because it affects the body just like medicine; indeed, even more so, since it continually clings to us, nor can we escape its alteration." As he says in book two of his *Therapeutics*, chapter five: "We can choose or avoid other materials, but it is not possible to escape the material that surrounds us; rather, it is necessary to use what is present." Air, which is cold in its composition compared to the innate spirit <note>The "spiritus" was believed to be a subtle substance that carried life and thought through the body.</note>, causes variations not only in the regimen of health, but also in the characters and natures of men, so that some seem to differ in their very species—which the Platonists concede regarding the souls of men. For just as you find those who are by nature timid, slow, sleepy, sluggish, lazy, and cowardly, so you may see those born spirited, strenuous, vigilant, industrious, vigorous, wise, and alert. You will also find some by nature pious, religious, just, temperate, modest, and kind; and likewise some impious, irreligious, unjust, greedy, and bold.

# Chapter III.

...shameless and monstrous. Those who are well-disposed by nature (as one may see with their own eyes) profit through the diligence of their teachers. But for those to whom nature has been difficult—as if with a stepmother’s hatred—they usually achieve nothing despite doing everything, and for the most part, they waste their effort and expense. We should not think that Anaxarchus the Epicurean (a poor philosopher), nor Anaxagoras and Parmenides, spent less effort on study than Plato and Aristotle; rather, they simply had less favor from nature. For that reason, the former are obscure, while the latter are honored among the heroic wise men.

<margin>Epithets of various nations.</margin>
It also appears that nations follow their own particular vices due to the diversity of the air. Thus, the Ligurians <note>People from Northwest Italy/Southeast France.</note> are said to be vain, and the Latins superstitious and proud. The Gauls are brave and naturally fierce; the Spaniards are boastful. The Italians are serious and fond of glory; the Carthaginians are oath-breakers. A well-known saying of the Greek poet Epimenides regarding the Cretans is cited by the Apostle Paul: <note>original: "Cretenfes semper mendaces: male bestie: vētres pigri." From Titus 1:12.</note> "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies."

I will say, then, in passing, and I will affirm summarily, that it matters greatly in what air and from what seed a person is sired; in what womb the embryo is formed; at what hours the infant is born; with what foods and exercises it is brought up; with what disciplines it is imbued; and under what part of the sky it is nourished. For the bodies of all nations are not equally suited for the perception of wisdom and intelligence. Hence we have heard that Thales (or as others would have it, Socrates) was accustomed to say that he gave thanks to God for three things especially: that he was born a man and not a woman; a human and not a beast; a Greek and not a barbarian.

For those who inhabit the extreme climates of the world are so far removed in their temperament from those who inhabit the "fifth climate" <note>Early geographers divided the world into "climates" or latitudinal zones. The fifth climate, encompassing the Mediterranean and Greece, was considered the most perfectly balanced for human intellect.</note> that a temperament which is healthy for one race is often fatal for another. And just as they differ in the disposition of their bodies, so do they differ in manners, laws, opinions, and character. For these reasons, the Thebans, Gauls, and Germans are considered more robust, while the Athenians and Egyptians are considered more clever.

So great is the influence of the body upon the soul that the Platonists (who maintain that demons and angels are corporeal) think they take delight in various things according to the variety of their bodies. Those who have a body of celestial substance are attracted by shapes and songs. Those of fire, by the smoke and scents of sacrifices. But those of air, they say, are accustomed to insinuate themselves into bodies and suck out the moisture of the human body. Herodotus, in his third book, affirms that he heard of no wise man from the race of the Scythians except for one, Anacharsis, who (as Cicero says in his *Tusculan Disputations*) was possessed of admirable wisdom. It shall suffice, therefore (as I judge), for us to have spoken about the air according to the requirements of this summary. But now I shall descend to the topic of rest.

<column-break/>

->¶ On excessive rest, the second monster.<-
->Chapter IIII.<-

<margin>What is rest.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative historiated woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a seated figure in a robe, possibly a scholar or a personification of Rest (Quies), set against a background with a building and landscape.</image-desc>
Rest is nothing other than
the privation of motion; and it
concerns a certain present
business. It is the privation
of exercise and labor, which
can be called idleness. When
this is excessive, as many and
as great harms overflow into the body as the benefits that exercise can bring. Regarding this, Isaac <note>Isaac Judaeus, an influential 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher.</note> says in his *Universal Diets*, chapter one: "Nothing exists more inimical to the maintenance of health than idleness and rest." Averroes <note>The great Andalusian philosopher and physician (1126–1198).</note> seems to have accepted this in the sixth book of his *Colliget* when he says: "Total rest of the body does not enter upon the path of health." From this it is clear enough that it enters upon the path of sickness, since it leads to many infirmities, and especially to the "ethical old age" <note>A term for premature aging or decline caused by lifestyle rather than years.</note>.

And Galen, in his book *On Good and Bad Juices*, chapter three, says: "For the greatest evil for the preservation of health is rest of the body, just as the greatest good is moderate motion." He himself gives the reason for this saying in his book *On the Types of Fevers and Tremors*, saying: "Rest is a corruption to bodies for which it is proper to be moved." Know, therefore, that daily exercises profit health more than doctors and medicine. For through exercise, says Fabius Quintilian, all things grow strong. Without it, as Galen says, it is impossible for a man to enjoy the most prosperous health for long.

<margin>Exercise.</margin>
Our Galen prefers exercise with a small ball to all others. Exercise also brings benefit, as Celsus teaches, through running, walking, and "clear reading"—which we use almost uniquely, shouting most contentedly in our daily public lectures. Plato and Aristotle approve of gymnastics above all, by which strength increases and health is preserved unimpaired. Aristotle, in the seventh book of his *Politics*, commands that youths be handed over to gymnastics and "pedotriuica."

<margin>Pedotriuica.</margin>
By "pedotriuica" (to explain this also in passing), we mean the exercise pertaining to a master trainer or "pedotribe." Now, a pedotribe, as Plato teaches in his book on philosophy, is a master of exercise whose duty it is (as he relates in the *Gorgias*) to make the bodies of men beautiful and robust. Plato so approved of gymnastics that in the fifth book of the *Republic*, he judged that women should be exercised in gymnastics; and in the seventh book of the *Laws*, he teaches that all warlike exercises are contained under the name of gymnastics. Therefore, for the preservation of the good of the body, we shall use exercise, which, as Cornelius Celsus says...

# Books on the Healthy Life. Chapters 5 & 6.

...is the first care of the body. It should always precede food in those who digest well; it should be more extensive in those who digest less, and gentler.

### ¶ What Phlegm Is and How It Should Be Avoided: 
### The Third Monster. Chapter 5.

Natural phlegm <note>original: "pituita." In ancient and Renaissance medicine, this was one of the four bodily humors, associated with water, coldness, and moisture.</note> is cold and moist and without flavor: nature always sends it through the veins so that it might digest it and nourish the body. For phlegm is food not perfectly cooked <note>The process of digestion was often described as "concoction" or cooking by the heat of the stomach.</note>: it can still be digested and nourish the body. We have said that when this increases, it is harmful to scholars. Therefore (to use the words of Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the famous Italian priest and physician whose medical advice for scholars this text adapts.</note>), so that phlegm does not increase too much: exercise must be used twice daily on a nearly empty stomach: yet never laborious, lest the "sharp spirits" <note>Spiritus: the subtle vapors that carry life and thought through the body.</note> be dissolved. Wastes should be most diligently purged from all passages. Dirt from the skin of the entire body, especially the head, should be thoroughly wiped away through both washing and friction. Foods that are too cold, fatty, poisonous, viscous, sticky, and all those things that tend to rot easily should be avoided. Let food be moderate, but drink more moderate still. The dwelling should be high up, far removed from heavy and cloudy air. Cold must be kept from the head: but especially from the neck and feet. A moderate use of spices in colder meals is beneficial.

### ¶ Why Melancholics Are Gifted and What Sort 
### of Melancholics They Are. The Fourth Monster.
### Chapter 6.

<margin>Democritus.</margin>
Someone might ask for what reason the greatest philosophers are either melancholic from the beginning or become so through study. Which indeed Democritus confirms: he says that no men can ever be great in talent except those who are stirred by a certain madness <note>original: "furore quodam perciti." Referring to the idea of divine inspiration or poetic frenzy.</note>. Aristotle also approves the same in his book of *Problems*. For he says that all men who have excelled in any field have been melancholic: whether they were born such, or became such through constant meditation. Which I believe happens for this reason: because the nature of the melancholic humor follows the quality of the earth: which

<column-break/>

is never spread wide like the other elements, but is more tightly contracted into itself. Thus the melancholic humor both invites and helps the soul to collect itself within itself. Again, if the soul frequently collects its spirits in this way into itself, because of the continuous agitation of the subtle parts of the humors being resolved, it makes the <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determines a person's physical and mental state.</note> of the body much more earthy than it had received; especially since by collecting itself, it makes the condition of the body more compressed: for such is the nature of the earth. I pass over the fact that such is also the nature of Mercury and Saturn: through which, while they collect the spirits into the center, they recall the sharpness of the mind in some way from external things to its own, and they fix it in contemplation and apply it to penetrating the centers of things. Neither, however, do planets or humors of this kind act as efficient causes; rather they either provide the opportunity or push away obstacles. But the mind itself, both invited and unhindered, accomplishes such things. In this melancholy we place philosophizing poets, priests, soothsayers, and prophets. They say that Epimenides the Cretan slept for fifty years: that is, as I believe, he lived removed from the senses. Similarly, they say that Pythagoras lay hidden for ten years, and Zoroaster for twenty. 

<margin>Socrates.</margin>
Socrates, as Plato writes, stood unblinking and immobile from sunrise until the sunrise of the following day, in the same tracks, with his mouth and eyes directed toward the same place, pensive and abstracted from his body. 

<margin>Plato.</margin>
Our Plato, when he had frequently withdrawn far from the body through the intensity of contemplation, at last passed away entirely in that very abstraction from the bonds of the body. His disciple Xenocrates was abstracted from his body for an entire hour every day. We read the same about Heraclitus and Democritus. Both withdrew into solitude. One seemed somewhat sad in appearance due to the intensity of study; the other, when he had begun to call his mind away from the senses and was hindered by his eyes, blinded himself. Archimedes of Syracuse, intent on geometric figures, did not feel the tumultuous destruction of his falling homeland or the enemy threatening his head. Porphyry, the disciple of Plotinus, writes that Plotinus was often accustomed to be released from his body and to change his expression; then he found certain wonderful things which he would later write down. He asserts that he himself was present four times at these miracles of Plotinus. He affirms that he himself, when he was in his sixty-eighth year, was once seized by the divine while contemplating. Great certainly is the power of the mind, which by its own virtue is released from the shackles of the body. Great is the wealth of the mind which, as often as it wishes, [can access] the precious treasures of God and nature, not...

### ¶ How sexual intercourse is to be avoided: The fifth monster. Chapter 7.
