The fifth monster is venereal coitus <note>sexual intercourse</note>, especially if it exceeds one's strength even a little. For it suddenly exhausts the spirits, weakens the stomach and the heart, and enfeebles the brain. Nothing can be more adverse to genius than this evil. Hence Avicenna <note>A Persian physician (980–1037) whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook in Europe for centuries.</note> says in the third [book], third [fen], chapter 5: "Frequent intercourse is more harmful than the loss of an eye." And the same author says in book 1, treatise 4, chapter 13: "Intercourse is among the things harmful to the stomach, and its cessation is among the things most beneficial to it." For Aristotle asserts that animals that engage in much intercourse have shorter lives. He proves this from sparrows, which live for only a year. He introduces a proof for this: that the blackness does not appear on the throats of those seen in autumn, which blackness signifies the old ones among them. Aristotle also says in the 21st problem of the fourth book of *Problems*: "Those who engage in intercourse are weakened and frequently become more infirm." And therefore, much intercourse debilitates the body and causes it to inherit various types of harm and pain. Why did Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine" in Ancient Greece.</note> judge intercourse to be similar to the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy; often called the "sacred disease"</note>, except because it strikes the mind, which is sacred? So 

<column-break/>

<header>Chapter 7 and 8.</header>

much does it hinder that Avicenna said in his *Book on Animals*: "If any of the seed flows out in intercourse beyond what nature can tolerate, it is more harmful than if forty times as much blood had flowed out." Thus, not without reason did the ancients wish the Muses and Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom and war; the Muses were patrons of the arts.</note> to be virgins. Therefore, nothing can be more adverse to genius than immoderate intercourse. For that reason, the wise have proposed this problem: "Why do many fools procreate very prudent children, while many very prudent men procreate fools?" Because fools, being vehemently overcome by the pleasure in intercourse, have their souls deeply immersed in the body; thus the seed, which shares greatly in the rational power, results in offspring who turn out more prudent. On the other hand, prudent and especially learned men are always thinking of something, and even during the act of intercourse, they discuss certain matters and, through reason, measure out those things which are necessary from the outside, and thus lift themselves up. Therefore, their outgoing seed is lacking in much of the soul's power. This is the solution for why dull and unlearned men procreate those stronger in body, while the learned procreate the more invalid. Therefore, the ancients held that intercourse harms not only the wise but also their future children even more than the wise themselves. Intercourse in the regimen of health <note>original: "regimine sanitatis"; a traditional set of rules for maintaining a healthy lifestyle</note> has nine canons:

1. That it be rare, and only when nature spontaneously demands it.
2. That it not be done when the stomach is full.
3. That it not be done during a time of hunger.
4. That it be done at the end of digestion.
5. That the bodily wastes have already been expelled.
6. That it be done with a beloved woman, not with one who is foul or whom you do not love.
7. That you sleep for a little while after it.
8. That if you seem to have become heavier from intercourse, you should abstain from it.
9. That it not be during the final days of the moon when the conjunction is imminent.

### The Seventh Monster: The Accidents of the Soul.
### Chapter 9

There have been some from the family of physicians who, in a certain way, envied the divine glory and detracted from our names, being addicted to nature more than is right. Among these is our prince, Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook.</note>, who tried to find natural causes for all miracles, even those which God showed for our benefit—such as the power that perfects the digestion of nourishment. # How sexual intercourse is to be avoided: the fifth monster. Chapter 7.

<margin>He condemns sexual intercourse</margin>
The fifth monster is venereal intercourse, especially if it exceeds one’s strength even a little. For it suddenly exhausts the spirits, weakens the stomach and the area around the heart, and enfeebles the brain. No evil can be more adverse to the intellect than this. Whence Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath and one of the most significant physicians of the Islamic Golden Age.</note> in the third tractate of his third book, chapter 5, says: "The multiplication of intercourse is the most harmful thing to the eye." And the same author in book 13, tractate 3, the last chapter of the first treatise, says: "Intercourse is among the things harmful to the stomach, and the giving up of it is among the things most beneficial to it." For Aristotle asserts that animals given to much intercourse have shorter lives. He proves this from sparrows, which live only for a year, bringing proof of this because the blackness does not appear on the throats of those seen in autumn—which blackness signifies the old among them. Aristotle also, in the fourth book of his *Problems*, problem 21, says: "Those having intercourse are drained and frequently become weaker." And therefore much intercourse weakens the body and makes it inherit various kinds of harms and pains. Why else did Hippocrates judge intercourse to be similar to the "comitial disease" <note>The "comitial disease" (morbus comitialis) is an old name for epilepsy, so named because meetings of the Roman assembly (*comitia*) were cancelled if someone had a seizure.</note> unless it strikes the wind, which is sacred?

<column-break/>

It is so harmful that Avicenna said in his *Book on Animals*: "If any seed flows out through intercourse beyond what nature can tolerate, it is more harmful than if forty times as much blood had flowed out." So it is not without justice that the ancients wished the Muses and Minerva to be virgins. Therefore, nothing can be more adverse to the intellect than immoderate intercourse. For this reason, the wise pose such a problem: "Why do many fools procreate very prudent children, while many very prudent men procreate foolish ones?" [The answer given is that] the foolish, being vehemently overcome by pleasure during intercourse, have their soul deeply immersed in the body; so the seed—which is a great participant in the rational power—results in children who turn out more prudent. But the prudent, and especially the learned, are always creating something or planning; even during intercourse they discuss certain things, or measure by reason those things which are necessary from the outside, and lift themselves up intellectually. And so their seed, in coming forth, is devoid of much "animal power." Hence is the solution as to why the dull and unlearned procreate those stronger in body, while the learned procreate those who are weaker. Therefore, the ancients held that intercourse is more harmful not only to the wise but also to their future children than to the wise themselves. Intercourse in the "regimen of health" <note>The *regimen sanitatis* was the traditional medical system of maintaining health through lifestyle choices like diet, sleep, and exercise.</note> has nine rules:

<margin>Rules for intercourse</margin>
First: let it be rare, and only when nature demands it of its own accord. Second: let it not happen when the stomach is full. Third: let it not happen at a time of hunger. Fourth: let it happen at the end of digestion. Fifth: let the "superfluities" <note>Bodily wastes or excrement.</note> have already been expelled. Sixth: let it be with a beloved woman, not with a foul one, or with a woman whom you do not love. Seventh: after it, sleep a little while. Eighth: if you seem to have become "heavier" <note>In this context, "heavier" refers to a feeling of lethargy or mental dullness.</note> from intercourse, abstain from it. Ninth: let it not be in the final days of the moon, when its conjunction is near.

# Satiety: the sixth monster. Chapter 8.

<margin>The detestation of satiety</margin>
The sixth monster is satiety <note>Overindulgence or excessive fullness.</note> of wine and food. Indeed, Aristotle says in the seventh book of the *Ethics*: "Pleasures impede prudence, and the greater they are, the more they cloud the mind, which is evident in aphrodisiacs—that is, in venereal matters." For no one, while attending to Venus <note>Engaging in sexual acts.</note>, can perceive anything with the mind. And Saint Jerome, in his work *Against Jovinianus*, says: "For when they are stirred up by excessive fullness, many have done more foully what they have foully taken in." Hippocrates also, the greatest of physicians, teaches that thick and obese bodies break out into paralysis and the worst kinds of diseases, unless they are reduced by a quick bloodletting. Whence even athletes, whose life...

### Chapter 9

...and the art of **fattening** <note>original: "sagina"</note> is this: as Galen, the most learned interpreter of Hippocrates, says, those who are overfed cannot live long. Nor can those whose minds are wrapped in fat enjoy lasting health; in them, there is nothing sublime, nothing refined. Socrates, the fountain of upright men, used to say that many men wanted to live in order to eat and drink, but that he himself ate and drank in order to live. Critolaus the Peripatetic <note>A philosopher of the school of Aristotle</note> said that pleasure is an evil and gives birth to many other evils from itself: namely, injuries, sloth, forgetfulness, and cowardice. Antisthenes the Socratic used to say, "I would rather go mad than be delighted by pleasure." I pass over how drunkenness makes men insane. Indeed, if the wine is either too much, too hot, or too potent, it will fill the head itself with the worst humors and rages. Truly, too much drink (to use these words) first calls back all the force of nature to the stomach to digest it. Thus it happens that the soul cannot attend to the head and to contemplation at the same time. Then, being poorly digested, it dulls the sharp edge of the mind with many thick vapors and humors. Even if it is digested well enough, nonetheless, as Galen says, the soul—suffocated by fat and blood—cannot perceive anything heavenly.

<margin>Rules to be observed regarding food and drink.</margin>

Regarding food and drink, learned men shall observe twelve **rules** <note>original: "canones"</note>. The **first** is that an excessive filling of any things whatsoever should be avoided. The **second** is that they should not eat except at that time when hunger is active. The **third** is that they should leave aside all things that produce vapors and fill the head, such as legumes <note>beans and peas</note> and fruits. For these are among the things that send the most vapors to the head. However, he allows cooked pears or quinces after a meal, and in hot weather, even the seeds of sweet or pomegranate, whose kernels should also be chewed. The **fourth** is that they should leave raw things alone, even if eaten with vinegar. The **fifth** is that they should flee brothy juices and all things too moist, for they add to the moisture which we are trying to cure. The **sixth** is that things which by their nature harm the memory should be set aside; for onions do this, as do garlic and leeks. The **seventh** is that dinner should always be light. The **eighth** is that every meal should end with coriander or juniper, or a crust of bread, after which they should not drink. The **ninth** is that "winey" wine <note>very strong or undiluted wine</note> should be avoided. For it is too vaporous and carries undigested matter to the head and other limbs; although it is hot, it nevertheless generates "cold" diseases, as Galen testifies; although it may be the cause of good digestion and quenches thirst better than water (as Aristotle says), it nevertheless suffocates the vital power, especially if drunk immoderately. The **tenth** is that all foods that remain a long time in the stomach should be avoided, such as cheese and all excessively fatty things and fish, because they generate a phlegmatic chyme <note>the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</note>. The **eleventh** is that all nut-like fruits usually cause harm, such as walnuts, hazelnuts, almonds, and chestnuts. The **twelfth** is that vinegar should be very sharp and hot, used in small amounts with cinnamon; and sweet flag <note>acorus</note> and pennyroyal <note>pulegium</note> should be placed in a small vessel—and this where phlegm is very abundant.

->The Seventh Monster: The Accidents of the Soul.<-
->Chapter 9.<-

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut drop-cap 'F'. Inside the bowl of the letter is a bearded man's head in profile facing left. The letter is surrounded by intricate floral scrollwork and vines.</image-desc>

**F**ormerly, there were some from the family of physicians who, perhaps envying divine glory and detracting too much from nature or being more devoted to it than is right—among whom is our prince Avicenna <note>The famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037)</note>—who attempted to find natural causes for all miracles, even those which God shows for our benefit, such as the perfection of digesting nourishment. Because of this, they say it has often happened that some, from the **imagination** <insert>imagination</insert> of the "falling sickness" <note>epilepsy</note>, have turned out to be epileptics, and from the imagination of leprosy, they became lepers. They also say that not only the body joined to the imagining soul obeys the imagination—which all physicians grant and the wise do not deny—but also external matter; this we deny. They say, however, that this power is not common to all souls, but is a singular privilege of certain ones which they think are more excellent and divine than others, such as they wish the souls of prophets, heroes, or demigods to be. And this way of speaking can be drawn from Avicenna when he says: "Any human soul, while the body is healthy, is sufficient to change the matter of its own body, because it rules it. Therefore, a noble and very strong human soul, on account of the constellations, will be able to transcend to operate on another's body through imagination alone without any other medium." Thus he spoke. Isigonus and Memphodorus, as Pliny testifies in the seventh book of his *Natural History*, report that in Africa there are certain families by whose praise things perish, trees wither, and infants die. Isigonus adds that there are people of the same kind among the Triballi and Illyrians who also bewitch and kill with a look those whom they stare at for a long time, especially with angry eyes; and that these people have double pupils in their eyes. There are, as they say, women of this kind in Scythia called the Bithye. But these things are not to be ascribed to imaginations, but either to a pestilential condition of the mouth or to a poisonous vapor that proceeds from the eyes. Just as it happens in those who...

...are infected by pestilence: for it is established that their souls possess a deadly power which, raging as a contagion against others, grows strong and creeps forward by multiplying itself. No doubt those who have the power of the **evil eye** <note>original: "effascinandi"; the belief that some could cause harm or enchantment through a look</note> suffer from something similar—it is harmless to themselves but lethal to others. And lest it seem impossible to anyone that such poisonous humors <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) were believed to govern health and personality</note> can be produced within us, I will add what Pliny says in Book 7 of his *Natural History*, Chapter 15, concerning the menstrual flow of women, from which human bodies are created. For he speaks thus: "Nothing is easily found more monstrous than the flow of women. New wine <note>original: "musta"</note> turns sour at its approach; crops become sterile when touched; grafted plants die; the buds of gardens are parched; and the fruits of the trees upon which they sit fall off. The brightness of mirrors is dulled by their very gaze; the edge of steel is blunted, as is the shine of ivory. Swarms of bees die; even copper and iron are immediately seized by rust; a dread odor fills the air; and dogs, having tasted it, are driven to madness, their bite inflicting an incurable poison." This is what Pliny says. From this, it follows that not all miracles are to be referred to natural causes, but some even to demons, and some—that is, those things which are true—to the good angels and to God.

<margin>Two modes of the imagination.</margin>

Regarding the **imaginations** connected with the passions of the appetite, and regarding those imaginations without such passions, which play a role in the regimen of health, two modes are granted by which they alter one's own body. The **first** is that, from the nature of the thing, the mental image <note>original: "species"</note> of heat and the imagination of it is productive of heat, and the image of cold is productive of cold—just as light is productive of warmth. And we gather this mode from Aristotle in his book *On the Cause of the Motion of Animals* when he says: "For fantasies, senses, and meditations alter us. For the senses are immediately certain existing alterations. Fantasy and intelligence, however, possess the power of things. For in some way, the understood image of hot or cold or pleasant exists in such a way as each of the actual things themselves." The **second mode** is through the movement of the **spirit** <note>In medieval medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that carried life, sensation, and motion through the body</note> toward the inside or the outside, or toward a specific limb. For in joy, the spirits are driven outward and the extremities become warm. In fear, however, the spirits are withdrawn inward, and they chill the extremities. And in certain passions, contrary motions occur in some way at the same time, so that the spirit is moved both outward and inward—as in the passion which is called in Arabic *elen* <note>Likely referring to a state of grief or anxiety</note> and in shame. Similarly, by a continuous and strong imagination and thought, the spirits are moved toward the brain; thus it happens that the body becomes either hot or cold, suddenly or gradually.

<margin>Rules for the accidents of the soul.</margin>

In the regimen of the learned, the **accidents of the soul** <note>emotions or mental states</note> have three **rules**. The **first** is that sadness should be entirely avoided. The **second** is that care for domestic affairs

<column-break/>

should be removed as much as possible. Whence Claudian says: "Our hearts do not admit two cares." The **third** is that the soul should be delighted by the thought and meditation of the sciences. For, according to Aristotle, "delight perfects the work."

### The eighth monster is staying awake very late at night, especially after dinner. Chapter 10.

Truly, in this matter, studious men err, and very many are deceived by the reasoning that they should frequently stay awake late at night, especially after dinner, which also forces them to sleep after the sun has set. Therefore, regarding how much this harms the talent, our **Ficino** <note>Marsilio Ficino, a famous Renaissance philosopher and physician</note> brings forward seven principal reasons in his book *On the Healthy Life*, which I have omitted on account of the brevity of this summary. Nevertheless, let those hours be chosen for study in which the stomach is empty, the talent is not darkened by vapors <note>It was believed that digesting food sent "vapors" to the head, clouding the mind</note>, and all things are silent. Therefore, let the morning songs of the cock be chosen, and let us take care that the movements of fortune do not break our calculation of time, lest we fail to complete those hours we have decreed for study. For if **Augustus Caesar** was accustomed to read and write daily even during the Mutinensian war; and likewise if **Julius Caesar**, when he had pacified the world, wrote down during the night by secret lamplight those things he had done by day—and especially with such elegance that he is wonderfully praised by **Quintilian** in Book 10, Chapter 1—then what, I ask, what could interfere with our urban leisure that would lead us away from the study of literature?

### The two principal enemies of memory: coldness and humidity. Chapter 11.

However, to return to the point from which we have now wandered quite far: the path that leads to the knowledge of truth and wisdom is very long, full of heavy labors of land and sea. Whoever, therefore (to use the words of our Ficino), enters upon this journey, as some poet might say, is often endangered by land and sea. Whether they sail in the sea, they are continually tossed among the waves—that is, the **humidities**—as if between Scylla and Charybdis. Or if they travel by land (as I might put it), two monsters first present themselves. The first is the image of death, namely **coldness**. The second is the mother of corruption, namely **humidity**. Indeed, **Avicenna** and **Galen** held that coldness harms more than humidity, because every natural operation is performed by natural heat. Coldness, however, confounds nature, nor does it enter into its work except as...

# Chapters 12, 13, 14, 15, & 16

...is the sub-dominating instrument: as is clear in the second collection, rule 7 and rule 4 of the first, from the "Conciliator" <note>Referring to Peter of Abano, known as 'The Conciliator', a famous 13th-century medical philosopher</note>, distinction 61. Therefore, in the second commentary on the *Song of Songs*, rule 95, he calls it the **heat of the elements** <note>original: "calorem elementorum"</note>; that is, that which is like a natural element. And in the third treatise, commentary 155: its contrary, which is **coldness**, is the most harmful. Truly, it harms indirectly, but **moisture** harms more directly. Since memory is strengthened by a proportionate **dryness**—whose nature it is to retain, as stated in Book 3 of *On the Soul*—it is therefore overwhelmed by moisture as something disproportionate. 

**Coldness** also universally hinders all operations. **Moisture**, however, seems more specifically to hinder the power of retention. And since things are so, excessive dryness can prevent forms from being imprinted, and thus it seems to hinder retention, though it strictly hinders the "capture" <note>The initial acquisition or learning of information</note> of ideas; but it hinders retention consequently, because what is not captured cannot be held. 

Truly, because coldness hinders the movement of the **spirits** <note term="spirits">In medieval physiology, these are subtle vapors that carry out the functions of the brain and nervous system</note>, since its nature is to quiet them—just as it is the nature of heat to move them, as Avicenna and Aristotle say in the 13th book of *Problems*, second text—therefore coldness hinders this movement necessary for remembering, but moisture hinders retention. Thus, the ambiguities can cease: whether coldness harms more—since its daughter is **oblivion** <note>forgetfulness</note>, as Paul says in chapter 28—or moisture, which is left in doubt by many. 

Because, according to Galen in his book *On Rigor*, natural heat is not pure heat, but a composite in which there is a proportion of all equality, therefore not every kind of heat produces a good memory, nor every kind of dryness, but only that which is certain and proportionate. Every immoderate **dyscrasia** <note term="dyscrasia">An imbalance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, bile, black bile) that leads to illness</note> casts down the action of its proper virtue. Truly, if excessive coldness is immoderately joined to dryness, the worst memory must arise: being ill-disposed for capturing information and dull in thinking. If, however, heat is joined to dryness, the movement of the spirits will indeed be swift, but the "inscription" <note>The mental recording of data</note> will become difficult. Thus, capture will be difficult, but recollection will be quite easy. Truly, all these variations in the proportion of heat and dryness will change [the memory] by degrees; and the same must be understood regarding other lapses of the bodily imbalances.

### ¶ Signs and Harms of Coldness. Chapter 12.

**C**oldness makes the mind dull; it brings on dizziness and induces slow recollection.

### ¶ Signs of Heat. Chapter 13.

**H**eat brings about speed of movements and of remembrance, and a head that is hot to the touch. If, therefore, two qualities are combined, it happens that the signs are complicated in the same proportion as the 

<column-break/>

qualities vary or intensify. For these imbalances can either be qualities alone—and here the matter of noble quantity is joined—or they can be joined with many humors of similar qualities. You will easily recognize the presence of this matter from its signs, which are explained sufficiently by physicians in their proper places, and have been collected by me quite extensively elsewhere.

### ¶ Signs and Harms of Moisture. Chapter 14.

**W**here **moisture** dominates, there is heavy and deep sleep. Such people are dull in all movements; they perceive present things well, but they remember things done long ago either not at all or with great difficulty. For moisture both admits and loses an impression easily.

### ¶ Signs and Harms of Dryness. Chapter 15.

**I**f **dryness** dominates, there will be wakefulness and a lightness of the head; and those superfluities <note>Excretions like mucus or phlegm</note> that are expelled by the palate, nose, and eyes will not be abundant; but there will be much **earwax**, which pertains to the memory. They "inscribe" <note>learn</note> present things with difficulty, but once inscribed, they are removed slowly. Hence it happens that they hold things better that were done long ago, and recall them better than things that are happening for the first time. We see this in the **elderly**, who remember well those things they did in their youth, but do not firmly retain things from the current year.

### ¶ How the Healthy Should Behave. Chapter 16.

<margin>Cornelius Celsus</margin>
**I**t remains for us to diligently show how it is fitting for the healthy to behave; and so that this may be performed more appropriately, we shall bring forward some items from the workshop of **Cornelius Celsus** <note>A Roman medical encyclopedist from the 1st century AD</note>. A healthy man, who is both well and his own master, should bind himself to no laws: he needs neither a doctor nor a masseur. He ought to have a varied way of life: sometimes in the country, sometimes in the city, and more often in the field; to sail, to hunt, to rest sometimes, but more frequently to exercise. 

For indeed, **idleness** dulls the body, while **labor** strengthens it. The former brings on an early old age, while the latter grants a long youth. It is also beneficial sometimes to use the bath, sometimes cold waters; sometimes to be anointed with oil, and sometimes to neglect it; to flee no kind of food that is commonly used. Sometimes to be at a banquet, sometimes to withdraw from it; sometimes to take more than is right, sometimes no more. To take food twice a day rather than once, and always as much as possible, provided he digests it. But while exercises and foods of this kind are necessary, those of the athletes are superfluous. For if interrupted because of certain civic...

# Book on the Healthy Life — Chapter 17

The order of exercise necessitates this: it wears down the body, especially those bodies that are filled after the manner of such people; they age and fall ill most quickly. **Sexual intercourse** <note>original: "concubitus"</note>, truly, should neither be overly desired nor too greatly feared. Rare indulgence excites the body; frequent indulgence dissolves it. However, when it is frequent, one can know it is not harmful—not by the number of times, but by nature, and by considering one's age and physical constitution—if neither weakness nor pain follows in the body. Likewise, it is worse during the day and safer at night; provided, however, that neither food follows the former, nor wakeful labor follows the latter immediately. These rules must be observed by the healthy, and care must be taken lest, in a state of secondary health, the defenses against illness are consumed.

## ¶ Care of the stomach and what should be done for those suffering in the stomach. Chapter 17.

<margin>Care of the stomach.</margin>
It remains that, following the advice of our **Ficino** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a celebrated Italian physician and philosopher whose work "De vita libri tres" is the source for much of this text</note>, we must have the most diligent care for the stomach, lest satiety ever bring on nausea or indigestion. When the weakness of the stomach is accompanied by little thirst, a slow descent of food from the stomach, and acid burping—and if all these occurrences are minor and not long-standing—the stomach should be treated with **rose lozenges** <note term="trocisci">Small, round medicinal lozenges or tablets made from a paste and then dried</note>. Of these, the patient should take a weight of 2 drachms every morning with 1 drachm of a decoction of seeds. This decoction of seeds is according to **Rhazes** <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD) was a Persian polymath and one of the most influential physicians in the Islamic Golden Age</note>. 

<margin>Description of the seed decoction</margin>
**Recipe:** Take Nabataean cumin and ammi <note>also known as Bishop's weed</note>, and let them boil in water until the water becomes red, which should be taken with the lozenges. The description of the rose lozenges, according to the same author, is as follows: 

<margin>Rose lozenges.</margin>
**Recipe:** Take 3 drachms of red roses; 1 drachm each of aloe pith, mastic, spikenard, camel grass, and wormwood. Let them be mixed with old wine and made into lozenges. One should be nourished by things that are quickly digested, produce few humors, and leave behind little waste. Food should be taken twice daily, in moderate and light portions, seasoned moderately with mace, cinnamon, and nutmeg. Let the person use much exercise before eating; let them drink less water than usual; and after eating, let them sleep plenty. Of wine, let them drink a little old, aromatic, and pure wine, and let this fortify the whole nutrition.

## ¶ On catarrh and heaviness and medicines against phlegm. Chapter 18.

Sometimes a humor drips from the head into the nostrils, which is mild; sometimes into the throat, which is worse; sometimes even into the lungs, which is the worst. If it drips into the nostrils, a thin phlegm flows through them and causes a slight cough. If it enters the lungs, besides sneezing and coughing, there is also heaviness of the head, weariness, thirst, and heat in the bilious urine.

### Chapter 18.

There is another ailment, not much different, called **congestion** <note>original: "grauedo"</note>, which is a heaviness of the head. This closes the nostrils, dulls the voice, and provokes a dry cough. Under its influence, the saliva is salty, the ears ring, the veins in the head throb, and the urine is turbid. Our **Coan** <note>Referring to Hippocrates, who was from the island of Cos</note> calls all these symptoms **head colds** <note>original: "coryzas"</note>. Although these symptoms are brief, they tend to become long-lasting if neglected. If the fluid drips into the nostrils or the throat, one must immediately, in the first days, walk a great deal. The lower parts of the body must be rubbed vigorously. A lighter friction should be applied to the chest and the head. Half of the accustomed portion of food should be removed, and eggs should be eaten, along with starch and similar things that make the **phlegm** <note term="pituita">one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture; here referring to mucus or discharge</note> thicker. Thirst must be resisted as much as can possibly be endured.

<margin>Syrup against phlegm</margin>
A syrup against phlegm, which our physicians call **catarrh** <note>original: "catarrum"</note>, is used when the matter is cold and flowing toward the chest. Take: 1 dram each of iris and elecampane roots; 1 scruple each of hyssop and maidenhair fern; 1 dram each of scraped licorice and cleaned raisins; 1 dram each of mastic and frankincense; half a dram each of nutmeg and cypress. With sugar, let a syrup be made, of which 2 drams should be given with 4 drams of the following decoction by **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"; a Persian physician (c. 865–925) whose works were foundational to Medieval medicine</note>. Take: 2 jujubes, 3 sebesten plums, 10 drams of pitted raisins, 3 drams of dried violets, 5 drams of finely cut licorice, and 10 citron figs. Let them be boiled in 3 pounds of water until reduced to one pound, then strained.

<margin>Solvents for phlegm</margin>
To dissolve cold phlegm from the head: **Cochia pills** <note term="pilule cochie">A common purgative pill in medieval medicine, usually containing aloes, colocynth, and scammony</note> perform this. Similarly, we shall give the **Hiera Piera of Galen** pills, or those which **Mesue** calls **Elefangi** <note>Mesue the Younger, an influential but likely pseudonymous Arabic medical author</note>, in the amount and frequency required. Certainly, this syrup is most beneficial in digesting phlegm even before the pills and especially after them. Other somewhat stronger pills can also be administered. For example, take: 1.5 drams of Cochia pills, half a dram of white **agaric** <note>a medicinal fungus used as a purgative</note>, half a scruple each of **colocynth** <note>bitter apple, a powerful laxative</note> pulp and **bdellium** <note>a semi-transparent oleo-gum resin</note>, and three grains of rock salt. Let them be finely powdered and mixed with **hydromel** <note>honey water</note> made with sage water, incorporated, and formed into pills the size of a chickpea. The dose is 1.5 drams at most.

Pills more familiar against phlegm when the matter is thin: Take: 3 drams of Elefangi pills, 1 dram of yellow **myrobalans** <note>astringent fruit used in Unani and medieval medicine</note>, 1 scruple of washed **Armenian bole** <note term="bolus armenicus">A medicinal red clay used as an astringent and to staunch bleeding</note>, and 1 scruple of purslane seed. Mix them, and with tragacanth mucilage made with rose water, let pills be formed. Give 1 dram (six pills) occasionally, or one pill four times a week when going to sleep.

Others for when the matter is thick: Take: 2 drams each of Elefangi pills and simple Hiera pills, 1.5 drams of **trochisced agaric** <note>agaric prepared into small lozenges</note>, and half a dram of mastic. Prepare with **oxymel of squill** <note>a mixture of honey, vinegar, and sea onion (squill)</note> and form them. Give 8 pills for 1 dram, as above.

Others against thin phlegm descending to the chest: Take: half a dram each of oak **polypody** <note>a type of fern</note>

<column-break/>

and trochisced agaric; 1 dram of washed Armenian bole; 3 drams of Elefangi pills; 4 scruples of licorice juice; and 2.5 drams of yellow myrobalans. Prepare with tragacanth mucilage made in violet flower water. Let pills be formed: 6 for 1 dram. Give one occasionally before dinner, but more often when going to sleep.

<margin>Electuary.</margin>
An **electuary** <note term="electuarium">A medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</note> to be administered in the evening upon entering bed is truly singular. Take: 1.5 drams of choice cinnamon; half a dram each of nutmeg and **calamite storax** <note>a fragrant resin</note>; 1 scruple each of aloeswood, mastic, and frankincense; 1 dram each of licorice and Corinthian raisins; half a dram of sugar candy; and a sufficient amount of white sugar to make an electuary. Let the sugar be liquefied with the decoction for the chest which we described above. The dose is half a dram.

We shall, moreover, command the chewing of frankincense at certain hours. For it wonderfully aids distillations, all the senses, and the memory.

<margin>Note on the use of frankincense.</margin>
However, we utterly detest the vehement and continuous use of frankincense, for it makes people furious and insane; it confuses the humors and darkens the spirits. For frankincense, as **Rhazes** holds, restrains the stomach and vomiting and sharpens the intellect; yet if a large quantity is taken, it burns the blood and makes people mad and wakeful. And **Dioscorides** <note>Greek physician and pharmacologist (c. 40–90 AD)</note> says: if frankincense is drunk by a healthy person, he incurs mania or even death. Therefore, our **Marsilio** <note>Marsilio Ficino</note> is not to be entirely believed when he orders one to chew frankincense often. Although it aids distillations, all the senses, and memory, he must be excused. For as the **poet** <note>The Roman poet Virgil, *Eclogues* 8.63</note> says:

<margin>Virgil.</margin>
"We cannot all do everything." <note>original: "non... omnia possumus omnes"</note>
And sometimes "even good Homer nods." <note>A reference to Horace's *Ars Poetica*, meaning even the best experts make mistakes</note>

A **laudanum apple** <note term="pomum">A "pomander" or scented ball of medicinal ingredients carried to ward off illness</note> for phlegm or catarrh: Take: 1 dram of the purest laudanum; half a dram each of aloeswood, calamite storax, and frankincense;

<margin>Phlegm apple.</margin>
1 dram each of nutmeg, cypress nut, and **sandarac** <note>a resin from a cypress-like tree</note>; 2 scruples each of **nigella** <note>black cumin</note>, cinnamon, and cloves; half a dram of nutmeg gall; 1 scruple each of myrrh, spikenard, mastic, and **costus** <note>an aromatic root</note>; half a scruple of amber; and three grains of musk. Let them be finely powdered and pounded with rose water, aromatic wine, and a little wax; let a "pomum" (apple) be made. A small bag for the head could also be made from the greater part of the aforementioned ingredients.

When the matter is hot, such a syrup could be made: Take: 20 each of jujubes and sebesten plums; 1 dram each of violet flowers, water lily, and red roses; half a dram of barley;

<margin>Syrup for the same.</margin>
1 dram of white poppy seed; and sufficient sugar. Let a syrup be made, and let 2 drams of it be given with the aforementioned decoction for the chest.

<margin>Potion.</margin>
The **rhubarb pills** of Rhazes dissolve hot matter. Indeed, another medicine could be administered: Take: 10 plums, half a dram of tamarind, and half a pinch each of water lily flowers and violets. Let a decoction be made, in which dissolve 1 dram of choice **cassia fistula** <note>the pulp of the Golden Shower tree, used as a mild laxative</note> and 1.5 drams of well-veined rhubarb infused as is customary, with 4 grains of spikenard.

...or in place of rhubarb, an equal amount of rose-juice electuary; let it be strained and given in the morning with warm water.
**A Fragrant Scent for a Hot Head Cold.** <note>original: "catarro calido"</note> **Take:** 2 drams each of red roses and white and red sandalwood; half a dram each of water-lily flowers and violet flowers; 1 dram of **spodium** <note term="spodium">ashes or metallic oxides, often zinc oxide, used as a cooling agent</note>; three grains of camphor; half a dram each of Armenian bole and nutmeg. With rose water and a binding of gum arabic and white wax, let a fragrant ball <note term="pomum odoriferum">literally an "odoriferous apple" or pomander, held to the nose to balance the humors through scent</note> be made.
Indeed, we utterly detest every violent and sudden expulsion and purging. For diseases (as **Plato** says) are not to be provoked unless they are extremely dangerous. Every sudden purging weakens the stomach and its contents; it exhausts many of the **spirits** <note term="spiritus">the vital fluids or "breath" believed to carry life and sensation through the body</note>; it confuses the humors; and it obscures the spirits with the dark vapors of the humors.

### On the Exact Cure of Black Bile. Chapter 19.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
We must now deal with that which we would have preferred to explain at the beginning. That kind of humor which we call **black bile** <note term="atra bilis">also known as melancholy; one of the four bodily humors, associated with the earth, autumn, and a cold/dry temperament</note> immediately mixes itself with the stability and nature of the entire body and throws it into confusion. For its temperament—as **Aristotle** testifies in the 14th book of his *Problems*—is both hot and cold. Since nature is both preserved and constituted by these two, black bile can be rendered both extremely hot and extremely cold. It is most suited by its very nature to endure both states: just as water, although it is cold, if it is heated enough (as when it boils), is felt to be hotter than a flame itself. Likewise, stone and iron, when heated by coal, turn out to be hotter than the fire, even though they are cold by nature.
<margin>See chapter six.</margin>
There is no doubt about this. But these things were spoken of more fully where we taught concerning the "fourth monster." <note>A likely reference to an earlier section describing the most dangerous or "monstrous" imbalances of the humors.</note> However, the nature of black bile is essentially cold, and it behaves exactly as has been said: if it exceeds its proper measure, it makes a person stunned, or dazed, or anxious, or fearful. Now, let us teach the remedies for curing it through syrups, pills, electuaries, drugs, and bloodletting.

### On Syrups. Chapter 20.

Many things have indeed been composed by many authors against black bile. For the present, I shall set forth certain types of remedies from among the many—the most select and safest of all—first accepted by the ancients, then confirmed by the moderns, and sometimes adapted by us for our own use. **Sabor, king of the Medes** <note>Likely referring to Shapur I or II, though often a legendary figure in medieval medical texts representing Persian/Arabic wisdom</note>, established the following syrup, which

<column-break/>

is beneficial for mania and **melancholy** <note>original: "melancholie"</note> and for the burning of yellow bile. **Take:** 2 pounds each of the juice of domestic and wild **bugloss** <note term="bugloss">an herb of the borage family, highly valued for "gladdening the heart" and tempering melancholy</note>; 2 pounds of the juice of sweet, fragrant apples; 4 drams of senna pods; 2 drams of saffron; 4 pounds of **tabarzet sugar** <note term="sachari tabarzet">a high-quality, refined white sugar originally from Persia</note>.
<margin>Syrup</margin>
Let it be made thus: let the senna be thrown into the juices for a day and a night after being crushed; then let them be softened by one or two boilings. Then, with the sugar, let a syrup be made. Let the saffron be rubbed in a cloth during its decoction. Give 2 or 3 drams with bugloss water; and sometimes, in case of necessity, it is given with goat's whey <note>original: "aqua casei," literally "cheese water"</note>.
¶ **Another digestive syrup for matter existing in the spleen.**
<margin>Another syrup</margin>
**Take:** half a quarter-pound each of the roots of fennel, parsley, and sweet flag, and cyperus root; 3 drams each of radish root and celery root; half a dram of caper bark; 5 drams each of tamarisk, ash, and broom; 1 handful each of hemp-agrimony, calamint, wormwood, maidenhair fern, endive, and scariola; 1 dram each of anise, fennel seed, pumpkin seed, purslane, and Indian melon seed; 6 drams each of scraped licorice and cleaned raisins; 2 drams each of the juice of borage and purified juice of fumitory; 1 dram each of borage and bugloss flowers, and Arabian stoechas; a sufficient amount of select honey; half a pound of white sugar. Let the barks be steeped in strong vinegar overnight; let a perfectly clarified syrup be made, up to one and a half pounds. Let it be administered with a decoction of borage flowers, tamarisk, and Arabian stoechas, taking half a dram of each; half a dram each of thyme, epithyme, senna pods, and oak polypody; 3 drams of anise. Let a decoction be made in goat's whey, and in the decoction let 1 dram of well-gummed myrobalan peels be steeped overnight. Let them be rubbed vigorously in the morning and strained; and to the strained liquid, for delicate patients, let 1 dram of white sugar or rock candy be added and sweetened.

### On Pills. Chapter 21.

<margin>Two types of pills.</margin>
There are indeed two kinds of pills. Some are suitable for the delicate; these are called **"Blessed"** <note>original: "benedicte"</note> by our people. Others are suitable for the robust, and they are more "attractive" <note term="attractive">in a medical sense, meaning they "draw out" or purge humors more forcefully</note>. 
<margin>Blessed pills.</margin>
They can be named **"Elephantine"** or **"Aromatic"** pills—partly in imitation of **our Ficino** <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a famous philosopher and physician whose "Three Books on Life" heavily influenced Renaissance health practices</note>, and partly by our own invention. They draw out phlegm, bile, and black bile without distress; they strengthen individual limbs; they sharpen and illuminate the spirits. 
**Take therefore:** half a dram each of frankincense, myrrh, saffron, aloeswood, cinnamon, lemon peel, lemon balm, raw silk, kermes, mint, white behen, and red behen; 1 dram each of purple roses, red sandalwood, red coral, and the three **myrobalans** <note term="mirobalanoꝝ">astringent plum-like fruits used in Ayurvedic and Greek medicine: here the emblic, chebulic, and Indian varieties</note> (namely emblic, chebulic, and Indian).

Rather, they should be taken together with syrup of fumitory or epithyme, or with the syrup we described above.

### On Liquid Medicine. Chapter 22.

<margin>Liquid medicine. A purging syrup for melancholy.</margin>
Where the greatest danger of drying out threatens, yet necessity compels a purging, we ought to pause the pills. Here, a liquid medicine is also useful. Take one and a half ounces of Indian **myrobalans** <note term="mirobalanozum">a plum-like fruit used as a laxative</note>; let them be crushed and boiled with one dram of dried prunes in eight ounces of water until half is consumed. Let it be strained, and to that strained liquid add ten drams of pomegranate manna <note term="manne">a sweet, crystalline substance used as a mild laxative</note>.

Likewise, in place of pills or other medicine, a decoction <note>original: "apozima"</note> or a laxative syrup can be given for melancholy. Take five drams each of borage flowers, bugloss, and Arabian stoechas; half an ounce each of oak polypody and select agaric; two drams each of basil seed and ginger; one dram each of purified borage juice and fumitory juice; and half a pound of white sugar. Let it be made into a syrup, lightly cooked and clarified. Let one to three drams be dissolved in syrup of **diacrydium** <note term="dyagredij">a preparation of scammony, a powerful purgative resin</note>. For this is often added to medicines to stimulate the virtues of other

### On Electuaries. Chapter 23.

<margin>Electuary.</margin>
Next follow the electuaries <note term="electuarijs">medicinal pastes made with honey or sugar</note>, among which I certainly praise what is described below. ### On Bloodletting. Chapter 24.

There are some (as a most learned neighbor wrote) who are too bold in the letting of blood; wise physicians detest them greatly. For blood is the tempering agent of **black bile** <note term="atre bilis">the humor associated with melancholy</note>, the fuel of the spirit, and the treasure of life. Indeed, the ancients judged that those of the first and last ages <note>infants and the elderly</note> could not endure this kind of help, and they were persuaded that a pregnant woman treated this way would suffer a miscarriage. But afterward, experience showed that none of these rules are permanent; rather, other potions and observations must be applied, toward which the counsel of the healer ought to be directed.

For it matters (as **Celsus** <note>Aulus Cornelius Celsus, a 1st-century Roman medical encyclopedist</note> excellently says) not what the age is, nor what is carried inside the body, but what the strength is. Therefore, if a youth is feeble, or if a woman who is not pregnant has little strength, blood is ill-let. Yet a sturdy boy, a robust old man, and a strong pregnant woman (as it pleases some) are treated safely. Nevertheless, an unskilled physician can be most easily deceived in these cases, because there is generally less strength underlying those ages. And a pregnant woman needs strength after the treatment, not only for herself but also to sustain the fetus. For there is a difference between a strong body and a fat one, and between a thin one and a weak one. Blood abounds more in the thin; flesh abounds more in the plump. It is more easily...

<meta>This page continues the medical instructions for scholars, moving from the conclusion of bloodletting treatments to the diagnosis and treatment of cognitive decline, specifically forgetfulness and mental dullness, citing authorities like Avicenna, Galen, and Plato.</meta>

Book: On a Healthy Life

...therefore they endure a withdrawal [of blood] of this kind: and it afflicts them more quickly if the blood is too fat. Therefore, the strength of the body is better estimated from the veins and from its appearance. Only when profuse laughter, great boldness and confidence, or a red color and swelling of the veins indicates an abundance of blood, ought we to let blood for scholars <note>original: "litteratis"; refers specifically to those dedicated to a life of study</note> when the situation requires. This should be done from the spleen vein of the left arm <note>original: "vena lienis sinistri brachij"</note> with a wide incision: four ounces in the morning and as many in the evening. Then after a few days, at least seven, one should irritate the blood through leeches <note>original: "sanguisugas"</note> so that three or four ounces of blood may drip from there. Nor does it seem that both should be done only for the more robust. But one is not permitted to let blood unless you have first softened the body with soothing medicines like manna or cassia, or with fat and soft clysters <note term="clysteribus">enemas used to clear the bowels</note>.

### On Dullness and Forgetfulness. Chapter 25.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a human face mask surrounded by scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
<margin>The cause of forgetfulness.</margin> It happens sometimes to those dedicated to study: either because they read or write with their head lowered too often, or when they are sluggish with excessive laziness, that a certain viscous phlegm <note term="pituita">one of the four humors, associated with cold and moisture</note> together with too cold melancholy <note term="melancholia">black bile, associated here with depression or sluggishness</note> occupying the head weighs it down, and makes them dull and forgetful. First, it must be known that these causes of forgetfulness sometimes differ by location. Either the cause is in the substance of the posterior [back] part of the brain, in which part memory is located according to the opinion of **Avicenna** <note>original: "Avicenne"; a famous 11th-century Persian physician</note>. Or it is in the sense itself, which is contained in the ventricle; or in the vessel, that is, on the surface of the posterior ventricle. For thus **Gentile** <note>Gentile da Foligno, a 14th-century physician and commentator</note> explains Avicenna’s words: though it could also be understood as being in the membranes <note term="panniculis">the meninges or coverings of the brain</note> or the sutures of the brain's substance in which the spirit is contained. Or it may be in the "vessel," that is, in the skull. And although **Galen** <note>the foundational 2nd-century Roman physician</note> himself says in the third chapter of the tenth book of *On Internal Parts* that a passion <note term="passio">an ailment or physical condition</note> cannot exist in the skull that would take away memory, if this passion is very great, it can diminish memory if not take it away, as Gentile believes. Indeed, the matter and every harm can be communicated to the memory from the temples and cause hindrance, for that is a location capable of holding such matter. There is also a various sensitive muscle, and the skull is thin there, as **Haly Abbas** <note>original: "Haliabas"; a 10th-century Persian physician</note> says in the second book of his *Theory* in the chapter on the causes of forgetfulness. And sometimes the matter itself creates an abscess <note term="apostema">an internal swelling or inflammatory mass</note>, as happens in **lethargy** <note term="lethargia">a clinical state of deep stupor or coma in medieval medicine</note>, and sometimes they do not.

### On Prognoses in Forgetfulness and Dullness. Chapter 26.

<column-break/>

Chapter 25. 26. 27. & 28.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'O' depicting a flowering plant with visible roots.</image-desc> Forgetfulness brought from birth is difficult to remove. That which is fixed from heat and dryness is also not easily removed. That which comes from moisture or coldness is more easily abolished, which usually happens to scholars. For it is easier and safer to dry and likewise to warm [the brain] than the reverse: especially in the brain, which is a principal organ and is naturally cold and moist; we proceed more boldly by warming than by cooling.

### On the Cure for Forgetfulness. Chapter 27.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with scrolling floral motifs.</image-desc> If the cause of forgetfulness is an abscess, let the cure for an abscess be applied, just as Galen, **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"; a 9th-century Persian physician</note>, and other wise physicians have handed down in their works. If, however, it contains "matter" <note term="materiam">harmful humors or fluids</note> but not an abscess, let it be digested and dissolved before the physician dares to apply remedies; otherwise, they might hinder more than help, and would never be of use. Nor indeed will I dwell on the means of digesting or dissolving, for the books of Galen, Rhazes, Haly Abbas, and the moderns are abundant on these things, and they are known even to mediocre physicians. Therefore, once the matter has been evacuated, these things which we are about to say should be observed.

### Intentions for Curing in Cold and Moist Causes. Chapter 28.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' featuring floral and botanical designs.</image-desc> I find there are three intentions for curing in cold and moist causes among the wise. The first is that with the body evacuated, the head is also particularly evacuated. For as **Plato** writes in the *Charmides*: 
<margin>One ought not to cure the eyes without the head, nor the head without the rest of the body. For this reason, in forgetfulness and dullness, once the body is evacuated, the head should also be particularly evacuated. And wise physicians were accustomed to do this in six ways.</margin> 
Just as one ought not to cure eyes without the head, nor the head without the rest of the body. For this reason, in forgetfulness and dullness, once the body is evacuated, the head should also be particularly evacuated. And wise physicians were accustomed to do this in six ways. The first way: that pills should be administered in whey, such as those we have shown sufficiently above in the chapter on pills. Truly, I shall write my own pills for forgetfulness, which were found partly by my own invention and partly by the intention of others. The recipe is: Take two scruples of **agaric troches** <note term="agarici trochiscati">medicinal lozenges made from larch fungus</note>; two drams of **hiera maior** <note term="hyere maioris">a "greater" version of a traditional bitter purgative</note>; half a dram each of **castoreum** <note term="castorei">a secretion from beavers used in nerve medicine</note> and colocynth; [and a certain amount] of male frankincense and myrrh...

## Chapters 25, 26, 27, & 28

Thus, the strength of the body is better estimated from the veins than from outward appearance. Truly, when a surplus of blood is indicated by excessive laughter, great boldness and confidence, or a ruddy color and swelling of the veins, we ought to draw blood from scholars when the situation demands it. This should be done from the vein of the left arm <note>original: "vena stenis sinistri brachij," likely referring to the basilic vein</note> with a wide incision: four ounces in the morning and as many in the evening. Then, at least eight days later, the blood should be stimulated by leeches so that three or four ounces of blood may trickle out. Both of these treatments seem suitable only for the more robust individuals. But one should not draw blood unless you have first softened the system with soothing medicines such as manna or cassia, or with rich and gentle enemas.

### On Dullness and Forgetfulness. Chapter 25.

<margin>
The cause of forgetfulness.
</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'C' depicting a scholar or physician seated at a desk with an open book.</image-desc>
It occasionally happens to those devoted to study—either those who read or write frequently with their heads bowed, or those who sometimes become sluggish through excessive inactivity—that a certain swift-acting phlegm <note term="pituita">viscous mucus associated with the "cold" humor</note>, together with an excessively cold melancholy, occupies and weighs down the head. This makes them dull and forgetful. First, it must be understood that the causes of forgetfulness sometimes differ by location. For either the harmful cause is in the posterior substance of the brain—the part where memory is located according to the opinion of Avicenna <note>a famous 11th-century Persian physician</note>—or it is in the sense itself, which is contained in the ventricle; or in the "vessel," that is, on the surface of the posterior ventricle. This is how Gentilis <note>Gentile da Foligno, a 14th-century physician</note> explains Avicenna’s words. It could also be understood as being in the membranes or the sutures of the brain substance in which the spirits <note>the "animal spirits" believed to carry thought and sensation</note> are contained, or in the vessel, meaning the skull. And although Galen <note>the most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> himself says in the third chapter of his tenth book *On Internal Affections* <note>original: "decimo interiorum"</note> that a sickness capable of removing memory cannot exist in the skull, nevertheless, if this sickness is very great, it can diminish memory even if it does not remove it, as Gentilis argues. Indeed, the matter and every harm in the temples can be communicated to the memory and cause obstruction, and there is ample space for such matter there. Furthermore, the sensitive muscle is varied, and the skull there is thin, as Haly Abbas <note>a 10th-century Persian physician</note> says in the ninth book of his *Theoretical Medicine* in the chapter on the causes of forgetfulness. And sometimes these matters themselves form an abscess <note term="apostema">a localized collection of pus or a swelling of humors</note>, as happens in lethargy, and sometimes they do not.

### On the Prognosis of Forgetfulness and Dullness. Chapter 26.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'O' depicting a bird among foliage.</image-desc>
Forgetfulness brought on from birth is difficult to remove. That which is fixed by heat and dryness is also not easily cured. However, that which arises from moisture or coldness is more easily abolished; this is what usually happens to scholars. For it is easier and safer to dry things out, and likewise to warm them, than the reverse—especially in the brain, which is a principal organ and is naturally cold and moist. We proceed more boldly with warming treatments than with cooling ones.

### On the Cure of Forgetfulness. Chapter 27.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'S' depicting a figure sitting in a chair.</image-desc>
If the cause of forgetfulness is an abscess, let the treatment for an abscess be applied to it, just as Galen, Rhazes <note>Al-Razi, a renowned Persian physician</note>, and other wise doctors have handed down in their writings. If, however, there is "matter" <note>excessive or corrupted humors</note> but no abscess, let it be "digested" <note>processed by the body's heat</note> and dissolved before the physician dares to apply remedies. Indeed, he must first expel the matter, otherwise the remedies could do more harm than good—or rather, they would never be beneficial. I will not dwell long on digestive or dissolving agents, for the books of Galen, Rhazes, Haly Abbas, and the modern authors are abundant on these topics and are known even to mediocre physicians. Therefore, once the matter has been evacuated, let these things we are about to say be observed.

### Intentions of Curing in Cold and Moist Causes. Chapter 28.

<margin>
On the evacuation of the body.
</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'I' decorated with floral and leafy designs.</image-desc>
Among the wise, there are found to be three intentions for curing a cold and moist cause. The first is that once the body has been evacuated, the head should also be specifically evacuated. For as Plato writes in the *Charmides*: "Just as it is not proper to treat the eyes without the head, so one should not treat the head without the rest of the body." For this reason, in cases of forgetfulness and dullness, after the body is evacuated, the head should also be specifically cleared. The wise physicians have been accustomed to do this in six ways. The first method is that pills be administered in the evening, such as those we have sufficiently shown above in the chapter on pills. Truly, for forgetfulness, I shall write of my own pills, which were found partly by my own invention and partly by the intention of others. The recipe for them is: <term>Recipe</term> <note>original symbol: ℞</note>. two scruples <note>a small unit of weight</note> of agaric troches; three drams of Hiera Picra <note term="hyere maioris">"Holy Bitter," a traditional purgative powder</note>; half a dram each of castoreum and colocynth <note>bitter apple</note>; and masculine frankincense and myrrh...

These actions are forbidden in a body full of bad humors <note>original: "cachochimico," or cacochymic</note>. Combing the head is of the same kind of treatment. On this matter, let our Celsus <note>original: "chous," likely a typo for "Celsus," the Roman medical encyclopedist</note> advise you: "For friction," he says, "if it is vigorous, hardens the body; if gentle, it softens it; if frequent, it reduces it; if moderate, it fills it out." 

The sixth method is a gentle enema to divert the matter from above. For this evacuates from the lower parts and diverts it from the upper parts. Take one handful each of mallow, marshmallow, violets, oregano, and calamint; two drams each of anise and fennel. Let a decoction be made, in which you dissolve one dram of fatty cassia fistula <note term="casiefistl">purging cassia, a mild laxative</note>, one dram each of *diaphœnicon* <note>a date-based purgative electuary</note> and *benedicta* <note>a "blessed" laxative compound</note>, one dram of well-skimmed honey, one and a half drams of red sugar, three drams of common oil, and one dram of salt. Let an enema be made, and it is sufficiently gentle.

### ¶ On Ointments for Forgetfulness. Chapter 29.

<image-desc>A large floriated initial "S" with leaf and vine motifs.</image-desc>
Many ointments are commonly made to be smeared on for forgetfulness. Take three pounds of the "blessed oil" or "oil of the philosophers" according to Mesue <note>a famous 9th-century Persian physician</note>, half a pound of henna oil, two drams of castoreum <note>a secretion from beavers used in medicine</note>, and two drams each of the fat of a weasel, a bear, and a mole.

Let all boil over a slow fire until a fourth part is consumed; afterwards, add these: Take one and a half drams of labdanum, half a dram of nutmeg, and two drams each of mace, cloves, euphorbium, and long pepper. Crush them all and store them together in a well-closed vessel for forty days; afterwards, distill it in a glass vessel. Let the back part of the brain be thoroughly anointed with it. Mix them all and let an ointment be made, with which the back part of the head and the pulse points of the head are to be anointed in winter, and especially at the beginning of spring and the end of autumn, once a week or twice a month.

### ¶ Things Beneficial Internally for the Forgetful.
### Chapter 30.

The "Anacardine Confection" <note>A medicine based on the cashew nut, *Anacardium*, famous in the Middle Ages for improving memory</note>, as is agreed by all philosophers and physicians, is most suitable for forgetfulness, premature graying, and for skin conditions like morphea and leprosy <note>original: "baras"</note>. ## ¶ The Book on Long Life by Master Symphorien Champier, Physician of Lyon, Begins

### ¶ The cause of the shortness of life and death: and that human life has not been shortened. Concerning the years of the ancient patriarchs. And that long life is necessary for the perfection of knowledge: which diligence also provides. Chapter 1.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter "E" showing a scholar or monk seated in a landscape with trees, looking towards the distance.</image-desc>

**E**ver since the beginning, the length and shortness of human life has been debated by many students of wisdom with no small difficulty. Some assert that from the world’s origin and before the inundation of the Flood, life was longer; others, on the contrary, claim that both before and after the Flood, life has remained within the same period of time.

<margin>The opinion of the astrologers</margin>
Therefore, I shall recount in few words, according to the measure of our understanding, what the opinion of the astrologers is regarding this question—an opinion that does not contradict the truth. One ought neither to wonder at, nor envy any age for, nor wish for oneself the great longevity of human life that existed before the departure of the general Flood. For those men, as astronomers say and as experience confirms, the heavens were more propitious <note>favorable or well-disposed</note>. Indeed, astronomers hold that there are two zodiacs: one in the eighth sphere, which is called the firmament, and another in the ninth. These were so disposed by God from the beginning of things and times that Aries was placed upon Aries, Taurus upon Taurus, and Gemini upon Gemini. With the powers of both spheres converging into one, a stronger influence was made upon the earth. Thus, there is no doubt that herbs were then more medicinal, the fruits of the earth were better, and the lives of living creatures were longer. But after this fellowship was dissolved by their motion and they moved away from one another, this entire lower world became ill. They add also that the moisture of the earth then supplied a pure, better, and more abundant nourishment for crops, which, after the Flood occurred, was weakened and corrupted by the saltiness of the sea. They say it was for this reason that God forbade Adam from tasting again of the tree which was called the "Tree of Life"—because it had the power to prolong life—lest he prolong his miseries along with his life.

<margin>The opinion of the theologians</margin>
Furthermore, our theologians add that the first parent <note>Adam</note> instructed his sons and grandsons in such disciplines that each person knew for himself what was useful and what was harmful to life.

<margin>The opinion proven by philosophers</margin>
Moreover, some of our philosophers prove that those men ought to have been in life longer than we are for this reason: namely, that since they had no inventions of predecessors, no arts, and no sciences at that time, it was necessary for them to learn those things through long experiments—things which

<column-break/>

we are taught easily and concisely from the writings of others and the nocturnal studies of our ancestors. At last, the sum of common human life was reduced, as David testifies in the Psalms, to seventy years, and it still perseveres in that same state. Furthermore, the opinion of those who say human life is being shortened must cease. For if the span of life was the same in the time of David and Solomon as it is now, how shall we say that human life is shortened daily? Indeed, two thousand five hundred years and more have passed between David and our own age, in which very long course of time a manifest shortening of life would have occurred. But if you say that in those times certain individuals survived until their hundredth year or more, a prudent person will respond that the same happened to some in later ages, and it happens even now.

<margin>Those who lived a long time</margin>
Avenzoar <note>Abu Marwan ibn Zuhr, a famous 12th-century Andalusian physician</note>, surnamed "The Wise," as Averroes testifies in the *Colliget* <note>original: "colliget" — from the Arabic *Kitab al-Kullyat*, meaning 'General Principles of Medicine'</note>, lived one hundred and thirty years because of his skill in medicine. Marcus Valerius Corvinus lived one hundred. Borgias the Sicilian lived one hundred and eight. Epimenides lived one hundred and fifty. Tinyras <note>Cinyras</note>, king of the Cyprians, lived more than that. Arganthonius, king of the Tartessians, lived one hundred and fifty. Terentia, the wife of Cicero, lived one hundred and seven years. A certain John, a squire of Charlemagne, king of the Franks, is said to have lived three hundred years, equal in length of life to Nestor <note>the long-lived King of Pylos from the Iliad</note>. Therefore, we should not grieve over the span of our life, but we must take every care to live for a long time in a holy and sober manner, and not in vain. For a long life is necessary for the perfect acquisition of knowledge, which diligence also provides. However, we do not wish these instructions to be shared with the idle or the lazy. For why would we desire those to live long who do not even truly live? Let us not nourish "drones" (to use the words of Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino, a famous Renaissance Neo-Platonist who wrote on health and longevity</note>), but rather bees. Nor should this be divulged to men dissolved by the lust for pleasures, who foolishly prefer a brief daily pleasure to a long one. Nor should it be revealed to the wicked and unjust, whose life is the death of the good; but only to prudent and temperate men who, with the strength of a skillful mind, will benefit the human race either privately or publicly.

<margin>The distinction of years</margin>
Regarding the years of the ancients, Pliny says the following in the seventh book of his *Natural History*, chapter forty-seven: "Some defined one year by the summer, another by the winter. Others used four-part seasons, like the Arcadians, whose years were three months long. Some defined them by the waning of the moon, like the Egyptians; thus, among them, some are reported to have lived a thousand years each." So says Pliny. By these words, he shows that he thinks the "years" attributed to the first patriarchs were actually months. But this opinion is sufficiently exploded <note>rejected or disproven</note> on its own. For we would live much longer than that antiquity which was still fresh at the beginning of the world. For one hundred years include one thousand two hundred months, which number...

<summary>Symphorien Champier examines the discrepancy between Biblical longevity and modern lifespans, arguing that while celestial and environmental conditions have changed, life is not actively shortening. He emphasizes that a long life is a tool for the wise to acquire knowledge and serve humanity, rather than a gift for the hedonistic.</summary>
<keywords>longevity, astrology, macrobiotics, Biblical patriarchs, Avenzoar, Pliny the Elder, Marsilio Ficino, medical philosophy</keywords>
