<meta>This page continues the discussion on the longevity of the Biblical patriarchs before transitioning into a philosophical exploration of the three stages of life, the necessity of death, and the theological problem of the resurrection of the body.</meta>

the number of years is ascribed to none of them. But what more evident argument can there be against those who say that the Hebrew years were actually months than that which Moses himself said: "Mahalaleel lived sixty-five years and fathered Jared." Certainly, if he took years to mean months, Mahalaleel would have fathered a child when he was only five years and five months old. Concerning the "age" <note>original: "seculo"</note>, which is defined as the longest span of human life between birth and death, enough has been said in passing.

# ¶ Three kinds of life which everyone must experience. Chapter 2.

<margin>
1 Corinthians 15
</margin>
For there are three kinds of life. The first is in the mortal body. The second is outside the body. The third is back in the body, when that which is corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and that which is mortal shall have put on immortality <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 15:53</note>. This is the perfect circle of souls: when, having been released from the body, they return again to their ancient limbs once their period is complete.

<margin>
The necessity of dying
</margin>
There is another necessity of dying (as some say): because we are clearly composed of contrary elements <note>The four humors or elements: earth, air, fire, and water, which were thought to be in constant conflict</note> which, by both acting and being acted upon, continually wear each other away. But in the judgment of wise men, this reasoning shows the brevity of life, but does not truly explain mortality. For it is clear that what is continually flowing away cannot stand for long. Yet even if the body were not made of contrary elements, but were molded from only one, the conflict of elements would be removed, but

<margin>
The corruptibility of the body
</margin>
mortality would not. For the body is corruptible whether it consists of one element or of many. Indeed, the elements themselves are by their very nature subject to death and corruption. For I do not think that water, if it were alone in the world and free from the opposition of other elements, would be 

<margin>
The opinion of the Platonists
</margin>
incorruptible. Plato, Plotinus, and Porphyry <note>Three major figures of the Neoplatonic school of philosophy</note> hand down another necessity of death based on the almost infinite number of souls. For they say that matter is not sufficient for the simultaneous creation of as many bodies as there are souls that are, have been, and shall be. And therefore, so that others may follow, it is necessary for the previous ones to depart, and to hand over the matter of their bodies to new souls, like a house to new inhabitants, so that the number of natural spirits may be fulfilled. To wish to live forever, therefore (if these things are true), is nothing else than to wish to occupy more than is fair of the matter owed to other souls, and to be an 

<margin>
Confutation of the Platonists
</margin>
impediment to those to come so that they are not born. How wicked this would be we may judge for ourselves: we would not yet have been born unless our ancestors had already departed. Therefore, according to these thinkers, God established the short days of man so that the sum total of all souls 

<column-break/>

might emerge in the race of a certain time. You, therefore, whoever you are who by living wickedly hold your limbs in the slavery of sin: remember that the matter of your body is expected by a perhaps better soul; a soul to whom you do an injury as long as you live, if the length of your obscene life stands in the way of its creation. From the aforesaid, it can be inferred (which is conceded by all upright men) that the matter of corruptible things is not itself destroyed. According to that saying of Naso <note>The Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso)</note>: "Nothing perishes entirely, believe me, in the world. But it changes and renews its face; and what is called being born is simply beginning to be something else" <note>original: "Non perit ex toto quicq[ua]m mihi credite mundo. Sed varie faciemq[uae] nouat: nasciq[uae] vocat." from Ovid's Metamorphoses</note>. For matter always seeks to be adorned with new forms, and form seeks to dominate matter. And when matter is destitute of one form, it never returns to that same form until the final day; though it does not return to a similar one immediately. It can, however, be recalled immediately—that is, in a short time—as if a human body were eaten by a man, as is the custom among the Anthropophagi <note>A Greek-derived term for cannibals</note>. For when part of the food passes into human seed, from that little portion of matter an embryo can be made, and it returns to the fellowship of a rational soul.

# ¶ An incidental question as to how it can be that the same part of matter which has been in several bodies might rise in the judgment. Chapter 3.

Human curiosity—among which number are a great many city-dwellers, and almost all who are eager for letters—asks perhaps how it could happen, or in what way it is possible, that the same part of matter which has been in several human bodies should rise in the judgment. Since it cannot rise with all of them, with which one shall it rise?

<margin>
The author here relates the opinion of certain theologians and does not assert it as his own.
</margin>
Some theologians say it will rise with the first owner, and that what is lacking in the others will be supplied by God. For just as He multiplied the loaves in the desert, He can also increase matter at the judgment. For if the whole matter of one became the whole matter of the other, it would be necessary for new matter to be given to the second, and then it would not be—as the Church teaches—the resurrection of one's own proper flesh.

# ¶ Various opinions on life: and whether there are "climacteric" years, both decisive and harmful. Chapter 4.

<margin>
The opinion of the astronomers
</margin>
Astronomers measure life by the heavens; and they wished to imitate the Etruscans, whose first ages were one hundred years long, here and in many other things. Furthermore, according to them, it can happen (as Varro <note>A Roman polymath</note> relates and as Dioscorides the astrologer wrote at Alexandria, where they are accustomed to preserve the bodies of the dead) that a man cannot live for more than a hundred years. Their human hearts declare this, for they perished

# Books on Long Life, Chapter 5.

...the human heart weighed, and they maintained that the increases and decreases of age correspond to this weight. They say it weighs one unit in the first year, two in the second, and four in the fourth; and so, it adds two units every single year until the fiftieth year. From that point—the hundredth year <note>original: "centu. 3." likely referring to a specific weight measurement or drachmae</note>—and from the fiftieth year, it likewise decreases by two units each year. From this, it becomes clear that in the hundredth year, the heart returns to the weight of the first year, and life cannot be extended any further. Epigenes <note>An ancient Greek astrologer and writer</note> denies that the years of life can exceed one hundred and twenty-two. Berosus <note>A Babylonian writer and astronomer</note> says one hundred and seventeen. The kings Petosyris and Necepsos <note>Legendary Egyptian authors of astrological texts</note> say that in Italy, it is possible for <margin>Climacteric years.</margin> the years of life to reach one hundred and twenty-six. Mathematicians <note>In this context, "mathematicians" usually refers to astrologers</note> warn that the "climacteric years" must be observed. These are the "climbing" and "stepping" years, which arise from the numbers seven and nine flowing together into one. For these two numbers are considered decisive and harmful, and are powerful enough to cut short a life. For this reason, they call the sixty-third year "the year of the elderly" and "the pestilential year," because nine times seven and seven times nine both result in that number. This astronomical superstition—as Lucius Suetonius <note>The Roman biographer</note> testifies—greatly disturbed Augustus himself. Let us instead run back to the Apostle Paul, who is conscious not of the secrets of the heavens, but of the secrets of God; let us learn from him that it is appointed for all men to die once. Let us also hear Cicero speaking on old age: "That we must die is certain, but it is uncertain whether it will be on this very day" <note>original: "Moriendum enim certum est: et incertum an eo ipso die"</note>. And Job says: "You have set his bounds, which cannot be passed." Nor should we grieve over the brevity of life in the manner of Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle</note>, who seemed to accuse Nature because she gave the longest life to crows, elephants, and stags, but was stingy to the point of appearing envious when setting the lifespan for man—to whom long life was most important and most deserved. On the contrary, if we believe Moses, God the creator of nature was so liberal in the distribution of life that he gave man the power never to die. But those who perfectly believe the divine words and lead their lives with justice and piety are content with the brevity of this present exile; they thank God more for opening heaven to man than they accuse Nature of being greedy with life.

### ¶ The length of human life according to the poets and certain philosophers. Chapter 5.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial N depicting a figure walking through a landscape with hills and a castle in the distance.</image-desc>Several members of the academy of philosophers and poets have spoken thus and left it in their writings: if we should fall from the "skiff"—that is, from this world—before a proper burial, we must wander for a hundred years, which seems to be the most fitting span of human life. They wish for

<column-break/>

the day of life to be long for everyone, provided it is not cut short. Whence comes that saying of Seneca: "He who reaches the end of his fate shall die an old man." However, among them, there are multiple paths for those who die, about which Servius <note>A famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> comments on that line in the fourth book of the *Aeneid*: "I have lived, and I have completed the course which fortune gave me" <note>original: "Vixit quem dederit cursum fortuna pegi"</note>. He says "Fortune," not "Human Nature" nor "Fate." For according to the poets, human life is contained by three things. First, Nature, to which no more than one hundred and twenty solar years are given. Second, Fate, for which ninety years—that is, three cycles of the planet Saturn—create an end, unless the kindness of other stars adds a third cycle. And third, Fortune—that is, chance—which pertains to all external things leading to ruin: shipwrecks, slaughters, and the like. Therefore, he rightly says "Fortune." So too Cicero in his *Philippics*: "Many things seem to loom over me beyond nature and beyond fate"—meaning the sword of Mark Antony, and so on. <margin>Virgil, 4th Book of the Aeneid.</margin> Thus says Servius. To this responds that line of Virgil: "For because she perished neither by fate nor by a deserved death, but miserably before her day and inflamed by sudden madness..." <note>A reference to the suicide of Queen Dido</note>. Therefore, according to them, the span of a hundred years is the middle ground between the times of Fate and Nature. For this reason, as Cicero says in *The Dream of Scipio*: "it is necessary that we fulfill the term of our life, waiting until God releases us." In some way, those who prevent the legitimate time—either by their own hand, or by gluttony, or by rashness, or by negligence—seem to escape the gift of God. Because of this, they wander for a hundred years. However, according to Virgil's opinion, only those whose bodies are unburied wander for a hundred years. For he had found the shade of Dido transferred into the Mourning Fields. They assign this kind of reason, saying that souls are subject to such great burdens of the body as long as the body is unburied. But with a legitimate or even a symbolic burial, the funeral rites are completed, by which the soul is absolved and transferred to its proper place. These things seem to be shrouded in shadows that suggest what we ourselves say: that the souls of those dying in a state of grace <note>original: "in charitate"</note> are not taken into the heavenly homeland until all the stains they contracted in the framework of the body have been purged. <margin>6th Book of the Aeneid.</margin> Indeed, Virgil himself expresses this sufficiently here: "Even when life leaves them with the final light, yet not every evil, nor all the plagues of the body, fundamentally depart from the wretched ones; it is entirely necessary that many things, long hardened, should grow inward in marvelous ways. Therefore they are exercised with punishments, and they pay the penalties for ancient evils. Some are stretched out empty, suspended to the winds; for others, the infected crime is washed away under a vast whirlpool, or burned out by fire. Each of us suffers our own ghosts <note>original: "Quisque suos patimur manes"</note>; thereafter we are sent through wide Elysium, and a few of us hold the joyful fields, until a long day, when the circle of time is perfected, has removed the hardened [stain]..."

# ¶ On the period of human life: and whether life can be prolonged: a question worthy of investigation. Chapter 6.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' featuring a bird and floral motifs within a square border.</image-desc>Since it was shown just before, according to the opinion of Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil</note>, that human life is contained by three things: namely nature, fate, and fortune. Therefore, Aristotle says in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*: that the life of each individual has a number by which it is determined. For there is an order for all things: and the time and life of all things are enclosed within a <term>period</term> <note>original: "periodo" — a fixed cycle or natural lifespan</note>: but the period is not the same for all; for some it is short, such as a year, while for others it is longer. Yet it often happens that one does not reach the goal of their period, but dies sooner because of the confusion of causes and the inequality of matter, which does not have the same virtues everywhere. <margin>The Question.</margin> Therefore, concerning this matter, it is asked whether every living thing has a certain and determined period of its life. And it seems not: because many things live through human industry, such as plants and seeds, and many animals; therefore they do not have a certain period of their life, since they live by human labor. Second: if every life were measured by a certain period, then the duration of any living thing's life could be known through nature; but this does not seem true, because nothing is more uncertain than the hour of death; therefore there does not seem to be a certain preset period for the life of any living thing. ¶ To satisfy the proposed question, it should be noted <margin>Where corruption arises.</margin> that corruption <note>the process of decay or dying</note> does not happen primarily and of itself in form or matter, but in the proportion of the mixable elements. Although the proportion of the mixture is not the medium of the union of form and matter, it is nevertheless the bond of continuation or the medium of duration. And therefore, since corruption happens through active and passive qualities, action and passion occur primarily and of themselves in the mixture or in the proportion of the mixed elements. Because of this, from whatever source the proportion of the mixture is held, the duration of being—or life—is also held as a result. Such a rightful duration through nature is called a "period." And therefore it must be said, since the proportion of mixable elements is held through the power of the planets under the oblique circle <note>the ecliptic or zodiac</note>, that the period of life is necessarily taken from under it. Therefore, the period of life which is taken from the proportion of nature—which is the bond of living and being—is both certain and infallible. ¶ To the reasons: regarding the first, when it is shown that many things live...

<column-break/>

...through human industry: it must be said that this is not true; but it should be understood that the period of life can be hindered by accident, such as by a violent killing, or the food and use of poisons, or by things contrary to nature; yet it cannot be prolonged, even if it can be hindered. ¶ It is not, therefore, by human industry that the period of life or life itself is prolonged, but rather that it is not hindered by accident. Regarding the second reason, when it is argued that the duration of any living thing's life could thus be known: it must be said that this is true if the "ascending concept" and the figure of the <term>alchocoden</term> <note>The planet that rules over the birth chart and "gives" the years of life in medieval astrology</note> are known, which is caused by the aspect of the planets and stars and degrees. Knowledge of this belongs to the second part of astrology, which is a great wisdom, as <term>Albumazar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer (787–886 AD)</note> testifies in the *Greater Introduction*; and these things hold truth unless contrary events occur miraculously. ¶ But for a clearer explanation of the above, several things worthy of being known present themselves to reason. First, it should be noted that since you feel the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The innate fluid or "fuel" that sustains life's heat</note> is continually dissolved by natural heat—and sometimes the dissolution is greater than the restoration <margin>of matter.</margin>—it follows that the life of a human or another animal cannot be made perpetual, but must necessarily fail by internal action. ¶ Second, it should be noted that in man there are four <term>complexions</term> <note>the balance of "humors" or bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note>: namely sanguine, choleric, phlegmatic, and melancholic. These complexions are not of equal duration; rather, the sanguine lasts longer. And if the sanguine sometimes die sooner than others, this happens by reason of their own excess and bad regimen <note>lifestyle or medical routine</note>. For if they lived temperately and were rightly governed, they would undoubtedly outlive the others for a longer time. ¶ Third, it should be noted that although someone might have naturally fallen into one complexion from the beginning of their birth, they could nevertheless accidentally fall into another through regimen. For if a phlegmatic person is governed by hot foods and temperately moist ones, they will accidentally become hot and moist, even though from the principles of birth they had been cold. And thus, that person would be naturally phlegmatic and accidentally sanguine. ¶ Fourth, it should be noted that although something can be corrupted from within by itself, it is not "firstly" so, because one part of a human acts upon another, yet nothing acts upon itself in the same part. ¶ Fifth, it should be noted that human life cannot be made perpetual, because corruption necessarily occurs from within by reason of dissimilar parts. ¶ Sixth, it should be noted that although human life can be prolonged beyond the limit of the individual complexion, <margin>The progression of human life.</margin> it cannot be prolonged beyond the limit of the species. The first part of this is clear, because by a good regimen one complexion can be changed into another better one. This leads to prolongation...

### Books on Long Life, Chapter 5.

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "period" or natural cycle of human life. Having previously discussed the influences of fate and the stars, the author now turns to a physical and medical perspective on whether these limits can be stretched or if they are absolute.</meta>

### Chapter 7.

The first part of this argument is contrary to what was said above: when it was stated that life cannot be prolonged through human industry. This remains true when considering celestial influences and their aspects. But now I speak more from a physical perspective and with respect to temperaments <term>complexionum</term><note>The "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—within an individual.</note>: not assertively, however, but only as a matter of probability. For God, through the ministry of the celestial bodies, can set boundaries that cannot be crossed, although beyond the influence of the heavens, they might be shortened or prolonged by God's infinite power. Hence, when the natural virtues are finally failing, medicines have no effective power at all. That life cannot be prolonged beyond the limit of the species is shown thus: because no matter how well an individual is governed by art or nature, they cannot live longer than a person of perfectly balanced temperament, living under the best rule and in the most suitable air; yet even such a person could not live beyond the limit assigned to the human species. ¶ Seventh, it must be noted that for any homogeneous thing, whether substantial or accidental, which exists at one time and not at another, there is a determined period for its duration. This is evident because nature determines that it cannot last beyond a certain point. And I say specifically "which exists at one time and not at another" because the elements and the light in the heavens, along with other accidental celestial virtues, do not have a determined period, for they are perpetual and eternal. From all this, it follows that every being that will eventually be destroyed has a determined period for its duration. And I say specifically "will be destroyed" rather than "is destructible" because the light of the firmament is destructible (just as the light of the moon is of the same species as it), yet it does not have a determined period because of its eternity.

<margin>
Conclusion.
</margin>
¶ From all the above, I infer one conclusion: that it is impossible for a physician, no matter how skilled, or an astrologer to restore the radical moisture <term>humidum radicale</term><note>original: "humidum radicale"; in medieval medicine, this was the "innate oil" or vital fluid we are born with that acts as the fuel for our life-fire. Once used up, it was believed it could not be fully replenished.</note> after the time of its peak; because it is continually failing and eventually life fails. The reason is this: because the moisture that comes in later is not as pure as that which preceded it, since the natural heat then cannot perform as much digestion as it could before. And if one asks for the cause, the answer is that this is from nature: because human virtues then begin to weaken across the whole species.

<margin>
Doubt concerning the corruption of homogeneous things.
</margin>
¶ But there remains a doubt whether truly homogeneous things are corruptible from within. To this, it must be said that although heterogeneous things <note>Bodies made of different parts or substances.</note> are corruptible from within, truly homogeneous things are not. The first part is clear because heterogeneous things are necessarily made of parts with dissimilar primary qualities, of which

<column-break/>

one necessarily acts upon the other, altering and destroying it. The second part is evident: for alteration and corruption made from within happens by reason of divisible qualities according to their strengthening or weakening. But in a truly homogeneous body, there is no such dissimilarity of primary qualities. And I call a body truly homogeneous here which is of equal intensity throughout, just as it is of the same essential name. From what has been said, it follows that since

<margin>
Natural things are contained in three times.
</margin>
man is a heterogeneous body in which there are contrary qualities: he must of necessity eventually be destroyed. For all natural things—if we believe Lactantius <note>Lucius Caecilius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325), an early Christian author who often harmonized Greek philosophy with theology.</note>—must be contained in three times: the past, the present, and the future. In the past is the origin; in the present, the substance; in the future, the dissolution. All these things appear in every individual human. For we begin when we are born, we are while we live, and we cease when we die. The first part begins the life of man; the second wears it away; the third breaks and finishes it. To be extinguished in one's own time—if we do not disagree with Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman orator; the author likely refers to Cicero's "On Old Age" (*De Senectute*).</note>—is desirable. For nature has a limit for living, just as it does for all other things. I had no more to say regarding the period of human life; and O mortals, I wish that you might eventually reach it, so that you might be able to prove by experience the things you have heard from us.

Take one dram of ancient theriac <note>original: "tyziace [tyriace] antique"—a famous polypharmaceutical "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh.</note>. Take eight pounds of "glorified" *aqua vite* <term>aqua vite</term><note>Literally "water of life"; high-proof distilled alcohol or brandy used as a solvent for herbs.</note> prepared according to the art, or at least of good wine distilled four times. Put in all the aforesaid ingredients, well-pounded and sifted; place them in a closed glass vessel and allow them to ferment well for forty days. Afterward, let it be poured into a glass alembic <note>A chemical apparatus used for distillation.</note> and let its "nose" be well-sealed with the receiver. Let it be distilled four times, always returning the liquid over its own dregs, except that in the fourth distillation, add two and a half drams each of all the myrobalans and cashew nuts <note>original: "anacardoꝝ"</note>. Pound them well and mix them; finally, let them rest for six days. Afterward, let it be distilled first with a slow fire, then gradually with a stronger one. You will see the color change three times: first it will be like water, then sub-citrine [pale yellow], and finally, with the fire greatly increased, it will become citrine [bright yellow]. It is fitting afterward that it be scented with ambergris and musk. The first water will be the weakest...

<column-break/>

the second will be for beginners and for summertime; and the second is also weaker than the third. The method of taking it is that one spoonful be taken twice a week in the evening without dinner, or in the morning on an empty stomach; and afterward, one should fast for six hours. If you also rub the temples and the "cell of memory" <note>Medieval anatomy located memory in the posterior ventricle (back) of the brain.</note> with it, it performs wonders. And although our Avicenna <note>The 11th-century Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the standard textbook in Europe.</note> said in the first part of the third book, first treatise, twenty-eighth chapter, that compresses <term>epithimata</term> should not be placed over that part [the back of the head] because of the lack of sutures, but rather over the coronal suture; he was speaking there of cold things which do not penetrate and do not help. It should not be denied that it ought also to be applied to the coronal suture. Let whoever uses this also beware of anger, labor, over-fullness, and even sexual intercourse, unless a sufficient evacuation has first been made. Likewise, it is a grand rule that when the brain has been sufficiently dried, we should stop there, lest we be cast headlong into a "dry imbalance" <term>dyscrasia sicca</term>, which is a greater misfortune than a "moist" one; indeed, it is better to stop short than to dry the brain too exquisitely. This water wonderfully strengthens the governing virtue of the whole body, and for that reason prolongs life, so much so that some, through its use, have reached one hundred and fifty years in good health. It produces a good complexion, fights cold diseases, kills "evil pustules" [sores], and heals all diseases caused by the rot of the humors; it especially helps with paralysis and spasms, and cures quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where fever recurs every fourth day.</note> and kidney ailments. Along with these benefits, however, it has its dangers: because it must be administered cautiously to those having a hot liver or head. I am also accustomed to apply substances appropriated to various members [organs] and to administer them for their specific diseases, and that indeed quite successfully. To those of a choleric temperament or those exercising in the summer and in a hot region, it should be offered prudently, so that the liver is tempered with a compress; however, a compress should not be applied when "plethora" <term>plectoria</term><note>An overabundance of blood or humors in the body.</note> is present, as per the fourteenth [chapter] of the third [book]; but also the water, as we have already said, should by no means be administered during plethora.

# The Book of Master Symphorien Champier, Physician of Lyon, on Obtaining Life from the Heavens begins.

## Preface to the following work. Chapter 1.

<margin>Aristotle, Book 1 of the *Meteorology*.</margin>
This lower world <note>The "lower world" or sublunary sphere refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which medieval thinkers believed was subject to change and decay, unlike the "higher" unchanging heavens.</note> is, by natural necessity, connected to the higher motions and celestial bodies, so that the entire power of the lower world is ruled and governed by the celestial world.

For since the motion of the heavens—as Aristotle testifies—is perpetual, having neither beginning nor end, but existing always in the beginning and always at the end; while the motions of lower things are not continuous or perpetual, the heavens are rightly the primary cause of these lower motions. It is probable among philosophers that things so beautiful <note>Referring to earthly life and complex organisms.</note> could not be sustained under the earth unless they were reached by a certain great effort of the heavens, and that a power once impressed upon them by that effort should endure. For in these matters of gathering and compelling, the heavens have labored for a very long time. And as our friend Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a central figure of the Italian Renaissance whose work on "celestial life" blended medicine, magic, and philosophy.</note> wrote most clearly: "If you grant that God has inserted wonderful powers into things below the moon, grant even more wonderful ones to the celestial things. Furthermore, if you judge it permissible for a man to use lower things <note>i.e., herbs and minerals.</note> for prosperous health, judge it also permissible to use the higher ones." And thus, one should temper lower things to the pattern of the higher ones through the physician's skill, just as they were also tempered by God from the beginning.

## What kind of influence of the celestial bodies over lower things philosophers and astrologers, along with our theologians, concede. Chapter 2.

<margin>Psalm 146 <note>In modern Bibles, this is Psalm 147:4-5.</note></margin>
No wise man doubts that a manifold power and operation was created in the celestial bodies by the Creator of all. Yet David indicates that very few of these have come to the knowledge of men, and all are known to God alone, saying: *He counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names.* It is established that names are imposed by the properties of things, which only He who created them knows perfectly. Hence the prophet, admiring divine wisdom, is compelled to exclaim:
<margin>as above</margin>
*Great is our Lord, and great is His power, and of His wisdom there is no number.* These things are to be understood regarding specific knowledge; for the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle.</note>, the Platonists, and the entire family of Stoics (by God's gift) recognized the general influx of the heavens which occurs through heat, light, and motion upon the earth. Whence—

<column-break/>

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin>
Aristotle (as we said) stated that this world is continuous with the higher motions. And in another place: "The motion of the sun along the oblique circle <note>The ecliptic, or the sun's apparent path across the sky.</note> brings about generations." And the holy father Augustine, in Book 3 of *On the Trinity*, Chapter 4, confirms the same, asserting that coarser and lower bodies are ruled in a certain order by the more subtle and powerful ones. And in Book 5 of *The City of God*, Chapter 6, while disputing with the mathematicians <note>In Augustine's time, "mathematicians" often referred to astrologers.</note>, he says: "It can be said, not altogether absurdly, that certain sidereal 'breathings' <note>original: "afflatus... sidereos," referring to celestial influences or emanations.</note> apply to the differences of bodies alone. Just as in the approaches and retreats of the sun, we see the seasons of the year vary; and in the waxings and wanings of the moon, certain kinds of things increase and decrease, such as sea urchins and shells, and the marvelous tides of the ocean. However, the mind and the will are not subjected to the positions of the stars." Augustine himself did not take away from astrology that which natural reason admits and the unchangeable tenor of the Sacred Scriptures does not reprove. Yet he does not say that the differences of bodies are *necessarily* caused by celestial influx, but that this can be conceded in certain cases. For as he says in the same place: "Diversity of offspring is from celestial influx," even when twins of different sexes can be conceived at the same time. Alexander of Hales, Thomas [Aquinas], Albert the Great, Bonaventure, Scotus, Ockham, and a numerous multitude of theologians all confirm the general influx of the heavens into lower things. I say "lower bodies," not human wills or minds. For as Augustine wishes in Book 12 of *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, bodily things cannot act upon the spirit. Others limit this to "of itself and immediately." For they say that since the intellect proceeds into its work through the mediation of images received from the senses, and the sensitive power uses bodily organs, it could be conceded accidentally and remotely that the intellect is hindered in its operation by changes in bodies—as can be seen in the melancholic and the "lunatic." <note>Those supposedly affected by the moon.</note> Whence the Scripture says: *The body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the sense that muses upon many things.* <margin>Wisdom 9.</margin> However, the Will, being the mistress of all its acts, is not bound to a bodily organ any more than the intellect is. It is even more free; it suffers no property of the heavens, nor is it subject to celestial influx. And therefore, acts proceeding from the will can by no means be foreseen or judged by astronomers. Some think that from the beginning of the world, the lifespan of people in ancient times was prolonged by God so that they could investigate astrology (or rather, astronomy) and the arts or other sciences that are acquired through long experience. Others say that a significant part of astrology was divinely revealed to the first parent Adam and the first patriarchs themselves. Whence also the Master of the Histories <note>Peter Comestor, author of the *Historia Scholastica*.</note>, Lactantius, and Josephus say that Abraham [taught] the Egyptians—

### Book on Obtaining Life from the Heavens, Chapter 7

...one spoonful at a time for three days: and it is effective for prolonging life if used sometimes in the morning during the winter season. An electuary <term>electuary: a medicinal paste or conserve made by mixing powdered drugs with honey or syrup</term> for maintaining good health and prolonging life: and it can be administered in all illnesses in which a general evacuation <note>original: "universalis evacuatio"; the process of purging the body of excess humors through the bowels or other means</note> is required: and for those who are constipated, it may be taken before and after food. For it evacuates yellow bile, phlegm, and black bile <note>these represent three of the four "humors" believed to govern human health and temperament; balancing them was the primary goal of medieval medicine</note> and purifies the blood: it soothes the chest and removes flatulence. Take: senna, cassia, tamarinds, rhubarb, violets, and polypody fern—half a dram <term>dram (ʒ): an apothecary weight, approximately 3.9 grams</term> of each; cleaned licorice, penidium <note>a traditional barley-sugar or "pulled sugar" preparation used to soothe the throat and act as a base for medicine</note>, and sugar candy—three drams of each. Let all these boil in a decoction <note>a concentrated liquid made by boiling down herbal material</note> previously made from one and a half 

<column-break/>

ounces of polypody. Strain the mixture, except for the cassia, tamarind, sugar candy, and rhubarb: and turn the said decoction into a syrup with a sufficient amount of sugar: afterwards add the remaining ingredients and let an electuary be made. Furthermore, eating two ounces of pitted raisins while fasting contributes to the path of rejuvenation, because it makes digestion better and reduces the phlegm within the body.

By natural necessity, this lower world is contiguous with the superior motions and celestial bodies: so that the entire power of the lower world is ruled and governed by the celestial world.

For since the motion of the heavens—according to the testimony of Aristotle—is perpetual, having neither beginning nor end, but existing in the beginning and always at the end; and since the motions of lower things are not continuous or perpetual: the heaven is rightly the primary cause of the lower world. For it is probable among philosophers that things so beautiful could not be sustained beneath the earth except by a certain great effort of the heavens, and that the power once impressed upon them from that effort remains. For the heavens labored for a very long time in fashioning and bringing these things together. And as our Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the Italian priest and philosopher whose work on "natural magic" and Platonic thought deeply influenced Champier</note> most brilliantly wrote: "If you grant that God has inserted wonderful virtues into things below the moon, grant even more wonderful ones to the celestial things." Furthermore, if you judge it permissible for a man to use lower things <note>i.e., herbs, minerals, and animal products</note> for prosperous health, judge it permissible to use superior things as well. And so, by the art of physicians, we should temper the lower things according to the norm of the superior ones, just as they were tempered by God from the beginning.

### ¶ What kind of influence of celestial bodies upon lower things philosophers and astrologers, along with our theologians, concede. Chapter 2.

<margin>

</margin>
No wise man doubts that a manifold power and operation was created in the celestial bodies by the Creator of all. David indicates that very few of these have come to the knowledge of men, but all are known to God alone, <margin>as above</margin> saying: "He counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names." It is established that names are imposed upon things according to their properties, which He alone who founded them knows perfectly. Wherefore the prophet, admiring divine wisdom, is compelled to exclaim: "Great is our Lord, and great is His power; and of His wisdom there is no number." Nor should these be understood as specific knowledge; for even the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, named for their habit of walking while discussing</note>, Platonists, and the whole family of Stoics (by the gift of God) recognized the general influence of the heavens, which occurs through heat, light, and motion on the earth. Wherefore

<column-break/>

Aristotle (as we said) stated that this world is contiguous with the superior motions. And in another place of his: "The motion of the sun under the oblique circle <term>oblique circle: the ecliptic, or the apparent path of the sun across the sky, which causes the seasons</term> brings about generations <note>original: "generationes"; the process of birth, growth, and the coming-into-being of physical things</note>." And the holy father Augustine confirms the same in Book 3 of *The Trinity*, Chapter 4, asserting that coarser and lower bodies are ruled in a certain order by those more subtle and powerful. Augustine himself did not take away from astrology what natural reason admits and what the immutable tenor of sacred scripture does not reject. Yet he does not say that the differences of bodies are necessarily from celestial influence, but that this can be conceded in some things. For as he says in the same place: the diversity of offspring is from celestial influence, even when twins of different sexes can be conceived at the same time. Alexander of Hales, Thomas [Aquinas], Albert the Great, Bonaventure, [Duns] Scotus, and Pierre d'Ailly—a numerous multitude of theologians—all confirm the general influence of celestial things upon the lower. They influence the bodies of lower things, but not human wills or minds. For as Augustine wishes in Book 13 on Genesis, corporeal things cannot act upon the spirit. Others limit this to influence "through itself" and "immediately." For since the intellect (they say), through the mediation of species <note>in medieval philosophy, "species" were the mental images or forms of objects received through the senses</note> received from the senses, proceeds into its work, and the sensitive power uses corporeal organs: by accident and remotely it could be conceded that the intellect, when the bodies are changed, is hindered in its operation—as can be seen in melancholics and lunatics. Wherefore Scripture says: "The body which is <margin>Wisdom 9.</margin> corrupted burdens the soul, and the earthly dwelling weighs down the sense that muses upon many things." But the Will, being mistress of all its acts, is not bound to the organs of bodies, just as the intellect is not. Indeed, it is more free; it suffers no obstacle from anyone, nor is it subject to the influence of the heavens. And therefore, acts and choices proceeding from the will can by no means be foreseen or judged by astrologers. Some believe that in the beginning of the world, God prolonged the span of life for the men of ancient times to such an extent so that they could investigate astrology or astronomy, and the arts or other sciences that are acquired through long experience. Others say that no small part of astrology was divinely revealed to the first parent Adam and to the first patriarchs. This lower world, by the necessity of nature, is adjacent to the superior movements and the celestial bodies: so that the entire power of the lower world is ruled and governed by the celestial world.

For since the movement of the heaven—as Aristotle testifies—is perpetual, having neither beginning nor end, but existing in the beginning and always in the end; and yet the movements of lower things are not continuous and perpetual; the heaven is deservedly the first cause of lower movements. For it is probable among philosophers that things so beautiful <note>Referring to the diversity and complexity of earthly life and minerals</note> cannot be sustained under the earth, except by some greatest effort from heaven, and that the power once impressed upon them by that effort endures in them. For the heaven has labored for a very long time in cooking and gathering these things. And as our Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), a famous Italian scholar who sought to harmonize Platonic philosophy with Christianity</note> wrote most clearly: "If you grant that God has inserted wonderful powers into things below the moon, grant even more wonderful ones to celestial things." Moreover, if you judge it permissible for a human to use lower things <note>such as herbs and minerals</note> for prosperous health, judge that it is also permissible to use superior things. And so, to temper the lower things according to the pattern of the superior by the skill of physicians, just as they were also tempered by God from the beginning.

<header>Books on obtaining life from the heavens. Chapters 3 and 4.</header>

<margin>Genesis</margin> ...testify that [Abraham] taught astrology: which I do not deny regarding the variations of the seasons; as it is written: "Let them be for signs and seasons" <note>Genesis 1:14</note>; but not regarding divination, which God specifically forbade to the servant of Abraham.

### ¶ Whether the effects of the heavens can be hindered according to astrologers who have some knowledge of the Christian faith. Chapter 3.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter E with foliage and strapwork patterns.</image-desc>Experience, authority, and reason show us that the effects of the heavens can be hindered. By experience indeed we see: that in the art of agriculture, some things to be produced naturally are so varied that those things which would happen to them by the course of the heavens occur very little: in sowing, seeding, planting, and pruning. Regarding the elements also, it is clear a similar alteration occurs: also regarding livestock, by killing: male with female: by amputating the right or left testicle: so that males or females might be generated <note>An ancient biological theory suggesting that physical interventions in breeding could override celestial timing for sex determination</note>. If all these things were left to the influence of the heavens alone, certainly diverse outcomes would follow: and two principles result: namely, nature and purpose. ¶ Many authorities can also be brought to the same point: not only of theologians and philosophers who posit the necessary and the contingent, virtues and vices: but even of astrologers. 

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin> Ptolemy, although he affirms these lower things do not happen inevitably from the heavens, just as those which happen by divine will. In the book of Aphorisms <note>Referring to the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms attributed to Ptolemy</note> also, it is said that the professor of this science can overturn many effects of the stars. Elsewhere: "A wise soul cooperates with the celestial power, just as the best farmer [cooperates] in cleaning and preparing." ¶ For choices <note>original: *electiones*, referring to the practice of "electional astrology"—picking the most favorable astrological moment to begin an undertaking</note> could not be beneficial unless the effects of the heavens could be changed. ¶ Likewise, reason suggests the same to us. For it can be a doubt to no one that the heavens can be hindered by a free cause not subject to them. 

<margin>The effect of the heavens can be varied.</margin> To understand this matter, one must observe a threefold kind of cause which can vary the effects of the heavens. The first cause indeed is the divine will, by whose power the heavens were established. For God is of much greater power in acting, without any proportion, than the heavens are in resisting; and since He is free—otherwise He would not be worthy to be God—He will be able to destroy the heavens and change the intermediate order and their powers. For just as a clockmaker <note>original: *horologij faber*</note> might have ordered the ninth hour to be struck at such a time, yet he can very easily order more or fewer or none to be struck. In this way, and much more easily, the heavens and their order can be changed by the First Cause, especially since all things require divine sustenance. A similar thing can happen with separate substances <note>referring to angels or celestial intelligences that move the planetary spheres</note>, if we only 

<column-break/>

consider their power and the resistance of the heaven: and this in a twofold way. First, on the part of the heavens. For an intelligence applied, or the souls of the heavens (if they are animate) do not act out of necessity of nature, but always act regularly because they choose better. Just as therefore a man is master of his own acts, so much more is an intelligence, by whose power many things are produced, able to vary them. Second, on the part of the patient <note>the "patient" is the person or object receiving the celestial influence</note>. For intelligences can move the subjects and vary them in many ways, by which the powers of the heavens are received in various ways or not received. ¶ They cannot, however, hinder all things, partly because of many things which are manifest to the intelligences. Similarly (though more weakly), it can happen from the third cause: which is the free human will. ¶ This is clear through all things that will be said below. From its operations, fortune follows. When a man has known some effect is to come, he can move, provide, and administer the lower causes helping or hindering—consequently removing future effects—in various ways: not only in things external to himself, as has been sufficiently deduced, but even in internal things: as when the senses instigate one to work at something, the free will can change the interior senses. Similarly, one unfortunate in riches can, by free will, dig the earth and find a treasure. Thus, therefore, the human will, or a man through free will, by applying lower things in a diverse way, can change the influences of the heavens. An angelic [will] can similarly do the same, and further, can do some things on the part of the heavens. The Divine [will], however, can in every way change both the influence and the causes of the influence. It is true, however, that if these hindering causes were removed, and assuming a particular order of the heavens, all things would happen by necessity; but by the universal order, the particular can be overturned. These are what some of the moderns living under the Christian religion feel concerning the influences of the heavens regarding human wills.

# Chapter 5

<margin>Against the mathematicians <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicians" was often a technical term for astrologers who calculated planetary positions.</note></margin>
...the lower part (we shall show how they resist the necessity of this kind of influence). Those who affirm that every single thing happens by necessity of the stars are themselves entangled in three especially pernicious errors—and they entangle the common people as well. For, as much as lies within their power, they strip the highest and almighty God of His own providence and His absolute rule over the whole world. Furthermore, they take away justice from the Angels, who, according to them, move the celestial bodies in such a way that all the crimes of men, all evils for the good, and all goods for the evil proceed from there. Finally, they take away liberty from men—who, in their view, are driven here and there no less than beasts—and they destroy the tranquility of everyone. For if they promise good things—which they are accustomed to do only rarely, barely, and quite obscurely—they usually involve those promises in the greatest difficulties, so that they are of very little use to us. But if at times (and this most rarely) they predict future things without extreme labor, we are rendered vain, proud, and negligent as a result. And if it happens by some chance as they promised, the long-awaited pleasure arrives as something hardly even pleasing. If, however, they threaten evils—which happens much more often—we anticipate for a long time evils that may come late, or we wretchedly imagine things that will never happen, and we suffer in the imagining. Finally, if the fates cannot be avoided, they are foreseen and predicted in vain. If they can be avoided by some means, then the "necessity of fate" is falsely defended by the astrologers. Perhaps one will say (as I suppose): this too is in the fates—that something out of many things may sometimes be foreknown and avoided. In this way, then, there will be a controversy among the Fates <note>Original: *Parcas*, referring to the Moirai or Fates of mythology.</note>, such that one decrees the man should be wounded, while another protects him. But let us grant them this for the present, if you please, lest we seem perhaps too stubborn to anyone; yet we will never concede to anyone that this too stands among the decrees of the Fates: that many people do not believe them, and many moreover contradict them. For how does fate now drive Marsilio <note>Referring to Marsilio Ficino, the author/philosopher.</note> to resist fate with the strength of his intellect? Surely he does not do this by the power of fate itself, but rather by some contrary power, or at least by the virtue of something higher he now rails against fate. For necessity itself cannot be entirely repugnant to itself, so as to deny that necessity exists, and by its own instinct and stings destroy itself. What does that most common saying mean: "We are driven by the fates; believe in the fates"? <note>Original: *Fatis agimur credite fatis*.</note> But if we consider the matter itself more diligently, we are not so much driven by the fates themselves as by the *fatuous* [foolish] defenders of the fates. Do not believe me, believe in the fates—if you will not believe the fools who involve things not in truths (as is said of the Sibyl), but in falsehoods, and who predict not what is specific to individual men, but what is common to all. These most talkative men bring so many things into the open that it is no wonder if, among many

<column-break/>

lies, they occasionally stumble by chance upon some truth. They wish to be wise for others when they are not wise for themselves at all. It is worth the effort to consider how destitute they are, how filthy, how unfortunate in their own affairs, how impudent and inept in conducting business. If by chance they practice trade, they foresee the outcome of commerce much less than other merchants. If they practice medicine, they predict the midpoint and end of a disease less than other physicians, and they care for bodies worst of all. And while they claim a power of divination, they themselves seem to rush and fall everywhere by chance. Arise therefore, early-ripening philosophers; arise all you who are precious lovers of liberty and tranquility! Come, act now, gird yourselves with the shield and spear of Pallas Athena. A war hangs over us at present against those nefarious "little giants" <note>Original: *gigantulos*, a mocking diminutive of giants.</note> who, through the foreknowledge of future things, attempt to equal themselves to the utterly immense God, and by the defense of celestial fate, attempt to take away free rule from the super-celestial God, who is supreme liberty. But those who so proudly strive to ascend to the heavenly ones shall be miserably cast down to the underworld. Reach out Your hand to us from on high, Almighty God. Supply strength to Your soldiers. We now move to defend this, Your empire. Help us, you divine powers who rotate the ethereal circles; help us, you who will excuse your own justice against the impious enemies who accuse you of an extreme injustice. Favor us also, O race of men, without envy. Truly, we protect this, your most precious liberty and tranquility. So that after we have triumphed over the diviners—not divine, but truly profane—who nevertheless enslave us with their deceptions, we may finally be able to cry out freely: "Impiety, therefore, placed under our feet, is in turn trampled; victory makes us equal to heaven." <note>Original: *Impietas ergo pedibus subiecta vicissim / obterit: nos exequat victoria celo.* A paraphrase of Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* 1.78-79.</note> Nor Marsilio.

# Books on Obtaining Life from Heaven. Chapters 3 and 4.

...testify that he taught astrology: which I do not deny, <margin>Genesis 1</margin> especially regarding the varieties of seasons: just as it is written: *That they might be for signs and seasons* <note>A reference to Genesis 1:14: "And let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years."</note>: not however for the reckoning of divination, which God specifically forbade to the seed of Abraham.

### ¶ Whether the effects of the heavens can be hindered according to astrologers who have some knowledge of the Christian faith. Chapter 3.

Experience, authority, and reason show us that the effects of the heavens can be hindered. By experience indeed we see: through the art of agriculture, some things naturally to be produced are so varied that those things which would have happened to them by the course of the heavens occur very little; this is seen in sowing, seeding, planting, and pruning. Regarding the elements also, it is clear that a similar alteration happens: also regarding livestock, even by killing them: or by mating a male with a female: or by amputating the right or left testicle so that either males or females are generated. All of which, if they were left to the influence of the heavens alone, different outcomes would surely follow: and two principles result: namely nature and purpose <note>original: "propositum," meaning a conscious plan or design</note>.

Many authorities can also be brought to support this: not only of theologians and philosophers who posit necessity and contingency, virtues and vices: but even of the astrologers themselves.

<margin>Ptolemy</margin> For Ptolemy affirms that these lower things do not happen inevitably from the heavens, just as things do not happen inevitably by divine will. Also in the *Book of Aphorisms* <note>Referring to the *Centiloquium*, a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms traditionally attributed to Ptolemy.</note>, aphorism 5: "The professor of this science can overturn many effects of the stars." And elsewhere: "A wise soul cooperates with celestial power, just as a best farmer does in cleaning and preparing the soil." ¶ For <term>elections<gloss>the astrological practice of choosing the most auspicious time to begin a specific task</gloss></term> could not be of use unless the effects of the heavens could be changed. ¶ Likewise, reason suggests the same to us. For it can be a doubt to no one that the heavens can be hindered by a free cause that is not subject to them.

<margin>The effect of the heavens can be varied.</margin> For the understanding of this matter, one must note a threefold kind of cause that can vary the effects of the heavens. The first cause indeed is the divine will, by whose power the heavens were established. For God is of much greater power in acting, beyond any proportion, than the heavens are in resisting. Since He is free—otherwise He would not be worthy to be God—He will be able to destroy the heavens and change their redundant order and their powers. For just as a <term>clockmaker<gloss>original: "horologij faber"</gloss></term> might have ordered the ninth hour to be struck at a certain time, yet he can most easily order either more or fewer or no strikes at all. So also, and much more easily, the heavens and their order can be changed by the First Cause, especially since all things need divine support. A similar thing can happen in <term>separate substances<gloss>immaterial beings, such as angels or the Intelligences that move the celestial spheres</gloss></term>: if we only 

<column-break/>

consider their power and the resistance of heaven: and this in a twofold way. First, on the part of the heavens. For the Intelligence applied to them, or the souls of the heavens (if they are animated), do not act from the necessity of nature: but they always act regularly because they choose the better path. Therefore, just as a man is master of his own acts, so much more is the Intelligence, by whose power many things are produced, able to vary them. Second, on the part of the patient <note>In medieval philosophy, the "patient" is the object that receives an action or influence.</note>. For Intelligences can move the subjects and vary them in many ways, so that the powers of the heavens are received in different ways, or not received at all. ¶ Yet they cannot hinder all things, partly because of many things which are manifest to the Intelligences. Similarly (though more weakly) it can happen from a third cause: which is human free will. ¶ This is clear through all things that will be said below. From the operations of free will, fortune <note>original: "fortuna"</note> follows. When a man has recognized that some effect is about to come, he can move, provide, or administer the lower causes that help or hinder—and consequently remove future effects—in various ways: not only in things external to himself, as has been sufficiently shown, but even in internal things. For when the senses instigate one to do something, free will can change the internal senses. Similarly, one who is unfortunate in riches can by free will dig the earth and find treasure. Thus therefore the human will, or man through free will, can change the influences of the heavens by applying lower things in a different way. Angelic power can similarly, and even further, do the same on the part of the heavens. Divine power, however, can entirely change both the influence and the causes of the influences in every way. It is true, however, that if these hindering causes are removed, and assuming a particular order of the heavens, all things would happen by necessity; but by the universal order, the particular can be overturned. Nor are those things true which some of the <term>moderns<gloss>original: "neotericorum"</gloss></term> living under the Christian religion believe regarding the influences of the heavens upon human wills.

### ¶ That celestial bodies do not influence human bodies by necessity according to the opinion of Catholics. Chapter 4.

Therefore, let no one laboring under the disease of envy, or who is not in control of himself, think that we approve the vain opinion of the mathematicians <note>At this time, "mathematicians" often referred specifically to astrologers who calculated planetary positions.</note> and astrologers, and that we depart from the confession of the Roman Church and the sincerity of the inviolable faith. On the contrary, we follow the professors of Catholic truth, and especially our Ficino in that book which he wrote against the judgments of astrologers (of which here is a great [number] of words)...

It specifically reconciles astrological study with Catholic doctrine by emphasizing that the soul and God remain superior to the material heavens.</summary>

# Chapter V

<margin>Against the mathematicians <note>In the Renaissance, "mathematicians" (*mathematicos*) was a common term for astrologers who cast horoscopes.</note>.</margin>
...the lower part (we shall show how they resist the necessity of this kind of influence). Those who affirm that individual things are necessarily caused by the stars are themselves entangled in three especially pernicious errors, and they entangle the common people as well. For they take away the particular providence of the highest and almighty God over these matters, as well as His absolute rule over the whole world. They also strip justice away from the Angels, who according to these men move the celestial bodies in such a way that all the crimes of men, all evils for the good, and all goods for the wicked proceed from there. Finally, they take away liberty from men—who, as it seems to them, are driven hither and thither no less than beasts—and they deprive them of all tranquility. For if they promise good things (which they are accustomed to do only rarely, with difficulty, and quite obscurely), they usually entangle those promises in such great difficulties that they are of very little benefit to us. If they ever do announce future events without extreme labor (and that most rarely), we are rendered vain, proud, and negligent because of it. And if by some chance it happens as they promised, the long-awaited pleasure arrives as something less than pleasing. If, however, they threaten evils—which happens much more often—we either anticipate late-arriving evils for a long time, or we wretchedly imagine things that will never happen, and we suffer in the imagining. Finally, if the fates cannot be avoided, they are foreseen and predicted in vain. If they can be avoided by some means, then the necessity of fate is falsely defended by the astrologers. Perhaps they will say (as I suppose) that this too is in the fates: that something among many things may occasionally be known in advance and avoided. Thus, there will be a controversy among the Fates <note>original: "parcas," referring to the Parcae or Moirai, the goddesses of destiny</note>, such that one decree might ordain a man to be wounded, while another protects him. But let us grant them this for now, if they like, lest we seem perhaps too stubborn to anyone; yet we will never concede to anyone that this too stands among the decrees of the Fates: that many do not believe them, and many, moreover, contradict them. For how does fate now impel Marsilio <note>The author, Marsilio Ficino, refers to himself in the third person.</note> to resist fate with the strength of his intellect? He is surely not attacking fate now by the force of fate itself, but rather by the power of something contrary, or at least something superior to it. For necessity itself cannot be entirely repugnant to itself, such that it denies its own necessity, and by its own instinct and stings destroys itself. What does that most common saying mean? *Believe in the fates, for we are driven by the fates.* <note>original: "Fatis agimur credite fatis." A quote from the Roman poet Manilius.</note> Yet if we consider the matter more diligently, we are not so much driven by the fates themselves as by the fatuous <note>A pun in the Latin: *fatis* (fates) vs *fatuis* (fools/fatuous).</note> assertors of fates. You will not believe me? Believe the fates! If you are fatuous, you will not believe those who wrap up falsehoods rather than truths in obscure sayings (as is said of the Sibyl), and who predict things for individual men that are not specific to them, but common to all. These most talkative men bring so many things into the open that it is no wonder if, among

<column-break/>

many lies, they occasionally stumble upon some truth by chance. They wish to seem wise to others when they are not wise at all for themselves. It is worthwhile to consider how destitute they themselves are, how filthy, how unfortunate in their own business, and how imprudent and inept in managing affairs. If by chance they engage in trade, they foresee the outcome of the trade much less than other merchants. If they practice medicine, they predict the course of a disease less than other doctors, and they treat bodies worst of all. And although they profess divination, they themselves seem everywhere to live and fall by chance. Arise then, herald of philosophers! Arise, all you who are greedy for most precious liberty and tranquility! Come, act now, gird yourselves with the shield and spear of Pallas <note>Pallas Athena, goddess of wisdom and strategic war.</note>. A war now looms over us against those wicked little giants, who try to equal themselves to the utterly immense God through their foreknowledge of the future, and who, by their defense of celestial fate, try to take away free dominion from the super-celestial God, who is supreme liberty. But those who so proudly strive to ascend to the heavens shall be miserably cast down to the depths. Reach out Your hand to us from on high, Almighty God. Supply strength to Your soldiers. We now set out to defend this, Your empire; help us, O divine spirits who rotate the ethereal circles; help us, for we are about to excuse your justice against impious enemies who accuse you of a certain extreme injustice. Favor us also, O race of men, without envy. Indeed, we are defending this, your most precious liberty and tranquility. So that after we have triumphed over these diviners—who are not divine, but truly profane, and who have enslaved us with their delusions for so long—we may at last be able to cry out freely: *Impiety, therefore, being subjected in turn, is trodden underfoot; victory makes us equal to heaven.* <note>A paraphrase of Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* 1.78-79.</note> And so says Marsilio.

# Books on Obtaining Life from the Heavens, Chapter VI.

...fret <note>original: "ringant"; this concludes a thought from the previous page about how deterministic astrologers might react to these arguments</note>: but Plotinus <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works Ficino translated into Latin</note> can in no way endure the idea that a man is necessarily driven in his individual behaviors by the celestial confluence of rays. This is because the human body is not a continuous part of the world, nor is the human soul a part of the World Soul <note>original: "anima mundi"; the Platonic concept of an intrinsic spirit that animates the entire universe</note>, nor is it procreated by the World Soul. Therefore, the human body possesses, in addition to its own shape, its own internal motor; it also has its own unique progression. I speak of an intellectual motor <note>The "motor" refers to the rational mind or intellect that drives human action</note>, which surely transcends the body and the life of the world through its intellectual nature. Indeed, it is not merely a part of the universe, but is itself a certain universe within itself. And since every motion is for the sake of the good, 

<margin>Motion is for the sake of the good.</margin>

our mind holds the very notion of the total good in its simplicity. Within this notion, individual goods are understood. Thus, the movement of the mind is not necessarily destined toward this or that specific thing as if it were the only good; rather, it can apply itself equally to anything through a variety of considerations. Now, the long consultation over individual things, the diligent weighing of opposites in turn, the exact choice made, and the subsequent withdrawal to other connections, all declare that the soul is not carried along by some natural force, or by habit, or by natural instinct, but rather by a universal and free eloquence of moving and acting. Since, therefore, we have our own nature and efficacy, and consequently our own unique action, we do not merely suffer under celestial action. Instead, we receive celestial influence according to our own effective property, and we ourselves perform something unique from it. Likewise, we carry out something by our own inner property. Furthermore, the celestial influence around us changes according to the nature of places. For even under a tiny portion of any climate, where the influence of the stars is the same, diverse things are born and happen at the very same moment and always, because of the diversity of the site—of the earth, air, water, winds, vapors, customs, and laws. Moreover, children are usually similar to their parents 

<margin>
From where the diversity of character arises.
</margin>

and nurses, no matter what hour they are born or nourished; for they receive much more from their own kin than from the hour of birth. And even if their forms are similar to one another due to the common nature of the place, generation, and nutrition, they often differ greatly in character and wit. Indeed, the diversity of souls—differing both in wit and character—arises from elsewhere than these corporeal causes. Finally, when the soul opposes bodily incitements for the sake of tranquility and intelligence, it declares that it both operates freely and does not depend on its own body, nor, therefore, on a celestial body. It seems that we can act through our body alone, but by the power and grace of the mind, we are able to resist our body and choose a life consistent with the

<column-break/>

mind, even if it is harmful to the body. And often, while the nature and incitement of the body remains the same, we are accustomed to choose things that are dissimilar to one another, based solely on a variety of conjectures. Also, even when the nature of the body has already become dissimilar, we have nonetheless been accustomed to choose similar things, if similar reason persuaded us; for in that case we do not depend so much on corporeal influence as on the abundance of intelligence and reason. As for those who pass down the idea that these things of ours are caused by the stars because they are *signified* by the stars, this has been more diligently refuted elsewhere. You should, however, conclude this: at any moment, and even in the same race-course, many very different things can be born at once—not only in individual accidents, but even in species and genus. To these, very different fates often fall, as if the nature and fortune of things were not drawn from the hour alone. This is also confirmed by the fact that many people often perish together in the same common destruction, even though they were not born in the same hour, nor did they flow together to the place of destruction at the same time.

### ¶ How the soul, according to the Platonists, 
### is above fate, in fate, and under fate.
### Chapter VI.

<margin>What fate is.</margin>

The common opinion of philosophers regarding fate is that it is a certain necessity brought upon things by the "conspiracy" <note>original: "conspiratione"; here meaning a harmonious breathing together or an interconnected web of causes</note> of corporeal causes. But since the motion of bodies proceeds from the soul, and the order of corporeal forms proceeds from the intellect, we rightly consider the intellectual soul to be naturally released from the necessity that is usually imposed by the motion and order or series of bodies. So far is the soul from being subject to fate, that it is even the very principle <note>The source or origin</note> of fate itself—provided that if there is a corporeal series, it depends on the intellectual soul. I say it depends on the Soul of the Universe for the universal series in common, and on other souls endowed with similar intelligence for their own series here and there. There are, therefore, two types of causes in fate: causes adapting themselves to the governance of bodies, and corporeal causes acting as the "fillers" <note>original: "complentia"; the material elements that complete the structure of fate</note> of fate. Furthermore, there is a triple order: of all bodies to the First Body <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the *Primum Mobile* or the outermost sphere that moves all others</note>; of souls to the First Soul; and of bodies to souls, and through those souls to the First Soul, and through that intellectual soul to the First Intellect. And thus the entire series of fates is finally reduced to Divine Providence. If, therefore,

He defines Fate as a web of physical causes but places the rational soul above this necessity, ultimately linking all cosmic order to Divine Providence.</summary>

# Chapter vii.

**Left Column:**

...if the soul is entirely outside the body: similarly, it is outside fate. If it is in the body insofar as it naturally yields to a body suffering under fate, it also suffers within fate to that extent. But if it separates itself from the body by its own powers, and provides only a life-giving <note>original: "vegetalez"; referring to the vegetative or basic biological force that sustains life</note> power to it, it is considered within fate only as an actor: yet it acts according to the condition of fortune. And indeed, the soul itself changes some things by its natural faculty, or corrects and amends them through a certain art, or endures them most easily through greatness of soul. But to what extent the soul undergoes fate insofar as it immerses itself in the body, the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue regarding the creation of the physical world</note> shows, saying: souls then first learned the laws of fate when they were joined to their vehicles <note>original: "vehiculis"; the celestial "chariots" or subtle bodies that carry the soul into the physical realm</note>. For from this point, the beginnings of fate are drawn. But meanwhile, that they may approach fate by free motion and thereafter be able to release themselves at some time, Plato declares both in the *Timaeus* and in the tenth book of the *Republic* <note>Specifically the Myth of Er, where souls choose their next lives</note>: that God taught the souls both the fatal laws and the reason of divine and human law alike, so that God might exist without blame <note>original: "extra culpam"; a reference to the Greek concept that the soul chooses its life and God is not responsible for those choices</note>. And he adds that virtue and reason are free. And so, according to the Platonists, the soul is sometimes an actor in fate, and sometimes a sufferer. And those who introduce a necessary series of things inevitably performing each detail, take away both contingency from the lowest things and liberty from counsel. Also, according to them, the intellectual nature acts freely, but its effect is sometimes hindered in its reasoning. And thus, not all things proceed from fatal necessity.
