### From Plotinus: Propositions on fate, on the world, and the soul of the world; on the stars and the power of the heavens regarding inferior bodies. Chapter vii.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' with white interlaced strapwork and stylized foliage on a dark square background.</image-desc>
Some things exist; others are made. Those which are made are made by a cause, and besides the immediate causes, we are often compelled to investigate more remote ones.
Because immediate causes are often not sufficient, therefore higher causes are searched out.
Neither can all things be compelled nor made by bodies; neither fate nor prophecy would exist if the principles of things were merely accidental.
Neither are we ruled by the heavens alone, nor do things happen from the heavens alone and of necessity.
Individual things here receive their specific quality in generation more from their own proper natures than from the heavens, although they are signaled by the heavens.
Order in the world does not happen by chance.
Worldly order does not proceed from matter.
Worldly order is not from a diversity of principles.

<column-break/>

**Right Column:**

The order of things does not happen only from the succession of things, but from the intention of the One.
The ends of things and of motions declare that things are made, arranged, and moved by divine providence.
Whatever things seem evil, whether regarding bodies or souls, are reformed into good.
Rational souls are not forced to base actions by either superior or inferior things.
Besides the qualities of bodies, there is everywhere an incorporeal life ruling all things rationally; and this universal nature rules over particular natures.
Universal nature, because it is all-forming, makes the universe all-formed, nor does it compel souls.
The ingenious works of nature are from providence, acting in the manner of art and nature. Nor are minds properly parts of this world.
The very seeds of the universe, which are universal nature, have prefigured within themselves even those things which are called evil.
Likewise, all worldly things are empty, in the manner of games.
As power decreases from superior to inferior things, it is replenished by number.
Human things are noted and arranged in both intellectual and natural providence.
The soul is indeed the cause for the heaven being immortal, and the heaven does not resist the soul in this.
Because the world is corporeal, it is neither from itself nor everlasting through itself, but through a cause that is entirely incorporeal.
The heaven is the spirit, breath, and word of the World Soul; and it is an occult power everywhere.
The heaven is the image of the soul, and individual things in the heaven reflect individual things in the soul.
Celestial things remain eternal both in species and in the individual. Composite things, however, remain only in species.
Individual elements are pure in themselves, even though in each there are certain qualities of the others as well.
The heaven is everlasting, by the benefit of both the soul and the body.
The heaven is moved by its own soul—rational and intellectual—and is driven in a circle, since the soul and the intellect perform circuits within themselves.
While the heaven moves, as much as it can, it is whole in any part of itself; and thus it attains the whole soul everywhere; it remains through an indivisible center just as the soul remains through intellect and substance.
The rational soul is moved by free motion. The irrational soul follows the universe.
In the universe, the circumference desires the center, and is finished by the circuit.
From the circuit of the soul and mind around God, the circuit in the heaven proceeds.
The motion of the heaven is produced by the intellectual soul, and it happens in a circle, both because of the soul and the intellect.

...they make a certain circuit within themselves; then, because the circular figure contributes to that circuit.
The **World Soul** <note>original: "Anima mundi"; the Neoplatonic concept of a cosmic spirit that connects the divine mind to the physical world</note>, through its higher power, turns the lower sphere into an orbit; and again, through its lower power, it bedews the heavens.
The nature of the planets is not malicious, nor is it changeable by a change of place; nor are natural things primarily generated from their rays and motions, but from their own specific natures everywhere and from the common Nature.
Celestial things signify even those things which they do not cause.
There are many things that cannot be brought about by celestial bodies and motions.
Planets do not change their nature by location, nor do they become evil.
In heaven there is only light, heat, and moisture.
Cold and dryness, however, are found around the center <note>the Earth, which in the geocentric model is the center of the universe</note>. Nor does anything celestial bring about cold by itself, or dryness, or anything harmful to life.
The stars signify our affairs rather than cause them.
Our soul has the character of a principle: it overcomes fate; it yields to fate; it is punished by divine law; it can even perform wonders, and in some way, it can even free the body from fate.
The rational soul is not subject to fate; but the irrational soul is subject to it.
The life proper to our body depends on the life of celestial things and on our own soul.
Those things which are generated here possess their own specific nature more from their own specific causes than from celestial ones.
All things are generated from the common life of the world and its **seminal reasons** <note>original: "rationibus seminalibus"; the Stoic and Neoplatonic "seeds" or formative blueprints that guide the development of physical things</note>, and simultaneously from the specific reasons of each thing.
Beyond the action of the World Soul, specific actions are common in most things; however, the **influences** <note>original: "influxus"; the "flowing in" of celestial power</note> of celestial motions seem to approach as if from the outside.
In the individual things that happen to men, we find sufficient causes within ourselves besides the celestial motions.
Before the soul is touched by fate, it is touched by love for the body.
All things are generated from the common nursery of the world and are contained within it. And those things which are born degenerate by departing from it once, and then through the ages, they fall away from their original states.
The seminal reasons of nature are not more known <note>or "notions"</note> just because they are made by the Mind. Likewise, they degenerate in nature first from the Mind, and then they fail in matter by falling away from nature.
If the stars are inanimate, they do nothing except physical things. If they are animate, they do not do evil things.
The stars do not change their nature by their motions, locations, or dispositions.
The significations of the stars happen because of the wonderful connection of things in the world.
The World Soul is the principle of natural things.
All rational souls possess freedom of choice.
The soul which in us depends on heaven is subject to

<column-break/>

fate; but that which is given to us by God is free from fate and is able to free us.
The stars do not produce anything except physical things; but the soul, through itself, enters into fate and fortune.
Things are generated primarily from the seminal reasons of nature; celestial influence disposes the matter.
Things that live by their own life have their own actions.
The evils that happen here are not sent from heaven.
Before the soul undergoes fate, it desires a body.
The soul has its own being, by which it also has its own action within fate; and it can release itself from fate.

### How astrologers can prognosticating in general regarding the fertility and sterility of the earth, pestilence, wars, and the change of kingdoms; and why they frequently err in their judgments. Chapter viii.

<margin>Augustine</margin>
Rarely do those who devote their labor to astrology restrain their judgments within the prescribed limits; rather, greedy for vain glory, they dilate themselves too much through **self-love** <term>original: "philautia"; an excessive or misplaced love of oneself or one's own opinions</term>. They long to divine from the stars what they cannot actually achieve. They also frequently descend to particular and local changes, noting the species of individual crops, and they pursue the outcomes of the inhabitants of lands separately—not attending to the fact that a general superior influence can be resisted. And (as Augustine says in the *City of God*, Book 5, Chapter 7), on a day chosen for sowing a field, so many seeds come into the earth at the same time; they germinate at the same time; and once the crop has emerged, they grow into grass, reach maturity, and turn yellow at the same time. And yet, from that crop, some ears of grain—of the same age as the others and, if I may say so, "womb-mates"—are killed by blight, others are devastated by birds, and others are plucked by men. One must judge other matters by the same standard. For the celestial causes are almost innumerable; of these, only a few things are known from the fixed stars, though the traditions of astrologers sing of how much their action can do. Added to this is the fact that many in our age delight in the practice of that "master of names" <note>likely a reference to superficial or popular prognosticators</note>, who have not yet begun to speak, let alone learned. Nevertheless, if it happens that the four parts of the year deviate much from their natural qualities, a disturbance of the air will very easily follow; and thus damage to the crops, either from excessive cold or parching heat, or from moisture suffocating them, or from dryness consuming the **radical moisture** <note>original: "humidum radicale"; the essential fluid believed by medieval doctors to sustain life and vitality</note>. Furthermore, when the elements are disturbed, the crops immature, and the air infected or putrefied—which we use diligently for breathing—he will rashly judge that illnesses are about to occur. Finally, physical reason suggests that from infected air and unsuitable nourishment, a turbulent **animal spirit** <note>original: "spiritum animalem"; the subtle substance that transmits sensory information and motor commands through the nerves</note> is generated. From this, illnesses...

It cites St. Augustine to argue that even things sharing the same astrological beginning, like seeds in a field, can have wildly different outcomes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous page regarding how the heavens and the soul interact. It concludes a warning about how mental disturbances can lead to social unrest and begins a detailed examination—and critique—of the twelve "houses" of astrology used to predict a person's fate from birth.</meta>

...sharp <note>original: "acute"</note> disturbances and many afflictions happen to the brain: when these dominate among the common people through the deceitful persuasion of a single son of Beelzebub <note>A name for the devil; here referring to a person acting under demonic or malevolent influence to incite the masses</note>, it is not difficult for an assault to occur. For if a prince strives to meet them with the law, they immediately attempt to shake off the burden of servitude and the scepter of the tax-collector from their proud necks. From this arise many sects, contentions, factions, seditions, wars, and other such things. And although (as Ptolemy says) a pious or wise man may rule the stars by resisting sensuality and his natural inclinations, Solomon wrote that the number of fools is infinite. 

<margin>Ecclesiastes 1.</margin>

Therefore, it is no wonder if, being skillfully aware of these dangers, not only astrologers and philosophers, but also physicians and farmers and sailors—taught by long experience—daily predict many true things about the future even without astrological rules: regarding diseases, the harvest <note>original: "annona"; refers to the yearly grain supply or price</note>, and storms. But enough of those matters.

<margin>On the houses of the planets.</margin>

Astrologers make prognostications regarding births <note>term: "nativities" (the positioning of stars at the moment of birth)</note> and "houses" <note>term: "houses"; the twelve divisions of the celestial sphere in astrology, each governing different aspects of life</note>. For they say that from the condition of the **first house** of the planets and the stars existing within it—and from the nature of the parts and various influences—they can tell wonders about the soul of the newborn. They predict, for instance, if he will be generous, a lover of laws, mild or warlike, a seeker of divine sciences, or a lover of some other study or occupation; they also predict what his physical condition will be. From the **second house**, they see the future prosperity or misfortune regarding the newborn’s wealth: whether he will possess it through inheritance, trade, or any other skill or labor; and further, whether he will squander what he acquired of his own accord, or lose it through some violence or misfortune. From the **third house**, they judge the newborn's siblings and his skill and observance of the laws. And there, through the "part" which astrologers call "hidden," they judge the secrets of the conscience toward God and toward men. For as the astrologer Abzaaz <note>likely referring to the Arab astrologer Abu 'Ali al-Khayyat</note> says in his exposition of this house: If Jupiter is strong at the birth and looks upon that part in any way, the newborn will both love God and be loved by God. But these ideas deviate from faith and truth. For the Scripture says: *No man knows whether he is worthy of hate or love.*

<margin>Ecclesiastes 9.</margin>

And the secrets of the conscience are open to God alone. Astrologers also name two "fortunes" among the planets: namely, **Venus** and **Jupiter**. Venus, as they say, grants the happiness of the present life, while Jupiter bestows the happiness of the future life. And one of them writes that **Saturn** positioned in Leo makes men long-lived, whose souls will pass to the heavens after death. And Albumasar <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous Persian astrologer</note>, piling impiety upon impiety, says: He who prays to God at the hour when the Moon is joined with the "head of the dragon" <note>term: "caput draconis"; the ascending node of the moon</note> and Jupiter, obtains whatever he asks for.

<column-break/>

...of magicians rather than astrologers. Come all to Job, and to Christ who says in the Gospel: *I give them eternal life.* For if astrologers speak the truth, why then do they not observe such an hour for themselves, so that they might once and for all obtain the power never to deceive anyone again in their judgments? Or why do they not obtain such riches that they would no longer have to sell their lies to others out of poverty? But now let us descend to the explanation of the houses.

The **fifth house** predicts if the one being born will father children and how he will feel toward them. This is the view of the Arabs. Ptolemy, however, judges children from the **tenth house**, and Wallius from the Ascendant. The **sixth house** announces future things regarding the infirmities of the newborn in the whole body and its individual parts, and when and how much he will be sick. From the **seventh house**, it is judged if he will be a lover of women and a follower of unspeakable lust; whether he will have one wife or many, old or young, and when he will marry them, and if he will live peacefully with them. From the **eighth house**, it is known by what death the newborn is destined to perish: whether by water, fire, the sword, hanging, or any other way. From the **ninth house**, whether the newborn will travel abroad, and how much by land or water, and what fortune he will experience in these travels. Likewise, whether he will hold his faith firmly or neglectedly. From the **tenth house**, judgment is made about the status of the mother, just as the status of the father is judged from the **fourth house**. Many, however, think the father’s status should be investigated from the tenth. Furthermore, it is hunted out whether the newborn will possess honor, power, or a good reputation. From the **eleventh house**, they speak of the newborn's friendships and what sort of people they will be with; likewise, they predict things regarding clothing. From the **twelfth house** of the figure of the heavens calculated at someone's birth, enmities and imprisonments are to be foreknown, if the newborn should perhaps have any or from where they might come. Similarly, the Egyptians judge servants from this house, but the Arabs think that should be done from the sixth house—and so on for almost innumerable other things. This part of astrology even judges the most minute and trivial accidents of a person's future from the "Lord of the Birth Hour," the *alcochoden* <note>term: "Alcochodon"; the planet that determines the length of life</note>, the *almutes* <note>term: "Almuten"; the planet with the most dignity or power in a chart</note>, the *hylech* <note>term: "Hyleg"; the planet designated as the "giver of life"</note>, and the projection of various "parts"; from the condition of the planets and fixed stars, and from the various aspects and directions of these same houses. To pursue each and every one of these further is not our present task.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether human fate and talent are determined by the stars or by God. ### Book III, On Obtaining Life from the Heavens, Chapter IX.

Perhaps some curious investigator will say: Why did God distribute gifts in this way? For instance, why did He give the gift of prophecy to David, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and those like them? Why did He give the wisdom of Solomon? Why did He grant the skill in divine laws to Moses among the Hebrews, to Mercurius Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with ancient wisdom</note> among the Egyptians, to Zoroaster among the Bactrians, to Charondas among the Carthaginians, to Minos among the Cretans, to Lycurgus among the Spartans, to Solon among the Athenians, to Numa Pompilius among the Romans, and to Peter, Paul, and the rest of the apostles and their followers among the Christians? 

Why did He grant poetry itself to Homer and Virgil? Rhetoric to Demosthenes and Cicero? Natural philosophy to Aristotle? Moral philosophy to Socrates? Metaphysics and divine matters to Plato? Medicine to Hippocrates and Galen? Astrology to Ptolemy? The discipline of civil law to Bartolus and Baldus <note>Famous medieval commentators on Roman law</note>? Canon law to Gratian? The art of war to Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar? Sagacity in counsel to Cato? Magic to Zoroaster? Arithmetic to Jordanus? Geometry to Euclid? Music to Pythagoras and Boethius? Logic to Chrysippus? Physics to Strato of Lampsacus <note>original: "Straboni lapsanseno"; likely referring to the Peripatetic philosopher Strato</note>? 

What was the reason for dispensing things so—was it by chance, or by celestial influence, or are these things governed by any providence? I am led back into the Scylla <note>A reference to the "Scylla and Charybdis" proverb, meaning a difficult dilemma where avoiding one danger leads into another</note> which I had just escaped. I will try, therefore, to slip away from here in few words; and if I find any "new wares," they can be applied to what we said above, so that from these passages a single truth of opinion may emerge, and from these two chapters, a single integrity of discipline. This question is one of great presumption, to which the Apostle <note>Paul</note>, a "vessel of election" caught up even to the third heaven, responds thus:

<margin>Romans 9; Psalm 35; Romans 11.</margin>

"Does not the potter have power over the clay, from the same mass, to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?" <note>original: "Nonne habet potestatem figulus..."</note> It would suffice to have said this, since "the judgments of God are a great abyss." And how incomprehensible are His judgments, how unsearchable His ways, and how hidden His counsels! Human temerity should not proceed so daringly as to wish to perceive those things which God ordained to remain hidden. For a servant will not be pleasing to his master if he tries to survey every inner chamber in the house; for such temerity seems more like the actions of a spy searching for traps than a servant performing his duty. Although I say it could be answered in this way, I will nonetheless say something, even if I am only "stammering." For it is written in the first chapter of Ecclesiasticus: "All wisdom is from the Lord God." And James says in his canonical epistle, chapter one: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights."

<column-break/>

And theologians frequently make use of the sentiment of Augustine for the restless. God so administers the things He created that He allows them to perform their own proper motions. Therefore, just as the soul is in the whole body, so God—always working in the whole world—added powers to various natures as a driving force <note>original: "pro mucrone"; literally "as a blade" or "point," implying a sharp, directing energy</note> and ordained that they should work. Indeed, He made them His instruments, which the Son of the Craftsman <note>original: "fabri filius"; a reference to Christ as the son of the carpenter, working alongside God the Father</note> uses even now. He neither prevents these powers from working, nor does He desert them while they work; but like a sailor with a ship, He helps and directs them—the sailor toward the port, and the power toward its end. And just as when the soul is idle the limbs are lulled to sleep, so when God ceases His influence—as was demonstrated in the fire of Babylon <note>A reference to the Biblical story of the three youths in the fiery furnace, where the fire lost its natural power to burn by divine will</note>—every effort of nature is in vain. 

Therefore, all good things are from God. But why He chooses one person and rejects another, human powers cannot know. For Jacob was most holy and good, while his brother Esau was the worst. Abel was most innocent and just, while Cain was the worst. Peter was the best, while Judas was the worst, though the other apostles were most holy. Therefore Christ says:

<margin>John 15.</margin>

"You have not chosen me, but I have chosen you." And Paul says in the third chapter of Titus <note>text says Timothy, but the quote is Titus 3:5</note>: "Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us." And Augustine says in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*: "He did not choose us because He foreknew we would be such, but He chose us so that we might be such through that very election of His grace." And the same Augustine says in the book *On Free Will*: "Not because of faith or any merits did God choose some from eternity... but by His free goodness He chose that they might be good."

<margin>Solution to the question.</margin>

Let us approach the solving of this according to natural reasons and the moral teaching of men, so that we may be able to learn and measure how much human powers can do in these things we have discussed. In all things said by me here and elsewhere, however, I wish it to be asserted only as much as is approved by the Roman Church. Whence, then, comes the excellence and majesty of such illustrious men as we have named?

<margin>The first opinion.</margin>

The first opinion is that of philosophers and physicians, who attribute the excellence of genius to the <term>complexion</term> <note>The specific balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) which was believed to determine a person's temperament and health</note>. Concerning this, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the first part of the 30th book of *Problems*: "Why is it that all men who have been outstanding in either politics, philosophy, poetry, or the arts, were melancholics?" But as we said in the book *On the Healthy Life*, the Philosopher does not mean that every melancholy or every melancholic complexion causes this; he means only that which is tempered with heat, which makes for excellent men.

It emphasizes that while all wisdom comes from God, the physiological state of "tempered melancholy" is a key natural factor in human genius.</summary>

### Chapter IX.

And so, according to Aristotle <note>original: "sm̃ Aristotelem"; "sm̃" is an abbreviation for "secundum" (according to)</note>, it seems that the first temperament that makes men excellent in talent is the **melancholic** temperament, provided it is moderately warm. But we have spoken enough about this type of melancholy in the book *On the Healthy Life*. Certain sharp-witted physicians have maintained that the primary temperament for creating a sharp and excellent talent is the **temperate** (balanced) temperament. After this comes the **sanguine**; after that, the **choleric**; third, the **melancholic**; and last is the **phlegmatic** temperament. 

However, others from the academy of physicians maintain that the first temperament after the temperate one is the **choleric**, and not the sanguine. While it is true that the sanguine is better regarding the duration of life, the choleric exceeds the sanguine in the excellence of talent. This is because in the choleric temperament, the "matter of the spirits" <note>Ancient science believed "vital spirits" were a subtle substance in the blood that carried thought and life through the body</note> is more subtle, and the heat is stronger, which digests that matter well; heat acts as the active force, while the matter is the passive. Furthermore, "cholera" (or yellow bile) is the fastest of all the humors. Such a temperament is hot and dry, and therefore has more open and ready passages and entrances; thus, it is most disposed toward the sciences and subtlety of mind. 

In contrast, the **phlegmatic** temperament is less disposed because its heat is more diminished. For by reason of the phlegm, the heat is more dull. In the production of the "spirits," the power of the heat matters more than the subtlety of the matter, though both concur. In the phlegmatic temperament, the heat is weaker and the matter of the spirits is thicker. Furthermore, **melancholics** possess greater dryness; they are more timid, more inquisitive, and more removed from allurements and pleasures; thus, they are better disposed toward virtues and the study of letters. 

But why are some phlegmatic and some melancholic people better disposed toward the sciences and fine arts than most choleric or sanguine people? They say this happens sometimes because a person may have a choleric temperament in the organs of the sensitive powers—specifically, the organ of the brain—even if the rest of the body's parts are of a phlegmatic or melancholic temperament. From all this, it is clear that the philosophers attributed the excellence of talent to one's temperament. Therefore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the second book *On the Soul*: "Those hard of flesh are inept of mind, but those soft of flesh are well-apt." 

As Averroes <note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Spain known for his commentaries on Aristotle</note> says in his twenty-eighth commentary: because of the excellence of the sense of touch, man is more subtle and discerning than all other animals. And since a temperament suitable for the quality of this sense is also suitable for discernment, the quality of the intellect's discernment does not seem to follow the quality of the other senses—namely, good sight, hearing, and the like. And when you look 

<column-break/>

upon intelligent men, you will always find them to be of such a temperament. Hence Averroes and Aristotle in the second book *On the Soul* say: Man has a more noble sense of touch than the other animals, and is therefore the most prudent of all animals. Galen <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> himself says in the second book of the *Tegni*: A man who is very out of balance is still more balanced than any "balanced" animal. And Avicenna <note>A famous Persian physician and philosopher</note> says in the first chapter of the first book *On Temperaments*: Man approaches the temperate state more than any other living thing. Therefore, the human being has a more certain sense of touch than other animals because he is more balanced. 

However, some animals surpass man in other senses, such as the eagle in sight (which looks directly at the rays of the sun), the boar in hearing, and vultures and tigers in smell. Regarding this, Averroes says in the second book *On the Soul* in the chapter on smell: Vultures and tigers came to the sites of a battle fought in the land of the Greeks from five hundred miles away because of their sense of smell. So he says.

It occurs here as something worthy of note: not every "softness of flesh" produces a clear-sighted talent. For sometimes softness of flesh follows a balanced temperament and a proper mixing of moisture with dryness; this is perfect and creates subtlety of mind. There is another softness that follows an abundance of "pituita" or phlegm; this indicates a cold and moist temperament, which does not indicate goodness of talent. This is the case in women, who have a watery softness which is phlegmatic, and this is also present in some phlegmatic men. There is also an "airy" softness found in the sanguine, and a "fiery" one in the choleric; these two softnesses are more perfect than the others. 

Thus, physicians and philosophers maintain that a temperament of airy or fiery softness creates an excellent talent. Even if some are hard and rough of flesh yet possess clarity of mind, this arises from the disposition of the brain, because the brain is well-tempered for animal and spiritual operations.

<margin>
The second
opinion.
</margin>

The second opinion is that of the **astrologers**, who say that temperaments follow the climates, so much so that some people seem to differ even in species. Whence it is said:
*   **Germans** are strong.
*   **Italians** are serious.
*   **Spaniards** are boastful.
*   **Gauls** (the French) are fierce in arms and faithful in religion (so that they are called "Most Christian").
*   **Latins** are said to be haughty and elated.

For the bodies of all nations are not equally fit for the perception of wisdom and intelligence. Whence, in the manner of Thales (or as others say, Socrates), I have been accustomed to say:

> I give the greatest thanks to God for three things: specifically, that I was born a man and not a woman; a human and not a beast; a Gaul and not a Bohemian.

For the Gauls are by their very nature more apt for philosophy and religion, because they have obtained bodies from the heavens and the temperament of the air that are...

### On the Life to be Obtained from the Heavens

...remote from the conflicts of opposites, as the philosophers say. For these reasons, among the Gauls <note>original: "gallos"; referring here to the people of France</note>, the **Parisians** are considered more ingenious, while the people of **Dauphiné** are more robust. This is clearly because the former live in a purer air, while the latter live in a thicker air due to the very high mountains. It is also worth noting that provinces that are neighbors or even touching seem to differ greatly in their men and animals. Thus, the people of **Lyon** are found to be more ingenious, but those of **Dauphiné** are stronger, more robust, weaker in their morals, more spirited, and more vigorous in arms. Those from **Forez** are vain, yet more ingenious and subtle. The natives of **Auvergne** are more robust and more uncivilized in their manners. Those of **Limoges** are more crafty and less urban in their behavior. The **Basques and Gascons** are more prone to blows. The **Normans** are more corpulent and talkative. The **Picards** are considered the most "hot-headed" <note>original: "cerebrosiores"; literally "more brainy," but used here to mean impulsive or headstrong</note> among the Gauls.

Indeed, those inhabiting temperate regions are wiser and better, because the influences of the stars and planets over these regions are optimal; whereas those inhabiting intemperate regions are wild and possess the manners of beasts. Therefore, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in part 14, problem 15, says that those inhabiting temperately warm places are more prudent and wise, while in intemperate places, the opposite is true. In the same work, **Aristotle** says that intemperate places are those that are either too hot or too cold; in these places, the inhabitants have beastly manners and fierce appearances. For **Haly** <note>Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note> in the second part of the *Quadripartitum* says that, universally, those whose latitude is between the 34th and 40th degree from the equator will be wiser than those inhabiting cold regions, such as those in the sixth and seventh climates. In such foreign places, men of a good **complexion** <note>The physical and mental balance of the four humors</note> or good sense cannot be born.

Our **Galen**, in the ninth chapter of *On the Virtues of the Soul*, speaks of **Plato** thus: In the *Timaeus*, at the beginning of his discourse, he writes: "Now indeed, God, having previously adorned the whole world and its order, caused us to inhabit it, choosing places in which **Eucraxia** <term>Eucraxia: a Greek term for the perfect "good mixing" or balance of the bodily humors</term> is generated; in these, the most prudent men are born." And at the beginning of the *Laws*, **Plato** says that in a temperate region, better men are born. **Avicenna** feels the same way, as cited by **Peter of Abano**. **Haly** also says that **Aristotle** and **Galen** were from the fifth climate, and they were the best natural philosophers and metaphysicians; while **Plato** and **Ptolemy** were from the third climate, and they were excellent in mathematics. And **Albu-

<column-break/>

-mazar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a leading Persian astrologer in the Abbasid court</note> in the third book of his *Introduction* says that the **Babylonians and Egyptians** are the wisest. For the sun is not very far from their heads, nor does it approach too closely. The motion of the sun is equal over them; therefore, their air becomes of a temperate complexion, neither excessively hot nor excessively cold. Their heat, their bodies, and their natures are temperate. Their senses, reason, and the quality of their souls are good; wisdom, intellect, excellence in things, and an honest quality of soul abound in them. This is the land of prophets and wise men.

But those who inhabit the second climate, such as the **Ethiopians**, have the worst manners; they have faces that are distorted, shameful, and fierce, and they are eaters of men, as **Haly** testifies he saw at the edges of the north and south. He says that there are evil spirits there, and beasts that eat men. Therefore, many say that the **Roman Empire** lasted longer and grew so great because the Roman region occupies a middle position between the northerners and the southerners.

Regarding **Noah**, the wise say he was famous in astrology, and his son **Shem** is numbered among the astrologers. Both father and son, most excellent men, came after the flood to **Chaldea**, a temperate region. Two years after the flood, this Shem fathered Arphaxad, who is said to have been **Melchizedek** <note>A mysterious king and priest mentioned in Genesis; the text here links biblical genealogy with the founding of civilization</note>; he was the first after the flood to found the city of Salem, which is **Jerusalem**. It is in the fourth climate, which is the middle of the seven climates. In this most famous city, all the great and admirable deeds of both the Old and New Testaments are read to have been performed. To demonstrate this truth through human reasons—which are sometimes found to be less valid and are rejected by the leading debaters and rivals of truth—hardly seems necessary for the present task. Nor, as they say in the poets' songs, "does the time itself demand these spectacles."

But any pious reader and lover of truth can easily learn this not only from the context of divine letters or (if you prefer) the **Holy Bible**—which no one dares to oppose except an infidel, a perpetual enemy of the Christian faith, or a heretic excluded from the bosom of Holy Mother Church—but also from many volumes of trustworthy historians who faithfully committed these deeds to literary monuments. From these, one can know that our Lord **Jesus Christ** according to his humanity, as well as **Abraham the Chaldean** (the supreme master of astrology), **Isaac**, **Jacob**, his son **Joseph**, and **Moses** (the greatest of prophets and the divinely taught interpreter of the whole Old Law), and the others...

<summary>This page discusses geographic determinism, arguing that temperate climates (like those of Rome, Jerusalem, and Egypt) produce wise and virtuous people, while extreme climates produce "beastly" behaviors. It notably identifies biblical figures like Noah and Abraham as masters of astrology and situates Jerusalem in the ideal "middle" climate zone.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how external and internal factors shape human intellect. Having established that the "climate" or geographic environment influences temperament, the author now explores the historical transmission of knowledge and the role of astrology and theology in determining the "perfection" of the human soul.</meta>

### Chapter IX

Prophets inspired by the divine spirit came from the fourth climate. **Albumazar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a 9th-century Persian astrologer influential in the Middle Ages</note> asserts that the **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient people of Mesopotamia</note> were the most skilled of all (for "Chaldeans" is interpreted as "wise men"), and after them the **Egyptians**. For the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> says in the prologue of his *Metaphysics* that the speculative sciences were discovered among the Egyptians, especially mathematics. And we have it from the Divine Scriptures that **Abraham** transferred astrology <note>often used interchangeably with astronomy in this period</note> from Chaldea into Egypt, where it was previously unknown. And as **Laertius** writes in the third book of the *Life of Plato*: **Plato** traveled to Egypt to see the prophets and priests. **Diodorus** <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> in his second book says it is contained in the sacred books of the Egyptian priests that **Orpheus, Musaeus, Melampus, Daedalus, Homer, Lycurgus, Solon, Plato, and Pythagoras of Samos** all traveled to Egypt. These many distinguished men learned everything in Egypt that made them wonderful among the Greeks. Furthermore, **Lycurgus, Solon, and Plato** brought many laws taken from the Egyptians back to their own republics. **Pythagoras** transferred geometry, arithmetic, the course of the stars, and the zodiac from the Egyptians to the Greeks. And **Orpheus** learned theology from the Egyptians.

<margin>Four famous centers of learning.</margin>

Indeed, there have been four most celebrated centers of study for literature and the sciences in the world: namely in **Chaldea, Egypt, Greece**, and lastly in **Italy**. And now **Gaul** <note>France</note> itself, or specifically the **University of Paris** (with all due respect to everyone), holds the primacy in theology. For the Gauls have always had their own eloquence, and the **Druids** as masters of wisdom, who professed to know the magnitude and form of the earth and the world, the movements of the heavens and stars, and what the gods intended. Just as the **Brahmans** were among the Indians, so were they called Druids among the Gauls; they were men of the most upright life.

Thus, astrologers maintain that all these things proceed from the influences of the heavens and the stars: namely, a temperate region, the most excellent men, the sciences and arts, and all kinds of good things from the aspects of the heavens themselves. This is because the concave surface of the heaven is the "book" of the First Cause, in which everything that exists in the world is written. If anyone, therefore, knew how to look into that surface, he would know all things: past, present, and future. Astrologers further maintain that not only does the influence of a temperate region make men wise and excellent, but also that a particular influence is required at the conception and birth of the individual. Similarly, they say that if someone is born and raised in a temperate region but has a bad influence at their birth, they will be most wicked. Thus they wish celestial influences to be so powerful that

<column-break/>

they attribute wealth, high offices, military service, war, victories, and the prosperity of all things to the heavens and celestial influences. Yet these are the things astrologers feel, even if they sometimes dream and shamefully wander like children from the path of wisdom and truth. No one from the assembly of philosophers or those studious of truth favors their foolish and tasteless opinions.

¶ The **third opinion** is that of the theologians, and especially those of **Paris**, who—in a general council celebrated at Paris (whose determination they assert no man may contradict or break with impunity)—determined that one soul may be more perfect than another in its natural state. Thus the soul of **Moses** was more excellent in its natural properties than the soul of **Pharaoh**; and the soul of **Christ** was more perfect in its natural state than that of **John**; and the soul of **Cain** was far inferior to the soul of his brother **Abel**. And thus a natural excellence or perfection of souls is granted, such that one soul differs from another in natural standing. Before this council, however, **Blessed Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, **Alexander of Hales**, and other most excellent theologians wrote that souls do not differ at all in their natural properties, but that all souls are equal in their nature. Yet **Bonaventure** and many others from the family of theologians asserted that souls do differ in their nature, so that one is more noble than another; and so our theologians hold, and the whole Church firmly confesses.

We say, therefore, that a temperate region, celestial influences, the excellence of physical temperament <note>original: "complexionis," referring to the balance of humors</note>, and the natural excellence of souls are "dispositions" and "aptitudes" for bringing about the perfection of arts, sciences, and virtues. Thus, they concur and operate as dispositions, not as the final causes. This is how true philosophers understood it, and no other way: that every perfection is made through frequent actions. This is confirmed by many reasons. The first of these is drawn from the authority of **Ptolemy**: "The wise man will rule the stars" <note>original: "Sapiens dominabitur astris"</note>. For influences do not flow into the soul, but into the body. Similarly, the physical temperament is in the body and not the soul, but the perfection of virtue is in the soul. The second reason is taken from the first and second books of the *Ethics*, where **Aristotle** says that virtue is not in us by nature; however, influences, temperament, and the excellence of souls are from nature. The third reason is that all skilled and famous men became learned through acts and exercises. Through much labor, they acquired goodness, skill, and arts for themselves. Therefore, the entire perfection of morality and science arises from repeated...

# On Obtaining Life from the Heavens

For these reasons, **Parisians** are considered the most clever among the Gauls, while those from **Dauphiné** <note>A province in southeastern France</note> are considered the sturdiest; this is clearly because the former live in a purer air, while the latter live in a thicker air (due to the very high mountains). It is also worth noting that provinces very near or even touching one another seem to differ greatly in their men and animals. Thus, the people of **Lyon** are found to be more clever, while those of **Dauphiné** are stronger and sturdier, though weaker in their habits, more spirited, and more vigorous in arms. The people of **Forez** <note>A former province of France, now part of the Loire department</note> are vain, yet more clever and subtle. The **Basques** and **Gascons** are <term>quick to strike<note>original: "ad verbera promptiores," meaning ready to fight or lash out</note></term>. The **Normans** are more stout and talkative. The **Picards** are considered the most <term>hot-headed<note>original: "cerebrosiores," implying a temperament driven by the "heat" of the brain</note></term> among the Gauls. For those inhabiting temperate regions are wiser and better, because the influences of the stars and planets over those regions are the best; conversely, those inhabiting intemperate regions are wild and possess the habits of beasts. Therefore, the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> says in Part 14, Problem 15, that those living in temperately warm places are more prudent and wise, while in intemperate places, the opposite is true. And in the same work, **Aristotle** says that intemperate places are those that are either excessively hot or excessively cold; in such places, the inhabitants have beastly habits and fierce appearances. Indeed, **Haly** <note>Haly Abenragel, an 11th-century Arab astrologer</note>, in his second commentary on the *Quadripartitum*, says that universally, those whose latitude is between the 34th degree from the equator up to the 40th degree are the wisest. Those inhabiting cold regions, such as certain regions in the sixth and seventh climates—and especially in such foreign places—men of good <term>complexion<note>The balance of bodily humors (blood, phlegm, etc.) which was thought to determine health and character</note></term> or good sense cannot be born. Our **Galen**, in his book *On the Powers of the Soul*, Chapter 9, speaks of **Plato** in this way: "In the *Timaeus*, at the beginning of his discourse, he writes this: 'God, first adorning and ordering this entire universe, made us to inhabit it by choosing places in which <term>Eucrazia<note>From the Greek 'eukrasia', meaning a perfectly balanced mixture of qualities or humors</note></term> is produced; in these places, the most prudent men are born.'" And at the beginning of the *Laws*, **Plato** says that in a temperate region, better men are born. **Avicenna** holds the same view, as cited by **Peter of Abano**. And **Haly** says that **Aristotle** and **Galen** were from the fifth climate, and they were the best naturalists and metaphysicians; **Plato** and **Ptolemy** were from the third climate, and they were excellent in mathematics. And **Albu-**

**-mazar** <note>Abu Ma'shar</note>, in the third book of his *Introduction*, says that the **Babylonians** and **Egyptians** are the wisest. The movement of the Sun is uniform over them; therefore, their air is of a temperate complexion, neither excessively hot nor excessively cold. Their heat, their bodies, and their natures are balanced. Their senses, reason, and the quality of their souls are good; wisdom, intellect, excellence in affairs, and an honorable quality of soul abound in them. This is the land of prophets and wise men. From these come our Lord **Jesus Christ** according to his humanity, as well as **Abraham** the Chaldean, the supreme master of astrology; **Isaac**; **Jacob**; **Joseph** his son; and **Moses**, the greatest of prophets and the divinely taught interpreter of the entire Old Law; and others.

### Chapter 9

Prophets inspired by the divine spirit came from the **fourth climate** <note>In ancient and medieval geography, the "climates" were zones of latitude; the fourth climate was considered the most temperate and ideal for intellectual and spiritual life</note>. **Albumazar** <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astrologer whose works were central to medieval European science</note> asserts that the **Chaldeans** <note>An ancient people of Mesopotamia, famous for their early developments in astronomy and astrology</note> were the most skilled of all (for "Chaldeans" is interpreted as "wise men"), and after them, the **Egyptians**. Indeed, the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note> says in the prologue of his *Metaphysics* that the speculative sciences were discovered among the Egyptians, especially mathematics. We have it from the divine scriptures that **Abraham** brought the art of astrology—previously unknown there—from Chaldea into Egypt. And as **Laertius** writes in the third book of the *Life of Plato*: **Plato** traveled to Egypt to consult with the prophets and priests. **Diodorus** also states in his second book that it is recorded in the sacred books of the Egyptian priests that **Orpheus**, **Musaeus**, **Melampus**, **Daedalus**, **Homer**, **Lycurgus**, **Solon**, **Plato**, **Pythagoras of Samos**, and many other distinguished men traveled to Egypt and learned everything that later made them marvelous among the Greeks. Furthermore, Lycurgus, Solon, and Plato brought many laws taken from the Egyptians back to their own republics. Pythagoras also brought geometry, arithmetic, the course of the stars, and the zodiac from the Egyptians to the Greeks. And Orpheus learned his theology from the Egyptians.

<margin>Four famous centers of learning.</margin>
Indeed, four most celebrated centers of study for literature and science have existed in the world: namely in **Chaldea**, **Egypt**, **Greece**, and finally in **Italy**. Now, **France** itself—or rather the **University of Paris** (if I may say so without offense to anyone)—holds the primacy in theology. For the Gauls have always possessed their own eloquence, and they had the **Druids** as masters of wisdom, who professed to know the magnitude of the earth and the world, the form and motion of the heavens and stars, and what the gods willed. Just as the **Brahmans** were among the Indians, so were they called Druids among the Gauls; they were men of the most upright life. 

Thus, astrologers maintain that all these things proceed from the influences of the heavens and the stars: namely, a temperate region, the most virtuous men, and the sciences and arts—all kinds of good things come from the aspects of the heavens themselves. They believe this because the concave surface of the heaven is the "book of the First Cause," in which all things that exist in the world are written. If anyone, therefore, knew how to look into that surface, he would know all things: past, present, and future. Astrologers further claim that not only does the influence of a temperate region produce wise and excellent men, but a particular influence is also required at the moment of a person's conception and birth. Similarly, they say that if someone is born and raised in a temperate region but has a bad celestial influence at their birth, they will be a most wicked person. Thus, they wish to show that celestial influences are so powerful that

<column-break/>

they attribute riches, high offices, military service, war, victories, and the prosperity of all affairs to the heavens and their influences. These are the views of the astrologers on these matters—though at times they "dream" and shamefully wander like children from the path of wisdom and truth. No one among the assembly of philosophers and seekers of truth supports their pride or their tasteless opinions.

The third opinion is that of the **theologians**, especially those of **Paris**, who determined in a general council held at Paris (whose tentative determination they assert no man may contradict or oppose with impunity) that one soul is more perfect in its natural qualities than another. Thus, the soul of **Moses** was more excellent in its nature than the soul of **Pharaoh**; the soul of **Christ** more perfect than the soul of **Peter** or **John**; and the soul of **Cain** far inferior to the soul of his brother **Abel**. Thus, a natural excellence or perfection of souls is granted, such that one soul differs from another in its natural merit. 

Before this council, however, **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, **Alexander of Hales**, and other most excellent theologians wrote that souls do not differ at all in their natural qualities, but that all souls are naturally equal. Yet **Bonaventure** and many others from the family of theologians asserted that souls do differ in their nature, such that one is more noble than another; and this is what our theologians hold, and the whole Church firmly confesses. 

We say, therefore, that a temperate region, celestial influences, the excellence of one's **complexion** <note>In medieval science, "complexion" refers to the physical balance of humors in the body</note>, and the natural excellence of souls are "dispositions" and "aptitudes" for achieving perfection in the arts, sciences, and virtues. Thus, they work together as preconditions (*dispositive*) and not as the actual cause (*effective*). It was in this way, and no other, that the true philosophers understood it: but every kind of perfection comes from repeated actions. This is confirmed by several reasons. The first is drawn from the authority of **Ptolemy**: <note>original: "Pius siue sapiens dominabitur astris"</note> "The pious or wise man shall rule the stars." For influences do not act upon or flow into the soul, but into the body. Similarly, the physical constitution is in the body and not in the soul, but the perfection of virtue is in the soul. The second reason is taken from the first and second books of the *Ethics*, where **Aristotle** says that virtue is not in us by nature; yet influence, physical constitution, and the excellence of souls are from nature. The third reason is that all skilled and famous men became learned through acts and exercise. Through much labor, they acquired goodness, skill, and the arts for themselves. Therefore, the entire perfection of morality and science, and the progress of the arts, comes from frequent practice.

### Book III: On Fitting One’s Life to the Heavens

...are completed and perfected by actions: a truth that no wise man has ever denied. The fourth reason is proven by experience. For not everyone living in a temperate region is the most learned or the best. Indeed, we have seen many from among the Italians, Greeks, and Hebrews who possessed a good <term>complexion (the physical balance of bodily humors)</term>, yet were lazy, sluggish, childish, and quite wicked. Conversely, others—both foreigners and our own people—who possessed a poor complexion have emerged as good, upright, skilled, and illustrious men. There is another proof from experience: if a physical complexion or <term>celestial influence (the astrological 'influx' of the stars)</term> produced good and learned men effectively and perfectly, then there would be no moral science, no teaching of skills or arts; the vast volumes of books would be in vain, and there would be no need for masters or disciples. The fifth reason is written in the third book of the *Ethics* <note>Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics, Book III, which discusses voluntary action and choice</note>: that no one is good against their will, and similarly, no one is evil against their will. Therefore, goodness and malice reside in the will, not in the physical complexion. If it were otherwise, free will would be abolished, all laws would be revoked, the reward for good work would be taken away, and the punishment of sins and of the wicked would be removed. No one would be worthy of praise or blame; no wicked person could be condemned, because no one should be accused or exalted for that which they cannot control—since virtue and vice must be voluntary. A man's physical complexion, celestial influence, and natural excellence of soul do not lie within his power, nor can they be subject to our will, because natural things are produced by nature and not by the will. For no one can create for themselves a natural excellence of the soul or a celestial influence.

<margin>The threefold perfection of arts and science</margin>

And so that these matters may shine more clearly, it must be further observed that the perfection of arts, science, and goodness—as pertains to our purpose—can be considered in three ways. The first is called "common," when someone is skilled according to the common course of other men, just as all people are commonly skilled; for instance, when someone is a skilled astrologer relative to other astrologers. The second perfection is called "eminently excellent," when someone is skilled above all men living in their own age. Such a person is not merely skilled according to the common course, but above others, exceeding all their contemporaries. The third perfection is called "most eminent," when someone exceeds not only all their contemporaries, but indeed everyone—including those who came before and those who follow. They exceed most eminently; that is, enough and more than enough. These are usually those who possess a huge spirit and a fervent nature aided by many <term>spirits (the subtle vapors in the body that connect soul and body)</term>, such as was found in Hector, Achilles, Hercules, and many others, who are called "demigods" by our people and "heroes" by the Greeks. These are men of brave and exalted spirit who always undertake great things, and whose stories we hear as much for their splendid deeds as for their enormous downfalls. Fleeing mediocrity, they either illustrate their lives with brilliant deeds or they

<column-break/>

stain themselves with famous crimes. Among their number was David and his son Solomon; both were fathers and sons who excelled at one time in religion and at another in vice. And from our own tradition, there is Paul the Apostle, who strove to destroy the Church of Christ, yet after he was converted to Christ, he complained of a "thorn in the flesh" and said he was "buffeted by Satan." <note>referencing 2 Corinthians 12:7</note> I will add also the most blessed father Jerome, who, while settled in the vast wilderness, seemed to himself to be among choirs of girls; as he himself said, while his body was freezing, the fires of lust alone were boiling over. <note>Jerome’s Letter 22 to Eustochium describes these temptations in the desert</note> In everyone’s hands is the book of the *Confessions* of Augustine, in which he frankly confesses that he was not only tempted by the love of women, but overcome by it. There was in these men a powerful nature, very similar to fertile soil which, by that one and same fecundity, produces both good and bad herbs indiscriminately unless it is restrained by a farmer. This is also manifest in horses: with the same strength with which they are able to run swiftly, leap nimbly, and carry warriors, they can also strike their master, throw their rider, and trample those in their path. In the realm of learning, some exceed others in the same eminent way: just as Homer, Virgil, Lucan, Ovid, Horace, and Juvenal exceeded all the poets who preceded them and those who followed. Similarly, in the medical art, Hippocrates, Galen, Avicenna, Rhazes, and Avenzoar <note>Avenzoar, or Ibn Zuhr, was a prominent 12th-century Moorish physician</note> preceded all physicians both before and after them. Likewise in philosophy, Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, Plotinus, and Porphyry surpassed everyone, both predecessors and successors, in skill and learning. However, it is not my intention here to speak of the perfection which God inspires divinely, or which the Holy Spirit illuminates; for we intend to define this here as a moral philosopher, and not according to supernatural illumination inspired by God. For even without "sanctifying grace" <note>original: "gratia gratum faciente," a theological term for grace that makes a person pleasing to God</note>, one can acquire arts, science, and moral virtues, just as we read that many most skilled craftsmen were strangers to the worship of the true God. There were also outstanding and distinguished philosophers without faith in the true God, such as Socrates, Plato, Pythagoras, Solon, Aristotle, Plotinus, and Porphyry. And in terms of pure moral goodness, many other illustrious men emerged, such as Brutus, the first consul of the Romans; Camillus, the dictator of the Roman city; and the Scipios and Catos. In military affairs, there were found the strenuous Miltiades, Themistocles, Aristobulus, Alcibiades, Pericles, Hector, Achilles, Romulus, Theseus, Alexander the Great, Hannibal, Pompey, and Caesar. And from the leaders of the Gauls: Brennus and Belgius; and Roland, Godfrey, and many other kings and leaders of the Franks whom...

# Chapter 10.

<columns>

...for the sake of [merit]; and lest I seem to commend my own people more than any others, I pass over them in silence. Thus, this triple perfection of arts, sciences, and morals can be acquired; we can attain it both through skill and through frequent actions. If, therefore, someone should ask us for a briefer conclusion to this inquiry: by what means or through what things do men become illustrious, excellent, and most upright in the integrity of their character? We shall respond that five things are universally required for this. The first is **skill**; the second is **imitation**; the third is **exercise** or frequent practice; the fourth is the **disposition of parts**; the fifth is **constant use from tender years**. <note>original: "Primum est ars: secundum imitatio: tertium exercitatio... quartum partium dispositio: quintum usus a teneris annis."</note> For by these five things, each person can attain for themselves this triple perfection of which we spoke a little earlier. But enough concerning these matters: now let us pursue the other things that remain.

## ¶ On the making of astronomical images: and what they are worth according to Catholics. Chapter 10.

<margin>
Rejection of the making of images
</margin>

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'A' at the beginning of the chapter, decorated with foliage patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
The final part of **Astrology** concerns the making of **astronomical images**. These are images carved or cast under certain <term>constellations (specific alignments of stars and planets)</term> so as to drive away harmful things or to entice and provoke useful and desired things. These are believed by the learned to be more superstitious than true, which can be very easily proven. For a <term>celestial influence (the 'influx' or energy from the stars)</term> is received into a thing either insofar as it is an artificial object, or insofar as it possesses natural matter. It is not the second case, because that matter already received its influence at the moment of its natural creation. Nor is it the first, because an artificial thing exists only through its "artificial form," which is its shape. But this shape is "whole in the whole"; it is not "whole in the part" or "part in the part." Therefore, in any one part of the shape—whether it be made of wood, stone, or other material—the "artificial form" does not exist in any way, neither in itself nor in any of its parts. Thus, it cannot receive the celestial influence. Experience has taught many that the intended effects have often followed the creation of such images; but, alas, it has miserably deceived them. For these things are not accomplished by the form of the image receiving power from the constellations, but by the **work of demons**. As **Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century philosopher</note> clearly testifies when writing against **Al-Ghazali**, asserting that images of this sort are entirely ineffective. For artificial things, insofar as they are artificial, neither receive celestial influence, nor are they the cause of any natural operation through themselves, as is clear from the study of nature; and <term>quantity (the physical dimensions or shape)</term> does not belong to the category of active forces. Therefore, an image fabricated from any material under whatever constellations

<column-break/>

receives nothing more of celestial virtue than the unshaped mass of material from which the image was made; nor do any of the inscriptions upon them have any power. All things, therefore, which are accomplished through images are done by the **work of demons**, as the **Blessed Thomas Aquinas** most clearly testifies in *Against the Gentiles* (Book III, Chapter 102), in the *Summa Theologiae* (Second Part of the Second Part, Question 96, Article 2), and in his book *On the Hidden Works of Nature*. These images are often buried in the middle of a place where their operation is expected, which is contrary to natural action; for active and passive forces act and are acted upon more strongly when they are directly applied to one another. Even greater vanity is indicated by the other ceremonies observed with them: such as when certain things are buried face-up with the **left hand**, or others are turned upside down with their feet up and heads down. All of these are signs of a **hidden pact** entered into with demons by those who use such things, rather than causes naturally contributing to an effect. The same is true of the <term>necromantic (death-magic)</term> images of angels, or rather the inscription of the names of demons and other unknown characters. Furthermore, the use of fumigations and invocations are manifest signs of a pact with demons. Theologians, and especially **Saint Thomas**, say that in this regard astronomical images differ from necromantic ones, although in both, specific times and constellations are observed. Alas, what great impiety lurks under the shadow of astrology! I pity this most miserable sect, which knows not how to pity itself. While it labors in vain to foretell health and good fortune for others, it is itself wasting away from an "elephantine disease" <note>likely a metaphor for a heavy, corruption-like spiritual leprosy</note>, allowing a cancer to crawl into the very depths of its soul. But against these things that have been said, **Ptolemy** says in the *Centiloquium*:

</margin>

Similarly, an effective image of a scorpion can be made when the Moon enters the sign of Scorpio. He says this sign was made in Egypt in his time and that he himself was present when the figure of a bull was pressed with a **Scorpio seal** into a **bezoar stone** <note>a stone-like mass found in the stomachs of animals, believed to be an antidote to poison</note>; it was given as a drink to one whom a scorpion had stung, and he was suddenly cured. **Hahamed the physician** affirms that this is effectively done, with **Serapio** confirming it. # Book: On Arranging Life Celestially

### ¶ On the creation of astrological images: and what they are worth according to Catholics. Chapter 10.

The final part of Astrology concerns the making of astronomical images: which, once begun, are carved or cast under certain <term>constellations (specific alignments of stars and planets)</term>; either to put to flight harmful things, or to attract and provoke useful and desired things. For the <term>influx (the invisible flow of celestial power)</term> is either received in the thing as an artificial project, or the project has a natural material. ¶ Not the second, because that thing receives its influx from the principles of its <term>generation (its biological birth or natural origin)</term>. ¶ Nor the first, because an artificial thing does not exist except through an artificial form, which is its shape: but the whole [form] is in the whole; it is not, however, the whole in a part, or a part in a part. Therefore, in one part of the shape—whether it be composed of wood, stone, or other material—the artificial form will not exist in any way, neither in itself nor in any part of itself. <meta>This page continues the investigation into "astrological images" (talismans). While the previous page began to define them, this page shifts to a defense of the author Marsilio Ficino, arguing that he describes these practices as a scholar rather than endorsing them as a believer, while also categorizing what can and cannot be predicted through the stars.</meta>

### Chapter 11 of the book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens* <note>original: "De vita celitus comparanda"</note>

In the small book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens*, chapter 13, he seems to affirm this. But it must be said that <term>Marsilio [Ficino]</term> <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was a central figure of the Italian Renaissance who sought to harmonize Platonism with Christianity.</note> himself does not so much approve of these images as narrate them. Listen to what he writes to the reader in the preface of that same work: "If you do not approve," he says, "of astronomical images otherwise invented for the health of mortals—which I myself do not so much approve as narrate—then, with my permission and even, if you wish, my advice, set them aside. But do not neglect medicines that are at least strengthened by a certain celestial support, unless perhaps you have no regard for life. For I have found through long and frequent experience that there is as much difference between medicines of this kind and others made without astrological selection as there is between pure wine and water." So says Marsilio. See how Marsilio himself speaks as one who is hesitant. Yet we can say that in that book, Marsilio was not speaking his own opinion, but that of <term>Plotinus</term> <note>A major Greek philosopher of the 3rd century and the founder of Neoplatonism.</note> himself. For a little later in the same place he says: "Henceforth, therefore, let us speak with Plotinus: only then intending to consult with you more diligently." And at the end of the same prologue, he says: "In all things that are treated by me here and elsewhere, I wish only so much to be asserted as is approved by the Church." See, therefore, in what way <term>Ficino</term> speaks doubtingly and not assertively concerning images of this kind. And just as <term>Abbot Joachim</term> <note>Joachim of Fiore, a 12th-century mystic.</note>, speaking against <term>Peter Lombard</term> <note>A 12th-century theologian whose "Sentences" became the standard textbook of medieval theology.</note> concerning the Trinity, said that Peter himself had posited a "quaternity" <note>A theological error suggesting there are four parts to God instead of three.</note> rather than a Trinity; so also Marsilio narrates astronomical images rather than affirming them—a fact which that little book he published against the judgments of astrologers shows most clearly.

->¶ Concerning astronomical judgments: and to<-
->which of them faith should be given. Chapter 11.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'T' containing a stylized landscape with plants and possibly mushrooms or small hills.</image-desc>
IT is useful to distinguish three kinds of future events: For some future things have a determined and infallible cause, such as those which depend on the motion of celestial bodies in which there is determination and the removal of every impediment; such are the conjunctions of planets, eclipses, and similar things. And concerning these, there is no "theological prophecy," but rather certain and evident astronomical science. Other things, however, have a determined cause but are nonetheless fallible, such as those which exist according to a lower nature; these have a determined cause because the "intention of nature" moves determinately toward one result. Yet they are fallible because many impediments can occur—for example, if a field is properly sown and the earth is good and well-

<column-break/>

-disposed, and a convenient arrangement of the celestial bodies brings forth good fruit. An astronomer can know these things in some way, though not with such certainty as the aforementioned things. Hence, if there were any divine prophecies concerning future events of this kind, the conjectures of astronomical judgments could be adapted to them in a certain way; for example, one could point to the prophecy <margin>Genesis 41</margin> of Joseph regarding the future famine <note>Referring to Joseph interpreting Pharaoh's dream of seven years of plenty and seven years of famine in Egypt.</note>. Still other things have an indeterminate and fallible cause, such as those which proceed freely from the human will, which is indeterminate because it can choose opposites; and it is fallible because even when a person wishes to accomplish something, many obstacles can arise. Therefore, such things cannot be known with certainty through astronomical or any other human science, but only through divine revelation. Hence, if there are any theological prophecies concerning such things, astronomical judgments cannot be fitted to them with any certainty, but only by a kind of meager conjecture. This is because (as has been said) a <term>constellation</term> <note>A specific alignment of stars believed to influence earthly affairs.</note> in some way disposes and inclines the human will; yet it is mostly animalistic men who obey it, those who do not resist evil inclinations through virtue. To the three aforementioned kinds of future events which occur according to the course of nature, a fourth kind can be added: those which happen miraculously by divine power alone. Although these have a determined and infallible cause—namely, the divine will—nevertheless, because that will is entirely unknown to us except through divine revelation, it is a matter of entirely empty and superstitious vanity to adapt astronomical considerations to prophecies concerning such futures, since such things exceed the power of nature and natural reason.

---

->¶ The end of this treatise On Obtaining<-
->Life from the Heavens.<-

## ¶ Concerning the Elysian Fields and the blessedness of the celestial paradise: and what the philosophers, and especially our divine Plato, think of them. Chapter One.
