**I** would not dare to say or assert anything rashly regarding the joys of paradise. For as it is written in Isaiah, chapter 64, and in the first Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 2: "No eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love Him." <note>original: "nec oculus vidit: nec auris audivit: nec in cor hominis ascendit q̃ preparavit deus diligẽtibus se"</note> Why should I, a man of poor wit, attempt to express in words what cannot even enter into human thought? Nevertheless, I shall speak and recount what our philosophers think regarding the <term>Elysian Fields</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the final resting place of the souls of the heroic and the virtuous.</note> and the blessedness of the celestial paradise. For Plato—who was named "Plato" because of his broad forehead, the width of his chest, and the richness of his speech <note>A common Renaissance etymology; 'Plato' derives from the Greek 'platys,' meaning broad or wide.</note>—seems to have spoken quite literally in the *Phaedo* regarding the likeness and analogy of the celestial earth. He says: "If it is necessary to tell a beautiful story, it is worth the effort, Simmias, to hear what those regions of the earth are like that lie beneath the heavens. Indeed, let us listen most gladly to this story. They say, therefore, my friend, that first of all, the face of that earth—if one were to look down from above—appears like those balls made of twelve pieces of leather: it is marked with various distinct colors. Of which our colors, which painters use here, retain a certain similarity. But there, the entire earth is made of such colors, and much more brilliant and pure. Part of it is purple, endowed with wonderful beauty; part is golden in color; part is whiter than plaster or snow. Furthermore, it is adorned with other colors similarly, and even more numerous and beautiful than those that have come to our knowledge. Indeed, these very hollows of the earth, filled with water and air, provide a certain splendid appearance of color among the variety of other colors, so that its single appearance always seems varied. In this kind of earth, according to a fitting proportion, similar trees, flowers, and fruits are born. Moreover, the mountains and stones there have, in the same way, a perfection and clarity,

<column-break/>

and colors that are much more beautiful. Certain particles of these are the little stones that are held in high price among us: <term>sardius</term>, jaspers, emeralds, and others of that kind. But there, nothing exists that is not of such quality, or even more beautiful. The cause of this matter is that those stones are pure, and not worn away or corrupted by rot and saltiness like ours—things which, flowing together in this place, cause the stones, the earth, the animals, and the plants to be infected and forced into sickness. But that earth itself is adorned with all these things, and even with gold and silver and other similar things. These shining things are born there in great number and size throughout the whole earth, so that to see it is a spectacle for happy spectators. Furthermore, there are many animals and humans there: some inhabiting the inland region, some living around the air just as we live around the shores of the sea, and some even on islands situated not far from the continent, surrounded by air. But to speak briefly: what water and the sea are to us for our use, the air is the same to them; and what air is to us, the <term>ether</term> <note>The "fifth element" or "upper air," thought by ancient philosophers to be the pure substance of the heavens.</note> is to them. The seasons there have such a temperate quality that the inhabitants live without disease continually and far longer than our people. Likewise, in sight, hearing, prudence, and other such ways, they excel us as much as air excels water, and ether excels air in purity. Moreover, there are temples of the gods and groves in which the gods truly dwell familiarly; and there are oracles, divinations, perceptions of the gods, and such familiarities for men to enjoy. The sun also, and the moon, and the other stars are seen by them as they truly are; and in other matters, they possess a blessedness congruent with these things."

<margin>The same author</margin>
Thus says Plato.
And elsewhere in the *Phaedo* he says: "He who has spent a pure and moderate life, having obtained the gods as companions and leaders, dwells there where it is fitting for each." And later in the same work: "Those who are found to have lived more piously than others are they who are released and freed from these earthly places as if from a prison, and ascend to higher things, dwelling in a pure region above the earth. Meanwhile, whoever has been sufficiently purified through philosophy lives entirely without bodies for all time, and they obtain even more beautiful habitations than these. The beauty of these is not easy to describe, nor would the present time suffice for the telling. But for the sake of these things which have been recounted, O Simmias, we must strive with every effort to pursue virtue, prudence, and wisdom in this life. For the reward is beautiful, and the hope is great." These things, therefore...

That things are exactly as I have described them, no man of sound mind should assert; yet that these things, or something like them, exist concerning our souls and their dwellings—since the soul itself appears to be immortal—seems to me both fitting and worthy of belief, as if we were venturing a noble risk. For the risk is a beautiful one. <note>original: "honeſtum em̄ periculum eſt" — This is a reference to Socrates’ famous "noble risk" from Plato’s Phaedo (114d), where he argues that even if one is not certain of the afterlife, it is a risk worth taking to live a virtuous life.</note> These are the words of Plato. ->¶ Concerning the happiness of the good, and the unhappiness and miseries of the bad, according to Plato. Chapter 2.<-

Plato, in the fourth book <note>Champier cites the "fourth book," but the famous "Myth of Er" actually appears in the tenth book of Plato's Republic.</note> of the *Republic*, writes that a certain Pamphilius <note>Champier refers to "Er the Pamphylian" as Pamphilius.</note> had been among those who fell in battle and had been dead for ten days. When he had died in battle and the other corpses were taken up on the tenth day already decayed, he was found whole and

<column-break/>

untainted in body. Finally, he was carried home for the office of burial. On the twelfth day after his death, while he was placed upon the pyre, he rose again and related what he had seen in the meantime. He said that after his soul had been separated from his body, it traveled with many others to a certain divine place, in which he saw two openings in the earth side by side, and two others in the region of heaven directly opposite them. Judges sat between these openings who, after they had judged the souls, commanded the just to ascend to the right through heaven, hanging the signs <note>original: "signa" — tokens or tablets recording their deeds.</note> of their judgment on their front side. Conversely, they commanded the unjust to go to the left and downward, bearing behind their backs the signs of everything they had done in life. When he himself approached the judges, he asserted that they replied that he must become a messenger to men concerning the things he saw there. They commanded him to listen and look diligently at whatever happened in those places. He had seen there, through each of the gates of heaven and earth, souls departing after the sentence was passed; through the other two gates, he saw souls ascending from the earth, covered in dust, filth, and decay; while from heaven, others descended bright and clean. He said that the souls coming from every direction appeared as if exhausted by a long journey, and they went gladly into the meadow that is there, as if into a great assembly, to lie down and greet one another, as many as had prior knowledge of each other. All those who had met, both those from the earth and those from heaven, questioned one another about what they had seen in their respective places. They responded to one another in turn: those from below, grieving and weeping at the memory of the evils they had suffered and seen on their journey under the earth (which he said was a journey of a thousand years); while those who had descended from heaven spoke of delights and spectacles of immense beauty. He recounted many things in a long sequence, which would be too lengthy a narrative for you, O Glaucon. But the summary was this: for whatever injuries it was established they had brought upon others, they paid the penalty ten times over for each one. This payment was for every hundred years—taking this as the span of a human life—so that they might pay a ten-fold penalty for their injustice. Thus, if any were the cause of many deaths, or betrayed cities and armies, or cast men into slavery, or were conscious of any other outrage or crime, they would pay ten-fold penalties for each misdeed. And again, if any had bestowed benefits or cultivated justice and piety, they received rewards in the same measure. Regarding those who died immediately after birth, or lived only a short time...

# Chapter 2.

...lest they waste time; he recounted some things hardly worthy of memory. However, concerning those who were pious or impious toward the gods and their parents, and murderers who had defiled their own hands with slaughter, he reported that they were affected by greater rewards and punishments. For he said he was present when someone asked another, "Where is Ardieus the Great?" This man had been a tyrant in a certain city of Pamphylia <note>A region on the southern coast of modern-day Turkey.</note> a thousand years before that time. He had killed his elderly father and his older brother, and had committed many other impious crimes. He asserted that the one questioned replied: "He has not come, nor will he ever come." O, what a dire spectacle! For as we were about to exit and sought the opening, having endured all else, we suddenly saw him, along with almost all the other tyrants. Among them were also some private citizens who had committed great crimes. Just as they were confident they were about to ascend, that opening would not permit them, but instead let out a horrific bellow whenever any of those who were incurable, or not yet purified, attempted to exit. Therefore, certain fierce men, fiery in appearance, were standing there; having heard the sudden bellow, they seized these souls separately and dragged them away. As for Ardieus and those like him, having bound their hands, feet, and necks, they threw them down and flayed them. <note>original: "excarnificabant" — literally "to strip the flesh from."</note> Then, having dragged them along a certain path toward the outer part, they tore them upon thorny bushes, <note>original: "tribulis" — likely refers to the thorny Mediterranean plant known as the caltrop.</note> indicating to those passing by the reason why they suffered such things and that they were being carried away to be cast into Tartarus. <note>In Greek mythology, the deepest abyss of the underworld, used as a dungeon of torment for the wicked.</note> While many and varied things terrified them there, this particular fear most vehemently vexed them: whether the bellow would be raised during their ascent; but when it was silent, each one seemed to ascend most gladly. He recounted such penalties and torments, and conversely, such benefits.

But when those souls mentioned in the upper regions had rested for seven days in the meadow, he said it was necessary for them to rise on the eighth day and depart from there, and finally arrive at a certain place on the fourth day. From there, they saw a light extended from above through the whole of heaven and earth, like a standing column, most similar to a rainbow, yet clearer and purer. Having proceeded toward it on a divine journey, they saw there, in the middle of the light, the ends of the celestial bonds extended from heaven. For this light is the bond of heaven, much like the undergirding ropes of triremes <note>Ancient warships with three banks of oars. The "undergirding" refers to the heavy ropes used to reinforce the hull.</note> which hold the entire circumference together. From these extremities hung the Spindle of Necessity, <note>term: "Fusus Necessitatis" — In Plato's vision, the entire universe turns like a spindle used for spinning wool, governed by the goddess Necessity (Ananke).</note> through which all the orbits are driven; its shaft and hook were made of adamant. The whorl, <note>term: "Vertiginem" — the weight at the bottom of a spindle that maintains its rotation.</note> however, was a mixture of this and other materials, the nature of which is as follows in its form, just as it is seen among us. Yet it must be noted from his discourse that

<column-break/>

it is as if within one large and hollow whorl, another smaller but similar one is inserted, having been carved out throughout, fitting together like those jars which are placed one inside the other; and thus a third and a fourth, and four others. For there are eight whorls in total, inserted into one another as circles showing their rims above, but forming the continuous back of a single whorl around the shaft. That shaft is driven straight through the middle of the eighth whorl and through the whole structure. The first and outermost whorl has the widest circle of the rim. The seventh is the second widest. The third is the fourth widest. The fourth is the eighth widest. The fifth is the seventh widest. The sixth is the fifth widest. The seventh is the third widest. The eighth is the second widest. <note>This complex description refers to the perceived widths of the orbits of the fixed stars and the seven "planets" known to the ancients: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Sun, and the Moon.</note> Furthermore, the circle of the first and greatest is variegated. The seventh is the brightest. The circle of the eighth whorl receives its color from the seventh shining upon it. The circles of the second and fifth are similar to each other, but somewhat yellower than the others. The third possesses the whitest color. The fourth is reddish. The sixth exceeds the second in whiteness. The spindle itself is turned as a whole in its rotation. But while the whole is rotated, the seven interior circles revolve more slowly in a motion contrary to the whole. Of these, the eighth is clearly driven with the most rapid motion. The second [group] follows one after the other: the seventh, the sixth, and the fifth. The third [group] is carried with such a motion that it seems to revolve with the fourth. The fourth [group] revolves with the third, and the fifth with the second. The spindle itself turns upon the knees of Necessity. Moreover, above each circle sits a Siren, carried around with the sphere, emitting a single voice, a single tone; thus from all eight, a single harmony rings out. <note>This is the origin of the famous concept of the "Music of the Spheres."</note> Furthermore, three others, the daughters of Necessity, sit upon thrones at equal intervals from one another, the Fates <note>original: "parcas" — the three goddesses who spin, measure, and cut the thread of life.</note> in white robes with garlands upon their heads: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos, who sing in accompaniment to the harmony of the Sirens. Lachesis sings of the past, Clotho of the present, and Atropos of the future. And Clotho, with her mother, touches the outermost circumference of the spindle with her right hand, turning it at intervals. Atropos, with her left hand, does the same to the inner ones. Lachesis, finally, touches both in turn with each hand. Therefore, when the souls arrived there, it was necessary for them to go immediately to Lachesis, where a certain prophet first arranged them each in order. Then, having taken the lots and the models of lives from the knees of Lachesis, he ascended a high platform and spoke thus: "This is the proclamation of the virgin Lachesis, daughter of Necessity. O ephemeral souls, this is the beginning of another cycle of a mortal and death-bringing race. No guardian spirit <note>original: "demon" — in the Greek sense of a "daimon" or personal guiding spirit, not an evil entity.</note> shall choose you by lot..."

### Chapter 2. On the Happiness of the Good and the Unhappiness and Miseries of the Wicked according to Plato.

Specifically, they seized Ardiaeus and those like him; and having bound their hands, feet, and necks, they threw them down and flayed them. <note>original: "excaruificabantesq" — likely a corruption of "excarnificantes," meaning to strip the flesh or torture severely.</note> Then, having been dragged along a certain path toward the outer part, they were mangled with thorny briars, indicating to those passing by for what reason they suffered such things and that they were being carried away to be cast into Tartarus. <note>Tartarus is the deep abyss in Greek mythology used as a dungeon of torment for the wicked.</note> While many and various things terrified them there, this fear vexed them most vehemently: whenever the roar was stirred up during an ascent; but when it was silent, everyone seemed to ascend most gladly. He recounted punishments and torments of this kind, and conversely, benefits of a similar sort. 

But when those souls had rested for seven days in the aforementioned meadows in the higher regions, he said it was necessary for them, rising on the eighth day, to depart from there, and finally on the fourth day to arrive at a certain place. From there, they could see a light extended through the whole of heaven and earth, like an upright column most similar to a rainbow, yet clearer and purer. Having proceeded toward it after a day's journey, they saw there, in the midst of the light, the ends of the celestial chains extended from heaven. For this light is the bond of heaven, much like the undergirding of triremes. <note>original: "subcincture" — refers to the ropes used to reinforce the hulls of ancient warships; Plato uses this to describe how light holds the universe together.</note> And thus the entire circumference is held together. From these extremities hung the spindle of the goddess Necessity, through which all the orbits are completed; its shaft and hook are made of adamant. <note>Adamant: a legendary, indomitable stone or metal, often associated with diamond.</note> Its whorl, however, is a mixture of this and other kinds, the nature of which is of such a shape as is seen among us. Yet it must be understood from his speech that it is arranged

<column-break/>

just as if, within one large and hollow whorl carved out through the whole, another similar but smaller one lay inserted, fitting so closely as to be like those jars that are inserted into one another, and so a third and a fourth, and four others. For there are eight whorls there, circles inserted into one another, showing their rims above, but forming a continuous back of a single whorl around the shaft. That shaft is driven straight through the middle of the eighth and through the whole. 

The first and outermost whorl, therefore, has the widest circular rim. The sixth has the second widest. The third has the fourth widest. The fourth has the eighth widest. The fifth has the seventh widest. The fifth has the sixth widest. The third has the seventh widest. The eighth has the second widest. <note>The author is detailing the relative widths of the celestial spheres or "whorls" of the spindle, representing the planets and the fixed stars.</note> Likewise, the circle of the first and greatest is variegated. That of the seventh is the most brilliant. The circle of the eighth whorl receives its color from the seventh shining upon it. Those of the second and fifth are similar to each other, though somewhat yellower than the others. The third possesses the whitest color. The fourth is reddish. The second, however, surpasses the sixth in whiteness. And the whole spindle is carried round in a circle with the same motion. But while the whole revolves, the seven inner circles are whirled around with a motion contrary to the whole. Of these, the eighth is clearly driven with the most rapid motion. The second ones follow one after another. The seventh, sixth, and fifth. The third is carried with such a motion that it seems to revolve with the fourth. The fourth with the third, and the fifth with the second. 

The spindle itself revolves on the knees of Necessity. Above, moreover, a Siren <note>In Greek mythology, Sirens were creatures whose song was irresistible; here, they represent the "music of the spheres."</note> stands upon each circle, carried along with it, emitting a single voice, a single tone. Indeed, from all eight, a single harmony sounds together. Moreover, the three daughters of Necessity sit on thrones at equal intervals from one another: the Fates, in white robes with crowns upon their heads: Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos, who sing to the harmony of the Sirens. Lachesis sings of things past, Clotho of things present, and Atropos of things to come. And Clotho, with her mother, at certain intervals of time, turns the outermost circumference of the spindle with her right hand. Atropos, with her left hand, does the same to the inner ones. Lachesis, finally, touches both in turn with each hand. 

Therefore, when the souls arrived there, it was necessary for them to go immediately to Lachesis, where a certain prophet first arranged them each in order. Afterward, when he had taken from the knees of Lachesis the lots and the models of lives, he ascended a certain high platform and spoke thus: "This is the word of the virgin Lachesis, daughter of Necessity. O ephemeral souls, <note>original: "anime diurne" — literally 'souls of a day,' emphasizing the short span of mortal life.</note> this is the beginning of another cycle of a mortal race that brings death. No guardian spirit shall cast lots for you..."

# Books on the Super-celestial Life.

<column-break/>

[...will be assigned] to you: but you will rather choose your own guardian spirit <note>original: "demonem." In the Platonic tradition, a *daemon* is a personal guiding spirit or destiny that the soul chooses before birth.</note>. Let the one who draws the first lot be the first to choose the life to which he will necessarily be bound. **Virtue**, however, is free and independent; according to how much each man honors or neglects her, he will possess more or less of her. **The fault lies with the chooser; God is without blame.** After saying this, he scattered the lots among them all, and each person picked up the one that fell near him. No one was allowed to know his place in the order of choosing until he had picked it up. Only then did he understand which number he had drawn. After this, he laid out the patterns of lives on the floor before them—many more than are visible here now. He asserted that the lives of all humans and animals were of every possible kind. There were tyrannies among them: some lasting for life, others temporary, collapsing midway into poverty, exile, and want. There were also the lives of famous men: some esteemed for their appearance, strength, and athletic success; others for the nobility of their ancestors. There were also lives of ignoble men, and those of women in the same variety. However, the condition and rank of the soul was not included, because the soul necessarily becomes different based on the life it chooses. Other things, however, were mixed together: wealth with poverty, health with disease, or a middle state between them. Here indeed, O Glaucon <note>Glaucon was Plato's brother and the primary listener in this dialogue.</note>, lies the greatest danger for man. For this reason, we must use every effort so that each of us, neglecting all other studies, may seek and follow this discipline: to be able to know and choose a good life from a bad one, and to always choose the better path from all those available. One must consider all that we are saying now: how these things, joined or separated, contribute to a virtuous life. One must understand what beauty combined with poverty or wealth does to the soul, and what kind of character it produces. Or what nobility, low birth, private life, power, strength, weakness, a quick mind, or a slow one—and all such natural or acquired traits—produce when woven together. Thus, from all these things, one can consider the nature of the soul and distinguish the better life from the worse, looking toward the soul’s nature. He calls that the "worse" life which makes the soul more unjust, and the "better" life that which makes it more just. All other things he should despise. For we have seen that this choice is the best for both the living and the dead. With this conviction, firm as a...

<column-break/>

...diamond <note>original: "adamantis." Referring to the hardest, most unbreakable substance; a metaphor for unshakeable resolve.</note>, one must set out for the underworld, so that even there, one is not dazzled by wealth and such evils, nor falls into tyrannies or similar actions that lead to many incurable crimes and the suffering of even worse things. Instead, one should know how to always choose the middle path between such extremes, both in this life and the next; for in this way, a person becomes most blessed. For as the messenger who returned from there reported, the prophet said: even for the one who comes last, if he chooses with prudence, a desirable life is available—not a bad one for the person who lives earnestly. Let not the first chooser be negligent, nor the last be discouraged. When he had said this, he reported that the one who had drawn the first lot immediately ran and chose the greatest tyranny. Out of ignorance and greed, he did not examine the details sufficiently; thus, he failed to notice that it was fated in that life for him to devour his own children and suffer many other evils. But when he examined the chosen life at leisure, he beat his breast and lamented the harmful choice, not following the prophet's warning nor blaming himself as the cause of his misfortunes, but rather blaming fortune, the spirits, and everything else instead of himself. He was one of those who had descended from heaven; he had lived his previous life in a well-ordered city and had practiced virtue by habit, but without the study of philosophy. Indeed, no fewer of those who fall from above are deceived in their choice than others, as they are inexperienced in suffering. Most of those who came from the earth, however—having themselves labored through calamities and seen others labor—did not choose their lives haphazardly. Because of this, and also because of the luck of the draw, a change of "good" and "bad" fortune happens for many souls. Furthermore, if anyone always philosophizes sincerely whenever he comes into this life, and if the lot of choice does not fall to him last, it appears from these reports that he will not only be happy here, but his journey from here to there and back again will not be an earthly and rough one, but smooth and celestial. He said it was a spectacle worth seeing: how the individual souls chose their individual lives. It was a miserable, ridiculous, and wondrous sight to behold. For the most part, the choice was made according to the habits of the previous life. For he said he saw the soul that had once belonged to Orpheus <note>The legendary musician and poet who, according to myth, was torn apart by women (the Maenads) and thus developed a hatred for the sex.</note> choosing the life of a swan; because of his hatred for womankind, he was un-

<meta>This page continues the "Myth of Er" from the end of Plato’s *Republic*. ### Chapter II.

...had been destined to be born. He said he saw the soul of **Thamyris** <note>A legendary singer who competed with the Muses.</note> choose the life of a nightingale. He also saw a swan choose to change to a human life, and other musical animals did the same, as is fitting. From among the other lots, one chose the life of a lion; he said this was the soul of **Ajax**, the son of Telamon, who fled from becoming a man because he was still brooding over the famous judgment regarding the arms <note>After the death of Achilles, Ajax lost a contest for his armor to Odysseus and died in despair; here he avoids humanity out of bitterness.</note>. After him came the soul of **Agamemnon**; out of hatred for the human race because of his past sufferings, he took up the life of an eagle. The soul of **Atalanta**, however, who happened upon a lot somewhere in the middle, saw the great honors bestowed upon an athlete and said she could not restrain herself from choosing the life of a competitor. Next, he saw the soul of **Epeius** <note>The builder of the Trojan Horse.</note>, the son of Panopeus, passing into the nature of a craftswoman. Far among the very last, the soul of the ridiculous **Thersites** <note>A soldier in the Iliad known for mocking his superiors.</note> put on the form of a monkey. By chance, the soul of **Ulysses** <note>Odysseus.</note> happened to have the very last lot of all. He said Ulysses came forward to choose last, but because of his memory of his former labors, his ambition had ceased. For a long time, he went around searching for the life of a private man who stayed out of trouble. He finally found it lying somewhere, neglected by the others. Upon finding it, he said he would not have chosen any other life even if he had drawn the first lot, and so he gladly embraced that life. He asserted that souls also pass from wild beasts into humans, and change in turn among themselves: the unjust into savage beasts, while the just take up the lives of gentle animals. In this way, all the mixtures of lives are completed. When all the souls had chosen their lives in the order the lot had given them, he saw them approach **Lachesis** <note>The first of the three Fates; her name means "Allotter."</note> in a long line. Lachesis then assigned to each the guardian spirit <note>original: "demonem." In Plato's thought, a *daemon* is a personal destiny or guiding spirit.</note> they had received, to be the guardian of their life and the fulfiller of the choices they had made. This spirit first leads the soul to **Clotho** <note>The second Fate; her name means "Spinner."</note>, placing it under her hand and the turning of her spindle to confirm the fortune it had chosen by lot. After touching the spindle, the spirit leads the soul to the spinning of **Atropos** <note>The third Fate; her name means "Inflexible." She cuts the thread of life.</note>, making the woven threads unchangeable. From there, they go quickly to the throne of **Necessity**. When they had all passed through it, they proceeded through a fierce heat and scorched air into the **Plain of Lethe** <note>The "Plain of Forgetfulness."</note>, a place utterly devoid of trees or anything that grows from the earth. As night approached, he said they camped by the **River Ameles** <note>The "River of Carelessness" or "Unmindfulness."</note>, whose water no vessel can hold. Every soul is required to drink a certain amount of this water, but those who are not guided by wisdom drink more than is proper. As one drinks, he begins 

<column-break/>

to forget everything. When they had slept until midnight, there was a sudden clap of thunder and an earthquake, and they were suddenly tossed upward, one here, one there, toward their new births, shooting up like stars. Er himself, however, was forbidden to drink from that river. He said he did not know how he returned to his body, but suddenly, looking around at dawn, he found himself lying upon the funeral pyre. And so, O **Glaucon**, the story was saved and did not perish. It will save us likewise if we obey it, and if we cross the **Lethe** (that is, the River of Forgetfulness) well, we shall not stain our souls with any blemish. Therefore, if we listen to my words, believing the soul to be immortal and capable of enduring all evils and all goods, we will always follow the path that leads upward. We will practice justice with wisdom in every way, so that we may be friends to ourselves and to the gods while we live this life, and after we have carried off the prizes of virtue like victors in a triumph. Thus, both here and in that thousand-year journey we have described, we may fare well. So says **Plato**. But is this a history or a fable? **Justin**, the Platonist and Christian martyr, wants it to be a history. I certainly will not refute that. However, where Plato calls it an "apologue" or "fable," it could be explained that a history can be called a fable when it contains an allegory deeper than the mere events themselves. For this reason, **Olympiodorus** also says that Plato often called histories and rational accounts "fables." And since he arranges the spirits, the places of justice, and the figures differently in the *Phaedrus*, the *Gorgias*, the *Phaedo*, and here, it is clearly evident that besides the literal form of the place, it contains an allegorical meaning. But why did he assert the mystery of immortality here through a historical example rather than through diligent argumentation? Because citizens are provoked to justice not so much by the artifice of words as by examples and deeds. Furthermore, why does he bring forward a man rising from the dead to confirm this? Because even if immortality is established by reason, along with the general execution of justice, it is still necessary to receive the description of the place, form, and arrangement of either reward or punishment from one who was actually there—which is hinted to us near the end of the *Phaedo*. Nor is it without reason that he testifies that **Er the Pamphylian** <note>Ficino uses "Herum Pamphilium." In the original Greek, Er is the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian.</note> rose again after dying in battle for the safety of his country: it signifies that those who die for the public good will rise again to the true life, just as he rose from among many the living to return to ours.

Book on the Supercelestial Life, Chapters 3 and 4.

## ¶ Regarding the celestial earth according to Aristotle. Chapter 3.

Although Plato has spoken abundantly about the celestial earth which our theologians call paradise, listen nonetheless to how **Aristotle**—who seemed to many to be so insane in his theology that they called him "demonic" while calling Plato "divine"—also approved this doctrine in the first book of *On the Heavens and the Earth* <note>Aristotle, *De Caelo* 1.9.</note> near the end, saying:
"Those things which have been brought forth outside the heavens are beings that possess the best life, and are in themselves most sufficient; they fulfill this life through all eternity, not aging with time, nor changing in place, nor subject to alteration or suffering, being foreign to all motion and change. As has been declared by many arguments regarding divine matters, every primary divine thing is unchangeable, necessary, supreme; there is nothing else better than it, nothing more divine, containing nothing wicked and lacking no good thing. It moves according to reason with unceasing motion. The end of all things is the time of each one's life, and a supreme perfection containing all time and infinity, eternal, always being, immortal, from which being and living are communicated to all other things—to some more clearly, to others more obscurely." Thus speaks Aristotle.

## ¶ Regarding the glory of the supercelestial paradise according to the Christians. Chapter 4.

But why should I continue to praise Plato, Aristotle, and the other philosophers who spoke of the celestial earth for so long? They are essentially nothing but shadows of the Christians, just as earthly things are shadows of the celestial. O true light above the ether! A light so true that it cannot be truly expressed. O truth shining wonderfully above the heavens, shining through so miraculously that no one can ever wonder at it enough according to its dignity, since it wonderfully surpasses wonder itself. Here alone one lives most truly, most clearly, most excellently, and most joyfully, where all life is nothing other than truth, clarity, goodness, and the fullest joy. Here, in that immense light of lights, we behold the lights of the **Ideas** <note>In Christian Neoplatonism, "Ideas" are the eternal forms or thoughts in the mind of God.</note> joined together, and in those lights we clearly see individual truths, just as if one were to look into the sun and see all the rays emanating from it, and within those rays, see the individual colors created there. Thus it happens that however much the desire of the intellect may gorge itself and drink here, it nonetheless remains always thirsty. But in paradise, because "man will see face to face" and "know just as he is known," <note>Quoting 1 Corinthians 13:12.</note> that which is partial, small, and incomplete shall be done away with. And our immense

<column-break/>

desire will be completely satisfied when 그 all-forming essence, which is the First Truth, reveals itself to our intelligence. Then at last that saying shall be fulfilled: "Be still, and see that I am God." <note>original: "Vacate ⁊ videre qm ego sum de?" from Psalm 46:10.</note> Of that city the Prophet said: "Glorious things are spoken of you, O city of God." <note>Psalm 87:3.</note> and "How lovely are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord." <note>Psalm 84:1-2.</note> And "As the deer longs for the fountains of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?" <note>Psalm 42:1-2.</note> Here the philosophers dispute concerning the "end of goods"—that is, concerning **blessedness** <term>beatitudo: the state of supreme happiness or the "Highest Good"</term>—and the curious industry of those seeking it in this life has increased so much, without ever finding it, that as **Augustine** witnesses in the 19th book of *The City of God*, the number of sects speaking about blessedness was brought by **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar.</note> to two hundred and eighty-eight. Our paradise abundantly includes the ends of all these sects, if any of them touch upon any true goodness. For it so intoxicates every appetite for pleasure with its own most redundant pleasure that the free will placed within it is deprived of the power to sin. Yet this is not a lessening of liberty, but an increase. For that liberty is far more excellent which is able to will only those things that will never be displeasing, rather than being able to will things which it must eventually wish it had not. Then "God will be all in all." <note>1 Corinthians 15:28.</note> This means that God will supply whatever each individual desires, for he will flow into our minds with such sweetness that what is said by the prophet will be perfectly fulfilled: "I shall be satisfied when your glory appears" (or as it is in the Hebrew: "your image"). <note>Psalm 17:15. The author notes a translation difference between the Latin Vulgate (*gloria*) and the Hebrew (*temunah*, meaning likeness or form).</note>

## ¶ To what glory the intellectual soul might arrive. Chapter 5.

No one shall dwell in the glory of the mountain of the Lord except him who walks here without stain, so that he may follow the "spotless lamb who takes away the sins of the world" <note>John 1:29.</note> wherever he goes in the most fertile pastures. But he who departs from this valley of tears carrying stains that have not been anointed with the oil of compunction <note>Sincere regret or remorse that "softens" the soul.</note> nor purged by the heat of fire, shall be cast forth into the outer darkness, into the lowest hell. Moreover, souls are led <margin>Luke 16.</margin> to this mountain of glory by holy angels, as the Lord witnesses concerning the soul of the beggar **Lazarus**. Nor <margin>Matthew 18.</margin> is it a wonder if they are led into rest by those whom they had as helpers and guardians in their labor, for they always behold the face of God; for the Lord says: "Their angels always see the face of my Father." Concerning which our **Saint Jerome** says: "Great is the dignity of souls, that each one from the beginning of its birth has an angel assigned for its protection." Study to please this angel with spiritual prayer, and in...

# Chapter V.

Fear to act wickedly always in His sight, so that when the proportions of your body are dissolved <note>That is, at the moment of death.</note>, He may lead your soul to the mountain of glory established in the field of delight. There, who could strive to enumerate how much glory, how much joy, and how much happiness there is? For the Apostle, caught up to the third heaven, says: <margin>1 Corinthians 2</margin> "Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, etc." <note>original: "Nec oculus vidit: nec auris audiuit zc." from 1 Corinthians 2:9, describing the wonders of heaven.</note> Indeed, for the soul which here has been pledged as a bride <note>original: "subarrata est," referring to a betrothal pledge.</note> to the Son of the Eternal Father through faith, hope, and charity, when she is brought to her Bridegroom, her heart will be adorned and endowed with corresponding **dowries**. These <margin>Dowries of the soul</margin> are **vision**, **love**, and **enjoyment** <term>fruitio: the ultimate spiritual satisfaction in possessing God</term>, in which the entire happiness of the soul is embraced—if you add the security of it never ending. For as Saint Augustine says in Book 13 of *The Trinity*, Chapter 8: "A life cannot be blessed unless it is immortal." The principal acts of glory by which the soul is turned toward God as the essential reward of blessedness are distinguished as three: namely, **to see**, **to love**, and **to enjoy**. For the **rational power**, whose role now is to believe through faith, will then see openly. "We shall see Him," <margin>1 John 3</margin> says John in his canonical letter, "as He is, face to face." The **desiring power** <term>concupiscibilis: the faculty of the soul that desires good</term>, whose role here is to love, will then love perfectly without interruption. The **spirited power** <term>irascibilis: the faculty of the soul that strives for difficult goods</term>, whose role here is to be raised up and strive for high things through hope, will then certainly grasp and hold them, continually and with security. Thus, first, the **intellect** will be perfected by the beatific and clear vision. Second, the **will** by the most perfect and sweetest love. Third, the **memory** by the firmest security and continual retention; and so the whole soul is perfected in the most joyful enjoyment. Hence, Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux, a 12th-century mystic.</note> says: "God will be the fullness of light to the intellect, the multitude of peace to the will, and the continuation of eternity to the memory." Someone might ask how we shall see God there, which our theologians teach is the essential reward of blessedness. The prudent reader will answer that God, according to the property of His nature, cannot be seen with bodily eyes, neither here nor after the final resurrection, since He is incorporeal. So Augustine argued when writing to Fortunatus. And if a scrap of hesitation or doubt remains, let him take as witnesses <margin>1 John 4</margin> the Apostle John, saying: "No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has made Him known." <margin>1 Timothy 6</margin> Also the divine Paul writing to Timothy concerning God: "Whom no man has seen, nor can see." However, where we read in many places of Scripture that God was seen by men, it was not through the proper nature of the Deity, but through an assumed creaturely form as it pleased Him. Therefore, we shall not see with these bodily eyes which we use here,

<column-break/>

but the most learned men already mentioned assert that God is to be seen with the eyes of the mind. Thus, they say, we must understand what Christ said: <margin>Matthew 5</margin> "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." Regarding these eyes, Paul also wrote to the <margin>Ephesians 1</margin> Ephesians, saying: "May He give you the enlightened eyes of your heart for the knowledge of Him." Concerning the happiness of souls in the homeland <note>original: "in patria," a common theological term for Heaven.</note>, Augustine writes as follows in the book *On the Threefold Dwelling*: "Indeed, there will be a constant reading of the **Book of Life**, that is, of eternal truth, supreme wisdom, and the Word of God, which is the vision of Jesus Christ, where whatever now lies hidden from us will be made manifest." There the reason is manifest: why this one was chosen and that one rejected; why this one was taken into the kingdom and that one reduced to servitude. Why one dies in the womb, another in infancy, another in youth, another in old age. Why one is poor and another rich. Why the son of an adulteress is baptized, while sometimes the son of a lawful wife dies before baptism. Why one who begins to live well sometimes ends poorly, and one who begins poorly often ends well. And all these things and many like them will be plain and open to everyone in the **Book of Life**. There the good of all will be open to all. There everyone will know each other's kinships. There the least person will undoubtedly have greater glory than one possessing the kingdom of the whole world, even if it were eternal. So great is the delight of eternal light that even if one were not allowed to stay in it longer than a single day, for this reason alone, the countless years of this life—though full of delights and surrounded by temporal goods—would rightly and deservedly be despised. For it was not said with false or small affection: <margin>Psalm 84</margin> "For one day in your courts is better than a thousand." And a little further down, the same Augustine says: "If all those shut up in the prison of hell saw the face of God, they would feel no punishment, no pain, and no sadness." If His presence appeared in hell with its holy inhabitants, hell would immediately be turned into a pleasant paradise. And further in the same work: "There, through the mirror of divine clarity, we shall see God Himself as He is, as far as is possible for a creature, and we shall know with certain knowledge." Then we shall see the hidden things of creatures and of hell itself. Then it will be manifest to the just how God is invisible, incomparable, without beginning, and without end, before all things. What is the difference between being "born" (which pertains to the Son) and "proceeding" (which pertains to the Holy Spirit), except that one is born of one, and the other proceeded from two. And how the Father did not precede the Son in time but in origin, nor the Holy Spirit. And how all...

# Book I on the Supercelestial Life, Chapter VI.

All things in God are one in God: except for what pertains to their relationship to one another <note>original: "excepto quod ad relationem pertinet." This is a standard theological point: in the Trinity, all is one except for the distinct relations between Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>. And how the world was in God before it was in itself: it was not the world, but God. And how He is everywhere entirely without being in a specific place; great without quantity; good without quality. And how He penetrates all things: the pure and the impure alike without polluting Himself. See these things which the divine Augustine pursues most clearly in the aforementioned book, and moreover in the *Soliloquy*, the *Manual of Meditations*, the *Enchiridion* (Chapter 94), and at the end of *The City of God*. In these "Elysian fields," the chosen will see as they gaze upon God, and this vision will satisfy the whole man, as the royal prophet says: <note>original: "regio propheta," referring to King David.</note> "I shall be satisfied when your glory shall appear."

## Chapter Six.

There are those among our writers who say that the immense pleasure of the intellectual part—the source of which is well known to everyone—overflows and, as it were, pours over and is channeled into the sensitive powers <term>potentias sensibiles: the faculties of the five physical senses</term>. This is just as we experience in various accidents of the soul <note>Here, "accidents" means temporary emotions or states of mind.</note> how the body is affected: a body that was healthy just a moment before when the mind was peaceful, now falls ill when the mind is disturbed. And what manner of glory might suffice for all the senses? Truly, concerning hearing and sight, something specific must be said according to what the Lord has granted to His humble servant. For the blessed shall hear the most delightful praises of God resonating from every side, according to that word of the prophet: 
<margin>Psalm 84</margin>
"Blessed are they who dwell in your house, O Lord: they will praise you forever and ever." Likewise, they shall see the heavens and perceive all the harmony of the spheres. They shall see Jesus Himself and Mary His mother, and all the glorious bodies of all the blessed. These bodies, so incorruptible and conspicuous in their miraculous beauty, will become so sweet a spectacle to the eyes' gaze that the blessed will not know what better thing could be desired. And as Augustine testifies in the book *On the Triple Dwelling*:
<margin>The threefold vision of the chosen</margin>
the chosen of God will have a **threefold vision**. **Intellectual**: by which they will see God in the spirit with the pure eye of the mind, as well as their own souls, their innermost virtues, and the angelic spirits. **Spiritual**: by which they will behold the likenesses of bodies in the spirit, not through a deceptive fantasy <term>fantasia: mental images or "phantasms" that can be misleading in this life</term>; the spirits of the righteous, currently released from their bodies, already enjoy this vision today. And **Corporeal**: by which they shall perceive physical bodies, some of which will be as splendid as the sun, others like the moon, and others like the stars. This too will be most delightful to the sight: for just as we now perceive the soul to be within the body by its motion,

<column-break/>

and see it give life to and rule the bodily members, so then we shall see, with a gaze beyond doubt, that God is innermost to the heavens, the elements, and all things, being whole in every part of the universe, and that He preserves, nourishes, and governs this machine of the world. Now, reason persuades us well enough of this and we believe it; yet, because of our natural ignorance, we do not fully grasp it. Then, however, turning our eyes in every direction, we shall grasp it. For so great will be the power in our eyes, and so sharp the keenness of our seeing, that the blessed, penetrating with their sight the sizes, numbers, proportions, harmonies, symmetry, and the entire nature of our bodies, the elements, and the heavens, shall be intoxicated by the abundance of the house of God, and shall say: 
<margin>Psalm 132</margin>
"This is my rest forever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen it." Indeed, knowledge will then be destroyed as far as the *act* is concerned, but not as far as the *habit* <note>In scholastic philosophy, "habit" refers to the permanent possession of knowledge, while "act" refers to the process of learning or thinking through something step-by-step. We won't need to "study" anymore because we will simply "know."</note>. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 13: "Charity never fails." And soon after: "Knowledge," he says, "shall be destroyed." For then the intellect, in understanding, will not turn itself toward mental images <term>fantasmata: the sensory data the brain uses to think</term>, for there will be none; however, the "species" <note>The essential forms or mental concepts of things.</note> will remain. Wherefore also the divine Augustine says in Book 4 of *The Trinity*, Chapter 2: "Then," he says, "we shall remember this mortal life, and we shall recall in our memory that we once believed what we did not see." Add to this that for the blessed, nothing will be impassable, nothing closed, nothing inaccessible; but by a wonderful subtlety and agility of the body, they shall be carried without the service of feet to wherever the fire of the will desires. Thus the body will be so obedient and subject to the command of the soul that no mass shall hinder the ascent, no weariness shall hinder continuous motion, and finally, no labor shall stand in the way. There have been those who said that in the instruments of the other senses, a quality would be generated by God through which they would grow sweet with a certain honey-flowing and nectar-like pleasure. But whatever should be said about a quality of this kind, one thing is certain: humans destined for eternal life are to be so established by God through **metamorphosis** <term>metamorphosim: a total transformation or glorification of the physical body</term> that there is nothing in them that is not blessed. They are gifted with these rewards and decorated with these crowns by God—not those who conquered cities or provinces, but those who conquered the flesh, the world, and the devil. Nor does He only render the rewards due to the victors, but He adds many great bonuses, gifts, grants, and a feast; all of which Christ promised in the Gospel, saying: 
<margin>Luke 12</margin>
"He will have them sit at table, and passing among them, He will serve them." By this it is implied that God will show His saints every kindness of humanity, every duty of liberality, every kind of magnificence, and every sign of charity. Then, moreover, when the soul has shed its fleshly weight, it will be able to freely and immediately abstract "intelligible species" <term>species intelligibiles: the pure concepts of things stripped of their physical matter</term> from the objects present; and it will understand not only through abstraction...

...tively <note>This continues a sentence from the previous page, likely discussing "abstractive" vs. "intuitive" cognition.</note> when objects are withdrawn, but also intuitively when objects are present. <margin>Avicenna</margin>

There are, however, Catholic men who assert that the knowledge which souls acquire anew when stripped of the body does not come through species <term>species: mental images or representations of things</term> received from objects, but through those flowed into them by God.

The soul itself is content by this very fact: that its own Good is incomprehensible; nor would it be content if that Good were capable of being fully grasped. And because the glory of the blessed is derived from the soul, he who shines with greater glory than others will not exalt himself, nor will he who has less envy the other.

### Chapter 7.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'Q' containing floral and leaf motifs inside a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
Why then, O living soul, are you content that He does not place a limit on your life? Why should you comprehend or define it, since it is infinite? Rather, I know that you rejoice in this very thing: that your life and your Good are without end. It is enough for you to be happily "grasped" by the Incomprehensible; indeed, nothing is enough for you unless it is incomprehensible. For whatever truth or goodness is offered that has certain limits, you require even more through your intellect and desire even further through your will. Therefore, you can rest nowhere except in the Truth and the immense Good, and you can place no boundaries except in the Infinite. Indeed, you depend upon the Infinite alone, and from that source you possess a power that is in some way infinite, by which you incline toward and progress toward the Infinite. 

But these things seem to contradict what was said before, where it was concluded that the blessed are satisfied by all good things. How can one be satisfied and at rest while seeing in others great goods that he himself lacks? This is impossible among the children of this world, where, according to the voice of the poet:
<margin>Ovid</margin>
"The envious man wastes away at the rich possessions of another." <note>original: "Invidus alterius rebus marcescit opimis." From Ovid’s *Epistles*.</note>

There in heaven, however, in place of envy there is charity; in place of hatred there will be a perfect love, and so great that in that same city (as Augustine expressed it) the possession of each will belong to all, and the possession of all will belong to each through charity. There, no superior will be proud, and no inferior will be envious. And in the *Manual*, in the penultimate chapter, the same Augustine says: 

"If any other person whom you loved entirely as yourself possessed the same happiness, your joy would be doubled, because you would rejoice no less for him than for yourself. If indeed two or three or many more possessed that same thing, you would rejoice just as much for each of them as for yourself, provided you loved each as yourself." 

Therefore, what will it be like in that perfect charity of 

<column-break/>

innumerable blessed angels and men, where no one will love another less than himself? For each one will rejoice for every other no differently than for himself. If, then, the heart of man can scarcely contain its own joy from such a great good, how will it be capable of containing so many and such great joys? And surely, since each person rejoices in another's good as much as he loves that person, so in that blessed happiness, each one will love God incomparably more than himself and all others with him. Thus, he will rejoice beyond estimation more in the happiness of God than in his own and that of all others with him. 

Such and so great will be the enjoyment <term>fruitio: a technical term for the joy found in possessing the ultimate Good</term> of the ever-blessed and most excellent Trinity (which things to be enjoyed are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as Augustine says in Book 1 of *On Christian Doctrine*), as great as the knowledge and love of it shall be. For "to enjoy" (as the same author writes) is to cling to something with love for its own sake; and "to use" <term>uti: the act of using a means to reach an end, contrasted with 'frui' or enjoyment of the end itself</term> is with joy, not yet of hope, but now of the thing itself. However, because we cannot love unknown things (as he writes in the same place), we enjoy known things in which the will, delighted by the things for their own sake, finds its rest. 

The same Doctor, in the *Manual* and the *Soliloquy*, prays to the Lord, saying:
> I pray you, my God, that I may know you, that I may love you, so that I may rejoice in you; and if I cannot do so to the full in this life, let my knowledge of you progress here, so that there it may be made full.

<margin>Daniel 12</margin>
The angel said to Daniel concerning the blessed:
> But those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto justice, like stars for all eternity.

There are, however, others who, with a more subtle deception, use "not learning" as a cover for their laziness. For they say that the celestial hierarchy is not bounded by the fullness of knowledge, but by the height of charity. Hence, the Seraphim <note>The highest order of angels, associated with burning love.</note>, who are named from the fullness of charity, are the supreme order, beneath whom are the Cherubim <note>The second order of angels, associated with the fullness of knowledge.</note>, who took their name from the fullness of knowledge. However, Catholic thinkers deny that there is less knowledge in the Seraphim than in the Cherubim, as is clear in the second book of the *Sentences*, distinction 9.
<margin>Thomas [Aquinas], dist. 9</margin>

Therefore, the Seraphim excel the Cherubim in knowledge just as much as they exceed them in charity. That supreme order is named after charity as the more noble gift of God, toward which knowledge is certainly ordered. The Cherubim, however, had to be named after knowledge rather than charity because the higher order had already claimed the name from charity for itself. Knowledge alone, therefore, does not lead to happiness, but it will be profitable if ordered toward charity. For knowledge, as the Apostle testifies, "puffs up" without charity. 
<margin>1 Corinthians 7 <note>The text cites Chapter 7, but this quote is from 1 Corinthians 8:1.</note></margin>
For the "puffed up" and the proud, no entrance will be open in that celestial region.

# Books on the Supercelestial Life
# Chapter 8.

Column 1:
<margin>God is one for a threefold reason.</margin>
### ¶ Concerning God according to the Platonists, Zoroaster, Orpheus, and the Sibyls. Chapter 8.

God is the highest of all things. Therefore, God is one and simple. Indeed, one supreme unity, one supreme truth, and one supreme goodness: one God. I say he is "one" according to the Platonists <note>Followers of the philosopher Plato, who emphasized the existence of abstract "Forms" and a single source of all being.</note> for a threefold reason. First, because he is the supreme unity. For if anything supreme is unique, what is more unique than the supreme unity itself? Every individual multitude of innumerable things is reduced back to its own proper unity. The multitude of innumerable men is reduced to one human species; of horses, to one equine species; and similarly for others. Next, take all these proper unities, which are limited to a certain number—that is, the species of things—and gather them into one common unity: namely, God, the prince of species. Just as the infinite multitudes of individuals are referred to the finite unities of species, so too it is fitting that the finite unities of species be referred to a single unity above all species. It is only right that just as each individual order of things is directed toward its own single principle, so the entire universe of things should be referred to one universal principle. And just as all individual matters are referred to one matter, and all members of the world to one body, so all the natures of the world are referred to one nature, all lives of the world to one life, all motions to one motion, and all movers to one mover of the world. Therefore, the ordainer of this one world is one God. He is "one," I say, by the first reasoning of the Platonists: because he is unity. He is also "one" by their second reasoning: because he is truth. For the supreme truth is one. If two supreme truths were said to exist, either one of them would have whatever the other has, or it would not. If the first is granted, then they are one, not two. If the second, neither is supreme; for this one lacks that truth which is in the other, and that one lacks what is in this one. Again, God is one by the third reasoning of the Platonists because he is the supreme goodness. Indeed, the supreme goodness embraces whatever good can possibly be found. Therefore, if you were to introduce two supreme goodnesses, whatever good is in one is also in the other; otherwise, neither would be supreme; and by the very nature of goodness itself, they are one, not two. Nor is there anything else mixed into them besides the nature of goodness; for if there were, they would not be supreme, but tainted. Therefore, they are altogether one. Nor is God prohibited from penetrating through all things by anything else, for nothing resists his infinite purity and power.

<column-break/>

Nor should it be thought that this Goodness is less present to the whole world than the soul is present to the whole body. For the world is less in relation to God than the body is to the soul, and the world needs God more than the body needs the soul. For if the "first patient" <note>original: "primum patiens," referring to matter or essence as that which receives action or form.</note> which is matter and essence, is propagated through all things, much more does the "first agent" <note>original: "primum agens," the active force or creator.</note> which is God, propagate himself through all things and beyond all things. God is therefore in all things because all things are in him; for unless they were in him, they would be nowhere, and they would not exist at all. For nothing is ever desired except the good, and nothing is ever found except the true. God is every good; God is every truth. God is amplitude and fullness itself. I do not see, therefore, why he would not amplify himself through all things and fill every single thing.

<margin>Orpheus on God</margin>
Wisely, therefore, Orpheus <note>A legendary Greek poet and musician whose "hymns" were central to a mystical philosophical tradition.</note> says in the *Hymn to Saturn*: "You who dwell in all parts of the world, the prince of generation." Let us often contemplate a certain most pure capacity, which no limits can ever contain, but which contains whatever can be or can be imagined. Reason dictates that what is everywhere named is nothing other than the universal nature of things, and that this is God. Therefore, when we say that God is everywhere, it must be understood that he is in himself, and vice versa—this is beyond doubt. For it is more excellent to "always be," which is, as it were, intrinsic, than to "be everywhere," which is, as it were, extrinsic. Therefore, that which can always be can much more easily be everywhere. For it is easier to exceed sluggish dimensions <note>original: "pigras dimensiones," likely referring to the static measurements of physical space.</note> than to exceed the effective motion of quality and time. God does not look upon things in themselves, but in himself; not through their images, but through his own essence. He is not distracted by many things, but beholds all things as one. He never labors, he does not seek, but he possesses. He is not diverted from weightier matters to consider lighter ones, because with the same intuition he sees these and those—like an eye which with one gaze beholds many stars in the sky. All of this Orpheus sang in the *Hymn to Apollo*: "You who hold the boundaries of the entire world. To you belongs the beginning and the end. Through you all things flourish. You temper the whole sphere with your resounding lyre."

<margin>Zoroaster on God</margin>
The followers of Zoroaster <note>An ancient Persian prophet whose teachings were often blended with Platonism in the Renaissance.</note> pass down the idea that God, in a certain way, acts upon himself. Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who expanded on Plato's ideas.</note> explained this in nearly the same manner as I am about to say: God is act—not of another, nor concerning another—but of himself and concerning himself. For he is act remaining within himself. Because he is act on account of the nature of the infinite good, and infinitely productive, he does not lack an "acted" thing—that is, a begotten thing—namely, an infinite "acted" reality. But since an internal thing is created through an internal act, and he alone is infinite, that which is acted upon or begotten therefrom...

Drawing on Orpheus and Zoroaster, the text describes God as an all-encompassing presence who beholds all of creation through his own essence rather than external images.</summary>

Concerning the divine nature, Orpheus sang divinely: "Rolling a swift impulse on a perpetual axis." <note>Orpheus was a legendary Greek poet and prophet; in the Renaissance, "Orphic" hymns were believed to contain ancient divine wisdom.</note> Concerning Jove <note>The Roman name for Zeus, here used to represent the supreme God.</note>, the same Orpheus said: "Begetter of all things: the beginning and the end." Zoroaster <note>The ancient Iranian prophet, seen by Renaissance thinkers as a primary source of "Ancient Theology" alongside Plato.</note> says: "The Father perfected all things and surrendered them to the second mind."

### ¶ Concerning the Word of God according to Plato. Chapter 9.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'P' featuring interlaced white vine-work patterns against a dark cross-hatched background within a square border.</image-desc>
Let us hear that Plato, whom holy men call "the Divine." He used words of this kind in the *Epinomis*: "I do not praise some for years, others for months, and others for no time at all, in which alone the world runs its course; one and efficient Word <note>original: "verbum" — translating the Greek "Logos," referring to the divine reason or speech that orders the universe.</note> of Him has ordained it, which is the most divine of all things." And in the letter to three of his dearest friends—I mean Hermias, Eraston, and Coriscus—he commended this most sacred doctrine to them with these very cautious words: "You three," he said, "shall read this letter together, or at least two of you together as often as you can, with confirmed diligence, elegance, and zeal, and its sister, doctrine: so that you may swear by the God who is the prince of all things present and future, and by the Father and cause of the prince and lord. If we philosophize rightly, we shall know clearly all that can happen to man." Does it not seem that Plato labored over the Hebrew scriptures? For from where else could he have learned to call God "Father and Lord," and to speak of the God who is the Father of the Prince and Lord?

<meta>This page continues the "testimony" of ancient philosophers regarding the divine Word (Logos). Having cited Orpheus and Mercury in the previous section, the author now turns to the heavyweight of the tradition, Plato, before moving into the Neopythagorean and Jewish-Platonic traditions represented by Numenius and Philo. The goal remains to show that the Christian Trinity was foreshadowed in the highest schools of ancient thought.</meta>

<header>The Book on the Supercelestial Life, Chapters 10 and 11.</header>

naming: Who among the Greeks, Egyptians, or Sicilians—those people Plato visited—ever claimed that the world was set in order by the most divine Word? Since Plato attributes the cause of things to the Mind, the followers of Plato argue in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue on the creation of the universe and the "Demiurge" or architect.</note> that the intellect of the Good itself was the son and architect of the world, existing from the beginning. Concerning this, as we have said, it is written in the *Epinomis*: "The most divine reason (or most divine Word) adorned the visible world." <note>original: "ratio divinissima" or "divinissimum verbum".</note> He calls this Goodness both "Father" and "Lord"—the first to designate the Father of the Mind, the second as the Lord of the Soul. 

Perhaps a Platonic mathematician would explain the numbers this way. So too would a "Platonic Christian"; however, an Arian <note>Followers of Arius, an early Christian priest who taught that the Son was a created being subordinate to the Father.</note> might understand the Holy Spirit as the Leader and the Son as the Mind. For where Plato says "Father," he implies "Son" as well. Even if someone posits one essence for the Three, they might seem to oppose the Platonists, but they would not clearly contradict Plato himself. Plato’s words in the new translation <note>Likely the Latin translation by Marsilio Ficino, which was standard in the Renaissance.</note> are: "Swearing by God, the leader of all things present and future, and the Father and Lord of the leader and the cause." 

In his second epistle, Plato spoke thus of God: "All things are around the King of all; all things exist for his sake; he is the cause of all beautiful things. Secondary things are around the second; tertiary things around the third." The human soul longs to understand what these are, looking upon things related to itself. Some interpret Plato's words thus: "All things are around the King of all," meaning Ideas are around the Good itself; for through Ideas, all things exist. "Around the second," meaning the Mind; around it are the reasons that follow the Ideas. "Around the third," meaning around the Soul of the World are the forms. 

He indicated that God is the *exemplary cause* <term>exemplary cause: the blueprint or model (Ideas) after which something is made</term> when he said "around." He showed God as the *final cause* <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or goal for which something exists</term> when he said "for his sake." Finally, he showed him as the *efficient cause* <term>efficient cause: the actual agent or force that brings something into being</term> when he added "He is the cause of all beautiful things." For even if some things are deformed, they are not so because they come from him, but because they have fallen away from him.

### ¶On the Word of God according to Numenius. Chapter 10.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial N decorated with floral motifs within a square woodcut border.</image-desc>
Numenius, that philosopher and theologian <note>Numenius of Apamea, a 2nd-century philosopher who famously asked, "What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?"</note>, in his book *On the Good*, uses these words: "He who desires to understand anything about the first and second God must first distinguish each in order; otherwise, his study will pour out its treasure in vain. Lest we suffer this, let us begin by invoking God as the leader of this discourse, that he may draw out the treasure of our thought. We must pray first, then distinguish. The first God, being in himself, is indivisible and simple."

<column-break/>

"The second and third God is one; and being inherent in matter (which is duality), he unites it, even though it would otherwise dissipate from that which contains and flows entirely." And a little later: "It is not fitting," he says, "for the first God to create, but to be the Father of the created gods." And progressing further: "The first God, the King of all, must cease from all labor. But we say the Creator God governs all things: from him, the inner mind is sent to all things, which are ordered for his communication. Therefore, when God turns toward us and looks upon us, it is by his rays that we live; our bodies too are nourished and live. But when God turns himself back into his own height, then bodies are extinguished, but the mind lives a more blessed life." 

And elsewhere Numenius writes: "Just as there is a certain logic for a farmer regarding plants, so it is with the first God in relation to the Creator. For the first, being the seed of all life, sows all things; but the Creator plants and distributes and transfers to each of us what has been cast from there." To show how the second God comes from the first: "Human things," he says, "pass from the giver to the receiver; but divine things are given by God and are not absent from him. This is like knowledge: he who receives it is made better, yet he who gave it loses nothing. A lamp is lit from another lamp so that the coal is not extinguished; for the matter of one is lit by the fire of the other. Thus knowledge does not depart from the giver, yet it has passed into the receiver, the cause of which is not human. The substance which possesses knowledge is the same with God who gives and with the person who receives." Thus says Numenius.

### ¶On the Word of God according to Philo the Jew. Chapter 11.

<image-desc>Ornamental initial P featuring a figure (likely a scholar or saint) in prayer or contemplation amidst foliage.</image-desc>
Let us also hear Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who used Greek philosophy to explain Hebrew scripture.</note> speaking of the Word. Though he does not speak correctly in all things, he explains these matters so clearly that one might believe the sense of Scripture is no different from what the Church preaches. In the book he titled *That the Worse is Wont to Attack the Better*, he used these words: "It befits all who seek knowledge to raise their minds to God the Father; but if they cannot, at least to his image—that is, the most sacred Word." 

Also in the same book: "And if someone is not yet worthy to be called a son of God, let him still strive to follow his firstborn Word, who is more ancient than all the angels and as it were the prince of angels. For the origin is both God and Word and the image according to which man was created and is called an Israelite." <note>Philo often interpreted the name "Israel" to mean "the one who sees God."</note> For this reason, I was a bit more lavish in their praise earlier; they all say...

We have also learned from a certain companion of Moses <note>The author is referring to Philo of Alexandria, a Jewish philosopher who lived during the time of Christ and sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> that it was said: "Behold the man whose name is the Rising Sun." <note>original: "oriens".
