### ¶ On the Holy Spirit. Chapter 11.

The Holy Spirit is the foremost witness, because He proceeds from the Father and the Son and possesses their substance. Moreover, He is called the Holy Spirit in a certain way according to His relation to the Father and the Son, because He is the Spirit of both. He is called the Holy Spirit of God because He is the holiness of both the Father and the Son. For since both the Father is Spirit and the Son is Spirit, and both the Father is holy and the Son is holy, He is nevertheless properly called the Holy Spirit as the co-essential and co-substantial holiness of both. The Holy Spirit is therefore not said to be "begotten," <note>original: "genitus". In Trinitarian theology, "begotten" is reserved for the Son to distinguish His origin from that of the Spirit.</note> lest it be suspected that there are two Sons in the Trinity.
<margin>John 16</margin>
Therefore, He is not preached as "unbegotten," lest two Fathers be believed to exist in the same Trinity; instead, He is said to be "proceeding" by the testimony of the Lord, who said: "I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when the Spirit of Truth comes, who proceeds from the Father, He will receive from what is mine and will declare all things to you." <note>A paraphrase of John 16:12-14.</note> Here, He does not only proceed by nature, but He always proceeds without fail to carry out the works of the Godhead. This is the difference between the Son being born and the Spirit proceeding: the Son is born from one, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both.
<margin>Romans 8</margin>
And therefore the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> says: "Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him."

### ¶ On the Trinity according to the philosophers and poets. Chapter 12.

The Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe.</note> held that a trinity was the measure of all things, for the reason that God governs things by the number three, and also that things themselves are limited by that number. That divine prophet and poet, Orpheus,

<column-break/>

meant the same thing when he called Jupiter the beginning, the middle, and the end of the universe. Zoroaster <note>The legendary ancient Persian prophet, often cited by Renaissance writers as a source of "pagan" wisdom.</note> also refers to this, saying: "The Father perfected all things and provided a seat for the Mind." Likewise, he continues: "The Father snatched Himself away, and did not shut His own fire into the mind of the one who follows." Aristotle himself proved that the perfection of those things which are enclosed within the sphere of actions and passions (to use physical terms) consists in three dimensions. That great man Virgil did not omit this in his *Bucolics*: "God delights in an uneven number." <note>original: "Numero deus impare gaudet". From Virgil's Eclogue 8. Medieval and Renaissance Christians often read Virgil's poetry as containing hidden Christian prophecies.</note> Furthermore, in the first book of *On the Heavens*, Aristotle says concerning the number three: "Of three we say 'all'." Through this he declared that we should apply ourselves to magnifying the one God, who is eminent by those properties of things that have been created. Mercury, the king and priest of the Egyptians, who is called by everyone "Trismegistus" (meaning "Thrice-Greatest"), says this in his book *On the Power and Wisdom of God* in the *Pimander*: <note>The *Pimander* (or *Poimandres*) is the most famous text of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greco-Egyptian wisdom texts.</note> "From the will of God, which encompassed the Word and imitated the beautiful world, He adorned the rest of the world according to that model from his own vital elements and seeds. Moreover, Mind, who is God, most full of the fertility of both sexes, being Life and Light, brought forth through His Word another Mind, the Craftsman, who is the god of fire and the divine spirit." So says Trismegistus. And to refute any doubt, should any arise, it should be hidden from no one what Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century theologian.</note> explained concerning the ancient philosophers. Indeed, although they did not know the divine mysteries of the Persons by their proper names—which are Fatherhood, Sonship, and Procession—it is certain they knew them through certain essential attributes which are "appropriated" to the Persons: attributing Power to the Father, Wisdom to the Son, and Goodness to the Holy Spirit. Therefore, no one should doubt that he has consulted wisely for himself when he observes the Christian religion, since this holy and true sentiment is even found among the Gentiles.

### ¶ On the Trinity according to Christians and Catholics. Chapter 13.

Although the investigation of the Trinity is difficult among other things that prove the faith—since faith does not consist in reason, but rather in a certain inclination by which men, through their rational appetite cooperating with divine light, are directed toward their proper end—it nevertheless seems most difficult because there are three Persons in the same essence. This is what turns almost all Jews and infidels away from this truth. Various faithful people have pursued this truth in order to grasp it. And although we should possess this truth more perfectly in our own country <note>That is, in Heaven (the true homeland of the soul).</note> where it will be seen through its essence, nevertheless the Holy Fathers...

# Book on the Supercelestial Life, Chapter 15.

Because of the persistence of those who oppose the faith, we are compelled to discuss these and other matters pertaining to the faith, albeit modestly and reverently, without the presumption of full comprehension. Such inquiry is not useless, as through it the soul is elevated to grasp something of the truth—at least enough to exclude errors. In considering the divine essence, which, as the most perfect, embraces all perfections within itself, we find among these the acts of *understanding* and *willing*, in which we are made like God. These are two essential acts in God; in us, however, they are accidental <note>In Scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that can change without changing the core nature of a thing, whereas "essential" acts are part of God's very being.</note>, and through an "immanent" action within us, the word is produced. When we wish to think about some matter, we form a representative image of it; in us, this is an accident, and it varies according to the diversity of things. In God, however, there is no accident; therefore, this "word" must be a subsisting substance produced by the divine intellect. It cannot be called the intellect itself, but rather a generated substance, like the producer in the same nature, yet distinct in "hypostasis" <note>original: "hypostasi". A Greek term used in theology to denote a distinct person or individual reality within the one Godhead.</note>. What this is cannot be easily grasped, but we can say what it is not: we say that such an image or Word is not an accident and is not finite, for it would not then be equal to the infinite divine intellect.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Nor can it be called the "intellect" since it is produced *by* the intellect; yet it is like the intellect in substance. This production can only be called "generation," because the production of something like oneself in substance is termed generation, as we have from Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul*: "the most natural work for living beings is to generate another such as itself." <note>original: "opus naturalissimum viuentibus est generare tale quale ipsum est"</note>

This Word, spoken or begotten, thus claims for itself the name of "Son." The first person (or "suppositum") <note>In logic and theology, a "suppositum" is an individual, self-existing subject.</note> who speaks or generates through the intellect is called the "Father," because He has produced one like Himself from eternity. This is clear from the first book of the *Sentences* <note>Referring to Peter Lombard's *Sentences*, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> and from Thomas Aquinas in the fourth book of *Against the Gentiles*. Regarding the Will, it presupposes the act of the intellect recognizing something as "good." Since goodness in God is infinite, and the infinite Will tends toward it, an infinite Love proceeds from it. Because the Will is infinite and the beloved is infinite, the Love is equal to the lover and the beloved. This Love cannot be called an accident, but a substance, since it is most unacceptable for there to be any accident in God. It will therefore be a distinct person proceeding from the Father and the Son through the Will; this is nothing other than Love, the Holy Spirit, whom we name the Third Person. Concerning this truth, it is said in Genesis 18: "Abraham saw three but adored one." <note>A common medieval interpretation of the three visitors to Abraham as a prefiguration of the Trinity.</note> It is also proven in Psalm 109: "The Lord said to my Lord"—that is, the Father to the Son—"sit at my right hand." And in the same Psalm: "From the womb before the morning star I begat thee." This "generation" spoken of by God cannot be understood as anything other than a divine generation, since before the morning star there was nothing

<column-break/>

human. And in Psalm 2: 
> The Lord said to me, "Thou art my son; today I have begotten thee," 

and he adds, 
> "Thy possession, the ends of the earth." 

These things can only be understood as referring to the Son of God. And in Psalm 71: 
> "His name endures before the sun." 

Therefore, He existed before the creation of the sun. The text of Psalm 44 expresses the same sentiment: 
> "My heart has uttered a good word," 

referring to the divine Word begotten of the Father. And it adds: 
> "Thy throne, O God," 

where "God" is in the vocative case. He is called God by God when speaking of the divine Word, and thus shows Him to be the second person in the Godhead. And in the same Psalm it says: 
> "God has anointed thee," 

that is, [the Father] has anointed you, the Word. "God" (the Father) anointed you, "God" (the Holy Spirit), always speaking to the second person. And Isaiah in chapter 45 says: 
> "Only in thee is God, and there is no God without thee. Truly thou art a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Savior." 

And in Psalm 66: 
> "May God, our God, bless us; may God bless us." 

Note that he says "God" three times, which must be understood as referring to the three divine persons; and let them "fear Him" [singular], to show the unity of the essence. And in Ecclesiasticus 1: 
> "The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God," 

meaning the Son of God. And in Wisdom 2, speaking of the Son of God:

These were the thoughts of the wicked, and they were deceived. And Isaiah says in chapter 6:

And in Proverbs 3, they place three things in God. For the Jews say there are in God three <term>midoth</term> <note>original: "midoth". Hebrew for "measures" or "attributes." Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah) often discusses the Sephirot or attributes of God, which the author is here linking to the Trinity.</note>, that is, three properties. Concerning the Holy Spirit, it is written in Wisdom chapter 9:

### ¶ On the angels according to the opinion of the Platonists, Zoroaster, Aristotle, Avicenna, and the Hebrews. Ch. 15.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous chapter regarding the nature of divine substances, transitioning from the internal logic of the Trinity to the external creation of intellectual beings, specifically angels. ...at once, and wills the same things: and as far as it is in itself: it acts suddenly in whatever it does. However, angels are those leading an **immobile life** without bodies. For who would deny that incorporeal substances, according to the nature of their own kind, are more suited to be outside a body than in a body? Therefore, there ought to be more species of that kind separated from the body than joined to it. For what is more natural to any genus exists in it for the most part. Such indeed are the angels: who, if they move the bodies of the world, are themselves in no way moved by the moved bodies. Yet souls, while they transport bodies, are themselves also carried along. A mover who travels together with the moved body does not preserve a perpetual and stable tenor and order of moving, unless an **immobile mover** <note>This refers to Aristotle's concept of the "Unmoved Mover," a primary cause of motion that does not move itself while causing movement in others.</note> presides over it. Therefore, the perpetual order of the world's revolution testifies that there are some immobile movers above souls. Thus, in some place, there will be action far from passion <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving an effect from an external source.</note>; so that just as bodies are moved but do not move [themselves], so angels move [others] and are not moved. Concerning these, **Zoroaster** <note>An ancient Persian prophet often cited by Renaissance philosophers as a source of "ancient theology" that prefigured Christian truths.</note> says: "The world has intellectual, immobile rulers." That angels exist, and are many, **Aristotle** proves sufficiently in the twelfth book of his *Metaphysics* <note>original: "diuinorum" — literally "divine things," the common title for Aristotle's Metaphysics in this period.</note>. The later Hebrew philosophers call those minds "angels" and "messengers." Our **Avicenna** <note>A famous Persian polymath whose philosophical works were central to medieval university education.</note> argues elsewhere that the chief among them are no fewer than ten. Elsewhere, however, he seems to indicate many more. Aristotle, however, admits they are no fewer than the celestial motions and confesses to have computed that number by probable reasoning. But as for what might be necessary, he leaves it to those wiser than himself, as if he suspected that those minds ought to be numbered according to their own primary and proper action—that is, intelligence—rather than according to a common and secondary action—that is, motion.

### On angels according to Dionysius the Areopagite, Iamblichus, and Proclus. Chapter 16.

<margin>Chapter 7.</margin> Intellectual substances, which are the best and exist through themselves, and are the ends of all corporal things which were created for their sake, are far more numerous than the motions of the spheres and all bodies. **Dionysius the Areopagite** <note>A 5th-century theologian whose work *The Celestial Hierarchy* became the definitive guide to the nine choirs of angels.</note> testifies to this, saying: there are more separate species of intellectual beings than of corporal ones. Justly, the most powerful Creator of the universe was able, knew how, and willed to render His work as similar to Himself as possible. Indeed, He created it most similar in this very thing: that He expanded absolute minds—which are most like Him—far beyond the forms joined to matter by an immense space (if I may put it that way). Hence that saying of the prophet Daniel

<column-break/>

"Thousands of thousands ministered to him; and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him." In distinguishing the orders of angels, Dionysius primarily uses the numbers **three** and **nine**, and sometimes **seven**. Furthermore, we find the number **twelve** in the Christian mysteries. **Proclus** and **Iamblichus** <note>Later Platonist philosophers who developed complex systems of divine hierarchies.</note>, the Platonists, observed the same after Dionysius. For they divide the supreme and middle angels by three and nine. They partition the following by seven, and finally the last ones by the number twelve. Since, according to the Platonists, the grades of bodies are shadows of rational souls, and the grades of souls are images of angels, therefore some distinguish the orders of angels according to the orders of both bodies and souls.

### On the order among spirits: and that it is false that angels and souls have always existed, according to the Platonists, Avicenna, and Plotinus. Chapter 17.

That supreme spirit is the one who always was and will be: this is **God**. There are also the lowest spirits of the beasts, which neither always were nor will be. There must be two middle spirits between these widely differing extremes, which have a part of that first spirit and a part of the lowest spirits. In what way, then, shall we compose these middle ones? Shall we say they have always been, but will at some point cease? Not at all. For what has always been has lived through infinite power into infinity; infinite power is never diminished. Therefore, if they had always been, they would also always be, and would be equal in duration to God, not middle spirits. Thus, so that they may be middle in their perseverance, it is necessary that they began at some point but never cease. And although they were **created from nothing**, they nevertheless do not turn back into nothing. That which we call "nothingness" in their creation is neither the matter nor the effect of the things from which they are made. Nor is it truly a boundary from which they are made, but it is only said to be so. Therefore, they are not compelled to follow the nature of nothingness through which they would return to nothing—a nature which they had left behind before they came forth into being. Rather, they preserve the nature of their cause, from which they received their essence, so that through the same infinite power they are preserved in being, far from nothingness. Through this power, they emerged from nothing into being, having left nothingness behind. It is therefore not absurd that what is procreated most closely by an infinite principle and an infinite end—that is, God—is thought to have no end; since many things which proceed from a finite beginning and end are rightly considered to proceed without end. Thus, for instance, **number** proceeds from unity. Thus, the **mathematical line** from a point. Thus, **future time** from the present moment: proceeding without end, with nothingness posing no obstacle.

It also refutes the idea that angels are eternal like God, arguing instead that they were created from nothing but will exist forever.</summary>

# Book III: On the Supercelestial Life, Chapter 18.

of which they are not streams, but shadows.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical exploration of the human soul's unique "middle" position in the universe, bridging the gap between eternal divine realities and the transient material world, a central theme in Renaissance Neoplatonism.</meta>

They meet: it is placed on the horizon, that is, at the boundary of eternity and time, because it possesses a middle nature between eternal and temporal things; and as a middle point, it has rational powers and actions rising toward eternal things. It also has powers and operations declining toward temporal things. <margin>Diverse inclinations of nature: where they arise.</margin> Diverse inclinations are born from the fact that we see the soul turning sometimes toward eternal things and sometimes toward temporal things; we recognize that it is constituted from both natures. That superior part of the soul, our **Plato** located in the kingdom of **Saturn**, that is, of mind and providence; but the inferior part he located in the kingdom of **Jupiter**, that is, of life and fate. Therefore, the soul seems to have a twin face like **Janus of the two faces** <note>original: "Janus bifrons"; Janus was the Roman god of beginnings and transitions, usually depicted with two faces looking in opposite directions.</note>, namely one golden and one silver. With the former, it regards Saturnian things; with the latter, Jovian things. By looking, however, it judges and desires.

It is better to love eternal things than to judge them. They are judged well only with the greatest difficulty. They can never be loved poorly as long as they are loved ardently, for they are never loved too much—indeed, never enough. It is far better to judge temporal things than to cherish them. They are mostly judged quite well, but for the most part, they are cherished basely. Surely the judge transfers the form of the thing to be judged into himself, but the lover transfers himself into the form of the beloved. It is better to lift inferior things up to us by judging them than to cast ourselves down to them by loving them. It is better to raise ourselves to superior things through love than to bring them down to us through judgment.

<margin>The soul when separated acts differently than when in the body.</margin> But when the soul is separated [from the body], it proceeds from individuals to species; from species, it passes to <note>The text here contrasts the embodied soul's inductive reasoning with the separated soul's intuitive grasp.</note> universal reasons. But when separated, it is the opposite. Indeed, beginning naturally then from its familiar cognitions, <margin>The soul separated knows differently than when joined.</margin> it knows, and in divine reasons, by a natural intuition, it sees natural species; and in these species, as if by a sudden argumentation, it nevertheless inspects individual things in a single moment. From this, a circle is made by it from time to eternity, and from eternity back to time. Therefore, just as it was so joined to matter that it might be separable and at some point exist as a separate thing, so thereafter it exists as a separate thing so that it is joinable again; and thus at some point, it is bound. Powers proceed from natures. Natures are judged by their powers. For it is ruled by infinite power, wisdom, and goodness. Therefore, these natural powers are not in vain. By this argumentation, the **Platonists** can perhaps use the likelihood of the eternal circuit of souls. By the same [argument], the **Hebrews**, **Christians**, and **Muslims** <note>original: "mahumetiste"; a common Renaissance term for followers of Islam.</note> seem to be able to most truly argue for the resurrection of human bodies.

The soul, therefore, in the body according to the Platonists, proceeds by knowing from individuals to species, and from 
<meta>catchword: species</meta>

<column-break/>

species to ideas. Outside the body, it proceeds in the opposite way: namely, from ideas to species, and from species to individuals. Also according to **Plato**, there is one soul in man, but three powers in that one soul. It is worthwhile to hear him disputing this matter in the fourth book of the *Republic*: <note>referring to Plato's "Republic," Book IV, 436b, where he discusses the tripartite nature of the soul: reason, spirit, and appetite.</note> so that he may hold this as certain: namely, that the substance of the soul is one, <gloss>things.</gloss> but there are several such powers in the soul at once. For he says: "One and the same thing can never act or be acted upon in contrary ways at the same time, in the same respect, and in relation to the same thing." Because if anything is seen to move and rest at the same time, it will either be moved through one part of itself and rest through another—as if someone moves one hand while the other rests—or certainly it will be moved by one reason and not at all by another, just as a sphere does not change its position in a straight line, but meanwhile rotates in a circle while it remains fixed around its center; therefore, it stays at the center, but the circumference is turned. For what prevents the soul from being one, fortified with three powers? Although these differ from each other in their specific properties, they are nevertheless everywhere in the same soul at once, wherever the soul is entirely present at once.

->¶ What are heaven, the soul, an angel, and God; and the difference between visible and invisible light. And what light is in the elements, heaven, the soul, an angel, and God according to the Platonists. Chapter 19.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'C' showing a classical courtyard scene.</image-desc>
The **Platonists** say that **Heaven** is a certain light without matter, which is in some way corporeal. They say the **Soul** is a certain great light without quantity. They say an **Angel** is a very swift light without motion. They say **God** is the best and most powerful light without quality, by whose heat and will we are driven more quickly, more certainly, and more vehemently than by the light of intelligence. In this, invisible light differs most from visible light: that visible light, whether in fire or in heaven, coming from the outside, illuminates before it heats. But invisible light, on the contrary, acting from within, in a certain way heats before it illuminates. Therefore, in the former, we proceed from sight to touch; in the latter, as if from a certain touch into sight. Human beauty is seen before it is loved. But Divine beauty is loved so that it may be seen. But in the former, that which is seen is possessed miserably; in the latter, to see is nothing other than to possess happily. Therefore, anyone labors in vain with too much order who believes he will possess God or hopes to find Him without a singular love and worship of Him, before he loves Him. According to the Platonists also, light in the elements is easily perceived by the eyes, whose composition consists of elements. Light in heaven, although more ample, is nevertheless more difficult to see. For the quality of the eyes is more distant from the light in heaven...

# Book I: On the Supercelestial Life, Chapter 18.

...is thought to proceed. That something created should exist forever, especially the soul, is proved not only by the Christian religion, but also by our **Aboali** <note>original: "Aboali"; refers to the Persian philosopher Avicenna (Ibn Sina).</note>, who proves it as the soul of philosophers. Thus, angels occupy a certain middle ground between God and the beasts. Human souls have obtained another middle ground 

<margin>
Differences of religion, souls, and angels.
</margin>

immediately after the angels, agreeing with the angel in that they will exist forever. They differ, however, because they have not existed for all time like the angels, who—having arisen from the beginning of things in the natural order before the course of heaven, of which time is the companion—have existed through all time, even if they have not existed through all eternity. Our souls, born after the origin of time, yield to the angels. Yet they are not temporal. For God, through that very point of his eternity which is always the same and universal, towers over and embraces the circuit of time in which he created the angels; he also creates the souls of men. Therefore, the souls of men are above the "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" refers to things that are acted upon or undergo change, rather than emotions.</note> of time, even though they are made after time's beginning. But the souls of brute animals are generated both after the origin of time and under the passions of time, because they are not made by God directly through his eternity, but through the revolutions of the heavens and the powers of souls. From this it happens that they do not live forever. For they are subject to the mutation of time, being made under time through the motion of heaven. And if they have anything excellent, it all flows continually from the fountain of the **third essence** itself, of which they are not even little streams, but shadows. Therefore, the Platonists do not think them to be certain idols <note>original: "idola"; here meaning likenesses or phantom reflections.</note> of the World Soul, or of the soul of that sphere which they inhabit; they place them as mediums between the third essence and the qualities of bodies. Yet they trace them back to this essence as shadows. Hence **Plotinus**, the greatest of philosophers, says: "Just as many images are spread from one face through many mirrors, so from the soul of the sphere many likenesses of the one soul [flow] into many bodies of beasts." I mean the bodies of beasts in which human souls are not present. For where these human souls are, there the irrational power follows the rational substance of our soul like a shadow. Our souls, however, are created daily. But why are new souls created daily by God? Could God not have created all souls at once when the world was constructed, just as he created all the angels at the beginning of the world? The Christian will answer: "It was not fitting." But more on these things elsewhere. Therefore, according to the Platonists, God is above the angel. Because the soul is a mobile multitude; the angel is an immobile multitude; and God is immobile unity.

### ¶ What the Rational Soul is According to the Platonists. Chapter 18

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>
The Platonists affirm that the rational soul is a **substance**; otherwise, they could not perfectly comprehend and define substance. They would not be able to be something more excellent than an **accident** <note>In philosophy, a "substance" is something that exists in itself, while an "accident" (like color or shape) only exists in something else.</note>, nor to judge and measure how much an accident falls short of substance. They say it is not corporeal and mortal. For if it were, they would not grasp incorporeal and immortal things, nor distinguish them from corporeal and mortal ones. They say that although it is a participant in reason, it is not reason itself, as some think it to be. For if it were, they could not wander from the truth in assigning reasons for things, nor from reason in acting. Therefore, he who affirms that the soul *is* reason wanders further from reason than he who denies it. Hence reason is either a substance or a quality. If reason is a substance according to its essence, it is the highest, absolute, and utterly infinite, which the soul is not; only God is. If it is a quality, it seems to be an accident and a virtue rather than the soul. But as for the soul, which freely rules the substance of the body by forming it, moving it in opposite directions, and bringing it to a halt, and which can successively put on contrary qualities, let no one dare to affirm that it is a quality or an accident. For in what way can it be called an "accident" <note>The author likely puns on *accidens* (an accidental property) and *occidens* (that which sets, falls, or dies).</note> when it runs equally through all genera and species of both substances and accidents? It also reflects upon itself, both in affection and in cognition, and therefore also in life, inasmuch as it inheres in itself and not in a subject or corporeal instrument; it acts as often as it touches, chooses incorporeal things, and rightly distinguishes them from corporeal things. It often resists corporeal inclination. Nor does it rest in the body.

The soul, therefore, is an **incorporeal, rational, and immortal substance**, adapted for ruling the body. Many among the Platonists believe this soul precedes the body. The Peripatetics <note>original: "Peripatetici"; followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note> believe the opposite.

# Chapter 19.

they meet: the soul is placed on the horizon, that is, on the boundary of eternity and time. This is because it possesses a middle nature between eternal and temporal things; and as a middle being, it has rational powers and actions that rise toward the eternal. It also has powers and operations that decline toward temporal things.

<margin>Where diverse inclinations arise from.</margin>

Rightly, therefore, since diverse inclinations are born from these diverse natures—by the very fact that we see the soul turning both toward eternal things and toward temporal things—we know it is constituted of both natures. Our **Plato** <note>original: "Plato noster"; a common way for Renaissance Humanists to refer to Plato as their intellectual guide.</note> placed that higher part of the soul in the kingdom of **Saturn** <note>In Platonic allegory, Saturn represents the pure Mind or Intellect.</note>—that is, of mind and providence—but the lower part in the kingdom of **Jupiter** <note>Jupiter represents the World Soul, which governs life and fate in the physical realm.</note>—that is, of life and fate. Wherefore the soul, like the two-faced **Janus** <note>The Roman god of transitions, depicted with two faces looking in opposite directions.</note>, seems to have a twin face: one golden and one silver. With the former it looks at Saturnian things, and with the latter at Jovian things. By looking, it either judges or desires.

It is better to love eternal things than to judge them. They are judged well only with great difficulty. They can never be loved badly as long as they are loved ardently; such things are never loved too much, but rather never enough. It is far better to judge temporal things than to love them. For the most part, they are judged well enough, but for the most part, they are loved basely. Certainly, the judge transfers the form of the thing to be judged into himself <note>By understanding it</note>, but the lover transfers himself into the form of the beloved. It is better to lift lower things up to us by judging them than to cast ourselves down to them by loving them. It is better to raise ourselves to higher things through love than to bring them down to us through judgment.

<margin>The separated soul knows differently than when joined.</margin>

Truly, when the soul is joined to the body, it proceeds from individuals to species; from species it passes to reasons. But when it is separated, it is the opposite. Truly, beginning naturally then from its own familiar concepts, it sees natural species in divine reasons by a natural intuition; and in these species, it sees individuals as if by a certain logical process, yet it inspects them all in a single moment. From this, a circle is made by the soul from time to eternity, and from eternity back to time. Therefore, just as it was joined to matter in such a way that it might be separable and at some time exist in a separated state, so then it exists separated in such a way that it is joinable again—and thus it was at some time bound. Powers proceed from natures. Natures are judged by their powers. For the soul is governed by infinite power, wisdom, and goodness. Therefore, its natural powers are not in vain. By this argumentation, the Platonists can perhaps usefully approach the eternal circuit of souls. The Hebrews, Christians, and Muslims seem to be able to use the same argument most truly for the resurrection of human bodies. Therefore, in the body, according to the Platonists, the soul proceeds in knowing from individuals to species; from spe...

<column-break/>

...cies to **Ideas** <note>original: "ideas"; the perfect, eternal forms in Plato's philosophy.</note>. Outside the body, it proceeds in the opposite way: namely, from Ideas to species, and from species to individuals. Also according to Plato, there is one soul in man, but three powers in that one soul. In his work, <gloss>the soul is</gloss> one, as one may hear in the fourth book of the *Republic*, where he disputes this matter in such a way that he holds this as certain: namely, that the substance of the soul is one, but there are several such powers in the soul at the same time. He says: "One and the same thing can never do or suffer contrary things at the same time in the same respect and toward the same thing." For if something is seen to move and rest at the same time, it will be moved through one of its parts and rest through another—as if one were to move one hand while the other is at rest. Or certainly it will move in one respect, but in another not at all; just as a sphere does not change its position in a straight line, but meanwhile rotates in a circle while remaining fixed around its center; thus the center remains, while the circumference is turned. For what prevents the soul from being one, fortified by three powers, which—though they differ from each other in property—are nonetheless everywhere together in the same soul, wherever the whole soul is present together?

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the soul, moving from its position on the cosmic "horizon" to the difficulty of perceiving it and the arguments for its immortality. It then transitions into a discussion on demons and the four types of life.</meta>

# Books on the Super-celestial Life. Chapters 20 and 21.

<margin>
Three obstacles of the mind.
</margin>
the soul is seen in no way: just as the light of the sun is not seen by the owl, because it is too great; nor does the bodily sense have any proportion to it; rather, it is thought of by some discourse of the rational soul. Light in an angel is neither seen nor even thought of. For it is above the proportion of the senses and above the capacity of temporal discourse; nevertheless, it is understood. For the soul agrees with the angel in its own stable intelligence, rather than through the mobile discourse of thought. Light in God, because it also exceeds the limits of the intellect, is not understood by any natural human intelligence at all; rather, it is believed and loved, and having been loved, it is seen as if freely infused. Indeed, the mind kindled by the love of this light, the more ardently it burns, the more brightly it shines; it also learns more truly and enjoys more sweetly. Hence **Plato** asserts that the divine light is not pointed out by the finger of reason, but is grasped by the clear serenity of a pious life. Therefore, among the Platonists, the taste of the soul, infected by the bitter humor of the body, tastes the flavor of divine things in no way, or only with difficulty and very rarely. Therefore, he enumerates three obstacles of the mind to beholding the light of intelligible things. First: because it is joined to the body. Second: because the mind is affected by the body. Third: because the mind turns its gaze toward bodily things. The reason for its immortality is that it understands incorporeal things without the instrument of the body. It reaches separated forms and separates those that are conjoined; it understands something for whose proper intuition a <term>phantasm</term> <note>In medieval psychology, a "phantasm" is a mental image derived from sensory experience.</note> is sometimes not necessary. Concerning its immortality, <term>Cato the Elder</term> <note>original: "Esto maior"; likely a corruption of "Cato Maior," the title of Cicero's dialogue on old age.</note> in the works of **Cicero** spoke thus: "But if I err in this, that I believe the souls of men to be immortal, I err willingly. Nor do I wish this error, in which I delight, to be wrenched from me. But if, when dead—as certain small-minded philosophers believe—I shall feel nothing, I do not fear that these dead philosophers will mock this error of mine." In almost this same manner, a certain most holy "mockery" is set forth more precisely, by which they say a certain impious philosopher was refuted by a religious man of ours. "I ask of you," he said, "is the soul immortal or not? If it is mortal, no benefits will accompany those who believe it is immortal. But if it should be immortal, and we did not believe it, the greatest harms will redound upon us." It must not be doubted that it is immortal, nor can anyone rightly dissent from this, unless they are of a disordered and utterly alienated mind. Therefore, setting aside the opinions and authorities of the pagans, and even the most effective reasons devised by our theologians who wrote in the <term>Parisian style</term> <note>Referring to the Scholastic method of the University of Paris.</note>, let us seek out **Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory,** and **Jerome**, who wrote quite abundantly on the immortality of the soul.

<column-break/>

### ¶ On demons. Chapter 20.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'S' depicting a serpent or dragon coiled within a circular frame with floral flourishes.</image-desc>

Those spirits are called demons who, created in heaven by the Maker of all things, were cast down from the height of heaven; they are damned, some to the lowest part of the earth, and some to this air as if to a suitable prison for themselves; they are always eager to harm, always alienated from justice, swollen with pride, clever in deceit, and pale with envy. And since **Porphyry** <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on the nature of spirits.</note> thinks some demons are good and others bad, come now, let us see and approve by certain reasons that all demons—whom the pagans worship in place of gods—are malignant. Indeed, we shall endeavor to demonstrate it in this way. Everything that is good cannot fail to be beneficial; and conversely, that which is evil cannot be so. But the demons and the gods of the pagans—**Saturn, Jupiter, Juno, Minerva,** and similar beings—and the invisible powers that work in and through their idols, delight greatly not only in the immolation of brute animals (which seemed unjust and abominable to **Theophrastus** and Porphyry) but even in the slaughter and blood of men. How, therefore, will these be good demons, and not wicked and ruinous spirits?

### ¶ Four kinds of life according to the Hebrews, Christians, and philosophers. Chapter 21.

<image-desc>A woodcut decorative initial 'I' featuring floral and leafy motifs.</image-desc>

<margin>
Celestial Life
</margin>
In the universe, there are four kinds of life: celestial, purgatorial, worldly, and infernal. Plato concludes the highest point of the blessedness of the celestial life in the *Epinomis*, where he says: The soul, most purified, with all mutability having been made firm and its multiplicity collected, confers itself entirely into its own unity, which is higher than the intellect; and through this, it now transfers itself into the divine intelligible unity, which is higher than the world; and it lives for God rather than for itself, to whom it is certainly joined by a certain wonderful reason beyond understanding. But concerning the celestial life, enough has been said in the preceding sections.

<margin>

# Books on the Supercelestial Life. Chapters 20 and 21.

The soul is seen in no way, just as the light of the sun is not seen by an owl: because it is too great, and the bodily sense has no proportion to it; rather, it is thought of through some discourse of the rational soul. The light in an angel is neither seen nor even thought of [discursively]. For it is above the proportion of the senses and above the capacity of temporal discourse; nevertheless, it is understood. Indeed, the mind is set on fire by love for this light through a certain stable intelligence, rather than through the shifting discourse of thought. Because the light in God even exceeds the limits of the intellect, it is not understood at all by the natural intelligence of man, but is rather believed and loved; and having been loved, it is seen as if freely infused. Indeed, the mind set on fire by love for this—the more ardently it burns, the more brightly it reflects; it also discerns more truly and enjoys more sweetly. Hence Plato asserts that divine light is not pointed out by the finger of reason, but is captured by the clear serenity of a pious life. Therefore, among the Platonists, the taste of the soul, infected by the bitter humor of the body, tastes the flavor of divine things either in no way, or only with difficulty and very rarely. Therefore, he enumerates three obstacles of the mind for beholding the intelligible light:
<margin>Three obstacles of the mind.</margin>
The first: because it is joined to the body. The second: because the soul is affected toward the body. The third: because the soul turns its gaze toward corporeal things. The reason for its immortality is that it understands incorporeal things without the instrument of the body. It reaches separate forms <note>Platonic "Forms" or "Ideas" that exist independently of matter.</note> and separates those that are joined; it understands nothing for whose proper intuition a phantasm <note>term: phantasm (a mental image derived from sensory experience). The author argues that high-level thought does not require physical imagery.</note> is sometimes not necessary. Regarding its immortality, it is as Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator.</note> spoke: *But if I err in this, that I believe the souls of men to be immortal, I err willingly. Nor do I wish this error, in which I delight, to be wrenched away from me. But if, once dead, I shall feel nothing—as certain minute philosophers <note>term: minute philosophers (a derogatory term for those who hold narrow, materialistic views, such as the Epicureans).</note> believe—I do not fear that these dead philosophers will mock this error of mine.* In almost this same manner, a certain most holy "quibble" is produced, by which they say a certain impious philosopher was refuted by a man of our religion. *I ask of you,* he said, *is the soul immortal or not? If it is mortal, no benefits will accompany those believing it immortal. But if it should be immortal, and we did not believe it, the greatest harms will redound upon us.* It must not be doubted that it is immortal, nor can anyone rightly dissent from this, unless they are of a disturbed and utterly alienated mind. Therefore, setting aside the opinions and authorities of the heathens, and even the most effective reasons devised by our theologians who wrote in the Parisian style <note>note: original: "parisiensi stilo." This refers to the Scholastic method of theology popularized at the University of Paris.</note>, let us seek out Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory, and Jerome, who wrote quite abundantly concerning the immortality of the soul.

<column-break/>

->¶ On Demons. Chapter 20.<-

Spirit spirits are called demons: those who were created in heaven by the Maker of all things and cast down from the loftiness of heaven; they were condemned, partly to the lowest parts of the earth, and partly to this air as if to a prison suitable for them. They are always desirous of doing harm, always alienated from justice, swollen with pride, clever in deceit, and sallow with envy. And since Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on spirits.</note> thinks some demons are good and others bad, come now, let us see and approve by certain reasons that all demons are malignant, even though the heathens worship them in the place of gods. Indeed, we shall attempt to demonstrate it in this way: everything that is good cannot fail to be beneficial, and conversely for what is evil. But the demons and gods of the heathens—Saturn, Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, and the like—as well as the invisible powers that work in and through idols, rejoice exceedingly not only in the sacrifice of brute animals (which seemed unjust and abominable to Theophrastus and Porphyry), but even in the slaughter and blood of men. How, therefore, shall these be good demons, and not rather criminal and pernicious spirits?

<margin>The celestial life.</margin>
The most purified soul—once its mutability is made firm and its multiplicity is gathered together—betakes itself entirely into its own unity, which is superior to the intellect. Through this, it transfers itself into the divine unity in the intelligible world above, living for God rather than for itself, to whom it is certainly joined by a certain wondrous manner beyond understanding. But enough has been said about the celestial life in the preceding sections. Plato also affirms the purgatorial life along with the celestial, though it is denied by many heretics. Whence he says in the *Symposium*: Purified souls, which loved divine beauty above all else, finally immerse themselves entirely into the very sea of divine beauty, and there they not only drink the divine liquors, but even pour them out from themselves into others. He understands Purgatory here when he says:
<margin>Purgatorial.</margin>

<meta>This page shifts from the previous discussion on Purgatory and scriptural proofs to a Neoplatonic philosophical treatise regarding the "super-celestial life." It explores the nature of the Divine Mind, the World Soul, and the relationship between the physical world and the realm of pure Ideas.</meta>

# Books on the Super-Celestial Life:

Existence itself is what is called "everywhere." The **sensible world**—the world we perceive with our senses—is truly small because it consists of small, finite parts. It exists within the **higher world** <note>original: "mundo superiore"</note>, not as if it were in a physical container or an empty space, but as something held within an active, preserving, sustaining, moving, and comprehending force.

The **intelligible world** <note>original: "Mundus intelligibilis," the realm of pure thought and divine forms</note> spreads its powers through every part of the universe by the greatness of its strength. It is present in its entirety to every single part, yet it remains supreme and above them all.

The **one first essence**—that is, the **Divine Mind**—is present as a whole everywhere. The **World Soul** <note>original: "anima mundi"</note> is the same. The great number of parts in the world does not stop this essence from being one and whole everywhere; nor does the unity of the soul prevent there being many other minds and souls existing alongside it.

Every **intellectual soul** is a clear image and a specific power of the **First Intellect**, which is unchanging in its essence; for from that which is unchanging, only essence can exist.

Our own soul is present to every limb of our body with its full power, even though different limbs receive different functions and strengths from it. The **World Soul** and the **Divine Mind** relate to the parts of the universe in this same way.

What we call physical size or "extension" in the material world is actually an **overflow of power** in the world of life. When we say the divine is "here" or "there," we should not imagine it occupies a physical location; rather, wherever anything exists, the divine is immediately present there in its entirety.

If that whole assembly of life—that is, the gathering of **intellectual souls**—acting together with the First Mind and First Soul, is always whole and indivisible everywhere, it follows that it does not reach bodies through physical movement. Instead, it reaches them through a certain effect. Bodies do not move toward it except by becoming prepared to receive its form—much like how fire affects nearby sulfur, or how light touches a transparent object.

The **sensible world** is scattered in three main ways: by physical extension and location, by the passing of time, and by the conflict of opposing qualities. However, the **intelligible world**—which is the first fullness of **Ideas**—allows no such division. Likewise, the world of life (the gathering of intellectual souls) remains wonderfully joined to the First Mind and its Ideas.

Since the intelligible world and the world of life admit no division of place, time, or opposition, and do not depend on any physical subject or location, they are rightly always present as a whole, everywhere.

It is the common opinion of all, and reason itself dictates...

<column-break/>

...that each of the gods exists everywhere at once. But for God to occupy every place simultaneously, He is not forced to be thinned out or divided; otherwise, He would be physical, and would become weak and perish. Therefore, He is the same and whole everywhere.

If you consider all the **Ideas** <note>original: "ideae," the perfect blueprints or forms of all things</note> within the First Mind, both individually and together, you will soon recognize the full abundance of all Ideas within each single Idea, while the distinct property of that specific Idea is still preserved. Likewise, if one intellectual soul forms many bodies one after another, it remains one within many. But in the intelligible world, it is rather that many things exist within one, or around one.

Our soul understands the fullness of these Ideas by turning toward its own intellect; it does not do so through mere images of Ideas. Therefore, through the intellect, the soul itself is the universe. In this way, within the universal form of things, all souls are in some way one, though each remains distinct by its own particular character. However, as far as they turn away from the intellect, they become separated from one another.

The **Divine Mind** acts upon matter through its Ideas, not from the outside like a human craftsman <note>original: "more artis humane"</note>, but from within, in the manner of a skillful nature. It is not separated from matter by location (otherwise it would be assigned its own specific place), nor is it mixed with matter (otherwise it would not rule over it at all).

This single **machine of the world** was built by one Mind and is brought to life by one Soul, which is present as a whole everywhere at once.

These **three principles of all things** are everywhere: **The Good** itself; the **Divine Intellect**, which is Beauty itself; and the **Life of the World**. Through hidden paths, these draw all things to themselves and gather them into one through a desire for goodness, beauty, and life.

Just as the Divine Mind—through an indivisible eternity that is the cause of time—equals and surpasses all time, so too through its indivisible essence and infinite power does it occupy and exceed all space. It creates and preserves space itself and everything within it, everywhere.

If the **One** and the **Good** are the same thing, then a multitude becomes worse the further it moves away from unity. Therefore, if one were to imagine a multitude that was either infinite or entirely lacking unity, that would be **Evil** <note>original: "malum"</note> itself.

**Man** is an intellectual, rational, and sensory soul all at once. This condition of the human soul is shaped precisely according to the character of our original Idea.

Our soul has the power of "sense" rooted in it by God, so that it may always make use of a certain kind of perception.

The **First Intellect**, with an overflowing fertility of light, naturally spreads itself inward into many **Ideal rays** <note>original: "radios ideales"</note>. From this propagation...

### Chapter 21.

...through both investigation and natural disposition: the natural forms of things flow outward like lights.

Since **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century philosopher and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose works heavily influenced Renaissance thought</note> maintains that the **Idea** of a human cannot be mixed with the Idea of a horse. Likewise, he holds that our intellect remains perpetually among divine things, and that our reason is guided by that primary intellect. Furthermore, since the divine nature of our soul is by no means cast down into lower things, but rather these lower things strive toward the soul, it followed that the human species is never transformed into that of a horse.

Since the "first number" <note>The mathematical or structural blueprint of the universe</note> exists in the **First Being** as the origin of all things, it is right that the full number of all things is found there. Likewise, since the **First Form** is there, things rightly differ among themselves by degrees of form, just as species do. Furthermore, in that perfect life and intelligence, every Idea of things is found; even things that do not possess life here have a certain life and intelligence there.

The **First Life**, the **First Intelligence**, and the **Perfect Living Being** <note>original: "animal perfectissimum," referring to the Platonic concept of the universe as a complete living entity</note> contain all possible degrees and species of lives, intelligences, and living creatures that can be imagined.

Just as the physical heavens contain the forms of lower, even lowly, animals in a way that is not lowly, so the **Intellectual Heaven** <note>The realm of pure thought above the physical stars</note> possesses the forms of the whole world in a manner even more excellent than the physical heavens do.

In the **First Life**, which is the maker of all things, all things are alive. And because it is the First Form, due to the marvelous efficacy of its life, it is entirely capable of propagating itself; all things living there are formally distinguished.

The **First Life** and **First Mind**, because they are the first of all forms, are the simplest of all and the most uniform. Yet, because they are the principle of all, they are also "all-formed" <note>original: "omniformis," containing the potential for every shape and identity</note>.

Since the **First Intellect** is the First Life, only the intellectual life is the true life.

That which was first procreated from **The Good** <note>The ultimate source of all existence in Platonism</note> itself is entirely good. In it, essence is a certain beginning and birth of a good work; life is the "adolescence" of the Good; and intelligence and the Ideal hope represent the "adulthood" of the Good.

To those asking what the Good itself is: the intellect appears to us clearly as the Good, since it is through the intellect that we truly judge between good and evil. Both the order and species of things, as well as life, proceed from the intellect. Indeed, the "adult life" which the soul desires is the intellect itself.

Life, intelligence, and species are to be desired because they have the "form of the Good" <note>original: "boniformia"</note>: life is the act directed toward the Good; intelligence is the act already determined by the Good; and species is the very boundary or impression left by the Good.

Without the wondrous grace of the **First Good**, no things can love, nor can they be loved.

The first principle of things is the same as 

<column-break/>

the Good itself.

The goal of the **intellectual soul** is the most unhindered act of intelligence, directed entirely toward the universal Good.

The Good itself, the principle of the universe, not only procreates the mind and soul, but also, by a ray twice infused—like a kind of **hook of love** <note>original: "amatorio quodam hamo," a metaphor for the divine attraction that pulls souls back to God</note>—it constantly calls them back to itself. There, it converts that ray first into the soul, then into the mind, and finally into a gracious and vital light. And this, in both cases, is happiness itself.

Since any beauty, by whomever it is loved, is always sought under the rationale of the Good, it is necessary that the Good itself is the principle of both beauty and love.

The Good itself is removed from any suspicion of multiplicity or change, so that the soul enjoying it is compelled to strip away its intelligence, which in some way resembles an action that is multiple and changing.

The **Scale** by which one ascends to the Principle has seven steps:
1. **The first** is the purgation <note>cleansing or purification</note> of the soul.
2. **The second** is the knowledge of individual divine works.
3. **The third** is the contemplation of the order by which lower works are led back to higher ones step by step.
4. **The fourth** is a proportional comparison which, through such order, brings itself to the divine.
5. **The fifth** is negation, by which you separate everything you can conceive from the Principle <note>The "Via Negativa," defining God by what He is not</note>.
6. **The sixth** is suppliant prayer to God, that the Father of the intellectual world may make you an intellectual world in act. For you have been this world only in potential from the beginning.
7. **The seventh** is that, when you have emerged as that intellectual world, you may—stirred further by the love of the Good—be transformed from the intellectual state into the Good which is above the intellect.

Since essence and reason are different and lower than the "Reason of the Good," it is not rightly said that essence belongs to the Good.

Even if the Good, due to its supreme simplicity, composes nothing of itself (speaking as if from within), it is nonetheless not obscure or uncertain to itself. Indeed, it is the origin of certainty and the **Father of Lights** <note>A reference to James 1:17, identifying the Platonic "Good" with the biblical God</note>.

There are three principal origins of things: **The Good**, **The Mind**, and the **World Soul**.

The **Intellect** lives freely in contemplation; and by a free decree, it determines to refer all private and public actions back to that contemplation.

If the soul becomes free at any time through intellectual virtue, it follows that the Intellect is first and foremost free. Likewise, if the Intellect possesses a life that is supremely free and voluntary, since it is closest to the Good, then the Good itself is rightly called **Liberty**.

One must not imagine that it happened by chance that this very thing which is now the Principle of all should be the Principle; as if it could have happened that something else, differently disposed, might have been the Principle.

<summary>This page outlines a Neoplatonic hierarchy of existence, identifying "The Good" as the ultimate source and goal of all life and intelligence. It provides a practical "Seven-Step Scale" for the soul's spiritual ascent, moving from basic purification to a final transformation beyond the intellect into the Divine.</summary>
<keywords>Plotinus, Neoplatonism, The Good, Divine Mind, World Soul, The Scale of Ascent, Seven Steps, Liberty, Father of Lights, Intellectual Heaven</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Neoplatonic metaphysics, shifting from the nature of the "First Principle" to the specific relationship between the Divine Mind, the rational soul, and the physical body. It specifically interprets Plotinus’s views on how the soul remains "pure" even while animating a "composite" living being.</meta>

->### Books on the Super-Celestial Life<-

The Supreme God is more rightly called **Freedom** by His very nature, as He is the master of His own nature. In whatever way essence, will, and reason might be named in God, they are fundamentally the same thing. Therefore, just as His essence is carried forth naturally, so too does God will and act; and conversely, in the same way He wills and acts, so His nature is constituted. He exists, therefore, not by fortune or by fate, but by His own **will**.

Whatever exists besides the "First" <note>The "First" or "The One" is the ultimate source of all existence in Neoplatonic thought</note> consists of many parts or powers reconciled into a single form of a whole.

Every essence possesses a natural multiplicity within itself from the beginning, and yet meanwhile, it remains a single unity. Nor does it do anything through a mere habit toward things; rather, things are made by it as if it were not "doing" them, just as things are changed by that which is itself unchanged.

Even though God is everywhere, He nevertheless shines clearly in the height of **Intelligence**. To perceive this light, all forms—not only those we imagine but even those we understand—stand in the way like clouds. Therefore, shake all of these away from you if you wish to happily perceive the divine light with a serene mind.

The **rational soul** <note>The part of the human soul capable of logic and divine contemplation</note> is the middle point between divine forms and natural forms. It is not "in" the body, but is "present to" it; it propagates life from itself into the body, and from this soul and body together, a single **composite animal** <note>original: "animal unum compositum"; here "animal" refers to any "animated" or living being, specifically the human person as a mix of soul and body</note> is formed.

The rational soul is the same as the rational nature of the soul itself; although it is separated from the body in its essential being, it nevertheless produces a life joined to the body within the existence of the single living being. In this way, the opinion of **Plotinus** stands as a middle ground between the opinions of **Alexander** and **Averroes** <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias argued the soul was a physical "form" of the body that died with it; Averroes argued for a single, universal intellect shared by all humans. Plotinus argues the soul is individual but independent of the body.</note>.

The rational soul, though it subsists in itself, nevertheless leans in a certain way toward the body, which is a state that hardly suits an intellectual substance.

Unless it is understood how the soul is joined to the body, it cannot be known which actions or passions belong properly to the soul and which belong to the **composite** <note>The "composite" is the human entity formed by the union of soul and body</note>.

The rational soul subsists in itself and has its own rational actions and a sense that is free from suffering. However, it produces an **irrational life** within the body, whose senses are occupied with the "passions" <note>In this context, "passions" refers to physical sensations, emotions, and things the body "undergoes" or suffers.</note> of the body.

The rational soul is coupled through its own **intellect** to the Divine Mind, and through that mind to God. In the same way, the irrational life is linked to the rational soul. Moreover, the intellect is both "private" (one's own) and "common" (shared). The cause of sin lies in the irrational soul and in our "animal" part, but the "consent" lies in the [rational] soul. Likewise, the "rational circuit" is the middle state between rest and straight motion.

Consider again from Plotinus how intelligence and reason relate 

<column-break/>

to one another and to the "image."

In the rational soul, there is properly neither sin nor punishment; these exist in the **irrational life**, which is the "image" of the soul. Although this image no longer exists once the soul departs from here, there remains a certain vital act of the soul that is rooted deep within it.

The rational soul reasons by itself, not through the instrument of the body. It also understands through its own intellect. It even understands through the **common intellect**, which is like a form for every individual intellect.

If the soul were not a "simple form" <note>A pure, indivisible essence</note> existing in itself, it would receive passions; but if it is such a form, it does not receive them.

The soul lives in itself and gives life to the body; using the body as an instrument, it is not subjected to the body's passions.

The soul is not mixed with the body, nor is it "in" the body, but it is present to the whole; therefore, it does not receive passions. And even if it were mixed or "in" it, the soul itself would not properly feel or suffer, but rather the **composite** would. It is difficult to say how disturbances refer to the composite rather than to one part or the other, because it is not yet clear how the composite is actually made.

The rational soul, existing in itself, presides over the human animal generated by it. In the soul, there is sense-perception without passion, as well as reason; in the animal, however, there is sense-perception accompanied by passion.

The rational soul is joined to the Divine Intellect through its own intellect, as if by a head; and through this, it is joined to God. Likewise, it is joined to its animal part through its **imagination**, and through this, to the body. Truly, even if all souls are brought back to a common mind, because each soul receives in its own unique way, that mind seems to become "private," and the souls carry away from it other intellects that are proper to themselves.

Those things that are proper to our "animal" part also pertain to us in a certain way; and the animal life is not extinguished, but accompanies the soul, which is its cause. Likewise, **intellectual virtues** are in the soul, while **moral virtues** are in the animal.

In children, the animal part and the soul's imagination reign. The intellect and reason are occupied with higher things. Likewise, the life of brute animals depends on a rational soul, either ours or another.

It is not the composite, but the soul itself that reasons and understands—sometimes through its own intellect, and sometimes through the common intellect.

Although the soul becomes similar to God through the **virtues**, God does not "possess" virtue; rather, He is the **exemplar** (the perfect model) of virtue. What is a "quality" of virtue in the soul is "essence" in God.

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic division between the rational soul and the "animal" composite, explaining that while the soul animates the body, it remains an independent substance joined to the Divine Mind. It clarifies that physical sensations and sins belong to the "irrational" or "animal" part of a human, while the true soul remains a pure, reasoning essence.</summary>
<keywords>rational soul, Plotinus, Divine Mind, composite being, intellect, virtues, passions, Neoplatonism, essence vs. quality</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the soul's relationship with the Divine. Having previously established that God operates by His own will rather than fate, the text now shifts to the practical and philosophical ascent of the human soul. It outlines how a person can move from the sensory world toward "Intellect," which the author identifies as the true state of blessedness.</meta>

### Chapter 22.

Understanding is spoken of through a certain analogy regarding both the Divine Intellect and the soul.
The Soul is neither the Good itself, nor is it properly called "good-formed" <note>original: *boniforme*; meaning something that has taken the shape or quality of the Good without being the Good itself</note>.
Wisdom in the Divine Mind is like a **touch**; in our mind, it is like **contact**; in our reason, it is like a **visible figure**.
The soul, through virtue, becomes similar to God, who is the exemplar <note>The perfect original pattern</note> of all virtues.
Through "civil virtues" <note>Social and moral virtues like justice or temperance that govern our conduct with others</note> acting as measures and forms, the soul approaches divine likeness more closely than physical matter does when it receives natural forms.
Purity must be sought so that the purified soul may turn toward its own intellect, and from there toward the Divine Intellect, so that it may be reformed by the "exemplary virtues" found there.
Plotinus confirms that the ultimate goal of virtue is to enjoy God.
The philosophical, musical, and amorous temperaments <term>ingenium: an innate disposition or natural talent</term> easily converge toward the same goal.
The philosophical disposition is more "free" than other temperaments and requires only a guide through the discipline of mathematics to reach metaphysical wisdom.
The task of the Metaphysician is to travel through all beings by **dividing, composing, defining, and demonstrating**, and finally to progress beyond being itself.
All faculties draw their principles from Metaphysics; if they do not, they are not true sciences, and their moral characters remain imperfect.
The "amorous" disposition must be recalled from the beauty of the body to the beauty of morals, then to the beauty of the sciences, and finally to the beauty of the mind.
The philosophical disposition is by nature "freed" from matter and needs only a guide to reach divine beauty through certain steps of discipline.
**Blessed** is the one who lives by the mind alone.
One life is supreme—that is, the Highest; all other lives depend upon it through many degrees.
The First Essence, the First Life, and the First Intellect are the same. Intellect itself is the highest peak of life.
Rational nature can achieve the **blessed life** <note>original: *vitam beatam*</note> when it is formed and acts through the intellect.
The happy person wants only the "single good"; they choose all other things for the sake of that one good.
There is an eternal wisdom in the mind; when reason reaches it, the soul is blessed.
If all things lived by the same degree of reason and perfection, all things could live equally well. But life itself is the Intellect. In other things, living is as different from the Intellect—that is, from life itself—as one species is from another.

<column-break/>

Man can attain the blessed life insofar as he attains the "intellect"—that is, when the whole soul becomes "intellect" in its active state.
The ultimate end is the **simple good**, which is the "intelligible good" <note>Good that is understood by the mind, rather than felt by the senses</note>. Other things are not the end itself, but lead toward the end.
The happy person desires only the intelligible good. He does not depend on other things, whether they are considered "goods" or "evils."
the blessed person keeps the intelligible good whole and unharmed even in the "blow of fortune" <note>meaning unexpected accidents or bad luck</note>.
The blessed person makes the "upper eye" of his reason one with intelligence; thus he is blessed, even if the "lower eye" of his reason looks upon other matters.
The blessed person lives more fully than anyone else, since his life is unified entirely within that which is best. He does not look toward external things as items to be desired or feared.
The blessed person does not need any pleasure outside of the mind. The highest act of intelligence is itself the **highest pleasure**.
**Man is solely the rational soul.** The blessed man is the soul that has already escaped into the Intellect; therefore, he thinks nothing of things belonging to the senses.
For one who possesses the "intelligible good," nothing can be added to his happiness by the presence of other goods, and nothing can be taken away by the opposition of evils.
The wise man, who is destined for blessedness, devotes himself only to the mind and depends only on God. He either despises all other things entirely or governs them without being disturbed.
All minds enjoy eternity forever. Rational natures, however, enjoy it at certain times; and as long as they enjoy it, they act with stability.
Rational nature both can and should be formed by the mind; and then, in a single act, it possesses all things.
Blessedness consists in a certain possession of the "present good," to which the passage of time adds nothing in terms of the past or future, but only in terms of the "now."
We consider a person happy in the highest degree when he beholds all truths and possesses all goods. But he sees all truths simultaneously in one "form of truth"—that is, in the Divine Mind. Likewise, he enjoys all goods in a single "fountain of goods"—that is, in the Good itself. Since he beholds truths and drinks in goods through this one form and one fountain, he surely contemplates all truths in a single gaze and drinks in all goods in a single draught.
**Beauty** is a certain grace, which is found more in things seen than in things heard, and even more in things thought; nor is it a matter of mere proportion <note>Ficino argues against the idea that beauty is just the mathematical symmetry of parts</note>.
The beauty that is seen represents the beauty of the mind. The beauty that is heard...

It emphasizes that a truly blessed person lives entirely through the mind, remaining undisturbed by external fortunes or physical pleasures.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general philosophical discussion of the soul and beauty into a formal index of commentaries on the Hermetic text known as the *Asclepius*. It bridges the Neoplatonic teachings of Plotinus with the Egyptian wisdom traditionally attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</meta>

->**Table of Commentaries.**<-

[It] refers to the beauty of the soul. Likewise, no one ought to, or even can, speak about the beauty of the mind and soul unless they possess it themselves. Matter has a natural deformity, but its beauty is foreign <note>original: *peregrinam*; meaning beauty is not inherent to matter but must come from an outside source or form</note>. But the soul’s ugliness is accidental <note>original: *aduentitiam*; something added or external to its true nature</note>, while its beauty is innate. Likewise, the beauty of the human mind—namely, in intellectual virtue—is like a most brilliant color. The beauty of the soul—namely, in moral virtue—is like a shape or figure.
The Good proper to each thing is a natural action directly and freely aimed toward the Good of the universe itself, which is the beginning and end of all things.
Things below the soul do not have true unity, essence, or form; therefore, they do not have true goodness. But the soul and higher things have those three truly, and thus have true goodness.
In all things there is something of the Good itself—that is, unity, essence, and form—and where these three are true, there is also true good; but where they are imaginary, the good is imaginary.
The intellect, both human and divine, is always in "act" <term>actus: the state of being fully realized or active, as opposed to mere potentiality</term>, although reason progresses from potentiality into act.

¶ These, most distinguished reader, are a very few points out of many that Plotinus himself, the Platonist, asserted concerning theology, which are not entirely discordant with Christian views. We can infer that his mind was not completely foreign to the Christian law from the fact that he was always a disciple of Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, the influential teacher in Alexandria who also taught the Church Father Origen</note>, who was a Christian, and always a friend of the most Christian Origen. He is said to have vowed, along with Origen and Herennius, never to depart from the teachings of Ammonius, and to have kept this vow just as he promised. Furthermore, his own disciple Porphyry is a witness that he once despised the worship of the pagan gods with a high spirit, even while Amelius <note>another student of Plotinus</note> was still urging him toward it.
