-># Prefatory letter to the following work<-

¶ To the most learned and most accomplished in the knowledge of all disciplines: likewise the prince of the philosophers of all Gaul, Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples. Symphorien Champier of Lyon, physician, sends his best greetings. <note>original: "S.P.D.", abbreviation for *Salutem Plurimam Dicit*</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' depicting a figure in a landscape with a building and trees.</image-desc>

<margin>The sentiment of Plato.</margin>
When I was revolving in my mind that sentiment of the divine Plato: in which he asserts that we are not born for ourselves alone, but that our country and our friends claim a part of our origin for themselves; and that men (as the Stoics like to say) are generated for the sake of men; you, most learned Jacques, seemed to me above all other mortals to be the one who has followed this principle most zealously. Indeed, not content with merely acquiring good disciplines for yourself, you have worked with "hands and feet" (as the saying goes) to communicate them to others through both words and writings. Nor were you content with that mediocre learning which satisfies others: you have penetrated into the more inward and abstruse depths of these subjects; indeed, you have reached as far as the very marrow to be sucked out. From the fountains—from which waters are drunk more pleasingly—you have strived to draw the pure flavor of truth itself, which you have learned without pretense and share without envy, and you do not hide its excellence. <note>This is a paraphrase of Wisdom 7:13: "What I learned without guile I impart without grudging; I do not hide her wealth."</note> 

<margin>Ovid. <note>original: "Qui-dius", likely a shorthand for Ovidius, though the text quoted is Biblical.</note></margin>
<margin>Jerome.</margin>
In the manner of Pythagoras and Plato, and other distinguished philosophers, you have traversed foreign regions and visited various peoples; you have also most laboriously traveled through Italy itself—famed throughout the whole world as the nurse of learned talents—partly so that you might see face-to-face those whom you knew from books and reputation, and partly so that you might bring back good literature from them to your own people. Whence, through your study and labor, many volumes in every kind of discipline have reached us; they have come forth from the workshops of the printers <term>calchographorum officinis: literally 'the offices of the copper-writers', a humanist term for print shops</term> most correctly edited, destined to bring no small fruit to students of the liberal arts. And letting pass your other works in dialectics and philosophy: the works of the divine Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist</note> are seen illustrated by your commentaries. Likewise, we have seen and read with great delight of soul two small works of that most ancient theologian whom they call Hermes Trismegistus: one on the wisdom and power of God <note>The *Poimandres*</note>, the other on the divine will, with your commentaries and explanation. Wherefore it happened that we took care to have printed and published the theological work of Asclepius—likewise a theologian and a disciple and listener of the same Hermes (or Mercury Trismegistus if you prefer)—which is known to very few, augmented or clarified by our own commentaries. 

But if anyone from the unlearned multitude or the countless crowd of the envious should dare to contend that this man [Asclepius] was not a listener of Hermes, let him read and understand the little book of Mercury Trismegistus himself regarding the divine will, which is titled *Asclepius*, in which Asclepius is introduced addressing King Ammon. If he does not believe this, let him hear and lend a patient ear to Lactantius Firmianus <note>A 4th-century Christian author</note>, a most learned man and no less Catholic, in the second book of his *Divine Institutes*. 

<margin>Lactantius.</margin>
For he says this of both: "Finally, Hermes affirms that those who have known God are not only safe from the incursions of demons, but are not even held by fate." And a little later he says of Asclepius: "But Asclepius, his listener, explained the same sentiment more broadly in that discourse which he wrote to the King, etc." 

But when for a long time my hesitant and uncertain mind wavered as to whose auspices I should rely upon to allow this little work to go forth into the light, you seemed to me most suitable because of your skill in all disciplines—you who do not cease to investigate most zealously the wisdom of the ancients. To you, we dedicate this good portion of our labors. For you, who cherish the teaching of the master and defend it from the teeth of the envious, will (in my opinion) by no means disdain to protect and vindicate from injury the doctrine of the listener who does not degenerate from the imitation of his master. But if you find anything in it that is crippled, mutilated, or imperfect, we earnestly entreat your kindness again and again that you may wish to correct it and restore it to its original truth. 

Farewell, ornament of all literature. Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1508, on the 24th of May. <note>original: "ix. kalendas Junij", the ninth day before the Kalends of June</note>

### ¶ On the intellectual substance.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring foliate and interlaced patterns.</image-desc>

I have sent you a great discourse, O King, which serves as the crown and commentary of all others; it is not composed according to the opinion of the many, but contains much that is contrary to them. Indeed, it will appear to you as inconsistent even with some of my own previous discourses. My teacher Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" sage and purported author of the Hermetic writings.</note> used to say to me often, both in private and sometimes when Tat <note>original: "Latio," likely a transcription of Tatius or Tat, the son and disciple of Hermes.</note> was present, that the philosophy found in my books would seem most simple and clear, yet would otherwise be a construction of confusion. On the contrary, it would possess a hidden existence from its opposites, and even an extremely obscure understanding of its concealed words. He said that for those Greeks who wish to interpret our own tongue, there will be a great perversion and obscurity of the writings. But a discourse expressed in its original tongue has a clear understanding of the words. For the very quality of the voice and the language of Egyptian names possesses within itself the power <note>original: "actum," referring to the inherent magical or energetic efficacy of the words.</note> of what is said. Therefore, O King, as far as you are able, keep this entire discourse untranslated, lest such mysteries reach the Greeks, and lest the proud, loose, and, as it were, "curled" <note>original: "calamistrata," a metaphor for overly ornate or artificial rhetoric, like hair curled with a branding iron.</note> speech of the Greeks should weaken the gravity, strength, and active power of the names. For the Greeks, O King, have only new words that are active in demonstrations. And this is the philosophy of the Greeks: a mere sound of words. But we do not use words; rather, we use voices great in their effects. I shall begin the discourse by invoking God, the Lord and Maker of all, the Father of the surroundings and of all existing things, who is the One, and the One who is all; for the fullness of all things is One, and in the One there is no second One, but both are the One. Keep this sense for me, O King, throughout the whole business of this speech. For if anyone attempts to separate that which is seen as "All" and "One"—which is the same thing—from the One, taking it as a name of the "All" or

<margin>On the naming of the One in multiplicity, and not in the fullness: for it is necessary that all things be One, if indeed they are One. They exist, however, and would never be One if they were separate existences, lest the fullness be dissolved. See, therefore, many springs of water on the earth; and in the earth, fire gushing out in the Mediterranean parts; and there, three apparent natures of fire, water, and earth hanging from one root, whence it is believed to be the treasury of all matter. And it indeed contributes to its own governance, but resumes its existence from above. Thus the sky and the earth are always the craftsman's work.</margin>

as a name of the "One," he dissolves the whole. I say indeed that the Sun is a substance bringing in certain things and leading back matter; drawing all things toward itself and to itself, and giving all things to all from itself. It grants a copious light.

<margin>On the sun. On the moon.</margin>

For it is he whose light and action reach not only the heaven and the air, but also the earth, even into the innermost depths of the abyss. If, however, there is a certain intellectual substance, this is its solidity, whose successive approach is its own light. Whence this consists or whence it flows, only he himself knows—or perhaps in a place and nature existing near him, so that he is not seen by us, but is known and understood by conjecture. The spectacle of this is not for the one who conjectures; but the most splendid vision itself illuminates the whole world, both that which is placed above and that which is placed below. For he is located in the middle, in the zenith, carrying the world; and like a good charioteer, confirming the course of the world and binding it to himself, lest in any way it should be carried along in a disordered fashion. The reins are life, soul, immortality, and generation.

# Introductory letter for the following short work

## To the most learned and most accomplished in the knowledge of all disciplines: likewise the prince of the philosophers of all Gaul, Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples. Symphorien Champier, physician of Lyon, sends many greetings.

<image-desc>A large historiated initial letter 'C' depicting a scholar in his study, seated at a desk and surrounded by books, representing the contemplative life of the author or the dedicatee.</image-desc>

<margin>Plato’s opinion.</margin>
When I was reflecting in my mind upon the sentiment of the divine Plato: in which he asserts that we are not born for ourselves alone, but that our country and our friends claim a part of our origin for themselves; and that men (as the Stoics please) are generated for the sake of men: you, most learned Jacques, seemed to me alone beyond all other mortals to have followed this principle most zealously. For you are not content to have acquired the good disciplines for yourself only: but you have labored with "hands and feet" <note>A Latin idiom (manibus pedibusque) meaning to do something with all one's might or by every possible means.</note> (as they say) to communicate them to others as well, both in words and in writings. Nor were you content with that mediocre learning which satisfies others: but you have penetrated to the inner and more hidden parts of those same disciplines; indeed, you have reached even to the marrow <note>Meaning the core or essence of the subjects.</note> to be drawn out. You have studied to drink the pure flavor of truth itself from the very springs from which the waters are drunk more gracefully. This truth you have learned without pretense, and you communicate it without envy, and you do not hide its honor. Like 
<margin>Saint Jerome.</margin>
Pythagoras and Plato and other distinguished philosophers, you have traversed foreign regions and visited diverse peoples; moreover, you have most laboriously traveled through that Italy, famous throughout the whole world, the nurse of learned geniuses: both so that you might see face to face those whom you knew from books and by reputation, and so that you might carry back good literature from them to your own people. Hence, through your study and labor, not a few volumes in every kind of discipline have reached us: and they have come forth in most corrected editions from the workshops of the printers <term>chalcographorum</term> <note>From the Greek for "copper-writer," a term used in the early days of printing to refer to those who used metal type.</note>, destined to bring no small fruit to the students of the fine arts. And if we set aside the rest, both in logic and in philosophy: the works of the divine Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> are seen illustrated by your scholarly notes. Likewise, regarding that most ancient theologian whom they call Hermes Trismegistus: we have seen two short works, one on the wisdom and power of God <note>Known as the *Pymander*.</note> and the other on the divine will <note>Known as the *Asclepius*.</note>, adorned with your commentaries, and we have read them through with great delight of the mind. Because of this, we have taken care to print and bring to light—augmented or clarified by our commentaries—this theological work of Asclepius the theologian, a disciple and listener of that same Hermes (or, if you prefer, Hermes Trismegistus), which is known to very few. But if anyone from the ignorant multitude or from the innumerable crowd of the envious should dare to contend that this man was not a listener of Hermes, let him read and understand the book of Hermes Trismegistus himself on the divine will, which is inscribed to Asclepius, in which Asclepius is introduced addressing King Ammon. If he does not 
<margin>Lactantius.</margin>
give credit to this, let him listen to Lactantius Firmianus <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often quoted by Renaissance humanists for his accounts of ancient wisdom.</note>, a most learned and no less Catholic man, in the second book of his *Divine Institutes*; and let him lend a patient ear. For concerning both of them he speaks thus: "Finally, Hermes affirms that those who have known God are not only safe from the incursions of demons, but are not even held by fate." <note>original: "Deniq; affirmat eos Hermes qui cognouerunt deū non tm̃ ab incursibus demonū tutos esse: verum etiā ne fato quidem teneri."</note> And a little later he says this concerning Asclepius: "But Asclepius, his listener, explained the same sentiment more broadly in that famous discourse which he wrote to the king, etc." But when my mind fluctuated for a long time, hesitant and uncertain under whose auspices I should allow this short work to go forth into the light: you seemed most suitable to me because of your skill in all disciplines, you who do not cease most studiously to investigate the wisdom of the ancients. It is to you that we dedicate this good portion of our nocturnal labors <note>original: "lucubrationū" - a common humanist term for scholarly work done by candlelight.</note>. For you who cherish the teaching of the master and defend it from the teeth of the envious will (in my opinion) by no means disdain to protect and vindicate from injury the teaching of a listener who does not degenerate from the imitation of his master. Nevertheless, if you find anything in it maimed, mutilated, or imperfect, we earnestly pray to your kindness again and again that you may wish to correct it and restore it to its pristine truth.

-> Farewell, ornament of all literature. Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507, the 9th day before the Kalends of June. <note>May 24, 1507.</note> <-

# ¶ Concerning the intellectual substance.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial M with foliage or strapwork patterns.</image-desc>

I have sent a great discourse to you, O King: a pinnacle and a commentary, as it were, on all others. It is not composed according to the opinion of the many, but rather holds much that is contrary to them. Indeed, it will appear to you as discrepant with certain of my own discourses. For Hermes, my teacher, often used to say to me—both in private and sometimes when Tat <note>The OCR reads "Latio," but in the context of Hermetic dialogues, this is almost certainly a transcription of "Tatio" (Tat), the son and disciple of Hermes.</note> was present—that any opinion falling into my books would seem most simple, yet it would be a manifest confusion (or elsewhere, a construction). On the other hand, because of the contrary [opinions], it would have a hidden and even most obscurely concealed understanding of the words. He said that the greatest perversion and obscurity of the writings would come from the Greeks who wish to interpret our own language into theirs. For a discourse expressed in its own native language has a clear understanding of the words. Indeed, the very quality of the speech and the language of the Egyptian names has within itself the power <term>actus: the active force or efficacy</term> of the things being said.

Therefore, O King, as much as it is possible, preserve this entire discourse (as you are able) untranslated; let such mysteries not reach the Greeks. Do not let the arrogant, loose, and, as it were, "curled" <note>original: "calamistrata." A metaphor for speech that is overly ornate or artificially styled, like hair curled with a hot iron.</note> style of the Greeks weaken the gravity, the strength, and the active power of the names. For the Greeks, O King, have only new words that are [merely] active in demonstrations. This is the philosophy of the Greeks: a sound of words. But we do not use [mere] words; we use voices that are greatest in works <note>The author argues that the original language (Egyptian) has a magical or inherent connection to reality that Greek lacks.</note>.

I shall begin the discourse by invoking God, the Lord and Maker of all, the Father, the Circle, and the One existing as all things. For the fullness of all things is one; and in that one, there is not a second "one," but both are the one that exists. Keep this sense for me, O King, throughout the whole business of this oration. For if anyone approaches that which is seen as "all" and "one"—which is the same thing—and tries to separate it from the "one," taking the name of "all" or "one" as a multitude and not as a fullness, they fail. For all things must be one, if indeed they are one. They are [one], and they would never be one if they existed [separately], lest the fullness be dissolved.

<margin>Concerning matter.</margin>
See, therefore, on the earth many springs of water; on the earth there is also fire gushing forth in Mediterranean parts. In the same place, three natures appear—fire, water, and earth—hanging from a single root. From this root, the treasury of all matter is believed to exist. And while it contributes to the governance of itself, it resumes its existence from above. For in this way, the Maker [governs] heaven and earth always.

<margin>Concerning the sun.</margin>
I say indeed that the sun introduces a certain substance, but leads back matter; he draws all things around himself and into himself, and from himself he gives all things to all. He bestows a copious light.

<margin>Concerning the moon.</margin>
For he is the one whose light and action reach not only into the heaven and the air, but even onto the earth, all the way into the innermost depth of the abyss. If there is a certain intellectual substance, this is its solidity; its successive approach would be its light. From where this light consists or flows, he alone knows—or perhaps in a place and nature existing near him, so that he is not seen by us. He is known and understood by conjecture. The sight of him is not for one who [merely] conjectures; rather, the most splendid vision itself illuminates the entire world, both that which is placed above and that which is placed below. For he is located in the middle, wearing the world like a crown. And like a good charioteer, he confirms the course of the world and binds it to himself, lest it be carried along in a disordered way. The reins are life, soul, immortality, and generation.

-># Introductory letter to the following small work<-

¶ To the most learned and most accomplished in the knowledge of all disciplines—likewise the prince of philosophers in all of France—Jacques Lefèvre d’Étaples <note>original: "Jacobo fabro stapuleñ." Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (c. 1455–1536) was a leading French humanist and theologian who recovered many ancient texts.</note>. Symphorien Champier of Lyon, physician, sends heartiest greetings.

<margin>The opinion of Plato.</margin>
<image-desc>Large ornamental initial C featuring floral and leaf motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
When I was reflecting in my mind on the sentiment of the divine Plato—in which he asserts that we are not born for ourselves alone, but that our country and our friends claim a part of our birth for themselves; and that humans (as the Stoics believe) are generated for the sake of other humans—you, most learned Jacques, seemed to me above all other mortals to be the one who has followed this principle most zealously. Indeed, you were not content merely to acquire good disciplines for yourself, but you have worked with "hands and feet" <note>An idiom meaning "with all one's might" or "by every possible means."</note> (as they say) to communicate these to others through both speech and writing. Nor were you satisfied with that mediocre learning that suffices for others; rather, you penetrated to the more inward and hidden depths—indeed, even to sucking the very marrow <note>Champier uses "medullas vsqz sugendas" (sucking the marrow) to describe deep, essential understanding versus superficial reading.</note>—and you studied to draw the pure flavor of truth itself from the very fountains from which the waters are drunk most pleasantly. This truth you have learned without pretense, you communicate without envy, and you do not hide its honor.

<margin>What Jerome says.</margin>
Likewise, in the manner of Pythagoras and Plato and other distinguished philosophers, you have wandered through foreign regions and visited diverse peoples. You have most laboriously traversed Italy itself—the most famous nurse of learned talents in the whole world—both so that you might see in person those you knew from books and fame, and so that you might bring back good literature from them to your own people. From this, no small number of volumes in every kind of discipline have reached us through your study and labor; they have emerged from the workshops of the printers <term>chalcographorum</term> <note>Literally "copper-writers," a term often used for early printers using metal type.</note> most correctly edited, destined to bring no small fruit to those eager for the liberal arts. To pass over your other works in logic and philosophy, the works of Saint Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist whose works Lefèvre d'Étaples edited in 1499.</note> are now seen illustrated by your scholarly notes. Likewise, we have already seen and read with great delight of soul two small works of that most ancient theologian whom they call Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric and philosophical writings called the *Hermetica*.</note>: one on the wisdom and power of God, the other on the divine will, both adorned with your commentaries. Thus it happened that we took care to print and bring to light this theological treatise by Asclepius—himself a theologian and a disciple and listener of the same Hermes (or, if you prefer, Mercury Trismegistus). This work is known to very few, but it has been augmented or clarified by our own commentaries. If anyone from the ignorant multitude or the countless crowd of the envious dares to contend that this Asclepius was not a listener of Hermes, let him read and understand the book of Mercury Trismegistus on the divine will, which is titled *Asclepius*, in which Asclepius is introduced speaking to King Ammon.

<margin>Lactantius.</margin>
If he does not trust this, let him listen and give a patient ear to Lactantius Firmianus <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325) often called the "Christian Cicero," who frequently cited Hermetic texts to support Christian doctrine.</note>, a most learned man and no less a Catholic, in the third book of his *Divine Institutes*. Concerning both of them, he says: "Finally, Hermes affirms that those who have known God are not only safe from the attacks of demons, but are not even held by fate." And a little later he says of Asclepius: "Moreover, Asclepius, his listener, explained the same sentiment more broadly in that discourse which he wrote to the King," etc. But when my mind wavered, hesitant and uncertain for a long time as to whose patronage I should allow this work to come to light, you seemed most suitable to me because of your skill in all disciplines, you who never cease to most zealously investigate the wisdom of the ancients. For you, who cherish the teaching of the master and defend it from the teeth of the envious, will surely not disdain (in my opinion) to protect and claim from injury the teaching of the student, who does not degenerate from imitating his master. However, if you find anything crippled, mutilated, or imperfect in it, we earnestly beseech your kindness again and again to correct it and restore it to its original truth. Farewell, glory of all literature. Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1506, May 24th <note>original: "ix. kalēdas Junij" (the ninth day before the Kalends of June).</note>.

### ¶ On intellectual substance.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' at the start of the paragraph, featuring scrolling foliage and vines in white against a dark background, enclosed in a square frame.</image-desc>

I have sent you a great discourse, O King: like a summit and a commentary upon all others. It is not composed according to the opinion of the many, but contains much that contradicts them. For it will appear to you to be at variance even with some of my own discourses. Indeed, Hermes—my teacher—often spoke with me, both privately and sometimes in discussion when reason was present, saying that the philosophy occurring in my books would seem very simple and a manifest confusion—or elsewhere, a mere construction. Yet, from these contrary things, a hidden existence and even the most obscure, concealed understanding of words would be held. He said there will be a great perversion and obscurity among the Greek writers who wish to interpret our own native language. A discourse set forth in its own tongue has a clear understanding of the words; for the very quality of the voice and the language of the Egyptian names has within itself the power of the things spoken. Therefore, O King, as much as you are able, keep the whole discourse untranslated, lest such mysteries reach the Greeks, and lest the proud, loose, and, as it were, frizzed <note>The Latin *calamistrata* refers to hair curled with a curling iron, here used as a metaphor for overly ornate or artificial Greek rhetoric.</note> speech of the Greeks should weaken the gravity, the strength, and the active speech of these names. For the Greeks, O King, have only new words that are active in demonstrations. This is the philosophy of the Greeks: the sound of words. We, however, do not use words, but voices [or sounds] of the greatest works.

I will begin the discourse by invoking the Lord and Maker of all, the Father who is around and through all existing things, the One who exists as all things; for the fullness of all is one. In the One, there is not a second "one," but both are the One. Keep this sense for me, O King, throughout the entire labor of this speech. For if anyone tries to separate from the "One" that which sees all and the "One" as being the same thing—taking the name of "all" or of "one" as a multitude and not as a fullness—he errs; for it is necessary that all things be one,
<margin>On matter.</margin>
if indeed they are one. And they are; and they would never be "one" unless they were a single being, lest the fullness be dissolved. Behold, therefore, many springs of water in the earth; and in the earth, fire also gushing out in the inland parts. There, three natures appear—fire, water, and earth—all hanging from one root, which is why it is believed to be the treasury of all matter. It contributes to its own governance, but it receives its existence from above. For thus the sky and earth are always the craftsman. I say indeed that the Sun brings forth a certain substance while leading back matter, drawing all things toward himself and toward matter, giving all things from himself to all. He bestows light in abundance.
<margin>On the sun.</margin>
For he is the one whose light and action reach not only into the sky and the air, but even onto the earth and down into the innermost depth of the abyss.
<margin>On the moon.</margin>
If, however, there is a certain intellectual substance, this is his solidity, and its successive addition would be his light. From where this consists or flows, he alone knows; or perhaps it is found in a place and nature existing nearby, though it is not seen by us, but only known and understood by conjecture. The sight of this is not for the one who merely conjectures; rather, the most brilliant vision itself illuminates the entire world, both the world above and the world below. Placed in the middle, at the summit, he bears the world. Like a good charioteer, he confirms the course of the world and binds it to himself, lest it be carried along in a disorderly way. The reins are life, soul, immortality, and generation.

# Definitions of Asclepius

He sent [his rays] to be carried out not far from himself—or rather (if the truth must be told) along with himself. And in this way all things are crafted. He grants eternal permanence to immortal things, and by the lifting up of light <note>Original: "sublatione luminis." This refers to the Sun's role in distributing divine light to the cosmos.</note>—extending as far as it reaches from either side toward the heavens—he gazes upon the immortal parts of the world. But for those parts occupying and circling every region of water, earth, and air, he provides life and stirs up generation. Through the imitations that exist in these parts of the world, he changes the living creatures by way of a revolution, transforming them from one kind of genus to another, and species to species, through a reciprocal change among themselves—just as he performs his workmanship in the great bodies. For the permanence of every body is change: the immortal body is indissoluble, but the mortal body is subject to dissolution. This is the difference between the immortal and the mortal, and the mortal and the immortal. For just as light is constant, so too the abundance of living creatures is constant and never-failing in its place and its provision. Indeed, many and various choirs of <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "demonum." In this context, daemons are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or "inner powers" that bridge the gap between the divine and the physical world.</note> surround him, like military cohorts. They are companions who are not far from the immortals. From their assigned station, they watch over the affairs of men and carry out what is commanded by the gods, using storms, tempests, lightnings, the changes of fire, and earthquakes, as well as famine and war, to punish impiety.

<margin>On God and men</margin>
For this is the greatest vice of men toward the gods: [impiety]. For it is the nature of the gods to do good, of men to practice piety, and of daemons to take vengeance. Other things that men dare to do are the result of error, or rashness, or necessity (which they call **Fate**), or ignorance. None of these offices are liable to judgment before the gods; only impiety is subject to judgment. The Sun is the preserver and nourisher of every kind. And just as the <term>intelligible world</term> <note>original: "intelligibilis mundus." The "intelligible" world refers to the higher realm of pure thought and divine forms, which cannot be seen with the eyes but only understood by the mind.</note> encompasses the sensible world, filling it and condensing it with various forms that match all things, so also the Sun, encompassing all things in the world, condenses the generations of all and strengthens them; and when things fail or flow away, he receives them back.

<margin>On daemons</margin>
Under the Sun is placed the choir of daemons—or rather, it is positioned within the reality of things. For these are many and various, ordained under the "angels of the stars," with an equal number assigned to each of them. Thus, they serve each of the stars, being good or evil according to their natures—that is, their operations. For the very substance of a daemon is its "operation" or activity. Some among them are mixed of both good and evil. All these who have obtained power over worldly business within themselves work turmoil upon the earth and various disturbances, both for cities and nations collectively, and for each individual privately. For they shape and stir up our souls toward themselves, dwelling within our nerves, our marrow, our veins, and our arteries, even reaching through the brain to the innermost organs. At the moment each of us is born and receives life, we are taken up by the daemons who serve that specific office of generation, those who are assigned to each of the stars. For these daemons move from moment to moment; they do not remain the same but revolve. These, therefore, enter into the two [lower] parts of the soul and turn the soul of each individual toward their own specific operation through the body. The **rational part** of the soul, however, remains free from the rule of daemons and resists them, being adapted for the reception of God. For this reason, a ray of light shines through the Sun into the rational part. Those who are thus illuminated are few, and for them, the daemons are idle; for no one—neither daemon nor god—has any power against a single ray of God. But all other men are driven and carried away, both in their souls and in their bodies, by daemons, for they cherish and love the operations of these spirits.

<margin>On Fate</margin>
And the truth is not for him who errs, or who causes others to err. Thus, they govern this entire administration of the lands through the instruments of our bodies. This governance Hermes called **Fate**. Therefore, the intelligible world depends [upon...]

->### Disciples of Hermes<-

The world comes from God, but the sensible world <note>The "sensible" world refers to the physical world we perceive through our five senses, as opposed to the "intelligible" world of pure thought and spirit.</note> comes from the intelligible world. The sun, however, through the intelligible and sensible realms, provides the upper world from the Good God. This is his workmanship. Around the sun are eight spheres hanging from him: one of the fixed stars, six of the wandering stars <note>The planets known to the ancients.</note>, and one around the Earth. From these spheres hang <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "demones." Intermediary spirits that act as messengers or governors between the heavens and humanity.</note>, and from the daemons, humans. In this way, all things and all people depend on God. Therefore, God is the father of all, the sun is the craftsman, and the world is the instrument of his craftsmanship. An intellectual substance governs the heavens; the heavens govern the gods; and the daemons, being subject to them, govern humans. This is the "military service" <note>original: "militia." Often used in Hermetic texts to describe the ordered hierarchy and duty of the celestial beings.</note> of the gods and daemons. 

God does these things through them for himself; indeed, all things are particles of God. If all things are particles of God, then God is all things. Therefore, in making all things, he makes himself. He never ceases, just as he himself is unceasing and, as God, has no end; so too his operation has neither beginning nor end. 

If you understand, O King, there are both bodies and incorporeal things, and there are bodies of incorporeal things. The King asked: "What kind, Asclepius?" 

Asclepius replied: "Those bodies that appear in mirrors; do they not seem incorporeal to you? For that is how it is, O Latius." 

Latius said: "You understand divinely." 

The King said: "But there are also other incorporeal things and bodies, such as <term>Ideas</term> <note>original: "idee." The perfect, eternal forms or patterns of things that exist in the divine mind.</note>." 

Latius replied: "It does not seem so." 

"Therefore," [Asclepius continued], "those existing in a body appear as both corporeal and incorporeal—not only in living beings, but even in inanimate objects." 

"You speak well, O Latius," said Asclepius. "Thus there are reflections of incorporeal things toward bodies, and of bodies toward incorporeal things. This is the link between the sensible world and the intelligible world. Therefore, O King, adore the images, for they themselves possess the Ideas from the intelligible world."

The King, then rising, said: "It is time to take care of the guests. In what follows, we shall afterward theologize about the rest, promising the harmony of a most sweet melody." 

If, in a display of instruments, discord should be an obstacle to readiness, the undertaking would be ridiculous. For when the instruments are "sick" <note>original: "egrotantibus." Meaning faulty, broken, or out of tune.</note> for use, the musician must necessarily be mocked by the spectators. Here, certainly, the instrument does not return the art to the player without labor. In those cases, the "sick" instrument is blamed. 

Indeed, according to nature, God the Musician not only works the harmony of songs, but also transmits the familiar rhythm of the melody down to the specific instruments. God is untiring; for weariness does not befit God. If a craftsman, wishing to compete most greatly in music, uses honeyed instruments—the flute, the reed, and the plectrum <note>A small tool used to pluck the strings of a lyre or lute.</note>—to perfect the sweetness of the song, yet the instrument fails, we do not blame the spirit of the musician. We do not blame the superior one; rather, we give him his due honor, but we condemn the raspiness of the instrument, which hindered the beauty. It hindered the music's melody and snatched away the sweetness and pleasant song from the listeners. 

And so it is with our body. Let no spectator blame our pious kind on account of our physical weakness. Recognize how untiring is the spirit of God, always possessing its own knowledge in the same way, continuing its happiness, and performing the same benefits for all. Even if you trust the craftsman greatly, but the material instrument does not obey him for the perfect variety of matter, the musician himself has done as much as he could. We should not bring blame upon him, but rather condemn the weakness of the instrument, which, by lowering or raising the pitch, destroyed the neighbor of the harmonious song. No one will ever accuse the musician for a weakness in the instrument. However much the instrument was a hindrance, the musician strove to keep the pitch from falling. The listeners treat that musician with even greater love because of his effort, while they turn the blame against the instrument. 

Thus you also, most honored ones, within yourselves, fit your own <term>lyre</term> to the Musician.

Asclepius.

-># Disciples of Hermes<-

The world comes from God. The **sensible world** <note>The physical world we can perceive with our senses.</note> comes from the **intelligible world** <note>The world of pure thought, forms, or divine ideas.</note>. The sun, however, through an intelligible and sensible influx, provides for the world from God the Good—that is, from the **Craftsman** <note>original: "opifici," referring to the Demiurge or the divine creator who shapes the universe.</note>. Around the sun there are eight spheres hanging from it: one of the fixed stars, six of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>, and one around the earth <note>the moon</note>.

From these spheres hang **daemons** <note>original: "demones." In Hermetic thought, these are intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil, who act as messengers or executors of the divine will.</note>, and from the daemons hang humans. And thus, all things and all people are hanging from God. For this reason, God is indeed the father of all, the sun is the worker, and the world is the instrument of his craftsmanship.

An intellectual substance governs heaven; heaven governs the gods; and the daemons, subject to the Lord, rule over humans. This is the "army" of gods and daemons. God performs these actions for himself through them, and all things are particles of God. If all things are particles of God, then God is all things. Therefore, in making all things, he makes himself; and he never ceases, for he is unceasing, and just as God has no end, so his operation has neither beginning nor end.

"If you understand, O King, there are both incorporeal bodies and bodies of incorporeal things."
"What kind?" said the King.
**Asclepius:** "The bodies that appear in mirrors; do they not seem incorporeal to you? For such is the case, O Latius."
**Latius:** "You understand divinely."
The King said: "There are also incorporeals and other corporeals, such as ideas."
**Latius:** "It does not seem so."
"Therefore, existing in a body, things appear corporeal and incorporeal, not only of living beings but even of inanimate things."
**Asclepius:** "You speak well, O Latius. Thus there are refractions of the incorporeal toward bodies, and of bodies toward the incorporeal; that is, the sensible world toward the intelligible, and the intelligible toward the sensible. Therefore, adore the images <note>original: "imagines," likely referring to sacred statues or icons.</note>, O King, as if they themselves possess the **ideas** <note>In the Platonic sense: the perfect, original patterns of things.</note> from the intelligible world."

The King, rising, then said: "It is time, O Prophet, to take care of our guests. In what follows, we shall hereafter theologize about the rest, promising the harmony of a most sweet melody."

If, in a display of musical instruments, a lack of harmony were a hindrance to readiness, the undertaking would be ridiculous. For if the instruments are 'sick' <note>malfunctioning or out of tune</note> for use, the musician is necessarily mocked by the onlookers. This certainly does not return the art to the player without labor; rather, the faulty instrument is blamed. Indeed, according to nature, God the Musician not only works the harmony of songs, but he also transmits the familiar rhythm of melody down to the specific instruments.

God is **untiring** <note>original: "indefessibilis."</note>; for weariness does not befit God. If a craftsman wishing to compete in music—even with flute-players using 'honeyed' instruments to create sweetness of melody, and perfecting that sweetness with reed and plectrum—fails, the listener does not disparage the musician's spirit, nor blame the masters. Rather, the listener gives fitting honor to the master but condemns the hoarseness of the instrument, because it was a hindrance to the most beautiful things. It hindered the music in its melody and sweetness and snatched away the sweet song from the listeners.

And thus our body surrounds [the spirit], lest anyone from the audience disparage our pious race because of our weakness. But know that the spirit of God is untiring, always possessing its own knowledge in the same way, continuing happiness, and providing the same benefits throughout all things. Even if you trust the craftsman most, if the material used does not comply with the perfect variety required, it is enough that the musician himself did what he could. We should not blame him; let us instead condemn the weakness of the instrument that, by lowering or raising the tone, destroyed the beauty of the harmonious song. No one will ever accuse the musician for a weakness occurring in the instrument. But as much as the instrument was a hindrance, so much more did the musician strive to compensate. The listeners of the musician show even greater love for him, even if they turn the blame against the instrument.

Thus also you, O most honored ones: go again and prepare the proper lyre for the Musician.

**Asclepius.**

# The Disciples of Hermes
### f ii

The world comes from God, but the sensible world <note>The "sensible" world refers to the physical world we can perceive with our five senses.</note> comes from the intelligible world <note>The "intelligible" world refers to the realm of pure thought or divine ideas, accessible only to the mind.</note>. The sun, through the intelligible and the sensible, provides for its own world from God the Good. This is the **divine craftsmanship**.

Around the sun, there are eight spheres depending on it: one of the fixed stars, six of the planets, and one around the earth. From these spheres depend the **daemons** <term>daemons: intermediary spirits that act as messengers or executors of divine will between gods and humans</term>; and from the daemons, humans depend. And so all things and all beings are dependent upon God. Therefore, God is indeed the father of all, the sun is the craftsman <note>original: "opifer"</note>, and the world is the instrument of that craftsmanship. 

Intellectual substance governs the heaven; the heaven governs the gods; and the daemons govern the humans subject to them. This is the "army" of gods and daemons. God performs these works through them for Himself; indeed, all things are parts of God. If all things are parts of God, then God is all things. Therefore, in making all things, He makes Himself; and He never ceases, for He is unceasing and, like God Himself, has no end. Thus, His operation has neither beginning nor end. 

"If you understand, O King," said **Asclepius**, "there are incorporeal things within bodies, and there are bodies belonging to incorporeal things." 

"What kind of things?" asked the King. 

"The bodies that appear in mirrors—do they not seem incorporeal to you?" 

"For that is how it is, O Latius," the King said.

**Latius** replied: "You understand divinely."

The King said: "But there are also other incorporeal and corporeal things, such as Ideas."

**Latius**: "It does not seem so." 

"Therefore, they appear as both corporeal and incorporeal things existing in the body—not only in living beings, but also in inanimate things." 

"You speak well, O Latius," said **Asclepius**. "Thus, there are reflections <note>original: "refractiones"</note> of incorporeal things toward bodies, and of bodies toward the incorporeal; that is, the sensible world toward the intelligible, and the intelligible toward the sensible. For this reason, O King, adore the images, as they themselves possess Ideas from the intelligible world."

The King, then rising, said: "It is time to attend to our guests. In the next session, we shall theologize about the remaining matters." 

He promised a harmony of the sweetest melody. If, in the display of instruments, a discordance were to hinder one's readiness, the attempt would be ridiculous; for when the instruments are failing in their use, the musician is bound to be mocked by the onlookers. Here, certainly, the art does not return a reward to one playing without effort. But in those cases, the failing instrument is blamed. 

Indeed, by His nature, the **Divine Musician** not only works the harmony of songs, but also transmits the rhythmic proportion of the melody down to the individual instruments. God is tireless, for weariness does not befit God. If, at that time, a craftsman wishing to compete in music—even if provided with honey-sweet flutes <note>original: "tybicinibus melleis"</note> producing sweetness of melody, and completing that sweetness of song with reed and plectrum—he does not disparage the spirit of the musician, nor does he blame the one who is superior. Rather, he renders decent honor to the musician, but condemns the hoarseness <note>original: "rauciditatem"</note> of the instrument, which was a great hindrance to beautiful things. For it obstructed the music's melody and sweetness, and robbed the listeners of the sweet song. 

And so it is with our body: let no spectator disparage our pious race because of its frailty. But recognize how tireless is the Spirit of God, always possessing its own knowledge in the same way, continuing its blessings, and manifesting through the same benefits throughout all time. Even if the use of the material did not obey the craftsman in its perfect variety, the musician himself has done as much as he could; let us not lay the blame upon him. Let us instead condemn the frailty which, by lowering the pitch or raising it, destroyed the closeness of the harmonious song. 

For no one will ever accuse the musician because of a weakness occurring in the instrument. Indeed, the more the instrument was a hindrance, the more the musician struggled to compensate for the failing pitch; and for this, the listeners regard that musician with even greater love, rather than turning blame against him. Thus you also, O most honored ones, adapt your own inner lyre to the Musician. 

**Asclepius**...

# Definitions of Asclepius

### f ii

Indeed, I see a certain craftsman <note>The "craftsman" here refers to the philosopher or speaker, Asclepius, who is comparing his oratory skills to a musician’s performance.</note> who, even without playing the lyre, shows his skill: if there was ever a great proof of his preparation, it is as if he used the instrument itself frequently. He adjusts the service of the strings through hidden means so that it works in such a way that the listeners, seated out of respect, are struck with wonder. It is said that there was once a certain **cithara-player** <term>cithara-player: a professional performer on the cithara, a sophisticated ancient Greek stringed instrument similar to a lyre</term> who, when a string was broken by a superior force, continued on. It is said that this musician, who was devoted to music, had a god who was favorable to him. For when he was competing in a cithara contest, a broken string became a hindrance to him; however, the kindness of the **Superior One** <note>original: "praestantioris." This refers to a divine or higher power, likely God or Providence.</note> supplied the string for him and granted him the grace of excellence. For a long time, in accordance with the providence of the Superior One, that power supplied sweetness to his strings as they fell, and kept the place of the broken string; the cithara-player, freed from the pain of the loss by the replacement of the string, held the excellence of victory.

So I feel and experience this myself, O most honored ones. For just now I seemed to confess my weakness and to fail a little while ago; but the power of the Superior One supplies the melody for the king's song. For this reason, the end of our utility will be the praise of kings and the duty of oratory for their trophies of victory. Come then, let us go: for the musician wishes this, and he has tuned it to the lyre; and he will play all the more sweetly and sing more gentle songs as nature provides a greater song.

After the lyre was tuned for me specifically for the king himself, and it holds the course of praise and the intention toward royal honors, it first stirred itself toward the **Supreme King of all, the Good God**. And having begun the song from a higher place, it will turn in the second order to the gods who, through His image, hold scepter-bearing majesty. Indeed, it is also pleasing to the kings themselves that the first song proceeds from on high; for from where victory was given to them, from there also the goods of hope are derived by consequence.

Let the musician come, therefore, to the Greatest King of all, God: who is indeed immortal throughout the eternal, and holds power from the eternal. He is the honorable Conqueror, the first, from whom all victories come. For the rest of time, victories are granted to those who follow. Our speech now hastens to descend to praises, and to the kings who are the overseers of our common security and peace, whose empire has long been greatly enlarged by the Superior God; to whom victory was granted before His right hand; for whom the prizes were prepared before the war was bravely waged; for whom there are trophies even before the battle; to whom not only kingdoms, but also the decree to act bravely was established; at whose very movement the **barbarian** <note>In this context, "barbarian" refers to those outside the civilized order or the enemies of the peaceful kingdom.</note> is struck with awe.

But the speech hastens to resolve the end in the beginning, and to move into the praise of the Superior One. Then, it will conclude the oration with the peace of the most divine kings who govern us. For just as we began from the Superior and higher power, so we shall bend the end back again toward that same Superior Being. And just as the **Sun** exists as the nourisher of all growth, he himself, rising first, gathers the first fruits of the harvest with his hands—using his rays as if for the picking of fruit. For his rays are his hands, picking the sweetest parts of the plants first.

In this way, since we have begun from the Superior One and have attained one spark of His wisdom, and are using this for our souls' **super-celestial plants** <note>A metaphor for the divine or intellectual faculties of the human soul that reach toward heaven.</note>, our praises must be stretched back toward Him again. He Himself will pour into us all our growth. It is fitting that the praise of the mouth and voices be returned to God, who is whole in every part, and to the Father of our souls, through this mystery. And if we cannot speak words equal to His dignity—since we are not equal to Him—neither could the ancient fathers celebrate Him according to His full dignity; yet they returned praise according to their human capacity, and for this they receive forgiveness. 

Indeed, it yields more glory to God that He is greater than His own creations. And the preface, the grace, the middle, and the end of all praises is to confess the **Father of infinite power** and of infinite boundaries. So it is with the praises of the king. For by nature, praises are within us humans, as we are offspring born from Him. But forgiveness must be sought. He especially grants these things even before the request is made of the Father. Just as the first-born and the ancients were not only removed from weakness by the Father, but also rejoiced through their desperation. So too is the knowledge of the whole, which provides life to all, and the praise to God which He has bestowed upon us.

# [The Disciples of Hermes Trismegistus]

For God, being good and always manifest, and possessing within Himself the goal of perpetual excellence through all things, is also immortal, encompassing within Himself an infinite limit. He is perennial through every action of His, offering to this world a protective promise <note>original: "pollicitationem auferuatricem." This refers to God's sustaining grace that preserves the universe.</note> of praise. In Him, therefore, there is no internal difference. There is no mutual change in Him. Rather, all things feel as one: there is one foreknowledge for all, one mind for them, and one fatherly sense operating through them to create the harmony of all things.

If indeed we praise God, let us truly descend to those who have received scepters from Him <note>This refers to earthly rulers who are seen as receiving their authority and "scepters" directly from the divine hierarchy.</note>. For it is necessary that those who began with kings, and were trained by them, should also accustom themselves to praises and celebrate piety toward that which is more excellent. And indeed, the first principle of praise begins with practice. They practice for this reason: that the practice of piety toward God and the praise of kings may be one and the same for us.

For it is right to return rewards to those who have unfolded for us the tranquility of such great peace. The virtue and the name of the King alone provides us with a father. For a King is so called <note>The author is engaging in a popular ancient practice of "etymology," linking the word for King (Rex) to the way he walks or rules (regno).</note> because he walks in royalty and greatness; he holds power for the sake of peaceful discourse, and because he was born to excel over barbarian kingdoms, his name is a mark of peace. Indeed, the very title of "king" has frequently been enough to make an enemy retreat at once. Furthermore, the acts of prostration before his statue are the greatest proofs of peace. Even the mere sight of the king’s image has brought about victory; it has granted fearlessness and safety from wounds to the native people.

# The Definitions of Asclepius

Indeed, I see a certain artist who, even without the active playing of the lyre, shows great proof of his preparation, just as if he himself frequently used the instrument. ¶ He arranges the service of the strings through secret means, so that the resulting work may strike the listeners—who are gathered for the sake of honor—with wonder. It is said of a certain artist, a cithara-player <note>The *citharedus* was a professional performer who sang while playing the cithara, a large and prestigious type of ancient lyre.</note>: when a string was broken, it was mended by a Superior Power <note>original: "a prestantiore." In this context, it refers to a higher divine entity or God Himself intervening to assist the human artist.</note>. It is said that a certain cithara-player, a master of music, had a propitious god. If, indeed, while performing in a cithara-playing contest, a broken string became a contemptible hindrance to him, the kindness of the Superior Power supplied the string for him and provided the grace of excellence. For a long time, according to the providence of the Superior Power, a sweetness had fallen upon those strings to supply them and guard the place of the broken string; the cithara-player, truly freed from grief by the supplement of the string, held the excellence of victory.

So therefore, as I feel and experience myself, O most honored ones: for lately I seemed to confess my weakness and, a little while ago, to fail; but by the power of the Superior One, a melody was supplied to modulate toward the King. For this reason, the end of our utility shall be the praise of kings, and the duty of our speech shall arise from their trophies of victory. Come then, let us go; for this is what the Musician <note>The "Musician" or "Modulator" here refers to the divine spirit or the inspired soul directing the praise.</note> wills, and he has tuned it to the lyre; and he will play all the more sweetly and sing more gentle songs as nature provides a greater theme for the song.

Therefore, after the lyre has been most greatly tuned by me for the King himself, and holds the tenor and intention of praise toward royal honors, it first roused itself toward the highest King of all, the good God. And having begun the song from a higher place, it turned in the second order to the gods who, through His image, possess scepter-bearing majesty. If indeed it is also dear to the kings themselves that the first song should proceed from on high: and from where victory was given to them, from there also the good things of hope are consequently drawn. Let the Musician come, therefore, to the greatest King of all, God; who is indeed immortal throughout the whole, everlasting, and possessing power from the eternal. He is the first fit Victor, from whom all victories come. For the remaining time, victories are granted to those who follow.

Our speech, therefore, hastens to descend to praises, and to the kings who are the overseers of common security and peace, whose empire has long since been greatly expanded by the Superior God; to whom victory was granted before His right hand; for whom the prizes <note>term: "brauia" (bravia). From the Greek *brabeion*, referring to the prize awarded to the winner of a contest or race.</note> were prepared even before the brave deeds of war; for whom there were trophies even before the clash of battle; for whom it was ordained not only to reign, but also to act bravely; at whose very movement the barbarian is struck with awe. But our speech hastens to resolve the end in the beginning, and to finish in the praise of the Superior One. Then, let us terminate our speech with the peace of the most divine kings who minister to us. ¶ For just as we began from a Superior and higher power, so we shall again turn our end back toward the Superior One Himself.

And just as the sun, being the nourisher of all growth, is himself the first to rise and collects the first fruits of the produce with his hands—as if using his rays for the gathering of the fruits—for the rays are his hands, plucking first the sweetest of the plants: so for us, having begun from the Superior One and having attained one part of His wisdom, and using this for the super-celestial plants of our souls, our praises must again be directed toward Him. He Himself shall pour into us all this growth. It is fitting that praise be returned to God, who is in every part whole, the Father of our souls, by the mystery of the mouth and voices. And even if we cannot speak as equals to His dignity, we do not cease by our speaking. For not even the ancient fathers could celebrate Him according to His full dignity; rather, they rendered praise according to their manly portion as was fitting, and for this, they have forgiveness. 

Moreover, it yields more glory to the God of glory that He Himself is greater than His own generations. He is the preamble, the grace, the middle, and the end of praises: to confess the Father of infinite power and of infinite boundaries. Such also are the praises of the King. For by nature, praises are inherent in us men as beings generated from Him. But forgiveness must be sought. For He especially grants these things even before the petition from the Father. ¶ Just as it is not only the removal of the Father's weakness for those born before and the ancients, but a cause for rejoicing through hope <note>original: "desperationem." In some Latin contexts of this period, this can imply a "surpassing of hope" or the state beyond human calculation, though it literally means "despair." Given the context of "rejoicing," it implies the divine resolution of human helplessness.</note>. And thus is the knowledge of the whole, which provides life to all, and the praise to God which He has bestowed upon us.

### Disciple of Hermes Trismegistus

For God, being essentially good and ever-present, contains within Himself the culmination of eternal excellence and immortality; or rather, He exists encompassing an infinite definition within Himself. Through His eternal activity, He offers to this world a saving promise of praise. Therefore, there is no internal division within Him, nor is there any change or turning back. Instead, all things perceive as one; there is one foreknowledge for all, one mind, and one Father—a single consciousness working through them to create the harmony of the universe.

If we are to praise God, we must also descend to those who have received their scepters <note>The scepter is used here as a symbol of legitimate royal authority granted by the divine.</note> from Him. For it is necessary for those who have begun with kings and been trained by them to accustom themselves to songs of praise, and to practice piety toward that which is most excellent. The very beginning of praise comes from practice; and they engage in this practice so that the exercise of piety toward God and the praise of kings may become one and the same for us. Indeed, we must offer due rewards to those who have secured for us the tranquility of such profound peace. 

The virtue and the very name of "King" presents the image of a father. He is called "King" because he moves with royal majesty and grandeur, holding authority over the discourse of peace; he is born to surpass any barbaric realm, and his name is a sign of peace. In truth, the mere title of "King" has often been enough to make an enemy retreat instantly. Furthermore, the statues of such a ruler are the ultimate expressions of peace. Indeed, the mere sight of the king's image has brought about victory, granting boldness and safety from harm <note>original: "insaucietatem," meaning the state of being un-wounded or invulnerable.</note> to his people.

# Commentary

## The Commentary of Lord Symphorien Champier, physician of Lyon, on the Theological Definitions of Asclepius, disciple of Hermes Trismegistus, addressed to King Ammon; divided into four parts.

<margin>
The first race of the gods.

A
Where the first humans were created.
</margin>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a floral design with several blooming flowers within a square border.</image-desc>

Since the poets tell tales that the first race of gods existed among the Egyptians, and that ancient observations of the stars were discovered by them—and since many famous and excellent deeds of great men are reported there—this history rightly begins with their affairs. The Egyptians claim (with Diodorus <note>original: "Diodoro teste." Refers to Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE who wrote extensively on Egyptian origins.</note> as witness) that the first humans were created in their land at the beginning of the world, both because of the goodness and fertility of the soil and because of the Nile. For the Nile generates many things and, by its own nature, easily nourishes what it has brought forth. Indeed, it provides the roots of reeds, the lotus, the Egyptian bean, and what they call *oxseum* <note>original: "oxseum." Likely referring to a type of sorrel or aquatic plant used for food.</note>, along with many other things laid out for the sustenance of men.

They use this conjecture to suggest that the first living creatures arose among them: even now in the fields of the Thebaid <note>The region around the ancient city of Thebes in Egypt.</note> at certain times, many large mice are generated. People are greatly amazed by this, for they see some of them animated and moving in their front parts as far as the chest and front feet, while the hind part is not yet finished but remains unformed earth. They say it is clear from this that Egypt produced the first humans at the very birth of the world; for in no other part of the world does it happen that animals are created in such a way. Therefore (as they say), those first humans born long ago in Egypt, beholding this adornment of the universe and marveling at the nature of all things, judged that there were two gods

<margin>
¶ Two gods: the sun and the moon.

L
</margin>

who were eternal: namely, the Sun and the Moon. They called the former Osiris and the latter Isis, for specific reasons. They called him Osiris (in the Greek interpretation) because he surveys the land and sea with his rays as if with many eyes; thus, they called him "the one with many eyes." <note>The author is connecting the name Osiris to the Greek "hosios" or "ophthalmos," following a common but linguistically incorrect Renaissance etymology.</note> Regarding this, the poets also heap up words, saying the sun "sees all and hears all." They assert that these gods, as they judged, travel around the entire world and nourish and increase all things through the three seasons of the year, completing the circuit with continuous motion: Spring, Summer,

<column-break/>

and Winter. These seasons do not conflict with one another but complete the year in established harmony. They say that one of the gods is fiery and spiritual <note>The Sun</note>, while the other is moist and cold <note>The Moon</note>. Air is common to both. From these, therefore, all bodies are generated and nourished, and the unique nature of things is perfected by the Sun and Moon.

They report, moreover, that others were born from these who were mortal, but through their wisdom and their benefits to the human race, they obtained immortality. <note>This concept, that gods were originally great human leaders deified after death, is known as Euhemerism.</note> Some of these reigned in Egypt; some were called by the same names as the celestial gods, while others were called by their own names: the Sun, Saturn, Rhea, and also Jupiter (whom some call Ammon), Juno, and furthermore Vulcan, Vesta, and finally Mercury Trismegistus.

<margin>
E
</margin>

The Egyptians maintain that this Mercury was the first

<margin>
The inventions of Trismegistus.
</margin>

to bring words into order and to give names to many things. They also say he was the inventor of letters and established the honors and sacred rites with which the gods should be worshiped. He was the first observer of the course of the stars and discovered the harmonies of voices. They record him as the discoverer of the wrestling floor <note>The *palaestra*, used here to mean physical education or athletics.</note>, of numbers, and of the medical art for healing bodies. Furthermore, he invented the lyre with three strings to match the three seasons of the year. For he established three tones: the high, the low, and the middle. He took the high from summer, the low from winter, and the middle from spring. He also taught the Greeks the interpretation of words, which is why they called him *Hermes* (that is, "the Interpreter"). <note>The name Hermes is linked here to the Greek word *hermeneus*, meaning interpreter or translator.</note> Finally, those who were writers of sacred letters in the time of King Osiris report that they received these same things from him.

</margin>

They say Osiris made great use of his counsel; even the planting of the Olive

The institutions of Osiris.
</margin>

was discovered by him, and not by Minerva <note>Athena</note> as the Greeks say. They report that Osiris, as a good man and one eager for glory, gathered a huge army so that he might travel safely through the world, teaching mortals how to plant vines, the crops of wheat and barley, and the benefits of livestock...

# On the definitions of Asclepius.

...remaining as he was, if he could lead men from a wild life to a more cultivated and gentler one, he would obtain the immortal honors he subsequently achieved. For not only those ancients, but even their descendants—mindful of the benefit of the grain crops discovered by him—held them as the greatest gods. They say that once the kingdom of Egypt was established, Osiris entrusted the care of all things to his wife Isis and gave her **Mercury Trismegistus** <note>Also known as Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure credited with writing the Hermetic corpus.</note> as an advisor; because he seemed to excel in wisdom, she used his counsel among her friends. He left Hercules as the leader of the army and of all matters pertaining to military pursuits.

<margin>
D 
Mercury Trismegistus regarded as a god
</margin>
To this Mercury they attribute the killing of Argus; they say he presided over the Egyptians and gave them laws and letters. He was held in such great veneration among men that he was numbered among the gods. Many temples were constructed to his divinity. Out of a certain reverence, it was not permitted for the common people to pronounce his proper name rashly. The first month of the year among the Egyptians is named after him. A town was founded by him which is even now called in Greek *Hermopolis*, that is, the city of Mercury.

<margin>
J 
Why he is called Trismegistus
</margin>
They called him **Trismegistus**, or "Thrice-Greatest," because he stood out as the greatest philosopher, the greatest priest, and the greatest king.

<margin>
M 
The custom of the Egyptians in choosing a king. The first theologian.
</margin>
After Osiris, he was called King by the Egyptians. For it was the custom of the Egyptians to choose priests from the number of philosophers, and to choose a king from the assembly of priests. Among the kings and philosophers, he was the first to turn from the study of physics and mathematics to the contemplation of divine matters. He was the first to dispute most wisely concerning the majesty of God, the order of demons <note>In the Renaissance sense, "demons" refers to *daimones*—intermediary spirits between gods and humans—rather than evil entities.</note>, and the transformations of souls.

<margin>R</margin>
He was therefore called the first author of theology. He was followed by **Asclepius**, his disciple, whom he introduced in the form of a dialogue in the book *On the Divine Will*, which is titled *Asclepius*. This Asclepius held the second place in ancient theology. **Orpheus** was initiated into these sacred mysteries by Asclepius.

<margin>Z</margin>
Moreover, many deeds of the ancient Egyptians are not only esteemed greatly by the natives, but also hold no small amount of admiration among the Greeks. Therefore, those who most excelled in learning traveled to Egypt so that they might perceive their laws and studies as worthy of 

<column-break/>

knowledge. For who would not know that entry into Egypt was difficult for foreigners? Nevertheless, they once sought to go there with all zeal; among these the more ancient were Orpheus and the poet **Homer**. Then came several descendants: **Pythagoras** of Samos and the lawgiver **Solon**. The Egyptians assert that letters, the courses of the stars, 

<margin>
O 
The invention of arts and sciences.
</margin>
geometry, and many arts were discovered by them. Furthermore, they claim the best laws were instituted by them. They say the greatest proof of this is that indigenous kings ruled Egypt for more than three thousand seven hundred years. This province was the most fortunate of all others in the world, which could in no way have happened unless they had lived by the best customs and laws, and had been learned in every kind of teaching.

<margin>
Priests of the Egyptians.
</margin>
For it was not as it is among the Greeks, where one man or one woman presided over the sacred rites; rather, many were engaged in the worship and honor of the gods, who passed down the same care of the sacred things to their sons. All of these were exempt from taxes and held the second place of honor and dignity after the kings.

<margin>
When the laws of Egypt were accepted
</margin>
For after the ancient life of the Egyptians, which they tell in fables existed in the time of the gods and heroes, they say that **Mina** <note>Refers to Menes, traditionally the first human king of Egypt.</note>—a man of great spirit and a life approved by all—first persuaded the multitude to use written laws. He feigned that these were given by the command of Mercury Trismegistus, as if they were to be the causes of great blessings.

<margin>
By what means the laws were given
</margin>
In the same way, they say that among the Greeks, **Minos** did this in Crete and **Lycurgus** among the Spartans; one said Jupiter was the author of his laws, the other Apollo. Many nations also report that they received laws in this manner, which were the cause of many blessings to those who obeyed them.

<margin>D.</margin>
For they write that **Zatraustes** <note>Zoroaster.</note> gave laws to the Iranians under a feigned name. In the same way, **Zamolxis** brought laws to the Getae <note>A Thracian tribe.</note>, presenting them from Vesta. Among the Jews, **Moses** claimed to give laws received through himself from **Abiao** <note>original: "Abiao." A rendering of the Divine Name (IAO/Yahweh).</note>, whom they call God; they did this either thinking that the law was a marvelous and divine thing and most useful to mortals, 

<margin>
P 
The lawgivers of the Egyptians.
</margin>
or thinking that the people would more quickly obey the laws out of fear of a god because of the excellence of the matter. Therefore, the first lawgiver among the Egyptians was a man of excellent prudence, **Mercury Trismegistus**, followed by **Mina**, a man of great spirit and proven character.

### The Commentary of Lord Symphorien Champier, physician of Lyon, on the theological definitions of Asclepius, the disciple of Hermes Trismegistus, addressed to King Ammon, divided into four parts.

<margin>
The first race of gods
A
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter Q containing floral patterns and leaves within a square border.</image-desc>Since the poets tell stories that the first race of gods existed among the Egyptians, and that ancient observations of the stars were discovered by them—and furthermore, since many famous deeds of excellent men are reported there as worthy of memory—this history shall begin with their affairs. They report (as Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BCE Greek historian known for his universal history, "Bibliotheca historica."</note> testifies) that at the beginning of the world, the first humans were created among them, both because of the goodness and happiness of the soil and because of the Nile. For the river generates many things and, by its very nature, easily nourishes what it has brought forth. Indeed, it provides the roots of reeds and the lotus, as well as the Egyptian bean, which they call *orseum* <note>Probably referring to the Nelumbo nucifera or a similar aquatic plant.</note>, and many other things set out for the sustenance of men. They use this conjecture to support the idea that the first living creatures arose among them: even now in the fields of the Thebaid <note>The region of ancient Egypt around the city of Thebes.</note> at certain times, many large mice are generated. People are greatly amazed by this fact, as they see that the front parts of some of them, as far as the chest and the front feet, are animated and move, while the rear part is not yet begun but remains unformed. They say it is clear from this that Egypt produced the first humans at the very birth of the world; for in no other part of the world does it happen that animals are created in such a way. Therefore (as they say), those first humans born long ago in Egypt, beholding the beauty of the world and wondering at the nature of the universe, judged that there were two eternal gods: namely, the Sun and the Moon. They called the former Osiris and the latter Isis, for specific reasons. They say Osiris means "many-eyed" in the Greek interpretation, as if he

<margin>
Where the first humans were created.

<margin>
Two gods: sun and moon.
