were surveying the land and sea with his rays as if they were many eyes. To this the poets also add their words, calling the Sun "the one who sees all and hears all." They claim these gods circle the whole world and nourish and increase all things through the three seasons of the year, completing the cycle with continuous motion: spring, summer, and winter. These opposites, in turn, complete the year through an established harmony. They say one of the gods is fiery and spiritual <note>original: "spiritualem," referring to the pneuma or breath of life</note>, and the other is moist and cold. Air is common to both. Thus, all bodies are generated and nourished by them, and the singular nature of things is perfected by the Sun and the Moon. They report, moreover, that others were born from these who were mortal, but who achieved immortality through their wisdom and their benefits to the human race. Some of these reigned in Egypt; some were called by the same names as the celestial gods, while others were called by their own names. These included the Sun, Saturn, Rhea, and also Jupiter (whom some call Ammon), Juno, and furthermore Vulcan, Vesta, and finally **Hermes Trismegistus**. The Egyptians believe that he was the first to organize words into order, and they say he was the inventor of many letters and established the honors and sacred rites with which the gods should be worshipped. He was the first observer of the courses of the stars and discovered musical harmonies. They report him as the discoverer of the movements of the gymnasium <note>original: "palestre," referring to athletic training</note> and the art of medicine for curing bodies; furthermore, he invented the lyre made of three strings, corresponding to the three seasons of the year. For he established three tones: the high, the low, and the middle. We take the high from summer, the low from winter, and the middle from spring. He also taught the Greeks the interpretation of words, which is why they called him *Hermes* <note>original: "hermen," the Greek name for the messenger god, which Champier associates here with "interpretation" or hermeneutics.</note>, that is, the interpreter. Finally, even the writers of sacred letters who lived in the time of King Osiris credit these same things to him. They say Osiris made great use of his counsel, and that the olive tree was discovered by him and not by Minerva <note>The Roman goddess of wisdom and war, equivalent to the Greek Athena.</note>, as the Greeks claim. Indeed, they say Osiris gathered a huge army so that he might travel safely through the world and teach mortals how to plant vines, and the sowing of wheat and barley, and the benefit of livestock.

# On the definitions of Asclepius.
**U**

The second man among the Egyptians to excel in human wisdom was Sasochis <note>Likely Sasychis, a legendary Egyptian king mentioned by Herodotus as a great lawgiver.</note>. They say he added many things to previous laws regarding religion and the worship of God; he was also the inventor of geometry and showed the courses of the stars to the inhabitants.

<margin>Q</margin>

They hand down that the third was King Soosis, who contributed many things to military matters and the duties of war through his institutions. The fourth recorded is King Bucchoris <note>Bocchoris (Bakenranef), an 8th-century BCE Pharaoh known in Greek tradition as a wise judge.</note>, who brought forth laws. After him, King Amasus added many laws, especially those pertaining to monarchs. They say the sixth, Darius the Persian <note>Darius I, who was respected by the Egyptians for his codification of their laws.</note>, added his own fatherly care to the laws of the Egyptians. Thus, their priests did not despise him; his theology and his sacred deeds were contained within their precepts. History has embraced the magnificence of the ancient kings and their humanity toward their subjects. Certainly, having imitated their virtue, he alone was called a "living god" by the Egyptians while still alive.

<margin>R</margin>

There were, therefore, kings among the Egyptians who handed down laws to them, the first of whom was Mercury Trismegistus <note>The Latin text uses "Mercurius" for Hermes.</note>. Among the theologians, Mercury was also the first. Asclepius, his disciple among the Egyptians, succeeded Mercury in theology.

<margin>
The Greeks
crossed over 
to the 
Egyptians 
for the sake 
of their 
learning.
</margin>

But we shall list those among the Greeks endowed with wisdom and doctrine who crossed over into Egypt in ancient times to perceive their theology, laws, and doctrine. Their priests write in the sacred books that Orpheus first crossed to the Egyptians, followed by Musaeus, Melampus, Daedalus, the poet Homer, and the Spartan Lycurgus. Next came Solon the Athenian, Plato, and Pythagoras of Samos; also Eudoxus the mathematician and Democritus of Abdera.

<margin>S</margin>

In Egypt, they certainly learned everything that made them admirable among the Greeks. For they say Orpheus brought back very many hymns of the gods, the secret rites <note>original: "orgia." Refers to the mystery religions or sacred ceremonies.</note>, and the poetic description of the underworld. And for this reason, Asclepius says here in this work to King Ammon:

<margin>T</margin>

"As much as possible, O King, preserve (as you can) every discourse unchanged, lest such mysteries reach the Greeks. Nor let the proud, loose, and, as it were, curled speech <note>original: "calamistrata." This refers to a style of rhetoric that is artificially ornate or affected, like hair curled with iron tongs.</note> of the Greeks weaken the gravity, strength, and active power of the names' pronunciation. For the Greeks, O King, have only new words, and their demonstrations are not

<column-break/>

active. And this is the philosophy of the Greeks: the sound of words. We, however—namely the Egyptians—do not use words, but voices of the greatest power." These are the words of Asclepius.

Asclepius, seeing his master Hermes accustomed to invoking God at the beginning of any work, whether great or small, said: "I will begin the discourse from there, invoking God, the Lord and Maker of all things, the Father of the circle and of all things existing as one, and the one existing as all." For the fullness of all things is one, and in the one, there is no second "one" existing, but rather one existing in both <note>This refers to the monistic idea that God is both the source and the sum of all things.</note>. For the Egyptians said that God, through love in all things toward all things, is the author and savior of all, and exists as the lord and master of all arts. This one Orpheus rightly called the "Skillful Twice-born" <note>original: "Solertem bigenium." A reference to the Orphic concept of a god born from two natures or origins.</note>, who holds the keys to all things. Therefore, that unity, truth, and goodness which we find above the angels in the mind of Trismegistus is the principle of all: the one, true, and good God.

<margin>BB</margin>

First, He is one because He is supreme unity. For if whatever is supreme is unique, what is more <insert>God is</insert> unique than supreme unity? He is primarily one because any multitude of innumerable things is reduced to its own proper unity. Therefore, the one God is the arranger of the one world. Second, He is one because He is Truth. For the supreme Truth is one.

<margin>CC</margin>

Third, He is one because He is supreme goodness. Indeed, supreme goodness embraces whatever good can ever be found. God is therefore in all things because all things are in Him; for unless they were in Him, they would be nowhere, and would not exist at all.

God is amplitude and fullness.

# Commentary.

God is that nature itself. I do not see, therefore, why he should not amplify and fill himself through all things and each individual thing. Let us often contemplate that most pure and full capacity which no limits can contain: which contains all things that can exist or be imagined. Reason dictates that what is named "everywhere" is nothing other than the whole nature of things:
<margin>CC</margin> and that this nature is God. Therefore, when we say that God is everywhere, it ought to be understood that he is in himself, and vice versa. It is more excellent to exist "always"—which is, as it were, intrinsic—than to exist "everywhere"—which is, as it were, extrinsic. For this reason, that which can exist always can much more easily exist everywhere. For it is easier to exceed sluggish dimensions of space than to exceed the effective motion of quality and time.

<margin>Matter as a subject.</margin>
<margin>DD</margin> While Asclepius says that all matter is believed to be a treasury <note>original: "erarium"; here meaning a storehouse or receptacle for forms.</note>, according to Aristotle it is a subject for each thing. And just as the first in nature, which is God, acts upon all things and suffers <note>In the philosophical sense: to be acted upon or to receive an impression.</note> nothing, so the last thing, which is corporeal matter, must suffer from all things. Indeed, it acts by itself upon another not at all, since there is nothing below it that might suffer from it. Therefore, matter which is subject to nature, since it is formless, is led to a natural form not by itself, but by the nature of form. On which account, beyond all
<margin>EE</margin> forms of this kind, there must be present in and presiding over all things a certain incorporeal substance penetrating through bodies, whose instruments are the corporeal qualities. This form Asclepius says is God. As Asclepius says: "I say indeed that the Sun is a certain inducing substance, bringing back matter, drawing all things around and toward himself, giving all things from himself to all, and bestowing a copious light." For he is the one whose light and activity reach not only into the heaven and the air, but even into the earth, down into the innermost depth of the abyss.

<margin>The powers of the Sun and Moon.</margin>
Understand the Sun to be the moderator of all things. Iamblichus narrates the opinion of the Egyptians thus: "Whatever good we have, we have from the Sun; namely, either from him alone, or if from others as well, it is either derived from the Sun or through others from the Sun." Likewise, the Sun is the lord of all elemental virtues. The Moon, by the virtue of the Sun, is the mistress of generation. Therefore, Albumasar <note>A 9th-century Persian astrologer and astronomer.</note> says that through the Sun

<column-break/>

and the Moon, life is infused into all things. <margin>FF</margin> Moses considers the Sun the lord of celestial things by day, and the Moon by night, as if it were a "nocturnal sun."

<margin>The Sun is placed in the middle.</margin>
Indeed, all have placed the Sun, the lord, in the middle of the world, although for different reasons. The Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers/astrologers.</note> placed him in the middle of the planets. The Egyptians, however, placed him between two groups of five in the world. Specifically, five planets above him; the Moon and the four elements below him. They believe he was positioned by providence closer to the earth than to the firmament, so that by his burning spirit and great light, the moisture of the Moon, air, water, and the thick matter of earthly things might be fostered.

<margin>Orpheus on the Sun</margin>
For these reasons, Orpheus called Apollo <note>The Greek god often identified with the Sun.</note> the life-giving eye of heaven. And briefly, these things which I say are gathered from the Orphic hymns: "But the eternal eye seeing all things. The supervening heavenly light, tempering heavenly and mundane things. Leading or drawing the harmonic course of the world. The lord of the world, immortal Jupiter, the all-running eye of the world, having a seal, fashioning all mundane things; the Moon pregnant with stars. The Moon, queen of the stars." Thus says Orpheus.

Among the Egyptians, in the temples of Minerva <note>Often identified with the Egyptian goddess Neith.</note>, this golden inscription was read: <margin>GG</margin> "I am those things which are, which will be, and which have been. My veil no one has revealed. The fruit which I have brought forth is the Sun born." Where it appears that the Sun is the offspring, flower, and fruit of Minerva—that is, of Divine Intelligence.

The ancient theologians, as Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> testifies, used to say <margin>HH</margin> that the queen of all, Justice, proceeds through all things from a throne in the middle of the Sun, directing all things, as if the Sun himself were the moderator of all. The ancient Physicists named the Sun the "heart of heaven." Heraclitus called him the fountain of celestial light; many Platonists located the Soul of the World in the Sun, which, filling the whole sphere of the Sun, pours out rays through that globe like fire, as if a spirit from there through all things, to which it distributes life, sense, and motion to the universe. But from where this consists or flows (says Asclepius), he alone knows; for he, like a good charioteer, confirming the chariot of the world and binding it to himself <margin>II</margin> so that it may not be carried along in an-disorderly way. The first principle acts for its own sake and moves all things divinely. Concerning Jove <note>Jupiter.</note>, he says...

# On the definitions of Asclepius

### Column 1

As Orpheus says: "Progenitor of all: the beginning and the end. You see all things within; you hear all things within; you distribute all things." In the works of Orpheus, God is called "eternal life" and "immortal wisdom." Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> says that this wisdom is the nurse of the human race. And the divine Plato, in the fourth book of the *Laws*, says that God contains the beginnings, the middles, and the ends of all things; He encompasses all and rightly disposes each individual thing. He is favorable to the strong and the religious, while He punishes the proud and the impious.
<margin>RR</margin> ¶ When Asclepius speaks concerning the spirits <note>original: "demonibus"; in this context, it refers to *daimones*, intermediary spirits between gods and humans, rather than exclusively "demons" in the modern sense.</note>, saying that some are mixed from good and evil, and that they have been allotted the management of affairs among themselves, etc.: what is said here does not seem to be entirely capable of being brought into a pious understanding, but rather follows the error of the gentiles. Nevertheless, Asclepius, as if full of prophecy, discourses much here regarding spirits and fate; regarding God, the Word <note>original: "verbo"; likely referring to the *Logos*.</note>, the world, and matter; and that nothing in the world is devoid of life. They call the governance of things "fate";
<margin>Fate.</margin> for indeed, divine law is fate. Regarding spirits, I think it has already been demonstrated that in Christian histories all such beings are seducers and evildoers; no practitioners of magic are more devoted to anything than to the subversion of truth. Thus, since they have looked upon great errors within the human race, they have deceived almost all nations with the false necessity of the fates. From these errors, no one has liberated mortals except our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. ¶ Asclepius writes that around the sun
<margin>22</margin> there are eight spheres depending upon it: one of the fixed stars, six of the wandering stars <note>The planets known in antiquity.</note>, and one around the earth. But because I know not why we are here under this Apollo <note>God of the sun and poetry.</note> as if we were poets,
<margin>QQ</margin> even if not good ones, let us be permitted to converse for a little while. Regarding the nine Muses, the ancients placed these powers in the sun. For we either contemplate his substance or his powers. Within his substance, we find essence, life, and intelligence.
<margin>Nine muses</margin> We name the essence "Heaven"; the life, "Rhea"; and the intelligence, "Saturn," according to their custom. If we contemplate the powers of the sun after his substance: we shall name his fecundity "Jove" <note>Jupiter</note> and "Juno." His light we name "Apollo" and "Minerva"; his color, finally, "Venus" and "Bacchus." Now, the ancients always depicted Phoebus and Bacchus—who rule most of all in the sun—as young men; for if anyone knew the light and color of the sun with that purity and property with which they exist there, and could receive them—

<column-break/>

### Column 2

—and accommodate them to his own use and measure, he would report perpetual youth therefrom, or at least fulfill one hundred and twenty solar years. But after these nine powers inward to the sun, let us proceed to the nine Muses around the sun. What, therefore, are the nine Muses around Phoebus, if not nine types of Apollonian powers distributed through the nine spheres of the world? However, the ancients recognized only eight heavens. Beneath the celestial fire, they added pure air as a ninth heaven, being celestial in its quality and motion. In any given sphere, they disposed divine spirits hidden from the eyes,
<margin>NN</margin> dedicated step-by-step to individual stars. These, the Platonist Proclus <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> calls "angels," and Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist who emphasized ritual and theurgy.</note> further names them "archangels" and "principalities." But those among them who are everywhere primarily "solar," the ancients called "Muses." These preside over all sciences, but especially poetry, medicine, music, purifications, oracles, and prophecies. But when Asclepius says, "From these spheres depend spirits, and from the spirits, men," it does not seem possible to be drawn toward true religion. All these things said here regarding the Muses and the spheres savor more of antiquity than of truth; they do not seem capable of being drawn into a pious understanding, but rather follow the error of the gentiles. Now let us return to Asclepius.
¶ Regarding God, Asclepius again says:
<margin>OO</margin> "But God does these things through these [powers] for himself; and all things are parts of God. But if all things are parts of God, then all things are God. Therefore, in making all things, He makes Himself and never ceases," etc. Here he teaches that all things are one, and all things are one [in God]: one as from Him by whom all things exist; one as all things effected are one in their cause. From this comes divine reason <note>original: "ratio"</note> and the divine Word <note>original: "verbum"</note>, most similar to a torrent of a river running from the summit with headlong speed; it permeates all things, glides into all things, and flows into all things. And what is this divine reason and divine Word other than Divine Wisdom, the architect of all things, which, since it is one, can do all things, and remaining in itself, renews all things. And Paul says to the Romans in chapter 11: "Since from him and through him and in him are all things."
<margin>PP</margin> ¶ Asclepius says that "Ideas" are the images of intelligible things. Indeed, among the Egyptians, "Ideas" are the realities: the reasons and the seeds. The forms of bodies are seen to be shadows of things rather than true realities. Just as—

# On the definitions of Asclepius

### Column 1

the shadow of a true body does not indicate the exact and distinct figure of the body. Thus, the bodies of the divine <note>original: "corpora divinorum"; referring to the manifested forms of higher beings or celestial bodies.</note> do not demonstrate their own proper nature.
<margin>QQ</margin> ¶ Concerning images, Asclepius says: "Adore the images, O king, as if they themselves possessed 'ideas' <note>In the Platonic sense, an 'idea' is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing in the divine mind.</note> from the intelligible world." But let me briefly explain what Christians feel regarding the adoration of images.
<margin>Christian Images</margin> In a gathering of three hundred and fifty bishops <note>A reference to the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 AD, which restored the use of icons in the Church.</note> celebrated at Nicaea—so that it might be decided once and for all whether the images of the saints should be restored to the temples or the practice abolished for all time—it was decreed by great consensus of all that they should be kept in temples according to the rite of the Roman Church. A form of veneration was added, contained in two verses, so that the matter might be free from any suspicion of idolatry. These verses are seen today in Venice, portrayed in the Golden House <note>The Basilica of St. Mark's in Venice.</note> in an ancient style of lettering, as they were translated from Greek into Latin: "For God is what the image teaches, but the image itself is not God. You may look upon this [image], but in your mind, worship what you perceive within it." <note>original: "Nam deus est quod imago docet: sed non deus ipsa. Hanc videas: sed mente colas quod cernis in ipsa."</note>
<margin>RR</margin> ¶ Asclepius, speaking of music or harmony, says: "Indeed, God the Musician possesses a nature that not only creates the harmony of songs, but also transmits the familiar rhythm <note>original: "numerum"; literally 'number', but here referring to musical meter or mathematical proportion.</note> of melody down to the specific instruments. God is tireless, for weariness is not appropriate for God," etc.
<margin>Two kinds of music.</margin> Two kinds of musical melody are handed down. One is grave and constant; the other is soft and wanton. Plato indicates in his books on the *Republic* and the *Laws* that the former is useful to those who use it, while the latter is well-known. In the context of a banquet, he made Urania <note>The Muse of Astronomy, representing the highest celestial music.</note> the Muse for the former, and Polyhymnia <note>The Muse of Sacred Poetry and Eloquence.</note> elsewhere for the latter. Some love the first kind; others the second. Those sounds which are to be applied to the regulation of character are to be sought after; the appetite for the others must be resisted. For the love of the former is celestial, while the love of the latter is common. Truly, if one were to offer to the sense of hearing a harmony of such great art and diligence of the Muses—with as much care of nature or art as flavors are offered to the taste, or soft things to the touch—we would undoubtedly recognize that Apollo <note>The Greek god of music, healing, and prophecy.</note> ravishes the soul with melody far more than Bacchus usually occupies the taste with wine, or Venus the touch with desire. For Plato described the soul—the maker, preserver, and mover of all natural things—chiefly through musical numbers and ratios; I say 'numbers' not as accidental mathematical values, as some falsely claim, but as established through ideal numbers and metaphysical principles. Therefore, as Asclepius

<column-break/>

### Column 2

writes so excellently: God not only creates the harmony of songs, but even transmits the familiar rhythm of melody down to particular instruments. Orpheus sang all of this in his Hymn to Apollo: "You who hold the boundaries of the entire world, you are the care of God. From the beginning and to the end, through you all things grow green. You temper the spheres with the resonance of the whole lyre." <note>original: "Tu habens usqz de mundi terminos universi... Tu spheras tota cythara resonante contemperas."</note> And in the eleventh chapter of Wisdom it is written: "You have ordered all things in measure and number and weight." <note>A famous biblical verse (Wisdom 11:20) used in the Middle Ages to justify the mathematical study of the universe.</note> And just as the most skilled physicians mix certain juices together by a certain reason, through which many diverse materials may unite into one new form—and beyond their elemental power, they miraculously obtain a celestial virtue, which is manifest in the Theriac of Andromachus <note>A famous ancient "cure-all" antidote containing dozens of ingredients, including viper's flesh.</note> and in the confection of Mithridates <note>Another legendary complex antidote named after King Mithridates VI of Pontus.</note>. Similarly, the most artistic musicians temper the deepest voices like cold materials, and the highest voices like hot ones, then moderately deep ones as moist, and moderately high ones as dry, with such great reason that one single form is made from many. This form pursues not only a vocal power, but a celestial one as well. This is evidently apparent from what Democritus and Theophrastus <note>Ancient Greek philosophers; Democritus is known for atomism, Theophrastus for botany and ethics.</note> say, and what Pythagoras proved by effect. For it is said that by certain harmonies, certain diseases of both the body and the soul were miraculously cured.
<margin>SS</margin> Thus it is no wonder that the ancient sages traced the origin of both medicine and music to the same source—that is, the Apollonian number. For each is a medicine: but one cures the soul through the body, while the other cures the body through the soul. Most appropriately, they also attributed prophecy <note>original: "vaticinium"</note> to Apollo, the fountain of melody. For melody alone, by drawing back the soul from all those things that distract it, contracts the soul into itself; into a certain—so to speak—inner hearing, by which not only the voices, but the reasons of the voices are perceived. When the disturbances are calmed, the soul is tempered to celestial harmony, and it pours out divine oracles from heaven. Indeed, every moving sphere, whether elemental or celestial, is moved in a circle by God through its own form with such great harmony that it may more fully enjoy its own place.
¶ Speaking of kingship, Asclepius says: "If
<margin>TT</margin> indeed we praise God, let us descend to those who have received scepters from Him. For it is necessary, having begun with kings and been trained by them,
<margin>The condition of a king.</margin> to also accustom ourselves to the praises of the Creator and to celebrate Him," etc. Plato wishes a king to be such that he truly perceives things in the manner of contemplatives.

# On the Definitions of Asclepius

### Column 1

[The king] should judge; and he should mandate that the laws to be carried out are not foreign ones, but his own. This follows from a very precise division of practical use, which is exceedingly necessary for both the definition and the science [of governance]. In the Homeric fashion, he calls the king the shepherd and caretaker of the human race. This indicates that there ought to be one single shepherd for the whole human race, as if it were a single sheepfold. Here he says that there was once a shepherd of the human race, under whom the Golden Age of Saturn existed. He also indicates that a king should be called the "pilot" of human life, as if he were steering a ship. This signifies that all power must be brought together into a single empire, so that human government might be as similar as possible to the divine government; for indeed, there is only one God who is the ruler of the entire world.

This is briefly confirmed by the following reasons: If you were to subdue the three parts of the world—Asia, Europe, and Africa—and distribute them among three kings, it would very easily happen that either one would eventually wage war against two, or two against one; or at the very least, they would be forced to argue over borders or some other matter. 
<margin>UU.</margin> Therefore, the judgment of the dispute would either have to be brought before one of those three, or before some fourth judge appointed besides the three. By whatever reason this is done, it will be necessary for that judge (if his sentence is to be obeyed) to have power over those between whom he judges. Otherwise, the judgment will be of no importance and will be judged in vain, as it might seem that the judgment could be dissolved by kings who are either more powerful or at least equally powerful. Therefore, there must be one king who is the judge of all, and who is undoubtedly to be revered by all.

As for what Plato disputes elsewhere concerning the motion of the spheres, providence, and fate, we have explained that sufficiently in other places. Certainly, Plato teaches us allegorically that we have no true and legitimate king except either in heaven itself, or on earth in the one whom the King of Heaven himself has placed over us as a shepherd—a shepherd, I say, not in name alone, but one who reflects the King of Heaven himself to the best of his ability through the similarity of his life. He also commemorates two kingdoms: namely, those of Jupiter and Saturn. He prefers the kingdom of Saturn to the kingdom of Jupiter, considering it more blessed. For under Jupiter, the active life and human action are signified; but under Saturn, the contemplation of divine things is signified. For Saturn, in his Greek name,

<column-break/>

is called *Chronos* <note>original: "chronos"; the Greek name for Saturn, often associated by Renaissance philosophers with "KRONOS" (Time) and "KOROS" (Purity/Fullness of Mind).</note>—as Plato also teaches in the *Cratylus*—and he encompasses the inviolable purity and integrity of the mind. When he said that men lived happily while Saturn was reigning, he showed that the human race would be blessed when a certain divine mind of a man is reigning, which might provide for actions for the sake of contemplation. 

Plato also compares the king to a physician, advising that in the manner of physicians, he should impose laws and bring healthy remedies both at opportune times and, when necessary, at inopportune times, both to those who are willing and sometimes to those who are unwilling. In his letters, he considers that the king himself should be held as sacred; and that, in the Egyptian fashion, he should be established as a priest and the overseer of sacred ministries. Because he is sacred, and so that he might never be contaminated, he does not permit the king to be present at trials where the matter concerns slaughter, exile, or prison. 

The same author proves that the royal dignity is the best of all forms of government, while the worst is tyranny, which rules neither by law nor by a legitimate mind, but rather by impulse and lust. For that reason, it was the custom of the Egyptians to choose priests from the number of philosophers, and to choose kings from the assembly of priests. For life consists of religion. By religion 
<margin>Lactantius</margin> (as the author Lactantius Firmianus <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author who argued that the word "religion" comes from *religare*, meaning "to bind" humanity to God.</note> states), Man excels all other living creatures. By the bond of religion, men are bound and tied back to God. From this "binding," religion itself is believed to have taken its name, although others derive it from elsewhere. 

All men owe servitude to God, which is called *latria* <note>original: "latria"; a Greek term used in Christian theology to denote the highest form of worship, reserved for God alone.</note> in Greek. But above all, the worship of God befits princes, which the Greeks call *theosebia* <note>original: "theosebia"; Greek for "god-fearing" or "piety."</note>. However, the most powerful worship of God is goodness. Seneca says: "Do you wish the gods to be favorable? Be good. Whoever has imitated them has worshipped them enough." Let the prince beware lest that which is so bad that nothing worse can be said, be deservedly said of him. Religion in a prince ensures that all subjects are restrained by a certain modesty and, as it were, by sanctity. Let the prince know, however, that God does not rejoice so much in the spending of the worshiper as in his holiness; for He prefers a pure mind to gold. Hence that line from Persius: "What does gold do in a holy place?" <note>original: "in sancto quid facit aurum?"; from Persius, Satire II. The poet argues that spiritual purity is more valuable than expensive offerings.</note> For I believe that a prince ought to be munificent toward God both in mind and by hand. For although God is in need of nothing, He nevertheless wishes princes to be neither unmindful nor ungrateful for His benefits.

<summary>This page argues for a singular, sacred monarchy that mirrors divine rule, contrasting the active life under Jupiter with the superior contemplative life of Saturn. It emphasizes that a true king must act as a "physician" to the state and be rooted in deep religious piety, prioritizing spiritual purity over material wealth.</summary>
<keywords>monarchy, Golden Age, Saturn, Plato, Lactantius, religion, piety, latria, theosebia, contemplative life, active life, Egyptian kingship</keywords>

# Commentary

<margin>yy</margin>
¶ God is called the King of Kings by all, for from Him all kings (as <term>Asclepius</term><note>A legendary disciple of Hermes Trismegistus in the Hermetic writings.</note> says) have received their scepters. For He is the one principle of all things: above all, and all things are from Him. In this way, He is both outside of all things and within all things, and all things are from Him, through Him, and directed toward Him. To the understanding of this "One," which is beyond essence, one ascends step by step.

<margin>Where the One is found.</margin>
Indeed, the "One" is found in a triple order. First, in those things that flow and are subject to the senses; these are called "sensible" things. Second, in those things that are always the same; these are called "intelligible" things, which are no longer perceived by the senses but by the mind alone. Nor is it found only in these, but even above both sense and sensible things, and above intellect and intelligible things, the One itself exists. For there is (as it pleases some to believe) a Mind diffused through the immense parts of the world and all of nature, joining them together. From this Mind, all things that are born and all living creatures receive their life.

<margin>From where "God" is named</margin>
Alternatively, God is a certain pre-eminent nature, than which nothing is better; by His providence, He continually governs the world He created. He is called <term>Deus</term><note>The author is using a common medieval etymology, though not linguistically accurate by modern standards.</note> from "giving" <note>Latin: *dando*</note>, because He gives to humans whatever is beneficial; or He is so named because nothing is lacking <note>Latin: *deest*</note> to Him.

<margin>zz Iamblichus on God</margin>
¶ <term>Iamblichus</term><note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who sought to synthesize Greek philosophy with theurgy and mystery religions.</note> writes thus about God: The first God, prior to being, is the sole Father of the first God, whom He begets while remaining in His solitary unity, and He is the same as the "super-intelligible." He is the exemplar of that which is called His own father, His own son, the "Single-Father," and God truly good. For He is the greater and the first, the fountain of all things, and the root of those things which are first understood and which understand—namely, the Ideas. From this "One," the self-sufficient God unfolded Himself. Therefore, He is called self-sufficient, His own father, and His own prince. For He is the principle, the God of gods, unity from the One, the principle of essence beyond essence. From Him comes essence, and for that reason He is named the Father of essences; for He is the principle of intelligible things, above true beings. Elsewhere, the same Iamblichus says: Nor are these the most ancient principles of all, which <term>Mercury</term><note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, identified by the Greeks with the god Hermes/Mercury.</note> placed over the ethereal, empyrean, celestial, and corporeal powers. He wrote one hundred books on the empyrean, just as many on the ethereal, and a thousand on the celestial realms.

<margin>Trismegistus on the Trinity.</margin>
¶ And if you desire to hear more fully about God and His Trinity from the Egyptians before the Word was veiled in flesh, listen to Hermes Trismegistus in that book which he wrote concerning the power and wisdom of God <note>Likely referring to the *Poimandres*.</note>. There, he saw the Son being born from the Father, and the Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son in a miraculous way, when he said: "Mind, however, G—"

<column-break/>

"—od, most full of the fecundity of both sexes, being Life and Light, brought forth with His Word another Mind, the Demiurge <note>original: *opificem*</note>, who is indeed the God of fire and the divine spirit." For in that book, he treats the Mosaic mysteries, though preserved under a shadow.

<margin>Genesis 1</margin>
For Moses saw darkness over the face of the abyss, and the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters. But this man <note>Hermes</note> saw a "dreadful shadow migrating into a moist nature," and he asserts that the shining Word (which illuminates all things) is the "offspring of the Mind" and the "Son of God." He states that the Mind-Father and the Word-Son do not differ in nature; he says they were <term>consubstantial</term><note>Meaning of the same substance; the same term used in the Nicene Creed to describe the relationship between God the Father and the Son.</note>, and he saw that there was a union of them. Let Moses be the leader of the Hebrew flock by divine decree, and Trismegistus the leader of the Egyptians.

<margin>Calcidius on Trismegistus.</margin>
¶ <term>Calcidius</term><note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his commentary on Plato's *Timaeus*.</note>, in the final part of his second book, asserts these things about Mercury, saying: Hermes Trismegistus—to whom common opinion, out of admiration for his virtue, consecrated divine honors—when he approached the final end of his life, addressed the disciples standing around him. "Until now, my children, I have lived as a traveler and an exile, driven from my homeland; but now I return to my homeland unharmed. When, after a short while, I depart from you, released from the stains of the body, do not mourn me as if I were dead. For I am returning to that most excellent and blessed city, to which all citizens shall come through the corruption of death. For there, God alone is the supreme Prince, who will fill His citizens with wonderful sweetness. Therefore, this which many consider 'life' ought rather to be called 'death' than life."

<margin>Socrates on death.</margin>
¶ We read that Socrates, in Plato's *Apology*, spoke in this manner: "Death is like a certain migration from here to another place. And the things that are said are true: namely, that all the deceased are in another place apart from us. What could be better than this, O judges? For if someone, having set out for that place, is free from those who claim to be judges, and finds the true judges who are said to judge there—Minos, Rhadamanthus, Aeacus, Triptolemus, and others of the demigods who lived justly—would such a migration be considered of little value? Again, to meet Orpheus and Musaeus, and Hesiod and Homer—for how much would any of us redeem that? Truly, if these things are true, I would wish to die many times over."

## On God A

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring a person sitting in a landscape with hills and trees.</image-desc>

<margin>Anaximander. Thales. Democritus. Pythagoras. Plato</margin>
Anaximander believed that the gods were infinite intellects. Thales, however, believed that the intellect of the world was God. Democritus thought that the intellect was a spirit within fire, serving as the soul of the world. Pythagoras said that God extended and governed the world. Plato was of the opinion that all things that move were brought into order by God and participate in what is appropriate for them. He also considers God to be unmixed with any matter and not bound by any potentiality <note>original: "nulli possibilitati complexum" — suggesting God is pure act or necessity, rather than just a possibility.</note>.

<margin>Opinion of the Stoics</margin>
The Stoics define God as an intellectual spirit, having no fixed shape, and changeable into whatever He wishes. Among the earliest philosophers, we find some who did not know that God existed, such as Anaxagoras, Diagoras <note>original: "Idium" — likely a corruption of Diagoras of Melos, known as the Atheist.</note>, and Theodorus of Cyrene; for they did not dare to say that God exists.

<margin>Aristotle. Epicurus.</margin>
Aristotle considers the supreme intellect of all things to be God. The Epicureans, however, think the gods exist in human form, are visible, and are incorruptible by nature.

<margin>Galen</margin>
And as our Galen <note>Galen of Pergamum, the famous Roman physician whose works were central to medieval medicine.</note> wishes, we have gained knowledge of God from the beauty and magnitude of His creatures that are visible to us.

<margin>Euripides.</margin>
For no good thing is made by itself, but by a wise creator, as Euripides said. Indeed, the stars in the sky vary in the beauty of their wise builder. We also gained knowledge of God from the fact that the sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars, making their journey beneath the earth, rise again with similar bodies, shapes, and sizes in the same places and times ordained by God.

<margin>Servius.</margin>
Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentary on Virgil.</note> says we call those who are eternal "Gods," while those made from men are called "Divi" <note>original: "diuos" — divine ones or deified mortals.</note>, as if they had met their day of divinity. Hence, we call even emperors "Divi."

<margin>Varro. Atteius.</margin>
However, Varro and Atteius hold the opposite view regarding those who are eternal.

<margin>Hermes.</margin>
And Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus.</note> said: "Finally, when you wish to see God, look up at the sun, my son; observe the course of the moon; look up at the order of the remaining stars."

<margin>Dionysius.</margin>
Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential Christian mystic and philosopher.</note> feels the same in his book *On the Divine Names*, when he says: "Perhaps we shall say this truly: we do not know God from His own nature (for that is unknown and surpasses all reason and sense), but from the most orderly arrangement of all creatures produced by Him, which bear certain images and likenesses of His divine patterns; through this path and order, according to our strength, we ascend to that which transcends all things."

<column-break/>

## On Matter. B

<margin>Aristotle. Plato</margin>
Aristotle and Plato say that matter is corporeal, formless, and void of species, figure, and quality insofar as it resides in its own nature; yet it is the receiver of forms, filling the role of a nurse or mother in the way of a seal <note>The "receptacle" or "nurse" of forms is a famous metaphor from Plato's Timaeus.</note>. However, those who say that water, or earth, or fire is matter are no longer calling it formless, but a body. Those who speak of "impartibles" and "indivisibles" call it formless.

<margin>Democritus.</margin>
The followers of Democritus call the first things "impartibles" <note>Atoms.</note>, the "indivisible," the "void," and those things that lack a body.

<margin>Stoics.</margin>
The Stoics, Pythagoras, and Thales of Miletus

<margin>Pythagoras. Thales.</margin>
say that all matter is entirely convertible, alterable, changeable, and in a state of flux.

## On Fate. C

<margin>Heraclitus.</margin>
Heraclitus says that fate is the reason <note>original: "rõnem" (rationem) — the Logos or governing principle.</note> proceeding through everything. Others have said that fate is an ethereal body; others, a seed following the generation of all things, or a law proceeding through all physical things.

<margin>Posidonius.</margin>
Others say it is a spiritual power; others, a universal dispensatory order; and others have said it is the rule according to which things that have been made were made, things that are being made are made, and things that will be are to be made. Posidonius said that the world is from God, and first there is God, then nature, and then fate.

<margin>Plato</margin>
Plato indeed admits fate in human souls and in the leading of human life. But he also applies a cause proceeding from ourselves <note>Referring to the concept of free will.</note>.

<margin>Chrysippus</margin>
Chrysippus, in his definitions, says that fate is the reason of the world, or the law of those things which are established in the world by providence; or the reason according to which all things that were, were made; and those that are, are being made; and those that will be, shall be made.

<margin>Posidonius.</margin>
Posidonius said that the first is Jove <note>Jupiter/God</note>, the second is nature, and the third is fate.

## On the Sun and Moon. D

<margin>Stoics.</margin>
The Stoics and likewise Heraclitus said that the sun and moon are spherical.

<margin>Empedocles. Anaximander.</margin>

For the shape of the moon appears either as crescent-shaped <note>original: "minoidalis" from the Greek 'menoeides'.</note>, or halved <note>original: "dicotoma" from 'dichotomos'.</note>, or gibbous <note>original: "amphikitra" from 'amphikurtos'.</note>, or fully illuminated. Then it recedes and becomes gibbous, then halved, then crescent-shaped, until it becomes invisible.

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
He says it has these shapes because the earth casts a shadow, some indeed according to a part of it, and some according to the whole of it.

<margin>Thales.</margin>
Anaximander said the moon has its own light. Thales and Aristotle say it is illuminated by the sun.

...stated that the circle of the moon is eleven times the size of the earth. Xenophanes, however, said it is a circle of fire. The Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that emphasized logic and natural law.</note> believed it was a mixture of earth and a fiery substance, though it possessed more fire. Anaxagoras and Democritus, on the other hand, believed the firmament was a fire containing cavities within itself. Furthermore, the Stoics estimated that the moon is larger than the earth. Parmenides thought it was equal in size to the sun and illuminated by it. Empedocles said the moon is twice as far from the sun as it is from the earth. The mathematicians, however, say it is eighteen times further. Eratosthenes states that the sun is 110,000 stadia <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note> from the earth, while the moon is 78 myriads <note>780,000</note> of stadia from the earth.

### On the Idea. E

<margin>
Eratosthenes
Galen
Socrates
Plato
Aristotle
Stoics
Plutarch
</margin>
According to Galen <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher.</note>, an Idea is an incorporeal substance that exists by itself; it gives form to formless matter and acts as the cause of their coming into being. Socrates and Plato believe that Ideas are substances separate from matter, residing in the things perceived by the senses, but originating in the divine mind. Aristotle, however, estimated that species and Ideas are not separate from matter. The Stoics, meanwhile, thought that our own thoughts were what constituted "ideas." Plutarch says an Idea (or species) is a substance devoid of body; while it does not exist by itself, it provides the shapes for formless matter and serves as the demonstrative cause for them.

### On Divine Substance. F

<margin>
Stoics
Thales
Anaximander
Democritus
Pythagoras
</margin>
The Stoics generally judge that the divine substance is an "artificer fire" <note>original: "ignem artificem" — a creative, designing fire that directs the universe.</note> proceeding along a path toward the creation of the world, containing within itself all the "seminal reasons" <note>The Stoic concept of *logoi spermatikoi*, the principles or "seeds" that determine how things grow and develop.</note> through which all things come to be by fate. They also see it as a spirit extending through the entire world, changing its name according to the various boundaries of nature through which it passes. Thales said that the mind of the world was the divine substance. Anaximander called the heavenly stars the substances of God and gods. Democritus defined the divine substance as God being an "ignited mind" and the soul of the world. Pythagoras stated that the principle "Monad" <note>The number one, representing unity and the source of all things.</note> was God, which is the nature of the One and the Mind itself.

### On Humanity. B

<margin>
Plato
Homer
</margin>
Plato used to say that a human being is not that which can be pointed at with a finger; just as a rider is not called "human-and-horse" but simply "human" (even though he sits on the horse), so in his judgment a human is not the animated body, but the soul alone, while it resides in the body. Homer, however, who says that the souls of heroes depart from the body, implies that the body alone is the human. For just as a cup

<column-break/>

is not called the drink itself, but merely the vessel in which the drink is sometimes held, so the human is only the body in which the soul is contained. Servius says this is the opinion of many philosophers: that our body is the only thing that is truly ours, as it is born and dies with us. The soul, however, belongs to the "generality" <note>The collective divine or universal soul.</note> and comes from God (as they believe), and is not uniquely ours, since it often passes into other bodies. Thus Servius notes that when Palinurus speaks in Virgil's *Aeneid*, he refers only to the body: "Now the waves hold me, and the winds toss me on the shore." <note>original: "Nunc me fluctus et palis habet: versantque in littore venti." (Aeneid VI.362)</note> Aristotle, more correctly, calls the composite of both "the human." For the whole is a composite that cannot be predicated of only one of its parts.

Anaximander of Chios, Metrodorus, and Chrates say the sun is established as the highest of all, after which is the moon, and below these are the wandering and non-wandering stars. Plato lists first *Phenon* (which is called Saturn); second, *Phaeton* (Jupiter); third, *Pyroeis* (Mars); fourth, *Lucifer* (Venus); fifth, *Stilbon* (Mercury); sixth, the Sun; and seventh, the Moon. The mathematicians say the sun is in the middle of all. The Stoics believe the stars are spherical, like the world, the sun, and the moon. Cleanthes says they are shaped like tops. Anaximenes says they are fixed like nails in a crystalline substance.

# On Asclepius
->B<-
<meta>catchword: os.</meta>

...the Egyptian: whom he writes discovered many aids for human life. For he invented the wrestling school <note>Latin: *palaestra*; a place for physical training and competition.</note> and the Lyre: which he made with three strings, to imitate the three seasons of the year. For he took the high <note>Latin: *acutam*; acute or high-pitched</note> voice from summer, the low <note>Latin: *graue*; grave or deep</note> from winter, and the middle voice from spring. He invented letters and the sacred rites of the gods. And because he taught the Greeks those things which pertain to interpretation, he was named "Hermes" by them, which means "Interpreter." He writes of a second Mercury born in Crete from Jove <note>Jupiter</note>, who invented the herald’s staff <note>Latin: *caduceatoriam*; the caduceus</note>, truces, and the treaties that are employed in war, especially so that heralds might be inviolable everywhere. This was observed for this reason: because Mercury was thought to be a mediator between both enemies; but in our own times, trumpeters are held in the place of heralds. They say he also invented weights, measures, and the profits of trade, and that he was a most great master of illusion in committing thefts. He places a third Mercury whom the Atlantic people say is their own. He was born of Jove and Maia, and they attribute to him almost everything said about the Cretan and the Egyptian Mercuries. Some say that this one was not Egyptian, but assert that he is the one who killed Argus <note>A hundred-eyed giant in Greek mythology</note>, and that he ruled over the Egyptians and handed down laws and letters. Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BC historian.</note>, however, as we have said, says he was the Egyptian through whom secret mysteries and stupendous oracles are revealed. For he speaks not only as a philosopher, but as a prophet often foretelling the future. He saw from here the ruin of the ancient religion. He predicted the rise of the new faith, the advent of Christ, the future judgment, the resurrection, the renewal of the age, the glory of the good, and the torments of the guilty. Therefore, Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD).</note> doubts whether he foresaw these things by the observation of the stars or by the revelation of demons. Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who saw Hermes as a pagan prophet of Christ.</note> numbers him among the prophetic Sibyls. Two principal books are circulated by this man: one concerning the Divine Will, and the other concerning the Will and Wisdom of God. The former is titled *Asclepius*, which Apuleius the Platonist <note>Author of *The Golden Ass* (2nd century AD).</note> made into Latin in earlier times. The latter is titled *Pimander* <note>Poimandres, the first book of the Hermetic Corpus.</note>; but we have recently seen this one migrate to the Latins through our own Marsilio Ficino the Platonist <note>The scholar who led the Florentine Academy and translated the Hermetic works in 1463.</note>. Our Asclepius, his disciple, followed this Mercury.
<margin>Apis was the first god of the Egyptians.</margin>
Since we wish to show the antiquity of Asclepius, Hermes, and Moses, I have decided to arrange the matter in this way. Apis was called the first god among the Egyptians, born from the daughter of Inachus, whom the Egyptians named Isis. Prometheus and Atlas also lived in those times. From Cecrops <note>The mythical founder and first king of Athens.</note> until the calamity <note>Likely referring to the Trojan War or the end of the heroic age.</note>, a little fewer than four hundred years are gathered, in which we are not ignorant that the flood of Deucalion and the fire of Phaethon occurred. Moreover, Cecrops is said to have been the first to call upon God

<column-break/>

as Jove, the first to establish an altar, and the first to erect a statue of Pallas <note>Athena</note>. After Cecrops, however, all the gods of the Greeks seem to have been born. Thus, from the times of Asclepius, Moses, and Hermes to the Trojan times, more than eight hundred years are found to have passed by the testimony of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who wrote on history and chronology.</note>.
<margin>L</margin>
Indeed, it is manifest that Homer and Hesiod were much younger than the Trojan War. It is well-established that Democritus and Pythagoras lived nearly seven hundred years after Troy. Therefore, by the authority of this philosopher, namely Porphyry, Asclepius, Moses, and Hermes lived one thousand five hundred years before the Greek philosophers. And so that the antiquity of the Hebrews may be held as beyond doubt, I shall use the testimony of many. Africanus <note>Sextus Julius Africanus (c. 160–240 AD), a Christian traveler and historian.</note>, therefore, in the third book of his annals, uses these words:
<margin>D</margin>
"Until the Olympiads <note>The four-year periods between ancient Olympic Games, starting in 776 BC.</note>, nothing certain is found in the history of the Greeks, but all things were written with confused timelines. After the Olympiads, however, since everything was noted most diligently every four years, no confusion of times occurs at all." Therefore, the migration of the Hebrews
<margin>The migration of the Hebrews.</margin>
into Babylon made by Nebuchadnezzar lasted seventy years. Cyrus reigned in the fifty-fifth Olympiad.
<margin>E</margin>
From the histories of Diodorus, Thalicostorus, Polybius, and Phlegon, it is clear in which year Jeshua the son of Jozadak made the first and partial leading back of the people, as it is written by Ezra the Jew. Moreover, from the native Ogyges <note>The mythical first king of Thebes or Attica.</note>, in whose times the first and greatest flood occurred in Attica, and while Phoroneus the Argive was reigning, until the first Olympiad, there were one thousand and twenty years. For so all assert who have written the annals of the Athenians, such as Hellanicus and Philochorus. Castor and Thallus also agree on this, who diligently treated Syrian history. Also Diodorus, who compiled the history of the world in libraries, and many others; and after a few points: We say, therefore, that Ogyges, from whom the first flood was named "Ogygian," lived in the times of Moses. This we prove in this way: From Ogyges, as we said, there were one thousand and twenty years until the first Olympiad, from which until the fifty-fifth Olympiad—that is, until the first year of Cyrus, king of the Persians, and the return of the Jewish people—there were 307 years. Therefore, from Ogyges to Cyrus there were 1,237 years; which if you subtract by ascending, you arrive at that year in which Moses led the
<margin>F</margin>
people out of Egypt. They say, therefore, that from Moses until Cyrus, 1,237 years are understood to have passed. Wherefore, Asclepius, Moses, and Hermes are much older than all the gods and heroes of the Greeks.

# Commentary.

...they find. And it is necessary to believe the elders far more, from whom the <term>juniors</term> <note>Referring to later generations of writers and thinkers.</note> have drawn their knowledge. For Hermes, Moses, and Asclepius are superior not only to Homer, but even to all those who wrote anything among the Greeks. 

<margin>Cadmus gave letters to the Greeks.</margin> Indeed, Cadmus—from whom the Greeks received their alphabet—lived much later than Hermes. Following him were Homer, Linus, Philammon, Amphion, Orpheus, Thamyris, Musaeus, Phemius, the Sibyl, Demodocus, and Epimenides of Crete (who traveled to Sparta). Also Aristeas of Proconnesus, Abaris, Centaurus, Dzimon, Cuculus of Cyprus, and Orius the Athenian <note>These are various legendary and semi-historical poets, seers, and "divine men" of Greek myth.</note>. It is established that there was only one master of Hercules, who lived one generation before the Trojan War. For his son, Tlepolemus, fought at Troy alongside Agamemnon. Orpheus, however, was a contemporary of Hercules, and Musaeus was a student of Orpheus. Amphion preceded the Trojan War by two generations. 

->B<-
But Demodocus and Phemius lived during the times of the Trojan War; the former in Ithaca and the latter among the Phaeacians. Thamyris and Philammon did not exist before them either. So much for the poets.

¶ But now let us speak of those who were considered <term>Sages</term> among the Greeks. Minos, who is seen to have excelled all others in wisdom and the skill of lawmaking, lived in the time of Lynceus (who reigned over the Argives after Danaus); he lived in the eleventh generation after Inachus. Lycurgus gave laws to the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> one hundred years before the first <term>Olympiad</term> <note>The ancient Greek system of dating based on the four-year Olympic cycle, beginning in 776 BCE.</note>. Draco brought laws to the Athenians in the thirty-sixth Olympiad. Pythagoras flourished in the sixty-second. Historians say that the Olympiads began four hundred and seven years after the destruction of Troy. Thales, the oldest of all those called the Seven Sages, lived in the fiftieth Olympiad. From Inachus to the Trojan times, twenty generations are counted—at least four hundred years. 

<margin>The Kingdom of the Assyrians was older than others.</margin> It is established that the Kingdom of the Assyrians was more ancient than all others. In its four hundred and second year—specifically the thirty-second year of Belochus VIII—Moses led the people out of Egypt. At that time, Inachus was the first king of the Argives and Amosis was reigning in Egypt. After Inachus, Phoroneus ruled Argos when the Ogygian flood occurred. And Aegialeus ruled in Sicyon, from whom the Sicyonian kingdom began; then also lived Cres, the first to reign in Crete. Acusilaus claims that Phoroneus was the very first of all men, which is why the poet of the *Phoronis* calls him "the father of mortals." 

<margin>R</margin> But from Inachus to Agamemnon, there were twenty generations. Troy was destroyed in the eighteenth year of Agamemnon's reign, while Demophon the son of Theseus ruled the Athenians. Theseus himself was an imitator of Hercules, one generation before the Trojan War. Thus, Trismegistus, Moses, and Asclepius...

<column-break/>

...are found to have existed six hundred and four years before the time of Dionysus. For when Perseus was already in the thirty-second year of his reign—as Apollodorus writes in his *Book of Times* <note>original: *de temporibus*; referring to the *Chronica* of Apollodorus of Athens.</note>—Dionysus departed from among men. From him to Hercules and Jason, and all the other Greek heroes who were at Argos, sixty-three years are collected; during which time Aesculapius and the Dioscuri also lived, as Apollonius of Rhodes testifies in his *Argonautica*. From the start of Hercules' reign in Argos until his passing and that of Aesculapius, thirty-eight years passed, as Apollodorus writes. From then until the assumption of Castor and Pollux was fifty-three years, which was also when Troy was destroyed. 

<margin>L</margin> <margin>The Jews</margin> The Jews, however (on the testimony of Josephus), left Egypt almost a thousand years before the Trojan times. Evidence from the Phoenicians even shows that the Temple was founded one hundred and forty-three years before Carthage was built by the Tyrians.

¶ But let us also say something of those who lived after Moses, Mercury Trismegistus, and Asclepius. 

<margin>O</margin> After them, Joshua held the leadership of the Jews for thirty years, as some say. Then, as the Scripture asserts, foreigners ruled for eight years. Again, foreigners ruled for twenty years, after whom were Deborah and Barak for forty years. The Midianites ruled for seven; Gideon <note>Bedeon</note> for forty; Abimelech for three; Tola for twenty-three; Jair for twenty-two; the Ammonites for eighteen; Jephthah for six; Ibzan <note>Esbon</note> for seven; Elon for ten; Abdon <note>Labedon</note> for eight. Foreigners ruled for forty. Samson for twenty. Eli the priest ruled for forty—during whose time Troy was destroyed.

Anaximander (also of Miletus) was followed by Anaximenes of Miletus, and he by Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, who taught Pericles, Archelaus, and Euripides. Among these, Pericles excelled in wealth and power among the Athenians. Euripides, however, devoted himself to the poetic and theatrical arts, and was called a philosopher by some. Archelaus first took over the school of Anaxagoras at Lampsacus; later, having set out for Athens, he had many others as listeners, including Socrates. Empedocles was a student of Telauges, at the time when Heraclitus—surnamed the Obscure <note>original: *scotinus*, which in Latin means *tenebrosus* (dark or obscure)</note>—was also flourishing. Xenophanes was succeeded by Parmenides; Parmenides by Melissus; and Melissus by Zeno of Elea. It is said of Zeno that when he attempted to overthrow a tyranny, and was being tortured by the tyrant to reveal his accomplices, he bit off his own tongue with his teeth and spat it into the tyrant’s face. The astrologer Julius Firmicus describes Plato's <term>geniture</term> <note>A birth chart or horoscope.</note>, and many consider his version more accurate than others. It is as follows: in the Ascendant, Aquarius contains Mars, Mercury, and Venus. In the Second House, the Sun is in Pisces. In the Fifth, the Moon is in Gemini. In the Seventh, Jupiter is in Leo. Julius Firmicus asserts that this nativity chart signifies a man who prevails with marvelous eloquence and who, by a celestial genius, approaches all the secrets of divinity. Aristotle and Xenocrates were students of Plato, and Plato used to say of them: "Alas, what a horse and what a donkey I have taken on to yoke together!" He meant that Aristotle needed a bridle, while Xenocrates needed

Many contend that he was from Samos, others that he was Tyrrhenian, and others that he was Syrian or Tyrian. <margin>R</margin>
from different people. No one has dared to say that he received anything from the Greeks; such was the poverty of learning and the liberal arts in Greece before Pythagoras taught everything he had collected with the greatest zeal. For this reason, he earned divine honors. From him proceeded the first philosophy, which they usually call "Italian," because he taught mostly there. 
<margin>S</margin>
The second is that which Thales, one of the Seven Sages, handed down, which is called "Ionic." The third is called "Eleatic," of which Xenophanes of Colophon is credited as the author. Many say that Thales was not Greek, but Phoenician; some think he was Milesian, and they record that he received most of his knowledge from the divinations of the Egyptians. As for Solon, one of the Seven who wrote the laws of the Athenians, he arrived in Egypt at the time when the Jews were living there in great numbers.

# Commentary.

<margin>
T
The Greeks and words.
</margin>
Plato testifies in his book on the universe <note>The *Timaeus*, which explores the origins of the physical world.</note>. In that book, we see him being taught by a barbarian <note>The term "barbarian" was used by Greeks and Romans for anyone outside their own culture; here it refers to an Egyptian priest.</note> who says: "Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; no Greek is ever an old man in his art, or at least no old discipline can be found among them." Plato himself, although he drank deeply of Italian philosophy <note>Referring to the Pythagorean schools in Southern Italy.</note>, is said to have traveled to Egypt to study the philosophy of Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus, whom the author identifies with the Roman god Mercury.</note>; he stayed there for a considerable time. Consequently, he professes with a grateful soul that all his best ideas were obtained from the barbarians. 

Democritus, long before this, boasted that he had learned from barbarians. He said: "I have been away from my homeland for eighty years out of a love for learning." 
<margin>
U
</margin>
Indeed, he sought out Babylon, Persia, and Egypt to learn. What shall I say of Heraclitus and other Greeks, through whom it is established that Greece was illuminated with teachings? For in the ages before them, Greece gaped at the prophecies and oracles of demons, and possessed no trace of solid discipline. 
<margin>
X
</margin>
Those miraculous responses of Apollo contributed absolutely nothing to humanity; rather, men wandered here and there with great effort, gathering for themselves the property of others. For they received geometry from the Egyptians, astrology from the Chaldeans, and other things from other peoples. But they never borrowed anything so great as what they received from the Egyptians and the Hebrews. 

For Moses, Mercury, and Asclepius were Egyptians. From them, the Greeks received the knowledge of the one God and rejected the multitude of their own demons. 
<margin>
Y
</margin>
We have rightly placed the writings of the Egyptians and Hebrews before Greek philosophy, since the Greeks stole all their good ideas from the Egyptians and Hebrews (whom they call barbarians), nor did they receive anything useful from their own gods. Many among the Greeks rightly despised those gods, preferring to be called ungodly rather than to worship demons. 

And therefore, Asclepius correctly says in the beginning: "As much as is possible, O King, preserve this discourse from being translated <note>original: *inconversum*, meaning "unturned" or "unchanged". The text argues that the power of the original Egyptian language is lost in Greek translation.</note>, lest the proud and dissolute—and, as it were, overly-ornate—speech of the Greeks should weaken the gravity, strength, and active power of the words." 
<margin>
Z
</margin>
"The Greeks, O King, have only words that are new and effective for demonstrations; and this is the philosophy of the Greeks: the sound of words. But we do not use words; rather, we use voices that are great with the power of deeds." Thus spoke Asclepius. Therefore, we have rightly placed the 'barbarian' scripture of the Egyptians before Greek philosophy. 

<margin>
z
</margin>
In the same way, one rightly prefers the discipline of the Gauls <note>The people of France.</note> to Italian writing and eloquence. Since the Italians stole all their good things from the Gauls, and had nothing of use from their own origins. Was not Lucius Plotius Gallus from Lyon, who was the first to teach the Romans 

<column-break/>

Latin rhetoric? For we read that Cicero asserts that he and his brother Quintus received the rudiments of the Latin language from him in the first years of their youth. Were not the famous poets Statius and Ausonius, and also Prosper—whose authority canon lawyers frequently rely upon—Gauls? From these men, the Italians received much. 

Why, then, do the Italians look down on and accuse the Gauls, rather than praising and admiring them? For the Gauls, despising falsehood, even followed theology, which alone is true and removed from all falsity. The princes of the Gauls did not fall into impiety like many Roman emperors who worshipped no god; nor, on the other hand, did they mix the knowledge of the High God with the falsehood of many gods, as did the wretched Christian emperors of Italy, such as Julian the Apostate <note>Roman Emperor (r. 361–363) who attempted to revive paganism.</note>, Constans, Maxentius, and many others. It is manifest that the Italians received not only rhetoric but also theology from the Gauls. 

Did not Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), who taught at the University of Paris.</note>, Peter Lombard <note>Author of the *Sentences*, the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages.</note>, Gregory of Rimini, and many others receive their theology from the Parisians and the Gauls? Why then do they rail against us and call us barbarians, if they themselves received rhetoric, other good disciplines, and finally sacred theology itself from the Gauls? What do you have, O Italian, that you did not receive from outsiders? If then you received it, why do you boast as if you had not? <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> 

And just as it is established that Lycurgus, and likewise Plato and Solon and other professors of wisdom, wrote many things in their books and laws that the Egyptians possessed before their time; so it is clear enough that Cicero, Virgil, Sallust, Thomas, and Peter Lombard, and many celebrated writers, wrote many things in their books and opinions that the Gauls possessed before their time. But enough concerning these matters.

# On Asclepius:

<margin>
The Seven Sages of the Greeks.
</margin>
The foundations of Jerusalem were laid by Shealtiel <note>Original: "Salathielis." A leader of the Jewish people during the Babylonian exile.</note> when he was led back to his homeland, while Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi were prophesying; after them, there was no longer a prophet among the Jews. In the times of Cyrus, however, the "Seven Sages" of the Greeks flourished—those to whom no Greek philosopher is considered older. Among them, Thales of Miletus was the first to be called a "natural philosopher" <note>Original: "physicus."</note> among the Greeks. Anaximander was his student. Anaximander was also from Miletus, and his own student was Anaximenes of Miletus. After him came Anaxagoras of Clazomenae, who taught Pericles, Archelaus, and Euripides. Of these, Pericles excelled among the Athenians in wealth and power. Euripides, however, devoted himself to the poetic arts and was called a "theatrical philosopher" <note>Original: "scenicus philosophus."</note> by some. Archelaus first took over the school of Anaxagoras at Lampsacus; later he set out for Athens and had many others as students, including Socrates. In the time of Anaxagoras, Xenophanes and Pythagoras also lived. Pythagoras was succeeded by his wife Theano and his sons Telauges and Menamechus. Empedocles was a student of Telauges, at the same time that Heraclitus—nicknamed "Scotinus" <note>Greek for "The Obscure."</note>, which in Latin means "the Dark One"—was flourishing. Xenophanes was succeeded by Parmenides; Parmenides by Melissus; and Melissus by Zeno of Elea. It is said of Zeno that when he tried to overthrow a tyranny and was being tortured to reveal his co-conspirators, he bit off his own tongue and spat it into the tyrant's face. Leucippus was his student, and Democritus followed Leucippus; Protagoras followed Democritus during the time of Socrates. Plato first studied under Socrates, then under the Pythagoreans. He surpassed all who had come before him in philosophy, both in eloquence and 
<margin>
D
The birth of Plato.
</margin>
wisdom. Plato was born in Athens or Aegina in the seven hundred and fifty-sixth year after the fall of Troy (as some prefer to calculate); in the three hundred and third year from the founding of the city of Rome; and four hundred and twenty-three years before the coming of Christ. This was near the end of the Persian Empire, a little before Alexander the Great, and about four hundred years or a little more before Augustus Caesar. Julius Firmicus, the astronomer, describes Plato's horoscope <note>Original: "genesim."</note>, an opinion many consider more accurate than others. It is as follows: in the Ascendant, Aquarius, with Mars, Mercury, and Venus. In the second house, the Sun in Pisces. In the fifth house, the Moon in Gemini. In the seventh house, Jupiter in Leo. In the ninth house, Saturn in Libra. Julius Firmicus asserts that this horoscope signifies a man who would excel with marvelous eloquence and, through celestial genius, approach all the secrets of divinity. 
<margin>
P
</margin>
Aristotle and Xenocrates were students of Plato, and Plato used to say of them: "Ha! What a pair I have yoked together: a horse and an ass. Aristotle needs a bridle, but Xenocrates needs 

<column-break/>

spurs." <note>A classic anecdote highlighting Aristotle's quickness and Xenocrates' perceived slowness.</note> Thus, all the philosophers of the Greeks are found to have existed after Cyrus, King of the Persians. But Cyrus lived seventy years after the Jewish captivity. He is also shown to have lived nearly one thousand and one hundred years after Moses, at which time Mercury Trismegistus and his disciple Asclepius were reigning. Thus, you must necessarily admit that Greek philosophy, and especially the Peripatetic <note>The school of Aristotle.</note> school, was much later than Mercury, Asclepius, and Moses. Indeed, the Greeks themselves confess that after Orpheus, Musaeus, and Linus—the most ancient "theologians" (as they call them) and the authors of many errors—there were seven admirable men so filled with wisdom that they were commonly called "Sages." All of these (as we have said) flourished in the times of Cyrus, King of the Persians. At that very time, the very last of the prophets lived among the Hebrews, more than six hundred years after the Trojan era, and no fewer than one thousand five 
<margin>
Ω
When philosophy began.
</margin>
hundred years after Moses. However, from those Sages, nothing was discovered except certain convenient and briefly spoken maxims for the benefit of human life. It is said that the class of "philosophers" began only after a great interval of time. For Pythagoras was the first of all, and it is established that he even invented the name "philosophy." Many contend that he was a Samian, others a Tyrrhenian, others a Syrian or Tyrian; thus, he who is called the greatest and first of philosophers by everyone was not clearly Greek. For all traditions hold that Pherecydes, the teacher of Pythagoras, was a Syrian. Pythagoras is said to have heard not only him, but also the Magi of the Persians and the diviners of the Egyptians, at the time when some of the Jews had migrated to Babylon and others to Egypt. He also heard the "Brahmins" <note>Original: "Brachmanas." The author identifies them here as "Jewish philosophers," likely conflating Eastern and Near-Eastern wisdom traditions.</note> of the Jews; thus, he obtained astrology from some, geometry from others, music from others, arithmetic from others, and various things from various people. But no one has dared to say that he obtained anything from the Greeks; such was the poverty of learning and the liberal arts in Greece before Pythagoras taught, with the greatest zeal, everything he had collected from those others. 
<margin>
R
</margin>
Because of this, he earned divine honors, and from him proceeded the first philosophy, which they usually call 
<margin>
S
</margin>
"Italian," because he taught mostly there. The second is that which Thales, one of the Seven Sages, passed down, which is called "Ionic." The third is called "Eleatic," of which Xenophanes of Colophon is credited as the author. However, many say Thales was not Greek, but Phoenician; some think he was Milesian. They record that he received most of his knowledge from the divinations of the Egyptians. Solon, one of the Seven who wrote the laws of the Athenians, reached Egypt at the time when the Jews were living there in great numbers.
