# Commentary

<sig>g ii</sig>

<margin>z</margin>
<margin>The Greeks rely on words.</margin>
Plato testifies in his *Book of the Universe* <note>Original: "Libro Universi," the title often used in the Middle Ages for Plato's *Timaeus*.</note>. In that book, we see him being taught by a "barbarian" <note>To the Greeks, a "barbarian" was simply anyone who did not speak Greek, particularly the Egyptians or Persians.</note> with these words: "O Solon, Solon, you Greeks are always children; there is no such thing as an old Greek." By this, he meant that no ancient discipline or tradition could be found among them. It is recorded that Plato traveled to Egypt to study the philosophy of Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, whom the Romans identified with Mercury.</note> and stayed there for a long time. Consequently, he himself admitted with a grateful heart that he had obtained all his best ideas from these foreigners. Much earlier, Democritus boasted that he had learned from the barbarians. He said, "For eighty years, I have been away from my homeland out of a love for learning." He traveled to Babylon, to the Persians, and even to Egypt to learn. What shall I say of Heraclitus or other Greeks? It is well known that all of them brought light to Greece through these teachings. For centuries before them, the Greeks were only interested in the prophecies and oracles of demons, and they possessed no trace of solid learning. Those marvelous responses from Apollo contributed absolutely nothing to humanity; rather, men wandered here and there with great effort, gathering what belonged to others. They received geometry from the Egyptians, astrology from the Chaldeans, and other things from other peoples. But they never borrowed anything as significant as what they received from the Egyptians and the Hebrews. For Moses, Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, and Asclepius were all Egyptians. From them, the Greeks received the knowledge of the one God and learned to despise their own multitude of demons. We have rightly placed the writings of the Egyptians and Hebrews above Greek philosophy, since the Greeks stole all their good ideas from the Egyptians and Hebrews (whom the Greeks call barbarians), while receiving nothing useful from their own gods. Rightly, many among them despised those gods, preferring to be called "impious" rather than worshiping demons. And therefore, Asclepius says correctly at the beginning: "As much as is possible, O King, preserve this discourse from being translated, so that such mysteries do not reach the Greeks. Let not the proud, loose, and, as it were, artificial <note>Original: "calamistrata," literally "curled with a hair-iron," meaning overly ornate or superficial.</note> speech of the Greeks weaken the gravity, strength, and active power of these names." For the Greeks, O King, have only new words that are active only for demonstrations. And this is the philosophy of the Greeks: a mere sound of words. But we do not use words; we use the greatest voices of actual works. Thus speaks Asclepius. Therefore, we have rightly placed the "barbarian" writings of the Egyptians above Greek philosophy. In the same way, the learning of the Gauls <note>Referring to the people of France.</note> is rightly placed above Italian writing and eloquence. For the Italians stole all their good things from the Gauls and received nothing of use from their own ancestors. Was not Lucius Plotius a Gaul from Lyon, and was he not the first to teach

<column-break/>

Latin rhetoric to the Romans? We read that Cicero asserts that he and his brother Quintus, in the first years of their youth, learned the rudiments of the Latin language from this same man. Were not the famous poets Statius and Ausonius, and Prosper—whose authority the canon lawyers so often rely upon—all Gauls? It was from them that the Italians received many things. Why, then, do the Italians hold the Gauls in low esteem and accuse them, rather than praising and admiring them? For the Gauls, despising falsehood, followed theology, which alone is true and removed from all deceit. The leaders of the Gauls did not fall into impiety like many Roman emperors who worshiped no god at all. Nor were they like those miserable Italian Christian emperors who, while knowing the High God, mixed the falsehood of many gods with the truth—such as Julian the Apostate, Constans, Maxentius, and many others. It is manifest that the Italians received not only rhetoric but also theology from the Gauls. Did not Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>, Peter Lombard, Gregory of Rimini, and many others receive their theology from the Parisians and the Gauls? Why, then, do they rail against us and call us barbarians, if they themselves received rhetoric, other good disciplines, and finally sacred theology itself from the Gauls? What do you have, O Italian, that you did not receive from outsiders? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as if you had not? <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> Just as it is certain that Lycurgus, and likewise Plato and Solon and other professors of wisdom, wrote many things in their books and laws that the Egyptians possessed before their time; so it is clear enough that Cicero, Virgil, Sallust, Thomas, and Peter Lombard, and many famous writers, wrote many things in their books and opinions that the Gauls possessed before their time. But enough of these matters for now.

<meta>This page transitions from a general defense of Gallic intellectual heritage to a specific dedicatory letter. Symphorien Champier is introducing his edition of the "Sentences of Sextus," dedicating it to the diplomat and cleric Philibert Naturelli. The previous page discussed the Greek debt to "barbarian" wisdom; here, Champier presents a specific example of that ancient wisdom being brought to the French printing press for the first time.</meta>

## To the most eloquent man: Lord Philibert Naturelli: both Provost of the church of Utrecht and Commendatory Abbot of Ainay at Lyons, his respected lord, Symphorien Champier, physician of Lyons, sends many greetings. <note>original: "S.P.D." stands for *Salutem Plurimam Dicit*, a standard formal greeting meaning "Sends many greetings."</note>

The ancient custom of the most learned men—which I do not think is hidden from you, the foremost of my friends—has been preserved and passed down to our own times: that they should greet those whom they follow with love and respect with some gift of their studies. <note>Champier is following the Humanist tradition of "gifting" a published work to a patron to secure both the patron's and the author's legacy.</note> By this, those who are greeted, knowing they are loved and respected, might realize that everlasting praise is derived from it; and in turn, those giving the greeting might make their own memory immortal for posterity through the singular excellence and friendship of their patrons. This is indeed what I intend to do at present. 

For while I was reading, I came across a certain little book by **Sixtus**, the Pythagorean philosopher <note>Sixtus, or Sextus the Pythagorean, was a philosopher whose "Sentences" were widely read. Although Champier calls him a Pythagorean, these moral maxims were actually likely written by a Christian in the late 2nd century.</note>, which was certainly brief but filled with very grave and frequent maxims. It struck me with wonder that this work had been printed by no one in Gaul <note>original: "gallorum." Referring to France.</note> until now (as far as I know), while every day many printers fill up their pages with trifles that will soon perish. I suppose they must be forgiven, however, since they study only for profit; they find more buyers for such trifles than for maxims of this kind. 

Nevertheless, moved by the common utility and my admiration for these things, I persuaded the honest men **Etienne Gueynard** and **Jacques Huguetan**, the booksellers, to see that this be printed. I am confident that it will be pleasing, if not to the common crowd, then at least to learned men and friends of virtue. Therefore, I have sent this especially to you, most learned of prelates, so that I might seek out your judgment, which is most exquisitely implanted in you by nature (from which your surname is derived). <note>Champier is making a scholarly pun on Philibert's surname, *Naturelli*.</note> No one is ignorant of the fact that you are distinguished both in all learning and in the excellence of your character. Therefore, I beg and beseech you that you wish to inform me of what you think of it. 

Farewell, most learned of men, and be mindful of your **Symphorien**. At Lyons, in the year of our Lord 1507, on the Nones of July. <note>July 7th.</note>

# Prologue to the Handbook of Sixtus the Pythagorean.

**Jerome against Jovinian.** It is beautifully said in the books of short sentences by Sixtus the Pythagorean: "An over-ardent lover of his wife is an adulterer." <note>Jerome here quotes a famous, albeit controversial, ascetic maxim found in the *Sentences* of Sextus to support his own arguments for celibacy.</note> A certain person, translating this book into the Latin language, wished to ennoble it with the name of the martyr Sixtus <note>Pope Sixtus II, a 3rd-century martyr. Jerome is accusing the translator, Rufinus, of deceptive branding.</note>; he did not consider that in the whole volume (which he divided into two parts), the name of Christ and the apostles is entirely unmentioned. Nor should he have translated a pagan philosopher for me as if he were a bishop of the Roman city. Similarly, Eusebius of Caesarea first defended the book of the martyr Pamphilus for the sake of Origen, so that he might more easily win over Roman ears to those books *On First Principles* by using such a praiseworthy name. Likewise, **Augustine** in the second book of his *Retractions*, chapter 42: "The book in which I responded to Pelagius, defending grace—not against nature, but that through which nature is freed and ruled—I titled *On Nature and Grace*. In this, Pelagius placed certain words as if they were of Sixtus, the Roman bishop and martyr; I defended them as if they truly belonged to that same Sixtus. I had indeed thought so, but afterward I read that they belonged to Sixtus the philosopher, not Sixtus the Roman Christian."

### ¶ Rufinus to his son Apronianus, many greetings. <note>original: "S.P.D." stands for *Salutem Plurimam Dicit*.</note>

Since the flock runs to the voice of its own shepherd, so also the religious listener rejoices in the warnings of a native shepherd. Therefore, my dearest son Apronianus, your sister, already your sister in Christ, was asking of me that I should compose something for her to read where she would not struggle to understand, written in an open and sufficiently plain style. I have translated Sixtus the Pythagorean into Latin; they say this Sixtus is a bishop, the one who among us in the city of Rome is called Sixtus and is adorned with the glory of a bishop and martyr. Truly, when she reads this, she will find it so brief that she will see great meanings explained in single lines; so powerful that the sentiment of one line can suffice for the perfection of an entire life; and so profound that a girl reading it might indeed plead that she lacks the intellect for it. Furthermore, the entire work is so short that it should never leave her hand; this whole book takes the place of a precious ring. And indeed, it seems fair that since the earthly ornaments have failed her for the sake of the Word of God, she should now be adorned by us in turn with the warnings of the Word and of wisdom. For now, let this book be held in the hands like a ring; a little later, advancing into a treasure-house, let it be kept in the whole heart for instruction

<column-break/>

and to suggest fellowships of good actions from its innermost secret depths. I have also added certain things from a religious parent to a son, but all of it is brief, so that the entire little work is rightly called a **Handbook** <term>Enchiridion: derived from the Greek word for 'in the hand,' meaning a manual or small book for constant use.</term> if in Greek, or a **Ring** if in Latin.

### ¶ End of the prologue.

### ¶ Here begins the Handbook of Sixtus, the Pythagorean philosopher.

A faithful man is a chosen man. A chosen man is a man of God. A man of God is one who is worthy of God. He is worthy of God who does nothing unworthy of God. Striving to be faithful to God, do nothing that is unworthy of God. A man doubtful in faith is dead while his body lives. He is truly faithful who does not sin; even in the smallest things, he acts cautiously. It is no small thing in the life of a man to neglect the soul. Consider every sin to be an act of impiety. For the hand or the eye does not sin, nor any such member, but rather the person using the hand or eye poorly. Every member of the body which persuades you to act against modesty must be cast away. For it is better to live with one member than to be punished with two. <note>This is a philosophical adaptation of the Gospel teaching in Matthew 18:8-9 regarding cutting off a hand or eye that causes one to sin.</note> Believe that honors and punishments remain for you immortally in judgment. Whatever you have of this world, even if someone takes it from you, do not be indignant. Do not offer yourself as blameworthy to the world. Yield all things to one who takes them from you, except for your liberty. A wise man and a despiser of money is like God. Use the things of the world only for necessary causes. Give what belongs to the world to the world, and what belongs to God to God. When you speak of God, know that you are being judged by Him. Be certain that you have received your soul—that is, a faithful deposit—from God. Consider the best purification to be harming no one. The soul is purified in the Word of God through wisdom. Never think that wisdom is without feeling. God is like a mind, which now exists and subsists of its own accord according to these things. You will not find the greatness of God, even if you were able to fly with wings. Do not seek the name of God, for you will not find it; because everything called by a name receives its name from something better—so that one might be called 'High' by voice, but another might be heard. Who is it, then, who imposed a name upon God? 'God' is not the name of God, but the indication of what we feel about God. Therefore, seek nothing concerning God that is not permitted. # The [Sentences] of Sixtus the Pythagorean.

[...An a]ngel. God is the first benefactor. The second is the human being who participates in His benefit. Live, therefore, as one who is second after God, and who has been raised up by Him. You have within you, I say, something similar to God; and therefore use yourself like a temple of God because of that which is within you that is like God. God undoubtedly granted freedom of choice to humans so that, by living purely and without sin, they might become like God. Let the world respect your life. Admit nothing that might bring a stain upon you. When those who live badly depart from the body, an evil demon will torment them until he exacts even the very last penny from them. <note>original: "nouissimum quadrantem"; this is a direct echo of the warning in Matthew 5:26.</note> Blessed is the man whose soul no one can reproach as it goes toward God. Whatever you honor above all things, that will rule over you. Therefore, honor God above all things so that He Himself may rule over you. If, however, God holds lordship over you, then you will finally rule over all things. The honor [due] to the Most High God is to know Him and to imitate Him. Indeed, nothing is similar to God in all respects; yet His grace is prior, just as to flourish in power is an imitation [of Him]. The mind is a holy temple for God, and a clean heart without sin is the best altar. The only sacrifice acceptable to God is to do good to humans for God's sake. A human being shows gratitude to God by living, as much as is possible, according to God’s way. God, however, lacks nothing; but the faithful person lacks God alone. <note>The text suggests that the believer's only true "need" is for the divine presence.</note> Imitate Him: he lacks nothing who needs only a few necessary things. Strive to be great before God, but flee from envy among men. If you are kind to the needy, you will be great before God. While a wise man’s life is in progress, the opinion of him among men is small; but after he is dead, his glory is proclaimed. Consider that time in which you do not think of God to be lost. Let your body indeed walk upon the earth, but let your soul always be with God. Understand what things are good, so that you may act well. A good thought is not hidden from the good God; therefore, let your thought be pure from all evil. Be worthy of Him who deigned to call you a son, and do all things as a son of God. You who call God "Father," remember Him in your actions. A man who is chaste and without sin has received the power from God to be a son of God. A good mind is the choir of God. An evil mind is the choir of evil demons. If you restrain an unjust person from acting unjustly, this is to punish according to God's way. Strive not to seem just, but to be just. It is certain that he is not [just] who wishes to seem to be [just]. Know that what is just is just for this very reason: because it is just. One who acts unjustly will by no means be hidden from God, nor even one who merely thinks it. A wise man will be chaste for God. Flee from all uncleanness. Always strive to speak of good things. Conquer lust by restraining the body in all things; for by [avoiding] luxuries and pleasures, you will escape uncleanness. God does not hear the pleasure-seeker. The end of follies is corruption. Let your deeds, not just your words, precede your actions. It is ruinous to serve vices; for as many vices as a soul has, so many d-

<column-break/>

-emons it has. The love of money indicates a love of carnal things. Acquire a firm possession. What is a firm possession but virtue or the strength of the soul? Renounce the things of the body while you still can, and as much as you can. Consider only that to be yours which is good. Whatever kind of person you wish to be while you pray to God, be such a person always. When you have cast away all your best estates, then, being purified, ask what you wish from God. <note>original: "praedia"; essentially, one must "sell all they have" to be spiritually ready for prayer.</note> Whatever you wish to be before God, be such a person right now. While you distribute the things of the world, despise them as one who knows they are apart from God. An evil-speaking tongue is a sign of an evil mind. Accustom your tongue to speak well, especially when the conversation is about God. No one can indeed do evil to God. But he is impious who blasphemes; for he has done what he could. The foundation of piety is self-restraint; the summit of piety is justice toward God. Hold a pious person in the same regard as yourself. Wish for what is beneficial for you to happen, not just what you want. Whatever you want your neighbor to be to you, be such a person yourself to your neighbors. Do not do the things you criticize. Do not agree with anyone urging you to seek what is not good. What God gives to you, no one can take away. Deliberate <note>The text reads "Libera," likely a printer's error for "Delibera."</note> before you act, and before you act, foresee what kind of thing it is you are about to do. If there is anything you do not want God to know, do not do it or even think it. Before you do whatever you do, think of God; let His light precede your actions. It is a great impiety against God to afflict a human being. The soul is enlightened by the remembrance of God. Strive to be content with modest things. Do not desire everything. Seek out opportunities for good things even with labor. Do not love the things of the body. A shameful act makes a person unclean. The soul of the foolish is purged when its hidden sense is reproved from within. God is the leader for humans in good actions. Consider no one an enemy. Love the person who shares the same nature as you. But love God even more than your own soul. It is worst for sinners to come together when they sin. Many things hinder your chastity, and a lack of restraint in food makes a person unclean. Eating any living creature is indeed a matter of indifference, but to abstain is more reasonable. <note>This reflects the Pythagorean tradition of vegetarianism, framed here as a "reasonable" choice rather than a strict commandment.</note> It is not the foods entering through the mouth that pollute the soul, but those things which proceed from evil acts. <note>A paraphrase of Matthew 15:11.</note> Whatever you receive while overcome by greed pollutes you. Do not strive too hard to please the multitude. In everything you do well, consider God the author. God is the author of no evil. Do not possess more than the use of the body requires. Gold does not rescue the soul from evils. It is certain that while you are immersed in the luxuries of the body, you are ignorant of those things prepared for you by God. Possess those things which no one can take away. Bear what is necessary as if it must be so. Strive to be magnanimous. Do not ask from God what is unworthy of God to grant. Let the reason within you be the very law of your life. And ask of God what you cannot receive from a human. In those things in which labor proceeds, let this happen to you...

Then speak when it is not beneficial to remain silent. Be silent about things you do not know. But about things you are certain of, speak at the right time. Speech out of season is a sign of a malicious mind. In a gathering, do not strive to speak first. It is better to be defeated speaking the truth than to win by lying.

# The Sentences of Sextus the Pythagorean

[It is a sin] even if you only think about adultery. Let the same reasoning apply to every sin. Having professed yourself a believer, you have likewise promised God not to sin. Let the adornment of a faithful woman be led by modesty. A man who divorces his wife <note>original: "uxore dimittit"</note> professes that he cannot manage a woman. A modest woman is the glory of her husband. By having reverence for your wife, you make her reverent in return. Let the marriage of the faithful be a contest of self-control. Just as you restrain your belly <note>meaning gluttony</note>, do the same for sexual impulses. Avoid the praise of the unfaithful. What you receive freely from God, provide freely to others. You will not find a great multitude of the faithful. For everything that is good is rare. 

Honor the wise man after God. When you are corrected so that you may become wise, give thanks to those correcting you. He who does not obey a wise man does not obey God. If you wish to be faithful, especially take care not to sin within yourself; but if by chance it happens, at least I ask that you do not repeat the same thing. Do not speak of doctrine that is not worthy of God. To wish to know many things must be considered a curiosity of the mind. He who knows what is worthy of God is the one who is truly wise. Specifically seek out that teaching from which you can grow in the love of God. A wise man is careful not to waste time. 

Hold onto confidence along with shame. Let children living wickedly cause you more torment than children who are dying. To live is not within our power, but to live *rightly* is within our power. Unfaithful children are not truly children. A faithful man does not take the loss of children with ingratitude. Do not judge one to be a philosopher to whom you do not entrust everything. Do not accept accusations against a philosopher. Strive to do good to everyone in common. Let it be a cursed thing to you to punish anything, even justly. If you wish to live with joy of soul, do not do many things. For in many actions, you will be diminished. 

What you did not put down, do not take up <note>An ancient maxim meaning: do not take what does not belong to you</note>; rather, let your own things be sufficient for you. Leaving behind what you possess, follow the word of God. For you will be free from all things when you serve God. Cease from all food not shared with the good. It is good to fast even for the sake of refreshing the poor. Let every drink be sweet to you that extinguishes thirst. Flee drunkenness as if it were insanity. A man who is conquered by his belly is like a beast <note>original: "belluo," likely a scribal variant for 'bellua' (beast)</note>. Nothing good arises from the flesh. The pleasures of shameful lust pass quickly. Words of integrity remain forever. Men are accustomed to cut off certain of their limbs for the health of the rest; how much more excellently shall this be done for the sake of modesty? <note>This refers to the radical idea of self-castration for the sake of purity, a controversial topic in early Christian asceticism</note>. Consider it a heavy penalty when you have obtained your desires. For the possession of things desired never restrains desire. It is not a wise act in which freedom is taken away. Treat necessary lust as if it were unnecessary. Some people hope to have good things. But those obtain them 

<column-break/>

who hand themselves over entirely to the word of God. Be a philosopher and an honorable person, and not a slanderer. Let your disparagement be rare and only when opportune. Excessive laughter is the sign of a negligent soul. Therefore, do not indulge yourself in such outbursts. Let the life of the chaste <note>original: "Castorum," referring here to the pure ones</note> be an example of honor for you. It is best not to sin, but for a sinner to be known is better than to be ignored. A boaster is not a philosopher. Know that it is great wisdom through which you can bear the foolishness of the unlearned. Consider it shameful to be praised by your own mouth. The souls of the wise are insatiable in the love of God. 

Take the beginning of every action from God. Before you act, have God in your mouth and in your mind before you even breathe. Do not try to do those things which must be learned before you have learned them. Do not love the flesh. Love a good soul second after God. It is the mark of a wise man to bear the anger of those in his household. The wealth of the wise is self-restraint. If you give away your own property to another so that you yourself have nothing, do not judge it to be good. Nothing is good which cannot be shared. Do not say that any sin is lighter than another. Just as you wish to be praised for good acts, so accept it patiently if you are blamed for misfortune. Do not value the praise or the disparagement of those you hold in contempt. 

To bury treasure is indeed inhuman, but for a philosopher to take what he has found is not right. As much as you labor for the body, if you labor that much for the soul, you will be wise. He who harms is not wise. For everything you do, call upon God as your witness. God confirms the good acts of men. An evil demon is the leader of bad acts. A wise man cannot be compelled to do what he does not want, just as God cannot. A wise man commends God to men. Among all works, God is glorified most in the wise man. There is nothing so like the true God as a wise man. Whom God possesses, the wise man also possesses. 

A bad man does not wish to be provident. An evil soul flees God. Everything that is evil is an enemy to God. Say that the thing in you which is wise is the "human" <note>The idea that the intellect is the true essence of humanity</note>. The wise man is a partaker of God. Where that which is wise in you is located, there also is your "good." Do not seek the good in the flesh. That which does not harm the soul does not harm the man. Honor a philosopher as a servant of God after God. To bear the "tent" of the body <note>A metaphor for the mortal body as a temporary dwelling</note> heavily is a sign of pride. But to be able to lay it down in peace when it is necessary is good. Do not become the cause of your own death. But if someone wishes to tear you from the body, do not be indignant. If someone excludes a wise man from his body unjustly, he provides a benefit to him in his own iniquity. For he releases him as if from chains. 

Fear saddens a person because of the soul's lack of skill. It would have been best if the iron with which men kill each other had never been made; nevertheless, let it not be found with you. No pretense will remain hidden for a long time, and especially at the end. As your character is, so shall your life be.

# Handbook

For devout character <note>original: "mores religiosi"</note> makes for a blessed life. He who thinks evil against another brings forth that very evil upon himself. Let an ungrateful man not hinder you from doing good. Consider nothing to be of greater price than what is asked for by the one who receives. He uses his resources best who gives willingly to those in need. If a brother wishes to withdraw from the faith, persuade him not to; and if he is incurable, take even greater care to preserve him. In faith, strive to surpass all men. You will not have understanding until you understand that you have it. Strive to maintain sufficiency <note>meaning contentment with what one has</note>. The limbs of the body are a burden to those who do not use them. It is better to serve others than to be served by others. He whom God does not release from the body should not take his life heavily. If you are not free from shameful deeds, do not argue anything about God. A true discourse about God is the discourse of God. If you know that those who hear you accept that you love God, then speak to them about God. Let works of God’s charity proceed from you, and only then speak about God. Do not dare to speak about God in a crowd. Utter the word about God more sparingly than your soul breathes. It is better to lose the soul than to utter a vain word about God. A lion and a tyrant alike have power over the body of a man who loves God. When a tyrant threatens you, then remember whose you are. He who speaks the word about God to those whom it is not permitted must be considered a traitor of God. It is better to keep silent regarding the word about God than to utter it more rashly than is fitting. He who says things about God which are not against Him does not speak a lie. A man who has nothing to say

<column-break/>

about God is truly deserted by God. He has not known God who has not worshipped Him. It is not true that he worships God who harms a human being. The foundation and beginning of the worship of God is to love men. He who takes care of men and prays for them is truly to be considered of God. It is God’s own nature to save those whom He judges worthy. But it is the duty of a worshiper of God to pray for the salvation of men. When that which you asked from God has been granted to you while praying, then understand that power has been permitted to you. A man worthy of God is a god among men. It is better to have nothing than, having many things, to share them with no one. If you do not give to the needy when you can, you do not receive from God when you ask. No man is wise who looks downward toward the earth. The immense freedom of the philosopher is not in the man, but in the soul. To lie in life is to deceive; and God recognizes what a lie is. And what is it in you that recognizes God? The good work of God. Those for whom the word of God is cursed are without God. Death does not take away the soul, but a bad life does. If you know by whom you were made, then you recognize yourself. To live according to God <note>original: "secundum deum"</note> is nothing other than to act modestly, well, and justly. The life of unfaithful men is a disgrace. Do not entrust the words of God to a bad character. Faith raises the soul from the earth to God. You will not find the magnitude of a wise soul, just as you will not find the magnitude of God. Whatever the world gives, no one holds firmly; whatever God gives, no one takes away. Divine wisdom is truly knowledge. O unclean soul, do not dare to speak from experience about God. A man's risk is in his works; and so let it be in your words. Do not entrust your ears to everyone. Indeed, to work concerning God is easy for everyone; however, to speak about God must be permitted only to the just man. Let your soul not torment your body, nor let the lust of the body torment your soul. Accustom yourself to provide to the body what is its own chaste due, and to the soul what is its own pious due. Feed your soul with the word of God.

### Maxims of Sixtus the Pythagorean

...and nourish the body with simple foods. Accustom your soul to those things in which it may rightly rejoice. The soul <note>original: "anima"</note> that rejoices in wicked things is unworthy before God. The soul of the wise man is always with God. The heart of one who loves God is established in the hand of God. The soul's ascent to God is through the word of God. The wise man follows God, and God follows the soul of the wise man. A king rejoices over those whom he rules; therefore, God rejoices over the wise man. A ruler is inseparable from those he rules; likewise, God is inseparable from the soul of the wise man, whom He protects and rules. The wise man is provided for by God, and for that reason is blessed. The soul of the wise man is acceptable to God, as is his mind. A wise man honors God even when he is silent. He who does not restrain the belly and those things below the midriff is not faithful. An unrestrained man pollutes God <note>meaning he defiles the divine image or presence within himself</note>. The knowledge of God makes a man of few words. To use many words concerning God is a sign of ignorance. The man who knows God is not consumed by great ambition. He who is the chosen one <note>original: "electus"</note> of God indeed does all things according to God's will, but he does not boast that he himself is chosen. A faithful man is always in a state of holy fear until he departs to be with God. A man who is satisfied by a second meal, who does not sleep at night, and does not flee from food <note>meaning he is preoccupied with gluttony</note> is not worthy before God. Fate does not make a man wise; for the grace of God is not subject to fate. Otherwise, God would not take the lusts of the body so seriously. The faithful man is nourished by self-restraint. Recognize those who are the children of God among His creatures, and honor each one according to their merit, after God. You should say that nothing which is evil belongs to God.

<column-break/>

A faithful soul is chaste, and a wise man is a prophet of God’s virtue. You will not love the Lord your God unless you possess something similar to God. Consider a friend to be like yourself, yet in a proper manner. You do not love God if you do not go toward God. Accustom yourself to always look back toward God. By gazing upon God, you will see God. Seeing God, you will shape your mind to be such as God is. Cultivate what is within you, and do not insult it through the lust of the body. Keep your body undefiled, as if you had received a garment from God; thus strive to keep the clothing spotless. The mind of the wise man is a mirror of God. But of an impure soul, dare to say nothing concerning God.

---

> Whoever desires to climb to the starry seats,
> And to visit the radiant roofs of the immense Thunderer <note>original: "tonantis" — a classical epithet for Jupiter, here used by the poet to refer to the Christian God</note>,
> Than which nothing more sublime occurs to human minds
> In the whole world: let him read and re-read this little book,

To the most honorable man: Master Philippe Laurent, well-deserving professor of the Apollonian art <note>original: "Apollinee artis," referring to medicine, as Apollo was the Greek god of healing</note>; the most diligent physician to the Queen of the French; Symphorien Champier, likewise a physician of Lyon, sends many greetings.

<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial 'C' featuring a floral design with several five-petaled flowers and curling vines.</image-desc>Most learned of physicians, Philippe, you were the first to call upon me with your kindness. Before I had any personal acquaintance with you—a man distinguished both by your lineage and your own virtues—you invited me to take a chance on your friendship. I, however, deem it entirely unmanly—and clearly an offense against what is right <note>original: "nefas," a word implying a sin against divine or natural law</note>—not to respond to affection. Therefore, I have decided to secure your love for me even more closely with this small gift: the instructional orations of Isocrates to Demonicus <note>Isocrates was an ancient Greek orator; his "Exhortation to Demonicus" was a popular Renaissance textbook for moral education</note>. May you hold this as a token of my regard for you until I can produce greater works for you—works that might better match your illustrious honors and the most serious medical treatments for which you have been so significantly distinguished. In this, you represent your father’s own image, reflecting the virtues of your parent’s soul just as you do the features of his face. For it is only right that sons should be heirs to their father's virtues just as they are to his estate <term>facultatis<gloss>In this context, the word refers to both professional skill and material inheritance</gloss></term>. In the meantime, let these few items serve as a light breakfast <note>original: "p ientaculo"</note>, until the dishes of a more sumptuous banquet are prepared. Farewell. From Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507, on the ninth day before the Kalends of July <note>June 23rd</note>.

Isocrates to Demonicus

## ¶ The advisory oration of Isocrates to Demonicus, translated from Greek into Latin.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'D' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>**We shall find**, O Demonicus, that the opinions of good and evil men are diverse in many matters. But they are by far most diverse regarding the habits of friendship. For some value friends only when they are present, while others cherish them even when they are absent. A brief passage of time dissolves the fellowships of the wicked, but not even an entire age could abolish the friendships of the good. Therefore, since I believed that those eager for glory and professors of learning ought to imitate the good and flee from the wicked, I have sent this oration of ours to you as a gift. It serves as a sign of the goodwill between us and no small proof of my intimacy with Hipponicus <note>Hipponicus was a wealthy Athenian and the father of Demonicus, to whom this letter is addressed</note>. For it is fitting for sons to be heirs to their father’s friendships just as they are to his wealth and property. I see, moreover, that fortune is assisting us and that a most timely opportunity has been offered. For you long for instruction, and I, for my part, endeavor to teach others. You are still a student of philosophy <note>original: "philosopharis," meaning to engage in the study of wisdom or character</note>, and I correct those who study it. Whoever, therefore, composes encouraging speeches for their friends undertakes a truly beautiful work; yet, they do not always dwell upon the best part of philosophy. Those who show the young not just how to exercise a certain greater power in their oratory, but how they might eventually be seen as established in good character—these men benefit their listeners far more than the former. The first group only invites the young to speak well, but the latter actually corrects their behavior. For this reason, we have used not just encouragements but authoritative rules <note>original: "regie," suggesting a kingly or guiding principle</note> and admonitions. we shall advise you on those things which a young man ought to seek, which things he should abstain from, with what sort of men he should associate, and finally, by what reasoning he should govern his life. For to those who have set such a path for their lives, it has been granted to reach a good harvest and true virtue. Certainly, no possession is worthier or more stable than virtue. Beauty either vanishes with time or wastes away through some sickness. Riches are more often the servants of wickedness than of honesty; for they provide a license for idleness and lure the young toward pleasures. Physical strength is very profitable when combined with prudence <term>prudentia<gloss>the practical wisdom to make right decisions</gloss></term>, but without it, strength is mostly a hindrance. While it may adorn the bodies of those who exercise, it casts a shadow over the

<column-break/>

sharpness and insight of the mind. But the possession of virtue alone grows old along with those in whose minds it has been sincerely poured and united. It is far better and more useful than all riches and any nobility. It makes possible for itself those things which seem impossible to others; it confidently and fearlessly endures those things which the common people think are terrifying; it considers cowardice a disgrace and labor a source of glory. We can learn this very easily from the labors of Hercules and the great deeds of Theseus <note>Legendary Greek heroes who achieved immortality through their virtuous struggles</note>. Virtue has erected such monuments of their good fame that not even the passing of all the centuries will bring their deeds into oblivion. Indeed, if you recall your father's counsels in your mind, you will have a beautiful and domestic example of these things I am saying. For that man neither neglected virtue nor spent his life in sloth; instead, he exercised his body with labors and sustained dangers with a spirited mind. He did not love riches at the wrong time. He used external goods as a mortal <note>meaning he recognized they were temporary</note>, but he cared for the things he had acquired as if he were immortal <note>meaning he managed his estate with a view toward a lasting legacy</note>. Nor did he live his life in a stingy way; rather, he was elegant and magnificent. He showed himself to be kind to his friends and approved of those who were devoted to him more than those who were merely joined to him by kinship. For he believed that nature was more powerful than law for the sake of fellowship, character more than race, and choice more than necessity. Time would fail me if I wished to recount all that man’s virtues; therefore, let us defer those things which can be said more accurately about him to another time. Meanwhile, we have brought forward the example of Hipponicus's nature, which you ought to imitate. You should establish your life according to this model, considering his character to be your law, and it is fitting for you to be an imitator and rival of your father’s virtue. Indeed, it would be most shameful if painters chose to represent beautiful animals by imitation, yet sons did not even wish to imitate their excellent parents. Believe that it is not so fitting for any athlete to train against his adversaries as it is for you to intent your mind on how you might best become like your father in his pursuits. This can in no way happen unless your mind is imbued with many of the most beautiful teachings. And since nature is so arranged that bodies are improved by tempered labors, but minds are increased by fruitful words, I will try to instruct you briefly on which studies I believe will allow you to make the most progress in virtue and be approved with glory among all men. 
¶ First of all, therefore, honor those things which pertain to the gods; not only by sacrificing, but also by remaining true to your oaths. For the former is a sign of an abundance of money, but the latter is proof of the honesty of one's character. Always honor the divine, but especially in the company of the community; for in this way, you will be seen both to sacrifice to the gods and to be bound by the laws.

# Isocrates to Demonicus

**Column 1:**

Behave toward your parents as you would wish your own children to behave toward you. Regarding the body, engage in those exercises that aim for good health rather than mere strength <note>The author distinguishes between 'robur' (brute force) and 'valitudo' (the balanced health of a gentleman)</note>. You can achieve this if you cease your labors while you are still capable of working. Do not love reckless laughter, nor offer bold speech; for the former belongs to a fool, and the latter to a madman. Those things which are shameful to do, consider them also not honorable to speak of. Accustom yourself to be modest; for because of this, you will appear prudent rather than insolent. Above all, consider that shamefastness <note>original: "verecundia," a sense of social or moral shame that prevents wrong-doing</note>, justice, and moderation are fitting for you and serve as an ornament; for in all these, the character of young men seems most to be contained.

When you have committed any shameful act, never hope it will remain hidden; for even if you hide it from others, you will certainly be conscious of it yourself. Fear the gods. Honor your parents. Revere your friends. Obey the laws. Pursue pleasures, but only those that are accompanied by glory. For delight joined with honor is the best thing, but without it, it is most foul. Avoid slanders even if they are false; for many who are ignorant of the truth look instead to public opinion. Appear to do everything as if you will hide it from no one; for even if you remain hidden for the present, you will surely be made known later. You would be most highly praised if you did not do those things which you would reprehend if they were done by others.

If you are a lover of learning, you will learn much. Those things which you have learned, preserve through frequent practice; but those things of which you are ignorant, acquire through instruction <note>original: "disciplinis"</note>. For it is equally shameful for one who has heard a useful discourse not to learn it by heart as it is not to accept a fruitful gift when it is offered by friends. Spend your leisure time in life in listening willingly; for in this way it will happen that you most easily learn those things which were discovered by others with great difficulty. Persuade yourself that many lessons are more useful than much money. For the latter fail very quickly, but the former remain with us forever. For wisdom alone of all possessions is held to be stable and eternal. Do not be burdened by undertaking a long journey to those who profess to teach something useful. For it is shameful that merchants cross distant seas solely to increase their current wealth, while young men do not even endure journeys by land to make their minds better and more refined. In your manners, be courteous in greeting others and affable in speech. He is courteous in greeting who receives those he meets with kindness; he is affable who conducts himself familiarly and benignly in conversation. Accommodate yourself to all, but associate only with the best 

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

people. For in this way, you will not be offensive to the former, and you will become a friend to the latter. Do not engage in frequent conversations with the same people, nor long ones about the same subjects; for there is a satiety in all things. Exercise yourself with voluntary labors so that you may be able to bear involuntary ones if the situation requires. Restrain yourself from all those things by which it is shameful for the soul to be conquered: profit, anger, pleasure, and grief. You will achieve this if you judge that to be profit through which you will acquire glory, rather than that which allows you to overflow with riches. In anger, behave toward those who offend you as you would think others should behave toward you when you err. In matters of desire, consider it shameful to rule over servants but be a slave to pleasures. In times of grief, look upon the calamities of others and remember that you are human.

Take greater care for the deposit of words than for the deposit of money; for honest men ought to display character that is more faithful than any oath. I would have you think it just as proper to withhold trust from the wicked as it is to believe the good. Tell your secrets to no one unless it is equally useful for you who are speaking and for those who are listening that those things remain silent. Accept an offered oath for two main reasons: either to free yourself from some infamous accusation, or to free your friends from great dangers. But never swear by any of the gods for the sake of money, even if you are swearing the truth; for you will seem to some to be a perjurer, and to others to be gripped by avarice.

Make no one your friend before you have examined how he treated his former friends; for expect that he will be toward you as he was toward them. Be slow to make a friend, but once made, remain constant; for it is equally shameful to have no friend as it is to treat many with inconstancy. Do not test friends at the risk of loss, but make trial of your companions. You will achieve this if, when you are in no need, you pretend to be in want. And if there are things you could safely say in public, commit them to them as if they were secrets; if you do not succeed in making them keep silent, you will suffer no damage at all, but if they do keep silent, then you will have known their character best. Test friends in the misfortunes of life and the sharing of dangers; for as we test gold in fire, so we test friends in some calamity. You will best use your friends if you do not wait for them to ask anything of you, but help them voluntarily and opportunely. Believe it is equally shameful to be outdone by enemies in evil deeds and by friends in kindness. From among your friends, choose those who are not only saddened in adversity but who also do not envy your success; for many grieve with their unfortunate friends

### Isocrates to Demonicus

¶ The preceptive oration of Isocrates to Demonicus, translated from Greek into Latin.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial letter 'F' depicting a detailed landscape with a town or castle in the distance, hills, and leafy trees in the foreground.</image-desc>

In many things, Demonicus, we shall find the opinions of the good and the bad to be far apart <note>The Latin text here uses a decorative 'F', likely for a word like 'Frequenter' (Frequently) or 'Fere' (Generally), though the underlying Greek text begins by contrasting the habits of the virtuous and the wicked.</note>. But they are most vastly different in those matters concerning friendship and social life. For the wicked value their friends only while they are present, whereas the good cherish them even when they are absent. The intimacies of the wicked are dissolved by a short course of time, but not even a whole lifetime could erase the friendships of the good. 

Therefore, since I believed that those eager for glory and professors of learning should imitate the virtuous and flee the wicked, I have sent you this speech of ours as a gift—a token of the goodwill between us, and no small proof of my friendship with Hipponicus <note>Hipponicus was Demonicus's father and a friend of Isocrates.</note>. For it is fitting for sons to be heirs to their father's friendships just as they are to his property. 

I see, moreover, that fortune is helping us, and a most timely opportunity has been offered. For you desire learning, and I attempt to teach others. You are currently practicing philosophy <note>In this context, 'philosophy' refers to the study of ethics and the art of living well, rather than abstract logic.</note>, and I correct those who study it. 

Now, whoever composes hortatory speeches for their friends certainly undertakes a beautiful work, yet they do not dwell upon the best part of philosophy. Those who show the young not merely how to exercise a certain greater power in oratory, but rather how they may be seen to be established in good character—these men benefit their listeners far more. The former only invite the youth to speak; the latter actually correct their conduct.

For this reason, we have used not exhortations but admonitions to counsel you on those things which a young man ought to seek, what things he should abstain from, what kind of men he should associate with, and finally, by what logic he should govern his life. For to whoever sets out such a path for their life, it alone is granted to reach the "good fruit" and true virtue. Certainly no possession is more worthy or more stable than this. 

Beauty either fades with time or is wasted by some sickness. Riches are more often the servants of wickedness than of integrity, for they provide license for sloth and entice the young toward pleasures. Physical strength is very profitable when joined with prudence, but without it, it is a great hindrance; and while it may decorate the body during exercise, it often 

<column-break/>

overshadows the sharpness and insight of the mind. But the possession of virtue alone grows old with those in whose minds it has been sincerely poured and united. It is far better and more useful than all riches and every nobility, making possible those things which seem impossible to others. It allows one to endure confidently and fearlessly those things which the common people think are terrible, judging cowardice to be a disgrace and labor to be a glory. 

We can learn this quite easily both from the labors of Hercules and the deeds of Theseus <note>Hercules and Theseus are cited as the ultimate Greek examples of 'virtus'—active, heroic excellence that benefits society.</note>. Virtue erected such monuments of good fame for them that not even all the ages of time shall bring oblivion to their deeds. 

Indeed, if you recall your father's counsel in your mind, you will have a beautiful and domestic example of these things I am saying to you. For that man neither neglected virtue nor spent his life in sloth; instead, he exercised his body with labors and sustained dangers with a spirited mind, nor did he love riches unseasonably. He used external goods like a mortal <note>Meaning he enjoyed them while he was alive.</note>, but he cared for the wealth he had acquired as if he were immortal <note>Meaning he preserved it for his heirs and his legacy.</note>. Nor did he live his life in a stingy way; rather, he was elegant and magnificent. He made himself accessible to his friends and valued those devoted to him more than any joined to him by blood; for he judged that for companionship, nature is more powerful than law, character more than lineage, and choice more than necessity. 

Time would fail me if I wished to recount all that man's virtues; therefore, we shall defer what can be said more accurately about him to another time. In the meantime, we have offered the example of Hipponicus’s nature, which you ought to imitate. You should establish your life according to this model, considering his character to be your law, and striving to be an imitator and rival of your father’s virtue. 

Indeed, it would be most shameful if painters represented beautiful animals by imitation, but sons did not even wish to imitate their own excellent parents. Believe that it is not as fitting for any athlete to train himself against his adversaries as it is for you to intent your mind on how you may become most like your father’s pursuits. This can by no means happen for someone who has not been imbued with many of the most beautiful teachings. 

And since nature is so arranged that bodies are improved by moderate labors, while minds are grown through fruitful discourse, I shall attempt to teach you briefly by what studies you seem to me to be able to profit most in virtue and be approved in glory among all men.

¶ First of all, therefore, cherish those things which pertain to the gods, not only by sacrificing, but also by remaining true to your oaths. For the former is a sign of an abundance of money, but the latter is a proof of the integrity of one's character. Always worship the divine, but especially with the community; for in this way you will be seen both to sacrifice to the gods and to be bound by the laws.

# Isocrates to Demonicus

### Isocrates to Demonicus.

Conduct yourself toward your parents in such a way as you would wish your own children to conduct themselves toward you. Regarding the body, employ those exercises not intended for mere brute strength, but those aimed at good health. You may achieve this if you cease your labors while you are still capable of working <note>Isocrates suggests moderation in exercise; one should stop while they still have energy left, rather than pushing to total exhaustion.</note>. Do not love rash laughter, nor offer bold speech; for the former is the mark of a fool, and the latter of a madman. Those things which are shameful to do, consider them no more honorable to speak of. Accustom yourself to be modest. For by the former you will seem insolent, but by the latter you will appear prudent. Above all, consider that modesty, justice, and self-restraint <note>Latin: *modestiam*. In this context, it refers to the classical virtue of Sophrosyne, or self-mastery and temperance.</note> are fitting and an ornament to you; for in these all the character of the young seems most especially contained. When you have committed any shameful act, never hope it will remain hidden; for even if you hide it from others, you will certainly be conscious of it yourself. Fear the gods. Honor your parents. Respect your friends. Obey the laws. Pursue pleasures, but only those that are consistent with glory. For delight joined with honor is the best thing, but without it, it is the most foul. Avoid slanders even if they are false. For many people, being ignorant of the truth, look instead to common opinion. Appear to do all things as if you were hiding nothing from anyone; for even if you are hidden for the present, you will eventually be made known. You could be most especially praised if you did not do those things which you would rebuke if they were in others. If you are eager to learn, you will learn much. Preserve those things you have learned through frequent practice; acquire those things you do not know through instruction. For it is just as shameful for one who has heard a useful discourse not to learn it by heart, as it is not to accept a fruitful gift when it is offered by friends. Spend your leisure time in life listening willingly; for thus it will happen that you most easily learn those things which others discovered with difficulty. Persuade yourself that many lessons are more useful than much money. For the latter fails very quickly, but the former remains with us forever; for of all possessions, wisdom alone is considered stable and eternal. Do not be burdened by undertaking a long journey to those who profess to teach something useful; for it is a shame that merchants cross distant seas for this reason alone—to increase their present wealth—but the young will not sustain journeys by land to make their minds better and more cultivated. Be courteous in your manners when greeting others, and affable in your speech. He is courteous in greeting who receives those he meets with kindness; he is affable who conducts himself in conversation with familiarity and benevolence. Show consideration to all, but associate only with the best. 

<column-break/>

For in this way you will not be hated by the former, and you will become a friend to the latter. Do not make frequent speeches to the same people, nor long ones about the same subjects; for there is a weariness in all things. Exercise yourself in voluntary labors so that you may also be able to endure involuntary ones, should circumstances require it <note>This reflects the Stoic-adjacent idea of "pre-rehearsing" hardship to build resilience.</note>. Restrain yourself from all those things by which it is shameful for the soul to be conquered: profit, anger, pleasure, and grief. You will achieve this if you judge that to be profit through which you gain glory, rather than that by which you may overflow with riches. In anger, conduct yourself toward those who fail as you would think others should be toward you when you err. In matters of pleasure, consider it shameful to rule over servants but to be enslaved by delights. In times of grief, look upon the calamities of others and remember that you are but a man. Have greater care for the "deposits" of words entrusted to you than for money. For honest men ought to exhibit a character more faithful than any oath. I would have you think it equally fitting to distrust the wicked as to trust the good. Tell secrets to no one, unless it is equally useful to you as the speaker and to those listening that they remain silent. Accept an offered oath for two main reasons: either to free yourself from some infamous accusation, or to free friends from great dangers. But for the sake of money, never swear by any of the gods, even if you were to swear truly; for you will seem to some to be a perjurer, and to others to be gripped by greed. Make no one your friend before you have examined how he treated his previous friends; for expect that he will be toward you as he was toward them. Be slow to make a friend, but once made, persevere constantly; for it is equally shameful to have no friend as to change many companions inconsistently. Do not test friends at the risk of loss; but do make trial of your intimates. You may achieve this if, though not in need of anything, you pretend that you are in want. And if there are things you could safely say openly, commit them to them as if they were secrets; for if you do not succeed in making them keep silent, you will suffer no damage at all; but if they do remain silent, you will best know their character. Test friends in the shared danger of life's misfortunes; for as gold is tested by fire, so we test friends by some calamity. You will best use your friends in this way if you do not wait for them to ask you for something, but help them voluntarily and opportunely. Likewise, believe it to be equally shameful to be outdone by enemies in doing harm as by friends in doing good. Choose those friends who do not only grieve in your adversity, but who also do not envy your success. For many people grieve with unhappy friends, but begrudge them when they are fortunate.

Isocrates to Demonicus

# Isocrates’s advisory speech to Demonicus, translated from Greek into Latin.

<image-desc>Large historiated woodcut initial 'A' featuring a central floral motif surrounded by leafy vines and blossoms within a square border.</image-desc> We shall discover, O Demonicus, that the opinions of good and evil men are opposed in many matters, but they are most widely divergent in those things concerning friendship and social interaction. For the latter <note>The "improbi" or wicked.</note> prize friends only when they are present, whereas the former <note>The "boni" or virtuous.</note> cherish them even when they are absent. A short course of time dissolves the intimacies of the wicked, but even the passage of an entire age cannot erase the friendships of the good. Therefore, since I judged that those who are eager for glory and professors of learning should imitate the virtuous and flee the wicked, I have sent you this speech of ours as a gift—a testament to the goodwill between us and a significant proof of my friendship with Hipponicus <note>Hipponicus was a wealthy Athenian aristocrat and the father of Demonicus; Isocrates uses his memory to guide the son.</note>. For it is fitting that sons should be heirs to their father's friendships just as they are to his property. I see, moreover, that fortune is helping us and a timely opportunity has been offered. For you desire learning, and I attempt to teach others. You are currently a student of philosophy <note>original: "philosopharis" — in this context, "philosophy" refers to the general study of ethics and the art of living well.</note>, and I correct those who study it. 

Whoever, therefore, composes exhortatory speeches for their friends undertakes a truly noble work; however, they do not dwell upon the best part of philosophy. Those who show young men not the means by which they may exercise some greater power in oratory, but rather how they might be seen as established in good character—these men benefit their listeners far more than the others. The former only invite the young to speak, but the latter actually correct their morals. For this reason, we shall resolve to use not merely exhortations toward you, but specific admonitions, advising you on what things a young man should strive for, what things he should abstain from, with what sort of men he should associate, and finally, by what logic he should govern his own life. For only those who have set such a path for their lives have managed to reach good fruit and true virtue <note>original: "virtutem" — the Latin equivalent of the Greek *Arete*, implying excellence in both character and function.</note>. Certainly, no possession is more worthy or more stable than this. Beauty is either vanished by time or wasted by some sickness. Riches are more often the servants of wickedness than of goodness, for they provide a license for laziness and entice the young toward pleasures. Bodily strength is very beneficial when joined with prudence, but when that is removed, it is most harmful; while it may decorate the bodies of those who exercise, it casts a shadow over

<column-break/>

the sharpness and perspicacity of the mind. But the possession of virtue alone grows old along with those in whose minds it has been sincerely infused and take root. It is far better and more useful than all riches and all nobility, making those things possible for itself which seem impossible to others; it endures confidently and intrepidly those things which the common people think terrifying, deeming laziness a disgrace and labors a glory. 

We can learn this very easily both from the labors of Hercules and the deeds of Theseus; virtue erected such monuments of good fame for them that not even all the passing ages shall bring oblivion to their deeds. Truly, if you recall your father’s counsels to mind, you will have a beautiful and domestic example of these things I say to you. For that man neither neglected virtue nor spent his life in sloth; instead, he exercised his body with labors and sustained dangers with a spirited mind, nor did he love riches unseasonably. He used external goods as a mortal <note>He used his wealth and resources during his lifetime, knowing he would die.</note>, but he cared for what he had acquired as if he were immortal <note>He managed his reputation and legacy as if it would live forever.</note>. Nor did he live his life in a sordid manner, but elegantly; he was magnificent. He gave of himself freely to his friends and valued those devoted to him more than those joined to him by mere kinship; for he judged that for the sake of companionship, nature is more powerful than law, character more than lineage, and choice more than necessity. 

I myself would fail if I wished to recount all that man's virtues; therefore, we shall defer what can be said more accurately about him to another time. In the meantime, we have presented the example of Hipponicus’s nature, which you ought to imitate, establishing your life according to that model—judging his character to be your law, and fitting yourself to be an imitator and rival of your father’s virtue. Indeed, it would be most shameful if painters represent beautiful animals by imitation, yet sons do not even wish to imitate their own excellent parents. Believe that it is as fitting for you to intend your mind toward following your father's pursuits as it is for any athlete to train against his adversaries. This, however, can in no way happen for one who has not been imbued with many beautiful teachings. And since it is so arranged by nature that bodies are increased by moderate labors, but minds by fruitful discourse, I shall attempt to briefly instruct you in those studies by which you might seem to me to make the most progress in virtue and be approved with glory among all men.

¶ First, therefore, above all else, cherish those things which pertain to the gods; not only by sacrificing, but also by remaining steadfast in your oaths. For the former is a sign of an abundance of money, but the latter is an argument for the integrity of one's character. Always worship the divine, but especially in the company of the community; for in this way you will be seen both to sacrifice to the gods and to be bound by the laws.

-># Isocrates to Demonicus<-

Conduct yourself toward your parents in the same way as you would wish your own children to conduct themselves toward you. In regards to the body, use those exercises not intended for mere strength, but those which look toward good health. You might achieve this if you cease your labors while you are still capable of laboring. Neither love reckless laughter, nor offer your speech with boldness; for the former is the mark of a fool <note>original: "amentis"</note> and the latter of a madman <note>original: "furentis"</note>. Those things which are shameful to do, consider them also not honorable to speak of. Accustom yourself to be neither of a harsh nor of a fierce countenance, but mild and modest. For because of the former you will seem arrogant, but because of the latter you will seem respectful. Above all, consider that modesty <note>original: "verecundiam"</note>, justice, and moderation are becoming and ornamental to you; for the character of the young seems to be most contained within all of these. When you have committed any act through disgrace, never hope that it will remain hidden; for even if you hide it from others, you will certainly be conscious of it yourself. Fear the gods. Honor your parents. Revere your friends. Obey the laws. Seek out pleasures, but only those that are accompanied by glory. For delight joined with honor is a most excellent thing, but without it, it is the worst. Avoid slanders even if they are false. For most people, being ignorant of the truth, look instead toward common opinion. Appear to do all things as if you were going to hide them from no one; for even if you are hidden in the present, you will eventually be made known to the public. You could be most greatly praised if you did not do those things which you would rebuke if they were in others. If you are eager for learning, you will learn much. Those things which you have learned, preserve through frequent practice; those things which you do not know, acquire through instruction. For it is equally shameful for one who has heard a useful discourse not to learn it thoroughly, as it is to not accept a fruitful gift when offered by friends. Spend your leisure time in life in listening willingly; for in this way it will happen that you most easily learn those things which were found with difficulty by others. Persuade yourself that many lessons <note>original: "auditiones" — literally "things heard," referring to oral teachings</note> are more useful than vast sums of money. For the latter fail very quickly, but the former remain with us forever. For of all possessions, wisdom <note>original: "sapientia"</note> alone is held to be stable and eternal. Do not be loath to undertake a long journey to those who profess to teach something useful; for it is shameful that merchants cross distant seas for the sole purpose of increasing their present wealth, yet the young do not endure journeys by land to render their minds better and more cultivated. Be courteous in your manners when greeting, and affable in your speech. He is courteous in greeting who receives those he meets with kindness; he is affable who conducts himself familiarly and benignly in conversation. Comply with the ways of all, but associate only with the best.

<column-break/>

For in this way, you will not be hated by the former, and you will become a friend to the latter. Do not make frequent addresses to the same people, nor long ones concerning the same matters; for there is a satiety <note>a "cloying fullness" or boredom</note> in all things. Exercise yourself in voluntary labors so that you might also be able to endure involuntary ones, if circumstances require. Restrain yourself from all those things by which it is shameful for the soul to be conquered: profit, anger, pleasure, and grief. You will achieve this if you consider that to be profit by which you acquire glory, and not that by which you might flow with riches. In anger, conduct yourself toward those who offend in such a way as you would think others should be toward you when you err. In matters of pleasure, consider it shameful to rule over servants while being a slave to your own desires. In times of grief, look upon the calamities of others and remember that you are a man. Have a greater care for the trust of words <note>original: "deposita verborum" — referring to keeping secrets or one's word</note> than for the trust of money. For it is necessary for honorable men to exhibit a character more faithful than any oath. I would wish you to think it just as fitting to withhold trust from the wicked as it is to believe the good. Tell your secrets to no one, unless it is equally useful for you who speak and for those who hear that they remain silent. Accept a proffered oath for two main reasons: either to free yourself from some infamous accusation, or to free friends from great dangers. For the sake of money, however, never swear by any of the gods, even if you were to swear truly; for you will seem to some to be a perjurer, and to others to be gripped by greed. Make no one your friend before you have examined how he treated his previous friends; for expect that he will be toward you such as he was toward them. Be slow to make a friend, but once made, remain constant; for it is equally shameful to have no friend as it is to treat many with inconstancy. Do not test friends at the risk of loss, but make trial of your familiars. You will achieve this if, not being in need of something, you nonetheless pretend to need it. And if there are things you could safely say in public, commit them to them as if they were secrets; for if you do not succeed in having them remain silent, you will suffer no damage, but if they do remain silent, then you will best know their characters. Test friends by the fellowship of life's misfortunes and dangers; for as gold is tested by fire, so we test friends by some calamity. In this way, it will be given to you to use your friends best: if you do not wait for them to ask something of you, but help them of your own accord and at the opportune moment. Believe it to be equally shameful to be surpassed by enemies in doing harm as to be surpassed by friends in doing good. Choose from among your friends those who not only grieve in your adversities, but also do not envy your success. For many grieve with their unfortunate friends, but...
