...indeed: yet they envy those who are fortunate. Remember absent friends when you are with those who are present, so that you do not seem to disparage these same men when they are eventually absent. Concerning the grooming of your body, be elegant and neat <note>original: "concinnus"</note>, yet not fastidious nor too delicately adorned. For to be neat is a mark of magnificence, but to be delicate is a mark of fussiness <note>original: "curiositatis"</note>. From the goods of fortune, do not love an enormous possession, but rather a moderate use of them. Despise those who are over-eager for riches but do not know how to use what is present and ready at hand; for such people are like a man who has a fine horse but does not rightly know the art of riding. Take pains to acquire riches, money, and estates; for to those who know how to enjoy them, money is indeed a true possession, just as strength is to those who are able to use it. Cherish your present riches for two reasons: so that you may easily repel some great loss, and so that you may help a friend who is diligent and devoted but otherwise unfortunate. As for the rest of your life's use, there is no reason to desire them greatly, but rather modestly. Cherish what you have, but seek better things. Never reproach anyone for their misfortune <note>original: "calamitatem"</note>. For fortune is common to all, and the things of the future are truly hidden and unproven. Do good to the good; for a debt of gratitude in the heart of an upright man is a most beautiful treasure. But if you do good to the wicked, it will happen to you no differently than to those who feed the dogs of others. For they do not stop barking at anyone else just because they are given something. Even so, the wicked, without any distinction, treat their benefactors with injury as if they were evildoers. Hate flatterers as much as deceivers; for when trust is placed in either of them, they cheat the gullible. If you approve of friends who congratulate you on a wicked deed, you will have no one to correct you toward better things. Toward your associates, show yourself easy-going, not harsh. For even servants can hardly bear the arrogance of the latter, by which a man despises all others; but all men bear the easy and pleasant manners of the former. Indeed, you will be easy-going if you are not contentious, nor fastidious, nor litigious about everything. Do not meet your angry friends harshly, not even if they become angry without merit; instead, yield to them for a little while while they are burning with rage, and rebuke them only when they are free from anger. Do not speak of serious things during moments of laughter, nor use jokes during serious matters; for that which is inappropriate is everywhere a nuisance. Do not grant a favor ungraciously, as many certainly do who, though they provide what was asked, nevertheless help their friends in an unpleasant manner. Avoid the reputation of an accuser and a critic <note>original: "censoris"</note>; for the former irritates men against you, and the latter is burdensome. Above all, avoid drinking parties at banquets. But if it should happen that you must attend one, get yourself away from there before drunkenness sets in. For when the mind is weakened by wine, it acts just like a chariot that has been stripped of its driver. For just as the chariot, wandering from its governor,

<column-break/>

is pulled along in a disordered way, so the soul, when the mind is corrupted, is unable to discern the right path. That you may be of a great spirit, contemplate immortal and divine things; but consider mortal things so that you may enjoy human affairs with moderation. Believe that modesty of speech is a much greater good than a reckless tongue, because while other vices can be a source of profit to all, those who possess this one fault are affected by no small disadvantage. For many a time, we pay the penalty in actual fact for things we have provoked with words. Of those whom you wish to make your friends, speak some good of them to those who will soon report it back to them; for praise is the beginning of friendship, just as blame is the beginning of hatred. When you deliberate, weigh the future by the past; for the hidden is most quickly discerned from the manifest. Deliberate while hesitating, but execute what you have decreed as quickly as possible. Consider it best to have good success from the gods, but good counsel from ourselves. Concerning things you are ashamed to speak of boldly, but which you would altogether wish to communicate to some friends, use speech as if you were talking about someone else's business. In this way, you will understand their opinion without having revealed yourself. Whenever you are about to have someone as a counselor regarding your affairs, consider first how he has administered his own; for he who has consulted poorly in his own business will never look out well for another’s. You will be most incited to take counsel if you look upon the calamities that have arisen from rashness. For we carefully guard our good health when we recall to memory how many evils threaten us from diseases. Imitate the manners of kings and follow their pursuits; for you will seem in a way to embrace and emulate them. Thus it will happen that you will be lovable among the common people and you will enter into a firmer favor with kings. Obey the laws laid down by the kings themselves, but nevertheless consider their character to be the most powerful law. For just as it is necessary for one living in a democracy <note>original: "statu populari"</note> to cherish the multitude itself, so it is fitting for one living under an empire to worship and admire the king himself. When you sustain the person of a magistrate <note>original: "magistratus"</note>, use no wicked servant in your administration; for in whatever things he sins, all the blame will redound upon you. Depart from the administration of the republic not wealthier, but more glorious; for praise coming from the multitude is better than much riches. Do not support or favor a dishonest thing; for you will seem to be the sort of person who commits the very things done by those to whom you bring help. Take pains so that you may seem able to be powerful, but be content with equity <note>original: "equitate"</note>, so that you appear to love what is fair and just not because of weakness, but because of modesty. Embrace honest poverty more than riches unjustly gained. For justice is so much better than riches, in that wealth is only of use to the living...

<meta>This page concludes the "Oratio Preceptiva" (Instructional Speech) of Isocrates to Demonicus. # Preceptive Oration

...help. That virtue, truly, brings glory even to those who have departed this life. Furthermore, the wicked find power in riches, but are utterly excluded from justice. Never envy anyone who profits from injustice; instead, approve more of those who have suffered some loss for the sake of justice. Indeed, even if the just do not possess more than the unjust, they nevertheless surpass them in the strength of good hope. Take diligent care of all things pertaining to life, but above all, exercise prudence <note>The Latin "prudentia" implies practical wisdom and foresight.</note>. For a good mind is the greatest thing within the small compass of a human body. Endeavor to accustom your body to labor, but your soul to the study of wisdom, so that you may execute what you have decided and foresee what is to your advantage. Whatever you are about to say, first consider it within your mind; for in most people, the tongue outruns the thought. Reflect that in human affairs, nothing is firm or stable; in this way, if you are established in happiness, you will not be carried away by joy, and if you are vexed by some misfortune, you will grieve less. Appoint for yourself two times for speaking: one concerning things you know well, and the other concerning things about which it is necessary to speak. For in these cases alone is speech better than silence; in others, quietness is preferable. When some good thing happens to you, rejoice; but when bad things occur, grieve only moderately. In either state, however, conceal your feelings. For it would be quite absurd to hide one's wealth within the house, but to walk abroad with one's mind exposed to all. Avoid infamy more than danger; for it is fitting for the wicked to fear a cruel end to life, but for the virtuous to fear disgrace as long as they live. Above all, endeavor to live your life with security. If by chance you must face danger, seek safety from war without any mark of shame. For all are condemned to die by the law of the fates; but nature has permitted only the high-minded to die well. Do not wonder if I have said more things than are suitable for your present age; for this fact was not hidden from me. But in this same little work, I wished both to advise your present life and to leave behind instructions for your future. You will easily recognize the use of these things, but you will find it difficult to find those who counsel you faithfully in such matters. Therefore, I thought nothing should be omitted from those things which I saw would bring you benefit, lest you search for what is missing from another, but rather that you might draw them out from this book as if from a storehouse <note>original: "cellam promptuariam," literally a pantry or storeroom of supplies.</note>. Furthermore, I would be most grateful to the immortal gods if the opinion I have formed of you did not deceive me. For we find that most people rejoice more in pleasant foods than healthy ones; likewise, they cling more to friends who sin alongside them than to those who give good advice. I believe you have chosen a path quite unlike theirs, using this as proof: that you do not shun the labor of other pursuits. For it is consistent with reason that he who has commanded himself to do only the best things should embrace those who urge others toward virtue. It would be a very great incentive for you to seek honorable works if you knew that the greatest and most solid

<column-break/>

pleasures are perceived from them. For in idleness and the love of excess, sorrow is the constant companion of pleasures. But to exercise oneself in virtue and to govern one's life prudently produces pure and more stable pleasures. For in the former, those who were first delighted grieve a little later; but here, after labors and hardships, we receive no small pleasures. In all affairs, we do not measure the beginning as much as we perceive the sense of the end. Since we do not do many things in life for the sake of the things themselves, but we labor for the sake of the outcomes. Consider besides that while the wicked are permitted to do anything indiscriminately—for they have immediately set such a course for their life—those who profess honor must either embrace virtue itself or certainly face many critics. For people do not pursue sinners with as much hatred as they do those who show themselves to be good but then do not differ from the base. And not without cause. For if we reprove those who lie in words alone, shall we not surely say that those whose whole lives are shameful are criminal? Rightly, therefore, would I believe such men not only commit a crime against themselves but are also traitors to fortune. For she bestowed on them riches, nobility, and friends; yet these most ungrateful men have made themselves unworthy of their present happiness. But if it is permitted for mortal nature to guess at the minds of the gods, I think they have shown through the fates—and even in those closest to them—how they conduct themselves toward good and bad men. For when Jupiter had fathered Hercules and Tantalus <note>Hercules and Tantalus are used here as archetypes: the hero rewarded for virtue and the king punished for pride/wickedness.</note> (as the myths tell and everyone believes), he consecrated the former to immortality because of his virtue, but tortured the latter with the greatest punishments because of his wickedness. Using these examples, one should seek uprightness, but also learn the best things from the poets and read through whatever useful things other wise men have said. For as we see the bee lighting upon every blossom and extracting what is useful from each, so it is necessary for those eager for learning to be inexperienced in nothing, but to gather useful things from everywhere; for even with such great diligence, one will scarcely manage to escape the errors of nature.

->The end of Isocrates's preceptive oration<-

### Isocrates to Demonicus

Indeed, they envy the fortunate. Remember your absent friends when in the presence of others, so that you do not appear to slight them when they are away. Regarding the care of your body and clothing, be elegant and neat, but not fastidious or overly decorated. To be neat is a sign of magnificence; to be delicate is a sign of vanity <note>Latin: "curiositatis" — in this context, it implies an excessive or fussy attention to detail.</note>. 

Of the goods of fortune, do not love excessive possession, but rather moderate use. Despise those who strive for riches but do not know how to use what they have; they are like a man who has a fine horse but lacks the skill of riding. Work to acquire wealth, whether in money or land; for to those who know how to enjoy it, money is a possession like that of Hercules <note>original: "sicut hercule possessiones" — likely referring to "Herculean" or legendary wealth, or perhaps an interjection emphasizing the scale of the benefit.</note> for those who have the strength to hold it. 

Cherish your current wealth for two reasons: to easily repel some great misfortune, or to assist a diligent and devoted friend who is otherwise unlucky. For the rest of life's needs, do not desire wealth excessively, but modestly. Cherish what you have, but seek better things. 

Never reproach anyone for their calamity. For fortune is common to all, and the future is hidden and unknown. Do good to the virtuous; for a most beautiful treasure is the gratitude owed by a good man. If you do good to the wicked, it will be the same for you as for those who feed other people’s dogs: they bark at those who give them food just as they do at anyone else. The wicked harm their benefactors just as they do their enemies. 

Hate flatterers as much as deceivers; for if you trust either, they will cheat the credulous. If you approve of friends who flatter you in an unjust matter, you will have no one to correct you for the better. Be approachable toward your intimates, not harsh. Hardship and fear, through which one treats everyone with contempt, can hardly be endured even by slaves; but everyone gladly bears the easy-going manners of a friend. Indeed, you will be easy-going if you are not argumentative, nor moody, nor litigious about everything. Do not respond harshly to angry friends, even if they are angry without cause; instead, yield a little to their outburst, and correct them once their anger has passed. 

Do not speak seriously in the middle of jokes, nor use jokes when discussing serious matters; for what is untimely is everywhere troublesome. Do not grant a favor ungraciously, as many do who help their friends but do so unpleasantly. Avoid the name of an accuser or a critic; the former irritates people against you, the latter is simply annoying. Above all, at banquets, avoid tight-knit cliques; if you must attend, leave before drunkenness. For when the mind is dulled by wine, it acts like a chariot that has lost its driver. Just as the chariot wanders without a guide, it is 

<column-break/>

dragged along in disorder; once the spirit is corrupted by the mind <note>Meaning the mind is clouded by intoxication.</note>, it cannot see what is right. 

To be of great soul, think on immortal and divine things; but use mortal things so that you enjoy human affairs moderately. Believe that restraint in speech is a great good compared to a reckless tongue; for while other vices can be profitable, this one brings no small disadvantage. Often, we suffer in reality for the things we have provoked with words. 

When you wish to make friends, speak some good of them to those who will report it back; for praise is the beginning of friendship, just as blame is the beginning of hatred. When you deliberate, weigh the future by the past; for the hidden is most quickly understood from the manifest. Deliberate slowly, but execute your decisions as quickly as possible. Consider it best to have success from the gods, but good counsel from ourselves. 

Regarding things you are ashamed to speak of openly, or which you wish to share with certain friends, speak of them as if they concerned someone else; in this way, you will learn their opinion without exposing yourself. Whenever you take someone into your counsel regarding your affairs, first consider how they managed their own. For he who has consulted poorly in his own business will never look out well for another’s. You will be most encouraged to seek counsel if you look at the calamities that come from rashness. We guard our health most diligently when we remember how many evils threaten us from disease. 

Imitate the manners of kings and follow their pursuits; for you will seem to embrace and emulate them. Thus, you will be lovable to the common people and gain firmer favor with kings. Obey the laws laid down by kings, but consider their own conduct to be the most powerful law. Just as one living in a democracy should cherish the multitude, so one living under a monarchy should honor and admire the king himself. 

When you hold a public office, do not use any wicked person as an assistant in your administration; for whatever he does wrong, all the blame will fall on you. Depart from public administration not richer, but more glorious; for the praise coming from the multitude is better than many riches. Do not assist or favor a dishonest cause; for you will seem to be doing the same things as those you help. Strive to show that you are capable of holding your own, but be content with equity, so that you appear to love what is fair and just, not out of weakness, but because of your moderation. Embrace a just poverty more than wealth gained through injustice. For justice is as much better than wealth as riches are only useful while we are living...

### Instructional Speech

...help. Indeed, virtue produces glory even for those who have passed from life. Furthermore, the wicked hold wealth in their power, yet they are utterly excluded from justice. Never envy anyone who profits from injustice; rather, approve of those who have suffered some loss for the sake of justice. Indeed, even if the just do not possess more than the unjust, they nevertheless surpass them in the possession of "good hope" <note>Latin: "bona spe" — a classical concept referring to the peaceful expectation of a good afterlife or a clear conscience.</note>. Take diligent care of all things pertaining to life, but above all, exercise prudence. For a good mind is the greatest thing found within the small body of a human. Endeavor to train your body so that you can execute whatever you have decided upon; this means providing for those things which are to your advantage. 

Whatever you are about to say, first reflect upon it in your mind; for in most people, the tongue outruns the thought. Consider that in human affairs, nothing is firm or stable; in this way, when you are established in happiness, you will not be carried away by excessive joy, and when troubled by some misfortune, you will grieve less. 

Appoint for yourself two specific times for speaking: one concerning things you know well, and the other concerning things about which it is necessary to speak. In these cases alone is speech better than silence; in all other matters, remaining quiet is preferable. When some good things happen to you, rejoice; but when evil things happen, grieve only moderately. In either state, however, you should conceal your feelings. For it would be most absurd to hide your riches within your house, yet walk about with your inner mind manifest to everyone. 

Avoid infamy <note>term: "infamia" — loss of legal or social standing; public disgrace</note> more than danger; for it is fitting that a cruel end to life threatens the wicked, but disgrace threatens the virtuous as long as they live. Above all, try to lead a life of security. But if by chance you happen to be in danger, seek safety from war without any mark of disgrace. For all are condemned to die by the law of the Fates; but nature has permitted only the magnanimous <note>term: "magnanimis" — great-souled or courageous people</note> to die well. 

Do not wonder if I have said more things than are suitable for your present age; for this fact did not escape me. Rather, in this same little work, I wished to provide for your present life and to leave behind precepts for your future. You will easily recognize the use of these things in time; however, you will find it difficult to find others who will counsel you so faithfully. Therefore, I thought nothing should be omitted of those things which I saw would bring you utility, lest you should have to seek what remains from someone else; instead, you can bring them forth from this book as if from a storehouse. 

Furthermore, I would be most grateful to the immortal gods if the opinion I have conceived of you does not deceive me. We find many people who, just as they rejoice more in pleasant foods than in healthy ones, so they adhere more to friends who sin with them than to those who advise them well. On this account, I believe you have chosen a different path from those people, using this as proof: that you do not flee from the labor of other worthy things. For it is consistent with reason that he who has commanded himself to do nothing but the best should embrace those who exhort others toward virtue. It would indeed be a very great incentive for you to desire honest works if you knew that the greatest and most solid

<column-break/>

pleasures are perceived from them. For in idleness and the love of excess, sorrow is the constant companion of pleasure. But to exercise oneself in virtue and to govern one's life prudently produces pleasures that are always sincere and more stable. In the former case, those who were delighted at first grieve a little while later; in the latter case, we receive no small pleasures even after labors and hardships. 

In all affairs, we do not remember the beginning as much as we perceive the outcome at the end. Indeed, most things in life we do not do for the sake of the actions themselves, but we labor for the sake of the results. Consider, moreover, that the wicked are allowed to do whatever is indiscriminate, for they have already proposed such a course of life for themselves. But for those who profess to be honest, it is necessary either to embrace virtue itself or certainly to face many critics. For people do not pursue those who sin with as much hatred as they do those who show themselves to be good yet do not differ from the vile. And not without cause: for if we reprove those who lie in words alone, shall we not say that those whose entire lives are shameful are utterly blameworthy? 

Justly, therefore, would we believe such people not only to commit a crime against themselves, but also to be traitors to their own fortune. For fortune has bestowed upon them riches, nobility, and friends; yet these most ungrateful men have made themselves unworthy of their current happiness. If it is permitted for a mortal to guess the minds of the gods, I think they have shown more than enough, even through those closest to us, how they conduct themselves toward good and bad men. For when Jupiter had fathered Hercules and Tantalus <note>Hercules was a hero rewarded with godhood; Tantalus was a king punished in the underworld for his crimes.</note> (as the stories tell and everyone believes), he consecrated the former to immortality because of his virtue; but the latter he tortured with the greatest punishments because of his iniquity. 

Using these examples, therefore, one should desire uprightness. Do not only remain within the things said by us, but also learn the best things from the poets, and read through whatever useful things other wise men have said. For as we see the bee sitting upon every bud, yet extracting the useful part from each, so it behooves those eager for learning to be inexperienced in nothing, but rather to collect useful things from everywhere. For hardly will anyone, even with such great diligence, succeed in escaping all the errors of nature.

->The instructional speech of Isocrates<-
->to Demonicus, son of Hipponicus<-
->The End.<-

### Isocrates to Demonicus

Indeed, people still envy those who are fortunate. Remember absent friends in the presence of those who are here, so that you do not seem to think little of these men when they are eventually absent as well. Regarding the grooming of your body's clothing, be elegant and well-fashioned, yet not overly fussy or too delicately adorned. For to be well-fashioned is a mark of dignity <note>original: "magnificentia" — in this context, a sense of noble stature or greatness</note>, while being over-refined is a mark of vanity <note>original: "curiositas" — implying an excessive or meddlesome attention to detail</note>. Concerning the goods of fortune, do not love an enormous possession, but rather a moderate use of them. Despise those who are zealous for riches but do not know how to use what they have at hand; for such people are like someone who has an elegant horse but does not properly understand the art of riding. Strive to acquire riches, money, and estates; for to those who know how to enjoy them, money is like a possession to be used, while for those who can only hold onto them, they are merely a burden. Love your current riches for two reasons: so that you may easily repel some great loss, and so that you may help a diligent and devoted friend who is otherwise unfortunate. For the remaining use of life, there is no reason to desire them greatly, but only modestly. Love what you have, but seek better things. Never mock anyone for their calamity. For fortune is common to all, and future events are hidden and incomprehensible. Do good to the good; for a most beautiful treasure is a debt of gratitude stored in an upright man. If you do good to the wicked, the same will happen to you as happens to those who feed other people’s dogs. For these dogs bark at anyone else even if they are given something. Likewise, the wicked treat those who do them good just as they treat those who do them harm, affecting them with injury without distinction. Hate flatterers just as much as deceivers; for both (if one places trust in them) cheat those who are credulous. If you approve of friends who congratulate you on a bad deed, you will not have anyone to correct you toward better things. Show yourself easy-going toward your familiars, not austere. For even servants will endure the pride of an austere man who despises everyone, but everyone joyfully bears the easy manners of a friendly man. Truly, you will be easy-going if you are not contentious, nor fussy, nor litigious about everything. Do not meet angry friends with harshness, even if they are angry without cause; rather, yield to them for a little while when they are boiling with rage, and rebuke them when they are free from anger. Do not speak of serious matters in ridiculous moments, nor use ridiculous jokes in serious matters; for whatever is poorly timed is everywhere troublesome. Do not grant a favor ungraciously, which many indeed do, who, while they do help their friends with what is requested, do so unpleasantly. Avoid the reputation of an accuser or a critic; for the former irritates men against you, and the latter is burdensome. Above all, avoid small, secretive gatherings at banquets. But if it should happen that you must attend, take your leave before drunkenness sets in. For when the mind is sluggish with wine, it acts like a chariot robbed of its driver. For just as a chariot, wandering from its governor,

<column-break/>

is carried along in a disorganized rush, so a soul, with its mind corrupted, cannot discern what is right. To be a man of great spirit, think on immortal and divine things; but regarding mortal things, enjoy human affairs with moderation. Believe that modesty of speech is a greater good than a sharp tongue, just as all other vices can bring profit to some, but this one brings no small disadvantage. For quite often we pay the penalty in reality for the things we have provoked with words. Concerning those whom you wish to make your friends, speak some good of them to people who will report this to them; for praise is the beginning of friendship, just as blame is the beginning of hatred. When you deliberate, weigh the future by the past; for the hidden is most quickly recognized by what is manifest. Deliberate slowly, but execute what you have decided as quickly as possible. Consider it best to have good success from the gods, but good counsel from ourselves. Regarding things you are ashamed to speak of confidently, but which you wish to communicate to some friends, speak of them as if they were someone else's business. In this way, you will understand their opinion without having revealed yourself. Whenever you are about to take someone into your counsel regarding your own affairs, first consider how that person has managed their own; for one who has consulted poorly in his own business will never look out well for another’s. You will be most incited to take counsel if you look upon the calamities that have come from rashness. For we diligently guard our good health when we recall to memory how many evils threaten us from diseases. Imitate the manners of kings and follow their pursuits; for you will seem in a way to embrace and emulate them. In this way, it will happen that you are lovable to the common people and gain a firmer favor from kings. Obey the laws laid down by the kings themselves, but consider their character to be the strongest law. For just as it is necessary for one living in a democracy <note>original: "statu populari" — a state of the people</note> to cherish the multitude, so it is fitting for one living under an empire to worship and admire the king himself. When you hold the role of a magistrate, use no wicked minister in your administration; for in whatever that man sins, all the blame will redound upon you. Depart from the administration of public affairs <note>original: "reipublice" — the common wealth or public business</note> not wealthier, but more glorious; for praise coming from the multitude is better than much wealth. Do not stand by nor favor a dishonest thing; for you too will seem to be committing such things as those whom you have helped are committing. Strive so that you may seem to be able to have the advantage, but be content with equity <note>original: "equitate" — fairness or justice that looks beyond the letter of the law</note>, so that you appear to love what is equal and just not because of weakness, but because of modesty. Embrace a just poverty more than wealth unjustly gained. For justice is as much better than wealth as...

# Preceptive Oration

[Virtues] help: for they truly bring glory even to those who have finished their lives. Furthermore, the wicked may have a portion of riches, but they are utterly excluded from justice. Never envy anyone who has profited from injustice, but rather approve of those who have suffered some loss for the sake of justice. For even if the just do not possess more than the unjust, they nevertheless surpass them in good hope. Diligently care for all things pertaining to life, but above all exercise prudence <note>original: "prudentia" — here meaning practical wisdom or moral discernment</note>. For a good mind is the greatest thing within the small body of a human. You should strive to accustom your body to labors, but your soul to the study of wisdom, so that you may be able to carry out what you have decided and foresee what will benefit your interests. Whatever you are about to say, first consider it within your mind; for in many people, the tongue outruns the thought. Reflect that in human affairs nothing is firm or stable; in this way, you will not be carried away by joy in prosperity, nor will you grieve too much when vexed by some misfortune. Appoint for yourself two times for speaking: one concerning things you know well, and the other concerning things about which it is necessary to speak. In these cases alone is speech better than silence; in others, silence is preferable. When good things happen to you, rejoice; when bad things happen, grieve moderately. In either state, however, learn to hide your feelings. For it would be absurd to hide your wealth within your house while walking about with your mind <note>meaning your internal emotions and thoughts</note> manifest to everyone. Avoid infamy more than danger; for it is fitting that a cruel end to life threatens the wicked, but disgrace threatens the upright as long as they live. Above all, try to live your life with security. But if it happens that you must face danger, seek safety from war without any mark of shame. For all are condemned to die by the law of the fates, but nature permits only the high-souled to die well. Do not wonder if I have said more things than are suited to your present age; for this fact was not hidden from me. But in this same little work, I wanted to both provide counsel for your present life and leave behind precepts for your future. You will easily learn the use of these things; however, you will find it difficult to find someone who faithfully advises you in such matters. Therefore, I thought nothing should be omitted from those things I saw would bring you utility, so that you would not have to seek from another what is missing, but could instead bring it forth from this work as if from a storehouse <note>original: "cella promptuaria" — a pantry or storage room for daily provisions</note>. Furthermore, I would give the greatest thanks to the immortal gods if the opinion I have formed of you does not deceive me. For we find many who rejoice in foods that are pleasant rather than healthy; in the same way, they cling to friends who sin with them rather than those who advise them well. However, I believe you have taken a different counsel, using this proof: that you do not shrink from the labor of other things. For it is consistent with reason that he who commands himself to do only the best things should embrace those who exhort others to virtue. It would be a great incentive for you to seek honest works if you recognized that the greatest and most solid

<column-break/>

pleasures are perceived from them. For in idleness and the love of satiety, sorrow is the constant companion of pleasures. But to exercise oneself in virtue and to prudently govern one's life produces pleasures that are always more sincere and more stable. In the former case, those who were first delighted soon after grieve; in the latter, after labors and hardships, we receive no small pleasures. In all affairs, we do not remember the beginning as much as we perceive the sense of the end. Indeed, many things involving life we do not do for the sake of the things themselves, but we labor for the sake of the outcomes. Consider further that it is permitted for the wicked to do anything indiscriminately, for they have immediately proposed such a way of life for themselves. But for those who profess to be honorable, it is necessary either to embrace virtue itself or certainly to have many critics. For all pursue with hatred not so much those who sin, as those who show themselves to be good while not differing from the base. And not without justice. For if we reprove those who lie in words alone, shall we not say that those who are wicked in their whole life are to be blamed? Deservedly, therefore, would we believe such men not only to commit a crime against themselves but also to be traitors to fortune. For she bestowed riches, nobility, and friends upon them; but these most ungrateful men made themselves unworthy of their present happiness. If it is permitted for a mortal nature to conjecture the minds of the gods, I think they have shown sufficiently and more than enough, even in those closest to them, how they behave toward good and bad men. For when Jupiter had fathered Hercules and Tantalus <note>Hercules was the hero of strength and virtue; Tantalus was the king who betrayed the gods' trust</note> (as the myths tell and all believe), he consecrated the former to immortality because of his virtue, but tortured the latter with the greatest punishments because of his wickedness. Using these examples, one may seek uprightness; and one should not only remain with what has been said by us, but also learn the best things from the poets and read through whatever useful things other wise men have said. For just as we see the bee lighting upon all blossoms, extracting what is useful from each, so it is necessary for those eager for learning to be inexperienced in nothing, but to collect useful things from everywhere. For hardly anyone will escape the errors of nature even with such great diligence.

# To the most kind and universally most learned Lord Gabriel Miro, most worthy professor of the art of Apollo <note>The "art of Apollo" refers to medicine, as Apollo was the Greek god of healing.</note>, most expert counselor and chief physician to the most serene Queen of the French: Symphorien Champier of Lyon, physician, sends many greetings.

<margin>
|| Hippocrates.
|| Pliny.
|| Jerome.
|| Luke.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C containing a floral motif with a central stem and three flower heads.</image-desc>When I more diligently revolve in my mind, my most excellent Gabriel, chief of physicians, the instability of time and the changing nature of all things, it seems to me that those ancient times—which they call the Golden Ages—were not praised by the most learned poets without reason. For in those times, nature is believed to have brought forth men studious of peace and all humanity; those who were especially noble did not give themselves over to shameful idleness, nor pant after damnable greed, nor waste their time (which Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was a Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> asserted was the most precious of possessions) in horrendous wars and the destruction of mortals. Instead, having cast down all the proud wealth and lofty honors of this world, they devoted themselves entirely to the investigation of truth—which *Cicero* <margin>Cicero</margin> attests is the proper characteristic of man—lest they spend their lives in silence like cattle, whom nature (as *Sallust* says) fashioned groveling and obedient to the belly. <note>original: "prona & ventri obedientia"</note> This is also read in the same author: how many mortals, devoted to the belly and sleep, unlearned and unrefined, have passed through life like travelers; but those intent on acquiring disciplines and sciences have sought the fame of noble deeds and good arts. By leaving behind for us the most excellent monuments of their lives, they testified that they once lived.

Who is so blind that he does not see most clearly how far the nobles of our age have degenerated from their way of living? (With very few exceptions). They lie prostrate under gluttony and luxury—indeed, every vice—detesting the sciences themselves and all arts along with those who cultivate them, and (what is most especially to be grieved) holding them in mockery; they only praise as much of them as they happen to need.

How is it that this science of ours (leaving aside others) is so worthy and so necessary for human use that it is undoubtedly believed that the best and greatest God revealed it to our ancestors for the safety of the human race? Hippocrates confirmed this in his letters to the people of Abdera, saying that medicine is a gift of the gods, and free. It was once valued most highly. Furthermore, as Pliny <margin>Pliny</margin> witnesses in the nineteenth book of his *Natural History*, it first dedicated its inventors to heaven. The Gentiles, moreover, would have it that the authors of this art were gods. Did they not pursue many most excellent physicians with divine honors? For they dedicated shrines to Chiron, Machaon, Podalirius, Hippocrates, and Hermagoras. Did not kings and princes and all the most noble men once profess this art?

But alas! We have been reduced to such a wretched condition of the times that everyone everywhere presumes to claim this art for themselves. The talkative old woman, the doting old man, the wordy sophist <note>A "sophist" here implies someone who uses clever but fallacious arguments.</note>—everyone presumes to handle it; they tear it apart; they teach it before they learn it. Others, weighing grand words with a knitted brow among the unskilled common folk and talkative little women, philosophize about medicine <gloss>Bibles</gloss> <note>The gloss "biblie" suggests they are quoting scripture or authoritative texts superficially.</note>. Others are not ashamed to learn from women what they should teach to men. And they do this not just with a certain ease of words, but rather with the audacity to explain to others what they themselves do not understand.

What is this rashness and presumption of spirit? Even farmers and masons, blacksmiths, woodcutters, wool-workers, fullers, and others who manufacture various furnishings and small works for the villa cannot be what they desire without a teacher. When I considered that this results in no small destruction for the human race, I felt that I must oppose and take counsel against such a harsh error. Therefore, I applied my mind to writing, and from several of the most approved interpreters of our profession, I have gathered a little book concerning "simples" <note>term: simples; natural, unmixed ingredients used as medicines, usually herbs.</note>; so that those panting to labor in the Apollonian art might have a localized and easier...

### **Medical Forests** <note>original: "Siluæ medicinales" — in the Renaissance, "Silva" (forest/woods) was a common literary term for a collection of miscellaneous notes or raw materials.</note> as a supplement to the

Lest anyone should mock us as being in-

**Lamb's meat** <note>original: "Agnina caro"</note> is moderately
hot and has an overflowing 
moisture; because of this, it 
is harmful to people of a 
moister temperament <note>The author uses the "humoral" system, where health depends on the balance of Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry qualities.</note>. It 
is suitable for those who are drier. The younger the animal is, 
the more easily it is digested, and the moister it is. And in

<column-break/>

other animals you will find the same: for the more youthful 
they are, the moister they are. However, **rams** (according 
to the testimony of **Isaac** <note>Isaac Judaeus (c. 832–932), a highly influential Jewish physician and philosopher whose works on diet and fevers were standard medical textbooks.</note>) remaining in their youth 
possess less moisture and stickiness because of the dryness 
of age dominating their temperament. Therefore, this meat 
is better than lamb and sheep, because if it is well digested 
it generates much good blood—especially if they are cas-
trated, because their heat and moisture are then balanced 
<note>original: "temperate"</note>. For this reason, they are of good flavor, 
unless they are decrepit with age, for then they are without 
doubt at their worst. Thus says Isaac.

**Almonds** <note>original: "Amygdala"</note> are moderately hot and 
nutritious in a beneficial way; they share in a thinning and 
cutting power. For this reason, they are said to be purifiers 
<note>original: "cathartica"</note> of the midriff <note>original: "precordiorum"</note> and the 
chest, though they are digested with difficulty. **Bitter 
almonds** are hotter than sweet ones; they are more thinning 
and cutting. They drive away obstructions <note>original: "oppilationes"</note> 
in the liver and spleen, and they break up stones in the 
kidneys and bladder. From almonds, a moderately hot oil 
is made, which is very profitable for the chest and lungs; 
it removes the blockages and obstructions of the liver. From 
bitter almonds, however, the oil is more effective for all 
things: it grinds down all stones, whether in the kidneys 
or the bladder, and brings forth the menses when used 
by women. According to the expert author **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasi" — Abu Bakr al-Razi (865–925), a Persian polymath and one of the most important figures in the history of medicine.</note>, 
sweet almonds are balanced in heat. Although they bring 
smoothness to the throat, they are heavy and remain in 
the stomach for a long time. However, they do not create 
obstructions themselves; rather, they open obstructions 
and soothe the burning of urine. Eaten with sugar, they 
increase the seed <note>i.e., sperm.</note>. Thus says Rhazes.

**Starch** <note>original: "Amylum"</note> is made from pure wheat 
sprinkled with water; it has the power of cooling and mod-
erately drying, and for this reason, it is suitable for colic 
<note>original: "torminibus"</note>. And as **Serapio** <note>Likely Serapio the Younger, a 12th or 13th-century author of a book on "simples."</note> says on the 
authority of **Galen**, that which is taken from starch cools 
and dries more than wheat. It is beneficial for humors 
flowing to the eye and for ulcers; when it is drunk, it cuts 
off blood coming from the chest and soothes the roughness 
of the throat.

**Dill** <note>original: "Anethum sive anetum"</note> is hot at the 
end of the third degree and dry at the beginning of the 
second <note>Medical substances were ranked in four degrees of intensity.</note>. It 
resolves, matures, and soothes pain; it also induces sleep. 
In the opinion of some, it harms the kidneys. As Rhazes 
maintains, it is unsuitable for the stomach and causes 
nausea; it increases the milk of the breast and softens 
the belly. According to Serapio, its property is to soothe 
hiccups and induce sleep, and the oil of dill is good 
for gas <note>original: "ventofitatibus"</note>.

<header>On the letter A.</header>

<note>This first section refers to Dill (Anethum), as indicated by the index on the preceding page.</note> It weakens the eyesight, especially if used in excess. It provokes urination, soothes <term>torsions</term> <note>Painful twisting or cramping of the bowels.</note> and bloating, and binds the belly. If it is cooked in oil, it dissolves <term>exituras</term> <note>Swellings or abscesses that are 'coming out' or coming to a head.</note> and ripens "cold" or "raw" <term>apostemes</term> <note>Inflammatory swellings or abscesses; in medieval medicine, "cold" meant they were caused by phlegm or melancholy rather than "hot" blood.</note>. When a woman sits in a decoction of dill, it helps with pains of the womb. When the seed of dill is burnt and made into a plaster over hemorrhoids, it removes them; when it is powdered over ulcers of the penis, it joins and heals them. It also heals old ulcers that are otherwise difficult to consolidate.

<margin>Serapion, chapter 252.</margin>
¶ **Anise** is hot and dry in the third degree. It is beneficial against old liver ailments caused by coldness. It is also good against the difficulties of gas which have the power of distraction caused by <term>pituita</term> <note>Phlegm, one of the four bodily humors.</note>. It has the power to remove gas from the belly and drives it out effectively; it also produces milk. ¶ Serapion, on the authority of Balem: The primary virtue of anise is that it heats and dries in the third degree. Secondly, it "resolves" <note>Breaks down or disperses morbid matter.</note>. Thirdly, it provokes urination, expels bloating of the belly, drives out windiness from the body, and soothes pains. It is suitable against poisons and binds the belly. It cuts off the white moisture flowing from the womb.

<margin>Isaac, in "On Particular Diets"</margin>
¶ **Asparagus** is the most nourishing of all vegetables. It induces urination and removes obstructions of the liver and kidneys. Asparagus is suitable for those with <term>colics</term> <note>Severe abdominal pains.</note> and kidney ailments caused by phlegm; it increases semen and is converted into blood more quickly than other vegetables. It brings forth the <term>menstrua</term> <note>Menstrual flow.</note> and is useful against tremors of the heart, except that it does not always agree with the stomach. For this reason, it is seasoned with <term>garum</term> <note>A fermented fish sauce popular since Roman times.</note> and oil. It should be used moderately cooked, not excessively.
¶ Isaac in "On Particular Diets": Asparagus is hot and moist in the first degree, whether it is the garden variety or the wild kind. The garden variety is more temperate than all other herbs and more nutritious; therefore, it increases sperm, agrees with the stomach, and provokes urination. The wild kind is hotter and drier; it opens obstructions of the liver and kidneys, provokes urination, and is effective for those with <term>icterus</term> <note>Jaundice, a yellowing of the skin and eyes.</note>. Eaten boiled, it moistens the belly.

¶ **Garlic** heats and dries in the fourth degree <note>The highest and most intense level of a quality in medieval pharmacology.</note>. When chewed, it helps with bloating and thirst; it draws apart and scatters thick and sticky humors. It possesses something of a medicinal quality and a "bad humor," which is removed when it is boiled in water. Frequent use is particularly for those with "hot" <term>complexions</term> <note>The specific balance of humors in an individual's body.</note>; however, for those with cold complexions, it often brings health. It offends the eyes, head, lungs, and kidneys.

<column-break/>

It destroys <term>lubricous</term> <note>Slippery or parasitic worms.</note> things and scatters gas. It is a remedy against nearly all snake bites, acting much like a <term>thiriaca</term> <note>Theriac, a famous "universal" herbal antidote against poison and disease.</note>. Because of this, our Galen says that garlic is the "peasant's theriac." Snakes flee from it as if it were most hostile to them. Thus, they say that those who have eaten garlic will be less harmed if a venomous creature strikes them. <margin>Dioscorides the Greek</margin> ¶ Dioscorides says: The virtue of garlic is hot; it soothes bloating of the belly and dries the stomach. It can ulcerate the skin, and when eaten, it expels <term>ascarides</term> <note>Intestinal roundworms.</note> and provokes urination. When garlic is eaten raw, roasted, or otherwise cooked, it clears the voice and soothes an old cough. It kills lice and nits when eaten regularly with food, and it benefits "moist eyes." <margin>Rufus</margin> ¶ Rufus: Garlic heats and cuts thick, viscous humors, but it harms the vision because it burns the tunics <note>The layers or membranes.</note> of the eyes and their moisture, disturbing the sight. It also harms the ears, liver, lungs, and kidneys, and generates windiness.

¶ Of **waters**, there are five types: rain, spring, well, river, and marsh. The lightest of these is rain water, whether it be from a well or a cistern, because it is easily transformed. It is suitable against fevers, <term>choleras</term> <note>Not necessarily the modern disease, but an excess of the "choleric" or yellow bile humor.</note>, and those with jaundice. It is easily excreted and poured out; if it lingers in the body, it makes the passages sluggish and yields with difficulty, producing "distillations" which the Greeks call <term>catharros</term> <note>Catarrh, or excessive mucus/drainage.</note>, especially if drunk cold. Therefore, it is more safely drunk with sugar. For hot complexions, burning fevers, <term>causonides</term> <note>A type of acute, high-burning fever.</note>, and tertian fevers, it is very useful. Light water should not be judged by its weight, but by how quickly it heats up and cools down, showing it is very dry and pure. If you do not have pure water, it should be pre-boiled and then drunk once cooled. For those with hot imbalances, nothing is as useful as water. <margin>Rhazes, Book 2 of Almansor, chapter 4.</margin> ¶ Rhazes: Natural water preserves the humors in the body and makes food penetrate by thinning it. By suppressing heat, it is more suitable than wine for those who are overheated or have a hot complexion. Furthermore, water that has a bad taste or smell is bad and should not be drunk. Turbid water generates obstructions in the liver and stones in the kidneys. Salty water first loosens the belly, but afterward constricts it and dries out the body; it generates <term>scabies</term> <note>A term for various itchy skin eruptions.</note> and <term>regadias</term> <note>Fissures or cracks in the skin.</note>. Standing and putrid water enlarges the spleen, corrupts the complexion, and generates fevers. Boiled water, until its substance is made finer, is less bloating and descends more quickly. Rain water is bad for those who quickly fall into fevers, though it is...

<margin>Galen</margin>
For as it is found in Galen, in the third book of *On the Regimen of Acute Diseases*, commentary 48, where he says: "Water finds no use except when it is drunk in acute diseases," this should be understood as referring to good water that has no defect. And there he generalizes that the speech of physicians praising or blaming any thing is understood to refer to the best examples of whatever things they are testing. Avicenna feels the same in the second book of the *Canon*, chapter two.

Goose meat is excessive and difficult to <term>concoct</term> <note>To digest or process within the body; in medieval medicine, digestion was viewed as a "cooking" process.</note>; and among all the farmyard meats, it is more humid and has thicker parts, so that it is ranked among the older meats and that of the ostrich. However, the wings are better digested and are not excessive. This fat, when dripped into the ears, helps and relieves earaches and assists with cracked lips. Some say that the testicles of geese aid in conceiving offspring after childbirth; the tongue is truly beneficial for <term>strangury</term> <note>A condition characterized by slow and painful urination.</note>. <margin>Isaac in *Particular Diets*, chapter on birds.</margin> Isaac says: Goose meat is more humid than others. Duck, gosling, and similar birds are harmful to the stomach; for they generate <unclear>bad humors</unclear> and putrefy food because of their excessive humidity.

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
<margin>Isaac, chapter on vinegar.</margin>
Vinegar is of a "cutting" essence and cold with a certain heat, though coldness dominates; it consists of thin parts and is a convenient medicine for drying; it is ranked in the third degree <note>Medieval medicine graded the intensity of a quality (hot, cold, wet, dry) from the first to the fourth degree.</note> when it is strong. Avicenna says: Vinegar is composed of heat and cold; both substances are subtle, but the cold is more dominant, and that in which there is sourness is hotter. Isaac says: Vinegar cools in the first degree and dries in the third. Hence, because of the weakness of its coldness, it penetrates the body quickly even to remote places. The cause of its subtlety is the heat it acquired from boiling. It is dissolving and thinning; when heated and given as a drink, it helps those having <term>orthopnea</term> <note>Difficulty breathing except when standing or sitting upright.</note>. It dissolves milk and blood

<column-break/>

clotted in the stomach. It is also effective against poison and things that bring death, such as opium, henbane, euphorbium, and the like. It helps those with a long-lasting cough; however, it harms a new cough, and especially those agitated by a dry one. If it is cooked with foods or eaten with something, it is a comfort to the stomach; it excites and increases the <term>appetitive virtue</term> <note>The body's natural power or "virtue" that creates the desire for food.</note> and resists bad humors in the stomach. <margin>Serapion</margin> Serapion says: In acute illnesses, vinegar is good for <term>choleric</term> people <note>Those with an excess of yellow bile, considered "hot and dry" in temperament.</note> and is not harmful to <term>melancholic</term> people <note>Those with an excess of black bile, considered "cold and dry."</note>; but it is harmful to women because it hurts their wombs. <margin>Galen</margin> Galen says: The substance of vinegar is composed of heat and cold, except that the coldness is greater in it than the heat. And it dries in the second degree, specifically near the end of it when it is processed. And he said of vinegar that it is harmful to the nerves, and experience testifies to this.

<margin>Galen</margin>
Oat is an herb whose leaves are similar to the leaves of wheat, except that they are softer; at the top of its stalk is a seed clothed in two or three tunics, from which come forth <term>awns</term> <note>The hair-like bristles on the grain.</note> similar to hairs in their fineness. Galen says: Its flavor is slightly sharp. Its primary virtue is that it resolves hard <term>apostemes</term> <note>Inflammatory swellings or abscesses.</note> and is useful for fistulas that form near the eyes, which are recognized by their itchiness. <margin>Dioscorides</margin> Dioscorides says: When an oat plaster is made with meal, it cures the itch and resolves hard apostemes; a juice is also expressed from it, which is mixed with meal, dried, and set aside.

Southernwood is hot and dry in the third degree; it also has the power of "cutting" and dispersing after a moderate application; it is quite bitter to the taste. Such a juice has an earthy essence. It shows a truly exuberant heat; it is made thin and therefore it heats and dries not inconveniently. Therefore, the herb cooked with its leaves and flowers in oil [is used] for conditions of returning fevers; one will feel less cold if applied before the <term>rigor</term> <note>The shivering or shaking fit that precedes a fever.</note> arrives. Its decoction, when drunk, also kills worms, and even more so when administered as a <term>clyster</term> <note>An enema; a liquid injected into the rectum for medicinal purposes.</note> than wormwood. Southernwood has a little sharpness; for that reason, it is also bad for the stomach. There are indeed two species of southernwood, male and female. Its fruit, crushed and drunk with water, helps with fractures, <term>convulsions</term> <note>The original term "vulsionibus" refers to tearing or twitching of the muscles.</note>, <term>dysuria</term> <note>Painful or difficult urination.</note>, and lethal medicines <note>Poisons.</note>; drunk with wine, it helps with <term>alopecia</term> <note>Patchy hair loss.</note>. Southernwood spread out drives away serpents; drunk with wine, it helps those bitten. It helps with swellings of the eyes when cooked with quince or with bread...

Hence, those metals that contain more mercury melt more quickly, such as lead and tin; by contrast, bronze and iron do not. ¶ Rhazes: Silver is cold and benefits the trembling of the heart.

...put by them and for the stomach. The dose is from half an <term>aureus</term> <note>A weight unit originally based on the Roman gold coin, roughly equivalent to 4.5 grams.</note> up to two drachms. And in infusions, from one aureus up to three drachms.
<margin>Rhazes, Book 8 of the *Almansor*, chapter 54.</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** From whom it is to be taken in doses of one to two aurei.

If anyone suffering in the anus wishes to take it—unless they have a "hot" <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four humors: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>—they should mix it with <term>bdellium</term> <note>A semi-transparent oleo-gum resin extracted from trees in the genus Commiphora.</note>. ¶ **Wormwood** <note>original: Absinthium</note> is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. Its juice is a much hotter herb, sharing in bitterness; it is notably astringent, therefore it cleanses, strengthens, and dries. For this reason, it also drives <term>bilious humors</term> <note>Associated with yellow bile and a fiery, choleric temperament.</note> out through the lower parts of the belly and drains them through the urine. Certainly, more so in the veins, it purges whatever is bilious through the urine; because of this, it does not help with <term>phlegm</term> <note>A cold, moist humor associated with lethargy.</note> trapped in the belly. This is also true if it is in the chest or the lungs. For its astringent power is stronger than its bitterness, because it possesses a certain sharpness more than is moderate. It wards off a hangover from excessive drinking and is suitable against bloating and pains of the belly and stomach when drunk with <term>hartwort</term> <note>original: seselis</note> or <term>Celtic nard</term> <note>A fragrant plant used in ancient and medieval perfumes and medicines.</note>. It cures <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: arquatestes</note> and sharpens the appetite. Its sprinkling or decoction, taken daily in the amount of three <term>cyathi</term> <note>A small measure, roughly 45ml.</note> with vinegar, helps against suffocation caused by poisonous mushrooms.
<margin>Rhazes, Book 3 of the *Almansor*, chapter 127.</margin>
<margin>Mesue.</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Wormwood is hot and dry; by making the stomach robust, it opens blockages of the liver and will assist with long-lasting fevers.
¶ **Mesue.** It is hot in the first degree and dry in the second; its juice and its flower are hotter.

There is no apparent harm in it. However, its juice harms the stomach because of its <term>saltiness</term> <note>original: bauracitatem; refers to a quality like borax or nitre.</note>. It is a weak laxative. By its purging action, it draws out <term>choler</term> <note>Yellow bile.</note> from the stomach, intestines, and liver. Its operation extends to the veins, and it cleanses them of choleric and watery humors, and sometimes draws them out by way of the urine.
<margin>Avenzoar</margin>
¶ And **Avenzoar** said: By its purging action, it also draws out phlegm. Others have said its effect on phlegm is not significant enough to be cared about. The dose of its decoction or infusion for a drink is from five to eight ounces, and its powder from three to four drachms, and its juice from three to four drachms.

¶ **Agaric** <note>original: Agaricum; a type of mushroom used in medicine, often Larch agaric.</note> has the power of heating, dispersing, and cutting through thick humors. It thoroughly purges

<column-break/>

the intestines and removes blockages; because of this, it heals the "royal disease" which we also call <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: arquatum and by the Greek word ictericum.</note>. It assists with pains of the liver, as well as with common illnesses. It wards off and calms the shivers of fevers that arise from thick and sticky humors. It is also beneficial for those who have suffered from wild beasts or cold environments. There is altogether a purging power in it.
<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Since Agaric is hot, it opens blockages of the liver. It also offers a remedy for asthma and epilepsy, as well as for old fevers. Furthermore, it expels thick humors from the head. The same author says in the *Book of Divisions*, chapter 62: Agaric draws out <term>melancholy</term> <note>Black bile, associated with sadness and cold/dry qualities.</note> and thick phlegm. Its dose is three drachms, and it is slow to act as a laxative.
<margin>Mesue.</margin>
¶ **Mesue.** Regarding the Agaric which the wise men have praised, and specifically the "female" kind: it has five good properties. Specifically, it should be white, smooth, easily broken, porous, and very light. It should appear sweet at first taste, followed by bitterness and astringency. It is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. Its operation is strengthened if a third part of <term>rock salt</term> <note>original: sal gemme</note> is added to it, or according to Galen, ginger. By its purging action, it draws out thick phlegm and red choler.
<margin>Galen.</margin>

<margin>Democritus.</margin>

It is a wonderful medicine for chronic <term>headache</term> <note>original: sodam; a medieval term for a splitting headache.</note>, epilepsy, and especially vertigo. It may be preserved for four years.

¶ **Aristolochia** <note>original: Aristoloche; also known as Birthwort.</note>, or *aristologia*, or *aristolochia*: the root of this plant offers immediate remedies; it is bitter and somewhat sharp. However, the round variety <note>Aristolochia rotunda</note> is of far finer parts <note>Referring to the "subtlety" or thinness of its medicinal essence.</note>, and is more effective in all things: and accordingly, for those in whom it is necessary to thin a thick humor, the round kind is needed. Because of this, it cures blockages and thickness, or the pain of raw spirits <note>In medieval medicine, "spirits" were vital vapors that moved through the body.</note>, and heals decay; it purges raging ulcers, and brightens the teeth and clears scars in the eyes. # Concerning the Letter B.

<margin>Galen, Book 6 of *Simple Medicines*</margin>
...ment, it is cold and dry, established in the first degree <note>Medieval medicine classified substances into four "degrees" of intensity regarding the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>, though he cites another opinion. ¶ Galen says: **Blite** <note>original: Bletum; a leafy green similar to spinach or beet.</note> is an edible vegetable, cold and moist in the second degree.

<margin>Beet. Isaac.</margin>
¶ **Beet**. ¶ Isaac says: *Cicla* <note>original: Cicla; refers to Chard or Sicilian Beet.</note>, which the common people call **Beet**, is hot and dry in the first degree; it provides poor nourishment to the stomach because of its certain sharpness and its great amount of moisture. However, if it is cooked in water and seasoned with vinegar, meat, and "omphacine" oil <note>Oil made from unripe olives.</note> or almond oil, it becomes easy to digest. It nourishes little, but it moistens the belly and opens blockages of the liver, 

<margin>Hippocrates. Rhazes.</margin>
especially if it is of the astringent kind. ¶ Hippocrates says: A decoction of beet is laxative, but the body of the plant itself causes constipation. ¶ Rhazes says: Chard is hot; being also bad for the stomach, it makes the belly flow and cuts through phlegm <note>To "cut" phlegm means to break up thick, sticky humors so they can be expelled.</note>.

¶ **Balsam** heats and dries in the second degree. It is also composed of "fine parts" <note>Substances with "fine parts" were thought to be more subtle and able to penetrate deep into the body's channels.</note>. <margin>Galen.</margin>

<margin>Rhazes, *To Almansor*, Book 3, Chapter 22</margin>
¶ Rhazes says: Balsam is vehemently hot; it even breaks stones <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note> and, when used as a pessary, it is effective for aiding conception.

¶ **Bugloss** <note>original: Buglossum; literally "ox-tongue," likely *Anchusa officinalis* or *Borago officinalis*.</note> is moist and hot in the first degree; when put into wine, it serves to temper it. It is suitable for those coughing due to roughness of the throat when cooked in mead <note>original: mulso; a mixture of water and honey.</note>. They say it is suitable for tertian fevers <note>A fever that spikes every third day, often associated with malaria.</note>. Some say that the herb which has three stalks, if crushed with its roots and seeds and drunk, cures these; while for quartan fevers, they use the one that rises with four stalks.

Rhazes says a decoction of it in wine is useful for abscesses,

<margin>Bryony or White Vine. Serapion.</margin>
¶ **Bryony**, according to Galen, moderately provokes urine. The root is cleansing and drying and of fine parts; it has a moderately heating virtue, because of which it thins the spleen. Applied externally with figs, it heals scabies and leprosy. ¶ Serapion, on the authority of Rhazes, says its virtue is that it heats moderately, cleanses, thins, and dissolves hardness of the spleen when a plaster made from it and figs is applied; it also cures scabies and diseases where the skin is raised. It removes "cloth" <note>original: pannum; refers to skin discolorations or melasma.</note>, black marks, skin eruptions, and the scars of ulcers. One <term>drachm</term> <note>A unit of weight, about 3.9 grams.</note> of it is drunk for epilepsy; and it is suitable for apoplexy <note>A stroke or sudden loss of consciousness.</note> when so administered, and for blockages; it kills the fetus <note>An abortifacient warning.</note>. Its root mixed with bitter vetch and fenu-

<column-break/>

-greek, when the skin is washed with them, purifies and cleanses it.

<margin>Bdellium. Rhazes. Dioscorides. Galen.</margin>
¶ **Bdellium** <note>A semi-transparent oleo-gum resin, similar to myrrh.</note> which is called Scythian is darker and resinous, and is quite effective at softening; the other is Arabian, which is clearer and dries more than it softens. There are some who use the Arabian kind for inflammations, eruptions of "blucher" worms <note>Possibly a reference to parasitic skin infections.</note>, and the bites of water-snakes, moistening it with foam to make a plaster. The Arabian kind is said to grind down stones in the kidneys when drunk, and to move the urine, and it treats the movement of undigested flatulence. ¶ Rhazes says: Jewish bdellium is hot; dissolving hard abscesses, it is proven useful for hemorrhoids; however, the bdellium from Mecca is cold and dry and binds the belly <note>Causes constipation.</note>. ¶ Dioscorides says: It is the gum of a tree that grows in the lands of the Arabs. Some of it is found to be filthy, brought from India; and some is brought from the region called *Batonainis*, resembling pine resin. ¶ Galen says: There are two species of bdellium, Scythian and Arabian; the Scythian is softer, the Arabian drier. The primary virtue of bdellium is heating and drying; the second is softening and dissolving. The third dissolves abscesses that form in the windpipe, and the swelling that occurs in intestinal ruptures <note>Hernias.</note> when it is dissolved with the saliva of a fasting man until it becomes like an ointment. It breaks stones in the kidneys when taken in a drink, provokes urine, expels thick windiness, dissolves hard raw abscesses, and cures pains of the ribs and weariness of the nerves. The dose of it alone is from 1 drachm to 2 drachms. Others say from half a drachm to one; it increases the power of coitus and improves it; it resolves clotted blood.

¶ **Bromus**, in Latin "Oats," is a stalk similar to the stalks and leaves of grain; its seed is as suitable for poultices as barley; a drink made from it stops the belly <note>Treats diarrhea.</note>. The juice in a gruel is suitable for coughs; it is moderately cold in temperament and has a certain tartness, and therefore it stops the flow of the belly. Enough has been said of this in the chapter on Oats.

<margin>Isaac.</margin>
¶ **Borage** is an edible vegetable, hot and moist in temperament, established in the first degree. ¶ Isaac says: It has the property of generating joy if it is given in wine to drink; it comforts the heart. The ancients mixed it into medicines effective for "cardiac passions" <note>Heart conditions or palpitations.</note>. Cooked with water, honey, and sugar and given as a drink, it excellently purges and cleanses the channels of the lungs and the throat.

¶ **Betony** heats at the first distance when chewed; its flavor is sharp and bitter.

# Concerning the Letter B.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ Galen says: Its first power heats in the first degree; its second power "cuts" <note>To "cut" (original: *incidit*) means to break down thick, sticky humors so they can be expelled from the body.</note> and cleanses; its third power breaks down thick humors, dissolves kidney stones, and purifies. It cleanses the lungs and liver and provokes the menstrual flow. It is helpful for epilepsy and heals strains of the nerves and muscles. When applied to the bite of a venomous or treacherous animal, it is beneficial; when taken as a drink, it helps with sciatica and sour belching.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ Dioscorides says: *Dromelle* <note>original: *dromelle*; a mixture of honey and water, similar to mead.</note> causes one to vomit up phlegm. Three or four drams of its leaves given with a *cotula* <note>A Roman unit of liquid measure, approximately half a pint.</note> of wine is used for venomous bites. Similarly, when a plaster made of its leaves is applied to a bite, it is effective. When one dram of the leaves is drunk with wine, it counteracts the malice of deadly medicines; if someone drinks this first and later consumes something containing poison, it will not harm them at all. It also provokes urine and loosens the belly. When taken as a drink with water, it cures those with epilepsy or apoplexy <note>A sudden loss of consciousness, often associated with a stroke.</note> and pains of the liver. When one dram is drunk with vinegar and honey, it cures pain of the spleen. When taken after a meal in the amount of a single bean mixed with clarified honey, it aids digestion. It is also given as a drink with wine and water to those who spit blood from the chest. When one dram is given with wine, it provokes the menstrual flow; when given with honey, it benefits old lung ulcers and pus in the chest. It is given to those with jaundice, and two drams are given with warm water for colic and intestinal pain. It is also helpful for head colds, catarrh, and difficult labor. If a woman does not have a fever, it should be given with wine and water. It draws out the poison from the bite of a rabid dog if it is left tied over the site of the bite.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Barberry** <note>original: *Berberis*</note> is a wasting bramble.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ Dioscorides says: It is a tree similar to wild pear trees, except that it is smaller. ¶ Galen says: Its power is styptic <note>A substance that shrinks or constricts body tissue to stop bleeding.</note>. Its second power is one that prevents and holds back any illness caused by "flux" <note>Any excessive flow of fluid from the body, such as diarrhea or hemorrhaging.</note> when it is eaten or drunk.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ Dioscorides says: When its fruit is drunk or eaten, it cuts off chronic flux and old moisture flowing from the womb. Its root, when made into a plaster and crushed, extracts arrows that are fixed in the flesh. It is cold and dry in the second degree; it "cuts" and prevents hot thirst, and strengthens the stomach and liver.

<margin>Platearius</margin>
¶ **Bistort** <note>original: *Bistorta*; also known as snakeweed.</note> is cold and dry in the third degree. Although an excess is not noted by authors, it has the power of consolidating, constricting, and strengthening conception. ¶ Platearius says: For dysentery, it should be given with plantain juice. To restrain and stop the menstrual flow, a warm soak made from rainwater

<column-break/>

and a decoction of its powder should be used. To aid conception, an electuary <note>A medicinal paste made of powder mixed with honey or syrup.</note> should be made from a half-pound of bistort powder and the same quantity of aromatic spices; this strengthens the retentive power of the womb. It is a twisted herb, and its root is similar to galangal, but it lacks the sharpness. Against vomiting caused by the heat of yellow bile, its powder should be mixed with egg white, cooked upon a hot roof-tile, and given to the patient.

<margin>Mesue. Rhazes.</margin>
¶ **Belleric Myrobalans** <note>original: *Bellerici*; the fruit of *Terminalia bellirica*, a staple of Ayurvedic medicine.</note> are among the "blessed medicines." ¶ Mesue says: They are cold in the first degree and dry in the second. ¶ Rhazes says: In their nature, they are close to the nature of Emblic myrobalans. He also says: Emblic myrobalans are cold and dry; they make the stomach robust and strengthen the roots of the hair.

<margin>Serapio. Rhazes.</margin>
¶ **Behen** <note>original: *Beben*; likely referring to *Centaurea behen* (White Behen) and *Salvia haematodes* (Red Behen).</note>. ¶ Serapio says: There are two species, namely the red and the white. Both are the size of a small parsnip root and are brought from Armenia. Its odor is good, and there is a certain stickiness in them. Both species are hot and moist, and they cause an increase in sperm. ¶ Rhazes says: Red behen is hot and incites the desire for sexual intercourse.

<margin>Isaac.</margin>
¶ **Wild Carrot** <note>original: *Baucia*; often used for parsnips or wild carrots in this period.</note>. ¶ Isaac says: It is hot in the middle of the second degree and moist in the middle of the first. There is both a domestic and a wild variety. It provides heavy nourishment; it is hard and nourishes less than a turnip. It has a certain sharpness, which makes it thinning and a producer of "diaphoresis" <note>The process of sweating.</note>. Therefore, it provokes urine and the menses. It also has a bit of "inflammation" <note>In this context, it refers to a stimulating heat that increases libido.</note>, which makes it helpful for sexual intercourse. If one becomes accustomed to it, it generates "unpraiseworthy blood" <note>Blood that is out of balance or contains bad humors.</note>; therefore, to temper it, it must be boiled twice. After the water is thrown out, it should be cooked a third time with lettuce, leek, and onion, and seasoned with "omphacine" oil <note>Oil made from unripe olives.</note>, vinegar, pepper, and caraway.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ Galen says: The domestic variety is "subtle" <note>Meaning it is composed of fine parts that can easily penetrate the body.</note>. Its first power is heating, its second is thinning, and its third excites sexual intercourse. But the wild variety is even subtler. Its first power is hot, its second is cleansing and does not cause bloating, and its third provokes urine and the menses.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ Dioscorides says: When a woman drinks the seed of the wild variety or uses it as a "nascale" <note>A medicinal pessary or suppository.</note>, it provokes the menses. When drunk, it helps with "strangury" <note>A condition where one can only pass urine drop by drop with pain.</note>, sterility, pleurisy, and venomous bites. Its seed, when drunk, aids in impregnation. The domestic variety is more suitable for food; it is useful for the same things as the wild kind, though its effect is weaker. Some people call both varieties "parsnip."

<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ Rhazes says: *Baucie* are hot and cause bloating; they are hard to digest, give sharpness to the sperm, and also expel urine.
