<margin>Isaac</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative large initial 'C' filled with intricate, swirling leaf and vine patterns.</image-desc>
**C**hestnuts are the best of the "sheep-acorns" <note>original: *ovium glandium*; a folk term for chestnuts.</note>. Among wild fruits, they provide suitable nourishment for the body, but they bring pain to the head—much more so than almost any other fruit. ¶ Isaac says they are hot in the first degree and dry in the second <note>Medieval medicine classified all things by their "complexion"—levels of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>.

¶ The Quince takes its name from Cydonia in Crete; our people call them *cotonea*. They are cold in the first degree and dry in the second. They contract and strengthen tissues. They fortify the stomach and bind the bowels; if taken before a meal, they provoke urine. If eaten in great abundance, they are difficult to digest; the sweet ones are less astringent <note>A substance that shrinks or constricts body tissues.</note>, while the acidic ones are better at stopping vomiting. If taken after a meal, they loosen the bowels. When eaten while drinking wine, they prevent the vapors of the wine from rising to the head. Some people claim that if a woman uses quinces frequently while pregnant, her child will be highly ingenious but wicked; however, this is considered false by our theologians. A preserve <note>original: *ra atuz* (likely *rhodatum* or a similar conserve)</note> made from quinces strengthens the stomach and liver.

<margin>
Psellus the
physician
on the
power of
theology
</margin>
¶ Psellus, in the book he wrote to Constantine, says: Quinces are very styptic <note>Highly astringent; used to stop bleeding or secretions.</note>. If one preserves them by cooking them with honey or sugar, they strengthen the stomach, and in cases of dysentery, they help by suppressing yellow bile and cheering the heart.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Rhazes,
Book 3,
Chapter 20.
</margin>
¶ Rhazes says: Sweet and sour quinces make the stomach robust, but the sour ones are stronger for this purpose; moreover, they excite the appetite. Their specific property is to bind the belly. However, if they are eaten after a meal, they cause the stool to descend quickly and expel it from the belly. If eaten before a meal, they prevent all of that. Those that taste more acidic are stronger at constricting the belly.

¶ The Cherry: some call it *cerasum*, others use the masculine *cerasus*. Properly speaking, "sweet cherries and autumn plums" come from the town of Cerasus in Pontus <note>A region on the southern coast of the Black Sea, modern-day Turkey.</note>. <insert>Serapion.</insert> ¶ Serapion says: Sweet cherries descend from the stomach quickly and provide little benefit to it. The sour ones, however, dry out phlegm and the "superfluities" of the stomach more than the sweet ones do.

¶ The Citron: its peels are hot in the first degree and dry at the end of the second. The flesh is hot in the first and moist in the second; the acid within them is cold and dry in the third degree; the seed is hot and dry in the second. The flesh is difficult to digest and generates thick phlegm; for this reason, it ought to be eaten with honey or sugar. The peel aids the digestion of food and works against the melancholic humor <note>The humor associated with sadness and "black bile."</note> and depression; it is beneficial to the stomach when used in moderation. For it is difficult to digest if taken immoderately. When preserved with honey or sugar, it is called "Diacitron"; it warms the belly, dries up its moisture, and digests food that would be hard to digest if unpreserved. Citron seed is useful against all poisons; it is especially effective against the venomous bites of scorpions, whether drunk or applied as a poultice. It wards off the plague and provokes the menstrual flow. Their acid greatly expels yellow bile. Some relate a marvelous thing: that if hot bread is placed inside citrons, it immediately wastes away. They also claim that if anyone uses them at night, it causes the eyes to become crossed and the vision distorted.

<margin>Avicenna</margin>
¶ Avicenna says: The peel is hot in nature in the first degree and dry at the end of the second. Its flesh is hot in the first and moist in the second. Some, however, have said it is cold and moist in the second—its coldness is greater, and its acidity is cold and dry in the third—and its seed is hot in the first and dry in the second. Its pulp is cold and moist.

¶ The Caper is hot and dry in the second degree. It consists of various different qualities: from a bitterness that cleanses, purges, and disperses, and from a sharp heat...

# Concerning the letter C.

...by which it heats, dissolves, thins, and sharpens by the power with which it compels and binds: and for this reason, it is beneficial for a hardened spleen—as much as anything else—whether it is eaten or applied as a poultice with vinegar or oxymel <note>A medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar.</note>. It also stimulates menstruation and is useful for toothaches when boiled with wine and vinegar. Its juice is even more potent, though the stalk and leaves are weaker; nonetheless, they soften the hardness of scrofula <note>Swelling of the lymph nodes, often associated with tuberculosis.</note>. The juice of this plant kills worms that have bred in the ears.
¶ But with vinegar, it removes obstructions of the liver and spleen and clears blockages. It helps the spleen especially through its specific properties; it is also beneficial for those with sciatica, though it harms the kidneys and bladder.

<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Capers** preserved in brine are hot and dry; being bad for the stomach, they induce thirst and cause the body to grow thin. That which is preserved in salt is vehemently hot. It causes headaches, though it provides aid to a stomach filled with many humors <note>The four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that medieval medicine believed governed health.</note> and for those whose digestion is very inconsistent. Capers preserved with vinegar are less hot than those placed in brine; they are also suitable for blockages of the liver and spleen.

<margin>
Rhazes
Book 2
Chapter 19.
Galen.
</margin>
¶ **Onions** are of a heating temperament in the fourth degree <note>The highest and most intense level of heat in medieval pharmacology.</note>; their essence consists of thick parts. Thus, when applied, they break open hemorrhoids; rubbed on with vinegar and oil, they wipe away vitiligo <note>Skin patches characterized by loss of pigment.</note>. When rubbed on the skin, they immediately rouse hair growth in cases of alopecia <note>Hair loss or baldness.</note>. When eaten, they heat the body and thin the humors with their sharpness, yet they also thin thick and sticky humors within the body. They induce wind in the belly due to the thickness of their substance, and they generate blood. ¶ Rhazes says: Onions preserved in vinegar neither heat nor cool, nor do they cause thirst, but they help the appetite. ¶ Galen considers them contrary to choleric people <note>Those with an excess of yellow bile, considered hot and dry.</note> but useful for phlegmatic ones. ¶ Galen, in book 7 of *On Simple Medicines*, in the chapter on onions: The onion is a heating substance of the fourth degree, and its substance consists of coarse parts.

¶ **Venison** <note>original: *Ceruina caro*; deer meat.</note> produces bad juice and is difficult to digest; it generates black bile. ¶ One must be careful when they eat serpents and vipers, for then—as nature teaches—the deer endure a great thirst and burn from it; at that time, the meat becomes poisonous. Therefore, it is safer to eat in winter, when it is also more easily digested, though even then it generates thick humor and obstructs the liver and spleen. It is said that if eaten continually and immoderately, it causes tremors in the body. Deer marrow and fat, when applied, soften hard cancers. Their horns are cold and dry; it is said that serpents are driven away by the smoke of burning them. They are effective against 

<column-break/>

strangury <note>Difficulty or pain in urinating.</note>, obstructions, and intestinal worms, though the lungs may be harmed by the smoke. Dried and powdered deer blood is effective against lethal bites, and drunk with wine, it helps against the bite of a viper.

¶ **Cinnamon** is of the third degree of heating and drying (or at least the second); it consists of very fine parts. Nothing dries so much while heating equally. It comforts the stomach and helps against coughs caused by moisture; it heats the belly and the liver. It dries out humors of the head and other parts. The best variety is said to be what is called "Mosul" from the city of Mosul. Indeed, there are seven species of cinnamon, which take their names from the places where they are produced; it would be superfluous to list them all. Truly, all species are useful to the stomach and easily digest food; they thin the phlegm, provoke urine, and remove blockages. They stimulate menstruation and expel the embryo <note>Used here as an abortifacient.</note> when drunk with myrrh. Applied to the anus, they dissolve virulent matter and poisonous bites; smeared on with honey, they cleanse vitiligo. They are also useful against "water between the skin" <note>Edema or dropsy.</note> and coldness of the kidneys; for this reason, those of a cold and moist complexion should mix cinnamon into the foods they eat. However, it harms the bladder. ¶ Rhazes says: Cinnamon is hot and dry; by strengthening the stomach and liver, it aids digestion and expels wind.

¶ **Cumin** is hot and dry in the third degree. There are some who say the second. It provokes urine and disperses gas, especially in the stomach. Drinking it brings on paleness; thus Persius says: "the seeds of pale cumin," <note>original: *pallentis grana cumini*.</note> and Horace says: "they would drink bloodless cumin." <note>original: *biberent exangue cuminum*; referring to the belief that cumin makes the skin pale.</note> ¶ Rhazes says: Cumin is hot and dry; providing help to digestion, it dissolves bloating, though less so than pepper. Drunk with wine, it is a remedy against poisons and virulent bites.

¶ **Coriander**, according to some, is cold in the first degree and dry in the third. There are those who say it is hot. It confirms and strengthens the stomach, keeping food in the stomach until it is digested. Toasted over a fire, it binds the belly <note>Acts as an anti-diarrheal.</note> and is useful against inflammations. For those of hot complexions, it stops the flow of blood whether drunk or crushed and applied. Drunk with wine, it excludes intestinal worms. Taken immoderately, it produces madness. Its juice, when drunk, is a toxin and kills; for those drinking it become mute and insane.
<margin>
Aver-
roes.
</margin>
Averroes, in book 5 of the *Colliget*: Coriander is hot in the first degree and composed of diverse substances.

# Concerning the letter C.

<margin>Isaac.</margin>
¶ **Isaac.** Coriander possesses both bitterness and astringency; for this reason, Hippocrates said it possesses heat because of its bitterness, and he said it is styptic <note>A substance that shrinks or constricts body tissue to stop bleeding.</note> because of its astringency. But Dioscorides maintains that it is cold; he also said that it dissolves scrofula <note>Swelling of the lymph nodes, often in the neck.</note>, which Galen denied. Galen says it is impossible for scrofula to be dissolved by coldness because scrofula are hard and thick tumors. He further said: I am unable to understand the intention of Dioscorides when he says coriander is cold, since the flavor of coriander <margin>Rhazes, Book 3, chapter 18.</margin> is bitter. ¶ **Rhazes.** Coriander is cold and dry; its nature is such that it causes what should nourish the stomach to remain there longer until its digestion is completed. Therefore, it is necessary that not too much of it be put into foods of a coarse nature. <margin>Platearius.</margin> ¶ **Platearius.** Coriander is hot and dry in the second degree <note>Medieval medicine ranked the intensity of a substance's "qualities" (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) on a scale of one to four.</note>. ¶ **Abugerig.** Coriander <margin>Abugerig.</margin> is a cold narcotic inducing stupor; it is toxic, and it prevents vapors from ascending to the head. For this reason, it is beneficial for headaches and drunkenness; it stops the flow of blood and binds the belly <note>Acts as an anti-diarrheal.</note>.

¶ **Saffron** is hot in the second degree and dry in the first. There are those who claim it is hot in the third; it is useful for the stomach and contributes much to the digestion of food, though it can cause obstructions. It is beneficial in cases of weakness caused by phlegm and for those with stones <note>Kidney or bladder stones.</note>, as it has the power to disperse them. It is beneficial to the intestines and against difficulty of breath; taken in moderate use, it maintains a beautiful complexion. But if taken immoderately, it generates both pallor and headache, and takes away the appetite for food. When applied with opium, milk, and rose oil, it helps those suffering from gout. There are some who add the leaves of a large beet to these. Some report that excessive and immoderate use of it causes perpetual laughter until the person finally dies. Others have reported the same thing happens if three ounces are drunk with water. <margin>Serapion.</margin> ¶ **Serapion,** on the authority of Rhazes, says there was a certain woman who labored for several days in childbirth; I gave her two drams <note>A small unit of weight.</note> of saffron in a drink, and she gave birth immediately. I have tested this always, and it has always happened thus.

¶ **Chickpeas** are hot with a little moisture; they are digested with difficulty. They stir up sexual desire more than the nourishing bean; they cause obstructions but stimulate menstruation. They share in both saltiness and sweetness. Because of the saltiness, they move the belly; because of the sweetness, <margin>Psellus to the Emperor Constantine.</margin> they move the urine, cause gas, generate milk, and have a cleansing power. Black chickpeas take the place of medicine because they are most effective at stimulating one's strength. ¶ **Psellus.** Chickpeas cause gas and nourish much

<column-break/>

just like the bean; they generate seed and arouse sexual desire. Their broth, cooked with the chickpeas, wears down stones in the kidneys, especially the small and black variety. If they are eaten fried, they are like beans: they bind the bowels and provide more nourishment. If the chickpea is eaten green, <margin>Serapion.</margin> it moistens the body itself. ¶ **Serapion.** Their first specific virtue is that they are hot with a little moisture; secondly, they resolve, open, and cut through humors; and thirdly, they cleanse and open obstructions of the liver and kidneys. They wipe away scabies and skin eruptions, resolve swellings of the testicles when they are hard, and cure bad sores when administered with honey.

¶ **Crabs** possess a certain salty humor; however, it is less in those that have a thin shell. They bind the belly because, during cooking, they lose that salty humor. But river crabs help against wounds of the lungs, though they may harm the bladder. Certain distinguished physicians report that if river crabs are cooked in oil, that oil, when dripped into aching ears, helps wonderfully against the heat. A drink made from them, when crushed, is also effective against every poison and venomous bite. They also claim that when toasted and applied, they soften all abscesses of the body and extract all splinters and thorns from the flesh. ¶ **Galen.** River crabs are effective against the <margin>Galen.</margin> bite of a rabid dog by their whole nature; and I have not seen anyone using this medicine who died from this sickness. See Serapion on this cure in chapter 432, concerning crabs.

¶ The meat of **pigeon chicks** <note>Squab.</note> is hot, moist, and abundant, especially that of <margin>Rhazes, Book 3, chapter 9.</margin> domestic ones. ¶ **Rhazes.** Pigeon chicks are of a vehement heat; they generate blood, cause inflammation, and quickly cause fevers. But if one eats them too frequently, it generates leprosy <note>In this period, "leprosy" often referred to various chronic skin diseases or "corruptions" of the humors.</note>; it also harms the head and the eyes, as some report. The meat of those born in the spring and autumn is considered better than those in winter or summer.

¶ All **cheeses** are bad, difficult to digest, phlegm-producing, and cause burning in the bowels; for they receive a sharp quality from the rennet. As cheese ages, it becomes sharper, hotter, and more burning; it is more difficult to digest, and its humor is worse, generating stones in the kidneys, and is therefore more destructive. Therefore, such cheese is to be avoided above all as having nothing good in it. Less bad is the cheese that is neither old nor sharp; the least bad is fresh cheese, being as it were midway between milk and cheese, and therefore easier to digest and producing a better humor, especially if it is soft and spongy...

<margin>Rhazes, Book 3, Almansor, chapter 15.</margin>
¶ **Fresh cheese** moves the bowels; old cheese binds them. We have found through experience that goat's milk cheese is superior to that of the cow, and following that of the cow, sheep's milk cheese is next in quality. ¶ **Rhazes.** Fresh cheese is cold and thick, and being something that increases the flesh, it suppresses the burning of the stomach. However, it is not said to be good for those who are cold by nature. Its properties vary according to its age. For that which is pungent in flavor is hot and burning, causing thirst and providing poor nourishment. Nevertheless, when a small quantity is taken after a meal, it strengthens the mouth of the stomach <note>The cardia, or the opening where the esophagus enters the stomach.</note>; it also removes excessive satiety and the nausea that arises in the mouth of the stomach from sweet and oily foods. However, both very fresh and very old cheese should be avoided.

<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Camphor.** ¶ **Rhazes.** It is cold and subtle; it helps to soothe hot illnesses occurring in the head and throughout the whole body. He who uses camphor excessively will suffer from insomnia, and if taken in a drink, it cools the kidneys and bladder, coagulates the sperm, and generates "cold" diseases, especially in cold regions.
<margin>Mesue the Elder.</margin>
¶ **Mesue the Elder.** Camphor is cold and dry in the third degree <note>Medieval medicine ranked the intensity of a substance's "qualities" (heat, cold, moisture, dryness) on a scale of one to four.</note>; it stops the flow of blood from the nose when a head-purge is made with it and the juice of sour grapes.

<margin>Ibn Masawayh</margin>
¶ **Cassia**, or **Cassia fistula** <note>Also known as the "golden shower tree," used as a laxative.</note>, is hot and moist, though not to a specific degree, for it is very temperate below every degree. ¶ **Ibn Masawayh.** Its vapor is sweet. Its primary virtue is that it is of an equal temperament. Its second virtue is that it is a resolving agent. Its third virtue is that it extinguishes the sharpness of the blood and soothes abscesses <note>original: "apostemata"</note> arising from it; it also resolves hard swellings in the gums and throat when used as a gargle with the decoction of raisins. It is beneficial for jaundice <note>original: "ycteritie"</note> and pain of the liver. Its specific property is to purge "burnt bile" <note>original: "cholera adusta," a toxic form of yellow bile in humoral theory</note> and to soften the belly with a moderate loosening. The dose is from 3 to 10 drachms <note>original: ".ʒ. iii. vsq[ue] ad .x."</note>, and it cleanses the nerves.
<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** The best kind is when it is extracted from the cane; it is balanced between heat and cold, and it relaxes the common bowels through its temperament. It helps with hot abscesses in the fistula <note>original: "fist'"</note> and especially of the throat; it inclines slightly more toward heat than toward cold, so that it almost reaches the beginning of the first degree. It is brought from Babylon and Basra.

Thus, it is suitably given for bilious diseases; it also greatly benefits those suffering from constipation due to the drying of the feces and those suffering from acute illness. Its third virtue is that it opens obstructions of the liver, kidneys, and gallbladder, and cleanses both thin and thick veins of thick, bilious humors; it strengthens the stomach and liver. It is cleansing, opening, and unsettling to the stomach, causing nausea; it possesses the power to induce evacuation through both vomiting and the bowels.

Therefore, when the water has been drawn off after being infused three or four times, it is a medicine that dries without stinging; it has the power to draw out when mixed with seawater.
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides.** The virtue of lime is inflammatory, stinging, burning, cauterizing, and softening. But if it is mixed with lard <note>original: "axungia"</note> or with oil, it becomes maturing and softening.

# Concerning the letter C.

<column-break/>

<margin>Galen</margin>
...it is restorative, flesh-forming <note>Original: *incarnatiua*, referring to the growth of new tissue in a wound.</note>, or consolidating. And that lime which has not been touched by water is stronger than that which water has touched <note>This refers to "unslaked" versus "slaked" lime.</note>. ¶ **Galen.** It burns strongly until it creates a hard, cauterized scab <term>eschar</term>.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Coral.** ¶ **Dioscorides.** The virtue of red coral is astringent <term>styptic</term> and cold with a balanced temperament. It provides manifest help for those with flowing blood and dysentery. When it is drunk with rainwater, it helps with pain in the stomach and the belly. 
<margin>Paul of Aegina</margin>
¶ **Paul.** It dries with a powerful drying action and binds because of its astringency. It is helpful for dysentery and blood-flows. It cleanses the vision and is good for watery eyes because it dries them with great force. 
<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Coral is cold; when well-ground and given in a drink, it helps those who spit blood <note>Original: *emptoicis*, a term for those suffering from hemoptysis or respiratory bleeding.</note>. When "red" is simply written, it is understood to be coral.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Great Centaury.** <note>A herb traditionally used for healing and digestive issues.</note> The root consists of contrary powers. To the taste, it is sharp and at the same time appears to become bitter, along with a certain brief sweetness. ¶ **Galen.** Its first virtue is that it heats; its second is that it forms flesh or "glues" tissue together; it cleanses and strengthens the limbs. Its third virtue is that it provokes the menses and expels a dead fetus; it also kills and expels a living one. It knits wounds together and helps with the spitting of blood. ¶ **The dose** is two *aurei* <note>A weight equivalent to a gold coin.</note>. If the person drinking it has a fever, let them drink it with water; if they are without fever, let them drink it with wine. It helps with the attrition of the nerves, shortness of breath, and an old cough. The juice of the root does the same as the root itself; it also purges viscous phlegm and bile <term>cholera</term> that looks like dregs, as well as "lemon-colored" water <note>Likely referring to serous fluids or jaundice-related fluids</note> with great strength.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Small Centaury.** The root of this is entirely ineffective and useless, but the branches and leaves are effective. The flowers are the most useful of all. A bitter quality dominates them, though they participate in a small amount of sharpness; because of this, it is an immediate remedy for drying out wounds without causing stinging pain. ¶ **Galen.** Its first virtue is drying without "biting" <note>Without a stinging or corrosive sensation.</note>; its second virtue is that it forms flesh, softens, and cleanses. Its third virtue is that it heals large wounds when it is placed fresh upon them in the manner of a plaster. It also forms flesh and consolidates old ulcers that are difficult to heal when applied fresh. It is indeed among the best and most noble medicines for blockages <term>oppilationes</term> of the liver, and it magnificently aids the hardness of the spleen when applied over it as a plaster,

<column-break/>

<margin>Mesue the Elder</margin>
or taken in a drink. ¶ **Mesue the Elder.** <note>Original: *Habenmesuai*, refers to the influential Persian physician Yuhanna ibn Masawayh.</note> The property of this plant is that it purges viscous phlegm that looks like dregs. It helps with sciatica when a decoction of it is taken in a drink, or when it is used as a clyster <note>An enema.</note>. ¶ The dose in a potion is two drachms; in a clyster, it is three drachms with sesame oil.

¶ **Wax** is in the middle-ground between heating and cooling substances, and between moistening and drying ones. It possesses something of a thickness of parts and a medicinal quality. Therefore, it does not only dry, but also appears to moisten "by accident" by inhibiting "distillations" <note>The leaking of fluids or catarrhs.</note>. For this reason, it is the base material for other medicines. On its own, it is counted among those things that "cook" <note>Mature or ripen</note> weak ailments when applied externally. It has a brief power to draw out or distract, in which it takes much from the nature of honey.

<margin>Abu-Jurayj</margin>
¶ **Abu-Jurayj.** <note>Original: *Abugerig*, a less common Arabic medical authority.</note> It softens the thickness of swellings <term>apostemes</term> and helps with roughness of the chest when placed upon it, or when a "loth" <note>A small measurement</note> is made with it and some oil, such as violet oil. It softens the nerves and viscera that have scabs <term>eschars</term>, and ointments are prepared with it.

¶ **Gourd or Colocynth** <note>Usually refers to the bitter apple or various squashes.</note> is of a moist and cold temperament in the second degree of both. It moderately cools hot burnings and provides moist and cold nourishment to the body—though only a little. It is digested reasonably well provided it does not begin to rot. This rotting happens through "wickedness" when a bad humor has gathered in the belly. 
<margin>Mesue the Elder</margin>
¶ **Mesue.** The juice of the gourd helps with a cough and chest pain that comes from heat; it cuts off thirst and helps with the anxiety that arises from bile. 
<margin>Rhazes, Book 3, Almansor, chapter 57.</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** The gourd is cold and moist; while being bad for the stomach by destroying the appetite, it also settles thirst and extinguishes the burning of the liver and stomach when heat abounds in them.

¶ **Costus** <note>A fragrant root used in ancient and medieval medicine.</note> has very little bitterness, but is of a sharp and hot quality and power. Likewise, it also "attracts" <note>Draws out humors</note>, which is why they grind it with oil before applying it to the bodies of those shivering from a high fever. It moves the urine and the menses. It is suitable for fractures and for pains in the sides. Because of its inherent bitterness, it kills the broad worm <note>A tapeworm.</note>.

# Concerning the letter D.

**Column 1**

<margin>Rhazes, Book 3, Chapter 22</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Costus <note>A fragrant root from the ginger family, used in ancient medicine and perfumes.</note> is hot and dry; it opens obstructions and cleanses: it eats away at superfluous flesh: it helps those suffering from rheum <term>discharge of fluids</term> due to cold if the nostrils are fumigated with it.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Maidenhair fern** <note>Original: *Capillus veneris*. A delicate fern used to treat hair and respiratory issues.</note> is midway between those things that heat and those that cool. ¶ **Galen.** Its primary virtue is a drying power, and there is no apparent heat in it. Instead, its temperament exists in a middle state between two opposite qualities, in the median degree between them. Its second virtue is one that thins and dissolves. Its third virtue is that it makes hair grow in cases of alopecia <term>hair loss</term> and dissolves scrofulas <note>Swelling of the lymph nodes, historically known as the "King's Evil."</note>: and when drunk, it breaks up stones and helps to bring up phlegm—thick, viscous humors in the chest and lungs—and it binds the bowels. ¶ **Mesue.**

<margin>Mesue</margin>
Its property is to cleanse the humors <note>Original: *chomesuai leram*, likely a corruption of terms for bile.</note> in the intestines and stomach; the dose is from 4 to 8 drams. ¶ **Dioscorides.**

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
It benefits those with jaundice, pain in the spleen, and difficulty urinating <term>strangury</term>: it breaks stones and binds the bowels when drunk with wine: it benefits the bites of venomous creatures and the flow of excess fluids to the stomach, and it provokes menstruation.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 3, Chapter 29</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Maidenhair fern is hot: if it is burnt and the bare areas of the scalp are rubbed with it, it causes hair to grow: it dissolves scrofulas: it also cleanses the lungs of the thick humors with which they are soaked.

¶ **Chicory** <note>Original: *Lycoree*.</note> says Acron, are herbs with many thin roots, which Virgil named *intyba* in the fourth book of the *Georgics*: "Strymonian cranes and endive with bitter fibers." Pliny, however, says: some among us call wild endive *ambula*; in Egypt they call it *Licorium* because it grows wild. Among us, they call it chicory <note>Original: *cicozeum*.</note>, the "sun-herb" or "bride of the sun," and the "sun-follower" <term>heliotrope</term> or *dionysia*. ¶ **Constantine.**

<margin>Constantine</margin>
It strengthens the stomach: it is effective against scorpions and the bites of other reptiles when mixed with myrrh: applied as a suppository for a woman, it provokes menstruation: it benefits the kidneys and stomach. For the purgation of women, when boiled in water, it is so beneficial that it draws out dead fetuses. And because it has a restrictive power, certain animals harmed by venomous creatures are healed by the touch of this herb; when eaten, it is effective for obstructions of the spleen and liver, and against inflammation of the liver.

¶ **Roe deer meat** <note>Original: *Lapreoli caro*.</note> has more good humor than other wild meats;

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

it is said to have an affinity with the human body. It benefits moist and overflowing bodies, as well as those with colic and "comitial" afflictions <term>epilepsy</term>: yet they bind the bowels and bring dryness to the nerves by their thinness.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'D' with stylized foliate and floral motifs in a square frame.</image-desc>
**Dittany** <note>Original: *Dictamum*. A medicinal herb from Crete, often confused with Origanum dictamnus.</note> consists of fine parts. ¶ **Dioscorides.** The action of dittany is like that of domestic pennyroyal, except that it is stronger in virtue: it is used in the preparation of ointments made against venomous bites: it provokes urine and menstruation. When it is burnt, venomous creatures are put to flight by its odor. Dittany differs from *diptamum*: yet it does the same things that *diptamum* does, except it is weaker.

¶ **Wild Carrot** <note>Original: *Daucus*, also called *staphylinos*.</note>: the wild kind is less edible than the domestic, but more powerful in all respects; the domestic is indeed edible, but weaker. Both have sharp and hot powers, and for this reason, they are thinning. The root, therefore, possesses a certain flatulent quality and consequently arouses sexual desire <term>Venus</term>. The seed of the domestic variety has something of a quality that drains the sexual urge, while the wild variety is entirely free of flatulence; for this reason, it provokes urine and menstruation.

<margin>Psellus</margin>
¶ **Dates.** **Psellus.** Sweet ones are more nourishing; those that are becoming tart are beneficial for the stomach and restrain the bowels entirely: all are difficult to digest and bind the belly if used in large quantities.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 2, Chapter 21</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Dates are hot and heavy, and they provide much nourishment. If they are taken in great quantities through habitual eating, they generate thick blood in the internal organs: they rot the teeth and cause blood and phlegm to increase.

<margin>Galen, On Theriac</margin>
¶ **Tragacanth.** <note>A natural gum obtained from the dried sap of Middle Eastern legumes.</note> ¶ **Galen.** Its primary virtue is a drying power: the second is a binding <term>conglutinating</term> power: the third is a virtue that breaks the sharpness of hot and acute things: and with this, it glues just like gum arabic.

The seed of the domestic kind does indeed have some power to sharpen sexual desire: while the wild kind is entirely without gas-forming properties: and for this reason, it moves urine and menstruation.

**Spurge.** <note>original: *Esula*</note> ¶ **Al-Tabari.** <note>original: "Dabir," likely referring to the Persian physician Ali ibn Sahl Rabban al-Tabari.</note> The *shubrum* <note>original: "fcebrem," an Arabic term for a type of spurge.</note> or spurge is hot in the third degree and dry at the beginning of the second: in it there is both astringency and sharpness: so that when someone takes it in a drink, they find astringency in their throat. Its harm is for those with a hot complexion <unclear>...complexion</unclear>: it induces a summer fever in the one drinking it, and harms the yellow bile <note>original: "aquam citrinam," literally "lemon-colored water."</note>: it also purges phlegm and melancholy. ¶ **Dioscorides.** One drachm of its root is taken and drunk with honey-water: and if one drachm of its seed is taken, it purges bile and phlegm. And itinerant doctors <note>original: "medici viatores," referring to traveling healers often criticized as quacks.</note> kill many people with it because of their lack of knowledge. These medicines are like fire: therefore they should not be called medicines, but rather poisons. See Serapion in the *Book of Simples*, chapter 371.

Dioscorides.

**Dwarf Elder** <note>original: *Ebulus*</note> or *chamaeacte*. <note>A Greek name meaning "ground elder."</note> ¶ **Dioscorides.** Its quality is astringent: when taken, it purges watery humors, but it is bad for the stomach. It softens the hardness of the womb and dilates its opening: its seed in a drink also does this. It is good for fire burns and dog bites, and it joins together fistulas and hollow ulcers. When a plaster is made with them and goat tallow, it benefits gout; and when used in a sitz-bath decoction, it expels the afterbirth and benefits dropsy <term>hydropisi</term>. When the leaves are crushed and their juice is expressed and distilled into the ears, it takes away whistling and thundering (otherwise called ringing) and kills the worms that are in them. When it is smeared on warm, it prevents scabies and itching. When taken in a drink, it benefits the bites of venomous animals and dissolves blood and milk when it is curdled in the stomach. It kills leeches that stick in the throat and benefits an old cough, though it increases a new one. It benefits the tightening of breath that forces a person to stand upright <note>This refers to orthopnea, a condition where one can only breathe comfortably while standing or sitting up.</note> and benefits catarrh descending to the throat, as well as quinsy <note>A severe inflammation of the throat/tonsils.</note> and enlargement of the uvula. When used as a mouthwash, it soothes toothache. When the tender tops are taken with their leaves and crushed, and their juice is given with wine in a drink, it benefits

kidney stones. A decoction of the root given in a drink heals hardness of the spleen. Elderberry and Dwarf Elder have the same quality: they have a drying, joining, and moderately resolving quality.

Serapion on the authority of Dioscorides, chapter 78.
</margin>

**Eupatorium** <note>Commonly known today as Agrimony or Hemp-agrimony.</note> is of a potency of subtle parts: it is cleansing and drying without manifest heat. Therefore, it purges obstructions of the liver. It has a certain brief bitterness by which it strengthens and firms the liver. Some say this herb is agrimony. If someone should perhaps demand of me that I reveal what the true Eupatorium is, I will finally say what I think. For many of the ancients, whom Dioscorides notes, thought this was the true *argemonium*, yet this is different from Eupatorium—an error that has persisted even to our time. For the herb which is the true Eupatorium is believed by many to be *argemonium*, and therefore by a corrupted name it is everywhere called Agrimony. It is described by Dioscorides and Pliny (who imitates Dioscorides) so that it almost seems to be placed before one's eyes. This is Dioscorides' description of the same herb: Eupatorium is an herb having a straight, slender, black, hard, rough stalk with hairs at the top; its length is almost one cubit <note>About 18 inches.</note> or more. It has leaves divided from each other around the stalk, cut with five or six incisions, and at the tip they are notched like a saw. Its leaves are similar to the leaves of cinquefoil <note>original: "pētafilon"</note> or the leaves of *sedenagi*, that is, hemp. Their color tends toward blackness. On its stalk from the middle up is the seed, and upon it are hairs; it hangs downward on the herb itself. In which description that herb is depicted which some have named *lapullam* <note>A "burr" or "little burdock."</note> from that clinging nature which Dioscorides attributes to the fruit; we commonly call it Agrimony. But there is another described as Eupatorium, such that no one unless blind to the nature of things would not recognize this as the true Eupatorium. Whence also a double error of our age is detected: one, that we receive the herb named Eupatorium by the ancients as the true *argemonium*; the other, that for Eupatorium we frequently use a common herb of which nothing is found among ancient authors except by reason or authority. ¶ **Mesue.** Eupatorium is an herb of half a cubit's length, of much bitterness, whose leaves...

Its leaves are like those of the lesser centaury <note>A common medicinal herb known for its bitter properties</note>, but they are rough and notched, and its stalk is slender. When it is dried, it turns a yellowish-citrine color. **Its complexion:** It is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. It is thinning, cutting, wiping, cleansing, and a preservative against rot; it is a resolving agent suited for gentle purging. Through purging, it easily draws out bile and phlegm. It strengthens the stomach, liver, and internal organs; it is a celebrated medicine for blockages and wonderfully aids those suffering from long-term fevers. **The dose:** As a potion, it is taken from four to six ounces; in its powder form, from two to three drachms <term>ʒ.ij. vsqz ad. iij.</term> <note>A drachm was approximately 3.9 grams.</note>.

¶ **Rocket** <note>original: *Eruca*; known today as arugula</note> is named from "leaping" <note>The author suggests a Latin etymological link between *eruca* and *salire* (to jump), implying sexual vigor</note>, which pertains to the union of arms. ¶ **Constantine.** Rocket is hot in the third degree and moist in the first; it increases semen, incites intercourse, and generates headaches. Therefore, it should be eaten mixed with lettuce so that its heat may be tempered. ¶ **Galen.** It is hot in the second degree and moist in the first. ¶ **Dioscorides.** It provokes urine, causes food to be digested, and softens the belly. ¶ **Psellus.** Rocket heats significantly, generates seed, excites the vigor of the flesh, and brings on headaches.

**The Bean** <note>original: *Faba*; usually referring to the broad bean or fava bean</note> cools and dries; it is of a moderate temperament and possesses a small degree of cleansing power.

For then it is worse and generates more windiness, descending slowly from the stomach. Therefore, he who eats it immediately finds sluggishness, heaviness in his body, a stretching sensation in the head, and thick windiness. However, if it is soaked in water until it sprouts and then is fried, its windiness and bloating are diminished. The eating of the bean is more commendable if it is cooked cleaned of its skins until it dissolves.

¶ **The Bean** <note>original: "Fasellus"; likely referring to the kidney bean or cowpea</note> is a middle-sort of food, between good and bad juice <note>The "juice" or "chyme" refers to the substance produced by digestion</note>; it is easy to cook but hard to digest. When soaked in garum, they are nourishing and generate good juice when well digested. They are better than fenugreek and are midway between good and bad juice, whether they are well-cooked or less so, and between slow and fast passage, and between being very nourishing or little.

¶ **Figs** are hot in the first degree. They benefit the chest against coughs and stir the urine. They are quite nourishing; if taken before a meal, they loosen the belly. However, if they do not descend immediately into the stomach, they generate bad blood; for this reason, those who eat their fill of figs often break out in scabies and lice. It is considered a useful food if eaten with walnuts or almonds. They cleanse the kidneys and remove blockages from the liver and spleen, except that they heat the body and cause thirst, and produce yellow bile in those with hot temperaments. Moreover, Galen <note>The most influential Greek physician of the Roman Empire</note> relates that due to the use of these kinds of tree fruits, he fell into illness quite often from the twentieth year of his age until old age; thereafter he abstained from others and took only figs and grapes, and these not immoderately. He also advised his friends of this, and none of them were afflicted by any lingering weakness afterward. Some have offered a remedy against poisons: if anyone

eats them with any thinning agent, such as rue <note>A bitter medicinal herb</note> or something of that kind. **Green figs** provide almost the same benefits; for they are hot in the first degree and dry in the middle of that same degree. They do not produce solid flesh, as bread and meat do. They cause wind in the belly, but they generate less "bad humor" than other fruits. They wipe the kidneys clean, though they do not produce entirely pure blood. <margin>Psellus, book 3 on the Rule of Health.</margin> ¶ **Psellus.** Figs, like other orchard fruits, generate bad juice, but these have less of it than the others. However, they should not be eaten for a long time. All these things should be taken sparingly.

Bread with much bran <term>cibarius</term> <note>often called "household bread" or "rations bread"</note> provides little nourishment. Bread made from fine wheat is difficult to digest, and if it is not well-digested, it generates raw humors. ¶ **Constantine.** All bread made from <margin>Constantine, *Pantegni*, book 5, theory chapter 15.</margin> wheat is hot in the first degree. It is, however, good for those who labor and exercise themselves. For those with a very hot stomach—so it is said in part <margin>Constantine in *The Pantegni*, book 5.</margin> five—it is good if well digested. Therefore, whoever is about to eat should eat unleavened bread or others with hot and diuretic substances. ¶ **Haly Abbas.** <margin>Haly Abbas, book 5 of the *Royal Book*, chapter 15.</margin> <note>A famous Persian physician (d. 982)</note> **Wheat** is more praiseworthy than all other grains and is closest to a temperate balance, except that it declines slightly toward heat. For this reason, it has been made more suitable and more beneficial for the bodies of men than all other grains. It is a more praiseworthy food; that which is solid, hard, declining toward red, and heavy is better and nourishes more, and is of a thicker substance. That which is white, tender, and light is thinner, nourishes less, and has more bran. If wheat is boiled, it nourishes the most and increases the strength of the body, but it generates a thick humor, especially if it is cooked with meat; for then it increases the strength and vigor of the body with a manifest increase, and it is suitable for men of great labor and fatigue. However, he who becomes accustomed to eating wheat uncooked produces windiness and generates longworms and roundworms in the intestines.

¶ **Bran.** ¶ **Galen.** It is less hot <margin>Galen, *On Simple Medicines*, book 5.</margin> and more temperate than the marrow of the wheat. # On the letter F.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides.** <note>Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD)</note> When it is cooked with strong vinegar and made into a plaster, it removes scabies <note>original: "scabiem"; a term used for various itchy skin conditions or mange</note>. It is also a useful plaster for hot abscesses <note>original: "apostematibus"; inflammatory swellings</note> at their onset. When it is cooked with rue and made into a plaster, it is beneficial for swellings of the breasts caused by the curdling of milk; it similarly treats scabies, intestinal stings, and the bites of vipers <note>original: "tyri"</note>.

¶ **Mushrooms** are a cold and moist food, and for this reason, they possess a deadly power. Among them, some are killers, even though that Epicurean <note>referring to a follower of Epicurus, often associated with fine dining</note> in the works of Horace says: "Nature has made meadow mushrooms the best; others are not to be trusted."
<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Galen.** <note>The most influential Roman physician (129–c. 216 AD)</note> The primary quality of mushrooms is excessively cold and moist, and because of this, they are close to being deadly medicines.

¶ **Pistachios.** ¶ **Constantine.** <margin>Constantine, book 5</margin> They are tempered between hot and moist. They support and warm the stomach and the liver; they are diuretic <note>original: "diuretici"; substances that encourage urination</note>, increase libido, and are nourishing. They are effective against the bite of a scorpion. ¶ **Rhazes.** <note>Persian physician al-Razi (865–925 AD)</note> Pistachios are hotter than <margin>Rhazes. almonds; they also open blockages of the liver.</margin>

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Ferns.** The root kills broad worms <note>original: "vermiculos latos"; tapeworms</note> when four drams are taken with honey-water <note>original: "mellicrato"</note>. It kills them whether they are healthy or diseased and drives them out. It dries out ulcers without causing stinging. ¶ **Galen.** Its primary quality is strongly drying without irritation. Its secondary quality is that it cleanses and strengthens. Its third quality is that it kills roundworms and tapeworms <note>original: "vermes cucurbitinos"; literally "gourd-shaped worms"</note> when four gold-weight measures <note>original: "aurei"</note> are drunk with honey-water.

¶ **Leaven** <note>Yeast or fermented dough</note> consists of fine parts and is moderately hot; for this reason, it is safe and does not cause stinging. It draws things out from the roots and disperses them. It is mixed from contrary powers: sourness, coldness, and a putrid heat, whether made from flour <margin>Rhazes, book 4 to Almansor, chapter 51.</margin> or other things. ¶ **Rhazes.** Leaven made from wheat flour helps with pains in the soles of the feet if a plaster is made from it; it also ripens abscesses.

<margin>Galen?</margin>
¶ **Fumitory.** <note>original: "Fumusterre"; literally "smoke of the earth"</note> ¶ **Galen.** Its primary quality is hot and cold with dryness in the second degree. Secondly, it strengthens and cleanses. Thirdly, it is beneficial to the stomach because there is a small amount of <term>stypticity</term> <note>original: "stipticitas"; a drawing or contracting sensation, like that of a tannin</note> in it, and there is no obvious amount of heat in it. ¶ **Abenmesuai.** <note>The physician Masawaih al-Mardini (d. 1015)</note> Its <margin>Aben- mesuai</margin>

<column-break/>

beneficial property is for the stomach, scabies, itching, and for purging <term>burnt bile</term> <note>original: "choleram adustam"; in humoral theory, bile that has become overheated and toxic</note>, as well as for cleansing the blood and provoking urine. The dose, when it is boiled, is from 5 to 10 drams; if raw, from 3 to 7 drams, with an equal amount of yellow <term>myrobalans</term> <note>an astringent fruit from the East used as a laxative</note>. The dose of its juice is from 4 to 8 drams, with 3 to 8 drams of yellow myrobalans. ¶ **Avicenna.** <margin>Avicenna</margin> <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), author of The Canon of Medicine</note> Fumitory is said to be cold in the first degree and dry in the second. There is coldness in it because of its styptic flavor, and heat because of its bitter flavor, but the coldness is stronger. ¶ **Constantine.** <margin>Constantine</margin> Fumitory is hot in the first degree and dry in the second. Thus it strengthens the stomach. The juice, when given as a drink, excites the appetite.

¶ **Fennel** heats intensely as if it were of the third degree of power, but it dries in the first order. Because of this, it produces milk, as it does not dry excessively. For the same reason, it helps with "suffusions" <note>likely cataracts or blurring of the eyes</note> and acts as a diuretic and provokes the menses. ¶ **Rhazes.** <margin>Rhazes, book 4 to Almansor, chapter 47.</margin> Fennel is hot and provokes urine; it is beneficial for chronic fevers. When it is fresh, it generates milk. Its juice, when placed in the eye, sharpens the sight.

¶ **Iron** is created from thick, impure, and burning sulfur with a small amount of unclean quicksilver <note>mercury</note>. The **Alchemists** call quicksilver "Mercury" because it joins with all metals, just as the planet Mercury, according to the astrologers, is joined with all the other planets in its influence. Thus, the more quicksilver they contain, the more quickly they melt, such as lead and tin. Copper and iron are the opposite. **Steel** <note>original: "Calibs"</note> is iron that has been purged and purified through many firings and quenchings. Thus it is made less oily and breaks more easily than iron; they are not entirely equal in weight. ¶ **Aristotle.** <margin>Aristotle, Book 2 (actually 4) of the Meteorology.</margin> In the second <note>it is actually the fourth</note> book of the *Meteorology*: Certain things are soften-able, such as iron and horn. Thus iron becomes soft and cuttable. Iron melted by heat is solidified; once cooled and worked, it is melted so that it becomes liquid, and meanwhile, it is solidified. ¶ **From the Book on the Nature of Things.** <margin>In the Book on the Nature of Things.</margin> Iron is cold by nature, hard, solid, and sharp; it tames all things by its strength, and is consumed only by itself <note>referring to rust</note>. ¶ **Averroes.** <margin>Averroes, book 5, chapter 43.</margin> <note>Andalusian philosopher and physician (1126–1198)</note> In the fifth book of the *Colliget*: Iron is of a vehement dryness. When it is ground down much and soaked many times in vinegar or in sour goat's milk, it is effective against sliminess of the stomach.

It is said that the marrow with gall <note>the bitter fluid from the gallbladder</note> causes memory to be destroyed <note>original: "abolendam facere memoriam"; this is a curious claim, as crane parts were often thought to aid vigilance or memory, but the text here specifies destruction or wiping away of memory</note>. ¶ **Pomegranates** are cold. The sweet ones are good for the chest: they produce good juice and share in the quality of chastity <note>medieval lore sometimes associated certain cooling foods with the suppression of lust</note>. <margin>Constantine, book 6.</margin> <note>Constantine the African, an 11th-century monk and translator of medical texts</note> Pomegranates are cold. The acidic ones are colder in moisture and dryness. The moderate ones extinguish red bile. They comfort the stomach and the liver; they remove "abomination" <note>original: "abomnationez"; referring to nausea or a deep aversion to food</note>. Brangra <note>likely a corrupted reference to another authority</note> in book 6 says: the dry parts of them are contrary to loosening the belly <note>i.e., they cause constipation</note>. They draw choleric humors so that they do not descend into the stomach.

<margin>Averroes, book 5, *Colliget*, chapter 42.</margin> gentian, is placed in the third degree. It is hot and dry, and this is manifested by the strength of its bitterness; and its root is very strong for thinning and opening blockages.

# On the letter J.

<margin>Paul [Aegineta], chapter on hermodactyl</margin>
¶ **Hermodactyl.** <note>original: "Hermodactilus"; likely *Colchicum*, or Meadow Saffron, used since antiquity for gout</note> ¶ **Paulus.** Hermodactyls are hot and dry at the beginning of the second degree. It is a herb, and around its roots, tuberous growths are found; these ought to be collected and reserved for use. They are gathered in the summer and stored; they can be kept for one year. Those which are white and solid should be chosen. They possess a dissolving, consuming, and attractive power. They primarily purge phlegm. Against arthritis, gout of the feet, gout of the hands, the "iliac passion" <note>a painful intestinal obstruction</note>, and diseases arising from phlegm where no fever is present. The "Theodoric sacred electuary" <note>original: "hieralogodion theodozicum"; a complex compound medicine</note> made from hermodactyls is very effective.

<margin>Mesué.</margin>
¶ **Mesué.** <note>Yuhanna ibn Masawayh (c. 777–857), a Persian Christian physician</note> Through its laxative effect, it draws out thick phlegm, specifically from the joints. Its dose is from one to two gold weight units <note>original: "aureo uno"; refers to the weight of a gold coin</note>. It may be preserved for three years.

### ¶ On the letter J.

Juniper.
St. John's Wort.
Henbane.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'U' featuring foliate designs within a square frame.</image-desc>
**Juniper** <note>original: "Uniperus"</note> is hot and dry in the third degree in both qualities; its fruit is also hot. It dries things out, as some say, in the first degree. The use of its bark, smeared on with water, wards off leprosy. The fruit is astringent; it benefits the stomach and the chest; it removes coughs, bloating, and upsets of the stomach. It provokes the flow of urine, and it wonderfully assists in cases of spasms, fractures, and those oppressed by "strangulation" <note>likely referring to a feeling of choking or respiratory distress</note>.

<margin>Averroes, volume 5, chapter 42</margin>
¶ **Averroes.** <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an influential Andalusian polymath</note> Juniper is hot and dry in the third degree and is very "subtle" <note>meaning refined or penetrating in its effect</note>. This is because the quality most found in it is a fiery substance, followed by a burnt earthy substance, and a small amount of cold earthy substance. Its secondary effects are to consume the putrefaction found in wounds and abscesses. Its tertiary effects are that it provokes urine and menstruation more strongly than others, even to the point of causing one to urinate blood. It causes abortion and extracts a dead fetus. Because of its subtlety and aromatic nature, it is sometimes used in place of a certain species of "Dorsini" cinnamon <note>original: "cynamomi dorsini"; likely Cassia or a specific grade of cinnamon</note>.

<margin>Galen.</margin>
¶ **St. John's Wort** <note>original: "Jpericon"; *Hypericum perforatum*</note>, or *ypericon*, or *reiofricon*. ¶ **Galen.** Its substance is subtle, and

<column-break/>

its primary power is that it heats and dries; its secondary power is that it refines. Its third power provokes urine and menstruation.

<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides.** When its seed is drunk with wine, it cures quartan fever <note>a fever, often malarial, that recurs every fourth day</note>; and when drunk in the same way for forty consecutive days, it cures sciatica. When a plaster is made from the leaves and seed, it cures burns from fire.

<margin>Galen.</margin>
¶ **Galen.** The fruit relaxes the belly and is beneficial for a type of paralysis which causes a person to bend backward <note>likely *opisthotonos*</note>. An ointment is made from it with laurel berries which assists in the paralysis that causes the head to bend backward. There are many other types of this herb which I have omitted because of the brevity of this summary.

<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
¶ **Henbane.** <note>original: "Jusquiamus"</note> ¶ **Dioscorides.** Its species are three. One of them has purple flowers and black seed. Another has honey-colored flowers and seed whose color tends toward redness. But the third species, in which there is benefit for medicine, has fat leaves full of moisture, and over them is a white down, and it has white seed. That species whose seed is black is to be avoided, for it is poisonous.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 3, chapter 29.</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** All species of henbane intoxicate and cause stupor; however, the black is judged the worst of all because it kills. Henbane, when crushed and applied to abscesses in which there is a violent pulse <note>throbbing inflammation</note>, destroys the sensation of pain.

# On the letter L.

**Column 1:**

...its primary power is hot at the end of the first degree, close to the second. Its secondary power is that it softens and dissolves through its softening; it tempers through its dissolution, and similarly it ripens. It gathers and strengthens hair that is falling out and heals <note>original: "incarnat", literally "to put on flesh"</note> ulcers that are difficult to close. When drunk with old wine, it binds the belly and provokes urine.

¶ **Lentil** <note>original: "Lens"</note> is cold in the second degree and dry in the third. It contains a thick humor and partakes of a harsh power and quality. If it is cooked in water and oil with salt is added, it is considered a suitable drink for dispersing [humors]. Twice cooked, it dries the belly and stops the flow of the bowels. It provides strength to the stomach, and for this reason, it is a suitable food for all the intestines of the belly, for those suffering from celiac distress and dysentery. Once the husk is removed, it loses much of its binding power. It creates slow and thick passages in the body. Those who use this food very frequently will fall into elephantiasis <note>a term used in the Middle Ages for severe skin diseases, including leprosy</note>, cancers, hardening [of the organs], nerve pains, and melancholic diseases. For its juice is suitable for producing thick, dry, and melancholic humor and blood. However, if there is a watery defect in someone’s flesh, this food is quite useful, just as it is most harmful to those who are already dry and withered. If one has healthy vision, it dulls it by drying; if the vision is already dull, it aids it by purging the humor. It produces thick blood that flows with difficulty. By drying, it keeps away the seed intended for sexual desire <note>original: "veneris intentum"</note>, and therefore it is useful for one practicing celibacy. It causes difficult sleep because of the melancholic humors it produces. If cooked with mint, it greatly reduces flatulence. Some mix in beet during the cooking for this reason. If it is thoroughly cooked and dissolved and applied to wounds from an arrow or a needle, it powerfully disperses the flow of blood. A short cooking of the lentil relieves griping pains, and when dropped into ears that are discharging pus, it helps.

<margin>Constantine, Book 5, ch. 75</margin>
¶ **Constantine.** Lentils are cold in the second degree and dry in the third, which is why they generate melancholic blood. If a choleric <note>someone with a hot and dry temperament</note> person uses them often, they become melancholic and will eventually suffer from melancholic disease, such as cancer, elephantiasis, mania, and the like.

¶ **Lupin**: one is domestic, the other wild. The domestic kind, when soaked for a long time in water, loses its 

<column-break/>

bitterness. When chewed in this way, it is difficult to digest. It is indeed nourishment for the body, but it generates a thick and raw humor. The wild kind is more bitter and more effective in all things than the domestic kind, though it shares the same power.

<margin>Psellus</margin>
¶ **Psellus.** <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine polymath</note> Lupin is difficult to digest and generates a thick humor. It has a moderate power to soften and bind the bowels.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 2 to Almansor, ch. 11 & 12</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Lupins are thick and hard to digest. However, when they are sweetened and eaten, they do not heat the body. While they are bitter, they are not suitable for nourishment but for medicine. For they dissolve scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes</note> and cleanse powerfully when administered while not very sweet. They also provoke urine and menstruation. Furthermore, they cause abortion and expel slippery worms from the belly. They also open the mouths of hemorrhoids.

¶ **White Lily** <note>original: "Lilium album"</note> heats and dries, as it is closer to sharp substances than the iris is, though not consisting of such fine parts. It is at the end of the second order of heating things, but it concludes the second order of drying things near the beginning.

<margin>Averroes, *Colliget*, ch. 42</margin>
¶ **Averroes.** The white lily is hot and dry in the second degree. We say this because it is bitter. It has a tempered wateriness; therefore, its oil is without any stinging <note>original: "mordicatione"</note>, and it is the highest among all things that dissolve matters in the womb <note>original: "matrice"</note>. Its leaves, cooked and placed upon flesh burned by fire, or mixed with boiling water and rose oil, bring immediate relief. The root is stronger than the leaves; therefore, it provokes menstruation and softens the hardness of all members, especially the womb.

¶ **Lettuce** <note>original: "Lactuca"</note>: a moist and cold vegetable, not in an extreme way, but like very cold spring water. Therefore, it is suitable against inflammations and mild "holy fires" <note>original: "sacros ignes", likely erysipelas or skin rashes</note>. As a food, it clearly quenches thirst and induces sleep, especially when chewed slightly cooked with oxycrate <note>a mixture of vinegar and water</note>. It is not cooked like other vegetables, nor does it move the bowels much, nor does it distend the belly. It does not generate bad blood, nor does it produce the most excellent humor. Its seed, when drunk, restrains sexual desire; hence it is given to those who suffer from [erotic] dreams. The juice of wild lettuce smeared on with breast milk soothes pains, inflammations, and heat.

# On the letter L.

<margin>Averroes, Book 5, Chapter 42</margin>
**Endive** <note>original: "Auer, intibi", referring to *Cichorium intybus*</note> has the same power as lettuce. Averroes says this herb is of a moist substance, like lettuce, but with a more gathered coldness. The wild variety is of a dry substance, but the domestic variety has a watery substance; for this reason, it ripens hot abscesses <note>original: "apostemata"</note>. However, it does not break stones located in the kidneys. For this reason, we place it in the first degree of coldness, tempered between moisture and coldness.

<margin>Galen</margin>
**Licorice.** Galen says: Its primary virtue is colder than the temperament of the human body, as if it were of a lukewarm heat; therefore, it is close to an equal temperament, and it is moist with a tempered moisture. Its secondary virtue is a power that softens. Its third virtue is that which soothes the roughness of the throat <note>original: "meri", referring to the esophagus or windpipe</note> and the bladder, and 
<margin>Rhazes</margin>
it cuts through thirst. Rhazes says: Licorice benefits the throat and the lungs by expelling the superfluities existing within them. Furthermore, it takes away thirst and the burning of urine.

<margin>Al-Kindi, 3.1</margin>
**Lapis lazuli.** Al-Kindi <note>original: "Alcanzi"</note> says it has a burning and purifying power, and therefore it removes warts. But when taken internally, it loosens melancholic humor <note>one of the four bodily fluids in medieval medicine, associated with depression or sluggishness</note> and purifies the blood from thick humors. The dose is two carats <note>original: "kirath", a small unit of weight</note> up to one dram <note>original: "3. j."</note>, mixed with other laxative medicines. When drunk, it benefits kidney pains and asthma <note>original: "asinati"</note>. If it is ground with vinegar and smeared upon morphea <note>skin lesions</note> and vitiligo <note>original: "baras", a term for white skin patches</note>, it cures them.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
**Litharge** <note>original: "Lythargirum", a lead oxide mineral</note> dries moderately, just as all others of that kind do; it both heats and cools, and it cleanses. In all these things, it acts moderately. Therefore, we often use the material itself by mixing it with others, such as wax, as a base.
<margin>Galen</margin>
Dioscorides says: The virtue of litharge is styptic <note>contracting tissues to stop bleeding</note>, softening, sedative, cooling, and "glutinating" <note>acting as a glue for wounds</note>. It fills putrid ulcers with flesh, removes the "superfluous flesh" <note>granulation tissue or proud flesh</note> that grows in them, and consolidates them. Galen says: Its primary virtue is equally drying, like other drying mineral medicines. Its secondary virtue is one that restricts and cleanses less than a tempered medicine. Its third virtue benefits the chafing <note>original: "excoriationi"</note> that occurs on the skin and other parts due to rubbing while 

<column-break/>

traveling. It serves as the base for all constricting medicines, much like wax.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial M depicting a seated male figure holding a book, surrounded by scrolls and floral patterns.</image-desc>
**Wild Mint** is hot in the third degree and dry in the second. The domestic variety is more moist than the wild. It benefits a cold liver and the belly; it strengthens the stomach and aids digestion. It soothes vomiting and the throat. It is useful for afflictions of the heart, sharpens the appetite, disperses gas <note>original: "flatus"</note>, and kills intestinal worms. The juice of the wild variety especially arouses lust <note>original: "venerem suscitat"</note> and removes obstructions of the liver and spleen. Nevertheless, one should not eat it continuously, because it thins the blood and generates a certain watery waste, changing its quality and turning it into yellow bile. It is advisable for those who have an abundance of yellow bile to abstain from it.

# On the letter L.

...its primary virtue is hot at the end of the first degree, nearly reaching the second <note>Medieval medicine categorized substances by "degrees" of intensity for qualities like heat and moisture, ranging from one to four</note>. Its secondary virtue is that which softens and dissolves through its softening action; it tempers through its dissolving action, and similarly matures. It gathers and strengthens hair that is falling out, heals ulcers that are difficult to close, and when drunk with old wine, it binds the belly and provokes urine.

**Lentils** <note>original: "Lens"</note> are cold in the second degree and dry in the third. They possess a thick humor and a harsh quality. If they are boiled in water, adding oil and salt is considered a suitable drink for dispersing [ill humors]. When boiled twice, they dry out the bowels and check diarrhea, bringing firmness to the stomach; for this reason, they are a suitable food for all intestinal complaints, such as celiac disease and dysentery. Once the husk is removed, much of their binding power is lost. They have slow and thick passages; those who use this food very frequently may fall into elephantiasis <note>original: "elephantas"; in this period, this often referred to leprosy or severe skin thickening</note>, cancers, hardening of the tissues, nerve pains, and melancholic diseases. Indeed, their juice is suitable for producing thick, dry, and melancholic humor and blood. If someone has a watery ailment in their flesh, this food is quite useful, just as it is most harmful to those who are already dry and withered. If one has healthy vision, it dulls it by drying; if one's vision is already dull, it helps by purging the humor. It produces thick blood that flows with difficulty. By its drying action, it fends off sexual desire; thus, it is useful for those practicing celibacy. It causes difficult sleep because of the melancholic humors it returns to the body. If boiled with mint, it greatly reduces flatulence. Some mix in beet during the cooking for this reason. If it is boiled thoroughly until dissolved and applied to wounds from a javelin or a needle, it powerfully stops the flow of blood. A short boiling of lentils relieves stomach cramps, and when dropped into the ears, it helps with ears that are leaking pus.

<margin>
Constantine,
Book 5.
</margin>
**Constantine** <note>Constantine the African, an 11th-century scholar who translated Arabic medical texts into Latin</note> says: Lentils are cold in the second degree and dry in the third, which is why they generate melancholic blood. If a person of a choleric temperament <note>someone naturally hot and dry</note> uses them often, they will become melancholic and eventually suffer from melancholic diseases, such as cancer, elephantiasis, mania, and the like.

**Lupin** <note>original: "Lupinus", a type of legume</note> is of two kinds: one domestic and the other wild. The domestic variety, when soaked for a long time in water, 

<column-break/>

loses its bitterness. In this way, when chewed, it is difficult to digest. It provides nourishment to the body, but it generates thick and raw humor. The wild variety is more bitter and more effective in all things than the domestic kind, though it possesses the same power.

<margin>
Psellus.
</margin>
**Psellus** <note>Michael Psellos, a Byzantine scholar and physician</note> says: Lupin is difficult to digest and generates thick humor; it has a moderate power to soften and to bind the bowels.

<margin>
Rhazes,
Book 2,
Chapter 51.
</margin>
**Rhazes** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi, a Persian physician whose works were central to medieval university education</note> says: Lupins are coarse and hard to digest. However, when they are sweetened <note>by soaking</note> and eaten, they do not heat the body. While they are bitter, they are not suited for nourishment but for medicine. For they dissolve scrofulas <note>original: "scrophulas", swellings of the lymph nodes, often from tuberculosis</note> and cleanse powerfully when administered while still somewhat bitter. They also provoke urine and menstruation. Furthermore, they cause abortion and expel worms from the belly. Moreover, they open the openings of hemorrhoids.

**White Lily** <note>original: "Lilium album"</note> heats and dries, as it is closer to the sharp qualities of the iris, though not composed of such fine parts. It is at the end of the second order of heating things, but it concludes the second order of drying things near its beginning.

<margin>
Averroes,
*Colliget*,
Chapter 42.
</margin>
**Averroes** <note>Ibn Rushd, a major Andalusian philosopher and physician</note> says: White lily is hot and dry in the second degree. We say this because it is bitter. It has a tempered wateriness, and therefore its oil is without any stinging sensation; it is the most excellent of all things for dissolving substances in the matrix <note>the womb</note>. Its leaves, when cooked and placed upon flesh burned by fire, and mixed with boiling water and rose oil, bring immediate relief. The root is stronger than the leaves; therefore, it provokes menstruation and softens the hardness of all members, especially the womb.

**Lettuce** <note>original: "Lactuca"</note> is a moist and cold morsel—not in the extreme, but like very cold spring water. Therefore, it is suitable against inflammations and mild cases of "holy fire" <note>original: "sacros ignes", usually referring to erysipelas, a painful skin infection</note>. As a food, it clearly quenches thirst and induces sleep, especially when chewed after being cooked with orach <note>original: "oricato", a spinach-like leaf vegetable</note>. It is not cooked like other vegetables, nor does it cause much movement or distension in the bowels. It does not generate bad blood, nor does it produce the most excellent humor. Its seed, when drunk, restrains sexual desire; hence it is given to those who suffer from [erotic] dreams. The juice of wild lettuce applied with woman's milk soothes pains, inflammations, and heat...

<summary>This page details the medicinal and dietary properties of lentils, lupins, white lilies, and lettuce, focusing on their effects on the bodily humors, digestion, and reproductive health.</summary>
<keywords>lentils, lupin, white lily, lettuce, humors, Constantine the African, Rhazes, Averroes, melancholy, reproductive health, medieval medicine</keywords>

# On the letter L.

<margin>
Averroes,
Book 5,
Chapter 42
</margin>
**Averroes** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century Andalusian polymath known for his medical encyclopedias</note> says that in **chicory** <note>original: "tibi", likely a corruption of "intybi", chicory or endive</note> there is the same power as in lettuce. Averroes states the herb is of a moist substance like lettuce, but with a more concentrated coldness; the wild variety is of a dry substance, but the domestic kind has a watery substance. Because of this, it matures "hot abscesses" <note>swelling caused by an excess of blood or yellow bile</note>, but it does not break stones located in the kidneys. For this reason, we place it in the first degree of coldness, being tempered between moisture and coldness.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Licorice.** ¶ **Galen.** Its primary virtue is colder than the complexion of the human body, as if it were of a lukewarm heat; therefore, it is near to a balanced complexion and is moist with a temperate moisture. Its secondary virtue is that which softens. Its third virtue is that it softens the roughness of the throat and the bladder, and
<margin>Rhazes</margin>
it quenches thirst. ¶ **Rhazes.** <note>A Persian physician, 865–925 AD</note> Licorice benefits the throat and the lung by expelling the superfluities <note>excess humors</note> existing within them. Furthermore, it takes away thirst and the burning of urine.

<margin>
Alcanzi:
1 drachm
</margin>
¶ **Lapis lazuli.** <note>A deep-blue metamorphic rock used as a pigment and medicine</note> ¶ **Alcanzi.** It has a burning and purifying power, and therefore it removes warts. But when taken internally, it purges the melancholic humor and cleanses the blood of gross humors. The dose is from four carats up to one drachm <note>term: drachm (a unit of weight roughly equal to 1/8th of an ounce)</note>, mixed with other laxative medicines; as a drink, it benefits pains of the kidneys and asthma <note>original: "asinati", likely "asthmati"</note>. If it is ground with vinegar and smeared upon morphew <note>skin discolorations</note> and white leprosy <note>original: "baras", an Arabic term for skin depigmentation</note>, it cures them.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Litharge** <note>original: "Lythargirum"; lead monoxide, a byproduct of refining silver</note> dries moderately, just like all other things of that kind; it heats, cools, and cleanses, and in all things it acts moderately. Therefore, we often use it as a base, mixing it with other things like wax.
¶ **Dioscorides.** <note>A Greek physician and author of De Materia Medica</note> The virtue of litharge is binding, softening, soothing, cooling, and
<margin>Galen</margin>
healing; it fills putrid ulcers with new flesh, removes the "proud flesh" <note>superfluous tissue in a healing wound</note> that grows in them, and heals them. ¶ **Galen.** Its primary virtue is equally drying, just as mineral medicines dry. Its secondary virtue is that it restricts and cleanses less than a balanced medicine. Thirdly, it benefits the chafing that occurs on the thighs <note>original: "coris", likely "coxis" (hips/thighs)</note> and other parts due to rubbing while on a journey. It serves as the base for all constricting medicines, much like wax.

<image-desc>A decorative capital letter 'M' containing a figure standing amongst swirling vines and leaves.</image-desc>

**Wild mint** is hot in the third degree and dry in the second. Domestic mint is more moist than the wild variety. It helps a cold liver and the belly; it strengthens the stomach and aids digestion. It mitigates vomiting and clears the throat; it is useful for ailments of the heart, sharpens the appetite, and disperses gas. It kills intestinal worms, especially the juice of the wild variety. It arouses lust and removes obstructions of the liver and spleen. However, it should not be eaten continuously, because it thins the blood and produces a certain watery humor, and by changing the blood's quality, it turns it into yellow bile. It is beneficial for those already full of yellow bile to abstain from it.
