# On the letter M.

When ground with salt and applied to the bite of a mad dog, it brings a cure. Its seed purges the belly but does not help the lungs. ¶ **Constantinus.** <note>Constantinus Africanus was an 11th-century monk who translated Arabic medical texts into Latin.</note>

<margin>Constantinus</margin>
**Mint** is hot and dry in the second degree, having a certain amount of moisture, from which the fire of lust is stirred. It is beneficial for the coldness of the liver and strengthens the stomach. ¶ **Galen.** <note>Galen of Pergamon (2nd century AD) was the most influential physician of the Roman Empire; his system of "degrees" of heat and moisture defined medicine for 1,500 years.</note> Its primary virtue is hot in the third degree; however, there is raw moisture in it.

<margin>Galen</margin>
Its secondary virtue is that which thins, cleanses, and strengthens; and the third is that which kills intestinal worms. It calms phlegmatic vomiting when drunk alone.

¶ **Fennel** <note>original: "Marathruz", from the Greek 'marathron'</note> or fennel heats sufficiently to be placed in the third order; and it dries, though not in the same way, but in the first. Enough has been said about it in the chapter on fennel.

¶ **Mallow** is cold and moist in the first degree. It passes through the belly easily, not only because of its moisture but also its stickiness, especially when prepared with oil and sprinkled with wine at mealtime. It helps the bladder, the chest <note>original: "thoracā"</note>, and the lungs, and it soothes a hoarse voice. Wild mallow, when applied to bites from wasps or bees, immediately frees one from pain. It is said that its decoction, when drunk, crushes stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, induces sleep, and easily eases the pains of childbirth <note>original: "puerperius"</note>; it softens inflammations, obstructions, and hardness. ¶ **Constantinus.** Mallow is moderately cold and moist; it moistens the belly and helps against a cough; it benefits the roughness of the throat, the lungs, and the chest if cooked with water and almond oil. Eaten in water and with oil, it loosens the belly.

<margin>Constantinus</margin>
¶ **Honey** is hot and dry in the second degree, consisting of fine parts and being cleansing. It contains something sharp as far as excreting is concerned; it rouses the belly and moves urine, but it does not move the bowels unless mixed with much water. Skimmed honey is suitable for the elderly of a cold temperament, but in those of a hot temperament, it turns to bile. When cooked by itself, it becomes less sharp and consequently less nourishing. ¶ **Galen.**

<margin>Galen</margin>
Its primary virtue heats and dries in the second degree. Its secondary virtue cleanses, and when it is cooked and matured, it becomes of little sharpness and little cleansing power; therefore, it is administered to heal fistulas and deep ulcers. But bitter honey is composed of diverse virtues, just as if you were to mix honey with wormwood. ¶ **Rhazes.** <note>Rhazes (865–925 AD) was a Persian polymath and one of the most important figures in the history of medicine.</note> Honey is hot and is quickly turned into red bile; it destroys phlegm

<column-break/>

as if by licking it away. This benefits those who have a cold complexion <note>the balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note> of the senses. However, in summer and for those who have a hot complexion, it is harmful.

¶ **Pomegranates.** <note>original: "Malagranata"</note> ¶ **Rhazes.**

<margin>Rhazes</margin>
The sweet ones do not cool, but they cause inflammation and thirst and soothe the throat. The sour ones, however, cause roughness of the chest and cool the stomach and liver. Those that specifically extinguish red bile are proper for the liver; they strengthen the stomach and

<margin>Constantinus</margin>
liver and remove nausea <note>original: "abominationem", literally a loathing of food</note>. ¶ **Constantinus.** Pomegranates are cold. The dry ones are colder; they are moderate in moisture and dryness. They extinguish red bile, strengthen the stomach and liver, and remove nausea. Their rinds <note>original: "brana"</note> are contrary to loosening the belly <note>meaning they cause constipation</note>; they contract the bilious humors so they do not descend into the stomach. The sweet ones are tempered between hot and moist; their tender seeds help those coughing from heat.

¶ **Medlars** <note>A fruit similar to a small apple, eaten only when overripe or "bletted"</note> partake of heat when ripe; when unripe, they are cold and astringent, and they bind the belly. ¶ **Psellus.** <note>Michael Psellus was an 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar.</note> Indeed, medlars, like service berries <note>original: "sorba"</note>, make the belly styptic <note>contracting or binding</note> and bind a flowing one; service berries are even more powerfully styptic.

<margin>Psellus: On the Reason of Diet</margin>
¶ **Millet** and panic grass are cold in the first degree and dry in the second; they are difficult to digest, bind the bowels, and provide little nourishment. They help those who need to be cooled and dried. When

<margin>Psellus</margin>
taken with milk or almond oil, they are more easily digested and become moister. ¶ **Psellus.** Panic grass and millet provide little nourishment; they cool and dry a moist bowel; they are also digested with difficulty.

¶ **Mastic** <note>A resin obtained from the mastic tree, used as a medicine and chewing gum</note> or mastiche is hot with a certain moisture. It is beneficial for those burdened with sticky phlegm; it draws out phlegm and has healing power. It helps cold stomachs, not only when chewed but also when applied externally. Likewise, an oil prepared from it is beneficial. ¶ **Galen.** It is composed

<margin>Galen</margin>
of diverse virtues, namely a styptic virtue and a softening virtue. Its primary virtue is that which heats and dries in the second degree; the second is that which softens, strengthens, and dissolves.

# On the letter A. <note>Though the header reads "A," the content clearly continues the letter "M" from the previous page, likely a typesetter's error.</note>

<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides:** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> **Mastic** <note>A resin obtained from the mastic tree.</note> helps with the spitting of blood and an old cough when it is drunk: and it is good for the stomach: it induces belching: and it causes the hair of the eyelids to stick; and when it is chewed, it makes the breath smell good: and it tightens the gums.

<margin>Galen</margin>
<margin>Rhazes iii. al.</margin>
¶ **Mandrake** has a dominant power of cooling, so that it is of the third order of cooling things: it brings on sleep. ¶ **Galen.** The primary virtue of mandrake is cold in the third degree: and with this, there is a little dryness: but in the apples of the mandrake there is moisture: and for this reason, they cause **lethargy** <note>original: "subeth," a medieval medical term derived from Arabic for a coma-like sleep</note>. ¶ **Rhazes.** <note>Abu Bakr al-Razi, a Persian polymath and physician.</note> Mandrake is cold, causing stupor: which, if put into wine, greatly intoxicates: but mixed with medicines, it takes away pain: if a very large quantity of it is drunk, it brings about death.

<margin>Rhazes</margin>
<margin>Isaac.</margin>
¶ **Pearls** ¶ **Rhazes.** Pearls are cold and dry in the second degree: and in them there is a little refinement; they help with the dimness of sight and the whiteness of the eye and its impurities: they restrain the menses and clean the teeth: and they dry up moistures. ¶ **Isaac Ibn Amram.** <note>A 10th-century Jewish physician in Kairouan.</note> Pearls are temperate in heat, cold, dryness, and moisture: and the thicker ones are better: and the clear ones are better than the dark. They help with **cardiac distress** <note>original: "cardiace"</note> and tremors of the heart: they clarify the thickened blood of the heart: they enter into medicines that restrain blood.

¶ **Melilot** <note>Sweet clover.</note> is of mixed power: it has a certain bitterness: otherwise it also disperses and digests. For there is more of a hot essence in it than a cold one. **Pliny** calls this **garland of Campania** <note>original: "certulam campanaz" / "sertula campana"</note>. ¶ **Dioscorides.** It is an astringent that softens hot **abscesses** <note>original: "apostematū"</note> and especially those of the eyes or also of the testicles. ¶ **Bedigozas.** <note>Likely referring to Al-Badigūras, an Arabic pharmacological source.</note> It is temperate: its properties dissolve superfluities; it ripens and resolves: and in its flavor, there is
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
<margin>Bedigozas.</margin>
an astringency.

¶ **Horehound** heats in the second perfect order: it also dries in the third perfect order: it removes the obstruction which we call **blockage** <note>original: "oppilationem"</note> of the liver and spleen: and it purges the chest: and the lungs, and moves the menses: and through the nostrils it purges those with **jaundice** <note>original: "ictericos" or "arquatos," the latter referring to the rainbow-like skin discoloration</note>: and it helps with old ear pains when applied, and it cleanses and disperses.

¶ **Melons** and **quince-melons** <note>original: "melopopones"</note> are by no means as moist or of such bad humor as large pumpkins <note>original: "pepones"</note>: nor are they as good for urine: nor for the belly: nor likewise

<column-break/>

for vomiting; nor are they as beneficial for the stomach.
<margin>Psellus</margin>
¶ **Psellus.** <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar.</note> Pumpkins are cold and moist and have some power of purging; therefore they moisten more than the **colocynth** <note>bitter apple</note> and quince-melons: and they generate bad juice in the body by their nature, especially when they are not well digested. Then they cause **choleric** <note>Original: "cholericos", relating to yellow bile</note> effects—not "bilious" as the common people think—but they upset the upper and lower belly: for before they are cooked [digested], they produce vomiting: especially in those who have devoured far too much. ¶ **Rhazes.** Sweet melons quickly
<margin>Rhazes iii. al. ch. xx.</margin>
turn into red bile. Others truly quench thirst and moisten: and provoke urine. If anyone uses too many melons in eating, he will suffer a choleric passion. ¶ **Cucumbers** and **watermelons** <note>original: "citroli"</note> are cold: which both take away thirst and cool the stomach, and provoke urine.

<margin>Rhazes in divisions ch. cxliv</margin>

**The Green Nut** <note>Walnut</note> is hot in the first degree and dry in the second; however, it has a superfluous moisture. When green, it moves the bowels. There are those who believe that if one eats walnuts with figs and **rue** <note>a bitter herb</note> before a meal, they will be immune to lethal medicine <note>poison</note>. Walnuts are certainly suitable for cold stomachs and are easily digested there, but in hot stomachs, they are more altered: they produce yellow bile, bring pains to the throat, and increase headache and cough. Taken before a meal, they cause vomiting; they also serve as remedies for the loosening of teeth.
<margin>
Psellus on the Rule of Living, book 2.
</margin>
¶ **Psellus:** <note>Michael Psellos, an 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar.</note> Walnuts provide little nourishment. When fresh, they have a watery power and are more easily digested and more useful to the stomach, especially when chewed with their skins removed along with **dried figs** <note>original: "caricisi"</note>. Dried walnuts soaked in water with the skin removed are held to be in the place of green and fresh ones.

¶ **Spikenard** <note>original: "Nardi spica"</note> heats in the first degree and dries in the completed second degree. It consists of a somewhat tart and sharp essence, not excessively hot, and with a brief bitterness. Therefore, it is very suitable for the liver and the stomach when drunk or applied externally. It moves the urine and removes bites and twinges; it cures the stomach and also dries up fluctuations in the belly and intestines. Furthermore, it benefits the head and the chest. The **Indian** variety is stronger, which is blacker than the Syrian. Read the chapter on the Spike.

¶ **Celtic Nard** has almost the same power as that already mentioned, except that it is weaker in all things, except for moving urine, as it is indeed hotter than the others, but less tart.

¶ **Pontic Nuts**, which are also **Hazelnuts**: they are hot and moist. They provide more nourishment than the aforementioned nuts, but they are more difficult to digest, they cause gas, and they cause distress.

# On the letter N.

...as some say, an intestine: that which is named the **fasting** <note>original: "ieiunum," the jejunum or middle part of the small intestine</note>: it is more easily digested, and it constricts the bowels less when the skin is removed. Some also report that if anyone eats them with **rue** <note>a bitter medicinal herb</note> before food, they will not be harmed by any bite or any poison of a scorpion that day; and scorpions will flee from the person if they are taken with dry figs. Those already bitten by scorpions are helped. Chewed hazelnut brings pain to the head.

---

<margin>Albasari.</margin>
¶ **Water Lily** <note>original: "Menuphar seu nilofar"</note> ¶ **Albasari.** It is cold in the third degree and moist in the second. Being made of subtle parts, it is penetrative. It takes away sleeplessness arising from heat. However, there is one species of water lily in which there is sharpness, heat, and subtlety; so much so that when we wish to provide heat in "cold" illnesses, we administer it and find it helpful. Syrup of water lilies benefits pain of the side <note>pleurisy</note>, the lungs, and coughs. It softens the bowels, induces sleep, and sedates pains. Oil of water lilies is stronger than violet oil; it is called "the killer of bees." It helps with hot **soda** <note>original: "sode," a term derived from Arabic for a throbbing headache</note> and provides relief when placed over hot abscesses.

<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides.** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist.</note> When its dry root is drunk with wine, it helps with chronic flux <note>diarrhea</note> and ulcers of the intestines, and it dissolves abscesses of the spleen. A plaster is made with it for pain of the stomach and bladder. When mixed with water and applied to white **morphea** <note>a skin condition causing discolored patches</note>, it cleanses it. When mixed with pitch and applied to **alopecia** <note>hair loss</note>, it cures it. It is drunk to stop nocturnal pollution <note>involuntary seminal emission</note>; however, if someone uses it too much, it weakens the genitals. Its seed has the same power in all these matters.

---

<margin>Galen.</margin>
¶ **Black Cumin** <note>original: "Nigella"</note> ¶ **Galen.** Its primary virtue heats and dries in the third degree. Its secondary virtue cleanses, cuts through [thick humors], and dissolves. Its third virtue cures **coryza** <note>the common cold or nasal congestion</note> when it is roasted, placed in a linen cloth, and smelled. It powerfully dissolves flatulence when taken internally and kills worms. It takes away warts and spots, and helps asthmatics. It provokes the menses when they are retained because of viscous humors. It dries up breast milk and helps against the bite of a **rutella** <note>likely a small venomous spider or insect</note>.

<margin>Abenmesuai.</margin>
¶ **Abenmesuai.** <note>Masawaih, a 9th-century Persian physician.</note> It kills **ascarides** <note>intestinal roundworms</note> and takes away phlegmatic and melancholic fevers.

<margin>Abenmesuai. Mesehaben.</margin>
¶ **Nutmeg.** <note>original: "Nux muscata"</note> ¶ **Abenmesuai.** It is hot and dry in the third degree. It is good for a cold stomach and liver. ¶ **Mesehaben.** <note>Likely Mesue the Younger.</note> It is hot and dry

<column-break/>

at the end of the second degree; it binds the bowels and makes the breath smell good.

<margin>Artran.</margin>
¶ **Coconut.** <note>original: "Nux indica," literally "Indian nut."</note> ¶ **Artran in the book on foods.** The Indian nut is hot in the second degree and moist in the first. It is heavy on the stomach, yet it does not produce bad **chyme** <note>the fluid mass of digested food</note>. Those of a choleric temperament should not use it. Its aged oil helps with flatulence of the loins, pains of the knees, and hemorrhoids that flow from phlegm. When the oil is drunk, it loosens the bowels and benefits the bladder. <margin>Abraam.</margin>

When its bark is taken, ground, and sifted, and one takes 1 drachm of it with two **aurei** <note>a weight unit, approximately 4-5 grams each</note> of ground dill or fennel seed, and it is prepared with sufficient honey and drunk with hot water: it induces vomiting and expels choleric and phlegmatic superfluities. It also loosens the bowels from below according to its power and the nature of the superfluities. <margin>Habic.</margin> ¶ **Habit.** It causes powerful vomiting on its own. <margin>Galen.</margin>
¶ **Watercress.** <note>original: "Nasturtium"</note> ¶ **Galen.** Its seed has a heating and drying power like mustard seed. Its second virtue is that it cuts [humors] strongly and burns. Its third virtue is that it calms sciatic pains and headaches, and any illness in which it is necessary to apply heat. Its seed is mixed into asthma medicines when it cuts through thick humors. It is said that when watercress is dried, its power becomes like that of mustard seed. But while it is fresh, because of the watery moisture in it, it has a weaker power than the seed. ¶ **Dioscorides.** Watercress seed is heating, sharp, and bad for the stomach. It softens the bowels, expels worms, and dissolves abscesses of the spleen. It causes abortion and incites the desire for intercourse. It cleanses ulcerated scabies and **impetigo** <note>a contagious skin infection</note>. Given in a drink, it helps against venomous bites and cures fire burns. There is another species called "roof watercress," and its power is also hot and subtle; it opens boils formed inside the body. It provokes the menses and destroys the fetus. When used as an enema, it helps with sciatica, though it sometimes draws blood. The seed purges bile through vomiting and flux of the bowels, and it provokes the menses.

**N**ux viridis <note>The Green Walnut</note> is warm in the first degree and dry in the second; however, it possesses a superfluous moisture. When green, it moves the bowels. ¶ **Pontic Nuts**, which are also called **Hazelnuts** <note>original: "auellane"</note>, are warmer and moister than the aforementioned walnuts. They provide more nourishment, but are harder to digest, and they cause bloating and offense to the stomach.

# On the letter N

...as some say, the intestine—specifically the one named the jejunum <note>The "hungry" or middle part of the small intestine.</note>—is more easily digested and less binding for the bowels once the husk is removed. Some also report that if anyone eats these <note>Referring to the hazelnuts mentioned on the previous page.</note> with rue before a meal, they will not be harmed that day by the bite or poison of any scorpion; scorpions will even flee from a person if they are consumed with dried figs, and those already bitten by scorpions are helped by them. However, chewing hazelnuts brings on a headache.

<margin>White water lily</margin>
¶ **Water Lily** <note>original: "Menuphar seu nilofar," derived from the Arabic *nīlūfar*.</note> or **Albafari**. It is cold in the third degree and moist in the second. Composed of subtle parts that can penetrate, it takes away sleeplessness caused by heat. There is, however, one species of water lily which possesses sharpness, heat, and subtlety; thus, when we wish to provide warmth in "cold" illnesses, we administer it and find it helpful. Syrup of water lilies is beneficial for pain in the side, the lungs, and for a cough. It softens the bowels, induces sleep, and soothes pains. Water lily oil is stronger than violet oil and is called "the killer of bees" <note>original: "interfectorum apum," likely a folk name or a reference to its potency/scent.</note>. It is useful for a "hot" headache <note>original: "sode calide," from the Arabic *suda* for headache.</note> and is beneficial when applied over hot abscesses.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides**. When its dried root is drunk with wine, it helps with chronic discharge <note>original: "fluxui antiquo," likely chronic diarrhea or dysentery.</note> and ulcers of the intestines, and it dissolves abscesses of the spleen. A plaster is made from it for pain of the stomach and bladder. When mixed with water and applied to white morphea <note>A skin condition involving discolored patches.</note>, it cleanses it; and when mixed with pitch and applied to alopecia <note>Patchy hair loss.</note>, it cures it. It is also drunk to stop nocturnal emissions <note>original: "pollutionem," referring to involuntary seminal loss.</note>; however, if someone uses too much of it, it weakens the genitals. Its seed has the same power in all these matters.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Black Cumin** <note>original: "Nigella," often *Nigella sativa* or Fennel Flower.</note>. ¶ **Galen**. Its primary quality warms and dries in the third degree. Its secondary quality cleanses, cuts through thick humors, and resolves them. Its third quality cures coryza <note>The common cold or a runny nose.</note> when it is roasted, wrapped in a linen cloth, and smelled. When taken internally, it powerfully resolves gas and kills intestinal worms. It removes warts and skin spots and is beneficial for those with asthma. It provokes menstruation that has been suppressed by viscous humors, dries up breast milk, and helps with the bite of a spider <note>original: "rutelle," likely a species of venomous spider or insect.</note>.

¶ **Nutmeg** <note>original: "Nux muscata"</note>. ¶ **Avenzoar**. It is warm and dry in the third degree; it is good for a cold stomach and liver. ¶ **Defehaben**. It is warm and dry

<margin>Artrum</margin>
¶ **Coconut** <note>original: "Nux indica," literally "Indian Nut."</note>. ¶ **Artrum in the Book of Foods**. The coconut is warm in the second degree and moist in the first. It is heavy on the stomach, yet it does not produce bad humors. Those of a choleric temperament should not use it. When drunk, the oil relaxes the bowels and helps the bladder; one dram <note>original: ".ʒ. i."</note> of it is taken with peach-kernel oil.

<margin>Abraham</margin>
¶ **Nux Vomica** <note>original: "Nux vomica," the seeds of the *Strychnos nux-vomica* tree, used as an emetic but highly toxic due to strychnine.</note>. ¶ **Abraham**. It is a nut whose color is between gray and white, slightly larger than a hazelnut, and there are nodes <note>bumps or markings</note> on it. When its rind is taken, ground, and sifted, and one dram of it is taken with two *aurei* <note>a unit of weight, roughly 1/6 of an ounce</note> of ground dill or fennel seed, mixed with sufficient honey and drunk with warm water, it induces vomiting. It expels choleric and phlegmatic superfluities and also relaxes the bowels below, according to its power and the nature of the waste. <margin>Habit</margin> ¶ **Habit**. It causes powerful vomiting on its own. The amount of its dose is two drams.

---

<margin>Galen?</margin>
¶ **Cress** <note>original: "Nasturtium," usually Garden Cress or Watercress.</note>. ¶ **Galen**. Its seed has a warming and drying power like mustard seed. Its secondary power cuts through humors strongly and stings the skin. Its third power soothes sciatic pains and headaches, and any sickness in which warming is required. Its seed is mixed into asthma medicines when it cuts through thick humors. It is said that when cress is dried, its power becomes like that of mustard seed. But while it is fresh, because of the watery moisture within it, it has a weaker power than the seed. ¶ **Dioscorides**. Cress seed is warming, sharp, and bad for the stomach. It softens the bowels, expels worms, and resolves abscesses of the spleen. It causes abortion and incites sexual desire. It cleanses ulcerated scabies <note>mange or skin sores</note> and impetigo. It is beneficial for venomous bites when given immediately, and it cures burns from fire. There is another species called "Cress of the Roofs" <note>original: "nasturtium tectorum," possibly Stonecrop</note>; its power is also warm and subtle, and it opens boils that have formed inside the body. It provokes menstruation and destroys the fetus. When a clyster <note>enema</note> is made with it, it helps with sciatica, though it sometimes draws blood; nevertheless, it purges bile through vomiting and flux of the belly and provokes menstruation.

**Rhazes.** It <note>Likely referring to the throat or an internal passage from the previous page.</note> dilates it. ¶ **Mixture.** **Myrrh** <note>A resin from the *Commiphora* tree.</note> is hot. It is suitable for a long-standing cough and makes the voice clear. However, it brings on dizziness <note>original: "scotomiam," a darkening of vision or vertigo.</note> and induces sleep; furthermore, it provokes menstruation and, when drunk, provides relief for scorpion stings.

<margin>
Avicenna.
Rhazes.
</margin>
¶ **Marjoram** <note>original: "Maiozana," likely *Majorana*.</note>. ¶ **Galen.** Its primary power is heating and drying in the third degree; secondarily, it dissolves and thins <note>original: "subtiliat," referring to the thinning of bodily humors.</note>. ¶ **Rhazes.** Marjoram is hot and thinning; it is beneficial for all "cold" ailments that occur in the brain.

<margin>
Arbabari.
</margin>
¶ **Mumia** <note>In this period, Mumia refers to bitumen or a resinous substance found in tombs, used as a panacea.</note>. ¶ **Arbabari.** It is hot and thinning; it is good for falls, blows, and flatulence. It restrains blood and is the most excellent of all medicines for spitting blood <note>original: "sputum sanguinis" or hemoptysis.</note>. It aids in fractures and bruising of the internal and external parts of the body; it is beneficial for the chest and lungs.
<margin>

Book 3 of the *Almansor*,
Chapter on
phlegm (?).
</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Mumia is good for those spitting blood; it restores a rupture or fracture quickly. Furthermore, it soothes pains of the throat, dislocations, concussions, and wounds. Those who have said that it heals perfectly have lied. Additionally, it helps pain caused by "cold" in the nostrils when blown in with elderberry oil.

<margin>
Avicenna.
</margin>
¶ **Lemon Balm** <note>original: "Melissa."</note>. ¶ **Galen.** Its power is like the power of horehound <note>original: "prassij."</note>, except it is less potent. It effectively provokes menstruation and helps with toothache, the sting of a scorpion, the bite of a spider <note>original: "rutelle," likely *tarantula*.</note>, and the bite of a dog; it gladdens the soul.
<margin>
Rhazes,
Book 3 of the *Almansor*,
Chapter 18.
</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Lemon Balm is hot. Because it is a thinning substance, it is suitable for those suffering from tremors of the heart. While it causes gas <note>original: "inflationem," bloating.</note>, it raises the penis <note>i.e., it acts as an aphrodisiac.</note>; furthermore, it provides a desire for eating and takes away vomiting and hiccups.

<margin>
Mesue.
</margin>
¶ **Manna** <note>A sweet exudate from trees like the flowering ash, used as a laxative.</note>. ¶ **Mesue.** It is balanced, though leaning more toward heat. It is soothing, cleansing, purifying, and sedative. There is no excess in it. However, it is among those substances that cause a weak bowel movement. It draws out yellow bile with ease. It softens the throat, chest, and belly, and it settles thirst. Its dose is from six to fifteen drams <note>original: ".a.z." is a common abbreviation for drams or ounces.</note>. It may be preserved for one year.

Platearius in
the book
*Circa Instans*.

¶ **Platearius.** Manna is more harmful than helpful when boiled <note>original: "in decoctiõe."</note>. It is never found pure; therefore, it should not be used in large quantities for acute fevers, because it is harmful due to being mixed with honey. See the chapter on Persian manna <note>original: "tereniabin."</note>.

**Green Nut** <note>The Walnut, *Juglans regia*.</note> is hot in the first degree and dry in the second; it has, however, a superfluous moisture. When green, it moves the bowels. There are those who believe that if anyone eats these nuts with figs and rue before a meal, they will be immune to lethal medicine <note>poison</note>. Nuts are certainly suitable for "cold" stomachs and are well digested there; in "hot" stomachs, they are more easily altered and produce yellow bile. They bring pain to the throat, and they increase headache and coughing. Taken before a meal, they cause vomiting; they also provide a remedy for the loosening of teeth.
<margin>
Psellus
on the rule
of diet,
Book 2.
</margin>
¶ **Psellus.** Nuts provide little nourishment. When fresh, they have a watery power and are more easily digested; they are more useful to the stomach when their skin is removed, especially when chewed with dried figs. Dried nuts soaked in water with the skin removed are held to be the same as green and fresh ones.

¶ **Spikenard** <note>original: "Nardi spica," *Nardostachys jatamansi*.</note> heats in the first degree and dries completely in the second. It consists of a somewhat sharp and pungent essence, not excessively hot, with a slight bitterness. Thus, it is very suitable for both the liver and the stomach when drunk or applied externally. It moves the urine and removes bites and twinges. It cures the stomach with its slight bitterness, and it also dries up fluctuations <note>gas or churning</note> in the belly and intestines. Furthermore, it benefits both the head and the chest. The Indian variety is stronger, which is darker than the Syrian. Read the chapter on "Spica."

¶ **Celtic Nard** has nearly the same power as that already mentioned, except it is weaker in all respects—unless used for moving urine, as it is hotter than the others; however, it is less sharp.

¶ **Pontic Nuts**, which are also **Hazelnuts**, are hot and moist. They nourish more than the aforementioned walnuts, but they are more difficult to digest and cause gas; they also cause harm <note>likely meaning they cause headaches, as noted on the previous page</note>.

# On the letter N

...as some say, the intestine: which is called the fasting <note>original: "ieiunum," referring to the jejunum, the middle segment of the small intestine.</note> intestine: it is more easily digested: and it constricts the belly less when the husk is removed. Some also report that if anyone chews them with rue <note>A bitter herb (*Ruta graveolens*) used in antiquity as an antidote to poison.</note> before food, they will not be harmed by either a bite or any poison on that day; scorpions will flee from the person. If they are taken with dried figs, they help those already bitten by scorpions. ¶ Chewed hazelnuts bring on a headache.

<margin>
Albasari
</margin>

¶ **Nenuphar or Nilofar.** <note>The Water Lily.</note> ¶ **Albasari.** <note>An Arabic name for the water lily.</note> It is cold in the third degree and moist in the second; its subtle parts are penetrating. It takes away insomnia arising from heat. However, there is one species of water lily in which there is sharpness, heat, and subtlety; thus, when we wish to provide warmth in "cold" illnesses, we administer it and find it helpful. Syrup of water lily is beneficial for pain in the side and the lungs, and for a cough; it softens the belly, induces sleep, and calms pains. Oil of water lily is stronger than violet oil; it is called the "bee-killer." It is beneficial for a hot headache <note>original: "sode calide," from the Arabic *suda*, meaning a localized headache or migraine.</note> and is helpful when placed upon hot swellings <note>original: "apostemata," inflammatory tumors or abscesses.</note>.

<margin>
Dioscorides.
</margin>

¶ **Dioscorides.** <note>The 1st-century Greek physician and author of *De Materia Medica*.</note> When its dry root is drunk with wine, it helps with chronic flux <note>Diarrhea or dysentery.</note> and ulcers of the intestines, and it dissolves swellings of the spleen. A plaster is made with it for pain of the stomach and bladder. When mixed with water and placed upon white leprosy <note>original: "morpheam," a term used for various skin discolorations or localized scleroderma.</note>, it cleanses it; and when mixed with pitch and placed upon hair loss <note>original: "alopiciam," alopecia.</note>, it cures it. It is drunk to prevent nocturnal emissions <note>original: "pollutionem."</note>; however, if someone uses it too much, it weakens the genitals. Its seed has the same power in all these things.

<margin>Galen.</margin>

¶ **Nigella.** <note>Black Cumin or Fennel Flower.</note> ¶ **Galen.** Its primary power is heating and drying in the third degree; secondarily, it cleanses, cuts <note>original: "incidit," referring to the ability to break up thick humors.</note>, and dissolves. Thirdly, it cures a cold <note>original: "corizam," nasal catarrh.</note> when it is roasted, placed in a linen cloth, and smelled. It dissolves strong bloating when taken internally. It kills intestinal worms, removes warts and spots, and helps asthmatics. It provokes suppressed menstruation caused by viscous humors, dries up breast milk, and helps with the bite of a shrew <note>original: "rutelle," likely referring to the *rutela* or a small venomous creature.</note>.

<margin>
Ibn
Masawayh
</margin>

¶ **Ibn Masawayh.** <note>Also known as Mesue the Elder, a Persian physician.</note> It kills pinworms <note>original: "ascarides."</note> and removes phlegmatic and melancholic fevers.

<margin>
Ibn
Masawayh
Mesue the

</margin>

¶ **Nutmeg.** <note>original: "Nux muscata."</note> ¶ **Ibn Masawayh.** It is hot and dry in the third degree; it is good for a cold stomach and liver. ¶ **Mesue the Son.** It is hot and dry

<column-break/>

at the end of the second degree; it binds the belly and makes the breath smell good.

<margin>Artram</margin>

¶ **Indian Nut.** <note>original: "Nux indica," usually referring to the coconut.</note> ¶ **Artram** in the *Book of Bees*. ¶ The Indian nut is hot in the second degree and moist in the first. It is heavy on the stomach; however, it does not produce bad chyme <note>The semi-fluid mass of partly digested food.</note>. Those of a choleric temperament should not use it. Its aged oil helps with flatulence in the loins, pains in the knees, and hemorrhoids that flow from phlegm. When the oil is drunk, it relaxes the belly and helps the bladder; one drachm <note>represented by the symbol 3. j.</note> of it is taken with peach kernel oil.

<margin>Abraham</margin>

¶ **Nux vomica.** <note>The seed of the *Strychnos nux-vomica* tree, containing strychnine; used historically as an emetic.</note> ¶ **Abraham.** It is a nut whose color is between blue-gray and white, slightly larger than a hazelnut, and there are nodes in it. When the husk is taken, ground, and sifted, and one drachm of it is taken with two gold coins' weight <note>original: "aureis," a unit of weight.</note> of ground dill or fennel seed, mixed with sufficient honey and drunk with hot water, it induces vomiting. It expels choleric and phlegmatic superfluities and relaxes the bowels according to the strength and nature of the superfluities. ¶ **Habie.** <note>An Arabic authority.</note> It causes strong vomiting on its own, and the amount of its dose is one drachm.

<margin>Galen.</margin>

¶ **Nasturtium.** <note>Watercress or garden cress.</note> ¶ **Galen.** Its seed has a heating and drying power like mustard seed. Its secondary power is that it cuts strongly and burns. Its tertiary power is that it calms sciatic pains and headaches, and any sickness in which it is necessary to apply heat. Its seed is mixed into asthma medicines when it cuts through thick humors. It is said that when nasturtium is dried, its power becomes like that of mustard seed. But while it is fresh, because of the watery moisture within it, it has a weaker power than the seed. ¶ **Dioscorides.** Nasturtium seed is heating, sharp, and bad for the stomach. It softens the belly, expels worms, and dissolves swellings of the spleen. It causes abortion and incites the urge for intercourse. It cleanses ulcerated scabies and skin eruptions <note>original: "impetiginem."</note>, helps with poisonous bites when applied as a plaster, and cures burns from fire. There is another species called "nasturtium of the roofs" <note>likely *Sedum* or a similar stonecrop.</note>; its power is also hot and subtle, and it opens boils formed inside the body. It provokes menstruation and destroys the fetus. When an enema is made with it, it helps with sciatica, though it sometimes draws blood. The seed purges bile <note>original: "cholera."</note> through vomiting and flux of the belly, and provokes menstruation.

<column-break/>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial "O" containing a bird and floral motifs. The word begins with this ornamental letter.</image-desc>
**Oil** is moderately warm and very moist. When raw and pressed, it is somewhat astringent <note>original: "astringit," referring to a substance that contracts body tissues.</note> and thus cooling. The older it is, the warmer it becomes and the greater its power to draw out humors, especially if it was thin to begin with. This is determined if it is pure and translucent. Its heat and dryness are distinguished by taste, for sweet oil is of moderate warmth. That which is becoming bitter, however, is cold, and is useful for the stomach.

<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Oil is warm; however, that in which a greater sharpness <note>original: "morsus," literally a 'bite' or stinging sensation on the tongue.</note> and a stronger odor is perceived is warmer. Furthermore, it does not cause a loss of appetite as other oily substances do, nor does it have their heaviness. ¶ **Nut oil** is vehemently hot and dissolving in nature. ¶ **Cyperus oil** <note>Oil from the roots of the Sedge or Galingale plant.</note> is warm and heats the kidneys. ¶ **Almond oil** is tempered; it provides help to the chest and lungs, as well as the bladder and kidneys, yet it causes a loss of appetite and descends slowly. ¶ **Radish oil** is hot and subtle <note>In Galenic medicine, "subtle" means thin and capable of penetrating deep into the tissues.</note> and dissolving; it provides a remedy for ear pain caused by cold or thick windiness <note>original: "ventositate," referring to gas or flatulence within the body's cavities.</note>. ¶ **Ben oil** <note>original: "Oleum de been," oil from the Moringa tree.</note> is hot and softening. ¶ **Lily oil** is hot and subtle, soothing the nerves and benefiting pain of the womb. ¶ **Narcissus oil** <note>original: "Oleum de narasco."</note> is like that made from lilies. ¶ **Violet oil** is cold and induces sleep. ¶ **Water lily oil** is similar to this, but acts more strongly. ¶ **Gourd seed oil** is judged similar to those two. It is also suitable for heat and wakefulness. **Butter** provides more nourishment than all other oily substances and is thicker. ¶ **Rose oil** is cold; it provides a remedy for headache and other ailments arising from heat. Ultimately, all oily substances retain the likeness of the things from which they are made. ¶ **Costus oil** <note>Oil from the root of the *Saussurea lappa*.</note> is hot; it warms the ner-

<column-break/>

-ves, providing help to those with tremors and paralysis. It benefits a cold stomach if applied as an epithem <note>A liquid medicinal poultice or wash applied externally.</note>, and if mixed with plasters, it is helpful. ¶ **Myrtle oil** is cold and makes the hair strong. ¶ **Wallflower oil** <note>original: "Oleum de keiri," from the *Cheiranthus cheiri*.</note> is hot and subtle, soothing and resolving, especially that which is made from the yellow variety. ¶ **Balsam** is vehemently hot; it even breaks stones <note>Refers to kidney or bladder stones.</note>. ¶ **Spikenard oil** <note>original: "Oleum nardinum."</note> is hot; it is suitable for a cold stomach when applied as an epithem. ¶ **Mastic oil** likewise provides a benefit when mixed into a plaster and placed over a cold stomach.

¶ **Basil** <note>original: "Ocimuz," commonly called Basilicum.</note>, which is called "basil" (for since it is a Latin name, it signifies what the Greeks call *erinon*), has a moderate warmth, though according to some it reaches the second degree. Its scent helps the brain; when sprinkled with rose water, it is more moist and induces sleep. Its seed succors those with heart ailments and brings those with black bile <note>original: "atra bili," associated with melancholy and depression.</note> from a state of lifelessness back to cheerfulness and alacrity.

<margin>Avenzoar</margin>
¶ **Avenzoar.** <note>Also known as Ibn Zuhr, a 12th-century Andalusian physician.</note> It is hot and dry at the end of the second degree; it opens blockages of the brain and benefits heart problems caused by phlegm and melancholy. When eaten or smelled, it helps a blocked nose, increases yellow bile, and is good for hemorrhoids. It benefits a cold stomach, causes coarse food to be digested, and helps the liver and heart.

¶ **Eggs** differ among themselves; those that are fresher are better because their effect is best. Those that can be sipped <note>original: "sorbilia," or soft-boiled eggs.</note> go down more easily, soothe the roughness of the throat, but nourish less. Hard-boiled eggs are difficult to digest and pass through slowly, providing a coarse nourishment to the body. Due to their poor quality, eggs roasted in hot ash are worse, and fried eggs provide by far the worst nourishment. Those prepared in hot water are approved. Goose eggs produce bad humors; hen eggs seasoned with butter are used extensively and are said to sharpen the intellect. Eggs cooked with vinegar constrict the belly by drying out distillations <note>original: "distillationes," the downward flow of catarrh or fluids.</note> and expelling phlegmatic humors in whatever way possible.

<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** The eggs most suitable for humans are those of the hen and the partridge; they greatly increase semen and incite arousal for intercourse. Likewise, the yolk, which is tempered in its warmth, nourishes well. The white, however, is cold and viscous, and is digested with difficulty; moreover, the blood generated from it is not good.
¶ Furthermore, eggs benefit the throat and the lungs...

# On the letter O.

<margin>Galen</margin>
[...] to harshness: and those in whom the blood is well-tempered and a generator of much strength, or those who are very fat, should not use them: at times they take the place of meat. ¶ **Galen.** The complexion of an egg is slightly colder than a tempered body: for it cools and dries in a moderate way without any biting sensation <note>original: "mordicatione," referring to a stinging or corrosive effect on the tissues</note>: and it is necessary that they be administered fresh: for old ones are not good.

¶ **Sheep's meat** is excessive <note>original: "redundans," implying it produces an overabundance of humors</note> and of bad juice <note>In ancient medicine, "juice" or "succus" refers to the quality of the fluids produced during digestion</note>: meat from a yearling is less harmful: that which is older is difficult to digest, possesses worse juice, and harms moist and phlegmatic stomachs.

¶ **Barley** is in the first rank of drying and cooling agents: it has a certain power of cleansing <note>term: "abstergent" — a substance that scours or cleanses the body's internal channels</note>. Sometimes it dries more than bean flour. For the bean is of a denser essence than barley: and therefore nourishes more than it. Barley certainly generates a thin and cleansing juice. Thus, it does not heat the body in whatever way it is prepared, for when prepared, it provides moisture. Barley flour made from crushed barley evidently dries; but barley-water <note>original: "ptisana," a medicinal porridge or decoction</note> moistens when it has been prepared as required. However, all barley breads nourish less than those made from wheat, and they move the bowels more than those.
<margin>Ali Abbas, Book 5 of the Theory, chapter 15</margin>
¶ **Ali Abbas.** Barley is cold in complexion in the first degree, and dry in the second. Its nourishment is less than that of wheat, and it is less viscous and thick; it generates windiness <note>flatulence</note>. But if it is cooked in water, it becomes cold and moist, and its dryness is expelled, and it becomes a suitable food for "burnt" diseases <note>likely referring to high fevers or inflammatory conditions</note>. For it cools, moistens, and smoothes. It is also suitable for those with fevers, for people of a hot and dry complexion, and for the thirsty. One should choose barley that is new, white, and hard, which is also firm: and which swells and inflates greatly while cooking: from this, let it be carefully prepared and moderately ground.
<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Galen.** Its first virtue cools and dries in the first degree: and its second virtue is that it cleanses with a slight scouring: and its third virtue is similar to the virtue of beans when applied externally: but it does not cause bloating as beans do.

¶ **Oregano.** There is a third species of this herb with the power of cutting <note>original: "secandi," the medicinal ability to break up thick humors</note>, thinning, drying, and heating. These are ranked in the third degree. For the Heracleotic kind is more effective than the *oritis* <note>original: "ouitide," a mountain variety of oregano</note>: it is wilder than the *heracleum* <note>referring to Panaces Heracleum</note>; others call it "stem," and there is also that which is called *tragozigonus* <note>goat-oregano</note>

<column-break/>

which also admits a certain bitterness.
<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides.** It is of three species: one is called Heracleotic oregano: and its primary virtue is heating and drying in the third degree: its second is thinning and cutting. The second species is called *orithis* and the third *tragorinus* <note>goat-oregano</note>.

¶ **Bitter Vetch** <note>original: "Orobus"</note> dries to a wide extent in the second degree; but it heats according to the first degree. To the extent that it admits bitterness, it also cuts and cleanses, and removes obstructions: but when taken in excess, it drives blood through the urine.

¶ **Opium.** ¶ **Dioscorides.** Opium is the gum of the black poppy: and its juice cools more than the seed; it also dries and thickens. ¶ **Mesue** <note>original: "Mesidennus," likely referring to Mesue the Younger</note> indeed says that the benefit of opium is only in its scent, causing sleep. In all other ways, its use is bad and very dangerous. ¶ **Galen.** Its second virtue cleanses, cuts, dissolves, and diminishes. And its third virtue is that when it is boiled in water until half is consumed, it is beneficial for diseases of the liver. The same author, in the eighth book of *Simple Medicines*: opium, which is made from the juice of the poppy, is cold in the fourth degree and dry in the third. ¶ **Platearius.** Opium is cold in the fourth degree and dry in the first.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical medical compendium, moving from the end of the letter O (eggs, mutton, barley) into the letter P. It focuses on the dietary and medicinal properties of fish, pears, apples, pumpkins, poppies (including opium), and leeks, citing authorities like Rhazes, Psellus, Averroes, Dioscorides, and Galen.</meta>

# On the letter P.

<margin>
Polypody (a fern)?
Purslane.
Pellitory.
</margin>

All **fish** are of a cold and moist complexion: but those that are more flavorful than others are better because they are easy to digest, possess good juices <note>term: "juice" (succus) — in ancient medicine, this refers to the quality of the fluids or "humors" produced by food during digestion</note>, and are moderately moisturizing, provided their flesh is not hard. In the second rank of quality are marine fish that live at the mouths of rivers. However, those nourished in mud and stagnant pools are wicked. The signs of fish with good juice are: having soft flesh, not being sticky, lacking an earthy smell, not being excessively fatty, not changing or rotting immediately when exposed to the air, and finally, being pleasant to the taste and having thin skin. For fish of this kind are easy to digest and produce proven blood, although the blood generated by all fish is thinner than that produced by land animals.

<margin>
Rhazes.
Book 2,
Chapter 16.
</margin>

¶ **Rhazes.** Indeed, all fish are hard to digest and remain a long time in the stomach; they also cause a foul stagnation <note>original: "situm," referring to a musty or decaying state of the humors</note>, and the blood generated from fresh fish is phlegmatic. Moreover, these fish moisten the body and increase semen; but they are harmful to those who are prone to cold illnesses. However, for those with a hot complexion and those dominated by red bile <note>original: "cholera rubea," one of the four humors associated with heat and dryness</note>, they are beneficial; nevertheless, their nutrition is generally bad, and many illnesses arise from them. Salted fish are by no means to be eaten, except on a day when one wishes to take medicine <note>likely referring to a day of purging</note>. If, however, someone craves them, let only a small quantity be taken.

¶ **Pears** are cold in the first degree and dry in the second: those that are sweeter and ripe share a certain moisture and heat; but those that are of a sweet yet tart quality, or even acidic, possess some heat, a moderate amount of other qualities, and a slight dryness. If taken before a meal, they bind the belly <note>original: "cohibent ventrem," meaning they act as an astringent to stop diarrhea</note>, especially the tart ones; taken greedily and to satiety, they cause colicky effects. They are suitable for hot stomachs, and their seeds are, by some specific property, useful for ailments of the lungs; however, they harm the kidneys. After a meal, they are useful to the stomach and also extinguish thirst.

<column-break/>

<margin>
Rhazes
</margin>

¶ **Rhazes.** Pears that are very sweet do not have a cooling effect. Nevertheless, they all bind the belly. If they are eaten after a meal, this occurs: once eaten, they quickly expel the stool, after which expulsion their final effect is to bind the belly.

¶ There are many species of **apples**: those that are tart have a cold and earthy juice; those that appear acidic are indeed cold, but of a thin essence; those of a medium complexion are sweet, leaning toward a warm quality.

<margin>
Psellus,
On the 
Regime of 
Life, 
Book 2.
</margin>

¶ **Psellus.** Apples that are tart have a cold and earthy juice, which is certainly thick; however, those that are acidic are cold and of thin parts, being of a middle temperament; the sweeter ones are judged to be warmer.

¶ The **pumpkin** <note>original: "pepo," likely referring to a type of melon or gourd</note> is cold and moist in the second degree; that which is sweet is less cold. Read concerning this in the chapter on melons.

¶ The **poppy** is cold and dry; the white is better than the black; it induces sleep, is difficult to digest, and provides little nutrition. Taken with honey, it increases bile. It settles the chest and the windpipe <note>original: "asperam arteriam"</note>, coughs, and the belly; it does not, as some claim, harm the head, though taken to excess it generates a heaviness in the head. The black poppy is colder and more sleep-inducing, such that if someone is excessive in its use, they will be buried in a most profound sleep, like those suffering from lethargy. Applied to the head with rose oil, it aids a headache caused by heat. Notable physicians record that, when applied with woman's milk and saffron, it relieves those suffering from gout. Its juice is lethal; for the juice of the black poppy is that which is named **opium**.

<margin>
Averroes.
</margin>

¶ **Averroes.** In the fifth book of the *Colliget*, chapter 42. Poppy-husks <note>original: "cascas"</note>, that is, the poppy, is cold and moist; the white is cold in the third degree, the black in the fourth.

<margin>
Dioscorides.
Galen.
</margin>

¶ **Dioscorides.** Its juice dries and thickens.

¶ **Galen.** Their primary power cools in the fourth degree <note>the most extreme level of a quality in medieval medicine</note>; and their secondary power is narcotic and deadening.

¶ The **leek** is hot and dry in the second degree; some, however, place it near the fourth. It has bad juice and encourages urine; it blurs the vision if it comes into constant use and makes sleep difficult. It is bad for the stomach, heats the semen, causes headache, and harms the liver, kidneys, and bladder. It is useful against hemorrhoids when boiled in water with vinegar and fish sauce <note>term: "garum" — a fermented Mediterranean condiment used both in cooking and as a medical base</note>.

It notably identifies opium as the lethal juice of the black poppy and warns of the narcotic effects of extreme "cold" substances.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical medical compendium for the letter P. It picks up mid-discussion regarding the properties of leeks and proceeds through partridges, pepper, peacocks, pheasants, pork, and peaches. It draws heavily on the "humoral" system of medicine, which balances the body's four fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</meta>

# On the letter P.

[...leeks] seasoned with oil and cumin are beneficial for cold stomachs. <margin>Galen.</margin> ¶ **Galen.** They possess such a degree of heating power that they can blister the skin when applied externally to the body. And I have indeed already said that all medicines that heat with such intensity are at the highest of degrees. <margin>Rhazes.</margin> ¶ **Rhazes.** The **leek** is hot and dry: although it may provide help to the appetite, it nevertheless causes the head to ache and brings about bad dreams; it is an evil thing for those accustomed to suffering from migraines <note>original: "cephaleam," a chronic or intense headache</note> and those who are harmed by heat.

¶ The meat of **partridges** is easy to digest, especially if it is not eaten immediately after death; for it then casts off the hardness it naturally possesses. It binds the belly <note>meaning it treats diarrhea or acts as a mild constipant</note> and generates thin blood; if it encounters thick blood, it thins it out—especially the saltwater-pickled parts <note>original: "alex," a fermented fish sauce or brine often used for preserving meats</note> and the meat under the wings. The rest, being easy to digest, is beneficial for those resting from exercise, those weak in power, and those on a thin diet. For moist stomachs, the marrow of partridges taken with wine helps those with jaundice <note>original: "arquatos," a term for the jaundiced, referring to the "rainbow" or golden color of the skin</note>. The liver, however, is for banquets; the bile <note>original: "fel"</note> is extremely beneficial for the eyes at the onset of "suffusions" <note>term: "suffusions" (suffusionum) — an early term for cataracts or clouded vision</note>. It benefits dim sight, and when placed in the nostrils with oil of jasmine <note>original: "inozatum," likely a corruption of "ozatum" or "anizatum" relating to jasmine or scented oil</note>, it improves the memory. <margin>Rhazes. / other version.</margin> ¶ **Rhazes.** Partridge meat, being thicker in comparison to chicken, binds the belly and nourishes greatly. <margin>Constantine.</margin> ¶ **Constantine.** Partridges are hard. <margin>Averroes. book 5 / Colliget / chapter 31.</margin> ¶ **Averroes.** The meat of partridges is among the most praiseworthy of bird meats, but it leans slightly toward coldness and dryness; they are like desert hens and have the property of binding the belly.

¶ **Pepper** is hot and dry in the third degree: it cuts through thick and sticky humors and disperses gas <note>original: "flatus," meaning wind or gas in the digestive system</note>; it also dissipates moisture in the chest, lungs, and belly. It harms the kidneys, and it is said that if placed in the anus after intercourse, it prevents female conception and causes sterility. Some have placed it in the fourth degree of heating and drying agents. <margin>Serapion.</margin> ¶ **Serapion.** If someone uses pepper excessively, it provokes urine; if one uses it only a little, it relaxes the belly—and in this, scammony <note>a harsh herbal purgative</note> acts as its opposite. It makes a person grow thin and dries up the semen; however, in white pepper, along with its sharpness, there is a moisture that increases semen. One kind is long, another is black and round. <margin>Platearius.</margin> ¶ **Platearius.** White pepper is hot at the start of the first degree and dry at the end of the fourth; it is called *leucopiper*. Long pepper is hot in the third degree and moist in the second; it is called *macropiper*. Black and round pepper is hot in the middle of the fourth

<column-break/>

degree and dry at its end; it is called *melanopiper*. Given in food, it strengthens digestion.

¶ **Peacock** meat is fibrous, abundant, difficult to digest, and produces bad juices. Some have claimed that broths <note>original: "apozemas," a decoction or herbal infusion</note> made from it have a specific property that benefits those with pleurisy, especially if the broth is succulent and fatty. Its fat, mixed with the juice of rue and honey, is said to be most helpful against colicky pains arising from cold humors. The eggs of this bird, burnt and mixed with vinegar and smeared on, are useful against leprosy and skin eruptions <note>original: "vitiligines," refers to patches of skin depigmentation or similar conditions</note>. Some say that peacock meat can be preserved for thirty years without rotting <note>This was a popular medieval belief famously cited by St. Augustine to prove the possibility of miracles</note>.

¶ **Pheasants** are easy to digest and generate good-quality blood; they should be considered entirely like chicken meat, as they do not differ much from them in similarity.

¶ **Pork** meat has good juice; when a year old, it is easy to digest and very similar to the human body. Indeed, it is said that certain people, forced by necessity to eat human flesh, reported that it seemed very similar to pork. It is more nourishing than all other foods. For unless it is very well tempered <note>processed or prepared correctly</note>, pork meat would make for bad food (since it feeds on all sorts of filthy things) and would not be transformed into the best flesh. Just as human bodies, if they are well-tempered, are not harmed by foods of bad humors; even if they grow weak afterward, they later transform back into a nature of good humor. <margin>Averroes. book 5 / Colliget / chapter 29.</margin> ¶ **Averroes.** And **Avicenna** says that the best of meats is pork, and he feels that this meat is, as it were, more natural to humans than the meat of other walking animals; experience teaches this.

¶ **Peaches** are placed in the second rank of cooling and moistening things. They generate a phlegmatic humor and are difficult to digest, rotting easily in the belly; because of this, those who fill themselves with them are seized by fevers. By their specific property, they harm the nerves. They ought to be eaten before other food, and one should drink pure wine with them. Those that are ripe loosen the bowels; those that are unripe are astringent <note>constipating</note>, and even more so if they are dried. The juice of the leaves, when drunk, kills worms. <margin>Constantine. Pantegni book 5.</margin> ¶ **Constantine.** Peaches are cold and moist in the second [degree].

...degree and generates phlegm. The food made from them is thicker when they are cooked: but they are not easily transformed <note>that is, digested and turned into blood</note> unless they are stripped and separated from the stones, in which case they are tender: they are quickly digested, but the opposite is true for the opposite parts.
<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** **Peaches** are cold and thick: although they benefit a burning stomach, they nevertheless descend with difficulty, and are converted into blood with difficulty. Whoever uses them as food will fall into the generation of phlegmatic fevers <note>fevers caused by an excess of the "cold" humor, phlegm</note>.

¶ **Bread** is not of just one kind: this arises from the material, the method of making it, and finally the baking. It also matters not a little how you eat it. The best is certainly from dense wheat and selected grain, so that it does not resist the teeth too much, and when broken it is porous and appears loose; color alone is not enough, but it should be easy to break. Ordinary bread <term>cibarius: "fodder" or household bread made for the common people</term> is of little nourishment and passes through the body quickly because of the cleansing power it has from the bran, which ejects from the intestines. That bread which is first-rate and made of select soft flour is slow to pass through the channels; the purer it is, the more highly regarded it is, and it generates blood and nourishes more.
<margin>Psellus, Book 2 on the Regimen of Living</margin>
¶ **Psellus.** Wheaten bread is the principal food in lunches and dinners; made with fine flour chosen by sifting the bran, slowly cooked and moderately tempered with leaven and salt. Second is that bread from fine wheat <note>original: "siligine"</note> and semolina <note>original: "similagine"</note>: it nourishes little. Bread full of bran, which is called ordinary bread, made from fine wheat is difficult to digest; and if it is digested, it generates raw humors. It also binds the bowels; therefore it suits bodies that exercise, but is bad for those who are idle. Pure bread from the finest flour <note>original: "polline"</note> suits exercised bodies but is useless for others. Ordinary bread nourishes little, is melancholic <note>tending to produce "black bile"</note>, and moves the bowels. Old breads dry the body out and nourish less than fresh ones; fried breads are drier and nourish less; less leavened ones are difficult to digest. Fresh fine-wheat bread refreshes all the senses of the head with its smell, confirms the spirits, and restores strength to the weak.
<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Bread made from wheat is the most suitable for the majority of people. It is also rendered better when it has much salt and much leaven, is well fermented, and is well cooked: whence it is both more quickly digested and found to be thinner and more refined. However, unleavened bread <note>original: "Azimus"</note> is digested with difficulty and descends slowly from the stomach. It causes pains in the belly, creates obstructions in the liver, and creates stones in the kidneys.

¶ **Cinquefoil** <note>original: "Pentaphylum," the five-leaved herb</note>, the herb of Mercury: the root of this dries in the third degree, but it is by no means sharp: therefore it is also considered very useful. For since it consists of thin parts, its use is very beneficial for ulcers of the bladder.

<column-break/>

<margin>Rhazes, book 2, chapter 22</margin>
¶ **Fleawort** <note>original: "Psyllium"</note>. The seed of this is primarily useful in the second order of cooling medicines; it is a medium between drying and moistening. ¶ **Rhazes.** Fleawort is cold. If it is drunk with julep <note>a sweet medicinal syrup</note>, it extinguishes an acute fever and calms the burning; it also soothes the chest. When roasted and drunk, it helps those who have bloody wounds in their intestines. If it is mixed with vinegar and stirred until it coagulates, and then placed upon limbs suffering from hot swellings <note>original: "apostemata"</note>, it calms the pain.
<margin>Platearius</margin>
¶ **Platearius.** Against a rough tongue in acute fevers, let it be placed and tied in a thin cloth and soaked in water; then let the tongue be smeared with such water, and let the tongue be scraped with a knife. Against thirst, let it be held under the tongue; it is appropriately used in syrups against acute fevers.

¶ **Parsley** <note>original: "Petroselinum"</note>; some have named it "sweet-parsley" <note>original: "glicydium"</note>. The seed of this is by far the most useful, as the herb itself is weaker. The seed is hot and dry in the third order, having the power of the second degree: therefore it draws out the menses and urine abundantly, and it works without causing flatulence.
<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Galen** says: as it appears to the taste, it is sharp with bitterness, thus in reality it is hot and "cutting" <note>referring to its ability to break up thick humors</note>. In Cilicia they call it "rock parsley" when it grows on Mount Amanus; it is also called *finyrmiū* <note>likely "smyrnium" or horse-parsley</note> or *petroselinum*; it does not differ much in power from [standard] parsley.
<margin>Constantine in the Book of Degrees</margin>
¶ **Constantine.** They say *Petroselinum* is a type of celery <note>original: "apiy genus"</note>, which is hot and dry at the end of the third degree. Its seed provokes urine and the menses; it dissolves windiness and flatulence. It is valuable for those with dropsy and periodic fevers; it cuts away pain of the kidneys and bladder; it cleanses the liver. It opens obstructions, especially in the kidneys; it dissolves the windiness of colic. Placed as a suppository in the womb, it provokes the menses and expels the afterbirth and the dead fetus.

¶ The **Poplar** tree is of a somewhat mixed temperament, consisting of a watery, lukewarm, and earthy essence: whence its nature is of a cleansing power, and it is somewhat bitter to the taste.
<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides.** When one ounce <note>original: "aur. .j."</note> of its bark is drunk, it benefits sciatica and the dripping of urine; and it is said that it prevents conception when drunk with the kidney of a mule <note>a common ancient folk belief for contraception</note>. And it is said the leaf does the same; and the juice of its leaves, when dripped lukewarm into the ear, benefits its pains; and when its fruit...

# On the letter P.

...is taken and mixed with honey: and an eye-salve <note>original: "collirium"</note> is made from it; it cures darkness of vision.

<margin>Rhazes, Almansor, chapter 20</margin>
<margin>Constantinus in the Pantegni, book 5</margin>
**Plums** move the bowels and do so quite effectively, yet they dry the body out less than other fruits. ¶ **Rhazes.** Plums are cold; although they move the stomach, they nevertheless repress red bile <term>cholera rubea: one of the four humors, associated with heat and bitterness</term> and take away the appetite. ¶ **Constantinus.** Plums and cherries are cold in the first degree and moist in the second. Acidic ones are colder and healthier; sweet ones are more laxative. Acidic ones extinguish heat; dry plums are less laxative than fresh ones.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 3 of the Almansor</margin>
**Pellitory** <note>original: "Pyrhetrum," likely Spanish Chamomile, Anacyclus pyrethrum</note>. We mostly use the root of the Pellitory, as it has a burning potency. Because of this, it mitigates pains in parts that have been chilled for a long time. Against the rigors <note>shivers or tremors</note> of persistent fevers, it is ground with oil before applications, and it helps those who are numbed or sleepy. ¶ **Rhazes.** Pellitory, being hot, is suitable for toothache and mouth sores; it also benefits paralysis and the rigors of fevers.

<margin>Galen</margin>
**Polypody** <note>a type of fern</note>. ¶ **Galen.** Its power is to dry strongly without "biting" or irritation.
<margin>Avenzoar</margin>
¶ **Avenzoar.** Its specific property is that it purges melancholy and phlegm without stinging or harmful side effects. The dose for its decoction or infusion is from 2 drams <note>original: "3 ij."</note> up to 5 drams. Without decoction or infusion, the dose is 1 to 2 drams.
<margin>Mesue the Younger</margin>
¶ **Mesue.** Some doctors were clever for those who could not bear to drink medicines: they would throw the ground plant into their food. It purges melancholy gently. Its dose by itself with sugar is 2 drams, and in decoction with other medicines, it is 4 drams.
<margin>Rhazes, Book 3 of the Divisions, chapter 115</margin>
<margin>The same, Almansor</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Polypody draws out melancholy and "false phlegm" <note>phlegm that has become salty or acidic</note>; it strongly heals the cracks <note>fissures</note> that occur in the hands. It is used in decoctions with epithyme <note>a parasitic plant, dodder of thyme</note>; the dose should be from two to three drams. ¶ **Rhazes.** Polypody, being hot, expels black bile and dissolves colic.

<margin>29. Constantinus, Book 5 of the Pantegni</margin>
**Purslane.** ¶ **Constantinus.** It is cold in the second degree and moist in the third. It helps those with a hot nature; the leaves are cooling; they benefit the teeth. The stems are styptic <note>substances that stop bleeding</note>; they help with the spitting of blood from the chest, and are good for those with dysentery and for women with a flux of blood. A poultice of its juice mitigates headaches and swellings caused by heat. One who is cold by nature should eat it with mint, rocket, and celery.
<margin>Rhazes, Almansor, chapter 18</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Purslane is cold; extinguishing thirst and internal burning, it binds the stomach. It takes away the "setting on edge" <note>original: "congelationem," the sensitive feeling in teeth after eating acidic things</note> of the teeth. It benefits those with an excess of red bile and those suffering from diarrhea caused by red bile; it also diminishes the production of sperm.

<column-break/>

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
**Pellitory-of-the-Wall** <note>original: "Paritaria seu vitriola"</note> or green glasswort has a quality that is not dry. The leaves are hot and dry in the third degree; it has a diaphoretic <note>sweat-inducing</note> power. The seed, however, is cold and moist. ¶ **Dioscorides.** The power of its seed is styptic and cold. Its seed, when used in poultices, extinguishes "holy fire" <term>ignis sacer: a term for various inflammatory skin conditions, often erysipelas or shingles</term>. It treats burns, restrains all tumors, clears pustules, and treats those with gout when mixed with "cypress saffron" or goose fat <note>original: "axungia apzina," likely a corruption of "anserina"</note>. It restrains tumors of the throat when used as a gargle or ointment. Mixed with rose oil, it mitigates earache.

<margin>Silvaticus</margin>
¶ **Silvaticus.** Pellitory-of-the-wall, heated in a pot without liquid, is placed on the painful part; or better yet, cooked in wine. When mixed with bran in a white wine that is somewhat acidic, it helps greatly. Prepared this way, it also cures coldness of the stomach and intestines and their pain. It is hot and dry in the third degree, and its seed is cold and moist. Against strangury <note>painful, drop-by-drop urination</note> and dysuria, it should be cooked in salt water and oil and applied as a poultice. For those who vomit blood, grind the pellitory, extract the juice, and let them drink it.

<margin>Averroes, Book 5</margin>
**Plantain.** ¶ **Averroes.** It is cold and dry in the second degree. Its root is less cold and more dry. When the leaf is dried, it is like the root. It has two qualities because it is composed of a watery and an earthy substance; this is shown by its tastelessness combined with its styptic <note>astringent</note> quality. Its secondary actions are that it dries and repels; it is effective against bad swellings and putrid matter, and it cures fistulas. Its third properties are against wounds of the intestines; it binds their blood and the ulcerations that arise from dysentery. Its root is effective against toothache and opens blockages of the liver and kidneys. This is because every plant's root is hotter than its leaves; yet the leaves are not devoid of heat, as we see that they scour and cleanse.
<margin>Rhazes, Almansor, chapter 39</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Plantain is cold, being suitable for hot swellings and fire burns. When placed on as a plaster, it also helps earache if the pain is caused by heat; its seed benefits ulcers of the intestines.
