<meta>This page continues the alphabetical entries for the letter P, specifically concluding a comparison of fruits (likely quinces and peaches) before moving into an extensive section on the dietary properties of different types of bread and the medicinal uses of herbs like Cinquefoil, Fleawort, and Parsley.</meta>

-># On the letter P.<-

...in degrees, it generates phlegm. The flesh of these <note>original: "coctanozū," referring to quinces</note> is thicker than that of peaches, but they are not easily converted; however, once stripped from the stones and separated, they are tender and quickly digestible; otherwise, the opposite is true.
<margin>*Rhazes.*</margin>
¶ **Peaches**. Peaches are cold and thick; although they benefit a burning stomach, they nevertheless descend with difficulty and are converted into blood only with hardship. Furthermore, whoever makes a habit of eating them will fall into the generation of phlegmatic fevers.

¶ **Bread** is not of a single kind; its variety arises from the material, from the making of it, and finally from the baking. It also matters not a little how you eat it. The best is certainly made from dense wheat and selected grains, so that it does not resist the teeth too much; when broken, it should appear porous and loose. It is not just the color that matters, but the sifting of the wheat. Therefore, **coarse bread** <term>cibarius panis: common bread containing the bran, often used by the lower classes or as "fodder" bread</term> provides little nourishment and passes through quickly because of the cleansing power the bran has in ejecting the intestines. That bread which is primary and made of selected soft flour moves through the passages slowly; the purer it is, the better blood it produces and the more it nourishes. <margin>*Psellus, Book 2 on the Regimen of Health.*</margin>
¶ **Psellus**. Wheat bread is the principal food at lunch and dinner; that made from flour sifted into fine dust is choice. It should be cooked slowly and be well-tempered with moderate yeast and salt. Bread from rye and semolina is second best. Bread with much bran, which is called coarse bread, nourishes very little. Bread from rye is difficult to digest, and if it is digested, it generates raw humors. It also constricts the bowels; therefore, it suits active bodies but is bad for the idle. Pure bread made from fine flour suits healthy bodies but is useless for those exercising. Coarse bread feeds little, is melancholic, and moves the bowels. Old bread dries the body and nourishes less than fresh; toasted bread is drier and nourishes less; bread with less yeast is difficult to digest. Fresh rye bread, by its smell, refreshes all the senses of the head, confirms the spirit, and restores strength to the sick. <margin>*Rhazes.*</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. Bread made from wheat is more suitable for most men. It is rendered even better when it has plenty of salt and yeast, is well fermented, and well baked; hence it is digested more quickly and is found to be thinner and more subtle. **Unleavened bread** <term>azimus: bread made without yeast or leavening agents</term>, however, is digested with difficulty and descends slowly from the stomach. It causes pain in the belly, blockages in the liver, and creates stones in the kidneys.

¶ **Cinquefoil** <note>original: "Pentha-phyllum," literally 'five-leaf'</note>, the herb of Mercury. The root of this dries in the third degree; it is by no means sharp, and therefore it is considered very useful. It consists of subtle parts; its use is very beneficial for ulcers of the bladder.

<column-break/>

¶ **Fleawort** <note>original: "Psyllium"</note>. The seed of this is primarily useful in the second order of cooling medicines; it is a middle ground between drying and moistening. <margin>*Rhazes, Almansor Book 2, chapter 17.*</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. Fleawort is cold. If it is drunk with a julep <term>iulep: a sweet, clear medicinal syrup</term>, it extinguishes acute fever and calms internal heat. It also soothes the chest. If roasted and drunk, it helps those having bloody wounds in the intestines. If it is mixed with vinegar and stirred until it coagulates and then placed upon limbs suffering from hot swellings <note>original: "apostemata"</note>, it calms the pain. <margin>*Platearius.*</margin>
¶ **Platearius**. Against roughness of the tongue in acute fevers, it should be placed in a thin cloth and tied, then soaked in water. The tongue should be smeared with this water and then scraped with a knife. For thirst, it should be held under the tongue; it is also appropriately placed in syrups against acute fevers.

¶ **Parsley** <note>original: "Petroselinum"</note>; some have named it *glycydum*. The seed of this is by far the most useful part of the herb. The seed is hot and dry in the third order and has a "cutting" power <note>referring to its ability to break up blockages</note>; therefore, it provokes menstruation and large amounts of urine, and it does so without causing bloating. ¶ Galen says: as is apparent to the taste, it is sharp with bitterness, and thus in reality it is hot and cutting. In Cilicia, they give the name *petroselinum* only to that which grows on Mount Amanus; it is also called *smirnium* <note>likely Alexanders, Smyrnium olusatrum</note> or *petroselinum*, and it does not differ much in power from common parsley. <margin>*Galen.*</margin>
¶ **Constantinus**. They say parsley is a type of celery <term>apium: a genus including celery and parsley</term> which is hot and dry at the end of the third degree. Its seed provokes urine and menstruation; it dissolves windiness and bloating. It is valid for those with dropsy and periodic fevers; it cuts away the pain of the kidneys and bladder and cleanses the liver. It opens blockages especially in the kidneys and dissolves the windiness of colicky passion. Applied as a suppository to the womb, it provokes menstruation and expels the afterbirth and the dead fetus.
<margin>*Constantinus Africanus, in the Book of Degrees.*</margin>

¶ **The Poplar tree** is in a way of a mixed temperament, consisting of a watery-tepid and an earthy essence; hence its nature is powerful for cleansing, though it is somewhat bitter to the taste. ¶ **Dioscorides**. When a dram of its bark is drunk, it helps with sciatica and the dripping of urine; and it is said that it prevents conception when drunk with the kidney of a mule. It is also said that the leaf does the same; and the juice of its leaves, when dripped warm into the ear, helps with its pains; and when its fruit...

# On the letter P. #
->k iij<-

...it is taken, ground, and mixed with honey: and from it an eye-salve is made [that] cures dimness of sight.

<margin>Rhazes, *Almansor*, book 2, chapter 20</margin>
¶ **Plums** loosen the bowels and do so quite effectively; however, they dry the body less than other fruits. ¶ **Rhazes**. Plums are cold: although they move the stomach, they nevertheless repress red choler <note>original: "choleram rubeam," one of the four bodily humors</note> and take away the appetite. 
<margin>Constantine, *Pantegni*, book 5.</margin>
¶ **Constantine**. Plums and cherries are cold in the first degree and moist in the second. Acidic ones are colder and more healthful; sweet ones are more laxative. The acidic ones extinguish heat, while the dried ones are less laxative than the fresh.

¶ **Pellitory of Spain**. We primarily use the root of the **Pellitory** <note>original: "Pyrethrū," *Anacyclus pyrethrum*</note>; it possesses a power by which it mitigates the pains of cold teeth. Against the shivers of persistent fevers, it is ground with oil before applications, and it helps those who are numb or drowsy. 
<margin>Rhazes, book 2 of the *Almansor*.</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. Pellitory, being hot, is suitable for toothache and mouth sores. It is beneficial for paralysis and the shivers of fevers.

<margin>Galen.</margin>
¶ **Polypody**. 
<margin>Galen: Its greatest virtue is that it dries strongly without causing a biting sensation.</margin>

<margin>Ibn Masawayh</margin>
¶ **Ibn Masawayh**. Its specific property is that it purges melancholy and phlegm without stinging or ill effect. The dose of its decoction or infusion is from 2 drachms <note>symbol: ʒ</note> up to 5 drachms; and without decoction or infusion, from 1 drachm to 2 drachms. 
<margin>Mesue.</margin>
¶ **Mesue**. Some physicians were clever for those who could not drink medicines, and they would throw the ground herb into some of their foods. It purges melancholy gently. Its dose by itself with sugar is 2 drachms, and in decoction with other medicines, 4 drachms. 
<margin>Rhazes, book 2, *The Division*, chapter 64.</margin>
<margin>The same author, *Almansor*, book 2, chapter 29.</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. Polypody truly draws out melancholy and salty phlegm: and it strongly heals the cracks <note>original: "scissuras"</note> that occur in the hands. It is placed in decoctions with epithyme <note>dodder of thyme</note>; the dose of which should be from two to three drachms. 
<margin>Rhazes: Polypody, being hot, expels black choler and dissolves colic.</margin>

<margin>Constantine, book 5 of the *Pantegni*.</margin>
¶ **Purslane**. 
<margin>Constantine. It is cold in the second degree and moist in the third. It helps a hot nature; the leaves "congeal" <note>soothe or set</note> and are good for the teeth. The branches are styptic <note>substances that shrink tissue or stop bleeding</note>: they are good for spitting blood from the chest, for those with dysentery, and for women with a flow of blood. A plaster made from its juice mitigates headache and swellings caused by heat. One who is cold by nature should eat it with mint, rocket, and celery.</margin> 
<margin>Rhazes, *Almansor*, book 3, chapter 18.</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. Purslane is cold: extinguishing thirst and burning, it binds the belly; it takes away the "setting on edge" <note>original: "congelationem"</note> of the teeth. It is beneficial for those having an excess of red choler, and for those who suffer a flux of the belly

<column-break/>

arising from red choler: it also diminishes semen.

<margin>Dioscorides.</margin>
¶ **Pellitory-of-the-Wall** or green **Glasswort** <note>original: "Paritaria seu vitriola"</note> has a virtue that is not dry. The leaves are hot and dry in the third degree; it has a diaphoretic <note>sweat-inducing</note> power. But the seed is cold and moist. 
<margin>Dioscorides. The virtue of its seed is styptic and cold. Its seed, when applied in plasters, extinguishes "holy fire" <note>likely erysipelas, a skin infection</note>. It treats burns. It suppresses all tumors and clears up pustules. It treats those with gout when mixed with saffron oil <note>original: "croco ciprino"</note> or with lamb fat. It suppresses swellings of the throat as a gargle or when rubbed on top. Mixed with rose oil, it mitigates ear pain.</margin>

<margin>Silvaticus.</margin>
¶ **Silvaticus**. Pellitory-of-the-wall, heated in a pot without liquid, is placed under the aching part; or even better, boiled in wine; and with bran in white wine that is somewhat acidic, it helps greatly. So prepared, it also cures coldness of the stomach and intestines, and their pain; it is hot and dry in the third degree, and its seed is cold and moist. Against strangury and dysuria <note>difficult or painful urination</note>, let it be cooked in salt water and oil and applied as a plaster. For those who cast up blood, grind the pellitory, extract the juice, and let them drink it.

<margin>Averroes, book 5.</margin>
¶ **Plantain** 
<margin>Averroes. It is cold and dry in the second degree. Its root is less cold and more dry. When its leaf is dried, it is like the root; and it has two qualities: because it is composed of a watery and an earthy substance, and its tastelessness combined with its styptic quality signifies this. Its secondary actions are that it dries, repels, and is effective against bad swellings and putrid matter, and it cures fistulas. Its tertiary properties are against wounds of the intestines; it binds their blood and heals the ulcerations that come from dysentery. Its root is effective against toothache, and it opens obstructions of the liver and kidneys; this is because the root of every plant is hotter than its leaves, yet those leaves are not deprived of heat, since we see that they cleanse and purify.</margin> 
<margin>Rhazes, book 3 of the *Almansor*, chapter 39.</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. Plantain is cold, being suitable for hot swellings and burns from fire. When applied as a plaster, it also helps ear pain if it arises from heat; its seed is beneficial for ulcers of the intestines.

## On the letters Q and R. ##

**Oak.**
**The Four Seeds.**
**The Five Roots.**
**Greater Wall Germander.**
**Lesser Wall Germander.**

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' with floral patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc> All parts of the **Oak** <note>original: "Quercus"</note> have an astringent quality; however, this is most concentrated in the cartilaginous material found beneath the bark and within the hardwood of the trunk. Regarding its medicinal power, enough has already been said in the chapter concerning the acorn.

¶ **The Four Seeds** <note>original: "Quattuor granatorum," referring to the Four Greater Cold Seeds of medieval pharmacy</note>. These are sometimes found labeled as the "four grains," and they are the four common larger "cold" seeds: specifically those of the melon, the cucumber, the gourd, and the *citrullus* <note>original: "citruli," likely referring to the watermelon or a specific citron-gourd</note>. The *citrullus* is a species of cucumber, but it is considerably longer than our local variety. Its seed is black—that is, its outer skin is—but the inner seeds are white. For more on these, see their individual chapters.

¶ **The Five Roots** <note>original: "Quinq; radices," known as the Five Opening Roots</note> consist of fennel, celery, rock parsley, butcher's broom, and asparagus. The word "root" <note>original: "radix"</note> is so named because it is fixed into the earth as if by certain "rays" <note>original: "radijs"</note> and is submerged into the depths. For natural philosophers say that the depth of the roots is equal to the height of the trees.

¶ **Greater Wall Germander** <note>original: "Quercula maior," literally "greater little oak"</note>, according to Simon of Genoa, is *chamaepitys* <note>Ground-pine</note>. Among the Greeks, this is interpreted as "lowly pine" <note>original: "infima pinus"</note>, from *chame*, meaning "brief" or "low," and *pitheos*, meaning "pine," because all species of this plant have the scent of pine. By more recent authors, this is called *uva vera*; Mesue praises it in his chapter on diseases of the nerves under the name *zigmai*, which is the same thing.

<margin>William [of Piacenza].</margin>
¶ **Lesser Wall Germander** <note>original: "Quercula minor"</note> is *chamaedrys*, not *chamaepitys* as Matthew Silvaticus falsely interprets it. ¶ **William of Piacenza** says: The "Oak of the Earth" or "Lesser Wall Germander" is *chamaedrys*, meaning lowly or small oak. It comes from *chami*, meaning "lowly," and *dris* or *dzia* <note>original: "dris dzia," Greek: *drys*</note> meaning "oak." Therefore, *chamaedrys* means a lowly or small oak.
<margin>Pliny. Avicenna, book 2 of the Canon, the chapter on *chamedreos*.</margin>
**Pliny** says: *Chamaedrys* is the herb that the Latins call the "little oak." ¶ **Avicenna** calls it "Oak of the Earth," and this is the plant that today is commonly called *calandrina*. ¶ **Abu Jarij** <note>original: "Abugerig," likely a reference to the 7th-century physician Ahrun</note> says a syrup is made from it for an old cough, for the corruption of digestion, for the onset of dropsy <note>edema</note>, and for spasms. The older the syrup is, 

<column-break/>

the greater its power will be. The crushed herb is beneficial for a tear duct fistula, and a decoction of it helps with "black jaundice." ¶ **Galen**.
<margin>Galen.</margin>
Its flavor is bitter, and with this, there is a certain sharpness. Its primary virtue is that it heats and dries in the second degree, though its heat is greater than its dryness. Its secondary virtue is that it cuts through and cleanses. Its third is that it dissolves hardness of the spleen, provokes urine and menstruation, cuts through thick humors, and clears the blocked passages of the internal organs.

**Turnips.**
**Rosemary.**
**Rue.**
**Rose.**
**Radish.**
**Rhubarb.**
**Currants.**

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'R' with stylized foliage and floral motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc> **Turnips** <note>original: "Rape"</note> are hot in the second degree and moist in the first. They provide significant nourishment, provoke urine, cause gas, and produce semen; they also soothe the throat and chest. If used continuously, they produce thick humors and block the liver. They neither loosen nor bind the bowels. Their seed, when ground and drunk, inflames the desire for love <note>sexual desire</note>. ¶ **Constantine**. The turnip is hot and moist, providing heavy food; it is flatulent, very nourishing, increases sperm, and is somewhat diuretic.
<margin>Constantine in the *Pantegni*, book 5.</margin>

¶ **Rosemary** is hot in the second degree and dry in the first; however, its exact degree is not determined by all authors. It has a certain astringent quality; it binds the bowels and dries them. It helps against coughs and catarrh <note>original: "destillationes"</note>. It provokes menstruation whether taken as a drink or as a suppository. Because its juice has the property of driving away the plague when used as an incense, it is useful during times of pestilence to frequently fumigate houses with rosemary, as it improves the quality of air that has been altered and corrupted.

¶ **Wild Rue** is hot and dry in the fourth degree, while the domestic variety is in the third. It cuts through thick and sticky humors and [is expelled] through the urine...

# On the letter R. #

[The text continues from the previous page regarding **Rue**] ...exhausts: it is suitable against inflations <note>original: "inflationes," referring to gas or bloating</note>: it restrains sexual desire: and **Rhazes** <note>original: "Rasis"</note> says it restores much. ¶ **Rhazes**. **Rue** is hot and dry; <margin>Rhazes.</margin> it dissolves [humors]. ¶ **Isaac**. <margin>Book 2, other chapter 17.</margin> **Wild Rue** is hot and dry in the fourth degree; <margin>Isaac.</margin> the **Domestic** variety is in the third: which is better for digestion because it has the power of "cutting" <note>A medical term for breaking down thick or sticky fluids in the body.</note> through thick and viscous humors and thinning them. ¶ **Dioscorides**. <margin>Dioscorides.</margin> **Rue** is among the things most helpful for inflations and windiness. It also extinguishes the desire for intercourse: it provokes urine and menstruation; it binds the belly: and its seed is used in medicines against deadly substances. It is the ultimate medicine for providing relief against deadly drugs and against the malice of poisons. It is helpful for pains of the side, the chest, for asthma, for coughing, and for abscesses of the lungs; for sciatica, for pain in the joints, and for shivering fits. It is especially effective if taken boiled with dried dill: it is also valuable for cramps of the belly and the womb, and for "suffocations" <note>A historical term for hysterical or respiratory distress related to the womb</note> of the same: it kills worms.

¶ **The Rose** is cold and dry, consisting of a sour and bitter quality: its scent helps "hot heads" <note>Those suffering from feverish or inflammatory conditions</note>: but it harms "moist" ones and triggers "distillations" <note>Runny noses or catarrh</note>. When taken internally, it helps those suffering from fevers caused by yellow bile. It strengthens the stomach and the liver: <margin>Bal. <note>Likely an abbreviation for a commentator or practitioner</note></margin> by its specific power it harms the testicles: it restrains sharp vapors so they do not climb into the head. ¶ **Galen**. Its primary virtue cools and dries: and its seed is even more drying. Its secondary virtue helps against blood-based abscesses at their beginning. ¶ **Rhazes**. Another person besides me and my friends experimented with taking ten fresh rose leaves; <margin>Rhazes.</margin> they caused him to void his bowels ten times, and its juice does the same. However, the **Dried Rose** is not laxative: and from this, it is signaled that there is a bitter virtue in it that cleanses; when the rose is dried, it becomes "styptic" <note>Astringent or tissue-contracting</note> because the bitterness is separated from it. The dryness in the rose is actually slight, for it is composed of both astringency and bitterness: which indeed cuts off desire and causes a strong purging.

¶ **The Radish** <note>original: "Rhaphanus"</note> warms in the third degree: but dries in the second. It is certainly of a "drawing" power: so that when applied, it moves old infestations and other flowing things that trouble the vision. It has a thinning power through its heat. **Aetius** says he marvels that some eat raw radishes after a meal—as they themselves say—so that they might digest better. For they say they have experienced this themselves; <margin>Rhazes Book 2, other chapter 18.</margin> many who imitated them were harmed. Water from the radish drives out stones <note>Kidney or bladder stones</note>. ¶ **Rhazes**. The **Radish**

<column-break/>

is hot and thick: making a long delay in the stomach, it "cuts" through phlegm and raises food toward the mouth of the stomach; it also moves one to vomit. Its leaves digest food and aid the appetite when a small amount of them is taken.

¶ **Rhubarb** <note>original: "Reubarbarum seu Raued"</note>. ¶ **Averroes**. <margin>Averroes.</margin> It is composed of diverse substances: from an earthy and cold substance, which is shown by its astringency; from a fiery substance, which is shown by its "cooking" <note>digesting</note> power; and from an airy substance, which is given by its rarity and sponginess. It is one of the most manifest things for helping the liver, for opening "oppilations" <note>blockages in the vessels or organs</note> and strengthening it. Similarly, it profits the stomach. **Galen** and other physicians say that it constricts the belly, yet we see that it purges. It is more miraculous than other purgative medicines because "its bridle is with it" <note>A famous phrase meaning it contains its own corrective: it purges the bile but its astringency prevents excessive diarrhea.</note>; for no purgative medicine is without some poison in some part of itself, except for this one. Because it strengthens all members of the body, we are able to restrain other medicines by using it as a purgative. ¶ **Rhazes**. <margin>Rhazes Book 2, other chapter 47.</margin> **Rhubarb** is hot: which, being beneficial to the stomach and liver, provides a remedy when drunk for falls and blows <note>Internal bruising</note>. ¶ **Mesue**. <margin>Mesue</margin> It is of a hot and dry complexion in the second degree: though it is said to be in the first, the former is more true. The nature of its action in dissolving blockages is due to the dominance of heat on its surface. There is no apparent harm in it. It may be given at any time and at any age, even to children and pregnant women. One should not omit adding its "spike" <note>Spikenard, often paired with rhubarb</note> to its company, for it is specifically helpful with it. Nor should you overlook the addition of a little clear, fragrant white wine in its infusions, especially when it is administered for the clearing of blockages. As a solution, it draws out yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> and phlegm. Its greatest property is to cleanse and strengthen the liver and the stomach: to clear the blood: to remove blockages and diseases of which blockage is the mother, such as dropsy, jaundice, an enlarged spleen, and the fevers caused by blockages. The dose of it in infusion is from 2.5 drams to 1 ounce <note>original: "a .3. ij. 7 s. vsqz .r."</note>; and the portion of it when ground is 1 dram. <margin>Girardus</margin> ¶ **Gerard of Cremona** in his third book: <margin>Cremonensis</margin> **Rhubarb** principally purges yellow bile; secondarily, <margin>in the book</margin> black bile; whence it is valuable against quartan fevers <margin>of medicine</margin> and daily fevers caused by "false phlegm"; and against <margin>in the chapter on</margin> "not-true" quartan fevers <note>A fever that does not follow the standard three-day cycle</note>. It is valuable against a distemper <margin>rhubarb</margin> of heat in the liver, its blockages, and jaundice: and it dissolves defects...

**S**ugar is hot and moist in the first degree. It has the power of cleansing and of moving the urine just like honey; yet it does not cause thirst as honey does, nor does it cause a stinging in the stomach. It stimulates the belly <note>acts as a mild laxative</note> and aids the stomach, the chest, the kidneys, and the bladder. Some have thought it to be cold, but they are refuted by other distinguished physicians because they say they have seen it turn to bile in a hot stomach. It is thought that old sugar is better [than new], as is the new when it is thinner and hotter, except that it brings pain to the head. When diluted with water, however, it takes on a coldness and refreshes. Used as a fumigant or smelled, it helps against a "distillation" <note>a runny nose or catarrh</note> of the head. ¶ **Galen**. <margin>Galen. Ibn Masawayh. Rhazes. Book 4, Chapter 20. New sugar is hot and moist; old sugar is hot and dry. ¶ **Rhazes**. **Sugar** <note>original: "Zuccarum"</note> softens the throat and the belly, and it does not heat except a little. ¶ **Paul** <note>Paul of Aegina</note>. **Sugar** is hot and moist in the first degree. It has the virtue of nourishing, cooling, and relaxing. Against pain of the eyes, let sugar be tempered with woman's milk and distilled <note>dropped</note> into the eye. ¶ **Constantinus**. **Sugar** is temperate, yet somewhat hot. Cooked with flour, it is difficult to digest. With almond oil, it is nutritious, but it causes constipation of the liver and may cause stones in the kidneys.

-># On the letter S.<-

[The plant] is beneficial for asthma <note>original: "asmati"</note> and for all cold, phlegmatic illnesses. It helps with epilepsy, asthma, and "suffocation of the womb" <note>A historical medical term, *suffocatio matricis*, once thought to be caused by the womb moving upward in the body</note>. It expels the fetus. 
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin> ¶ **Dioscorides:** When goats and other animals eat from this plant during their time of mating, it greatly helps them to conceive.

## ¶ Sulfur
Sulfur is composed of an oily, airy, earthy, and subtle substance, refined by fieriness. From quicksilver <note>original: "argento viuo," or mercury</note> and sulfur joined together in various ways and refined in the mines of the earth, diverse metals are generated. As some scholars believe, if they remained in the earth, nature would repeat the refinement of the quicksilver until it was stabilized into silver, and the sulfur would be turned into gold. 
<margin>Galen.</margin> ¶ **Galen:** The substance of all sulfur is subtle. Its second power resolves and draws out [humors]; its third power resists poisons, such as sea-poisons and other similar toxins. When it is mixed with "white glue" <note>original: "glutino alborin," possibly referring to a lead-based ointment or lime</note>, it cures scabies and the illness where the skin is raised up. 
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin> ¶ **Dioscorides:** Its power—especially that of the variety not touched by fire <note>original: "que nō appropinquat igni," native sulfur</note>—is that it heats and resolves. It matures [abscesses], helps a cough, and draws out pus from the chest. When it is swallowed with a soft-boiled egg or used as a fumigant, it helps with asthma. When used as a fumigant, it also helps with deafness and forgetfulness. It is mixed with honey and wine to cure scars and bruises of the ears when they are smeared with it. 
<margin>Rhazes, Book 2, chapter 38.</margin> ¶ **Rhazes:** Sulfur is hot and causes a burning sensation. It helps against scabies if used as an ointment; if drunk, it offers aid for asthma.

<margin>Constantinus.</margin> ## ¶ Dragon’s Blood
¶ **Constantinus:** The juice of this plant is called Dragon's Blood <note>original: "sanguis draconis," a bright red resin from several different plant genera</note>. It is intensely red and its flavor is styptic <note>astringent or mouth-puckering</note>. Its primary power cools in the third degree; its second power helps with cuts in the flesh; and its third power heals wounds and binds together ulcers. When made into a suppository, it binds the belly <note>cures diarrhea</note>. Taken internally, it strengthens the stomach, and it does the same when applied externally.

<margin>Galen.</margin> ## ¶ Stoechas
¶ **Galen:** Its substance is composed of a cold and dry earthy substance (in small part), making it slightly styptic; it is also composed of much fiery and subtle substance, which is why it has a bitter taste and is only slightly styptic. Its second power cleanses, strengthens, opens, and thins [humors]. Its third power strengthens the entire body and all internal organs.

<column-break/>

It prevents all putrefaction and thins [humors].
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin> ¶ **Dioscorides:** A decoction of it helps with chest pain, just like hyssop, and it is used in the preparation of medicines. ¶ **Rhazes:** Furthermore, all herbs in whose scent one perceives sharpness, pungency, and stimulation—such as the flower of Arabian Stoechas <note>original: "sticados arabi," French Lavender</note> and wild mint <note>original: "mentastruz"</note>—are hot. 
<margin>Rhazes, Book 2, chapter 21.</margin> However, those whose scent is delicate and by which the soul is soothed—such as the water lily <note>original: "nenufar"</note>, the willow flower, and the rose—are all cold. 
<margin>Rhazes, Book 2, chapters 40 and 53. The dose is from 2 to 3 drachms.</margin> ¶ **The same Rhazes elsewhere:** Stoechas is hot; it expels black bile and phlegm. It also provides a benefit for epilepsy and melancholy when drunk frequently so that it may purge the belly. The same author in Book 8, chapter 53: the dose is from 2 to 3 drachms.

## ¶ Spodium
<margin>Mesuë.</margin> ¶ **Mesuë:** Spodium <note>Historically referring to burnt ivory or metallic oxides like zinc oxide</note> is cold in the third degree and dry in the second. It helps with the inflammation of choler <note>yellow bile</note> and strengthens the stomach. It helps with mouth ulcers and heartburn <note>original: "cardiace"</note>; it also helps with hot swellings <note>original: "apostematibus"</note> of the eyes and fainting. 
<margin>Rhazes.</margin> ¶ **Rhazes:** It binds the belly and helps with mouth ulcers and the inflammation of choler. It strengthens the stomach. It helps with cold pustules <note>original: "bothoz," an Arabic medical term for skin eruptions</note> in the mouths of infants. It is cold and dry in the third degree. 
<margin>Rhazes, Book 2, chapter 46.</margin> **The same elsewhere:** It is cold and dry, which helps with acute fevers, thirst, excessive diarrhea, and vomiting. It also aids pustules that grow on the mouth and tongue, as well as tremors of the heart.
<margin>Platearius in his book. [Burnt] marble is often found among us as a substitute through burning into a cindery substance.</margin> ¶ **Platearius:** The best spodium is made from burnt elephant bones. It is often faked using the root of a certain cane or with marble changed into a cindery substance by burning. But that [fake] is too heavy; it is more noteworthy for its price than its power. Good spodium is rarely found among us.

## ¶ Savin
<margin>Galen.</margin> ¶ **Galen:** Its primary power heats and dries in the third degree. Its second power thins and dissolves when drunk. Its third power cleanses the rot of foul, eating, and ancient ulcers. Similarly, it cleanses foul "melancholic" ulcers when placed upon them with honey. It removes erysipelas <note>a skin infection</note> and provokes the menses more than any other medicine. It causes blood to be passed in the urine, kills a living fetus, and expels a dead one. It is also an ingredient in "death-bringing" ointments <note>original: "vnguentis mortiferis," likely referring to highly toxic or abortifacient preparations</note>. 
<margin>Dioscorides.</margin> ¶ **Dioscorides:** When made into a plaster by itself, it removes bruises of the skin and those blemishes which happen because of a superfluity of the body; it also removes the scars of fire <note>original: "estiaram ignis," likely eschars or burn scars</note>. When drunk, it makes blood come out with the urine and expels the fetus.

-># On the letter S.<-

¶ **Salt** is hot and dry in the second degree. It possesses a sharp quality and is beneficial for those with a phlegmatic temperament <note>original: "pituosis," referring to an excess of phlegm in the four humors theory</note>. It stimulates the bowels and dries out the body; it has the power to cleanse and sharpens the appetite. However, if one uses it immoderately, it burns the blood, dims the eyesight, diminishes the semen, and causes itching. It also irritates the intestines. When rubbed upon the teeth, it consumes the moisture lingering between them, and it dissolves excessive fluids in the belly. It is said that salt mixed into drinks can cure the ill effects of a wine hangover.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides:** There are two types of salt: one from mines and another from the sea. The mined salt is stronger and drier.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Galen:** The primary quality of salt is hot and dry in the second degree. Its second power gathers, cleanses, and dissolves. Its third power prevents the rotting of bodies that are prone to corruption due to their excessive moisture.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 3 to Almansor, chapter 16</margin>
¶ **Rhazes:** Salt is hot and dry. When added to food, it removes the harm of daintiness <note>original: "fastidii," perhaps meaning a lack of appetite or pickiness</note>, thins the humors, and excites and restores the appetite. Furthermore, in those who consume too much of it, it burns the quantity of the blood, weakens the vision, diminishes the sperm, and generates itching and scabs.

<margin>Platearius, in the Book "Circa Instans"</margin>
¶ **Scabious.** ¶ **Platearius:** This is hot and dry in the second degree. It is effective when green; when dried, it has little power to dissolve, consume, or cleanse. It is effective against scabs, deafness caused by ear-pus, hemorrhoids, ringworm, and skin eruptions <note>original: "impetiginem"</note>. Against the form of leprosy called alopecia <note>A historical term here used for a skin condition causing hair loss</note>, drink four or five drams <note>A dram is a small unit of weight, about 3.9 grams</note> of its juice and bathe in a decoction made from it.

¶ **Sage**, or *elelisphacus* <note>The Greek name for Sage</note>, is clearly of a hot temperament and mildly sharp. When used as a fumigant <note>A treatment involving herbal smoke or steam</note>, it particularly helps women by restraining immoderate menstrual flow and other discharges.

<margin>Agrippas on Sage</margin>
¶ **Agrippas** says that lions eat this "sacred herb" before mating, for it is most powerful for conceiving offspring. Therefore, when a woman drinks a measure of its juice (about one *acetabulum* <note>A small Roman cup, roughly 2 fluid ounces</note>) with a little salt and then sleeps with her husband, she will conceive without fail. They claim that in Egypt, after a great plague had wiped out many people, the surviving women were forced to use this herb to replenish the population.

<margin>Orpheus. Galen, Book 6 of Simple Medicines. Serapio.</margin>
¶ **Orpheus** says: give half a measure of cooked sage juice with one ounce of honey to those coughing up blood <note>original: "hemaptoicis"</note> to be drunk on an empty stomach, and the bleeding will stop immediately.

¶ **Galen:** The temperament of this herb is manifestly hot, possessing sufficient heat, and it is slightly styptic <note>Tending to shrink tissues or stop bleeding</note>.

¶ **Serapio:**

<column-break/>

**Serapio:** A decoction of its leaves and branches, when drunk, provokes urine and menstruation, expels the fetus, and helps against the venomous bite of the sea-stingray. It also darkens the hair, stops the flow of blood, and cleanses foul wounds.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides:** Its power is diuretic; it governs the menses, causes abortion, binds blood flowing from wounds, and purges dirty sores.

<margin>Habir</margin>
¶ **Senna.** ¶ **Habir:** Its temperament is hot and dry, though only slightly hot; its dryness is nearly equal to its heat. It has great power when it reaches the stomach to purge melancholy and choler <note>Two of the four bodily humors associated with bile and sadness</note>. It strengthens the substance of the heart when mixed with the medicines I have mentioned, such as violet. A drink made from its decoction is more beneficial than the powdered herb itself. The dose for the dried, powdered form is one dram, while in a decoction (following Mesue), it is five drams.

¶ **Mesue:** Older senna lacks spirit, and its stalks are useless. It is hot at the beginning of the second degree and dry in the first. The leaves are hot in the first degree. It is a cleansing, purifying, and resolving agent. It is weak and slow to act, and it can weaken the stomach. Its action is improved when combined with sharp things like ginger and rock salt; cordial and stomachic medicines mixed with it make its work more successful.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Galen:** When taken with chicken or meat broth, it purges the bowels without distress. If it is infused in whey with spikenard and then cooked slightly, it is a good medicine; it easily draws out melancholy and "burnt" choler, and it cleanses the brain, heart, liver, spleen, the sensory organs, and the lungs. It opens blockages of the internal organs and preserves youth if taken during one's younger years. It generates joy and cuts away the cause of sadness; it improves the vision and is a medicine for melancholic and long-standing fevers. The dose of the infusion is between three and four *aurei* <note>A weight equivalent to a gold coin, roughly 12 to 16 grams</note>.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 3 to Almansor, chapter 23</margin>
¶ **Rhazes:** Senna and fumitory <note>original: "fumusterre," a medicinal plant</note> quickly and easily lead out dry choler. The dose is between four and twelve drams in a decoction, and similarly for violets.

<margin>The same, Book 8 to Almansor, chapter 12</margin>
¶ **And elsewhere:** Senna and fumitory expel burnt humors. They also help with scabs and itching; for these conditions, it is appropriate to administer between four and seven drams.

-># On the letter S.<-

<header>Regarding the letter S.</header>

## Salt
Salt is hot and dry in the second degree <note>Medieval medicine categorized substances into four degrees of intensity for the four "humors" (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile)</note>. It partakes of a sharp or sour quality. It is beneficial for those with a phlegmatic constitution; it moves the bowels and dries out the body. It possesses a cleansing power and sharpens the appetite. However, if one uses it immoderately, it scorches the blood, makes the vision dull, diminishes the seed <note>original: "semen," referring to reproductive fluid</note>, and provokes itching. It harms the intestines. When rubbed upon the teeth, it consumes the moisture lingering between them; it also dissolves moistures within the belly. Ground salt is said to heal the harms of a wine hangover...

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides:** There are two types of salt: one from the mines and another from the sea. The mineral type is stronger and drier.

<margin>Galen, Book 3, Chapter 17</margin>
¶ **Rhazes:** Salt is hot and dry. By removing the harm of aversion to food, it refines [the humors] and excites and sharpens the appetite. Furthermore, for those who consume a great quantity of it, it scorches the blood, weakens the sight, lessens the sperm, and generates itching and scabies <note>a general term for itchy skin diseases or mange</note>.

<margin>Platearius, in the book *Circa instans*</margin>
## Scabious
¶ **Platearius:** It is hot and dry in the second degree. It is effective when fresh [green]; when dried, it has little power for dissolving, consuming, and cleansing. It is effective against scabies and deafness of the ear caused by discharge [pus], as well as for hemorrhoids, "creeping sores" <note>original: "serpiginem," a term for spreading skin rashes</note>, and impetigo. Against the leprosy called *alopecia* <note>original: "alopicia," here likely referring to a skin condition causing hair loss</note>, one should drink 4 or 5 drams <note>symbol: ʒ</note> of its juice and bathe in the water of its decoction.

<margin>Agrippa on Sage</margin>
## Sage or Elelisphacus
It is clearly of a hot constitution and mildly sharp. When used as a fumigant for women, it restrains immoderate menstrual flow and "womanly flux." ¶ **Agrippa**, moreover, says that lionesses eat this "sacred herb" when mating; for it is most powerful for conceiving offspring. Therefore, when a woman has drunk the measure of one small cup <note>original: "acetabuli," a Roman liquid measure</note> of its juice with a little salt, and has slept with a man, she conceives without doubt. They say that in Coptos, Egypt, many died from a plague, and the population was restored by compelling the women to use it.
<margin>Orpheus</margin>
¶ **Orpheus**, however, says: give to those spitting blood <note>original: "hemaptoicis"</note> 2 [units] of cooked sage juice with 1 ounce of honey, to be drunk while fasting, and it stops immediately.
<margin>Galen, Book 6 of Simple Medicines, chapter on Elelisphacus</margin>
¶ **Galen:** The constitution of this herb is hot with a manifest and sufficient heat, and it is slightly styptic <note>astringent or tissue-contracting</note>.
<margin>Serapion</margin>
¶ **Serapion**

<column-break/>

The decoction of its leaves and branches, when drunk, provokes urine and menstruation; it also expels the fetus, helps against the poisonous bite of the sea-dragon <note>original: "strigonis marini," likely the weever fish</note>, blackens the hair, cuts off the flow of blood, and cleanses "fraudulent" <note>stubborn or slow-healing</note> ulcers.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides:** Its power is diuretic; it regulates the menses, causes abortion, binds blood flowing from wounds, and purges foul wounds.

<margin>Habir</margin>
## Senna
¶ **Habir:** <note>likely an Arabic medical authority, possibly Al-Harith</note> Its nature is hot and dry, yet of little heat; its dryness is nearly equal to its heat. It has great power when it reaches the stomach for purging melancholy and yellow bile. It strengthens the substance of the heart when mixed with the medicines I mentioned elsewhere, such as violet; a drink of its decoction is more beneficial than the ground herb itself. The dose of the ground dry herb is one dram; in the decoction of Mesue, it is five drams.
¶ **Mesue:** Old senna is without spirit, and its stalks are useless. It is hot at the beginning of the second degree and dry in the first. The leaves are hot in the first degree. It is detergent, cleansing, and resolving. It is weak and slow to move the bowels, and it weakens the stomach. It is strengthened by sharp things like ginger and rock salt; cordial and stomachic medicines combined with it make its work successful.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Galen:** Taken with chicken broth or meat, it purges without distress. If it is infused in whey <note>original: "aqua casei," literally cheese-water</note> with spikenard <note>original: "spica"</note> and then cooked a little, it is a good medicine; it draws out melancholy and "burnt" bile with ease and cleanses the brain, heart, liver, spleen, sense organs, and lungs. It opens blockages of the internal organs and prevents "burning" <note>likely inflammation or fever</note> in youth. It generates joy, cuts off the cause of sadness, and improves the sight. It is a medicine for melancholic and long-standing fevers. The dose of its infusion is a drink of three to four *aurei* <note>gold coins used as a weight measurement</note>.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 6, Chapter 8</margin>
¶ **Rhazes:** Senna and fumitory [taken together] are beneficial for daily itching and *bothor* <term>pustules or skin eruptions</term>, and they draw out bile easily. The dose should be from four to six drams in a decoction when required; and likewise for violets. Elsewhere: Senna and fumitory expel "burnt" humors in the same way; they also help with scabies and itching. For these, it is appropriate to administer between four and seven drams.

# Regarding the letter T.

<margin>Aben Mesue</margin>¶ **Savory** <note>original: "Saturegia"</note> ¶ **Aben Mesue.** It is hot and dry in the third degree <note>Medieval physicians ranked the intensity of a medicine's effect from the 1st to 4th degree</note> and is mostly of the wild variety. Its property is that it expels windiness, bloating, and intestinal griping, and it aids in digesting food. It expels superfluities <note>excess waste or humors</note> from the stomach, provokes urine and menstruation, and sharpens vision that has been weakened by excess moisture. <margin>Galen</margin>¶ **Wild Thyme** <note>original: "Serpillus"</note> ¶ **Galen.** Its primary virtue is heating; its second is its thinning and dissolving power; and its third is that it provokes urine and menstruation. <margin>Rhazes, Book 8, Chapter 53</margin>¶ **Scammony** <note>original: "Scamonea"; a powerful herbal purgative</note> ¶ **Rhazes.** It vehemently expels yellow bile <note>original: "cholera rubea," literally "red bile," referring to the humor of yellow bile</note>. The smallest dose given is one-sixth of a drachm <note>a "drachm" or "drachma" (ʒ) was a unit of weight, roughly 3.9 grams</note>; the largest is two-thirds of a drachm. When we fear it may cause harm and wish to remove its ill effects, we should mix it with the juice of an acidic quince, or a "Macian" apple, or with rose water mixed with enough sumac to prepare it. From this mixture, small, thin, round pieces should be made in the manner of lozenges and dried in the shade. One should know the weight before it is prepared, and the dose given should be from a quarter-drachm to half a drachm. <margin>Rhazes, in the Book of Divisions, Chapter 141.</margin> And elsewhere, the same Rhazes says: Scammony dissolves yellow bile and moist humors with great power; when it is combined with aloe and myrobalan, it is corrected <note>tempered or made safer</note> by them.

Similarly, quince syrup and quince water correct it; when quinces are included with it in medicinal preparations—such as the electuary of quinces and similar recipes—it works more quickly and with less malice <note>fewer side effects</note>. Its dose is from seven and a half grains to a quarter-drachm.

<margin>Mesue</margin>¶ **Mesue.** It is of a hot complexion in the third degree and dry to the same extent. Democritus says that it is the "purgative by excellence" <note>original: "solutiuum antonomastice"</note>, and that it is the primary type of purgative, more universal than all others. <margin>Averroes, Colliget, Book 5, Chapter 12</margin>¶ **Hart’s-tongue Fern** <note>original: "Scolopendria"</note> ¶ **Averroes.** It is temperate in heat and dryness. It is evident that it dissolves the hardness of the spleen and opens its blockages, just as laurel berries do for blockages

# Regarding the Letter T.

...a sublime medicine of little malice <note>The author uses "malice" to mean harmful side effects or toxicity.</note>. However, the white variety which is fresh and gummy does not require much rectification <note>original: "rectificatione," the process of purifying or refining a substance</note>: and indeed, by purging, it draws out humors and phlegm that are not overly viscous. The dose is from 2 to 3 drams <note>original: "3. ij. vsqz ad. iij." using the apothecary symbol for drams</note> when it is boiled. If it is taken in its usual manner, the dose is from 1 dram up to 1 aureus <note>original: "aureum," a weight equivalent to a gold coin, roughly 4.5 grams</note>.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Frankincense.** <note>original: "Thus"</note> ¶ **Dioscorides.** <note>A 1st-century Greek physician and botanist</note> Frankincense is effective against skin eruptions, spider bites, burns, and bruises, as well as for pains in the ears and breasts, and internal tumors. However, if it is drunk by a healthy person, they may suffer from mania or even death.

<margin>Constantine in the *Book of Degrees*</margin>

It warms and constipates; it clears the vision; it solidifies fresh wounds; it restricts the flow of blood wherever it may be; and it also strengthens the memory.

<margin>Rhazes, *Almansor* book 2, chapter 38</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** <note>An influential 9th-century Persian physician</note> Frankincense, being hot and dry, creates flesh in wounds. It also wards off stomach troubles and vomiting, and sharpens the intellect. However, if a great quantity is taken, it burns the blood and causes a sluggish chill; it likewise helps with tremors of the heart.

<margin>Isaac</margin>
¶ **Tereniabin.** <note>A type of Manna, specifically "Persian Manna" secreted by the camel-thorn plant</note> ¶ **Isaac Israeli.** <note>An 10th-century Jewish physician and philosopher</note> Tereniabin is a dew falling from the sky; it resembles aggregated, granular honey and is called "honey of dew." Most of it falls upon trees in the land of Khorasan <note>original: "coraseni," a region in the Persian East</note> in the Orient. Its virtue is equally softening to the belly and moistening to the chest. It is beneficial for those with "hot natures," especially when it is dissolved in jujube water or plum water. Its dose is from 10 up to 20 aurei.

<margin>Abir</margin>
¶ **Abir.** <note>Likely referring to a specific Arabic medical authority</note> Tereniabin is better than sugar; it calms the inflammation of hot fevers, removes thirst, and softens the belly with a moderate loosening effect. It is the manna that falls from the air just as manna falls; it also soothes the chest and cough.

<margin>Rhazes, *Almansor* book 2, regarding manna, chapter 20</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** Tereniabin is hot; it also loosens the belly and soothes the throat. Regarding this, read the chapter on manna.

¶ **Caltrop** <note>original: "Tribolus seu tribulus," a spiked plant</note> consists of a moderately moist, cold, and dry essence. When drunk, the terrestrial fruit grinds down stones in the kidneys.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Galen.** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire</note> Its substance is composed of a moist substance of little coldness, and a dry substance of significant dryness according to its coldness. Its third suitability is that it prevents hot abscesses <note>original: "apostemata"</note> from hardening; and universally it benefits all members to which humors flow. ¶ **Alcanzi.** When Sealed Earth is of good quality, if it is powdered in a mouth from which blood flows, it stops it immediately; there is no medicine that cuts off all flows of blood as effectively as this one.

**V** <note>A large historiated woodcut initial 'V' showing a man in a wide-brimmed hat and cloak walking through a landscape with trees and hills under a shaded sky.</note>

Wine is of the second degree of heating; quite old wine is of the third; while must <note>new, unfermented wine</note> is of the first. Some use wine because it is beneficial; others because it cheers the mind; others so that it may provide pleasure to the taste; and others for all these reasons.
It has a nature for nourishing the body; but red and thick wine turns into blood. Very old wine is in the third degree; medium wine is in the second degree of nourishing the body. Red and thick wine, I say, is the most suitable.

<meta>This page continues the medical encyclopedia under the letter V (transcribed as U in the Latin text), specifically focusing on the properties and uses of wine (Vinum) and grapes (Uva), citing major classical and medieval authorities.</meta>

# Regarding the Letter V.

...to the blood: from which it becomes black, sweet, and thick; then harsh; then reddish; and the least of all, white and thin. Therefore, the most approved wine, suited for both the healthy and the sick, is that which is reddish in color and thin in substance, and somewhat tart. Generally, there are four colors of wine: white, tawny <note>original: "fulvus," a brownish-yellow or amber color</note>, blood-red, and black. The blood-red variety is considered the best. The effectiveness of wine is more apparent in cold and dry bodies, and in those where less internal heat resides, such as in the elderly and the faint. However, the use of wine should be avoided by those who are hot-natured and those suffering from fevers.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ Indeed, Galen says regarding constitutions <note>original: "complexionibus," referring to the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) in the body</note> that wine possesses an extraordinary speed of transformation. For it is like a torch, or a wick soaked in oil, or tinder and fire. The use of wine must be avoided by children and youths.

<margin>Plato, book 2 of the *Laws*</margin>
¶ As Plato writes in the second book of the *Laws*: Young men should abstain entirely from drunkenness and the filling of themselves with wine. I would grant wine to no one during the day unless it is needed as a drink for the sake of physical exercise or because of disease. Nor should it be used at night by a man or woman when they wish to focus on conceiving children. I would also strictly prohibit governors and judges from wine when they are about to undertake their duties. Likewise, those who are about to deliberate on matters that should not be neglected. Indeed, the use of wine should be most moderate and sparing for almost everyone.

<margin>Rhazes in the *Alphabetical Book*, chapter 5</margin>
¶ **Rhazes.** All wine that intoxicates heats the body. Furthermore, wine generally always warms the stomach and the liver, and it causes nourishment to penetrate the body; it also increases the blood and the flesh, and augments the innate heat. It even assists nature in its own proper actions, and therefore digestion becomes stronger. Through wine, the expulsion of superfluities <note>original: "superfluitatum," waste products or excess humors</note> and their exit from the body becomes easy. This is the reason why health, sturdiness, and strength endure, and old age is delayed. Moreover, wine gladdens the soul; but if it is taken in excess, it hinders the liver, the brain, and the nerves; it also generates tremors, spasms, paralysis, apoplexy, and sudden death. If drunk temperately, however, it is a cause of much good in the body, especially in the elderly. Likewise, pure wine with very little water mixed in is beneficial for those accustomed to suffering from thick windiness <note>original: "ventositatem," meaning gas or bloating</note> in the belly, and for those whose stomach and liver are cold. Refined wine with a large mixture of water provides help to those who suffer headaches from wine or who become easily intoxicated by it, although it may cause bloating in the belly. Thick, sweet, and new wine is harmful to those who have internal obstructions or "thickness." However, it is good for those wishing to gain weight quickly. Wine

<column-break/>

that is white and clear, which does not tolerate much mixing with water, provides less heating but is a greater provoker of urine. In color, the fiery and bitter wine, which can receive a larger mixture of water, provides greater heating. ¶ Likewise, wine that is black, thick, and sweet, in which there is a certain harshness <note>original: "ponticitas," a sharp or astringent quality</note>, is of a thicker nature. Furthermore, new wine generates more blood and fills the veins more quickly; old wine is found to be the opposite of this.

<margin>Ali Abbas, *The Theory*, chapter 30</margin>
¶ **Ali Abbas.** <note>A 10th-century Persian physician</note> Wine strengthens the natural heat; it increases and unfolds it into all the limbs; it strengthens the soul, to which it brings happiness and joy, and it adds boldness to the spirit and strength to those who are sluggish. It tempers choleric humors <note>The "hot and dry" humor associated with yellow bile</note> and purges through urine and sweat. It also tempers black bile <note>original: "choleraz nigram," the "cold and dry" humor</note> by its own heating and moistening. It softens the nature, moistens the principal organs, and builds up and restores bodies that have suffered dryness from immoderate heat or those rising from illness. For it increases the appetite for food, aids in the digestion of the same, and assists in its transmission to the limbs. It carries the moisture of water to them; thus, it moistens them if by chance dryness has occurred; it dissolves windiness and inflation. All these things occur if wine is taken in a moderate quantity, such that it does not burn with excessive drunkenness. The constitution <note>original: "complexio"</note> of pure wine is universally hot and dry; except for that which is new and close to the wine-press: the heat of the first does not exceed the first degree; however, the heat of old wine does not pass the second degree <note>Medieval medicine graded the intensity of a substance's qualities—hot, cold, moist, or dry—on a scale of one to four</note>. According to how near or far it is from its pressing, there will be a decrease or increase in this constitution. It is among the most opportunistic and best causes for protecting health if it is taken in a temperate way and when it is needed. The natures of wine vary based on five things: first is the color; second is the liquidity; third is the odor; fourth is the flavor; and fifth is the time <note>Referring to the age of the wine</note>.

¶ Grapes nourish less than figs. They are beneficial when chewed grapes leave the belly quickly. If they stay too long in the belly, they cause the most harm. For they are not digested, but they overflow to the liver and the veins, generating raw humor; they are not easily changed into blood because of the surrounding skin. Therefore, it is not bad that the skin is spat out by some, sucking out only the flesh and juice, by which the belly is eased. Grapes preserved for the winter are more useful for eating.

<margin>Psellus, book 2 on the *Rule of Life*</margin>
¶ **Psellus.** <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine monk and scholar</note> Grapes themselves, like other fruits, nevertheless nourish more than all others except figs; they generate less bad humor when they have ripened well. They nourish less than figs; they are beneficial when they are easily excreted; when that is not the case, they cause harm.

It emphasizes moderation, age-appropriateness, and the benefits of wine for digestion and the elderly, while warning against its effects on the young and the feverish.</summary>

### ¶ Violet leaves possess a watery and somewhat cold power. And their first virtue cools a little: their second softens: and their third quiets hot swellings <note>original: "apostemata," used here for inflammatory swellings or abscesses</note> when the leaves are applied: either by themselves or with barley flour. And they help with inflammation that occurs at the mouth of the stomach and in the eye.
<margin>Rhazes, book 4 of the *Almansor*, chapter 22</margin> ¶ Rhazes. Violets are cold and sleep-inducing: and they soothe a headache caused by heat.

<margin>Galen</margin>
### ¶ Nettle. ¶ Galen. Its first virtue is a virtue that heats, though not with much heating: and it dries without biting or sharpness. And its second virtue is one that dissolves <note>original: "resoluit," meaning to break down or disperse humors</note> with much power: and along with this, its virtue is flatulent <note>original: "inflatiua," meaning it causes "wind" in the body</note> and for this reason it stimulates sexual intercourse. And its third virtue is a power that heals sores and swellings that occur behind the ears. And it causes one to cough up thick, viscous humors from the chest and lung when it is drunk. It also cures corrosive ulcers, and cancer, and everything for which drying is suitable. <margin>Abenguefit</margin> ¶ Abenguefit <note>Abenguefit was the Latin name for the 11th-century Arab physician Ibn Wafid</note>. When the seed of the nettle is husked and ground and mixed with honey and taken, it relaxes the bowels with great strength. And one must take care that it does not touch the tongue, nor the top of the throat, lest it burn them.
<margin>Isaac Ebenamram</margin>
And its dose is from twenty grains up to thirty. ¶ Isaac Ebenamram <note>A 10th-century Jewish physician from Kairouan</note>. ### ¶ Wind. ¶ Rhazes. The wind from the northern pole: coming from the direction of the Lesser and Greater Bear <note>The constellations Ursa Minor and Ursa Major</note>, is cold and dry. It makes bodies hard and renders them robust: it makes the senses and the

<column-break/>

head clear <note>original: "lema," which usually refers to eye-discharge, but in this context likely means the wind dries up such fluids, making the head "clear"</note>. Being better than all other winds, it removes putrefaction more effectively. However, it does cause a cough. It also brings on diseases that occur in the lung and throat, as well as rheumatism or a common cold: moreover, it binds the belly but provokes urine. But the wind coming from the southern pole, from the direction of the midday sun: dissolves bodies: disturbs the senses: and causes headache and eye disease: it also causes epilepsy to accelerate before its usual times: likewise, it produces fevers because of its putridity: however, it does not cause irritation to the throat, chest, or lung. It is also more prone than all other winds to bring on disease, and most especially if it blows in summer or at the end of spring. But the wind which blows from the furthest point of the spring sunrise to the furthest point of the winter sunrise <note>The East/Southeastern winds</note>: and that which comes from the furthest point of the spring sunset to the furthest point of the winter sunset <note>The West/Southwestern winds</note> are entirely temperate in heat and coldness. The one that tends toward us from the East is better, but the one from the West is worse and is more thick.

### ¶ Mistletoe consists of a mostly airy and watery hot substance: to which a little earthy matter is mixed: there is therefore more sharpness in it than bitterness: which can be seen from its effect. It is not, however, among the medicines that heat immediately in the first degree: but acts like thapsia <note>A plant known as "deadly carrot," used as a skin irritant and purgative</note>. <margin>Rhazes, book 3 of the *Almansor*, chapter 31</margin> ¶ Rhazes. ...of blood: hence it is black and sweet, and thick; then harsh; then reddish; the least of all is white and thin. Therefore, the most approved wine, suited for both the healthy and the sick, is that which is reddish in color, thin in substance, and somewhat tart. There are generally four colors of wine: white, tawny, blood-red, and black. The blood-red excels the others. The efficacy of wine is more manifest in cold and dry bodies, and in those in whom less heat resides, such as the elderly and the faint. The use of wine should be avoided by those who are hot and suffering from fevers. ¶ Galen says concerning temperaments: <margin>Galen</margin> there exists in wine an exceptional speed of change. For it is like a torch, or a wick soaked in oil, or tinder and fire. The use of wine should be avoided by children and youths. ¶ For as Plato writes in the second book of the *Laws*: <margin>Plato, Book 2 of the *Laws*</margin> Young men should abstain entirely from drunkenness and the overfilling of wine. I would grant wine to no one at all during the day, unless it is needed for the sake of physical exercise or diseases. And this is why health, stoutness, and strength endure, and old age is delayed. Moreover, wine gladdens the soul; but if it is taken in excess in drink, it causes hindrance to the liver, brain, and nerves; it also generates tremors and spasms, as well as paralysis, apoplexy, and sudden death. However, if it is drunk temperately, it is the cause of much goodness in the body, and especially in the elderly. Likewise, pure wine to which a little water is mixed benefits those who are accustomed to suffering from heavy gas <note>original: "ventositatem," referring to flatulence or internal wind</note> in the belly, and those whose stomach and liver are cold. But it is good for those wishing to grow fat. Wine

Furthermore, new wine generates more blood and fills the veins more quickly; however, old wine is found to be the contrary of this. ¶ Ali Abbas. <margin>Ali Abbas, *Theoreum*, Chapter 30</margin> ¶ It comforts the natural heat; it increases and spreads it into all the limbs; it comforts the soul, to which it brings happiness, joy, and distinction, and adds boldness to one's virtue and strength; it balances choleric humors <note>The "choleric" humor was associated with yellow bile, fire, and a hot, dry temperament</note> and purges through urine and sweat. All these things happen if it is taken in a moderate quantity—specifically, that which does not burn with excessive drunkenness. However, it is among the more opportune and better causes that protect health, if it is taken in a balanced way and when it is needed. The natures of pure wine vary based on five things: first is color; second is liquidity; third is odor; fourth is flavor; fifth is time.

¶ Grapes nourish less than figs. Eaten grapes are beneficial when they pass quickly from the belly. If they stay too long in the belly, they cause the most harm. But the wind coming from the South Pole—from the direction of *Suhayl* <note>original: "stublel," a Latinization of the Arabic name for the star Canopus, indicating the South</note>—dissolves bodies, disturbs the senses, and causes headaches and ailments of the eyes. It also causes epilepsy to hasten before its usual time, and causes fever because of its tendency toward rot; yet it does not cause irritation to the throat, chest, or lungs. It is more prepared to bring on sickness than all other winds, especially if it blows in summer or at the end of spring. The wind that blows from the end of the spring rising to the end of the winter rising <note>the Northeast</note>, and that which comes from the end of the spring setting to the end of the winter setting <note>the Northwest</note>, are entirely temperate in heat and cold. That which tends toward us from the East is better, but that from the West is worse and is more thick.

¶ **Mistletoe** <note>original: "Viscum"</note> consists of much airy and watery substance and is hot, to which a small amount of earthy matter is mixed; therefore, there is more sharpness in it than bitterness, which can be seen from its effect. For it draws and pulls out deep-seated moisture—not only thin moisture, but also thick—and it pulls it apart and dissipates it. It is not, however, among the medicines that warm immediately in the first degree, but acts like *thapsia* <term>thapsia; a plant known as "deadly carrot," used as a powerful skin irritant and purgative</term>.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 2 of Almansor, Chapter 31</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. Mistletoe is hot and dry; it dissolves gas and swellings.

<margin>Averroes, Book 5 of the Colliget, Chapter 42</margin>
¶ **Averroes**. The operations of mistletoe are the same as *thapsia* in their primary and secondary effects; it is extremely hot with superfluous moisture, and it draws from the depths of the body; it does this with much slowness because of the superfluous moisture existing within it.

¶ **Vitriol** <note>original: "Uitriolum"</note>. ¶ **Galen**. I have seen in the mines three veins extended one over the other for a long distance. The virtue of all these is caustic, burning the flesh and creating a hard, burnt scab <term>eschar</term>; and along with this burning, it is styptic <term>styptic; a substance that shrinks tissues and stops bleeding</term>.

<margin>Averroes, Book 5 of the Colliget, Chapter 42</margin>

The thickest is red; after that is *colcothar* <term>colcothar; a reddish-brown iron oxide residue left after distilling vitriol</term>; after that is green and red. The green is, as it were, the material of the *colcothar*; such is the comparison of *colcothar* to green. The red has less "bite" than the green because of the thickness of its substance; the red and green do not dissolve, because the red is hardened with a stony hardness, and the green is...

### ¶ Regarding the Letter X.

**Xylalohe or Aloe-wood.**
**Xylocerata <note>Carob</note>.**

Xylalohe, or aloe-wood <note>also known as agarwood</note>, is a tree that grows in many places in the East as well as in the South. The Eastern variety indeed escapes all decay and has no difference in scent compared to other trees. When split, it gives off a scent that is not particularly remarkable. However, the inhabitants cut it and bury it under much earth; then, a long time later, they dig the wood up and sell it to merchants. In Egypt and other regions, they scrape the woods and remove the bark; in this way, they prepare the various types of aloe-wood. They are all hot and dry; they bind the bowels, strengthen the stomach, remove blockages of the liver, and dissolve excess moisture in the belly.

<margin>Isaac Eben Amram</margin>
¶ **Isaac Eben Amram** <note>A 10th-century physician from Kairouan</note>. It is hot and dry in the second degree; it is good for the brain, strengthens ulcers, expels excess moist humors, and its smoke causes phlegm to descend from the brain.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 3 of Almansor, Chapter 23</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. Aloe-wood is hot and dry, and it is suitable for a moist stomach that is filled with viscous fluids.

<margin>Galen</margin>
¶ **Xylocerata: or Carobs.** <gloss>Galen attacks these; he prays that no one would ever have brought them into his region, because they are of bad juice, are woody, and are difficult to digest.</gloss> More modern writers think the stomach is strengthened by them if they are taken after food; they also firmly check the flux <note>diarrhea</note> if they are eaten before the rest of the meal.

<margin>Dioscorides</margin>
¶ **Dioscorides**. When these are administered fresh, they are bad for the stomach and soften the bowels; but when they are dried and served, they are better for the stomach than when they were moist, for they bind the belly and provoke urine, especially when they are prepared with fruit syrup <note>original: "rob"; a thickened fruit juice</note>.

<margin>Rhazes</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. When warts <note>original: "verne", likely a corruption of "verrucae"</note> are smeared with these while they are green, it eradicates them.

### ¶ Regarding the Letter Z.

**Ginger.**
**Zedoary.**
**Sugar.**

Ginger <note>original: "Zynziber"</note> is hot in the third degree and moist in the first; it clears blockages and digests food; it arouses lust and disperses gas. It is beneficial against dimness of the eyes caused by moisture by making the sight sharp, and it aids against coldness of the belly and liver, as well as against sticky humors.

<margin>Rhazes, Book 3 of Almansor, Chapter 23</margin>
¶ **Rhazes**. Ginger is hot and moist; it digests food and moves the bowels. It benefits a cold stomach and liver; it likewise helps the darkness of the eyes caused by moisture, whether it is applied to the eyes or eaten.

<margin>Abenmesuai</margin>

It is hot and dry in the second degree; it fattens the body in a healthy way and removes windiness. Its special property is that it takes away the odor of garlic, onions, and wine.

<margin>Bedigoras</margin>
