<header>Introduction.</header>

# The Introduction to Medical Practice, collected by the same Lord Symphorien Champier, physician: It begins.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' containing floral and leaf patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
Since a different method of practice has become common among our more recent professional interpreters than that which our ancestors used, it was my intention to add certain general principles—gathered from the most famous professors of this faculty for the benefit of beginners in the Hippocratic art—to these simple medicines. We shall begin by proceeding from enemas <note>original: "clisteribus"</note>, as they are the most common treatments, to those remedies specifically suited for the cure of certain fevers.

<margin>A soothing enema.</margin>
¶ A soothing enema for the belly: it draws out hardened waste, reduces febrile heat, and serves other similar purposes. ℞ <note>Take</note>: half a handful <note>original: "ʍ. β."</note> each of mallow leaves and spinach; one and a half pounds of river water. Let them boil until a third of the liquid is consumed; then let them be strained and strongly squeezed. Of this strained liquid, take one quarter <note>approx. 5 ounces</note>, to which add 3 ounces of violet oil; this is if the cause of the illness is "hot." But if the cause is "cold," add 3 ounces of common oil and 2 drachms <note>original: "ʒ. ij."</note> of common salt. If you wish to cleanse the bowels more thoroughly, add more blite <note>a leafy green similar to spinach</note> and sugar. In a hot condition, add white sugar; in a cold one, add red sugar. If you wish to soothe further, add cassia fistula <note>the "pudding-pipe tree," used as a laxative</note> or manna <note>a sweet plant resin</note>. Some, such as Avicenna <note>the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>, add egg yolks. If the feces are very hardened, the enemas should be very fatty, containing oil or marrow, so that they add 6 ounces of oil; many practitioners use oil alone.

<margin>A soothing laxative.</margin>
¶ A soothing medicine can also be given "from above" <note>orally</note>. For sometimes enemas cause more harm than soothing medicines taken by mouth, as I have often seen. ℞: 1.5 drachms of newly extracted cassia fistula; 4 ounces of barley water. Let the cassia be extracted with the said water. Another recipe: ℞: 1 ounce of manna; 2 ounces of violet syrup; 2 ounces of barley water. For the same purpose, the "water of fruits" from the seventh distinction of Mesue <note>an influential medieval medical authority</note> is useful. The doses are usually 4 ounces, though it is sometimes necessary to increase or decrease these doses according to the patient’s physical disposition—considering their tendency toward constipation <note>original: "stipticiratis"</note> or looseness, their habits, age, and so forth. Finally, note that some prepare these enemas using the juices of herbs, hoping to soothe the patient more effectively.

<margin>A minorative.</margin>
¶ A "minorative" <note>a gentle purgative</note> is so called because it evacuates common "minutiae" <note>small impurities</note> or those existing in common vessels, such as the stomach and intestines. ℞: half a drachm of tamarinds, or in their place an equal amount of plums. Let them be boiled in 10 ounces of water until a third is consumed; let them be strained and strongly squeezed. Of this strained liquid, take 8 ounces and add 1 drachm of manna (or an equal amount of cassia if you lack manna); this is particularly aimed at "choler" <note>yellow bile, one of the four humors</note>. If you wish to cleanse the blood of choler, put tamarinds in the whole decoction. But if the problem is "phlegm" and choler—but principally phlegm—add agaric <note>a medicinal fungus from larch trees</note> to the decoction and let it boil with the tamarinds. Use 3 drachms of agaric, not ground into powder, but sliced into small pieces.

<column-break/>

¶ A minorative specific to choler, addressing it as the primary offending matter. ℞: 6 ounces of the aforementioned tamarind decoction; 1 ounce of manna or an equal amount of cassia; 2 drachms of rose juice, or half a drachm of "electuary of rose juice" <note>a medicinal paste</note>, depending on the body's disposition as noted above. But if the offending humor is phlegm: ℞: 1 drachm of cassia; 1.5 drachms of "Indian electuary." Let it be extracted with a decoction of hops, sebesten <note>Egyptian plum</note>, and tamarinds, as described above. For the same purpose, the "elephantine pills" made of simple hiera <note>a traditional "holy" bitter medicine</note> are effective.

<margin>What must be done first.</margin>
¶ As soon as you encounter a patient suffering from an acute fever, give them a soothing enema for its many benefits; this also prepares the intestines for the purgation <note>original: "solutioni"</note> to be performed the following day. This is most beneficial even when other medications might be prohibited. It can be made thus: ℞: one handful <note>original: "ʍ. j."</note> each of fennel, violet, mallow, and blite. If you wish to make it stronger, add one handful of water lily <note>original: "nenufa"</note>; if even stronger, add a quarter handful of mandrake bark. Let them boil until a third is consumed; then squeeze the mixture. Of this liquid, take 1 pound and 2 ounces; add half a drachm of camphor, 2 drachms of sandalwood, 3 ounces of violet or rose oil, and 2 drachms of salt. You may add to or subtract from these ingredients as you see necessary and suitable for your purpose.

¶ Since in acute fevers—and especially in "peracute" <note>extremely sharp or sudden</note> ones—the humor <note>the matter of the disease</note> is "furious" <note>highly agitated</note>, one should not wait for "digestion" <note>the natural maturation or settling of the humors</note>. Instead, the humor should be evacuated immediately with an eradicating drug. Note here that many physicians prefer to give "blessed medicines" <note>gentle, safe remedies</note> in these cases, fearing those that work with great intensity, such as scammony <note>a harsh purgative resin</note>, scammony-based preparations, turbith <note>a medicinal root</note>, and the like. In such cases, they give an infusion of rhubarb with a decoction of 1 drachm of tamarinds and half a drachm of plums. Let them be lightly boiled, then placed in a cloth, well rubbed, and strongly squeezed. Of this liquid, take 4 ounces, 2 drachms of rhubarb, and 4 grains of spikenard. Many who dislike spikenard use "quinantum" <note>camel grass or lemongrass</note> in the decoction instead. Let it sit for 6 or 8 hours; then let it be strained and a strong extraction made. Give this at dawn, following the standard rules for administering drugs. Truly, these medicines evacuate easily and do not pull humors from remote parts of the body, performing their work gently. Therefore, even scammony-based medicines are not to be feared when they are perfectly balanced, just as...

<header>Introduction.</header>

...electuary of rose juice <note>A medicinal paste made of rose juice and sugar or honey</note>; indeed, also that of Nicolaus <note>referring to the *Antidotarium Nicolai*, a standard medieval pharmacological text</note>, although it may not be as comforting. From there, manna or cassia can be given: for example. ℞ <note>Take</note>: manna or cassia, half an ounce; electuary of rose juice according to the description of Mesuë <note>Mesuë the Younger, a celebrated but semi-mythical pharmaceutical authority</note>, 3 ounces; or Nicolaus’s version, 3 ounces. Or, you may increase the dose of cassia and decrease the electuary. Certainly, we have seen such things benefit those who used mild remedies more; however, you must consider the strength, the temperament <note>original: "complexionem," referring to the balance of the four humors</note>, and the physical condition of the patient, because some can tolerate these while others cannot.

<margin>A digestive for fevers.</margin>
¶ Set down here—so that you do not leave empty-handed—is a digestive <term>digestive: a medicine intended to "ripen" or process harmful humors so they can be expelled</term> and a quencher for an acute fever. ℞: fine sugar, 3 ounces; orange juice, 3 ounces; the "greater cold seeds" <note>seeds of cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon</note>, cleaned, 2 ounces; seeds of endive and lettuce, 2 ounces each; endive water, 6 ounces; sorrel water, 4 ounces; water lily water, 3 ounces; and violet and rose water, 2 ounces each. Let those which need pounding be pounded; then mix everything and let them boil lightly. Afterward, let them be scented with a little red sandalwood and coral, of each a portion, and let all be put through a strainer. The feverish patient should use this digestive up to and including the peak of the illness, giving half an ounce of it regularly at dawn. It should be given cold in hot weather and warm in cold weather, and many times throughout the day and night as much as the patient wishes.

<margin>Cooling in fevers.</margin>
¶ Another intention in treating fevers is the cooling of the liver with things applied externally. To complete this perfectly, it would be necessary to cite many things here, which would be very long and should not be attempted in this place; it will be enough for you if I describe some epithems <term>epithem: a liquid medicinal application, usually soaked into a cloth and applied to an organ</term> as an example. ℞: endive water, 5 ounces; rose water, 3 ounces; red sandalwood, 2 ounces; spodion <note>originally a term for metallic oxides, in pharmacy it often referred to burnt ivory or bone used for cooling</note>, 1 ounce; vinegar, 2 ounces; and let an epithem be made with a linen cloth. Let it be lukewarm in summer and more than lukewarm in cold weather. If you wish to make it stronger, add water lily water, nightshade <note>original: "solatri"</note>, and a little camphor.

¶ Similarly, if you wish to make a cooling ointment, you can do it this way. ℞: rose oil and water lily oil, 1 ounce each; red sandalwood, 1 ounce; spodion, half an ounce; and a little wax. If you desire to cool even more, wash the said ointment afterward with endive water or its juice.

<margin>For the kidneys and liver.</margin>
¶ Because by cooling the kidneys, the liver is also cooled—and this is especially true for a young person with hot kidneys—make an ointment or an epithem for the kidneys as well from these ingredients. ℞: rose oil (made from unripe olives), 7 ounces; white wax, 1 ounce; white vinegar, 1 ounce; ivory shavings, 1 ounce; and red sandalwood, 1 ounce. Mix and make an ointment. If you wish to cool further, wash it with nightshade water or water lily water as above, or add an ounce of camphor. Likewise, an epithem is often made with water of "true coldness" from rose water, water lily water, and nightshade juice if

<column-break/>

mixed with ivory shavings, the "greater cold seeds," and similar items. Take note of these things.

¶ The reduction of heat in the heart is likewise achieved with epithems, sachets, and ointments. Also, by the drawing in of air from cold things and other ingenious methods to be seen in the third book of the *Cure of a Hot Bad Complexion of the Heart*. For an epithem: ℞: rose water, 3 ounces; sorrel and bugloss water, 2 ounces each; water lily water, 1 and a half ounces; red sandalwood, 2 ounces; coral, 1 and a half ounces; camphor, 3 grains; saffron, 2 grains; and white vinegar, 1 and a half ounces. Mix and make an epithem with a linen cloth.

¶ A sachet for the same purpose in cooling the heart: ℞: red sandalwood, 1 and a half ounces; "lambuze" <note>unclear; likely a preparation of coral or silk</note> and coral, 1 ounce each; rose leaves, 1 and a half ounces; coriander, 1 ounce; camphor, 2 grains; dried sorrel, 1 and a half ounces; and pearls, half an ounce. Let the camphor and pearls be ground by themselves, and let a sachet be made with crimson silk <note>original: "sindone de grana"</note> and applied to the heart. From these same things, with cold oils—such as violet, rose, water lily, and the like—mixed with white wax and a little vinegar, a cooling ointment can be made, but it is not commonly used. Also, by drawing in air while standing over cold water and holding cold things before them, such as ice, fresh rose leaves, cold fruits, and similar things.

<margin>For the brain.</margin>
¶ The tempering of the heat of the brain is done with moderating and soothing remedies, since it has to balance the heat of the heart; it is primarily the reduction of the heart’s heat that is sought. It is tempered with liniments, ointments, plasters, embrocations <note>a liquid rubbed onto the skin</note>, sachets, scents, and such. A common mild soothing remedy: ℞: rose oil, 1 and a half ounces; lettuce water or its juice, rose water, and white vinegar, half an ounce each. Shake and mix well together, and soak a piece of cloth large enough to cover the space of the forehead and temples. If you wish to make it stronger, add camphor, an emulsion of white poppy seeds, henbane juice, and the like. And if even stronger, add a little opium, so that you may compose a weak, strong, or very strong version according to the pressing necessity. You can make an ointment from the same things with oils of rose, violet, water lily, and the like, with a little vinegar and white wax. For example: ℞: rose oil, 1 and a half ounces; violet oil, 1 ounce; water lily oil, half an ounce; houseleek juice, half an ounce; enough white wax; and half an ounce of vinegar. Let the forehead and temples be anointed. Among the Italians, an epithem is made from nightshade water or its juice with rose water and egg white, with a little vinegar.

<margin>For the testicles</margin>
¶ An epithem for the testicles is made from those things that suddenly induce coldness throughout; for I have seen a sick man so heated that he could be cooled in no other way. An epithem for this: ℞: rose water, 2 ounces; violet water, half an ounce; water lily water, half an ounce; red sandalwood and red coral, 1 ounce each. Shake and mix, and apply with a cloth as many times as you see necessary.

# On Clinical Practice

...at a timely moment according to the state of the heat and the cooperating vital power.

<margin>How to proceed in medical matters</margin>
¶ In the art of medicine, one must begin with the milder remedies and progress toward the stronger. Therefore, in the first rank of those things that can be applied both internally and externally, place chamomile and its oil. In the second rank, wormwood and its oil. In the third rank, celery. In the fourth rank, southernwood. In the fifth rank, agaric <term>agaric: a medicinal fungus used as a laxative and to treat phlegm</term>. In the sixth rank, French lavender. Then laurel, anise, seseli, calamint, marjoram, birthwort, costus, and similar items. Among the compound medicines for a "cold cause" <note>referring to diseases caused by an excess of the cold humor, phlegm</note>—which have been tested in quartan fevers and daily fevers arising from thick phlegm, as well as in "false" tertian fevers—a beneficial remedy is a portion of "water of life" <note>original: "aque vite"; likely an early distilled spirit or brandy</note> with half a dram of clove powder. This should be given half an hour before the onset of the paroxysm <term>paroxysm: the sudden attack or increase in symptoms of a fever</term>, preceded by a therapeutic rubbing, and with the rubbing continued without interruption after it is administered. Some provide this with a small amount of fermented and aged theriac <note>a famous polypharmaceutical "universal" antidote</note>, and this is a powerful remedy. Another milder treatment is an application made from oil of chamomile and oil of lilies. Another is from oil of rue and oil of lilies. Such things, which are actually warm, ought to be applied with warm cloths for an hour, or at least half an hour, before the feverish fit begins. For the same purpose, a recipe (℞) of several of the simple herbs already mentioned and oil of costus, chamomile, or rue is effective; this is common practice, or one might use oil of euphorbium. If you wish it to be stronger or milder, you may add or subtract ingredients as seems expedient. Likewise: ℞ ginger, pellitory, and calamus, half a dram each; let them be given with one dram of warm wine.

<margin>For removing shivering</margin>
¶ A tested remedy for removing shivering and the "typus" <note>the periodic pattern of the fever</note>: ℞ one part spider webs and mix with nettle seed and the strongest white or red vinegar; apply this to the pulses before the onset of the fit. And Avicenna <note>a Persian physician whose 'Canon of Medicine' was the standard medieval text</note> in the second book of the *Canon*, in the chapter on myrrh, says that myrrh taken with pepper and water before the start of the shivering removes it. Let what has been said suffice for shivering, "horripilation" <note>the sensation of skin crawling or hair standing on end</note>, and cold.

<margin>Against weakness of the retentive power</margin>
¶ Against the weakness of the "retentive power" <term>retentive power: the body's internal faculty responsible for holding onto nourishment and fluids</term>, one should proceed with cooling styptics <note>substances that contract or "tighten" tissues</note> applied both internally and externally. An external rubbing made of rose oil and "omphacine" oil <note>oil made from unripe olives</note> mixed with myrtle and willow leaves is effective. Likewise, this is useful: ℞ one dram each of rose and myrtle oil; half a dram of quince; one dram each of pomegranate flowers and "dragon’s blood" <note>a bright red resin from the Dracaena tree</note>; a little vinegar and a small amount of wax to make a liniment. For the same purpose, provide troches <term>troche: a medicinal lozenge</term> of amber and "sealed earth" <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay from Lemnos</note> with water lily water, syrup of myrtle, and so on. To hold back excessive sweating, the juice of houseleek is effective. And Bertruccius <note>original: "Bertilis"; likely referencing the 14th-century physician Nicolas Bertruccius</note> used to praise the "new rose-honey" of Nicolaus and gave it several times a day. Finally, note that the places which ought to be anointed in this case are the forehead, the temples, the pulses of the arms, and the spinal cord. Likewise, nightshade is effective when mixed with cooling styptics such as Armenian bole <note>a medicinal red clay</note>, tragacanth, gum arabic, gallnuts, and similar things with vinegar and

<column-break/>

the aforementioned styptic oils.
¶ Diarrhea <note>original: "fluxu ventris"</note> resulting from an excessive weakening of the vital power is much to be feared in fevers, because the natural heat can easily be extinguished by it. In such a case of diarrhea, take care not to give narcotics. Among the domestic remedies recommended for such things are: water of toasted barley in which myrtle, or the flesh of quinces, or something similar has been boiled with tragacanth. Likewise, syrup of myrtle, of currants, of Mesuë’s verjuice <note>original: "agresta mesue"; juice of unripe grapes</note>, quince pulp, troches of spodium <note>ash of burnt ivory or bone</note>, and the like. Regarding foods, use hulled lentils, boiled twice and made acidic with the juice of sour pomegranates or with vinegar. Externally, use plasters, ointments, fomentations, and such.

<margin>Against heaviness of the head</margin>
¶ Against heaviness of the head, apply things that "resolve" <note>disperse or dissolve harmful vapors</note>, yet are temperate, such as chamomile, which resolves without drawing more humors, or melilot and the like. If you lack simple herbs, make a compound by mixing hot things with cold: for example, ℞ one handful of chamomile flowers; half a handful each of red roses, melilot, and French lavender; one dram of mace. Let them be ground and made into a small bag for the head. But if there is a vehement heat in the head, apply only cold things; and let the cold things be scented with vinegar, rose water, and the like. Take note that in this case, you must avoid applying "milk emulsion" to the head or anointing it with oil, since such things, by causing "oppilation" <note>original: "oppilando"; blocking the pores</note>, prevent the escape of vapors. Therefore, Avicenna forbade "embrocations"—specifically cold, blocking ones—but later allowed those that open the pores; you must consider this.

<margin>Cooling the fever</margin>
¶ Excessive wakefulness and restlessness, especially due to vehement heat, sometimes brings on a fever; for this, proceed as follows. First, apply cooling things externally, such as embrocations <term>embrocation: a liquid medicine rubbed on the body</term>, ointments, or scented substances. For example: ℞ half a dram each of coral and "spodium"; half a handful each of white poppy bark and chamomile flowers. With this decoction, let the feet and arms be bathed, and cloths soaked in it should be applied to the temples. Be careful with anointing the temples if the head is "full" <note>replete with humors</note>. Second, you shall give a sleep-inducing agent by mouth; a common one is: ℞ one dram of poppy syrup with water lily water, given two or three hours after a meal, or an emulsion of poppy seeds, which is also given in food. It is said that anointing the soles of the feet and the palms of the hands with the fat of a crane induces sleep. Likewise, if the forehead is smeared with the juice of henbane and mint, the patient will sleep. But if he does not sleep from this, death is to be expected.
¶ For the same purpose, and this is strong: ℞ one dram each of oils of rose, violet, and chamomile; half a dram each of the juices of mandrake, henbane, and lettuce; half a dram of opium dissolved in wine; and a little wax. Let them all boil until the juices are consumed; then strain and add the opium; with this, anoint the pulses of the temples and arms, and the forehead.
¶ For the same purpose, though it is weaker: ℞ of mandrake...

# Introductory Treatise

<column-break/>

Take myrrh, opium, saffron, and frankincense, 1 dram <note>original: "ʒ. i"; a dram is about 3.9 grams</note> of each. With wax, make small lozenges, and when needed, stretch one of them over the navel. While the actual stomach pain persists, let "diversions" <term>diversions: treatments intended to draw "bad humors" away from a painful area to another part of the body</term> be performed with rubbings and cupping, and place a large cupping glass over the navel or the parts adjacent to it. But note that if possible, first induce vomiting; then give oxymel <term>oxymel: a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term> made from syrup. If the pain is caused by windiness <note>referring to gas or flatulence</note>, the aforementioned large cupping glass, rubbings, and diversions are helpful. Also, take warm bread fresh from the oven, soak it in oil or honey, and apply it. Also, take chamomile, anise, and rue, 1 dram of each; let them be boiled, and in that decoction place a cloth, then apply it to the stomach once squeezed out. Diversions are safer; always begin with the milder ones.

<margin>Against roughness of the tongue.</margin>
¶ Roughness of the tongue sometimes occurs, and when it is accompanied by a thick and viscous "limosity" <term>limosity: a slimy or muddy buildup of humors, often associated with phlegm</term>, then take 4 ounces of warm barley water and 1 ounce of simple honey-water; mix them and wash the mouth with it. Then, let the tongue be cleaned with a linen cloth, or do this with a sponge soaked in that liquid; or use a reed, or a wooden or silver instrument to scrape the tongue. Then, let the mouth be washed with the aforementioned water. Also, first let the patient hold rock candy in the mouth, or a compound made of common seeds and rose honey, or licorice juice with violet julep <term>julep: a sweet liquid medicine, often flavored with flowers</term>, so that the harmful slime is sufficiently softened; then scrape it with wool or wipe it away with a sponge as was said. Or, take starch and soak it in violet julep, and proceed as described. Likewise, an ointment made of violet oil and the like applied around the neck is effective. Above all, ensure that the patient does not keep their head on the pillow, nor stay flat on their back, nor lie upon their neck. If possible, have them breathe over cold water and hold it in their mouth.

---

### ¶ Now follows the section on fevers in particular: and first, concerning the pure tertian fever.

The syrup of Saint Ambrose <note>a remedy named after the patron saint of Milan</note>, which produces a wonderful sweat and extinguishes thirst: Take a suitable quantity of hulled millet and let it boil until it bursts. Then take 5 ounces (or thereabouts) of its boiling broth and pour in 2 drams of fragrant white wine. Give it to the patient while hot, and then cover them well; they will sweat wonderfully. He used to cure the people of Milan this way, and they still use it. It is also said that 1 dram of gentian root drunk with wine before the fit takes away the fever. The juice of ground-pine <note>original: "ypiceois"; likely *Iva arthritica* or ground-pine</note> works similarly. A plaster made from soot, salt, and water-celery <note>original: "aspio aqtico"</note> placed upon the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet three hours before the onset also takes it away. These, however, are empirical remedies <term>empirical: remedies based on folk experience or observation rather than formal medical theory</term> which I do not entirely agree with, but I found them described by Nicolaus <note>referring to Nicolaus Praepositus, author of the *Antidotarium Nicolai*</note>, and for that reason, I have included them here.

<column-break/>

¶ A master syrup: Take flowers of borage, bugloss, and roses, half a handful of each; violets, lettuce, white poppy, endive, and prickly lettuce, one handful of each; seeds of endive and lettuce, half a dram of each; and the "four cold seeds" <term>four cold seeds: a standard mixture of cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon seeds used to cool the body</term>, 6 drams of each. Let them be boiled. From this decoction, take 1 pound; add 4 ounces of sugar, 1 ounce of vinegar, and 1 ounce of pomegranate wine. Let a syrup be made. If you wish to make a "long" <note>diluted or extended dose</note> version, give 4 drams of it in place of a digestive. If it is a "short" version (properly boiled down), give 2 ounces with 3 ounces of endive water. Or, take 1 ounce of simple vinegar syrup, half an ounce of sugar, 2 ounces of endive water, and 1 dram of vinegar; and so on for others.

<margin>A laxative.</margin>
¶ You had the laxatives <note>original: "solutiua"</note> above; but here, take 1 ounce of cassia <term>cassia: the pulp of the *Cassia fistula* pod, used as a mild laxative</term> extracted with endive and wormwood water, 2 drams of choice rhubarb, and 6 grains of spikenard or camel grass. Mix them. The "Abbot's Rose Powder" <note>original: "Dyarodon abbatis"; a famous digestive powder containing roses and spices</note> is very suitable for this case; give it six hours before the fit.

¶ For a pure tertian fever, a tested remedy is the warm juice of bindweed <note>original: "corrigiole"</note> drunk for three hours before the paroxysm <term>paroxysm: the sudden onset of a fever fit or shivering</term>; the dose is 5 ounces. Indeed, it prevents the paroxysm from occurring. The juice of unripe grapes works the same way if drunk for nine mornings. So too does chicory juice. You should prepare these with sugar as a julep, or make a julep from their juices and waters and administer it; for this is effective. And if 3 ounces of wine made from sweet or sour pomegranates is given with 2 ounces of endive water two hours before the onset of the paroxysm, it takes it away or diminishes it, especially if continued for several days. However, in this, consider the condition of the stomach; then, on the following day, give an evacuation of pills or other means so that the retained matter may be cleared out. I have tried this and it succeeded well.

---

### ¶ Following is the section on the non-pure or "bastard" tertian fever.

<margin>A digestive.</margin>
When the mixture is of bile <note>original: "cholera"</note> and thin, watery phlegm—which is called "citrine" <note>a yellowish bile</note>—take 1 ounce of endive water, 1.5 ounces each of prickly lettuce and chicory water, and 1 dram each of wormwood and fennel. Mix them. Or it may be made from syrups: Take 1 ounce each of simple vinegar syrup and strained rose honey, with 2.5 drams of endive water. Or if you want a master recipe: Take one handful each of endive, prickly lettuce, lettuce, maidenhair fern, hyssop, and chicory; 2.5 drams of fennel roots; 1 dram of celery roots; and 1 dram each of endive and prickly lettuce seeds. Let a decoction be made; and for every 1.5 pounds of the decoction, add 4 ounces of sugar and 4 ounces of vinegar. Make it "long" or "short" as you please, and give it as stated; and flavor it with cinnamon.

<margin>A laxative.</margin>
¶ A laxative: 1 ounce of extracted cassia with 2 drams of prepared turbith <term>turbith: the root of a plant in the morning glory family used as a strong purgative</term>; draw it out with wormwood and endive water. Or take 1.5 drams of "Electuary of Indus" <note>a purgative compound from the East</note> and 2 drams of Nicolaus’s rose juice electuary with 1 dram each of endive and wormwood water.

# On practical application

¶ Compose **confections** and **electuaries** <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term> from both hot and cold ingredients. For example: Take of the aromatic rose species from the description of Gabriel, 1.5 drams <note>original: "ʒ. i. β."; a dram is about 3.9 grams</note>. Take of the species of the three sandalwoods, 2 drams, because the bile prevails in its vigor. Take of Tabarzet sugar <term>Tabarzet: a highly refined, white crystalline sugar</term>, 10 drams. Let a solid confection be made; or with similar ingredients and violet-borrage sugar, make an electuary. From the **troches** <term>troches: small medicinal lozenges or tablets</term>, the lesser rose troches are especially beneficial after thirteen days.

¶ If the ailment arises from **vitelline bile** <term>vitelline bile: a type of "yellow bile" thought to resemble the color and thickness of egg yolks</term>, speak similarly of the simple medicines. For the compounds: Take 1.5 drams of simple **vinegar syrup**, half a dram of strained honey of roses, and 1.5 drams each of endive and fennel water. For the "magistral" <note>expertly formulated or physician-prescribed</note> recipes: Take 1 dram each of fennel and asparagus roots; half a dram each of hart's-tongue fern, endive, wild lettuce, and hazelwort. Let a decoction be made, and with 1.5 pounds <note>original: "℔. j. β."</note> of liquid, add 4 drams of Tabarzet sugar and 5 drams of vinegar—or squill vinegar <term>squill: the sea onion, used as a powerful cleansing agent</term> if you wish to "cut" the humors more effectively—and do this as the treatment progresses. Take 4 drams and let it be made into a **long or short syrup** <note>referring to the cooking time and resulting thickness</note>, and let it be given as described above for **pure tertian fever** <term>tertian fever: a fever that recurs every third day, historically associated with malaria</term>, either with other appropriate ingredients or without waters.

¶ Among the laxative medicines, it is appropriate to take 2.5 drams of "diaphoenicon" <term>diaphoenicon: a purgative electuary made primarily of dates</term> or the "Indian electuary"; 1.5 drams of the electuary of rose juice, or cassia, "diaprunum" <note>a plum-based laxative</note>, or manna; and 2 drams of prepared gummy turpeth <note>a root used as a strong purgative</note> or an equal amount of agaric <note>a type of medicinal mushroom</note>. And in this chapter, **Avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), one of the most influential physicians of the Islamic world</note> praises scammony, turpeth, and agaric. Rhubarb is also valuable, given both in substance and as an infusion. And remember well, because of the chronic nature of the illness, you must proceed from the weak to the strong and repeat the treatment often. Among the troches, those of hemp-agrimony are commended.

¶ From the confections: Take 2 drams of the "Diarhodon of the Abbot" <term>diarhodon: a rose-based medicinal powder used to cool the body</term> or of the three sandalwoods; 1.5 drams of the aromatic rose species of Gabriel; 4 pounds of sugar. Make a confection from which the patient may take one morsel of 2 drams an hour before eating, and afterward drink a little aromatic wine, very well strained. Or prepare an electuary from 1 dram each of bugloss and violet sugar; half a dram each of rose and rosemary; 1.5 drams of "Manus Christi" <term>Manus Christi: literally "Hand of Christ," a restorative sugar-based tablet often containing pearls or gold</term>; and 1.5 drams of the electuary of gems <note>a recipe containing crushed precious stones</note> or the three sandalwoods. Add more or less of this according to how far you see the fever differing from a "pure" fever, as has been said.

¶ And if the fever is not "pure" due to an admixture of **melancholy** <term>melancholy: the "black bile" humor, thought to be cold and dry</term> generated within by "combustion" <note>the "burning" or overheating of humors that turns them into black bile</note>, then look for the simple medicines that benefit both pure bile and melancholy, and combine them. For example, for a magistral recipe: Take one handful each of violet flowers, borrage, bugloss, red roses, endive, wild lettuce, and garden lettuce; 3 drams each of the "greater cold seeds" <note>seeds from melons, cucumbers, and gourds</note>, hart's-tongue fern, borrage juice, and the juice of fragrant sour apples; and 2.5 drams of fumitory juice <note>original: "fumiterre," literally "smoke of the earth"</note>. Let them boil in 6 pounds of water until one-third has been consumed; and with 2 pounds of sugar and 2 drams of squill vinegar, let a syrup be made, clarified, and given in greater or lesser amounts depending on the duration of the illness, as above. Or take from the compound syrups: 1 dram of violet syrup, half a dram of syrup of fumitory,

<column-break/>

2 drams of bugloss water, and 1 dram of fumitory water. Mix them.

¶ From the laxatives: Take 1.5 drams of choice rhubarb and five grains of spikenard; infuse them in "milk water" <note>whey</note> and a little white wine. Let it stand for eight hours in the infusion, then squeeze it out. To this strained liquid, add 1 dram of cassia or manna; let the cassia be extracted with equal parts of fumitory, borrage, and endive water.

¶ Fabricate confections and electuaries: for example, take 1 dram of the electuary of gems; 2.5 drams of the three sandalwoods or Diarhodon of the Abbot; and 10 drams of the whitest sugar.

¶ If the fever is "unnatural" because of an admixture of black bile coming from the outside: work similarly with the simple medicines. For example: Take one handful each of lemon balm, hart's-tongue fern, endive, wild lettuce, borrage flowers, bugloss, and violet; 1.5 drams each of fennel and parsley roots; and 1 dram each of licorice, roses, and raisins. Let a decoction be made, and with one pound of the decoction, add 3 drams of sugar and 2 drams of vinegar. Let a long or short syrup be made, as has been said. Or take 1 dram of acetous violet syrup, half a dram of fumitory syrup, and 1.5 drams each of hart's-tongue fern and bugloss water. For the laxative: Take 1 dram of cassia or manna, half a dram of "diasena" <term>diasena: a compound medicine made primarily of senna leaves</term>, or 2.5 drams of the "Electuary of Hamech" <term>Hamech: a famous purgative used specifically to expel melancholy humors</term> with appropriate waters, and give it, etc.

### Following is the section on phlegmatic fevers, and first on intermittent ones.

**Avicenna** says in the second book of the *Canon* that **bedeguar** <gloss>white thorn</gloss> is effective for long phlegmatic fevers, the cause of which is a weakness of the stomach, and for all ancient fevers—especially its root; and in its place, one may use fumitory. Likewise, nigella <gloss>black cumin</gloss> resolves phlegmatic fevers, because its powder is given with oxymel <term>oxymel: a medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term>, especially once the matter has already been "digested" <note>meaning the humors have been ripened or prepared for expulsion</note>. Likewise, the juice of hemp-agrimony drunk with honey of roses removes phlegm. A remedy of the country folk, especially during the decline of the illness: **Cyranides** <note>an ancient book of lore and magic</note> said that a spider weaving on the walls, if taken in the name of the patient, enclosed in a reed, and hung around the neck, takes away a one-day fever. The seagull is also useful. **Apuleius** <note>referring to a 4th-century herbalist</note> says that **scordion** tied around the body of a man takes away daily fevers. **Scordion** <gloss>wild garlic</gloss>. **Cyranides** says that with common oil of scorpions, if you anoint the entire back, feet, hands, and forehead with it while warm, it takes away the daily fever—and not only that, but also the tertian and quartan fevers, as has been proven. **Constantine** <note>Constantine the African, a famous medieval translator of medical texts</note> confirms the same, especially when the moon is in decline. Water of "cucusta" <note>possibly dodder or a similar climbing plant</note> with oxymel does the same.

### ¶ Now follows concerning fevers in particular: and first concerning pure tertian fever.

**S**t. Ambrose’s Syrup, which induces sweating wonderfully and extinguishes thirst. Take a suitable quantity of **hulled millet** and let it be boiled until it evaporates; then take about 5 ounces of its boiling broth and infuse it with 2 ounces of fragrant **white wine**. # On Practical Medicine

¶ Compose **confections** and **electuaries** <term>electuary: a medicinal paste or conserve made by mixing powdered herbs with honey or syrup</term> from both "hot" and "cold" ingredients: for example, **Take** 1.5 ounces of aromatic rose spices <note>original: "specier' aromatici rosati"</note> following the description of Gabriel, and 2 ounces of the "three sandals" spice blend <note>A mixture of red, yellow, and white sandalwood used to cool the body</note>, which overcomes bile through its vigor. Take 10 ounces of Tabarzet sugar <note>A high-quality refined white sugar</note> and make a solid confection. Or, using similar ingredients with sugar of violets and borage, make an electuary. Among **troches** <term>troche: a medicinal lozenge or tablet</term>, the "lesser rose" troches are most effective, especially after fourteen days.

¶ If the fever arises from **vitelline bile** <term>vitelline bile: "yolk-like" bile, a medical sub-category of yellow bile thought to be thick and bright like an egg yolk</term>, use the same simple medicines mentioned before. From the compound medicines, **Take** 1.5 ounces of simple acidic syrup, 0.5 ounces of strained rose honey, and 1.5 ounces each of endive and fennel water. For professional recipes, **Take** 1 ounce each of fennel and asparagus roots, and 0.5 ounces each of hart’s-tongue fern, endive, escarole, and asarabacca <note>original: "asari"</note>. Make a **decoction** <term>decoction: a concentrated liquor made by boiling down herbal materials</term>. Then, **Take** 1.5 pounds of this liquid and 8 ounces of Tabarzet sugar, with 5 ounces of vinegar—or squill vinegar if you wish to more sharply "cut" the humors—and throughout this process, take 4 ounces [of the mixture] to make either a "long" or "short" syrup. Let it be given as described above for pure tertian fever, either with specific accompanying waters or without.

¶ Among **purgatives**, it is suitable to **Take** 2.5 ounces of *diaphenicon* <note>A laxative confection made primarily of dates</note> or Indian electuary, 1.5 ounces of rose juice electuary or cassia, or *diaprunis* <note>A plum-based laxative</note>, and 1 ounce of manna. Add 2 drams of gummed turbith <note>A root used as a powerful purgative</note> prepared for use, or an equal amount of agaric <note>A type of medicinal fungus</note>. In this chapter, **Avicenna** <note>The famous 11th-century Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> praises scammony, turbith, and agaric. Rhubarb is also valuable, whether given as the substance itself or as an infusion. You should commit well to memory that for **chronic illnesses**, you must proceed from weak to strong medicines and repeat the treatment often. Among troches, those made of eupatorium <note>Hemp-agrimony, used for liver and bile disorders</note> are recommended.

¶ From the **confections**: **Take** 2 drams of "the abbot's rose" spice blend or the three sandals blend, 1.5 drams of Gabriel’s aromatic rose spices, and 4 drams of sugar. Create a confection from which the patient should take one 3-dram morsel an hour before eating. Afterward, let them drink a little aromatic wine, very well diluted with water. Alternatively, make an electuary from 2 drams each of borage and violet sugar, 0.5 drams each of rose and rosemary, 1.5 drams of *Manus Christi* <note>A "hand of Christ" sugar tablet, often containing pearls or precious stones</note> with pearls, and 0.5 drams of the "gem" electuary or the three sandals. Add more or less of this depending on how much you see the condition differs from "pure" bile, as was said.

¶ And if the condition is not "pure" due to a mixture of **melancholy** <term>melancholy: "black bile," the humor associated with earth and cold/dryness</term> generated within by "adustion" <term>adustion: the historical medical theory that humors could be "scorched" or "burnt" by excessive heat, turning them toxic and dark</term>, then look for simple medicines that benefit both pure bile and melancholy, and combine them. For example, professionally: **Take** 1 handful each of the flowers of violet, borage, oxtongue, red rose, endive, escarole, and lettuce. Take the "greater cold seeds" <note>Usually a blend of cucumber, melon, gourd, and watermelon seeds</note>, hart’s-tongue fern, and 2 ounces each of borage juice and fragrant acidic apple juice. Add 2.5 ounces of fumitory juice. Boil these in 6 pounds of water until a third of the liquid has evaporated. With 2 pounds of sugar, make a syrup including 3 ounces of squill vinegar; let it be clarified and given in greater or lesser amounts depending on the duration of the illness. Or: **Take** from the compound syrups 1 dram of violet syrup, 0.5 drams of fumitory syrup,

<column-break/>

2 drams of oxtongue water, and 1 dram of fumitory water. Mix them.

¶ From the **purgatives**: **Take** 0.5 drams of choice rhubarb and five grains of spikenard. Infuse them in "milk water" <note>Whey or a milky infusion</note> and a small amount of white wine. Let it stand for eight hours in infusion; then press it out. To this liquid, add 1 ounce of cassia or manna. The cassia should be extracted with the waters of fumitory, borage, and endive.

¶ Fabricate **confections** and **electuaries**: for example, **Take** 1 dram of the "gem" electuary, 2.5 drams of the three sandals or the abbot's rose spice, and 0.5 ounces of the whitest sugar.

¶ If the condition is "unnatural" due to an external mixture of **black bile** coming from outside the body, act similarly with simple medicines. For example: **Take** 1 handful each of lemon balm, hart’s-tongue fern, endive, escarole, borage flowers, oxtongue, and violet. Take 1.5 drams each of fennel and parsley roots, and 1 dram each of licorice, roses, and raisins. Make a decoction, and with one pound of this decoction, add 3 ounces of sugar and 2 ounces of vinegar. Make a long or short syrup as instructed. Or: **Take** 1 dram of acidified violet syrup, 0.5 drams of fumitory syrup, and 1.5 drams each of hart’s-tongue and oxtongue water. For the purgative: **Take** 1 ounce of cassia or manna, 0.5 drams of *diasene* <note>A compound laxative based on senna</note>, or 2.5 drams of Hamech’s electuary with suitable waters, and administer it.

### ¶ Following is the treatment for phlegmatic fevers, and first, those that are intermittent.

D**avicenna** <note>Ibn Sina</note> says in the second book of the *Canon* that **bedeguar**—that is, the "white thorn"—is effective against long-lasting **phlegmatic fevers** <term>phlegmatic fever: a fever caused by an excess of phlegm, characterized by chills and a slower onset</term> caused by a weakness of the stomach. It is good for all old fevers, especially its root; in its place, one may use fumitory. Likewise, **nigella** <note>Black cumin</note> resolves phlegmatic fevers because its powder, given with **oxymel** <term>oxymel: a traditional medical mixture of honey and vinegar</term>, works especially well once the "matter" of the illness has been digested <note>Historical medicine believed a disease had to "ripen" or be "digested" before it could be purged</note>. Likewise, the juice of **eupatorium** drunk with rose honey removes phlegm.

**A remedy of the peasants**, particularly for when the fever is fading: **Kirannus** <note>A reference to the *Cyranides*, an ancient book of magico-medical lore</note> said that a **spider** found weaving on the walls, if taken in the name of the patient, enclosed in a reed, and hung from the neck, takes away an "ephemeral" <note>one-day</note> fever. The fat of a hedgehog is also useful. **Apuleius** <note>referring to the Herbal of Pseudo-Apuleius</note> says that **scordium**—that is, wild garlic—bound around the human body removes **quotidian** <note>daily</note> fevers. **Crato** claims that if you rub the whole back, feet, hands, and forehead with common **scorpion oil** after it has been warmed, it removes the daily fever—and not only that, but also the tertian and quartan fevers. This is a proven remedy. **Constantinus** <note>Constantine the African, a 11th-century translator of Arabic medicine</note> confirms this, especially when the moon is waning. Water of *cucusta* <note>Possibly a spelling variant for a type of gourd or dodder</note> with oxymel does the same.

# Introductory.

### ¶ Next follows periodic fever from sweet phlegm.

¶ Regarding the usual compounds for a phlegmatic fever caused by **sweet phlegm** <term>sweet phlegm: a variation of the phlegm humor considered to be naturally sweet and often associated with less severe inflammation</term>. **Take**: 1.5 ounces of simple vinegar syrup, 3 ounces of boiled river water, and 1.5 ounces of sugar. I move now to a stronger remedy: give 1.5 pounds <note>original: "lib. j. ß."</note> and 1.5 drachms <note>original: "ʒ. i. ß."</note> of oxymel <term>oxymel: a medicinal mixture of honey and vinegar</term> with 3 ounces of fennel water. Furthermore, for a stronger dose, give vinegar of two roots with fennel water, as prescribed. And for the strongest, give vinegar syrup of five roots, or Byzantine syrup with eupatorium <note>Hemp-agrimony</note> water, wormwood water, and the like. Proceed always from the weak to the strong, and then to the strongest, giving these digestive medicines for five, six, or seven days. Occasionally, pause the treatment so that nature may rest from the burden of the medicines; then, it may be seen what nature will accomplish when not hindered by these remedies.

¶ If you desire a **professional digestive** <note>original: "digestiuuz magistrale"</note>, do this: **Take**: 1 drachm each of agrimony, wormwood, and rose gall <note>original: "bedeguar"</note>; 0.5 ounces each of fennel root, celery root, licorice, and raisins; 3 drachms each of roses and Bishop's weed <note>original: "ameos"</note>; 2 drachms each of endive and fennel seeds. Let them boil in four pounds of water until the liquid is reduced by half. With one pound of skimmed honey, let a syrup be made—this is especially for winter; in summer, make it with sugar. Note here that this is a strong remedy and suitable for the end of the treatment. You have the usual laxatives in the preceding pages. However, for the digested matter: **Take**: 1 scruple each of agaric <note>A medicinal fungus</note> and turpeth <note>A root used as a purge</note>; 4 grains each of spikenard and rock salt; 0.5 drachms of these should be infused in honey-water, then sufficiently strained. In this water, dissolve 1.5 ounces of cassia or manna.

¶ A confection of turpeth is prepared in this manner, to be eaten in this case: **Take**: 2 drachms each of galangal and long pepper; 0.5 scruples each of mace and saffron; 12 drachms of gummy and choice turpeth; 1 pound of the whitest sugar; and with wormwood water and a little citron wine, let a solid confection be made, of which the patient should take a "morsel"—namely, 3 drachms.

¶ Among the confections, these are suitable: **Take**: 1 drachm of aromatic rose spices, 0.5 drachms of the Abbot's Rose-restorative <note>original: "diarodon abbatis," a cooling powder made of roses and sandalwood</note>, 2 drachms of the electuary of gems, and 5 ounces of the whitest sugar. Let a solid confection be made with wormwood water, of which a morsel should be taken an hour before eating, both morning and evening.

¶ An electuary is ordered thus: **Take**: 6 ounces each of sugar flavored with borage, bugloss, and violet; 1 drachm of pulverized marble <note>original: "thos," likely referring to a mineral powder</note>; 1.5 drachms of aromatic rose spices; 1 drachm of the Abbot's Rose-restorative; and 0.5 drachms of the electuary of gems. Mix these with water <note>original: "eauora," likely a transcription of 'aqua'</note>, and give as described for the confection above.

¶ Regarding troches <term>troche: a medicinal lozenge or tablet</term>: **Take**: 2 drachms each of the Rose-restorative species and choice cinnamon. Incorporate them with agrimony juice; and although powders are not commonly used,

<column-break/>

give them in the form of pills. You may also make a confection from these same ingredients using sugar.

¶ **Rose troches** are also praised, because they are comforting to the stomach, which, as has been said, must necessarily be comforted in a phlegmatic fever. Therefore, rub the stomach externally with an ointment: **Take**: 2 drachms of mastic oil, 0.5 ounces of nard or spikenard oil, 2 drachms of wormwood oil, 0.5 drachms of powdered cloves, 2 drachms of aloeswood, 1 drachm of red coral, 0.5 drachms of prepared coriander, 1 scruple of rose powder, and a little black vinegar; with wax, make an ointment. Among proven remedies, a powder of cinquefoil <note>Five-leaf grass</note> given with one grain of pepper and potent wine one hour before the fever's onset—always understand this timing for similar gifts—resolves the daily fever. Ground mustard given with hydromel <note>honey-water</note> removes the daily fever by driving the matter to its limit. Theriac <term>theriac: a famous "universal" antidote and medicine containing dozens of ingredients</term> performs the same when given with warm water two hours before the onset, and this should be done from the fourth day to the fourth day following previous evacuations.

¶ An **Alchif** <note>A specific Arabic-influenced medical recipe or authority</note> against fever from sweet or natural phlegm: **Take**: 1 drachm of fumitory juice, 0.5 drachms of agaric, and 1 drachm of fennel juice. Let it be given three hours before the fever's onset, and the sick person shall be freed.

### ¶ Next follows periodic fever from false phlegm.

¶ Regarding **professional digestives**: **Take**: 1 handful <note>original: "M. j." / manipulus</note> each of endive, escarole, and bugloss; 0.5 handfuls each of fennel and celery roots; 1 handful each of bugloss, violet, and borage flowers; 1 drachm of cold seeds <note>usually a mix of melon, cucumber, gourd, and pumpkin seeds</note>; 6 drachms each of licorice and raisins; 2 drachms each of anise and fennel. Let a decoction be made in four pounds of water until half is consumed. Then, with one pound of sugar and half a pound of honey, let a syrup be made, of which you shall give 2 drachms with 1.5 ounces of endive water and 1 ounce of bugloss water.

¶ You have many more **laxatives** in the preceding pages in abundance. But so you do not leave empty-handed: **Take**: 0.5 handfuls of violets, 0.5 ounces of raisins, and 2 drachms of fennel roots. Let a decoction be made from these with water, with which you extract 0.5 ounces of cassia, 1 drachm of *diasenicon* <note>a laxative electuary made with senna</note> or Indian electuary. Or, with the said decoction, give 4 drachms of *diasenicon*. Or, **Take** rhubarb <insert>concerning rhubarb</insert> soaked overnight in a fine wine with spikenard; give it with the preceding decoction, 1 drachm of cassia, and 1 drachm of the electuary of rose juice.

¶ For confections, **Manus Christi** <term>Manus Christi: "Hand of Christ," a refined sugar-based lozenge, sometimes containing pearls or gold leaf</term> prepared with a small amount of sandalwood is suitable. Also: **Take**: 1 drachm of red coral, 4 scruples of cinnamon, 0.5 drachms of pearls, 1 drachm of red sandalwood, 0.5 drachms each of aloeswood and mace, and 8 ounces of the whitest sugar. Let a confection be made in morsels with rose water, which you should take as in the previous section. Or, let a confection be made from the species of the Abbot's Rose-restorative and the electuary of gems, or the aromatic rose.

# On Practical Medicine.

¶ Let an electuary be made from sugar of roses, violets, and bugloss, 2.5 ounces of each; *manuschristi* <term>manuschristi: 'Hand of Christ', a medicinal sugar confection often shaped into sticks or tablets</term> and *diarodon abbatis* <term>diarodon abbatis: 'The Abbot’s Rose', a cooling compound of roses and sandalwood</term>, 1.5 drachms of each; and half a drachm of the species for the electuary of gems. Let it be gilded <note>original: "deauretur" — medicinal preparations were often coated in gold leaf to increase their prestige and supposed efficacy</note>.
¶ Regarding troches <term>troches: small medicinal lozenges or cakes</term> which are not much in use now: **Take** troches of eupatorium <note>Hemp-agrimony</note> and troches of *spodion* <term>spodion: an astringent powder made from burnt metallic or vegetable matter</term>, of each [an equal amount]. Prepare with violet julep and give as described in the previous section.

### On the cure of periodic phlegmatic fever caused by mucilaginous, glassy, and watery phlegm.

¶ From the usual digestive compounds for such a fever: **Take** 1 drachm of strained rose honey, half a drachm of simple vinegar syrup, and 1.5 drachms each of fennel and bugloss water. From this, transition to stronger doses by degrees as said before. **A Professional Recipe**: **Take** 1 drachm each of asparagus, butcher’s broom <note>original: "brusci"</note>, and fennel roots; 1 pound each of balm <note>lemon balm</note> and bugloss; 1 drachm each of anise and fennel seeds; half a drachm of Bishop’s weed <note>original: "ameos"</note>; and 4 drachms of raisins. Let a decoction be made with four pounds of water until it is reduced by half; then with 1 pound of honey and 4 drachms of vinegar, let a syrup be made. In winter, use honey; in summer, use sugar. Make it more or less acidic as seen fit. This is useful once the matter has been digested <note>prepared for expulsion</note>. In the beginning, use less "opening" <note>original: "aperitiuis" — medicines meant to clear blockages in the vessels</note> remedies; see the conditions of the digestive in this matter as mentioned in the previous chapters.
¶ Regarding laxatives, you have pills and other things which you should know for yourself. **From the professional recipes**: **Take** 2 drachms of *hierapigra* powder <term>hierapigra: 'holy bitter', a famous ancient purgative based on aloes</term>; 1 drachm each of agaric <note>a medicinal fungus</note> and turbith <note>a purgative root</note>; half a drachm of spikenard; and 6 scruples of rock salt. Let them be formed with oxymel <term>oxymel: a mixture of honey and vinegar</term>. In this case, agaric is the specific medicine. Confections are appropriate as said for sweet phlegm, though you should increase the level of heat more, since "glassy" phlegm is colder than "sweet" phlegm. Regarding ointments, see for yourself.

### On the cure of mixed periodic phlegmatic fever.

¶ According to the composition of the humor, compose the simple ingredients. Thus, for common digestives: **Take** 1 drachm of strained rose honey, half a drachm of simple vinegar syrup, 1 drachm of sugar water, and 2 drachms of fennel water. **From the laxatives**: **Take** 1 drachm of cassia and 1 drachm of turbith; let it be extracted with a decoction of tamarinds, maidenhair fern, raisins, and licorice. Prepare the following confection: **Take** 2 scruples of cinnamon, 1.5 scruples of red sandalwood, half a drachm of pearls, and 1 pound of sugar. Prepare with bugloss, borage, and fennel water.
¶ Prepare an electuary: **Take** 2 drachms each of borage sugar and the *manuschristi* mentioned above; half a drachm of the species of the electuary of gems; half a scruple of red coral; and enough lemon syrup as suffices. Gild it.

<column-break/>

¶ Prepare troches and others as for "false" <note>salty</note> phlegm. A common digestive, at least in the beginning: **Take** 1.5 drachms of simple oxymel, half a drachm of strained rose honey, and 1 drachm each of bugloss water, fennel water, and sugar water.
¶ **From the laxatives**: **Take** half a drachm of "Indian pills" and 1 drachm of turbith pills. Incorporate them with simple oxymel and give up to five. Then transition to a stronger syrup, such as a professional one. **Take**: 2 drachms each of the "five roots" <note>celery, asparagus, fennel, butcher’s broom, and parsley</note>; 1 drachm each of maidenhair fern and hyssop; and 2 drachms each of hart's-tongue fern <note>original: "scolopēdrie"</note>, endive, chicory, and bugloss. Let a decoction be made, and at the end add 2.5 drachms of dodder of thyme <term>epithimi: a parasitic plant used to purge melancholy and phlegm</term>. Strain it, make into a syrup with sugar, and aromatize it with cinnamon, especially in summer. In winter, however, you can make the syrup with honey.
¶ **A professional laxative**: **Take** licorice, raisins, maidenhair fern, polypody fern, thyme, and dodder of thyme. Let a decoction be made with water and extract 6 drachms of cassia or manna; to which add 1 drachm of agaric, 1.5 drachms and 1 scruple of turbith, half a scruple of ginger, and 6 grains of rock salt.
¶ **From the confections, this is suitable**: **Take** 1 drachm of the species of "The Abbot’s Rose", 2 scruples of the species of the electuary of gems, and 10 drachms of sugar. Make it with fennel and bugloss water.
¶ **An electuary of gems**: **Take** 4 drachms each of bugloss and borage sugar; 1.5 drachms of the species of gem confection, or musk-based compound <note>original: "diamuschi"</note>, or aromatic rose; and half a drachm of "The Abbot’s Rose". Gild it, etc.

### On Epiala or Epialos.

¶ A common digestive, at least in the beginning: **Take** 1.5 drachms of simple oxymel, half a drachm of wild fruit syrup <term>rob: a thickened fruit juice or syrup</term>, and 1 drachm each of bugloss, fennel, and wormwood water; aromatize with cinnamon. And because Avicenna <note>a famous 11th-century Persian physician</note> praises one laxative, I wish to tell it to you here: **Take** 1 drachm each of yellow and black myrobalans <note>astringent plum-like fruits from India</note> and 1.5 drachms and half a scruple of turbith. Infuse in simple oxymel for ten hours; then add 4 ounces of goat's milk whey and heat it slightly. Then perform a strong pressing and add 6 drachms of manna or cassia. Administer this when you perceive there is some melancholy and you fear a conversion to a quartan fever.

### On the cure of quartan fevers.

Some give, after three evacuations, a wine made from a decoction of mint and horse-mint mixed with 1 or 2 drachms of theriac <term>theriac: a complex medical paste used as a universal antidote and panacea</term> and 4 drachms of "water of life" <term>aqua vite: distilled spirits or brandy</term>. This is given half an hour before the "accession" <note>the onset of the fever fit</note>. The wine is warm, and they cover the patients well; they do this three or four times as it seems beneficial to them, and thus they free them. Some [do] the same...

...are mixed with water for men and with clove powder <note>original: "puluere gariofiloz"</note>. Some give warm, pure aromatic wine with gentian powder, and it is a secret. Likewise, the seed of **St. John’s Wort** <term>hypericonis: St. John’s Wort, traditionally used to "drive away demons" and treat fevers</term> given with wine dissolves a quartan fever <term>quartana: a fever characterized by paroxysms that occur every fourth day, historically linked to the "black bile" of the spleen</term>, and this is proven by experience. And you know from what was set down above that such things ought to be given about one hour before the onset of the fever fit. **Catmint** <note>original: "nepita"</note> given in powder form with warm water works the same way. So does **yarrow** <note>original: "millefoliū"</note> with wine. Likewise, 1.5 drachms of **laurel berries** <note>original: "baccarū lauri"</note>; let 1 scruple of this powder be given with a thin wine before the onset; then let the patient be covered and let hot cloths be applied and left there. From the proven remedies: **Take** 2 drachms each of asafoetida, rue leaves, and long pepper; combine with honey and give before the onset. Someone told me he had many times proven the efficacy of half a drachm of **gentian** with thin wine. Some prepare this ointment: **Take** 2 drachms of theriac <term>tiriache: an ancient "universal antidote" containing dozens of ingredients, including viper flesh and opium</term>, 1 drachm of spikenard, 1 drachm of cloves, and 2 ounces each of old oil and wine. Let them boil over hot coals; with this ointment, rub the back and the entire spine near a large fire; afterwards, give warm thin wine in which gentian has been decocted with a little sugar, or the "confection of Adrian" described by Nicolaus <note>referring to the *Antidotarium Nicolai*, a famous medieval pharmacopeia</note>. The "Arogon" ointment of Nicolaus works the same way, but consider well the strength of the patient, for in such cases the sick person must be strong. Four seeds or leaves of **clover** <note>original: "trifolij"</note> drunk with wine before the onset take away a quartan fever, according to **Avicenna** <note>the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>. 1 drachm of powdered **human skull** <note>original: "cranei humani"</note> works the same way. Someone taught this as a "great secret"—using powdered skull in a drink. The same is confirmed if a large piece of a skull is held under the left armpit near the heart. The **heart of a rabbit** recently killed, hung from the neck or the left arm, also takes away a quartan fever.
¶ **An experiment of Platearius** <note>Matthaeus Platearius, a 12th-century physician from Salerno</note> for quartan and quotidian fevers: he said, "We have an excellent and proven experiment using **asarabacca** <term>assara: Wild Ginger, used as an emetic to induce vomiting</term> against quotidian <note>daily</note> and quartan fevers." Wine from a decoction of asarabacca berries should be given before the onset; if the matter is in the stomach, it draws it out through vomiting; if in other parts, it consumes it. Both the root and the leaves are medicinal. The root should be chosen for its fragrance; it should not be too light but weighty, and not worm-eaten but solid. It can keep its potency for three years.
¶ **Another most certain experiment** by the same Platearius, according to him: Let the patient use every day the powder of **carpobalsamum** <term>carpobalsami: the fruit of the balsam tree</term> with the outer bark removed, against "vices of the womb" arising from a cold cause, because it cleanses it. One should choose that which is not worm-eaten and is aromatic. Wine from a decoction of **cloves** with rose water is effective against all pain of the stomach caused by coldness and against the "cardiac passion" <term>cardiacam passionem: historically referring to severe heartburn or palpitations rather than a modern heart attack</term>.
¶ **An experiment of Platearius** against epilepsy and paralysis. **Take** a green lizard with its head and tail cut off

<column-break/>

and place it in warm common oil for 40 days until it putrefies; afterwards, let it be cooked in that same oil, and with asphalt and red wax added, let an ointment be made which is effective for epilepsy and paralysis if the spine is rubbed with it. It is also effective for **alopecia** <note>hair loss</note> caused by the putrefaction of cold humors.

...root of **plantain** <note>original: "stris radix" likely referring to *Plantago*</note>, when drunk, most effectively drives away the **fear of water** <term>aquae pauorem: hydrophobia, the hallmark symptom of rabies</term>. ### The Mithridatic Antidote
Doctors praise the **Mithridatic antidote** <note>named after Mithridates VI of Pontus, who supposedly made himself immune to poisons</note>; they offer various versions of its composition and demand huge sums of money for these precious ointments because of their rarity. They value single pounds of it at twenty sesterces, preying on the desperation of the unfortunate; they even use their wits to deceive them, persuading them to buy things that are actually harmful. For some versions hurt the stomach, others the head, and others bring on a lethargy or weigh down the body with wasting. Thus it frequently happens that those who used these "antidotes" died more miserably than if they had simply drunk the poison. However, **Pompey the Great**, after defeating Mithridates, found in the king's own cabinet a recipe written in his own hand. By taking this daily, the king kept himself safe and unharmed against all poisons. **Take** two walnuts, two dried figs, twenty rue leaves, and one grain of salt; pound them together and eat them while fasting. **Electrum** <term>electrum: a natural alloy of gold and silver</term> is gold in which a fifth part of silver is found. If anyone uses a drinking vessel made of this, he will escape the traps of poison; for in the presence of poison, rainbow-like arcs appear in the metal with a fiery hissing sound, and in this way, the crime is detected by a double sign. There is also "fake" electrum made by adding a fifth part of silver to gold, but this performs just as well as the natural kind. Thus we have shown which antidote prevents poison and which vessel detects it. Now I shall suggest further remedies. **Centaury** <note>a medicinal herb</note> drunk as a potion ejects harmful medicines through the bowels. A weight of one denarius of **birthwort** <note>original: "Aristologie"</note> root is drunk in goat’s wine. Dog's blood is drunk

<column-break/>

against toxins. Lamb's rennet taken in a potion is effective. A stork's stomach with sheep's milk is given in food. Common weasel, dried and aged, is drunk in doses of two drachms. The blood of **Pontic ducks** <note>ducks from the Black Sea region, famous for eating poisonous hellebore without harm</note> is kept thickened and then diluted with wine. Donkey's blood, when drunk, restrains poisons. Goat's blood is also usefully drunk.

Since the medical faculty—on whose investigation kings and princes of old spent no small effort because of its excellence—has always been held in the highest esteem, it is pleasing at the conclusion of this little work to attach the **privileges** in which the professors of this art rejoice, drawn from the body of Imperial Law <note>original: "iuris cesarei"</note>.

### The Privileges of Physicians.

¶ Physicians are not bound to undertake civic duties <note>referring to Law "Medicos", Code "On Professors and Physicians", Book 10</note>.
In every city, a certain number must be established <note>Law 1, Digest "On the decrees to be made by the order"</note> who must have the care of healing bodies.
Both they and their children and wives are excused from all public burdens <note>Law "Medicos" and the final law of "On the vacation and excuse from duties"</note>.
They are not required to receive guests <note>billeting soldiers or officials</note> in their homes, even upon the arrival of the Prince <note>Digest "On duties and guests", final law</note>.
For physicians, during the time they are in battle to care for the sick, the statute of limitations <note>original: "prescriptio"</note> does not run against them <note>Law 3, Code "To whom a long-term prescription does not apply"</note>.
They ought not to be brought into court against their will <note>Law "Medicos", Code "On Professors and Physicians"</note>.
They are excused from guardianship and curatorship <note>Law "Final two", section "Grammarians", Digest "On excuses from guardianship"</note>.
A physician who is still under his father's legal power <note>original: "filiusfamilias"</note> can make a will regarding property acquired in his professional service <note>Law "With the ancients", Code "On undutiful wills"</note>.
He has, or ought to have, a salary from the public treasury <note>Law "Medicos", Code "On Professors and Physicians"</note>.
Physicians treating the poor are permitted to receive a salary from the public treasury <note>Law "Archiatri", Code "On Professors and Physicians", Book 10</note>.
If physicians are found to be insufficient or incompetent after being approved, they can be rejected <note>Law "That step by step", section "To be rejected", Digest "On duties and guests"</note>.
All privileges granted to physicians are seen to be granted to their children, wife, and household <note>Law "Often", cited above, and the final law near the end of the Code "On Professors and Physicians"</note>.

# Introductory Handbook

...are mixed with vine water and powdered **cloves** <note>original: "gariofiloꝝ"</note>. Likewise, **St. John’s Wort** <term>sebypericonis: Hypericum perforatum</term> given with wine breaks a **quartan fever** <term>quartanam: a fever, often malarial, that returns every third day</term>, and this is proven. And you know from what was stated above that such things ought to be given about one hour before the onset of the fever fit. **Catnip** <note>original: "nepita"</note> works the same way when given as a powder with hot water. So too does **yarrow** <note>original: "millefolium"</note> with wine, or laurel berries. 

**Recipe for a powder to be given before the onset:** 
Take 1 drachm of the powder with thin wine; then let the patient be covered and let warm cloths be applied and left there. 
**From the proven remedies:** 
Take **asafoetida** <note>a pungent plant resin</note>, rue leaves, and long pepper, 2 drachms each. Mix with honey and give before the fever begins. Someone told me he had often found success with half a drachm of gentian in thin wine. 

**Some prepare this ointment:** 
Take: **Theriac** <term>tiriache: an ancient "universal" herbal jam or panacea</term> 2 drachms, **spikenard** 1 drachm, cloves 1 drachm, and 2 drachms each of old oil and wine. Let them boil over hot coals. With this ointment, grease the back and the whole spine before a large fire; then apply warm cloths. Afterward, you shall give thin wine made from a warm decoction of gentian with a little sugar, or the "Confection of Hadrian" according to the description of Nicolaus. The "Arogon" ointment of Nicolaus works the same, but consider well the strength of the patient, for in such cases the sick person must be strong. 

Four seeds or leaves of **trefoil** <note>clover</note> drunk with wine before the onset take away quartan fever, according to **Avicenna** <note>the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina</note>. One drachm of powdered human skull works the same. Someone taught this as a great secret—drinking the powdered skull. It is likewise confirmed that if a large piece of a skull is held under the left armpit, or the heart of a recently killed hare is hung from the neck or left arm, it removes the quartan fever.

**Experiment of Platearius for daily quartan fevers:** 
He said: We have an excellent and proven experiment using **asarum** <note>original: "assara," likely hazelwort</note> against daily and quartan fevers. Wine from a decoction of asarum berries should be given before the onset; if the "matter" of the illness is in the stomach, it brings it out through vomiting; if in other parts of the body, it consumes it. The root is medicinal, as are the leaves. The root should be chosen for its fragrance, not too light but heavy, and solid rather than worm-eaten. It can keep its power for three years.

**Another experiment by the same Platearius, most certain according to him:** 
Let the patient use daily the powder of **carpobalsamum** <note>the fruit of the balsam tree</note> with the upper bark removed, for disorders of the womb arising from a cold cause, because it cleanses it. One should choose the fruit that is not perforated and is aromatic. Wine from a decoction of cloves with rose water is good against all stomach pain from "coldness" and against heart palpitations.

**Experiment of Platearius against epilepsy and paralysis:** 
Take a green lizard, and having cut off its head

¶ Since the medical faculty—to whose investigation kings and princes once devoted no small effort because of its eminence—has always been most highly esteemed, it pleased me at the end of this little work to annex the privileges which the professors of this art enjoy, drawn from the body of **Imperial Law** <term>iuris cesarei: Roman civil law</term>.

### The Privileges of Physicians.

¶ Physicians are not bound to undertake civil duties <note>such as public offices or mandatory community service</note>. *Law: medicos, Code of the Profession and Physicians, Book 10.*
In every city, a certain number [of doctors] should be established by decree who must have the care of healing bodies.
Both they and their children and wives are excused from all public duties. *As said in the law "medicos" and the final law on Vacations and Excuses from Duties.*
They are not bound to receive guests <note>billeting or quartering soldiers/officials</note> in their homes, even upon the arrival of the Prince. *Digest on Duties and Honors, final law.*
For physicians, during the time they remain in battle for the sake of curing the sick, the **statute of limitations** <note>original: "prescriptio"</note> does not run against them. *Code: To whom long-term prescription does not apply.*
They should not be brought into court against their will. *Said law: medicos, Code of the Profession and Physicians.*
They are excused from guardianship and caretaking <note>legal duties to manage others' estates</note>. *Digest on Excuses from Guardianship.*
A physician who is a "son under authority" <term>filiusfamilias: a son still legally subject to his father</term> can make a will regarding his **quasi-military property** <term>quasi castrensi peculio: earnings from professional service that the father could not claim</term>. *Law "cum antiquis," where the Gloss and Doctors comment.*
He has, or should have, a salary from the public treasury. *Said law: medicos.*
For physicians treating the poor, it is permitted to receive a salary from the public. *Law: archiatri, Code of the Profession and Physicians, Book 10.*
If physicians are found to be insufficient <note>incompetent</note> after being approved, they can be rejected. *Digest: on Duties and Honors.*
All privileges granted to physicians are seen as granted to their children, wife, and family, as in the law cited above.

O God, who presented the blessed Louis <note>Saint Louis IX (1214–1270), the only King of France to be canonized as a saint.</note>, powerful in the French dominion, as an example to others of both mercy and total devotion from his earliest youth: grant, we beseech you, that we—who have cast down the insane pleasure of the present age through chastity, great wealth through piety, and pride through true humility—may by your grace, and accompanied by his merits, be granted to live in a manner like his, and be bestowed the eternal enjoyment of heavenly glory. Through our Lord.
