<meta>This page transitions from the general index of the work to the "Introductory Letter" (Epistola prohemialis). It serves as a formal dedication by the author, Symphorien Champier, to Cardinal Georges d'Amboise, shifting the focus from historical tables to the moral and political philosophy underpinning the work, specifically the value of peace and wise leadership.</meta>

# Introductory Letter

<margin>
The peaceful
reign of 
King Numa
Pompilius.
</margin>
To the most reverend father in Christ and lord: **Lord Georges d'Amboise**, Archbishop of the Church of Rouen <note>original: "Rothomagensis"</note>, Cardinal, and most worthy Legate in France; a man distinguished both by his learning and his virtues: **Symphorien Champier**, physician of Lyon, wishes much health.

---

<image-desc>A large woodcut decorative initial 'N' containing a scholar or ruler figure seated at a desk within a vaulted classical interior, surrounded by books and architectural details.</image-desc>

<margin>
The principle
for 
maintaining
peace.
</margin>
Most pious father, the writers who have committed the noble deeds of kings and princes to the monuments of literature extol **Numa Pompilius**, the second king of the Romans, with the highest proclamations of praise. He was a man born of the Cures <note>A town of the Sabines.</note> among the Sabines, so distinguished in all religion, piety, peace, prudence, and justice that subsequent ages believed him to have been a disciple of Pythagoras. Yet, he was instructed not so much by foreign arts as by the severe and somber discipline of the ancient Sabines. He diverted the Roman people from the savagery of war to the pursuits of peace and religion. He is surely an exemplar to all who are powerful in royal authority, that they might follow his institutions.

<margin>
Commendation
of peace.
Invective 
against
Lycurgus. <note>Lycurgus was the legendary lawgiver of Sparta, often contrasted with Numa because his laws focused on military discipline rather than Numa’s religious and peaceful reforms.</note>
</margin>
Since, among all living beings, man is especially born for society and peace—as the author Lullius <note>Likely referring to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a philosopher whom Champier admired, though the sentiment is also found in Cicero.</note> maintains—who would not think that man alienated from every condition of nature and humanity who, as a supporter of war and discord, delights in raging like a tyrant over others, often abusing the powers of his empire? Thus, I judge that race of men to be impious whose arts, or rather deceits, undermine and dissolve the most pleasant bond of human benevolence, and who endeavor to pull apart and separate souls joined by charity—without which no society can exist. Therefore, let princes be of a tranquil and benign spirit; if they easily demonstrate their prosperity and deeds, they will find that a kingdom is acquired and preserved far more by skill and beneficence than by threats or even force. By what means did **Cyrus** transfer the empire from the Medes to the Persians? Was it not by prudent industry and greatness of soul?

<margin>Alexander</margin>
By what means did **Alexander** penetrate as far as the Ganges? Was it not by prudence and kindness?

<margin>Caesar</margin>
By what means, finally, did **Julius Caesar** attain the leadership of the whole world? Was it not by counsel and clemency? For as long as **Romulus** showed himself to be humane <gloss>mankind</gloss> and gentle, he was regarded as a near-divinity on earth. But from the moment he wished to use his mind’s power and legal right to deal with things by force, he became a tyrant toward those to whom he should have been dearer and more pleasant. For this reason, that wise King **Philip of Macedon**, the father of Alexander the Great, is recorded by Theophrastus to have stood out as greater and more moderate than other kings, not only in his royal lineage and dignity but also in his kingly fortune and character. Because he understood the temperaments and customs of the Macedonian people, he advised his son Alexander, not without reason, that he should show himself to be charming and gracious to the Macedonians, so that he might secure for himself the strength of the multitude. For the minds of the people are captured not by threats, nor by terrors, but by various duties of humanity and, most especially, by charms. And although these duties of the human soul are equally appropriate for all, they are most fitting for the prelates who emulate Christ, who—when he was about to depart for heaven—left peace to be perpetually preserved by his followers. While I see that your ancestors were very studious of this, you yourself, more than all others, seem to me to imitate that peaceful Numa; for I see that many even among the pastors of the Lord’s flock abuse the peace, which they ought to use for the study of the good arts and the duties of virtue, by being devoted to obscene pleasures.

<margin>
Cato
of the 
Latins.
</margin>
If they commend **Cato the Censor**—a just man—for the exceptional virtues of his soul, the songs of poets, and the eloquence of orators, they must hold you as no less worthy of praise than him.

# Introductory Letter

->¶ To the most reverend father in Christ<-
->and lord: Lord **Georges d'Amboise**,<-
->Archbishop of the Church of Rouen,<-
->Cardinal, and most worthy Legate in<-
->France; distinguished both by<-

<margin>
A peaceful 
kingdom
for
Numa’s 
people.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'N' containing a figure within a classical landscape framed by foliate and architectural motifs.</image-desc>

**W**riters who have committed the illustrious deeds of kings and princes to the records of literature extol **Numa Pompilius**, the second king of the Romans, with the highest heraldry of praise. A man of most pious character, born in Cures, a city of the Sabines, he was so distinguished in all religion, piety, peace, prudence, and justice that subsequent ages believed him to have been a disciple of **Pythagoras** <note>A famous Greek philosopher and mathematician; historical chronologies now show Numa lived long before him, but the legend of their connection persisted in the Renaissance.</note>. Yet he was instructed not so much in foreign arts as in the austere and somber discipline of the ancient Sabines. He transformed the Roman people, through the severity of war, toward the pursuit of peace and religion. He is surely an exemplar to all those holding royal power, that they might follow his institutions. For since, among all living creatures, man is especially born for society and peace—according to **Tullius** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and orator.</note>—who would not think him alienated from all conditions of nature and humanity who, as a supporter of war and discord, delights in acting the tyrant over others by abusing the great powers of his empire? Thus it is that I judge that race of men to be impious whose arts and deceits weaken and dissolve the most pleasant bond of human benevolence, and who attempt to divide and separate souls joined together by charity, without which no society can exist. Let princes, therefore, be of a tranquil and kind spirit; if they wish for prosperity, their deeds easily demonstrate that a kingdom is ruled and preserved far better by art and beneficence than by threats or even by force. By what means did **Cyrus** transfer the empire from the Medes to the Persians? Was it not by prudence and greatness of soul? By what means did **Alexander** penetrate even to the Ganges? Was it not by prudence and kindness? By what means, finally, did **Julius Caesar** attain the leadership of the whole world? Was it not by counsel and clemency? For **Romulus**, as long as he showed himself merciful and mild to the human race, was regarded almost as a divinity on earth. But when he first wished to use his power to rule the minds of others with harshness, he was treated with cruelty by those to whom he ought to have been more dear and pleasant. For this reason, that wise King **Philip of Macedon**, the father of Alexander the Great, is recorded by **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle.</note> to have stood out as greater and more moderate than other kings, not only in his royal lineage and dignity but also in both fortune and character. Because he understood the temperaments and customs of the Macedonian people, he advised his son Alexander—not without reason—that he should show himself gracious and flattering to the Macedonians, so that he might secure the strength of the multitude for himself. For the minds of the people are captured not by threats, nor by terrors, but by other duties of humanity and, most especially, by kindness. And although these duties of the human soul are equally appropriate for all, they are most fitting for prelates <note>High-ranking church officials like bishops or archbishops.</note>, who are the emulators of Christ; for He, when He was about to depart into heaven, left behind peace to be perpetually preserved by His followers. While I see that your ancestors were greatly devoted to these studies, you yourself, more than all others, seem to me to imitate that peaceful Numa. Many other pastors of the Lord's flock abuse the peace—which they ought to use for the study of the good arts and the duties of virtue—by dedicating themselves to obscene pleasures. But if they commend **Cato the Censor** <note>Marcus Porcius Cato (234–149 BCE), known for his strict morality and opposition to Hellenistic influence.</note> for the exceptional virtues of his soul, the songs of poets, and the eloquence of orators, they must hold you as no less worthy of praise than him.

# Letter

History does not grant **Pompey the Great** <note>Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (106–48 BCE), a leading Roman general and statesman.</note> mediocre honor for his very famous deeds, yet you stand here, by no means to be placed after him. If, finally, we wished to bring forward the illustrious gifts of our great ancestors, we would easily find you distinguished by a good part of them; you are so noted that you provide an example to others in both all academic disciplines and in virtues. Nor is it a wonder that you are a lover of virtues and a cultivator of honesty, which is—as they say—cooked into the very roots of your lineage.

<margin>Parents</margin> Therefore, your character could not be weakened either by long spans of time or by the evil contagions of this life of ours. It is indeed, as I seem to see, a great aid to virtue to be born of noble parents. For young men who have some natural talent are accustomed to emulate the dignity of their ancestors so as not to seem degenerate, and they aspire to the happiness of the praises earned by their fathers. Thus the name of **Philip** [of Macedon] inspired **Alexander**. Thus the glory of the elder **Africanus** inspired the younger **Scipio**. Thus the fame of **Julius Caesar** excited **Octavian**. Thus also **Pyrrhus**, the son of Achilles, was emboldened by the image of his father. 

You also, most worthy archbishop, since you love virtue—not a little because of God and nature leading you, and by your own striving studies—can nonetheless be helped by the images of your predecessors, whose character leads you to equal them. Though it is arduous and difficult, it is certainly both beautiful and laudable. 

<margin>Praise of the House of Amboise</margin> For what thing worthy of the **House of Amboise** could I now bring to light? It would surely be much better not to enter such a vast sea at all than to wish to sail it in such a small boat <note>Champier uses the common "modesty trope" of the Renaissance, comparing his writing ability to a small boat and his patron's greatness to a vast ocean.</note>. However, lest I seem to pass over said house entirely in silence, I will draw out at least a minimal part of their most extensive praises. 

If we seek the immense generosity of this house, we will easily find it approaching the nobility of the ancient kings of the Franks. If we seek antiquity, this house alone surpasses the memory of the ancients in its illustrious deeds and high offices. What other race of men will we find more excellent than this one? 

And keeping silent about others, let us mention only those who are alive in our age. First occurs Lord **A.** [Aimery d'Amboise], mature in counsel and outstanding in prudence, whom they call the **Grand Master of Rhodes**—and not without reason, for he is a most fierce defender and a tower of strength for the orthodox faith against the face of the enemy of unsullied Christianity. He is followed by a company of prelates to be treated with the highest honor: namely, Lord **A.** [Louis d’Amboise], Bishop of Albi; Lord **Jean** [d’Amboise], prelate and Duke of Langres and Peer of France; Lord **A.** [Louis d’Amboise the younger], Bishop of Poitiers; and Lord **A.** [Jacques d’Amboise], Bishop of Clermont and most worthy Abbot of Cluny. 

If I should try to describe their innumerable gifts of both body and mind, to use the words of **Virgil**: *Evening will close Olympus and settle the day before I finish* <note>original: "Ante diem clauso componet vesper olympo" from Virgil's Aeneid, I.374.</note>. But yet you, most excellent of archbishops, far exceed so many and such great men, so that concerning you that same poet's words may truly be said: *As much as the flexible willow yields to the pale olive, or the humble wild-nard to crimson rose-beds* <note>original: "Lenta salix quantum pallenti cedit olivae, Puniceis humilis quantum saliunca rosetis" from Virgil's Eclogues, V.16-17.</note>. In our judgment, the rest yield to you by just as much. 

<margin>Virgil in the Bucolics, Eclogue Five. Virgil in the Bucolics.</margin> For although they themselves have turned out to be quite distinguished, you confer no small ornament upon them, so that of you the same poet’s words are verified: *As the vine is the glory of trees, as grapes of the vine, as bulls of the herd, as corn of the rich fields: you are all the glory of your kin* <note>original: "Vitis ut arboribus decori est, ut vitibus uvae, Ut gregibus tauri, segetes ut pinguibus arvis: Tu decus omne tuis" from Virgil's Eclogues, V.32-34.</note>. 

We pray with bended knee that you might make us a sharer in this glory; which we will frankly confess ourselves to have obtained when we know that you have looked with a cheerful brow and relaxed gaze upon our little work—composed with no small nighttime diligence and dedicated to you as the sole protector of men of letters—which bears on its front the title **On the Victories of the Gauls Against Foreign Nations**. For with you favoring it, it will go forth into public more securely, nor will it fear the barking of the envious. Farewell, support of the whole kingdom, and deign to admit us among those devoted to you. 

From **Lyon** <note>original: "Lugdunum"</note>, in the year of our Lord 1508, on the 17th of June <note>original: "xv. kalendas Julij" (the 15th day before the Kalends of July).</note>.

# The Trophies of the Gauls: First Treatise

# ¶ On the division of Gaul. Likewise on the origin of the Gauls. And their virtues against other nations, and especially the Romans.

### ¶ First Treatise.

<margin>Division of Gaul</margin>
<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'G' depicting a landscape with a river, trees, and buildings in the distance, set within a double-lined rectangular frame.</image-desc>
All Gaul (as **Caesar** <note>Julius Caesar, in the opening of his *Commentaries on the Gallic War*.</note> testifies) is divided into three parts: one which the **Belgae** inhabit, another the **Aquitani**, and the third those who in their own language are called **Celts**, but in ours **Gauls**. Caesar does not mention the province of **Lyonnaise** <note>Lugdunensis</note>. However, all of "Long-haired Gaul" <note>original: "Gallia comata"; so named by the Romans because the inhabitants wore their hair long.</note> (as **Pliny** testifies) is called by one name and divided into three types of people: the **Belgian**, the **Lyonnaise** (or Celtic), and the **Aquitanian**. **Ptolemy** <note>The Greco-Roman geographer.</note> adds the **Narbonensis** province by the Mediterranean Sea. **Belgica** extends from the **Scheldt** river to the **Seine**. From that river to the **Garonne** is **Lyonnaise**. From there to the ridge of the **Pyrenees** mountains is **Aquitania**.

<margin>Fertility of Gaul</margin>
The land is especially fertile in grain and pasture; here it is productive for all kinds of crops due to its temperate warmth and there because of its lucky and timely rains. It is so abundant that it suffices not only for the inhabitants themselves, but also provides a wealth of all things to **Spain**, **Italy**, and especially to the **Genoese**. For here there is not only a great supply of grain, but also of wine, oil, and honey. It is least frequent in harmful types of animals. It is watered by rivers and springs, and distinguished by two great rivers, the **Rhine** and the **Rhone**. It is most blessed in its offspring for the use of living creatures. It joins Spain only at the single ridge of the Pyrenees mountains. From the east, the peaks of the **Alps** protect it; from the west, the **Ocean** encloses it; from the north, the streams of the Rhine and **Germany**. **Cisalpine** Gaul (meaning "on this side of the Alps") and **Transalpine** (that is, "across the Alps" toward the north) are the parts of Gaul, as we have said.

<margin>Regions of Gaul</margin>
If we wish to distinguish the specific provinces of Gaul, there occur: **France** <note>Referring to the Île-de-France region.</note>, **Normandy**, **Brittany**, **Touraine**, **Picardy**, **Flanders**, **Holland**, **Zeeland**, **Burgundy**, **Lorraine**, **Luxembourg**, **Switzerland** (or **Alsace**), **Provence**, and the **Dauphiné**.

<margin>Characteristics of the Gauls</margin>
The race is most Christian and religious. Their bodies are prepared for fasting and labor, and their minds for death. They prefer war to leisure. They are military men, and their arms are dearer to them than their own blood. They have always had masters of wisdom as their properties <note>A reference to the Druids.</note>, who profess to know the magnitude and form of the earth and the world, the movements of the sky and stars, and what the gods wish. But hear what the Gauls were capable of in such a long series of ages, who frequently exhausted even the Romans with varying victory.

<column-break/>

Listen to **Trogus Pompeius** <note>A Roman historian whose work survives via the epitome of Justin.</note> speaking thus in **Justin's** 20th book of epitomes: "While **Dionysius** <note>Tyrant of Syracuse.</note> was waging war, ambassadors of the Gauls—who a few months earlier had burned **Rome**—approached him seeking an alliance and friendship. They affirmed that their nation was placed among his enemies and would be of great use to him, either fighting in the battle line or attacking the enemies from the back while they were intent on the fight." This embassy was pleasing to Dionysius. Thus, having struck an alliance and being reinforced by Gallic aid, he renewed the war as if from scratch. However, the cause for the Gauls coming into Italy and seeking new homes was internal discord and constant dissensions at home. Out of weariness for these, when they had come into Italy, they expelled the **Etruscans** <note>original: "Thuscos"</note> from their seats and founded **Milan**, **Como**, **Brescia**, **Verona**, **Bergamo**, **Trento**, and **Vicenza**. Thus far Justin. And as the historian **Antias** writes, in the year 642 from the founding of the city <note>642 AUC, or roughly 112 BCE.</note>, the proconsuls **Caius Manlius** and **Quintus Caepio** were sent against the **Cimbri**, **Teutones**, **Tigurini**, and **Ambrones** (Gallic tribes who had then conspired to extinguish the Roman Empire); they divided the provinces between themselves with the Rhone river in the middle. There, while they disputed among themselves with the gravest envy and contention, the Italians were defeated by the Gauls with great danger to the Roman name. Indeed, in that battle, **Marcus Aemilius** was captured and killed. Two sons of the consul were slain. 80,000 Romans and allies were slaughtered in that time of glory; 60,000 camp servants and followers were killed. Thus, it is reported that from the entire army only ten men survived to bring back the miserable news to increase the miseries. The Gauls, having gained two camps and huge plunder, destroyed everything with a new kind of curse: clothing was torn and thrown away, gold and silver were cast into the river, the breastplates of the men were cut up, the trappings of the horses were destroyed, the horses themselves were drowned in the whirlpools, and men with nooses placed around their necks were hung from trees, so that the victor recognized no plunder and the conquered recognized no mercy. There was then at Rome not only the greatest mourning, but also fear. Thus far Antias. And around the year 484 from the founding of the city, the **Cisalpine Gauls** emerged as new enemies of the Romans, against whom it was fought with varying fortune. For in the first conflict under the consul **Valerius**, 3,500 Romans fell. And as the historian **Fabius** <note>Fabius Pictor, the earliest Roman historian.</note> attests, in the year 545 from the founding of the city, during the consulship of **Lucius Aemilius**, **Lutatius Baebius**, and **Atilius Regulus**, the Senate was struck with great dread by the revolt of Cisalpine Gaul, since it was also announced that a huge army was approaching from further Gaul, especially of the **Gaesatae** <note>Gallic mercenaries armed with a distinct spear called a gaesum.</note>, which is the name not of a race, but of mercenary Gauls. So...

It emphasizes the Gauls' military prowess and religious nature, recounting their ancient migrations into Italy and their devastating victories over Roman armies.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the historical account of the Gauls, moving from the geographical description of the previous page to their military conflicts with the Romans and their migrations into Greece and Macedonia during the 3rd century BCE.</meta>

# The Trophies of the Gauls.

The consuls were moved to gather the forces of all Italy for the protection of the empire. In doing so, it is reported that there were 800,000 armed men in the armies of both consuls. Among these, the Roman and Campanian <note>Inhabitants of the Campania region of Italy, known for their alliance with Rome.</note> infantry numbered 368,000, while the cavalry numbered 26,000, with the rest making up the remaining multitude. When battle was joined at **Arezzo** <note>original: "Arretium"</note>, the consul **Attilius** <note>Gaius Atilius Regulus, who died at the Battle of Telamon in 225 BCE, though the text here refers to the broader Gallic Wars in Italy.</note> was killed. 72,000 Romans were slain—or at least a portion large enough that it should have terrified them—yet they fled. Indeed, historians record that 3,000 of them were killed then; it is for this reason all the more ignominious and shameful that such great ranks fled after losing so few. In the following year, dire portents terrified the wretched city.

<margin>Prodigies seen.</margin>
The city was indeed wretched, terrified on one side by the roar of enemies and on the other by the wickedness of demons. For in the **Picene** river, blood flowed out; and among the **Tuscans**, the sky was seen to burn. At **Rimini**, in the deep of night, bright lights shone forth, and three moons were seen to rise in different regions of the sky. At that time also, **Achaia** <note>A region in Greece.</note> and the island of **Rhodes** were so shaken by a great earthquake that, as buildings fell everywhere, that famous and massive **Colossus** <note>The Colossus of Rhodes, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note> also collapsed.

<margin>The entry of the Gauls into Italy.</margin>
The entry of the Gauls into Italy is recorded by **Trogus Pompeius** in the works of **Justin**, book 24 of the *Epitomes*, when he says: The Gauls, with an overflowing multitude, since the lands that had fathered them could not hold them, sent out 300,000 men to seek new homes, as if on a pilgrimage. Of these, a portion settled in Italy, which also captured and burned the city of Rome. Another portion penetrated the **Illyrian** gulfs, guided by birds—for the Gauls are skilled beyond all others in the study of <term>augury</term> <note>The practice of interpreting the will of the gods through the flight or behavior of birds.</note>—and through the slaughter of barbarians, they settled in **Pannonia** <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note>. They are a harsh, bold, and warlike race who were the first after **Hercules**—to whom that feat gave admiration for his virtue and a belief in his immortality—to cross the unconquered peaks of the **Alps** and places made impassable by cold. There, having tamed the Pannonians, they waged various wars with their neighbors for many years.

<margin>3</margin>
Soon, following such success, the Gauls divided their ranks: some sought **Greece**, others **Macedonia**, laying everything waste with the sword. So great was the terror of the Gallic name that even kings who had not been provoked sought to buy peace with huge sums of money. Only **Ptolemy**, the King of Macedonia <note>Ptolemy Ceraunus, known for his violent rise to power.</note>, heard of the Gauls' arrival without fear. Driven by the furies of his own <term>parricides</term> <note>The act of killing one's close relatives; Ptolemy had murdered his half-brothers to seize the throne.</note>, he went out to meet them with a few disorganized troops, as if wars were no more difficult to wage than his own crimes. He even scorned a diplomatic mission from the **Dardanians** offering 20,000 armed men in aid, adding further insult. He said it would be the end of Macedonia if, after they had conquered the whole East alone, they now needed Dardanians to defend their borders; he claimed his soldiers were the sons of those who, as victors under **King Alexander**, had served in campaigns across the whole world.
<meta>catchword: would have served [fecerint]</meta>

<column-break/>

When these things were reported to the Dardanian king, he said that the famous kingdom of Macedonia would soon fall due to the rashness of a premature youth. Therefore, the Gauls, under their leader **Belgius**, sent envoys to Ptolemy to test the spirit of the Macedonians, offering peace if he wished to buy it. But Ptolemy boasted among his people that the Gauls sought peace out of fear of war. He behaved no less fiercely toward the envoys than he did when boasting among his friends, stating he would not grant peace unless their chiefs were given as hostages and their weapons handed over; for he would not trust them unless they were unarmed. When the embassy's report was brought back, the Gauls laughed everywhere, shouting that he would soon realize whether they had offered peace out of consideration for themselves or for him. A few days later, battle was joined. The defeated Macedonians gave way. Ptolemy the Macedonian, weakened by many wounds, was captured; his head was cut off and, fixed upon a spear, was carried around the entire defeated line to terrify the enemy. Flight saved a few of the Macedonians; the rest were either captured or killed. When this was announced throughout all Macedonia, the gates of the cities were closed and everything was filled with mourning. Now they grieved for the loss of their sons; now they feared the destruction of their cities; now, invoking the names of their kings **Alexander** and **Philip**, they called upon them as gods for aid. They prayed that those under whom they had not only been safe but had emerged as conquerors of the world would protect their fatherland, which they had made first in the heavens by the glory of their deeds, and bring help to the afflicted whom the madness and rashness of King Ptolemy had destroyed. While everyone else was in despair, **Sosthenes**, one of the Macedonian nobles, thinking that action rather than vows was required, gathered the youth and both restrained the Gauls (who were exulting in their victory) and defended Macedonia from hostile depopulation. Because of these virtuous services, he, though not of royal blood himself, was preferred over many nobles who were seeking the kingdom of Macedonia. And when he was hailed as king by the army, he compelled the soldiers to swear an oath to him not under the name of "King," but as "Leader." Meanwhile, **Brennus**, the leader under whom a portion of the Gauls had poured into Greece, heard that those under Belgius had defeated the Macedonians. Indignant that the victory had been so easily abandoned after it was won, he himself broke into Macedonia with 150,000 infantry and 15,000 cavalry. As they were plundering the fields and villas, Sosthenes met him with an organized army of Macedonians. But a few are easily conquered by many, and the fearful by the strong. And so, when the defeated Macedonians had hidden themselves within the city walls, the victorious Brennus, with no one to stop him, plundered the fields of all Macedonia. And as the same **Justin** affirms in book 25...

# First Treatise

<margin>
Kings trust in the Gauls.
</margin>
At that time, the youth of the Gauls was of such great fecundity that they filled all of Asia as if in a swarm. In short, neither did the kings of the East wage any wars without a mercenary army of Gauls, nor did those driven from their kingdoms flee to any others but to the Gallic kings. Such was the terror of the Gallic

<margin>
The name of the Gauls always terrified the Romans.

name, or rather the success joined to their arms, that kings believed they could neither keep their majesty safe nor recover what was lost without Gallic courage. Thus, having been called to aid by the king of Bithynia <note>An ancient kingdom in northwest Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note>, they divided the kingdom with him after victory was won, and they named that region Gallograecia <note>Also known as Galatia, where the Gauls settled in Asia Minor.</note>. The same **Justin** <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian whose work preserved much earlier history.</note> in Book 28 says of the Gauls and their courage against the Romans: they heard that the peoples of Transalpine Gaul, having entered Italy, possessed many of its greatest cities; and that they occupied a broad territory within the borders of Asia, which is said to have been taken by those same Gauls in wars. Rome was said not only to have been defeated by the Gauls, but even captured, so that only the peak of a single mountain <note>The Capitoline Hill, which legend says was saved by the honking of sacred geese.</note> was left to them; and the enemy was removed not by war, but by a price <note>Refers to the gold paid to the Gallic leader Brennus to end the siege of Rome.</note>. Moreover, the name of the Gauls, which always terrified the Romans, he [Justin] considers part of their strength. For those Gauls who inhabit Asia are distinct in location from those who occupied Italy, yet they have almost the same origin, courage, and lineage. Regarding their religion and the worship of the gods as the time permitted, hear the same **Justin** in Book 43 speaking of **Massilia** <note>Modern-day Marseille, France, founded as a Greek colony.</note>, which was founded near the mouth of the Rhone River in a remote bay, as if in a corner of the sea. Massilia flourished everywhere in the fame of its deeds, the abundance of its wealth, and the glory of its strength, suddenly the neighboring peoples gathered to wipe out the name of the Massilians, as if to extinguish a common fire. By unanimous consent, the petty king **Catamandus** was chosen as leader. While he was besieging the city of the enemies with a great army of most select men, he was terrified in his sleep by the appearance of a fierce woman who called herself a goddess. Of his own accord, he made peace with the Massilians. Having asked that he might enter the city and worship their gods, when he came to the Citadel of Minerva, he suddenly cried out upon seeing the statue of the goddess in the portico—whom he had seen in his sleep—that she was the one who had terrified him at night and ordered him to withdraw from the siege. Congratulating the Massilians because he perceived that they were under the care of the immortal gods, he gifted a golden torque <note>original: "tozque" (torque), a traditional Celtic neck ring.</note> to the goddess and joined in perpetual friendship with the Massilians.

<margin>
The noble deed of the Massilians.
</margin>
Peace having been won and security established, the ambassadors of the Massilians—who had been sent to bring gifts to Apollo at **Delphi**—returning home, heard that the city of Rome had been captured and burned by the neighboring Gauls. When this news was announced at home, the Massilians observed a period of public mourning; they contributed public and private gold and silver

<column-break/>

to complete the weight for the Gauls, from whom they had learned that peace had been purchased. For this merit, immunity was decreed for them, a place for spectacles was given to them in the Senate, and a treaty of equal rights was struck. These were the slaughters of the Italians carried out by the Gauls. But I shall briefly set forth what they also suffered from others. It is recorded in memory that to **Hannibal**, when he was hurrying with burning hatred against the Italians, there appeared in his dreams a serpent of horrific size, which, following the army from behind, laid low the woods and forests with a great crash. What else was that terrible serpent but Hannibal himself, through whose ministry God wished to punish the crimes of all Italy? We read in the Christian annals that **Attila**, the most ferocious king of the Huns, when he was devastating Italy with so many and such great slaughters, said with a free voice that he was the "Scourge of God." Likewise, histories sing that while the Roman prince **Zeno** was reigning, the Goths under the leader **Theodoric** invaded Italy, and it was afflicted by various incursions of barbarians and then occupied by the tyranny of **Odoacer**. Did not **Frederick**, called **Barbarossa** <note>Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I, known for his conflicts with the Italian city-states.</note>, overthrow the most flourishing city of **Milan** among the internal Italians, and pursue Pope **Alexander III** at Venice? What is to be said of the Roman emperors? Did not **Julius Caesar** usurp power through violence and tyranny against the state of the Republic? For when he had come into Italy returning from Gaul, he demanded that a second consulship be decreed for him in his absence. This was opposed by the consul **Marcellus**, with **Pompey** striving against him. Then it was decreed by the Senate that Caesar should not come into the city except with his army dismissed. Pompey and all the Senate, trembling as Caesar's strength grew, as if driven from Italy, crossed over into Greece and chose **Dyrrachium** <note>Modern Durrës, Albania.</note> as the seat for waging war. Caesar came to Rome, and when money from the public treasury was denied to him, he broke down the doors and invaded it, taking from it 4,175 pounds of gold and nearly 400,000 pounds of silver. Departing from there and crossing the Alps, he came to Massilia; then he proceeded to the Spains. Returning from there, he defeated Pompey and his men in the **Battle of Pharsalus** and put them to flight. Later, he returned to Rome, where, while he was arranging the state of the Republic according to the examples and ordinances of his ancestors, he perished—slain by 22 wounds in the Curia—at the hands of the instigators **Brutus** and **Cassius**, and with the knowledge of much of the Senate, because he had usurped an impious power with a violent hand. In this conspiracy, they say there were more than sixty partners in this deed. The two Brutuses and Gaius Cassius and many others of the conspirators, with drawn daggers, withdrew to the Capitoline. After Caesar was extinguished, armed ranks arose from his ashes; wars were begun, which should not be read by children as testimony to a miserable fertility, but should be watched by the people...

# Trophies of the Gauls.

The consuls, stirred by the danger, gathered the forces of all Italy for the protection of the empire. When this was done, they report that there were 800,000 armed men in the combined army of both consuls. Among these, the Roman and Campanian infantry numbered 367,000, while the cavalry was 26,600. The rest were a multitude of others. When the battle was joined at Arretium <note>Modern-day Arezzo in Tuscany.</note>, the consul Attilius was killed. 80,000 Romans fled; it was not so much the size of the slaughter that should have terrified them, but the manner of their flight. For historians record that only 3,000 of them were killed then; it is therefore more ignominious and shameful that such a great host fled after losing so few.
<margin>Prodigies seen.</margin>
In the following year, dire prodigies terrified the wretched city. It was wretched indeed, for it was frightened on one side by the roar of enemies and on the other by the wickedness of demons. For in the region of Picenum <note>An area on the Adriatic coast of Italy.</note>, blood flowed in a river; among the Tuscans, the sky seemed to burn; and at Ariminum <note>Modern-day Rimini.</note>, a bright light shone late at night, and three moons were seen rising in different parts of the sky. At that time also, a great earthquake shook Achaia <note>A region in Greece.</note> and the island of Rhodes so violently that, as buildings fell everywhere, that famous Great Colossus <note>The Colossus of Rhodes, a massive bronze statue of the sun god Helios and one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note> also collapsed.
<margin>The arrival of the Gauls in Italy.</margin>
**Trogus Pompeius** <note>A Roman historian of the 1st century BC whose work is preserved primarily through Justin's summaries.</note> records the entry of the Gauls into Italy in the 24th book of his *Epitomes* of **Justin**, when he says: The Gauls, being of an overflowing population, when the lands that had birthed them could no longer contain them, sent 300,000 men to seek new homes as if on a pilgrimage. Of these, one portion settled in Italy, which even captured and burned the city of Rome. Another portion, led by birds (for the Gauls are more skilled than others in the study of augury <note>The practice of interpreting omens from the flight of birds.</note>), penetrated the Illyrian bays through the slaughter of barbarians and settled in Pannonia <note>An ancient province covering parts of modern Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note>. A harsh, bold, and warlike people, they were the first after Hercules—whose deeds gave him the admiration of courage and the belief in immortality—to cross the unconquered ridges of the Alps and places impassable with cold. There, having tamed the Pannonians, they waged various wars with their neighbors for many years. Soon after, following such success, they divided their columns; some sought Greece and others Macedonia, laying everything low with the sword. So great was the terror of the Gallic name that even kings, unprovoked, sought to buy peace with vast sums of money.
<margin>3</margin>
Only the King of Macedonia, **Ptolemy** <note>Ptolemy Keraunos, who gained the throne by murdering his benefactors.</note>, heard of the arrival of the Gauls without fear. Driven by the furies of his own crimes, he went out to meet them with a few disorganized troops, as if wars were no more difficult to manage than murders. He even scorned an embassy from the Dardanians <note>A Balkan tribe.</note> that offered 20,000 armed men in aid, adding an insult. He said it was over for Macedonia if, having conquered the entire East alone, they now needed the Dardanians to defend their borders; he said his soldiers were the sons of those who, under King Alexander, had served as victors throughout the whole world.

<column-break/>

When these words were reported to the Dardanian king, he said that the famous kingdom of Macedonia would soon fall through the recklessness of this headstrong youth. Therefore the Gauls, under the leader **Belgius**, sent envoys to Ptolemy to test the spirit of the Macedonians, offering peace if he wished to buy it. But Ptolemy boasted among his people that the Gauls sought peace out of fear of war. He behaved no less fiercely toward the envoys than he did among friends, declaring he would only grant peace if they gave their princes as hostages and surrendered their weapons. For he said he would only trust them if they were unarmed. When the embassy’s report returned, the Gauls laughed, shouting from all sides that he would soon realize whether they had offered peace for their own sake or for his. After a few days, the battle was joined. The defeated Macedonians retreated. Ptolemy, faint from many wounds, was captured. His head was cut off, fixed on a spear, and carried around the whole battle line to terrify the enemy. Flight saved a few of the Macedonians; the rest were either captured or killed. When this was announced throughout all Macedonia, the city gates were closed and everything was filled with mourning. Now they grieved for the loss of their sons, now they feared the destruction of their cities; now they called upon the names of their kings, Alexander and Philip, as if calling upon gods for help. They prayed that those under whom they had not only been safe but had also emerged as victors of the world might protect their fatherland, which they had raised to the heavens by the glory of their deeds; they begged for aid for the afflicted whom the madness and recklessness of King Ptolemy had ruined. While all were in despair, **Sosthenes**, one of the Macedonian nobles, believing that they should act rather than just pray, gathered the youth and checked the Gauls who were exulting in their victory, defending Macedonia from hostile plundering. Because of these acts of courage, he was preferred over many nobles who sought the Macedonian throne, despite being of lower birth himself. And when he was called "King" by the army, he compelled the soldiers to swear an oath to him not as a king, but as a leader <term>dux<note>Sosthenes refused the title of 'Basileus' (King), preferring to be seen as a general or military commander during the crisis.</note></term>. Meanwhile, **Brennus**, the leader under whom a portion of the Gauls had poured into Greece, heard of his people's victory under Belgius over the Macedonians. Indignant that the victory had been so easily abandoned, he himself broke into Macedonia with a force of 500,000 infantry and 15,000 cavalry. As they were plundering the fields and villas, Sosthenes met him with a prepared army of Macedonians. But a few are easily defeated by many, and the fearful by the strong. Thus, when the defeated Macedonians had hidden themselves within the walls of their cities, the victor Brennus plundered the lands of all Macedonia with no one to stop him.

# First Treatise

<margin>Kings put their trust in the Gauls.</margin>
In those days, the youth of the Gauls were so numerous and fertile that they filled all of Asia like a great swarm. Indeed, no kings of the East waged any wars without an army of Gallic mercenaries. Nor did those driven from their kingdoms flee to anyone other than the Gallic kings. So great was the terror of the Gallic name and the success of their arms that they believed their majesty could not be safe, nor lost power recovered, without Gallic valor. Therefore, called to aid by the King of Bithynia <note>A region in what is now northwest Turkey.</note>, they divided the kingdom with him after their victory and named that region Gallo-Graecia <note>Better known as Galatia; the inhabitants were the "Galatians" mentioned in the New Testament.</note>. The same **Justin** <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a Roman historian of the 2nd century AD.</note> says in his 28th book regarding the Gauls, their virtues, and the Romans: they heard that the peoples of Transalpine Gaul had entered Italy and possessed it with many great cities; they occupied a territory somewhat wider than that which they are said to have seized in Asia through war. I would say Rome was not only conquered by the Gauls but even captured, so that only the peak of a single mountain <note>The Capitoline Hill, which was the only part of Rome not taken during the Gallic sack around 390 BC.</note> was left to them; and the enemy was removed not by war, but by a bribe. Moreover, the name of the Gauls, which always terrified the Romans, became a source of their own strength. For those Gauls who inhabit Asia are far removed from the seats of those who occupied Italy, though they have almost the same origin, courage, and lineage. Regarding their religion and the worship of the gods, as time allowed, listen to the same **Justin** in his 43rd book speaking of Massilia <note>Modern-day Marseille, France.</note>, which was founded near the mouth of the Rhône river in a remote bay, as if in a corner of the sea.

<margin>The seed of the Gauls terrified the Romans.</margin>

Having requested permission to enter the city and worship their gods, he came to the citadel of Minerva. Upon seeing the statue of the goddess in the portico, whom he had seen in his rest, he suddenly cried out that she was the one who had terrified him at night and had ordered him to withdraw from the siege.

What should be said of the Roman emperors? Did not **Julius Caesar** usurp power through violence and tyranny against the state of the Republic? For when he had come into Italy returning from Gaul, he demanded that a second consulship be decreed for him in his absence. <meta>This page follows a discussion on the military history of the Gauls, specifically their expansion into Asia and their conflicts with Rome. # Trophies of the Gauls.

...it should suffice to explain: the beginning of all these evils was ambition and pride. Therefore, it should not be considered an unjust punishment, nor even a slaughter, for those who—aspiring through right and wrong to the pinnacle of power against the liberty of the Republic—behave like tyrants and rage against their subjects like ravenous wolves among sheep. Nor should it seem strange or improper to anyone if sometimes the crime is punished along with the author, so that evil may be removed from our midst. We are certainly not ignorant of the fact that this was verified not only in Julius Caesar, the first emperor of the Romans (of whom we spoke a little earlier), but also in many of his successors and those like him. For just as the sin of the first-created man <note>The "protoplast," referring to Adam.</note> passed down to all posterity, so too did the ambition of Caesar, the first emperor, corrupt all Roman princes (excepting the Christians). Consequently, those who were his imitators in their way of life became his companions in the manner of their deaths. 

<margin>Roman emperors who died badly</margin>

So that the narrative may begin from the first: Julius Caesar (mentioned above)—I omit how many cares, how many labors, how many dangers and costs he endured to reach the throne, for that is impossible to relate—was not yet sailing with full sails in his empire when, behold, a storm of conspiracy arose by which he was so overwhelmed that he died after receiving twenty-three wounds. **Caligula**, after reigning for three years and ten months, was butchered by his own people. **Claudius**, in the thirteenth year of his reign, was poisoned. **Nero**, still a youth and established in the flower of his age—who, while Rome was burning, had sung of the *Fall of Troy* <note>original: "Troie halosin" (Greek: ἅλωσιν). Nero famously performed a song about the destruction of Troy while watching Rome burn.</note>—stabbed himself with his own dagger. **Galba**, an old man, was butchered in the city at the Lacus Curtius in the seventh month of his reign; and his head, which had given laws to the whole world, was cut off by a common soldier and thrown to the camp followers. **Otho**, on the ninety-fifth day of his reign, pierced himself with a dagger. **Vitellius**, dragged from his palace with the greatest ignominy, spattered with mud and dung, had the point of a sword placed under his chin so that he could not bow his face in shame; he was led to the Gemonian stairs <note>A flight of stairs in ancient Rome where the bodies of executed criminals were displayed.</note> and butchered limb by limb. **Domitian**, who from the best of sons became the worst, and was a most cruel persecutor of Christians, was killed by his own people in the fifteenth year of his reign; he was all the more unhappy as his power had lasted longer. For what was the prolongation of such a cruel tyranny but an accumulation of divine indignation? **Commodus**, who was (as they say) "inconvenient" <note>A pun on his name, Commodus (meaning "convenient" or "suitable"), and the Latin word "incommodus" (troublesome).</note> to everyone, was strangled in the twelfth year of his reign. **Helvius** <note>Likely referring to Pertinax (Publius Helvius Pertinax).</note>, because he was illiberal and sordid, was openly killed in the sixth month of his reign. **Caracalla**, in the seventh year of his reign, while he had dismounted from his horse for the sake of relieving his bladder, was struck down by the Parthians. **Heliogabalus**, a most disgraceful man, was killed in the fourth year of his reign during a riot 

<column-break/>

of the soldiers. **Decius**, an enemy of the Christians, was killed by barbarians in the second year of his reign, and his corpse was never found. **Valerian**, who reigned with Gallienus, was captured by the King of the Parthians <note>Historically Shapur I, though the text names him Pacarus.</note>; he was not killed immediately but reserved for a lingering death. For he served as a footstool for the King when he mounted his horse—which is otherwise called a stepping-stool.

But why do I proceed to recount the slaughters of tyrants? It should be concluded with that satirical verse: 
*Few kings descend to the son-in-law of Ceres* <note>The "son-in-law of Ceres" is Pluto, god of the Underworld; the original Latin quote is from Juvenal's Satire 10.</note> *without slaughter and blood, and few tyrants by a "dry" death.* <note>meaning a natural death.</note> Here one could cite **Antimachus**, the Greek poet, who, when he wished to soften the grief he felt from the death of his dearest wife Lycidice, wrote an elegy in which he recounted all the calamities of heroes. But for the present, let these remarks on the beginnings and ends of tyrants suffice.

And to return to Caesar, from whom we have digressed somewhat, it seems worthwhile. He was, by military law, the most outstanding of all Italians. Although none of his predecessors or successors can be compared to him, nevertheless, many among the Gauls emerged not only as his equals in military affairs or the virtue of arms, but even his superiors (though sometimes with unequal fortune). This is clear to almost everyone regarding **Belgius** and **Brennus**, the leaders of the Gauls (mentioned a little earlier), who even preceded him. I pass over in silence the Trojans, from whom the Franks themselves drew their origin. For from **Francus** (or Francio), the son of Hector, the region of Francia and its inhabitants, the Franks, were named.

And in later times there was **Charlemagne**, the son of King Pepin of the Franks, whom our people rightly prefer to Caesar himself in matters of war. Having defeated Desiderius, the King of the Lombards in Italy at Pavia, he came to Rome and was elected Emperor by the Senate and the Roman people, and confirmed by the Supreme Pontiff. He was a helper of the Church, and because a wicked woman, **Irene**, was ruling in the East <note>The "translatio imperii" (transfer of empire) was justified by the claim that the Byzantine throne was vacant because a woman (Empress Irene) was ruling.</note>, he became the greatest prince of the Christians. He recovered the Holy Land in the East which had been occupied by the Saracens, and in the West, he liberated all of Spain from their hands. He was the greatest champion and protector of the Christian faith and the Roman Church. He lived seventy-one years and died—not by violence like Caesar—but happily among his own, after reigning over the Gauls for forty-seven years. He ruled as Emperor after the end of his wars not for a mere three years and seven months like Caesar, but for fourteen years, with the great approval of all his people. Many of the Gauls flourished in the Empire after Charles, such as **Louis the Pious**, son of Charlemagne; **Lothair**, son of Louis the Pious; **Louis II**, son of Lothair; **Charles II**, called the Bald, son of Louis the Pious and uncle of Louis II and brother of Lothair; **Charles the Younger**, grandson of Charles the Bald; and **Arnulf**.

# First Treatise

...he was of the lineage of the Charleses: he who destroyed the Northmen <note>The Normans.</note> with a wondrous slaughter and took Rome. Louis III, the son of Arnulf. These were the kings of the Gauls <note>The author uses "Gauls" (Galli) to refer to the Franks and the French, tracing their ancestry back to Troy.</note> who obtained the Roman Empire happily, not through tyranny, but through a rightly celebrated election.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus, Chapter 10</margin>
What more remains to be said of the Gauls? Truly nothing, except that there is one true God who transfers kingdoms from one people to another because of injustices, injuries, insults, and various deceits, disposing of the times and also punishing sins. For He sometimes chooses the weak things of the world to confound the proud.

<margin>Virgil</margin>
For after the affairs of Asia fell and proud Ilium <note>Troy.</note> perished, and the Trojans were fugitives throughout almost the entire world, the kingdom of the Franks finally took its beginning from them. Moderated for a long time by dukes and other officials, it was gradually raised to the heights and expanded into Normandy, Picardy, Aquitaine, and Lyon, as well as other surrounding regions. At last, divine mercy deigned to bestow this kingdom upon a most powerful king who occupied all of Gaul, both on this side of the Alps and no small part of the region beyond the Alps, holding all regions from sea to sea under his jurisdiction. With a strong hand, an outstretched arm, a provident organization, and always mature counsel, he governed them. To this race of men, whom almost all other nations admired and—not without merit—honored with a mixture of love and fear, the true God (who was worshiped through anxious superstition by those who were ignorant) opened the fountain of His understanding. Intending to rule men through a man forever, He bestowed no small virtues upon the King of the Gauls, often performing wonders among foreign nations so that he might defend His Church—which has neither wrinkle nor stain—from the infidels who had increased throughout the world due to the negligence of the Emperor Heraclius and had grown strong against the Christians. To ensure that the liberty of the faithful among the Gauls was safe, He willed them to be practiced in military support. Because of this, and since he often restored the Supreme Pontiffs to their place after they had been driven out of Rome, the race of the Franks seemed more devoted to divine religion than others. Hence, by a just title, the kings of the Franks were called **Most Christian.**

<margin>Kings of the Franks</margin>
From the time of Clovis, who was the first among them to receive the faith of Christ, we read of no one among the kings of the Gauls who was either an infidel or held wrong views on the faith. Among the Roman Emperors, however, even after they recognized the way of truth, many deserted it and turned back, holding wrong views about Christ.

<margin>Roman Emperors who left the faith badly</margin>
First of all, was not Constans, the son of Constantine the Great, an Arian <note>A follower of Arianism, a belief that denied the full divinity of Christ, considered a major heresy.</note> who persecuted Christians? Likewise, his brother Constantine [II] was similar—an Arian like his brother. Julian the Apostate was treacherous against the faith—whence he is called "the Apostate"—who withdrew from the Christian faith after Constantine and held Christians in the greatest hatred, to whom

<column-break/>

he forbade public offices and the study of the sciences. The Emperor Valens in the East, as an Arian official, persecuted the faithful of Christ; wherefore he commanded that monks should serve as soldiers under a temporal lord. Was not the Emperor Anastasius made a principal heretic? Justin the Younger, the nephew of Justinian, was a greedy, rapacious man and a heretic. The Roman Emperor Leo III was certainly a most wicked man, who caused the images of the Blessed Mary and other saints to be publicly burned <note>Referring to the Iconoclasm movement.</note>. Constantine V was a persecutor of the Church who killed many Catholic monks, impiously devoting himself to the magic arts. Were not all these emperors iniquitous, stubborn, unfaithful, heretics, and of ill-sentiment toward Christ? Thus, in their age, by the just judgment of God, the impious Empire barely flourished even in name. For in the East, barbarians occupied everything; and the Romans, alienated from the use of arms and the custom of making war, became unarmed, inert, and faint-hearted. Basely surrendered to idleness, they looked toward the Gauls as strenuous and warlike soldiers, who were always most ready as helpers and protectors of the Roman Church, and who never hesitated to face death when necessity required it. For this reason, they elected Charlemagne, the son of Pippin, as Roman Emperor. Almost all the kings of the Gauls ended their final day happily, either fighting bravely in arms or among their own people with affairs well managed and peace acquired for the kingdom. But a no small part of the Roman princes (as has already been said) perished either ignominiously by their own people or through some other misfortune. And omitting those already commemorated a little above—lest there be a superfluous repetition of those to whom the Sun of Justice <note>A common metaphor for Christ.</note> did not communicate His rays—did not these also die badly? Tiberius perished by poison, he who was transformed from a mild prince into a most savage beast. The Emperor Pertinax was killed in his own house by soldiers. Didius Julianus was killed in the palace. Bassianus <note>Commonly known as Caracalla.</note> was killed at Carrhae. Macrinus was killed by his own people after Bassianus. Alexander [Severus], the son of the varied Heliogabalus, was killed in Gaul by soldiers through the work of Maximian <note>Maximinus Thrax.</note>. Maximian was killed at Aquileia with his son by soldiers. Gordian III was slain by soldiers. Philip and his son of the same name were both killed in a military tumult through the fraud of Decius: the father at Verona, and the son at Rome. Quintillus, the brother of Claudius, was killed. Florianus was killed by the treachery of soldiers. Probus of Pannonia was killed by soldiers. Carus the Roman was struck by lightning along with his army. Carinus was killed by Diocletian, and his brother Numerian was killed by the treason of his father-in-law Aper. Diocletian drank poison. Valerius, after many troubles...

...he had afflicted the Christians, he wasted away from a long-lasting disease; and when worms swarmed from his body, unable to endure the agony, he killed himself with his own hand. <note>This likely refers to the Emperor Galerius, whose gruesome death was often cited by Christian historians as divine punishment for his persecutions.</note> Licinius <note>original: "Lucinius"</note> was killed by his own men. But he himself was conquered and killed by one of his own soldiers whom he had exiled. <margin>Baruch, chapter 3</margin> Were these not the princes of the nations, who ruled over the beasts that were upon the

<column-break/>

earth? Who played with the birds of the air; who treasured up silver and gold, in which men trust, and there was no end to their acquisitions? Who worked in silver and were anxious, and there is no trace of their works? They were certainly exterminated and went down to the underworld, and others rose up in their place. <note>A quotation from the Book of Baruch 3:16–19, used here to emphasize the vanity and downfall of earthly rulers.</note> Were these, therefore, true emperors? Perhaps someone will answer: "Not at all; rather, they were tyrants." And because they raged against their subjects like most savage beasts, they perished torn to pieces just like beasts. But concerning these and many others—whom I pass over in silence in my pursuit of brevity, and whose deeds are better known from the annals of the most esteemed historians than "the grove of Mars" <note>A classical idiom (originally from the Roman satirist Juvenal) used to describe something so common and well-known that it is a cliché.</note> or one’s own home—I believe I have said more than enough for the narrow limits of this summary.

## ¶ Concerning the illustrious deeds of Charles VIII and Louis XII, kings of the Franks. Second Treatise.

It remains, therefore, for us as well—following in the footsteps of others, even if we speak with a stammering tongue—to bring into the public eye something of the excellent deeds, worthy of eternal memory, which in our own age the most Christian kings of the Franks performed through brave fighting against foreign nations, namely the Italians, and especially the Neapolitans and the Insubrians <note>A term for the people of Milan</note> or Milanese. When, therefore, King Louis XI had yielded to fate <note>original: "fato concesserat"; a polite phrasing for his death in 1483</note> with the kingdom of the Franks pacified on every side, divine wisdom—through which kings reign <margin>Proverbs 8</margin> and makers of laws decree just things, through which princes rule <margin>Luke 19</margin> and the powerful decree justice—granted that the son of the same Louis, Charles, the eighth of this name, become king.

Although he was of tender and weak limbs and of short stature (much like that Zacchaeus mentioned in the Gospel), he nevertheless possessed a milder disposition and a more kindly nature, so that the poetic saying might not undeservedly be proven true of him: "A greater virtue reigned in a small body." For he courageously subdued whatever enemies rose up against his kingdom on its borders, and often brought them under control without great loss to the realm, so that universal peace was restored to the kingdom. When Charles was finally able to rest from these wars, a concern took hold of him: concerning the Kingdom of Sicily <note>Charles VIII claimed the throne of Naples, often called the Kingdom of Sicily, through the Angevin line</note>, which he contended belonged to him by right of inheritance.

<column-break/>

Nor could he be moved from this opinion. He would not even listen to the ambassadors of the Parisians sent to him for that very purpose. Therefore, having gathered forces by land and sea, primarily at the urging of Pope Alexander VI <note>A member of the notorious Borgia family</note> and Ludovico Sforza <note>The Duke of Milan</note>, who were hostile to Alfonso of Naples, he led his army into Italy. He stayed first in Lyon for several days, not quite certain whether he himself should cross the Alps. At last, having crossed the Alps, he followed his army, a good portion of which he had sent ahead well-equipped. Making his way through Italy, after capturing cities that attempted to block his passage and resist the greatness of his power, he came to Rome. 

The Roman Pope, fearing his arrival because of its scale, and being unable to prevent his entrance, retreated into the Castel Sant'Angelo <note>The fortified papal fortress near the Vatican</note> as a most secure place. The King, having entered the city, ordered the soldiers to refrain from rioting. He inflicted the ultimate punishment—death—on some who did not obey the royal edict, erecting three gallows throughout the city. While the king spent a few days in the city and no military riot was heard, Alexander, feeling more secure, left the fortress and admitted the king to a meeting. After many words were exchanged back and forth, and many conditions and articles were added by both sides, a true friendship was contracted between them. I have taken care to insert the content and copy of these articles here, since they have been omitted by other writers. The agreement between the Pope and the King is as follows: First, all injuries between the Pope and the King of France are forgiven. And they published several articles, the summaries of which are these. First, the Pope shall remain a good father to the King, and the King a good son to the Pope. Also, the Pope is content...

Also, the King agrees that provisions may be brought to the city of Rome both through Ostia and the Old City, provided they do not come from the side of his enemies. Also, the Pope shall give the King of France commissioners so they may provide him with travel supplies through the lands of the Church. Also, all fortresses, castles, and cities of the Church shall be opened to the King of France if he should happen to go there himself, until he is in safety. Also, when the King returns, all places shall be restored to the Pope within fourteen days after the King's departure. Also, upon returning, he shall restore Ostia into the hands of the Cardinal of San Pietro in Vincoli <note>Giuliano della Rovere, the future Pope Julius II</note>. Also, the Old City and other fortresses shall remain in the King's power for his own security. Also, the Pope pardons all those who served the King, namely those of Aquapendente, Montefiascone, Viterbo, and others. Also, the Pope restores all Cardinals to their liberties from this moment, on the law and condition that they be faithful from now on. Also, the Pope pardons and grants remission to the Colonna and Savelli families. Item, similarly in the legation of the Patrimony <note>The Patrimony of Saint Peter, a province of the Papal States</note>. Also, the King shall appoint in Campania one Cardinal who is a friend to him. Also, the King takes the Lord Prefect of the City <note>Giovanni della Rovere</note> into his protection. and the same Prefect shall remain in his former state and dignity. Also, the King transfers and takes upon himself the dispute and every controversy which is turned between the Supreme Pontiff regarding the plunder of 40,000 ducats and certain other goods. Also, the Lord Cardinal of San Pietro in Vincoli is restored to his legation in Avignon. Also, the Cardinal of Barcelona shall receive the emoluments of his hat <note>original: "capelli"; referring to the income associated with his rank</note> both in his absence and in his

<column-break/>

presence; and he shall remain in his former dignity. Also, the Pope shall restore Cardinal Savelli to his legation in Spoleto. Also, the Pope shall restore the Colonna and Savelli families, with their other friends, to their former status. Also, the Pope releases the Cardinals from the obligation made by them in the conclave, namely regarding not withdrawing without license and consent. And similarly from the oath sworn by them. Also, the King shall restore the city of Rome to the Supreme Pontiff with the keys and other fortifications. Also, the King shall not require the Castel Sant'Angelo from the Supreme Pontiff. Also, the King shall offer personal obedience to the Supreme Pontiff. Also, the King himself shall not offend the Supreme Pontiff in anything, nor bring any injury upon him; and if anyone should be troublesome to him, or hurt him in any way, the King shall be bound to defend him. Also, the Supreme Pontiff promises security to the King: and that neither the King’s person nor anyone of his followers shall be offended or harmed in any way by the Roman people.

<margin>C</margin> Therefore, with these pacts made between the Supreme Pontiff and the King of the Franks, the King himself pursued the journey he had begun. and, storming certain cities that resisted him, he marched toward Naples. Alfonso, who then held Naples, fearing his arrival, left the kingdom to his son Ferdinand. He himself, fleeing into Sicily, departed from this life a little while later. <margin>The King</margin> Ferdinand, with his father fleeing, retreated into the Castel dell'Ovo as Charles arrived at Naples. Entering the city, Charles—with the most honorable people he could find and the common folk applauding him—took possession. Ferdinand, however, refusing the most honorable condition offered to him by the most humane King, was forced to flee. Success followed for Charles: first Apulia, then Calabria, and soon even Lucania. Envying such prosperous successes, the Supreme Pontiff—having allied himself with the Venetians and Maximilian, King of the Romans <note>Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I</note>, joined by the King of Spain and Ludovico of Milan <note>Ludovico Sforza, "Il Moro"</note>—all these <margin>The King's rivals</margin> sent legates to Charles. <margin>D</margin> They demanded that he either leave Naples free, or lead his forces against the Turks as he had promised. To this, the King, somewhat indignant, was the first to respond. "You have all," he said, "conspired most closely against me; but one thing shall frustrate your gatherings: so that you Venetians may learn, by my decree, to govern your trade and not the empires of things." With this word, the ambassadors were dismissed. He remitted the heavier taxes on the Neapolitans with which they were being oppressed by Alfonso. <margin>The King turns toward Gaul</margin> With Naples pacified and governors with a strong garrison placed throughout the regions, he committed the supreme command to Gilbert of Montpensier. He himself prepared to return to France with part of his forces. As he was returning, Alexander closed the gates of the city to him...

# Second Treatise

### B

...departed, and although he had fortified it with ditches and ramparts, he nevertheless withdrew with the cardinals to Orvieto <note>The Latin "Venetun̄" is likely an OCR error for "Urbevetum" (Orvieto), where Pope Alexander VI fled to avoid the returning French army</note>. Charles, entering Rome with the favor of the people, made a stop there. He freely relinquished the cities he had held from Pope Alexander, except for Ostia and Prince Cem <note>original: "zyzimum turchuz"</note>, the Turk who had died at Naples. Setting out from there, he took Siena under his protection. As he approached Fornovo <note>original: "fornouium"</note>, not far from the city of Parma, he received word that the Venetians and the other conspirators <note>The League of Venice, a coalition formed to expel Charles from Italy</note> were occupying the roads <margin>E</margin> through which he was to pass. There were forty thousand armed men in the enemy camp. Charles led at most seven thousand choice fighters, exhausted by their long journey and no less in need of supplies. For he had left a good part of the rest of his army in Naples and elsewhere as garrisons. He had also sent another significant force to Genoa under the leaders Philip of Savoy and Hugues d'Amboise, because Cardinal Giuliano <note>Giuliano della Rovere, the future Pope Julius II</note> had given him hope of recovering those cities. Because of this, the elevated enemy held it as almost certain that Charles would fall into their power, or truly die from some wound. The leaders of the opposing forces also promised victory to the Venetian envoys, and above all the Duke of Bozzolo <note>original: "Bonziacus dux," referring to Gian Francesco Gonzaga of the Bozzolo branch, a commander in the Italian league</note> repeatedly testified that in this one battle, which seemed imminent, the Gauls <note>The French</note>, warned of their own vanity, would easily understand that Italian valor was not—as they themselves falsely proclaimed—entirely extinguished. Indeed, they had offered fifty thousand—others say one hundred thousand—ducats to anyone who brought the King into the camp either alive or dead. To him who presented the head of a Frenchman, a reward of six ducats was established. With the hope of such gain, the Venetian enemy encouraged his soldiers. But the high-spirited Charles was no less active; having arranged his battle lines, he was like a second Judas Maccabeus with a tiny army against a vast multitude. To his men, <margin>1 Maccabees 3</margin> he said:

> It is easy for many to be enclosed in the hands of a few; and there is no difference in the sight of the God of heaven to deliver by many or by few. For the victory of battle stands not in the multitude of an army, but strength comes from heaven. They come against us in stubborn and proud strength to destroy and despoil us. But we will fight for our lives, and the Lord himself will crush them before our face.

By these and other similar words, the army of the Gauls was encouraged, and they fearlessly awaited the arrival of the enemy who were confident in their own numbers. The presence of the King also increased the spirit of the soldiers significantly; at this time, his authority was worth more than the rest of the army. When the enemies saw this kind of order, preparation, and the perseverance of the Gauls, who considered it more honorable to

<column-break/>

die bravely in arms while fighting than to basely turn their backs to the enemy by retreating, they wondered at the battle very much and were afraid. The Gallic forces were stationed on one side of the Taro River <note>original: "Tarri fluminis"</note>. In Fornovo, on the other side, the Duke of Bozzolo, eager for conflict and battle, exhorted his men. Without delay, as the signals sounded, an assault was made on the Gauls in several places at once. The Italians, entering the river with a roar and a shout, reached for the further bank. Here a grim struggle arose, and a dire battle was joined. At last, the French, fighting like spirited lions, drove the Venetians down the slope and compelled them to retreat basely to the river and return to their own side. The Sforza troops <note>Soldiers of Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan</note> also fought, but having been defeated, they turned their backs to the French in headlong flight, like fleeing Parthians. Therefore, when the enemy could prevail nothing against the armed battle line of the French, they were led by shame—since they had done nothing worthy of mention—to turn their warlike fury toward the unarmed multitude of camp followers, porters, and others who carried the provisions, as well as the pack animals of the muleteers. Upon them, they exercised the greatest cruelty, whom the soldiers were unable to help. Many strenuous soldiers fell on both sides in this battle, but on the opposing side, there was no comparison—far more died, among whom these men of greater reputation are recorded: Rodolfo Gonzaga; Giovanni Maria Gonzaga; the Favorite of the Lord Marquis; Count Roberto di Bagno; Count Galeotto Ippoliti; Antonio Scarampo; Lord Ascanio di Martinengo; Guido Gonzaga; Bernardino Parente; Alessandro d'Este; Ranuccio Farnese; Count Bernardino di Montano; Roberto Ferreza; Alessandro Berardo; Vincenzo Corso; Lord Galeotto di Cozegia; Francesco del Fia; Francesco of Mantua; Jacomino di Boso; Leonardo Locacorno; Bartolomeo di Domenico Pio; Benedetto di Cozegia; Giovanni Francesco di Grossi; Evangelista di Gregori; Pietro Francesco Penna; Dondazio Barbo; Luca Terzo; Carlo Forlano; Luchino Forlano; Giovanni Todescho; Bergamo of Verona; Ercole di Montecucolo; Americo Coute; Rezolo del Sesebalco; Ligorola; Ludovico Farda; Giovanni Giacomo; Tommaso di Quagra; Lingneia da Modena; Mozleto Bocaccio; Travaino de la Volta; Ezechiele Boccalino; Bonifacio Gonzaga; Alessandro Alolgiazio; Antonio de la Fibre; Bartolino da Palu; Silvestro Bagnolo; Bartolino Piceti; Venturino de Chirin; Andrea de Brizello; Guglielmo de Raventa; Polidoro Ca...
