->### Trophies of the French<-

...and I shall name them. Johannes Augustinus Bandello, Jacobus de Bicharia, Petrus de Monte, Ludovicus de Rezo, Lord Theophilus de Piscaro the chancellor, Federicus Bocalino, and Molet de Hostilia. Many others also received fatal wounds in this dire conflict. These were the principal men among the famous nobles who fell in this struggle, numbering about fifty. It is rumored that these were among the "gilded knights" <note>original: "equites auratos"; a title of high nobility often associated with the Order of the Golden Spur</note> to whom the Prince of Mantua <note>Francesco II Gonzaga</note> or the Venetians had entrusted the command of all their forces.

<margin>B</margin>
Of the French army, however, very few fell, except for the unarmed servants upon whom the enemy fell like ravenous wolves gasping for prey. Matthias, the natural son of Bourbon <note>Matthias, the "Bastard of Bourbon," a prominent French commander</note>, was the most spirited among the brave, the strongest among the strong, and the most warlike among the martial. Like a second Hector, he was carried with great force into the most heavily armed ranks of the enemy, most impetuously carving a path for himself. Prostrating many of them, now with his spear and now with his sword, he spared no one. But where he conducted himself so strenuously and performed many illustrious deeds in that battle, inconstant and fickle Fortune envied him such great honor. For his horse, on which he sat, was spurred and heated by the fury of war; its bridle snapped, and it carried its rider hither and thither, and finally into the enemy's line. There, alone and surrounded by many, he was at last taken captive.

<margin>The French achieve victory</margin>
Having been distinguished by so noble a victory, the French army, with the enemy turned to flight, pursued their intended journey. Many light cavalry soldiers followed them, with their leaders following behind, but at a distance, lest they should again experience the fortitude of the French.

<margin>D</margin>
At last Charles reached Asti with his army. While staying there for several days, he learned that Louis, Duke of Orleans <note>the future King Louis XII</note>, was being very closely besieged at Novara by the Milanese. For the sake of liberating him, Charles entered into a peace with the enemy. When this was done, and he had returned safely to France, he bypassed Paris and went to the Abbey of Saint Denis <note>original: "Dionysij cenobiuz"</note> to fulfill the vows he had made to the heavens.

<margin>The death of King Charles.</margin>
As soon as Charles returned to France, Naples defected from its allegiance. After the death of Gilbert de Montpensier, the remaining governors, barely defending their garrisons, retreated to Charles. Charles hurried to recover it again, having gathered forces by land and sea. But his unexpected death thwarted his purpose. He passed away at Amboise <note>original: "ambasie"</note> in his twenty-seventh year, on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the year of salvation 1498, on the day before the Kalends of May. This Charles was small in stature <note>original: "pusillus"</note> but greatest in soul, adorned with many virtues. For in him was the highest humanity, praiseworthy courtesy, commended liberality, and a wide-reaching affability that offered access to him to all.

<sig>B 3</sig>

<column-break/>

In wars he was so fortunate that he dared to attack nations feared by his predecessors. Who ever—even among the kings of the French—did not dread declaring war on the British except this Charles? He strenuously fought them down along with their supporters. Who besides him crossed the Alps? He not only conquered all of Italy but also struck no small fear into transmarine nations, so much so that even the Turk himself <note>The Ottoman Sultan, Bayezid II</note> feared his approach. For it was he who, with a tiny hand of men, courageously defeated the massive forces of both the Venetians and the Milanese, as well as the rest of the Italians, at Fornovo. There he obtained such an excellent victory that other most excellent victories often achieved by the French seem to yield to this one in no small measure. For this reason, since statues are decreed for each of the kings of the French in the high places of the Parisian palace for their egregious deeds, the most excellent of all was decreed for him.

<margin>K</margin>
By his authority and favor, the King of the English <note>Henry VII</note> obtained the royal scepter among his own people. But let these few things be said of the many virtues of Charles.

<margin>The expedition of King Louis XII into the lands of the Milanese</margin>
In his place, by the supreme consensus of all princes, Louis, Duke of Orleans, was substituted. With the kingdom at peace, he was mindful of the injuries he had received at Novara from Ludovico Sforza <note>The Duke of Milan, known as "Il Moro"</note>. At the same time, determining to recover the Duchy of Milan as belonging to him, he sent ahead forces to cross the Alps with a large, prepared army, which he soon followed. The King, having crossed the Alps, attacked, captured, and finally plundered several towns of the Sforza party, though not without inconvenience to our men. Soon the people of Pavia passed into the King's power. Shaken by this event and doubtful of the loyalty of his people toward him, Sforza thought to withdraw himself from danger. Having placed soldiers in the Citadel of Milan for a garrison, and having most copiously fortified it with everything pertaining to both provisions and war and defense, he himself secretly departed with his son and a few others. Sforza having fled, the Milanese admitted the King not long after. The prefect of the Citadel was warned to do the same; he resisted once or twice as if he would preserve the Citadel for Sforza with sincere faith. But yielding to avarice (which is innate to the Lombards), he promised he would surrender the Citadel if he were allowed to receive as a royal gift whatever furnishings Ludovico had left behind upon departing. The condition was partly accepted, and the prefect received half of the furnishings. With Milan and its Citadel received, the remaining towns of the region, along with all the castles, were brought into the King's power by free surrender a little later. Furthermore, the Genoese came, to whom he gave as prefect Philip of Ravenstein, his relative by his mother's side. To the Venetians, he gave Cremona along with some...

### Second Treatise

He entrusted the borders of the Milanese principality to the local inhabitants (as they had agreed from the beginning). Once affairs among the Insubrians <note>original: "insubres"; a classical name for the people of the Milanese region</note> were settled, the King returned to France. Upon his departure, behold, the Milanese defected to Cardinal Ascanio Maria Sforza, the brother of Ludovico, and they were the first to receive Ascanio within their walls. Soon, Ludovico himself arrived with hired Swiss and German soldiers. Consequently, after recalling his forces and sending new reinforcements from France, they captured Ludovico Sforza alive without a fight and sent him to France to the King. Cardinal Ascanio, who was then staying in Milan, was struck with grief by this bitter news regarding his brother; he abandoned the city and took flight, accompanied by many of his friends. But he unfortunately fell into the hands of the Venetians. Taken to Venice, he was sent within a few days by the Venetians—who were allies in the war—to the King, where he remained until the death of Pope Alexander VI. When the Pope died, the King permitted him to depart for Rome to help elect a new Supreme Pontiff, and he later passed away there. Louis also set his mind on recovering the Kingdom of Naples, entering into an agreement with King Ferdinand of Aragon and Queen Isabella <note>original: "Elisabeth"; referring to Isabella I of Castile</note> of Spain on these terms: that they would divide the conquered Kingdom of Naples equally between them. Pope Alexander VI granted to both whatever rights pertained to the Church. At the start of spring, he immediately sent his forces there. There, with the god of war watching for a long time, the battle was fought on both sides.

<margin>
D
The Neapolitan expedition.
</margin>
The French, however, first drove the Spaniards from the field and forced them into Barletta <note>original: "Barolum"</note>. Having obtained the opportunity to wander more freely through all the borders of the kingdom, they neglected to besiege the Spaniards, who were holding Barletta and several other citadels with a garrison.

<margin>
P
Philip, King of Castile, comes to Lyon.
</margin>
At about that time, the most refined prince Philip, Archduke of Austria <note>Philip the Handsome</note>, returning from Spain and distinguished with the royal crown of Castile, sought out Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunuz"</note>, where he was received quite honorably. For the most reverend Lord George d'Amboise, Cardinal of Rouen and most worthy Archbishop, acting as legate in France, went out to meet him with a noble company of associates. Likewise, the ecclesiastical persons (of whom there are very many in Lyon) came in procession. Others adorned the walls and partitions with tapestries and embroidered hangings or curtains. Still others exhibited spectacles and many types of plays filled with various mysteries for him as he entered. The rest climbed to higher places or occupied windows. The common folk, enticed by the desire to see him, flocked through the streets and crossroads. The counts and canons of the church of St. John the Baptist, maintaining a significant gravity, waited before the porch of the temple with the other ministers of this sacred house; they received him most kindly and into the sacred building 

<column-break/>

introduced him to adore the best and greatest God along with their patron saint; he was also received by them with hospitality. Thus, finding the discord between the two most illustrious kings—to both of whom he was closely joined—most troubling, he stayed in Lyon for several days awaiting the King’s arrival, intending to strive "with hands and feet" <note>original: "manibus t pedibus"; a Latin idiom meaning to try with all one's might</note> to lead them to the unity of peace. When the King arrived, the matter was discussed quite diligently by them and by the mature counsel of their farsighted advisors; finally, a treaty was struck. It would have remained an indissoluble bond had the Spanish King not lent a patient ear to "womanly counsel" <note>original: "muliebri consilio"; a likely reference to the influence of Isabella of Castile</note>, by whose nod all the business of the kingdom was arranged.

<margin>2</margin>
While these things were being negotiated, the enemy, intent on every opportunity, departed Barletta in the silence of a late night and arrived at Ruvo <note>original: "Rubum"</note>. The French, suspecting nothing of war since peace was being discussed, lost the garrison town as it was stormed. At almost that same time, German infantry hired by the Spaniards had arrived, which gave the enemy such confidence that—even though they had been shamefully routed many times before and suffered great disadvantage—on the 21st of April <note>original: "ix. kal. Maij"; 9 days before the Calends of May</note> in the year of our Lord 1503, they led out all their forces and encamped at the bridge of Cannae, not far from the French camp, which was situated along the banks of the River Ofanto <note>original: "Aufidi"</note> near Canosa.

<margin>
Battle of the French and Spaniards
</margin>
The next day, as the Spaniards attempted to take the town of Cerignola <note>original: "Cydoniole"</note> by force, and the French came to its aid, the battle was fought fiercely on both sides. Finally, the French knights on the far flank—partly because they were exhausted by the fighting and partly because they were far inferior in number—were forced to give way for a short time. Noticing this, the Italian knights serving as auxiliaries to the Spaniards attacked the flanks of the French who were fighting at the front and threw them into confusion. For I believe they dreaded looking upon or attacking them face-to-face. With the French thus weakened and put to flight, the victory remained with the Spaniards. In that battle fell the most noble Louis, Duke of Nemours, of the lineage of the Counts of Armagnac, who held the person and office of the King’s legate. The Spaniards, elated by their success, not long after captured the city of Naples and its citadel, and as the other towns surrendered, they took possession of the kingdom. The remnants of the French who survived the war and the flight first halted at the bank of the Liris <note>the Garigliano river</note> at Genuessa; then they retreated to Gaeta, where, surrounded by the enemy's naval forces, they sustained the attack with constancy and courage, awaiting help from their own people. This calamity was made more mournful by the ruinous desertion of those who ought to have brought aid. For the French paymasters, or as they are commonly called, the treasurers <note>original: "thesaurarij"</note>, provided almost no support at all.

### Triumphs of the Gauls

Because they had received public funds to send pay to the soldiers, but, led by greed, they kept it for themselves—reaching a sum rumored to be 300,000 ducats—and did not supply the necessary travel expenses. Therefore, the most courageous soldiers—who not only could have held Naples <note>original: "Parthenope," a classical name for Naples</note> now conquered, but could also have recovered all of Sicily and kept the enemies at a further distance—were forced by hunger and distress of spirit to be miserably reduced to nothing. But such a shameful crime did not remain unpunished. <margin>Their punishment.</margin> For once the truth was uncovered, they were summoned to the Parliament of Paris and forced to give an account; in this matter, the greatest justice was found. For this reason, some of them were punished by the seizure of their goods, others were sent into exile, and others, had they been caught, would have suffered capital punishment by the King's command. The head of all these aforementioned evils was a woman’s nature, prone to every evil, for she easily turned the King's mind in whichever direction she wished. Indeed, many other women have been the cause of the betrayal of the bravest men and the destruction of cities and kingdoms. Did not Cleopatra destroy Mark Antony? Did she not also delay the most courageous Caesar in Egypt from his undertaking—after the Battle of Pharsalus, which was so bloody—while he was still entangled in civil wars and had not yet achieved full victory? Was not a woman the cause of the destruction of Troy? And did not Hecuba give the counsel by which Achilles, the bravest of the Greeks, was treacherously slain? It would have been far more pleasing and much more agreeable to us to report the happy wars of Italy and France than these lamentable disasters; yet because the times have brought this about, we follow the shifts of the times, the mutability of fortune, and the cleverness of the enemies. And the war by which almost all of Sicily was overturned, we describe in passing in this defense <note>original: "apologetico"; a work written to defend or explain a position</note>. It is indeed a sorrowful subject, but very necessary for the knowledge of our times. Nor does Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian</note> deserve less praise when he reports the city of Rome captured by the Gauls and consumed by fires than when he narrates the victories of Scipio Africanus. <margin>The duty of history.</margin> It is indeed the duty of history to commit to literary monuments deeds both prosperous and adverse. Therefore, better things are to be hoped for, but whatever has happened must be written. This is something that Venetian man certainly does not seem to have done—a man otherwise endowed with eloquence, but under which a lethal poison lurks within the sweetness of honey. For he is not to be called a historian, who writes only the truth of both adversity and prosperity, but rather a poet. Unless, perhaps, he wishes to say that he wrote not for historical accuracy, but as an image of a perfect war; and not how the Spaniards and Italians were

<column-break/>

against the Gauls, but how they ought to have been. Thus, under the instruction and example of the Spaniards, we might see a most excellent kind of royal administration clearly expressed. This is the same form in which that Cyrus, King of the Persians, is described by Xenophon: not for historical accuracy, but as the image of a perfect commander—not as he was, but as he ought to have been. But enough of these things. It remains for us to recall our pen to the continuation of the task we have begun, and to bring into the open those things which the Venetian writer (I know not with what intent) either diminished or passed over in silence. There has come into our hands the work of that (if he can be so called) historiographer; it is, in my opinion, not inelegant, and in it he has endeavored to weave a history of the wars between the Gauls and certain peoples of the Italians and Spaniards. But (if I may say so without offense) he does not seem to have sufficiently pursued the pure truth of history in it, since he explains the successes of our adversaries more clearly than the light, while highlighting our adversities. Since indeed even they sometimes fought unsuccessfully, and our men often fought successfully, I do not deny that the outcome of the war was unhappy for us—partly because of the trouble caused by the attacking enemies, but rather because of the infidelity of our officials, who withdrew necessities from the soldiers. Nor is it a wonder that our men sometimes labored under adverse fortune, for the outcome of war is varied and doubtful. <margin>Maccabees</margin> Was not that most courageous Judas Maccabeus, after fighting bravely and spiritedly for a long time, finally destroyed along with his entire brothers' lineage under the successors of Alexander the Great, as the history of the Maccabees testifies? <margin>The King.</margin> The Jews who wished to revere and observe the law were miserably slaughtered; among them was Eleazar, one of the elder scribes, a man advanced in age, handsome in countenance, and venerable for the holiness of his life. When he was forced to eat swine’s flesh against the statutes of the law established by God, he preferred to die justly and religiously rather than prolong a shameful and ignoble life a little further. Therefore, while he was subjected to torments and saw death approaching, he is said to have cried out groaning: "Lord, who has holy knowledge, you clearly know that although I could be delivered from death, I endure hard pains of the body, but in my soul, I willingly suffer these things because of your fear." Did not David, whom God found according to his own heart and anointed as <margin>About David</margin> king, suffer the ambushes of King Saul, the foreigners <note>original: "allophilorum"; often referring to the Philistines in biblical Latin</note>, and his own most beloved son? Was not Abel, whom Christ calls just in the Gospel, the first of all the saints to be killed by his wicked brother Cain? Was not Jeremiah overwhelmed by stones? Was not Isaiah [sawn] into two...

### Second Treatise

...was cut into pieces. Was not Zechariah, son of Berechiah, killed between the temple and the altar? <note>A reference to Matthew 23:35; Zechariah was a prophet whose murder within the sacred precinct was a symbol of ultimate injustice.</note> Was not Elijah driven into flight by Jezebel? I say nothing of the apostles. I say nothing of John the Baptist. I say nothing of the martyrs, for no one’s own home is better known to them than these are to us. For as many as have pleased God from the beginning of the world until our own age have carried the cross of suffering in their mortal bodies. Listen to what is said in the Psalms: *For your sake we are being killed all day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.* <note>original Latin: "Propter te mortificamur tota die: estimati sumus sicut oues occisionis" from Psalm 44:22.</note>

It is no wonder, then, if the Gauls <note>The French</note>—circumvented by the ambushes of the Spanish who used their own cunning and did not obey the king's commands—sometimes fought with little success; for inconstant Fortune does not always smile upon the same people. Nevertheless, our men carried out many memorable battles quite fortunately, both in the time of King Charles <note>Charles VIII</note> and of Louis XII, who currently moderates the royal scepter; many of these deeds the future writer will pass over in silence.

Likewise, there is that singular combat of Pierre Terrail, Lord of Bayard, a most noble man from Dauphiné. <note>Known as the "Chevalier de Bayard," the legendary "knight without fear and beyond reproach."</note> For when, in a certain engagement of war, he had captured a certain Spaniard most noble and most practiced in arms, and held him as a captive, he treated him kindly and humanely enough as befits a nobleman. Yet, when the Spaniard was restored to liberty, unmindful of the favor, he complained of Bayard’s inhumanity toward him. Because of this, he challenged the Lord of Bayard to a singular combat—specifically on foot, where he believed he had the advantage. Bayard, feeling himself exhausted from long labor and lack of food, initially declined the condition. Finally, provoked by many insults and judged as faint-hearted, he cast aside all softness of spirit and accepted the condition. The place was designated; the day of the contest was set. 

The Spaniard even sent to the said Lord of Bayard a letter, written by a scribe and signed with his own hand, which I have both seen and read through. Lest anyone think we are making these things up to favor our own people, I wanted to insert it here in its own language, though set forth in Latin translation <note>The author provides the Spanish text first, then a Latin version; both are translated to English here.</note>, along with the response of the aforementioned Lord of Bayard. 

**The Tenor of the Spaniard's Letter:** "Lord Pierre de Bayard, I have heard how you have come to the place where I was assigned to perform deeds of arms from my person to yours. This pleases me, and I

-> **To Lord Alonso de Sotomayor.** <-

The explanation of the letter just mentioned is as follows: "Lord Pierre de Bayard, I have heard that you have seen the place of battle assigned to each of us, which pleases me greatly. But I wish that if anyone from our side or yours should be a hindrance to either, or if any trickery is used, the lord of that person shall be the captive of the other, just as if he had been defeated by the strength of arms; and I wish for no other security. Written in Andria, November 26, in the year of our Lord 1503. By me, Pedro de Cardona." 

**The Spaniard’s subscription:** "Lord Alonso de Sotomayor." 

The response of Lord Pierre Terrail follows: "Lord Alonso, I have seen the letter given to me, and the condition pleases me: that if anyone from our side is a hindrance to the other, he shall be that person’s captive as if overcome by the force of arms. For I desire only to defend my honor and to repel the injury done to me, as if I had not treated you with the humanity I ought to have; for this and nothing else I desire. Farewell. Written this 29th of November, in the year of our Lord 1503. By me, Pierre Terrail, Lord of Bayard." 

When these things were finished, they both came courageously to the fight. They joined hands fiercely; but the Lord Pierre Terrail, though pitying him (for he is exceedingly humane), killed the Spaniard with a third strike. He freely permitted his body, along with his arms—which he could have kept for himself by the law of war—to be carried away so that it might be given to burial with the appropriate decency. 

Likewise, someone might describe a certain contest in which a certain number of Gauls fought unsuccessfully with a certain number of Italians; yet he might omit another in which a certain number of Spaniards 
<margin>Lord Bayard holds the bridge.</margin>

In that battle, though seven of the Gauls' horses were killed, two Gauls—of whom the oft-mentioned Lord of Bayard was one—resisted the Spaniards so courageously and rescued their companions from danger that they gained the victory, while the Spaniards, accomplishing nothing, returned ignominiously to their own people.

These men can say with David, that brave and warlike man: *We went through fire and water, and you led us out into a place of refreshment.* <note>original: "Transiuimus per ignem & aquam & eduxisti nos in refrigerium" from Psalm 66:12.</note> Nor were there among so many evils and adversities of the French few glorious struggles out of many, which that Venetian historian <note>Likely a reference to a contemporary historian like Marcantonio Sabellico, whom the author accuses of bias.</note> has either shrouded in silence or recorded with diminished literary monuments. You, therefore, O bravest young men of the French, whose ancestors fell in Sicily far from their native soil: recall your soul from grief and sadness; preserve yourselves for favorable things; and rejoice the more, and give immense thanks, because they met death in a just war, fighting bravely like vigorous soldiers, even if circumvented by the deceits and ambushes of the enemy. But Roman emperors—such as Julian the Apostate, Constans, Maxentius, and the others whom historians report to have lived shamefully—God corrected so that his justice might punish their perfected wickedness with both temporal and eternal penalties, as justice demands. Of them we can say what we find written 
<margin>ps.</margin>
in Isaiah, where God complains of the impious and ungrateful Jews. For as long as they clung to God by living well, with him who said: *But for me, to cling to God is good: and to put my hope in God,* <note>original: "Mihi autem adherere deo bonum est: & ponere in deo spem meam" from Psalm 73:28.</note> so long did he feed them and direct them like a pious father. But after they withdrew from God the Father like the prodigal son, going away into a distant region and dissipating their substance by living impiously—and because, once it was consumed, they never returned to the father—they were fed with the food of pigs and permitted to pass into a bestial nature. Among these was that impious Herod the Second <note>Herod Agrippa I.</note>,

<column-break/>

who, after he had killed James to please the Jews, seized Peter also; while he allowed 
<margin>Acts 12</margin>
himself to be called a god, he was soon seized by the wrath of God. In vengeance for such great impiety, his whole body suddenly began to swarm with worms; he was shaken by pains of the belly, tormented by dysentery, and while still alive, he drank the cup of bitterness as the first fruits of perdition. Likewise, that Julian the Apostate, a wicked man and the worst of Roman emperors—who in derision called Jesus Christ "the Galilean" and "the carpenter's son"—was pierced by an arrow in the Persian (or as others say, Parthian) war; while he was expiring, he was forced to cry out: *You have conquered, O Galilean, you have conquered.* <note>original: "Vicisti galilee vicisti."</note> Therefore, God struck us not as a physician would to heal, but rather as a just judge to punish, no longer by the benefit of medicine but by the duty of his office. Certainly, although many things disturb me as I write these words because of my singular love for my fatherland, I am nevertheless consoled by this reason: that even if France suffered great adversities in those Frenchmen (on account of the treachery of the enemy), she has nonetheless remained the conqueror of foreign nations until now, and at present remains most powerful by both land and sea. And the cities in her, most adorned with great wealth and great authority, have flourished until now and flourish today; their glory and kingdom are extended far and wide, so that one should not groan so much for those adversities that happened then, as one should rejoice for the prosperous things that remain. Just as his great labors made Hercules more famous, so it would be for France, for he would never have been so celebrated if he had not labored so dangerously. I say nothing of the disciplines of the liberal arts, in which the one incomparable city of Paris is found to have no equal and to be a nurturer of such things. But there will be another time for that commendation.

### Third Treatise.

...[their] misfortunes as well as their successes, just as faithful writers have committed to literary monuments: let them bring these propositions into the open. For us, however, there shall be no small praise for these matters found in the commentaries of the most studious and highly-trusted Italians. Therefore, just as with many other things, we have sought to restore these matters—though so thoroughly erased—to the knowledge of our people. And we have done so all the more gladly because other nations have not failed to weave histories of their own praises, whereas this work is entirely about ours. In this work, it will be worthwhile to explain clearly in a few words: how much the virtue of the Gauls <note>The author uses the Latin *Galli* (Gauls) to refer to the ancestors of the modern French, a common practice in Renaissance humanism to link modern France to ancient glory.</note> once prevailed throughout Italy, other regions, provinces, and finally through almost the entire world; which cities were besieged, which were stormed and conquered, and in what places battles were joined by the Gauls themselves. For it is a most beautiful thing to know all these matters, and a most shameful thing to be ignorant of them. Indeed, it is the mark of a diligent man not to be ignorant of his fatherland’s origin and progress, and whatever has happened to it through former times. Therefore, I have taught above—using Justin and other men of no small authority—about the struggles of the Gauls against the Romans and other nations. Now, however, I have decided to confirm the glory of the Gauls and our own judgment through the Italians themselves; a task I shall consider correctly done if it is approved by the most learned and wise Italians. We shall, therefore, take the beginning of our narrative chiefly from Caesar himself, both on account of the authority of the speaker and the authority of the one about whom he speaks.
<margin>
B
Plutarch
on
Caesar
</margin>
Thus Plutarch, speaking of Caesar, says: Caesar, campaigning for nine years, subdued all of Gaul—from the Pyrenian forest and the Alps to Mount Cevennes <note>original: *Gebennam*</note>, and the Rhine and Rhone—to the Roman People <note>original: *P. R.* for *Populus Romanus*</note>. As another historian writes: after Gaul was pacified by Caesar, it was a greater glory for him than if he had subdued the whole world for himself. Yet Caesar confesses in the first book of his *Commentaries* that he crossed the Rhine not of his own accord, but at the request of and summoned by the Gauls, not without great hope and great rewards. He proclaimed that they had left their homes and kin but held seats in Gaul granted by these people; that hostages were given by their own will; and that they took tribute by the right of war, which victors are accustomed to impose on the conquered. He claimed not that he had brought war upon the Gauls, but that the Gauls had brought war upon him. What, therefore, must be said of the Gauls, if Caesar seems to have earned greater glory on account of Gaul—not so much because it was conquered as because it was surrendered by the Gauls themselves—than if he had pacified the rest of the world for himself? O glorious race of Gauls! O most brave race! O warlike nation: a nation harsh, yet no less religious. Through you kings reign,

<column-break/>

through you emperors triumph. If Caesar had not known Gaul, not only would he not have usurped the empire, but he would not have obtained the name of perpetual dictator. Only the Franks <note>The author now shifts from *Galli* to *Franci* (Franks/French), treating them as the same people.</note>, only the princes and leaders of the Franks out of the number of all nations, dared to consult the interests of Caesar and to attack and weaken the audacity of Pompey in the Pharsalian war. Many more were fighting under Pompey than under Caesar. But Caesar, by the virtue of the Gauls who fought under him and with a great charge, attacked the enemy; and by killing and wounding many, he laid them low.
<margin>
Caesar
conquered
Pompey
with the
help of the
Gauls.
</margin>
The Caesarians, in the manner of the Gauls, striking the faces of the enemy, harassed them with their spears and points; terrified by this kind of striking due to the danger to their eyes, the enemy were forced to turn their backs. Caesar, moreover, commanded only twenty-two thousand men, the greater part of whom were Gauls. Under Pompey, truly, fought many more than twice that number. But this victory was not the Italians’, but the Gauls’; who fought as if for themselves under one leader <note>The transcription reads *Lyra*, likely a corrupted reference to a leader or a specific formation; the sense is fighting with singular focus</note> against the Erepseans and Assyrians—timid men.
<margin>
Julius
Celsus.
</margin>
Likewise Julius Celsus <note>A 14th-century scholar often confused in the Renaissance with the author of Caesar's biography.</note>, though a rival of the Gauls, says this of the Gauls in the fifth book of the *Wars of Caesar*: The Gauls are open men and not at all treacherous; they are accustomed to fight through virtue rather than through ambushes. And Caesar says in his *Commentaries*: That matter also increased the care of the most provident leader: that he was conducting business with a most treacherous king, while he was accustomed to fighting with Gauls, who are open men and ignorant of ambushes, and who wage war not with frauds, but with virtue. Likewise in the same chapter: Caesar stands his battle line, and the few fight excellently against the many. In which encounter, the virtue of some Gallic horsemen who followed Caesar was remarkable and difficult to believe. Indeed, thirty or fewer repelled two thousand Moorish horsemen from the field and drove them into the town. But let these suffice from the sayings of ancient writers.
<margin>
Francesco
Filelfo
on the
Franks.
</margin>
We shall briefly touch upon what even more recent Italian writers have felt about the Gauls. Francesco Filelfo <note>1398–1481; a famous Italian humanist scholar.</note>, a man the most learned and elegant of his age among the Italians, says this in a letter to Charles VII, King of the Franks: "If it is permitted to confess the truth without envy toward anyone: since that impious, cruel, and most wicked sect of Muhammad became strong, there is no race of men to whom the Christian religion owes more than to the invincible and most noble virtue of the Franks. For while almost all other Christian kings and peoples had grown faint, as if by a certain sluggish numbness of soul, only the Franks were found who, with a great and lofty spirit, [withstood] every attack of the barbarians and infidels..."

...not only did they withstand them, but they repelled them. Nay, what is more than repelled: they routed them, put them to flight, and crushed them. Not even Filelfo <note>Francesco Filelfo (1398–1481), a famous Italian humanist who often wrote about Italian and French history.</note> can deny this. Was it not that Charlemagne, as we said above,

Charlemagne defeated the Saracens.
</margin>

And was he not adorned with the insignia of the Roman Empire by Pope Leo, as Hadrian had previously decreed? As soon as he returned to Further Gaul, not content with present praise, but meditating on something greater and more famous in his mind, he sought Spain with robust and very firm troops. For at that time, it was serving the followers of the wicked and lost Muhammad. It was entirely under the foul and most shameful dominion of the Saracens. The war was long and most dangerous. There were many battles, many slaughters on both sides, and varied outcomes. But finally, by divine kindness, through the prudence and perseverance of Charles and the virtue of his army, those same impious enemies of Christ were equally crushed by extreme calamity, so that the allies of that same perfidy were destroyed by the same Charles at the rugged mountain of Africa. Was it not the same cause of honor for Louis the Pious, 
<margin>
Lord Louis expelled the Saracens.
</margin>
son of this Charlemagne, when with such labor and danger he liberated the city of Rome from the harshest yoke of the Saracens? These enemies, led by the Egyptians, had been summoned into Italy by the wicked conspiracy of certain Romans. Was it not that most holy King Louis <note>King Louis IX of France, known as Saint Louis.</note>, who was called "the most Christian" by many? Who first, so that he might stand by his agreements, keep his oath, and protect what we call honor, exhausted all his treasures? 
<margin>
Saint Louis against the Saracens.
</margin>

Then, having again gathered an army from all of Gaul, out of that same force of honor, he crossed into Africa with the plan and intention not only of avenging the calamity received in Egypt but of removing all the superstition of the most impure Muhammad from the land of the living. He would have easily accomplished this, had he not been seized by the force of a <insert>l</insert>ethal plague at Tunis, which he was besieging, and passed from this light along with his son Louis, the Cardinal of Albano, and an almost infinite number of Christians. For what other desire do we believe those Franks and other Gauls had, who under the leadership of Godfrey <note>original: "Borthifredo." Likely referring to Godfrey of Bouillon, a leader of the First Crusade.</note> 
<margin>
Godfrey against the same.
</margin>
when they had arrived in Asia, overcame the Saracens in battle at Damascus, and crushed the Persians and Turks at Antioch? 

<column-break/>

They recovered all of Mesopotamia; and again, having routed the Saracens in Syria to the point of extinction, and having stormed the very populous and fortified cities of Dara and Barka, they liberated the Holy City and all of Palestine—something which had happened during the reign of Emperor Henry III. Likewise, Bohemond <note>Bohemond I of Antioch, another key leader of the First Crusade.</note> liberated them from the shameful servitude of the infidels, and they possessed them with a wonderful increase of the Christian name for eighty-eight years, until the time of Saladin. And we not only read of the Franks in the histories of the Italians, but we study them thoroughly. Great praise was given to the Blessed Julius Caesar because he had overcome the Britons in a difficult war—a people who had even turned Liber and Hercules <note>Bacchus/Liber and Hercules were legendary figures often claimed to have reached the edges of the known world; Caesar’s victory over the Britons was thus seen as exceeding myth.</note>, two most skilled, famous, and powerful leaders, to flight, and had never been conquered by anyone. But Gaul shows that these same people [the Britons] were not only overcome and conquered by the English, but exterminated from their native soil. How much the English are inferior to the French is declared by the frequent and very great victories held over them by Charles VII, King of the French. Among the Italians, you will find few Caesars—men such as Julius Caesar. Among the Gauls, however, it is certain that many such most famous and powerful kings have flourished. 
<margin>
Victory in war is won by three things.
</margin>
The wise say there are three things by which victory is won in war, all of which you will find in the kings of the Gauls: the excellence of the commander, the multitude and strength of the soldiers, and the convenience of financial resources. For money is, as it were, the very sinews <note>original: "nerui." The author uses the common metaphor of money as the 'nerves' or 'sinews' of war, meaning the essential source of strength.</note> of war. All of which you will find in Gaul. For though I remain silent about the abundance of money—which everyone knows the King and Kingdom of the Gauls possess in wondrous plenty—among the Gauls, there is an army which is both large and strong. For a very long time, through constant military service, this army has been trained with the highest praise against those same greatest and most formidable forces of the English and Germans, by which nearly all of Gaul is surrounded, so that they do not fear even the whole human race. I believe the excellence of a commander consists of two things: prudence and virtue, by which both all authority and prosperous outcomes are born. For reason and counsel, while they have great value in all things, are most important in waging war. For he who is ignorant of military affairs and command can do nothing rightly, neither in fighting nor in commanding. From the beginning of their reign until this very age, the French have conducted themselves so prudently regarding the military art that no industry of commanders or soldiers, no practice, and no method can remain hidden from them.

...moreover, among the kings of the French, there was as much greatness as there ever was in any other kings or emperors. <margin>Sabellicus, Book 3</margin> Regarding the virtues of the French, hear what their adversaries were compelled by the truth to say. There were few minor kings in the entire nation; now the king's authority holds everything far and wide. They celebrate marriages according to the Italian rite. Many care for the liberal arts, and especially the study of divine arts. The University <note>original: "Gymnasium." Referring to the University of Paris (the Sorbonne).</note> which is in Paris declares this: it is the most famous of all that exist on earth. They are also most eager for Roman literature, nor do they despise Greek. Judgments are in the hands of magistrates; it is the kings' role to choose them. In wars, they use the armored knight <note>original: "cataphracto equite."</note> and lightly armed infantry. They also use archers, who stretch longer bows—not made of horn like those of the Scythians and almost the whole East—but of a rare and harder material. The Franks are descended from the Trojan line." <note>A popular medieval and Renaissance myth claimed the Franks were descended from Francus, a survivor of Troy.</note>
<margin>The remarkable deed of Joan the Maiden.</margin> In the same book, he says: "In the times of Charles VII, King of the French, I would believe that the deed of Joan, the French Maiden, occurred—memorable in every age. When the French resources lay broken by the English wars, a girl, warned by a heavenly voice (as it is believed) and equipped with manly clothing and arms, began to lead the army. Then, having frequently engaged with the enemy, fighting among the foremost, she recovered the greatest part of the French territory from the English." Sabellicus says that during these times—or certainly not much earlier—Charles expelled John, Count of Armagnac, from his principality, a man infamous for the incestuous love of his sister and seeking marriage with her. How far this is from the truth, all men know. For it is the most common report that John of Armagnac was killed in Gascony, not by Charles, but by Louis XI. It is no wonder, therefore, if Sabellicus has erred in many places and felt poorly toward the French, since he erred in more recent history regarding the House of Armagnac. And in the eighth book of the *Eneades*, the same Sabellicus writes thus about the French: "There were in Spain many mortals who abhorred the true worship of the faith; most of the cities of these nations fell to French arms. -> ### Third Treatise ### <-

...was indeed so great among the kings of the Gauls <note>The author uses "Gauls" (gallorum) to refer to the French people and their monarchs.</note>: as great as has ever been among any other kings or emperors. ¶ Hear what even their adversaries were forced by the truth to say concerning the virtues of the Gauls. For Marcus Antonius Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506), an influential Venetian historian known for his universal history, the *Enneades*.</note>, a man of great eloquence in both tongues, 
<margin>Sabellicus, Book 3, on the Franks.</margin>
speaks thus in his third book on the customs of the Gauls: "The religious rites of the Gauls are entirely different from what they once were. Formerly, they were worshippers of evil demons like other nations; now, they are most observant of true piety. In those days, the people lived each for themselves, as did the cities. There were only a few petty kings in the whole nation; now, the authority of the King holds everything far and wide. They celebrate marriages according to the Italian rite. Many care for the liberal arts, and especially the study of divine arts. The University <note>original: "Gymnasium." Here referring to the University of Paris (the Sorbonne), established as a center of medieval learning.</note> which is in Paris declares this: it is the most famous of all that exist on earth. They are also most eager for Roman literature, nor do they despise Greek. Judgments are in the hands of magistrates; it is the role of kings to choose these men. In wars, they employ the armored knight <note>original: "cataphracto equite." A heavily armored cavalryman.</note> and lightly armed infantry. They also use archers, who draw longer bows—not made of horn like those of the Scythians and almost the entire East, but of yew or some other harder material. The Franks are descended from the Trojan line." 
<margin>The extraordinary deed of the Virgin Joan.</margin>
And in the same book, he says: "In the times of Charles VII, King of the Franks, I believe there occurred that deed of Joan, the French Virgin <note>Joan of Arc (c. 1412–1431), the peasant girl who led French armies against the English during the Hundred Years' War.</note>, memorable in every age. When the wealth of the Gauls lay shattered by the English wars, a girl, warned by a heavenly voice (as it is believed) and equipped with male clothing and arms, began to lead the army. Then, having engaged the enemy many times and fighting among the first ranks, she recovered the much larger part of the French territory from the English." Sabellicus says that during these times—or certainly not much earlier—Charles expelled the Count of Armagnac, John, who was infamous for the incestuous love of his sister and for attempting to marry her, from his principality. Everyone knows how far this is from the truth. For it is a very common report that John of Armagnac was killed in Gascony, not by Charles, but by Louis XI. It is no wonder, then, if Sabellicus has erred in many places and thought poorly of the Gauls, since he erred even in recent history regarding the Armagnacs. And in the eighth book of his eighth *Ennead*, the same Sabellicus writes thus of the Gauls: "There were many mortals in Spain who shrank from the true worship of the faith; most of the cities of these nations fell to Gallic arms, and among these, most flourishing in wealth and fame, Augusta <note>Likely Zaragoza (Caesaraugusta).</note> and Pamplona <note>original: "Papilonia."</note> were taken by force and plundered as enemies. At that time, Ibnalachus and Denizes <note>Moorish rulers in Spain.</note> held Spain widely; 

<column-break/>

distrusting their own strength, they redeemed peace for themselves on these conditions: that Charles, beyond a great weight of gold given as tribute, should hold hither Spain. There are those who write that there were three kings who entered into these treaties. Furthermore, Charles the victor, when he was leading his victorious army back into Gaul, fell into an ambush of the Basques <note>original: "vasconum." This refers to the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778.</note> near the Pyrenees. For a whole day, the battle was fought in an unfavorable place. Many of the Gallic name perished in that battle, and among them Anselm, Eggihard, and 
<margin>Roland perished.</margin>
the bravest of all the Gauls, Roland, the nephew of Charles by his sister; his fame, more than heroic, has flowed down to posterity. That bravest of men perished after a huge slaughter of his own people—not by the sword, as they say, but by thirst. The Basques, barely repelled by the Gauls, withdrew to safety laden with plunder. However, if they felt any joy from that bloody victory, Charles made it very brief for them; he immediately pursued the nation itself with a fierce war. Indeed, often weary and variously afflicted by the calamities of war, they paid the deserved penalties for their treachery." Thus says Sabellicus. Roland died at the age of forty-two, as Turpin <note>A reference to the "Pseudo-Turpin Chronicle," a 12th-century legendary history of Charlemagne's campaigns in Spain.</note> writes. This is attested by the short poem which Charles is said to have always had on his lips: "You return to your fatherland; you leave us in a sad world. A shining hall holds you; a tearful day holds us. But since you have spent eight lustra plus two years <note>original: "lustra geris octo binos super annos." A lustrum is five years; 8x5+2 = 42 years.</note>, snatched from the earth, you return as a just man to the stars." And in the ninth book of the ninth *Ennead*, the same Sabellicus writes thus of Charlemagne: "Wonderful are the things that have been handed down to memory concerning the nature and character of that man. He was equally eminent in the arts of peace and war. His piety, beneficence, and humanity were distinguished—greater than in any of the previous princes. It is difficult to say whether his military virtue or his good fortune was greater. No one ever subdued more nations in Europe. No one cherished the study of the liberal arts more indulgently or loved them more dearly. Albinus, who is given the surname Alcuin <note>Alcuin of York (c. 735–804), the English scholar and advisor to Charlemagne who led the Carolingian Renaissance.</note>, sent from Britain by kings to obtain peace from him, was embraced by Charles for his exceptional erudition; from an envoy he made him his guest, and from a guest, his teacher, imitating the ancient example of the Athenians, who, when Gorgias was sent to them publicly by the people of Leontini, detained him in Athens after he had performed his duty as envoy, captivated by his eloquence. He established a University 
<margin>The University of Paris.</margin>
of divine and human wisdom in Paris, and another in Pavia <note>original: "Ticini."</note> in Italy, as I see some are pleased to believe. They add a memorable event: Two men of the monastic profession, brought from Ireland <note>original: "hybernia."</note> into Gaul with British merchants, while others were offering various wares, they..."

-> # Trophies of the Gauls # <-

...testified with a loud voice that they had **wisdom for sale**, if they could find a buyer. At first, they were believed to be raving; but soon, as they began their daily preaching, their assertions began to be noticed by a few, as is often the case. Meanwhile, when the rumor reached the royal palace, they were summoned into the presence of **Charles** <note>Referring to Charlemagne (r. 768–814).</note>. When asked about their "merchandise for sale" before the king, they testified to the same thing. They were asked at what price it was set for one wishing to buy. "The food and clothing of a teacher," they replied. 

However, Charles was hindered by the cares of war—for these events occurred somewhat before he obtained the title of Emperor. One of these men he settled in **Paris**. They say his name was **Clement**; young men from every rank of the city were given to him to be instructed. The other was ordered to cross into Italy, to **Ticinum**—which is now called **Pavia**—to teach wisdom. 

There is also another account regarding the **Parisian Gymnasium** <note>The University of Paris.</note>: that it was established by four men of the monastic profession: **Rabanus**, **Alcuin**, **Claudius**, and **John the Scot** <note>These are famous Carolingian scholars: Rabanus Maurus, Alcuin of York, Claudius of Turin, and Johannes Scottus Eriugena.</note>. I deliberately set aside other things which **Sabellicus** <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506), a Venetian historian.</note> himself wrote concerning the stature and strength of Charles in praise of the Gauls. It is a wonder that such an excellent writer, who so greatly praised the deeds of the preceding kings of the Gauls, should speak so fearfully—falling short of the manifest truth—concerning the deeds of those whom our own age has known, even though they did things no less great than the rest. 

Regarding **Clovis** <note>Clodoueus/Clovis I (c. 466–511), the first King of the Franks to unite the tribes and convert to Christianity.</note>, he writes in the third book of the tenth *Ennead* as follows: "Clovis, who was the first of the Frankish kings to cherish Christian piety, defeated **Syagrius** (the son of Aegidius) in war and expelled him from his kingdom; when he was driven out and had fled to the Goths, Clovis demanded him back and, when he was surrendered, killed him as an enemy." Then Clovis brought war against the Goths and Aquitanians; he vowed a horse in exchange for victory. Having been granted his vow <note>term: "voti damnatus" — literally "condemned of his vow," meaning he was now obligated to fulfill it because his prayer was answered.</note>, he attempted to redeem the animal with a small sum of money. But the war-horse stood motionless until a greater price was given for it. Then the good king said: "The Saint <note>original: "diuus," likely referring to St. Martin of Tours.</note> was kind and favorable to me in battle, since this horse is his (for the thing had been vowed to heaven), but his businessman is too greedy." He says many other things about the kings of the Gauls, their customs, and their virtues. 

But when he happens upon
<margin>Sabellicus thinks poorly of the Gauls.</margin>
**Charles VIII**, a liberal, pious, and merciful man, and upon **Louis XII**, a most Christian and prudent man, he writes many things not as a historian, but—disregarding the laws of history—with poetic and fabulous license. This is especially true regarding that victory of the Gauls at the banks of the **Taro River** <note>The Battle of Fornovo (1495), where Charles VIII fought the League of Venice.</note> when he says: "The Venetian cause was superior that day, because once the Gauls' baggage was taken, 

<column-break/>

the enemy was forced to go where the Venetian wanted, not where he had intended to go." On the contrary, the Gaul may claim the victory for himself, because after the Italians had been repulsed by him with slaughter, he held to his destined journey. 

That the Venetians gained the victory is a claim not so much false as it is ridiculous; for a most certain report of it has long since flown even to the farthest Indians. For the Gauls may most justly claim the victory for themselves. For just as **Xerxes**, the King of the Persians, was put to flight with so great an army by **Themistocles** no less by skill than by strength, so the Italians were not only put to flight by the one Charles, but were slaughtered on that day. 

For Sabellicus himself, as if compelled by the truth (which is the strongest of all things), speaks thus: "The number of the injured could hardly be entered into the record. It is well enough established that a number **twice as large** from the Italian army fell as from the Gallic." There fell among the Venetian leaders **Rodolfo Gonzaga**, his uncle **Francesco**, **Ranuccio Farnese**, and many other illustrious men. So says Sabellicus. 

He ought not to have said "a number twice as large," etc. For he should have made no proportion at all, since there is no proportion between "none" and "very many." As for his claim that "many more of the Gallic leaders fell," this is utterly foreign to the truth, since it was found that **none** of the number of leaders died in that clash, except for one **Julian**, acting in the place of a certain general of the Gallic army, who, fighting bravely, finally fell. I do not, however, deny that the **Bastard of Bourbon** (of whom I spoke above) and some others were captured. 

Likewise, the same Sabellicus says: "It must be confessed that on that day it was fought by the Venetian leaders with more courage than counsel." But I ask, let the Venetian tell me: where then did that Senate's so mature "counsel" go? Where was that "prudence" of theirs which the outcome of events deserves, and which is so greatly commended by Italian writers? Perhaps he will answer that on the day they fought at the Taro River, the Venetians did not wish to commit such a treasury of counsel and prudence to their generals, nor expose it to the hazard of war, lest it perhaps be endangered with them, and thus they might lose their "treasury" along with their soldiers. 

But I am led by conjecture to think that they hid this kind of "treasury" away on that day with their treasuries of money (in which they trust), so that it might be reserved there in safety under the protection of **Saint Mark**. But enough of joking. In recounting the virtues of King Charles, I shall cite as witnesses not Sabellicus, but others from among the Italians who experienced his strength—and first of all, **Jacobus Philippus** <note>Giacomo Filippo Foresti (1434–1520), an Italian chronicler and monk from Bergamo.</note>...

### Third Treatise ###

...Bergomensis of the Order of Hermits, in the work he titled *The Supplement of the Supplement of the Chronicles*: a book in which, although he wrote much besides the truth, he was nonetheless compelled by the truth to write several things in praise of the Franks.

<margin>Bergomensis on King Charles VIII</margin>

In the sixteenth book of that same volume, he says this regarding **Charles VIII**, King of the Gauls: "I confess that I have read of no French king since the time of **Hugh the Great** <note>Referring to Hugh Capet (r. 987–996), the founder of the Capetian dynasty.</note> who is to be preferred to this small king, whether in conducting wars and acquiring kingdoms, or in magnanimity of soul, clemency, and especially piety. None of those kings ever dared to enter Italy. I would even dare to say of him what I believe Virgil said of Octavian: *A greater virtue reigns in a small body.* <note>Charles VIII was famously short and of frail appearance, contrasting with his massive military ambitions in Italy.</note> Indeed, the incredible fame of his victories shook all of Europe and even Asia with fear and admiration. Because of this, **Bayezid**, the Emperor of the Turks, began to contemplate war. This most excellent king was certainly to be commended for all these marvelous praises." 

Yet even **Jacopo Bergomensis** <note>Jacopo Filippo Foresti (1434–1520), an Augustinian friar from Bergamo whose world chronicle was highly popular but often criticized for inaccuracies.</note> was not always reliable. Although in this instance he wrote the truth about King Charles—much like **Balaam** <note>A biblical figure who was compelled by God to bless the Israelites instead of cursing them.</note> was compelled by an angel—nevertheless, in many other histories (if not all) regarding the kings of the Gauls, he spoke so erroneously that a leopard does not seem defiled by more spots than this man is by errors and lies. Indeed, he is found to be contradictory to himself in many places. For this reason, as was said above, he claims the victory at **Fornovo** <note>A significant battle in 1495 where the French fought the League of Venice.</note> belonged to the Venetian leaders. Yet elsewhere he says: "Even if the victory is credited to the Gaul, it was not bloodless."

<margin>On King Louis XII</margin>

Now, this man, along with **Baptista Mantuanus** and **Sabellicus**, felt so poorly toward the deeds of the Gauls that he should be called neither a historian nor even a poet, but rather a **Zoilus** <note>A historical figure known as a "harsh critic," used here to mean a spiteful detractor.</note> who is a stranger to the duty of a true poet. Furthermore, let them hear what he said regarding **Louis XII**, the most Christian King of the Gauls at the present time. For he says in the aforementioned book, where he speaks of the battle of Charles VIII against the Bretons at **Saint-Aubin** <note>The Battle of Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier (1488), a decisive battle in the "Mad War" where the French royal army defeated the rebel lords and the Duke of Brittany.</note>: "When **Francis, Duke of Brittany**, had called the **Duke of Orléans**, the **Prince of Orange**, and his subject barons to his side, he [the King] sent his commander **Jacques Galeotto** against the same Duke of Brittany with a large force. They fought a very great and sharp battle against each other. In this battle, six thousand men on both sides were

<column-break/>

slain. Among them, Galeotto himself, though the victor, fell in the slaughter. When the Duke of Brittany saw himself defeated, he escaped by flight so as not to fall into the hands of the enemy. But the Duke of Orléans and the Prince of Orange were captured and brought to the King; he immediately ordered the Duke of Orléans, named **Charles**, to be beheaded by a centurion. After his death, peace followed immediately." So says Jacopo Bergomensis.

<margin>The error of Bergomensis</margin>

Nothing is further from the truth than this lie. And to further corroborate this same lie, he says a little later: "**Louis, Duke of Orléans**, having succeeded to the kingdom without much difficulty this year after **Charles, King of the Franks**, died without any children, has reigned for five years until the present. He primarily had **Charles** as his father, whom the same King Charles, his predecessor, had ordered to be struck by the executioner's blade after he was captured on account of a mark of conspiracy and rebellion and for violating the public faith." Thus writes Jacopo. He brings these and six hundred other ridiculous absurdities against the Gauls—the man who is said to have written a *Supplement of the Supplement* not of histories, but of fables. He is the most inept of all men, were he not a member of the clergy <note>The author implies his status as a monk protects him from harsher social consequences, or perhaps that his only "skill" is religious ritual.</note>; he knows no sound except that of bells or drums. It would seem vain and most foolish to respond to every single instance of his madness, which is so inconsistent with the facts. I do not think he has read—or at least if he did read, he did not remember well—that precept of **Horace**:

<margin>Horace, *On the Art of Poetry*</margin>

> "You who write, take up a subject equal to your strength; and ponder long what your shoulders refuse to bear and what they are capable of." <note>original: "Sumite materiam vestris qui scribitis equam Viribus: et versate diu quid ferre recusent: Quid valeant humeri."</note>

Nor did this "poet" sufficiently consult the annals of ancient or even recent writers which contain the pure truth without any flattery. Jacopo himself committed to writing that **Charles, Duke of Orléans**, the father of this present King Louis, was captured with the Prince of Orange by Charles VIII, who ordered him to be punished with the ultimate penalty. What could be further from the truth than this error? What closer to a falsehood? For **Duke Charles of Orléans**, the father of this Louis, had departed this life many years before this war—indeed, even before the coronation of King Charles VIII. Furthermore, his son Louis, having been elevated to the throne in the year of our Lord 1500, ordered his father's body to be brought out for burial; he had it carried to **Paris** in a funeral procession and buried there in the **Convent of the Celestines**, in the chapel where his ancestors chose their place of burial. Not...

<meta>This page continues the author’s sharp critique of contemporary historians. Having just discussed Sabellicus, he now focuses on the work of the Augustinian monk Jacopo Filippo Foresti of Bergamo (known as Bergomensis), specifically examining his accounts of the French kings Charles VIII and Louis XII.</meta>

### Third Treatise

...the man from Bergamo <note>Jacopo Filippo Foresti, or "Bergomensis" (1434–1520)</note>, of the Order of Hermits <note>The Augustinian Friars</note>, in that work which he titled *The Supplement to the Supplement of Chronicles*. In this book, although he wrote many things that fall short of the truth, he was nevertheless compelled by the weight of reality to write several things in praise of the French. 

<margin>Bergomensis on King Charles VIII.</margin>
In the sixteenth book of that same volume, he says of **Charles VIII**, King of the Gauls: "I confess that I have read of no King of the Gauls, from the time of **Hugh the Great** <note>Hugh Capet (c. 941–996), founder of the Capetian dynasty</note> until now, who—whether in finishing wars and acquiring kingdoms, or in magnanimity and clemency of soul, and especially in piety—should be preferred to this young King. None of those kings ever dared to enter Italy. Indeed, I would venture to say of him what I believe **Virgil** said of Octavian: *Greater virtue reigned in a small body* <note>original: "Maior in exiguo regnabat corpore virtus"</note>. For the incredible fame of his victories surely shook all of Europe and even reached Asia with fear and wonder. Thus even **Bajazet**, the Emperor of the Turks, began to contemplate war. This most excellent King was certainly to be commended with all manner of wonderful praises." 

Thus far the words of Jacopo Bergomensis. Although in this matter he wrote the truth about King Charles—being compelled by the facts just as **Balaam was by the angel** <note>A reference to the biblical story where Balaam is forced by divine intervention to speak the truth against his original intent</note>—nevertheless, in many other histories concerning the Kings of the Gauls (if not all of them), he spoke so falsely that he seems no less defiled by errors and lies than a leopard is by its spots. Indeed, he is found to be contradictory to himself in many places. 

For instance, as was mentioned above, he claims the victory at the little village of **Fornovo** <note>original: "furnouum rusculum"</note> belonged to the Venetian leaders. Yet elsewhere he says: "Even if the victory is credited to the Frenchman, it was nonetheless a bloody one." This man, along with **Battista Mantovano** and **Sabellicus**, felt so poorly toward the achievements of the French that he should not only be denied the name of "historian," but should not even be called a "poet." Instead, he should be called a <term>Zoilus</term> <note>A "Zoilus" is a term for a harsh, spiteful, or pedantic critic, named after a Greek grammarian who famously nitpicked the works of Homer.</note>, a stranger to the true duty of a poet. 

<margin>On King Louis XII.</margin>
Furthermore, let us hear what he said concerning **Louis XII**, the most Christian King of the Gauls at the present time. In the aforementioned book, where he speaks of the battle of Charles VIII against the Bretons at **Saint-Aubin** <note>The Battle of Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier (1488)</note>, he says: "When **Francis, Duke of Brittany**, had called the **Duke of Orleans** and the **Prince of Orange**, his subjects and barons, to his side, he [the King] sent his commander **Jacques Galiot** <note>original: "Iacobū galeoti"</note> against the same Duke of Brittany with a large force. They fought a great and bitter battle between them, in which about six thousand men were killed on both sides."

<column-break/>

<margin>An error of Bergomensis.</margin>
"...Among whom the commander Jacques himself, though the victor, fell slain. When the Duke of Brittany saw himself defeated, he escaped by flight so as not to fall into the hands of the enemy. However, the Duke of Orleans and the Prince of Orange were captured and brought to the King; and he immediately ordered the Duke of Orleans, named Charles, to be beheaded by a centurion. After his death, peace followed at once." Thus says Jacopo Bergomensis. 

Nothing is further from the truth than this lie. And so that he might further corroborate this same lie, he says a little later: "**Louis, Duke of Orleans**, having succeeded to the kingdom without much difficulty this year after **Charles, King of the French**, died without any children, has reigned for five years until the present. This man had as his father the first Duke Charles, whom the same King Charles, his predecessor, had ordered to be struck with the axe after being captured, on account of the mark of conspiracy and rebellion and the violation of public trust." 

These are the words of Jacopo himself. He heaps these and six hundred other ridiculous follies upon the French—this man who is said to have written a *Supplement to the Supplement*, not of histories, but of fables. He is a most foolish man (were he not initiated into holy orders), who knows no sound other than that of bells or drums. It would seem vain and utterly stupid to respond to every single one of his insanities, which are even more inconsistent than what came before. 

I do not think he has read—or at least if he did read it, he did not hold it well in his memory—that precept of **Horace**: 

<margin>Horace, *On the Art of Poetry*</margin>
*Choose a subject, you who write, that is equal to your strength; and consider long what your shoulders refuse to bear and what they are able to carry.* <note>original: "Sumite materiam vestris qui scribitis equam Viribus: et versate diu quid ferre recusent: Quid valeant humeri."</note> 

Nor has he sufficiently pored over the annals of ancient or even recent writers which contain the pure truth, free from all flattery. This Jacopo put into writing that **Charles, Duke of Orleans** (the father of this current King Louis), was captured by Charles VIII along with the Prince of Orange, and that the King had ordered him to be executed. What could be further from the truth than this error? What could be closer to a falsehood? 

For the Duke Charles of Orleans, the father of this Louis, had departed this life many years before that war—indeed, even before the coronation of King Charles VIII. Furthermore, his son Louis, having been elevated to the throne, ordered his father’s body to be exhumed in the year of our Lord 1506 and carried to **Paris** in a funeral procession; and there, in the **Convent of the Celestines**, he had him buried in the chapel where his ancestors had chosen their place of burial. Not...

He argues that Louis's father had actually died years prior to the events described, proving his point by citing the 1506 reburial of the Duke of Orleans.</summary>

### Trophies of the Gauls

Therefore, it is hardly surprising if he erred in most things, since he has fallen here into a most manifest error. It is not surprising, I say, that that deluded man spewed his venom against us; for out of an innate weakness of mind, he followed **Marcantonio Sabellico**, **Battista Mantuanus**, and other minor Italian writers. These men, moved partly by spite and envy, and partly corrupted by money (which all things obey), lash out at the Gauls in their writings. Out of a certain perversity of soul and empty glory, they despise, blame, and scorn all those ancient and illustrious Gauls whose memory has been celebrated with the highest praise and veneration throughout all ages; they do so with a certain wild and immense insolence. As if holding the wheel of fortune in their hands, they turn and twist everything up and down, dragging it to their own judgment. 

But it is not surprising that they think ill of other nations or disparage them, since (as is known to everyone) they attack one another not only with words and writings, but even with arms. For there is an innate desire among Italians for disparaging and slandering, 
<margin>The envy of Italian writers</margin>
which is bred and grows within them. To set others aside and speak only of the learned: did not **Sallust** <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus (86–34 BCE), a Roman historian</note> lash out against **Marcus Cicero** in his writings, of which his invectives still exist? Did not the famous **Lorenzo Valla** <note>A leading Italian humanist (1407–1457) famous for his biting critiques</note> testify that **Priscian**, **Donatus**, **Servius**, **Nonius Marcellus**, **Pompeius Festus**, **Varro**, **Aristotle**, **Cicero**, **Livy**, **Sallust**, **Lactantius**, and other authors of the Latin language were neither elegant nor correct in their use of words in many places? He even disapproved of **Saint Jerome**, asserting that many things in the Holy Scriptures were wrongly translated by him into Latin. He even claimed that **Blessed Augustine** did not think correctly regarding fate, the Trinity, and divine providence. 

Did not a certain **Merula** write against **Galeotto**, and vice-versa? Did not **Poggio the Florentine** <note>Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459)</note> write against Valla, and vice-versa? And among the theologians, did not **Pico della Mirandola** lash out at a certain brother of the Dominican Order, and that same man against Pico? Did not **Lucio Bellanti** also attack Pico? Among the physicians, did not **Giacomo da Forlì** write against **Gentile da Foligno**? **Ugo of Siena** against Giacomo da Forlì? **Sermoneta** against Ugo and Giacomo? Did not **Giovanni Ercolano** write against the same, asserting that Ugo and Giacomo did not even know how to prepare a single enema or clyster <note>A medical procedure for injecting fluid into the lower bowel</note>? And among more recent doctors, the one who wrote the *Greater Light* <note>original: "Lumen Maius," a pharmaceutical text by Quirico de Augustis</note> calls the author of the *Apothecaries’ Light* a "non-illuminating light," a "badly-shining light," and a "shadowed light." And **Zerbi** <note>Gabriele de Zerbis (1445–1505)</note> criticized many others.

<column-break/>

It is therefore not at all surprising if they lash out at foreign nations and, with their "dog-like teeth" <note>An idiom for biting or snarling criticism</note> turned to madness, petulantly tear them apart and blame them, since they provoke one another with insults and disagree so greatly among themselves. 

In our own times in Paris, we saw a certain **Girolamo Balbi** <note>An Italian humanist teacher (c. 1450–1535) known for his quarrelsome nature</note> stuttering and chattering against **Fausto** <note>Publio Fausto Andrelini, a court poet to the French kings</note> and **Guillaume Tardif** so much that he stirred up and disturbed the entire University with his talkativeness, like a magpie. Having finally incurred a mark of infamy, he was forced (as they say) to leave without saying goodbye to his host; he betook himself to the English (whom the poet **Virgil** asserts are "Britons entirely divided from the whole world"). 
<margin>Virgil</margin>
For these are the men who abuse the free gifts of God, being of that number of whom **Battista Mantuanus** himself says in his book against poets who speak shamelessly:
> There are those to whom the eloquent 
> golden vein of a poet is given; 
> But it falls into filth 
> and is infected with mud.

But it is rather more surprising regarding this same **Battista Mantuanus**—a man of religious profession, initiated into sacred orders, and by far the most learned prince of poets of our age. He has always been held in the highest estimation by all, both the learned and those distinguished by exceptional virtue, because of his volumes filled with singular learning. Yet, having cast aside the truth for the sake of some prince's favor, he turned his mind to writing a short work titled *A Trophy for the Expulsion of the Gauls* <note>original: "Tropheum pro gallis expulsis," celebrating the retreat of Charles VIII from Italy in 1495</note>. It is most full of the most evident lies and fictions, containing nothing or at least very little of the truth. This brought no small disgrace upon him; indeed, it is said to have inflicted a significant stain both on his other works and on his good reputation (than which nothing is more excellent). 

This is much like what many tell of **Albert the Great** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a famous scholar-saint</note>, easily the prince of theologians of his time: because of a small work commonly called *On the Secrets of Women*, he is said to have contracted no small infamy, even though he wrote many volumes of the most exquisite doctrine. But enough of these things. It remains for me to bring forward the testimony of certain man of letters who celebrate the King in their poems.

Bound his empire by the ocean and dwell among the stars.

### An epitaph for the same King Charles by Publius Faustus Andrelinus of Forlì, Royal Poet Laureate.

Whoever you are, O Prince, do not trust in a powerful scepter;
In this way or another, death comes to all equally.
Behold, here lies Charles: to whom conquered Britain yielded,
And Naples was captured along with its ancestral soil.
He who flooded the Insubrian <note>Lombard (Milanese)</note> fields with Latin blood,

He who received the fugitive king from the English domain,
And gave him the scepter won by a victorious cohort <note>A reference to Charles VIII supporting Henry VII's claim to the English throne.</note>.

<column-break/>

While terror and love stood firm in all regions.
He always waged victorious wars on the appointed day:
Such was the strength in his magnanimous breast.
The Iberian <note>Spanish</note> ruler owed as much to his noble mind,
To whom he returned fortified towns with no fear <note>Refers to the Treaty of Barcelona (1493), where Charles returned Cerdanya and Roussillon to Spain to secure neutrality.</note>.

Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, known for his piety.</note> was not better in steadfast religion.
Did the palms of Augustus pour forth more gifts?
Gifts that testify to a magnanimous leader.
While he strives to adorn his kingdoms with a learned assembly,
And to place holy fathers in every sacred house;
While he seeks to relieve the people oppressed by excessive tribute,
And to perform more splendid deeds with an invincible hand,
He dies, cut off and extinguished in his prime—
Alas, sudden death envied such a great leader.
But new glory compensates for an untimely death;
His illustrious deeds surpass the final funeral pyre.
