Neither gold, nor lineage helps; neither beauty, nor age,
Nor the imperial peak of kings over their people.
Death dissolves all things; nor do the fates allow anyone
To resist death; yield to the fates: life is nothing.

### Another by the same author on the same king:

Religion, goodness, spirit, generosity, justice:

<margin>D</margin>
Now something must be said of Louis XII, the most Christian King of the French: yet we shall say less than his virtue deserves. He is the greatest cultivator of justice among all kings, and most observant of equity; of admirable clemency and urbanity. With admirable virtue and success, he magnificently enlarged the kingdom of the Gauls. Endowed with a subtle genius and outstanding eloquence and modesty, he now happily moderates the scepters of the realm among his people. He strives to preserve his people in tranquility more than others who held the scepter of the kingdom before him. He relieved them of the heavy burden of tributes and other impositions by which they were previously pressed. He used the greatest piety and prudence toward his subjects and all other matters concerning the state of the commonwealth. The wisdom of his mind, his counsel, and his other virtues are an object of admiration to all, so much so that it is very difficult to judge in which of them he excels, or for which he deserves greater praise. He is also a great lover of good letters, and most observant of learned men, and most greedy for books, like Ptolemy Philadelphus <note>A King of Egypt (3rd century BCE) famous for the Library of Alexandria.</note>, who placed Demetrius of Phaleron over his library, handing him a large sum of money so that from all sides for the king's library he might buy...

He gathered books by either purchasing or transcribing them. And when he <note>Referring to Ptolemy II Philadelphus, the famous King of Egypt and patron of the Library of Alexandria.</note> asked how many books were already in the libraries, he replied: more than two hundred thousand, but he believed that in a short time the number could reach five hundred thousand. # The Preparations of the Genoese

### ¶ Benedictus Portuensis to the distinguished man Bartolomeo Giustiniani, regarding the arrival of the most serene Louis XII, King of the French, into the city of Genoa.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' featuring floral and leafy motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc> It is a well-established fact that many great and excellent men have often been seen in our city: the most famous princes of lands, dukes, kings, emperors, and supreme pontiffs. Many sights worthy of memory have also been seen. However, I find no record that any King of the French was ever in Genoa at any time—a fact which no one would have either seen or read about until these recent days—with the possible exception of that Louis <note>Referring to Louis IX, known as Saint Louis (ruled 1226–1270), who stopped in Genoa during the Crusades and was later canonized as a saint.</note> whom we worship, as some prefer, because of the holiness of his life. Therefore, since after so many centuries have passed, the new and admirable sight of Louis XII, King of the French, the most glorious of all who came before him, has shone before our eyes, I thought I would be relating a truly pleasant memory if I were to write down his most happy arrival into this city. At the same time, I will show with what preparation, what zeal, and what affection the city welcomed and honored its revered king. Although I know I cannot offer or promise any oratorical ornament that might delight the minds of readers, perhaps the novelty of the subject itself and the presence of our most pleasant prince in this account will be of help. Therefore, to you, Bartolomeo Giustiniani <note>A member of the prominent Giustiniani family of Genoa, often involved in the administration of the Aegean islands and Corsica.</note>, most kind man—who, being absent at that time in your most worthy governorship of Corsica, which you administered for so many months with great praise, missed that spectacle—and who, given your great learning, always desire to learn everything, I have decided to dedicate this little gift of mine. This is so that you may see for yourself in its proper order what you perhaps learned less coherently from elsewhere. Farewell.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' featuring floral and leafy motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc> It was the third year since Louis XII, King of the French, had conquered the Principality of Milan by force of arms—a territory he claimed was owed to him by hereditary right through his father's line. He first drove out, then captured and brought to France Duke Ludovico Sforza <note>Ludovico "Il Moro" Sforza (1452–1508), the Duke of Milan who was famously captured by the French in 1500.</note>. The entire Genoese dominion was also taken into his power through a free and spontaneous surrender. Two years later, he also acquired the Kingdom of Naples after 

<column-break/>

King Frederick <note>Frederick of Naples, who was deposed in 1501 during the Second Italian War.</note> yielded, which, according to a treaty, was to be shared with Ferdinand and Isabella, the monarchs of Spain. In the division of the kingdom, a contention seemed to arise between the Spaniards and the French, and because of this, they came to arms, which was the origin of the war that followed. At that time, Cesare Borgia <note>Cesare Borgia (1475–1507), the son of Pope Alexander VI, whose military campaigns across Italy were legendary for their ambition and ruthlessness.</note>, the Duke of Valentinois and son of the Supreme Pontiff Alexander, held a powerful army in Italy, and it was not easily apparent toward which side he would lean. However, the constant opinion of all was that victory would be wherever the Duke attached himself. For he had prepared a great name and empire for himself, having conquered almost all the rulers in Flaminia, Piceno, and Tuscany. And while he was pondering greater things in his mind, having entered the territory of Florence, he had compelled the city of Florence itself to change <note>A reference to the political instability in Florence where the French and Borgia interests often clashed with the local republican government and the exiled Medici family.</note>, with the members of the Medici faction, who were exiles, following him. That matter indeed seemed to be of great importance (as it was), and it was believed that it could bring no small risk to the quiet state of the King's affairs. In this agitation of things, therefore, the most prudent King came into Italy. Having sent an army ahead into Naples—which he thought was sufficient to resist the enemy—he himself stayed for some days in Milan and Pavia. There, by his wisdom, having settled the affairs of Florence in a very short time, he drew to himself the Duke of Valentinois himself, whom some thought had been alienated from friendship with the French. He held him with him for several days in great favor and esteem. After this, being now secure about the affairs of Italy, he decided to complete the journey he had long intended to visit the city of Genoa. When this became known in Genoa, a decree of the Senate was made that the royal arrival should be celebrated with the greatest possible honor. Therefore, twelve leading men were chosen from the city, to whom the entire care of honoring the royal arrival was committed. These men first of all arranged for the necessary money; to ensure it was provided quickly, the credit of the Bank of Saint George <term>magistratus sancti georgij: The Bank of Saint George, a powerful financial institution in Genoa that often funded the state's public works and diplomatic missions.</term> intervened with a huge consensus of votes. Then, since they had decided that ambassadors should be sent to the King to congratulate him in the name of the Republic on his arrival into Italy and to invite him to visit their city as he had already promised, it pleased the Senate that ambassadors be appointed by them. These were four: Brizio Giustiniani, Paolo Fieschi, Bartolomeo Ceva, and Gerolamo Doria. Brizio and Gerolamo were senators at that time. Paolo was one of the Twelve <note>original: "duodecimum" - referring to the Council of Twelve, a high-ranking executive body in the Genoese government.</note>. Thus, while they were detained either by public business or by preparing and equipping themselves to carry out the duty of the embassy, a period of many days slipped by. Furthermore, because of the longer delay, it happened that this embassy [arrived] at a less opportune time...

# The Preparations of the Genoese

...it seemed it could be resolved. The task of performing this duty was given by letter to the famous interpreter of law, Domenico Spinola <note>original: "dominico spinule"</note>, who for another cause had long been serving as an ambassador to the kings. Meanwhile, news arrived that the king’s arrival was being hastened, and the necessary things in Genoa were prepared with the greatest zeal. Nothing stirred the minds of the citizens more than the shortage of fodder; in this sterile region, it seemed most difficult to provide for as many horses as were said to be coming. However, as was later discovered, not so great a number of horses actually reached Genoa, and a larger supply of fodder and other necessities was provided.

Now the day was approaching on which the king was to depart from Pavia. Therefore, four men were chosen by the Twelve <note>The "Twelve" refers to the ruling council of the city</note> from every rank of the city: Andrea Ciceri, Bartolomeo Senarega <note>original: "cena"</note>, Agostino Doria <note>original: "auria"</note>, and Franco Fieschi <note>original: "fliscus"</note>. These were to travel as far as Tortona to greet and honor the king in the name of the public. Groups of youths, which they call "societies" <note>The *societates*, or festive youth brigades often organized for civic ceremonies</note>, were also prepared, each one to go out to meet him as far as they were commanded.

Lodgings and houses were prepared throughout the city to receive the king and the royal retinue; these were distributed among the families and other ranks of the city, as was the ancestral custom. Many stables for horses were constructed, so that in this maritime city, where they are rare and very narrow, there would be no lack of space for stalling the horses and the rest of the king's pack animals. Everywhere the roads within and without the city were restored. The Carignano hill <note>original: "Cliuus carinianis"</note>, which leads to the Church of the Inviolate <note>The church of Santa Maria in Passione, likely</note>, where the king was to be lodged, was not only paved from bottom to top but also widened where it had been narrow. The road from the Gate of Saint Thomas to the lighthouse tower <note>The Lanterna, Genoa's famous lighthouse</note> was paved with flint and brick. The palace was also painted all around with lilies <note>The fleur-de-lis, the heraldic symbol of the French monarchy</note> and other royal insignia, as it is seen now. In short, no diligence was omitted to celebrate the arrival of such a great king.

While these things were being done by the citizens, Philip of Ravenstein <note>Philip of Cleves, Lord of Ravenstein, the French-appointed governor of Genoa</note>, the prince who then presided over the city of Genoa, arrived from Pavia at full gallop. He announced that the king would have departed from the Ticino <note>Pavia</note> before the appointed day, had he not decided to attend a duel which was to take place on the following Sunday between two Mantuan cousins of the Gonzaga family. But he assured them that the king would undoubtedly begin his journey the day after; he therefore urged that all nearby necessities be ready. Having learned what had been planned, he did not approve of sending anyone far away to meet the king; instead, on the day he was to enter the city, the Senate with the other citizens ought to proceed as far as the gravel shore <note>original: "glarea," likely referring to the Bisagno riverbed or the coastal shingle</note>. There, everyone would see the king in an open and visible

<column-break/>

place. There, each would honor their prince. This finally would please the royal majesty; other things would be less welcome and superfluous. These words of the governor ensured that the four men who were to go out to meet the king, as had been decreed, were not sent, nor was anyone else sent in the name of the public to any place beyond the designated spot before the day of arrival.

Meanwhile, the ministers who distribute the royal houses arrived, who in their language are called <term>forrerij</term> <note>From the French "fourriers," the harbingers or quartermasters responsible for arranging logistics and lodgings</note>. These men, going around through all the suburban regions of the city, inscribed the doorposts of individual houses with French signs and titles, and assigned them according as the condition of each lodging and future guest required. Although this practice was new to the eyes of the citizens and never before seen in Genoa until that time, it was nevertheless carried out by everyone not only with obedience but even with an eager desire to please and serve the king. In this, it was truly pleasant for the citizens that these same ministers performed their duty most modestly and even said that whatever lodgings they found were beautiful and acceptable to them. Thus, the care previously undertaken by the citizens in their own manner for preparing lodgings was rendered unnecessary.

While such things were being prepared in the city, some primary men went to the Senate. They proposed that, while the king delayed his arrival, they should consider those matters of the republic which ought to be discussed with him when he arrived. The advice was praised, and it was decreed that this task be entrusted to prudent men who would devise what seemed most relevant to the republic. Therefore, eight men of singular authority and prudence among the citizens were appointed: Giovanni Battista Grimaldi, Simone Bianco, Andrea Ciceri, Anfreone Usu di Mare, Ambrogio Zerbi, Nicola Spinola, Antonio Sauli, and Stefano Doria <note>original: "auria"</note>. These men, after maturely consulting among themselves, reported a few things out of many which seemed of greater weight and necessary to be explained to the king. Of these, two especially concerned the city. One was the Spanish trade, which is most necessary to the Genoese, and which it seemed would be prohibited in many and various ways by the imminent war. The other was the term of the magistrates' jurisdiction, being longer than the laws of the city permit. Therefore, they decided to deal with the king chiefly regarding these matters.

The royal arrival was approaching, and now a large part of the courtiers had arrived, for all of whom lodgings were open; these were recognized by the signs on the gates which we mentioned were inscribed above. It was sufficiently clear from the letters of Bartolomeo Senarega, then performing the public embassy at the royal court, that the king himself—the eleventh day before the Kalends of September <note>August 22nd</note> having already passed from Pa[via]...

### The Preparations of the Genoese

...that [the King] had departed from Pavia; and that he would be five days on the journey, three of which had already passed when Bartholomew’s letters <note>Bartholomew Senarega, the author and chronicler</note> were read aloud. Meanwhile, the Cardinal of Rouen <note>original: "Cardinalis rhoromagensis"; Georges d'Amboise, the King’s chief minister and a powerful figure in the French court</note>, who held supreme authority with the King, preceded the royal arrival and entered the city. He was accompanied by the president and a long line of senators and citizens, and was lodged in Carignano at the Church of the Virgin. On the following day, when the King was to enter, all the magistrates and citizens of every rank, as well as crowds of young men, were ordered—at the signal of the bell—to gather in the palace square so that they might proceed with the Senate to meet the King. 

The Twelve <note>The council of twelve citizens governing the city's affairs</note> came into the Senate and asked what their place would be in the procession. They had intended in their minds that the place immediately following the Senate was owed to them. The Senate replied to the Twelve that their place would be after the Treasury officials—the office which is called the Common Mint <note>original: "monete cōmunis"</note>. They took this answer poorly, complaining that they were being treated unjustly, relying on examples from former times that were irrelevant; finally, they said they would only go if they preceded the Treasury officials. Indeed, it was not the authority of the magistracy—which was only for that time and for one single purpose—that caused this dispute, but rather the private dignity of the men themselves. For in that number were Knights of the Golden Spur <note>original: "aurati equites"</note> and patricians, men who were considered the leaders of their respective orders in the city without controversy. The Senate, however, persisted in its decision so as not to detract from the dignity of a most ancient magistracy of venerable authority.

The King had spent the night in the small town which the common people call Borgo Fornari <note>original: "Burgum furnariorum"</note>, fifteen miles distant from this city. Departing from there at dawn and crossing the mountain pass, he descended into the Polcevera valley and turned aside to the villa of the late, most distinguished citizen Lazzaro Doria <note>original: "Lazari aurie"</note> in the fields. There he dined at a lavish and splendid banquet prepared by the brothers Stefano and Girolamo. That day was Friday, the 26th of August <note>original: "vij. kal. septembris"</note>, in the year 1502 after the life-giving birth of Christ our God. The whole city was crowded and poured out in honor of the King; the shops were closed, the streets were strewn with green branches, and the walls of the houses were adorned with hangings and tapestries draped everywhere. Women were stationed in the streets and porticos, dressed in precious robes, gems, large pearls, and necklaces. The temples resounded with the sound of bells, the ships in the harbor and the fortress of Castelletto itself with the blare of trumpets and the roar of cannons. The palace also joined in with banners raised. Finally, every part of the city displayed signs of immense joy. Everywhere it was a festive day, everywhere it was

<column-break/>

celebrated with solemnity. But the Senate and the rest of the citizens and the crowds of young men, dressed in silk robes, exited the palace around midday. They met the King at the gravel banks of the Polcevera. As soon as they saw him coming, they dismounted from their horses and, bowing down with their knees to the ground, they saluted their prince with veneration. Then Brizio Giustiniani <note>original: "Brixius iustinianus"</note>, the head of the Senate, spoke: 

<margin>The Speech</margin> "Most glorious King, we, the most faithful servants of your Majesty, receive you with such veneration and eagerness of soul that no other could be greater, truer, or more sincere. We rejoice indeed on our own behalf and on behalf of the whole city, which we now represent, to behold your most serene face, which we contemplate as if it were a divinity sent down from heaven. We give thanks to your immense kindness and clemency, which has deigned to come to visit your Genoese people among these rocks and crags. The entire city congratulates you; everyone rejoices, men and women alike; the very walls themselves exult, as you will soon see, at your most longed-for arrival. We shall mark this most happy day with a white stone <note>A classical idiom for a lucky or memorable day</note> and record it in our archives. Receive, therefore, O most illustrious of kings, a people most devoted to you, who with the most constant hearts are ready to pour out not only all their resources and strength, however small they may be, but even their sons, their very lives, and their blood for the glory of your name."

The King, with a cheerful expression and having given his right hand, ordered them all to rise. Together, they took up the journey toward the city on horseback. The senators, hastening their journey a little, arrived at the Gate of Saint Thomas. There they awaited the King at the entrance to the city itself under a canopy of gold and crimson silk, which bore his colors, namely red and yellow <note>original: "rubri scilicet croceiq; coloris"</note>; there they received him. And so, in succession through fixed intervals of space, the citizens were arranged to take turns carrying the canopy. 

The order of the citizens processing was as follows: the groups of young men went first, all of them a sight to behold, and the younger ones were first, dressed in half-French garments <note>original: "vestibus semigallicis"; likely referring to a fashion style blending local and French trends</note>. These were followed by others of a slightly older age, dressed in different clothing. Thus the rest of the youths followed by age groups. Then came the older men, after them the magistrates, and finally the senators themselves. Truly, the spectacle of the city that day was beautiful. But as for which nobles and leading men, both Italian and French, accompanied the King in that entry into the city, and in what order they walked, it could not easily be discerned in the thick and dense multitude. However, among the many who then came to Genoa, the more noble are: the Duke of Valentinois <note>Cesare Borgia</note>, the Marquess of Montferrat, the Marquess of Saluzzo, and Gian Giacomo Trivulzio <note>original: "Johannes iacobus triultius"; a famous Italian condottiero in French service</note>...

### The Preparations of the Genoese

...and the Marquis of Vigevano <note>original: "Marchio viglebii"; Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, a celebrated Italian general in French service</note> himself; and François the Marshal. These four were Italians. From the French, however, were Philippe of Ravenstein <note>original: "Philippus rauẽstein"; Philippe de Clèves, the Governor of Genoa and the King's cousin</note>, Lord Governor of Genoa; the Marshal of Gié <note>Pierre de Rohan</note>; the Lord of Dunes; the Lord of Ligny; the Lord of La Trémoille; the Lord of Chaumont, Great Master of the royal household; the Vidame; and the Lord of Ravel, nephew of the Cardinal of Rouen—and both of these were commanders of the nobility. Also present were the Infante of Navarre; Rainier, Duke of Albany; and the Bastard of Savoy <note>René of Savoy</note>. There were, furthermore, ambassadors from the Emperor, the Venetians, and the Florentines, as well as many other nobles. All of these, or many of them, preceded the King as he entered that day.

Federico, the former King of Naples <note>Federico d'Aragona, who had been deposed by Louis XII a year earlier</note>, had also intended to come; his lodging had already been prepared for him at Carignano in the villa of the most illustrious citizen Antonio Sauli, but a painful condition in his feet <note>original: "aduersa pedum valitudo"; likely gout</note> prevented him. However, several members of his household set out for this place. Shortly after the King's departure, Federico's wife also arrived; having stayed here for a few days, she set out to join her husband in France. The Duke of Ferrara, the Marquis of Mantua, and others turned back, either deterred by the roughness of the road or because they would have been hemmed in by the crowds at Genoa.

Now is the moment where you might look upon the distinguished King, carried on a white horse and dressed in a golden cloak <note>original: "chlamyde"; a formal mantle</note>, surrounded only by footmen carrying French weapons in their hands. He was joyful wherever he passed, greeting everyone most kindly, even with his head uncovered. From the children and the rest of the crowd, the cry went up everywhere: "France! France!" and "Long live the King!" Following him were the Cardinals: Giuliano of San Pietro in Vincoli <note>Giuliano della Rovere, the future Pope Julius II</note>, Raffaele of San Giorgio, and Federico Sanseverino; and Cesare Borgia, Duke of Valentinois. Immediately following them were four hundred mounted archers chosen for the King's guard. They were all of nearly the same age, dressed in a single distinguished royal uniform, carrying bows and quivers; they presented a most beautiful sight.

When they arrived at the Temple of Saint Lawrence <note>San Lorenzo, the Cathedral of Genoa</note>, the clergy and priests were ready, holding sacred objects in their hands. They were supposed to meet the King at the city gate according to custom, but because of the immense multitude of people rushing together, they had been ordered to wait there. As soon as they saw the King dismounting, they went to meet him. After the King had kissed the True Cross from the hands of the bishop, he proceeded to the high altar, which was adorned with the most celebrated signs and statues of the saints. Having poured out his prayers, he mounted his horse again as the day was waning and proceeded to Carignano, leaving behind all the citizens in the palace square as had been decreed.

<column-break/>

The King himself, along with the Duke of Valentinois and other leading men, entered the palace prepared with royal luxury and magnificence in Carignano, next to the Temple of the Inviolate Mary <note>original: "inuiolate Marie templum"; Santa Maria in Via Lata</note>, by the distinguished man and head of his family, Giovanni Ludovico Fieschi <note>original: "Iohāne Ludouico flisco"</note>, who had devoted many days of work to this with the greatest zeal. All the other houses of Carignano were occupied by the King's courtiers. Night had now arrived, and the whole city glittered with lights; the festive displays surpassed the night itself. Clanging bells and the voices of people rejoicing were heard everywhere. Moreover, the villas all around showed signs of great joy by lighting bonfires. The magistrates ordered the same to be done for the entire following three days.

At dawn the next day, the King set out for the Temple of Holy Mary of the Castle; once the sacrifice <note>The Mass</note> was completed, he returned to Carignano, where the rest of the day was given either to rest or to necessary business. For access to the royal court was open to few besides the members of the household. On the following Sunday, he visited the fortress of Castelletto; having dined there and stayed not long, he returned to Carignano. Immediately, the senators and other primary citizens set out there for the sake of showing their respect; they were received by him in a very kind and refined manner. After they had respectfully performed the duty of greeting him, Giacomo Forno <note>original: "Iacobus furnius"</note>, a legal expert learned not only in Latin but also exceptionally in Greek, delivered this most elegant speech, having been delegated this task:

### On Kingship

Whether by hereditary succession or by legitimate election—such as yours is, most Christian and therefore invincible King—if a reign is obtained (even if by other means, provided it is not unjust), it is the greatest of all things among the people of the world. No one who considers the matter can doubt that it is better and more advantageous than popular rule, the rule of the elite <note>original: "optimatum imperium"; aristocracy</note>, tyranny, or the power of a few. For anyone who reflects on the substance of God knows that He is not only one, but necessarily one, and there cannot be more; since He alone is the maker and ruler of the whole world, no other type of governance from all those mentioned above approaches Him more closely or can be more similar than the rule of one, which we call a monarchy or a kingdom. Added to this is the fact that in the rule of one, even if only moderately established, no discord or disagreement need be feared. All these things must frequently happen in other modes of command, as the leaders themselves argue among one another, while they either envy each other or each tries to seize for himself alone the glory or profit, if there be any in leadership. Homer, noticing this—whether seized by poetic fury or (as I would rather believe...

# The Preparations of the Genoese

...[it must be noted] that, moved by a certain divine power, he introduces Agamemnon speaking in harmony: *It is not good for many to rule; let there be one king.* <note>original: "Non multos regnare bonum est: rex imperet vnus"; a famous quote from Homer's Iliad (Book 2) often used in the Renaissance to justify absolute monarchy.</note> Since, therefore, the kingdom of one man is of such a nature and greatness as has been demonstrated, it is fitting that the king be equal to such a kingdom—indeed, even much greater. For every moved thing is inferior in power to its mover. To those who argue otherwise, it must necessarily follow that the king will be unequal to bearing the burdens of his kingdom: either the kingdom will eventually oppose and overthrow him, or he himself, laboring under the mass of the kingdom as if under an unjust bundle and an unfair weight, will be crushed and ground down. Therefore, a king is greater and more powerful than his kingdom.

But as for you, King Louis—not to compare you with your ancestors, all of whom you have surpassed and left behind by vast intervals—you shine forth and excel beyond the greatest kings of all ages in the clarity of your name, your splendor, the glory of your deeds, your skill in military affairs, your fortitude, prudence, faith, piety, justice, gravity, constancy, gentleness, clemency, and other royal virtues. You excel as much as the height of royal fortune stands apart from other private men. If I, a most speechless man, should dare to select and pursue even the smallest particle of your innumerable and inaccessible virtues, I fear that what happens to eyes straining to look at the sun would happen to me. Just as their ability to see is taken away by the sharp glare, so too does the veneration I feel repel me at the very entrance as I approach more closely and inquire more curiously.

Nor indeed am I so stupid, or so lazy, nor of such a dull heart, that I do not sense the nature and scale of your empire, or who and how great you are yourself—all of which are the greatest of things, and more than the greatest, as has already been sufficiently proven above. Let others speak who have drunk more deeply of the Castalian spring <note>Castalian spring: a spring on Mount Parnassus in Greece, sacred to the Muses; drinking from it was said to grant poetic inspiration.</note>, those upon whom the Muses smiled more sweetly at birth, and those to whom it was given to be able to sound the Meonian trumpet <note>original: "meonia... tuba"; a reference to Homer, who was sometimes called the "Meonian" poet, meaning a grand epic style of writing.</note> for the noble deeds of famous leaders. Let them tell how great you rise against the enemy, whether you choose to go on foot or dig spurs into the flanks of a foaming horse and hurl the spear with strong arms. You are the first to enter the fray and the last to set aside the war. You perform all the duties of a strenuous soldier and the best commander; no one chooses a camp location better than you. Let them recount in you alone all the virtues of Philopoemen <note>Philopoemen: a Greek general (c. 253–183 BC) known as "the last of the Greeks," celebrated for his tactical genius and personal austerity.</note>.

<column-break/>

Let there be no nation so remote, no people so separated, no corner of the earth so hidden or inaccessible that they do not carry within them the terror of your arms. Let them extol as they wish the strength, ferocity, and number of your soldiers and legions. Let them proclaim, sing, and celebrate your innumerable victories won from the enemy.

May you be greater than Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Great: founder of the Persian Empire, famously cited by ancient and Renaissance authors as a model of the "cured" or merciful conqueror.</note> in how most mercifully you have spared some of your enemies. To others who preferred to surrender and submit themselves to your kindness, gentleness, clemency, and faith rather than experience the insuperable strength of your fortitude, you left the royal name and granted royal ornaments and expenses—may you be held greater than Alexander. Many indeed are honored by you, but few are trusted; thus you rule stably and safely. No nation among so many fierce and unbridled ones bordering your kingdom may stir against you, thanks to the firmest fortifications of your power and the strongest garrisons of your borders.

Indeed, let this rather be credited to your love and your character, through which you have already achieved this: that you are believed to have rendered the kingdom not only safe, but secure. Your flanks are not only enclosed, fortified, girded, hedged, and surrounded by the most faithful soldiers, most devoted attendants, and incorruptible guards, but also by counts, marquises, dukes, kings, and cardinals—who are themselves also judged worthy of royal dignity. This is attributed to their more inclined love and anxious benevolence toward you.

Let others write of you as secure at home and intrepid abroad—to all people everywhere you are one to be feared, roused by the mere fame of your arrival. Tumults are settled, wars are composed, arms are laid down; you yourself bring and speak the laws of peace. You recall the severed friendships of peoples and nations into their former harmony; you lead them back into ancient grace. You persuade everyone toward peace and quiet, while you yourself are always restless so that you may prepare rest for your subjects and friends. It is debated whether you excel more in the arts of peace or war, when in both matters you are the most outstanding, best, and greatest.

I say, let others speak of these and other gifts, and I wish they would speak in a manner worthy of the dignity, sublimity, and highness of your majesty! I myself have decided not to attempt those things at all, freely, ingenuously, and openly confessing my humility and weakness. For you are greater than can be proclaimed now by this narrow mouth. I will, however, compensate you for this injury, O King: though I myself say nothing of you that is worth reading, I shall certainly provide the materials for what they may read. From me, the argument...

# The Preparations of the Genoese

...and the Marquis of Vigevano <note>Gian Giacomo Trivulzio, a prominent Italian condottiero in French service</note> himself: and a Marshal of France. These four were Italians. Among the French, however, were Philip of Ravenstein, the Governor of Genoa and the King’s cousin; the Marshal of Gié; the Lord of Dunois; the Lord of Ligny; the Lord of La Trémoille; the Lord of Chaumont, the Grand Master of the Royal Household; the Lord Vidame; and the Lord of Revel, the nephew of the Cardinal of Rouen. Both of these latter men were commanders of the nobility. Also present were the Prince <term>Infans</term> <note>A title for a royal prince of Spain or Portugal</note> of Navarre; the Duke of Albany; René, the Bastard of Savoy; and furthermore, legates of the Emperor, the Venetians, and the Florentines, as well as many other nobles. All of these, or at least many of them, preceded the King as he made his entrance that day. Federico, formerly the King of Naples <note>Frederick of Aragon, who had been deposed by Louis XII and Ferdinand of Aragon</note>, had also intended to come with them, and a lodging had already been prepared for him at Carignano in the villa of the most distinguished citizen, Antonio Sauli; but the poor health of his feet <note>original: "aduersa pedum valitudo"; likely a reference to gout</note> prevented him. Nevertheless, some members of his household set out for this place. Shortly after the King’s departure, Federico’s wife also arrived; she stayed here for a few days and then set out for her husband in France. The Duke of Ferrara, the Marquis of Mantua, and others turned back, either terrified by the roughness of the road or because they had already been to Genoa quite often. 

Now is the place where you might behold the distinguished King, carried on a white horse and clothed in a golden cloak, surrounded only by footmen carrying out French deeds <note>likely referring to the King's personal guard or Swiss mercenaries</note>. He was joyful wherever he passed, and with his head even uncovered, he most kindly greeted everyone. Everywhere the children and the rest of the crowd shouted: "France! France! and long live the King!" Following him were the Cardinals: Giuliano of Saint Peter in Chains <note>Giuliano della Rovere, the future Pope Julius II</note>, Raffaele of Saint George, and Federico Sanseverino, as well as Caesar, the Duke of Valentinois <note>The infamous Cesare Borgia</note>. Following immediately after were four hundred mounted archers chosen for the King’s protection. They were all of nearly the same age, dressed in one distinguished royal uniform, carrying bows and quivers, and they presented a most beautiful sight. When they reached the Cathedral of Saint Lawrence, the clergy and priests were ready, holding sacred objects in their hands. They ought to have met the King at the city gate according to custom, but due to the immense multitude of people rushing together, they had been ordered to wait there so they might see the King as he dismounted, and they immediately went to meet him. And the King, after kissing the True Cross from the hands of the bishop, proceeded to the high altar, which was adorned with the most celebrated images and statues of the saints. After pouring out his prayers and mounting his horse again, as the day was already declining, he proceeded to go to Carignano, leaving behind all the citizens in the palace square, as had been decided. 

<column-break/>

The King himself, with the Duke of Valentinois and other princely men, entered the lodgings in Carignano—prepared with royal luxury and magnificence near the Church of the Inviolate Mary <note>The Basilica of Santa Maria Assunta</note> by that distinguished man and leader of his family, Giovanni Luigi Fieschi, who had devoted several days of labor to this with the greatest zeal. The rest of the court officials occupied all the other houses of Carignano. Now night had arrived, and the whole city glittered with lights; torches overcame the night itself. Clanging bells <note>original: "era... crepitantia"; literally "clashing bronzes"</note> and the voices of those exulting were heard everywhere. Furthermore, a thousand fires lit all around showed signs of great joy. The magistrates ordered the same to be done for the entire following three days. At the next light, the King set out for the Church of Saint Mary of the Castle; after the sacrifice was performed, he returned to Carignano, where the rest of the day was given either to rest or to necessary business. For the entrance to the royal quarters was open to few besides the household servants. On the following Sunday, he visited the fortress of the Castelletto; having dined there and not delayed long, he returned to Carignano. This is a Latin translation of a famous line from Homer’s Iliad, often used in the Middle Ages and Renaissance to justify absolute monarchy.</note> Since, therefore, the kingdom of such a great man is of the nature that has been demonstrated, it is fitting that the king be equal to his own kingdom—or rather, much greater. For everything that is moved is inferior in power to its mover. To those who decide otherwise, it will necessarily happen that the king will be unequal to bearing the burdens of his kingdom: either the kingdom itself will eventually be cast down and overturned, or he himself will be oppressed and crushed under the mass of the kingdom, as if under an unjust bundle or an uneven weight. Therefore, a king is greater and more powerful than his kingdom.

Indeed, you, King Louis—not to compare you with your ancestors, all of whom you have bypassed and left far behind in the longest of valleys—shine forth and excel so much beyond the greatest kings of all ages in the clarity of your name, the splendor and glory of your deeds, your skill in military affairs, your fortitude, prudence, faith, piety, justice, gravity, constancy, mildness, clemency, and other royal virtues. This excellence is as great as the height of royal fortune is distant from all other private men. If I, being a most speechless man <note>original: "infantissimus"; literally "unable to speak," a common trope of humility in Renaissance oratory</note>, should dare to even touch upon or follow the smallest broken-off particle of your innumerable and inaccessible virtues as a reckless praiser, I fear that what usually happens to eyes straining to look at the sun might happen to me. Just as those eyes lose their faculty of seeing due to the piercing light, so too, as I approach more closely and inquire more curiously into these things, the reverence of the subject repels me right at the very entrance.

Nor am I so stupid, or so lazy, nor am I of such a dull heart, that I do not perceive how great and of what quality your empire is, or what kind of man you are yourself. All these things have already been proven above to be the greatest, and even greater than the greatest. Let others speak—those who have drunk more deeply of the Castalian spring <note>A reference to the fountain on Mount Parnassus sacred to the Muses; it implies poetic inspiration</note>, those upon whom the Muses smiled more sweetly at birth, and those who have been granted the ability to sound the trumpet for the noble deeds of famous leaders. Let them tell how greatly you rise up against the enemy, whether you choose to go on foot or pierce the foaming flanks of a horse with spurs and hurl the spear with strong arms; how you are the first to enter the fray and the last to leave the battle. You alone perform, fulfill, and exceed all the duties of a strenuous soldier and an excellent general. No one chooses a place for a camp better than you; let them recount in you alone all the virtues of a Philopoemen <note>A famous Greek general and statesman known as "the last of the Greeks."</note>.

<column-break/>

Let there be no nation so set apart, no race so remote, no corner of the earth so hidden or inaccessible, into which they do not carry the terror of your arms. Let them extol as they please the strength, ferocity, and number of your soldiers and legions. Let them preach, sing, and celebrate your innumerable victories won from the enemy. Because you have most mercifully saved some of your enemies, you are greater than Pyrrhus <note>King of Epirus, known for his military brilliance but also his complex character.</note>. Because you have left the royal name and granted royal finery and expenses to others who preferred to trust and surrender themselves to your kindness, mildness, clemency, and faith rather than experience the insuperable strength of your fortitude, you are considered greater than Alexander <note>Alexander the Great.</note>. Because many are indeed honored by you, but few are trusted, you rule as a stable guardian.

Because no nation among so many fierce and unbridled ones bordering your kingdom is moved to action, this is ascribed to the firmest defenses of your power and the strongest protections of your borders. Or rather, let it be credited to your love and your character, by which you have now achieved this: that you are believed to have rendered the kingdom not only safe, but truly secure. Your sides are closed, fortified, surrounded, hedged, and crowded not only by most faithful soldiers, most devoted attendants, and uncorrupted bodyguards, but also by counts, marquises, dukes, kings, and cardinals, who are themselves also esteemed with royal dignity; this is attributed to their more leaning love and narrow benevolence toward you.

Let you be described by others as secure at home and intrepid abroad, but everywhere you yourself are to be feared by all, as people are stirred by the mere rumor of your arrival. Let tumults be settled, wars be composed, and arms be laid aside; you yourself bring and dictate the laws of peace. You recall the severed friendships of peoples and nations into their former concord; you lead them back to their ancient grace. You persuade all to peace and quiet while you yourself are always restless <note>original: "inquies"; meaning the King is untiring in his work for the state</note>, so that you may prepare rest for your subjects and friends. It is debated whether you excel more in the arts of peace or of war, though you are the most excellent, greatest, and best in both.

These things, I say, and innumerable others, let others tell; and I wish they would speak in a manner worthy of the dignity of your highness and the loftiness of your majesty. I myself have decided not to attempt those things at all, having freely, ingenuously, and openly confessed my own humility and weakness. For you are greater than can be sounded through this narrow mouth of mine. I will, however, compensate you for this injury, O King: if I have said nothing of myself about you that is worth reading, I will certainly provide things for others to read. This very fact—that we cannot fulfill it—is the most certain and powerful argument for your greatness. Therefore, if in any way we have not served you according to your dignity, or if our services are found to be too small, we are far from simply confessing it; we acknowledge and admit it. Good King, may you take it in good part, as you might hear similarly from God: for you do not lack for our goods. Nor should you measure our services by the scale of our resources, but rather by the measure of our devotion; so that even if we have not fulfilled what we wished to fulfill, it shall still be enough to have wished to fulfill it. We do not accuse any of those who currently perform the office; for no such thing has been commanded of us. However, we ask and pray that our most honorable and sacred laws be preserved." The eight replied in turn that it was far from their minds that any thought should be given to diminishing his authority; that they were moved not by hatred or ill-will toward anyone, but were speaking purely and sincerely, telling the truth, which looked both to the royal honor and the benefit of their republic; that he was greatly deceived if he thought such things of them; and finally, that it was not their office to accuse anyone. But since by law no one outside the senatorial order was permitted to be present for an election of this kind, except for the governor and those who record the acts of the senate, this praetor whom I named above was always present; this was seen as tolerable for the reason that the president, being ignorant of the Latin language, used him as an interpreter. Some of the senators were whispering then, however, which was later reported to the King and the Cardinal, making his case even more grave. # The Preparations of the Genoese

...now, with a broader freedom than the others, he was held as if he were one of them. Then, with the sun already setting, having returned home, he found eight men <note>Referencing the "Eight of Peace," a Genoese magistracy mentioned on the previous page.</note> waiting for him. Looking upon them with a cheerful and serene countenance, he led them into the hall. There, he graciously listened as they gave thanks for his many kindnesses. He most kindly approved the concessions that had been granted to the city regarding Spanish affairs, legal questions, the appointments of magistrates, and other matters pertaining to the republic, and he commanded them to be of good heart. 

Turning then to jokes, he most calmly recounted what he had done at the villa of Lorenzo <note>Likely the villa of Lorenzo Lomellini, where the King stayed.</note>, how he had played, and everything else that had taken place. He added, moreover, that he would never seek to visit Italy in the future without also visiting Genoa. Thus, being joyful himself, he dismissed the eight joyful citizens. 

When he was about to depart on the following day, which was the 4th day before the Nones of September <note>September 2, 1502.</note>, the senate issued a decree that the magistrates and all citizens should be present at the courtyard of the palace at early dawn, ready to escort him as he departed in the same order they had received him upon his arrival. But the King, setting out before daybreak, had already left the city by the time either the senate or the citizens had gathered at the government house. Nonetheless, some, having hastily mounted their horses, followed him without any formal order, blaming their own negligence and that of others. 

It was truly a wonder how much the King himself and all the rest were delighted by the sight of the city and the service of the citizens. It is said that as they returned to France, they spoke most pleasantly among themselves about this throughout the whole journey. The most serene Queen <note>Anne of Brittany (1477–1514), Queen of France.</note>, having then been informed of our services toward the King, is said to have been so grateful that she did not hesitate to give thanks to our merchants who are in Lyon <note>original: "Lugduni". Lyon was a major center for Genoese banking and trade.</note>, and for this reason alone, she extended the duration of the passing trade fairs. 

Indeed, the entire city remained so joyful and satisfied by this arrival of the King that he left behind a most pleasant memory of himself and a great longing among everyone. There is now no one at all who does not carry the royal name to the heavens, and who does not hope with all their prayers for the King's safety and the growth of his empire. For my part, I believe that this most happy arrival ought to be forever consecrated for our city and for the whole Genoese name, since from this time, having witnessed firsthand the admirable and divine virtue of their King's body and mind, everyone has been filled with greater hope regarding the affairs of the city.

As soon as the little book <note>original: "libellus". Referring to the manuscript or pamphlet this text comprises.</note> was presented to me, which you wrote to me concerning the arrival of Louis XII, King of the French, into this city—written with no less elegance than faithfulness—I snatched it from the hands of your modest youth, Hieronymus, and ran through it with immense eagerness. Then, when I had reviewed each detail more attentively, I could not help but greatly praise your zeal, diligence, and the elegance and dignity of your speech. I am so delighted by the daily reading of it that I keep the book itself as a companion even at my table. 

For the sequence of events, the consultations, the enthusiasm of the citizens, the preparations of the city, and the decorations of the houses were so aptly expressed by you that I, who was absent in the prefecture of Corsica <note>The island of Corsica was then a territory of the Republic of Genoa.</note>, seem to have seen each thing with my own eyes and touched them with my hand. But it pleased me above all to know that charity and kindness which our most excellent King showed to his Genoese, and the immense devotion and veneration of our entire city, of every rank and of the whole people, toward the King. 

While I consider these things in my mind (and I consider them daily), I cannot help but leap with the greatest joy. O, what a King the best God has sent down to us from heaven, who is decorated no less by the most illustrious virtues than by the noblest kingdoms, many provinces, cities of the sea, and peoples; and who is both willing and able to lift up the Genoese, afflicted for a long time by various calamities, and restore them to their former glory. Rightly, therefore, ought we to rejoice in such a great good, than which—by the testimony of the philosophers—nothing more blessed can happen to mortals in human affairs. 

Everyone owes a debt to you, for you have committed this noble and memorable matter to letters. And I give and hold no small thanks to your kindness, for you have filled my mind with great pleasure, which I am accustomed to take from repeated reading, and you have decorated it with a distinguished title and praise. Continue, therefore, in writing as you have begun, from which you will acquire glory for our fatherland and praise for yourself. Farewell. Genoa, the 15th day before the Kalends of December <note>November 17.</note>, 1502.

### Speech of the Genoese.

¶ Decree of Genoa to be observed annually, enacted in the year of our Lord 1502, on the 17th day of November.

[Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring floral and architectural motifs.] The illustrious and exalted Lord Philip of Cleves <note>Philip of Cleves, Lord of Ravenstein (1456–1528), was a Flemish nobleman serving as the French Governor of Genoa.</note>, Lord of Ravenstein, Royal Admiral, and Governor of the Genoese; and the magnificent Council of the Lords Ancients <note>The *Antiani*, the executive council of the Republic of Genoa.</note> of the Commune of Genoa, assembled in full number, whose names are as follows: Barnaba di Fieschi <note>original: "Bernardus de flisco"</note>, Prior; Cristoforo Cattaneo; Battista Vivaldi; Girolamo Loggia; Ambrogio de Zerbi; Quilico de Negro; Stefano Spinola, son of the late Ambrogio; Battista Lomellini; Edoardo Scalia; Paolo Fauli; Niccolò de Ghirardis; and Antonio de Canali. Considering how much it befits all Genoese to provide constant proof of their true documents of faith, devotion, and observance toward the Most Christian King, our Lord <note>King Louis XII of France.</note>; and to be grateful and mindful of the singular affection and benefits conferred upon this city, among which that which seems truly worthy of eternal memory is that his Sacred Majesty deigned to visit this very city in person this year. His arrival was not only welcome and pleasant to all, but also most salutary for the entire Genoese Republic. Therefore, by this solemn decree to be valid for all time, they have sanctioned and decreed that the day of the arrival of the Most Christian King himself into this city—which was the twenty-sixth day of the month of August last past—shall be observed as a holiday and celebrated as a festival every year by the entire city. Furthermore, it shall be celebrated with the ringing of bells, salutes <note>original: "falodijs," likely referring to festive salutes or displays of joy.</note>, and other expressions of gladness, so that the memory of his arrival may appear most joyful to all. They command that the present decree be published henceforth throughout the entire city, and that its observance be proclaimed every year by the voice of the herald.

¶ Speech delivered in Genoa before the King of the French by Niccolò Brignole <note>original: "Nicolaum briznalem," a prominent Genoese diplomat and orator.</note>, a Genoese citizen, on the day before the Kalends of September <note>August 31.</note> in the year of salvation 1502.

[Decorative drop cap 'E' with foliage and scrollwork.] We receive you with reverence and congratulations alike, as one sent down to us from heaven by the favor of the Great God, by celestial blessings, by the most favorable stars, and by the most happy auspices, O most glo-

<column-break/>

-rious and most invincible of kings. We do so with such alacrity of spirit and such great and incredible joy that, if it were permitted to unlock and look into the depths of our hearts, one would see our souls leaping for joy within our breasts. For when we gaze upon such a great king, now our guest by his own clemency, and contemplate your most distinguished majesty, we falter in the consideration of your magnitude, and speech fails. Otherwise, in such a great abundance of all marine matters <note>A reference to Genoa’s maritime power and the wealth of topics it provides an orator.</note>, an opportunity for the most rich speaking would have been found. Therefore, your highness is the reason why I may say little of many things, or almost nothing at all, O most excellent of all kings; for we cannot endure the radiance of your heavenly serenity. To me personally, to whom the Senate delegated this task of expressing the public joy, there is such alacrity in my soul that the more I strive to speak well, the more I hesitate. My mind cannot supply a speech while joy hinders it; for even if my speech were to flow, and all my thoughts were ready, I could not equal even the smallest part of this common joy with words. You will therefore grant pardon, most clement Prince, even if you now see us to be less prompt or ready in speaking than the celebration of this place and time requires; you will find the city and the whole people all the more prompt in obeying and bravely executing matters for the glory of your sublimity. Indeed, no duties, no services, and finally no servitude of ours can be so great that they could even approach your greatness and charity toward us, let alone be sufficient. We confess that your benevolence and the inclination of your most high soul toward us conquer the strength of all the Genoese—and we pray that it may long conquer—which (if I may say so with your kind permission) are neither small nor to be despised. But, illustrious King, that is your true greatness: to be both able and willing to bind your peoples to you by your merits. Conversely, there is no service of the peoples, however great, that can be equal to your merits. This is the true way of reigning; these are the laws of ruling: that peoples be won over and held by benefit and charity rather than by wicked command. Indeed, that security of yours, with the greatest wisdom, brought it about that you left the Kingdom of the French without anxiety or any agitation of mind, and decided to cross into Italy in safety, so that, having confirmed your empire in Italy by these same laws, you might return again to the French lands without care. You have no need for further armies, most powerful King; no leaders, so to speak, are necessary for you. If you are free from taxes and stipends, you can still protect and preserve so wide an empire, largely acquired by your wisdom and strength. For even if some external force were to attack, the citizens themselves, bound by your kindness, will defend the cities by themselves.

The previous page established the city's official decree to commemorate the visit; here, the text describes the King’s personal interactions with the citizens, his early departure, and a celebratory letter from Bartolomeo Giustiniani to the Republic’s Chancellor praising a written account of these events.</meta>

# The Preparations of the Genoese.

He was now treated with such generous freedom that he was regarded as one of them. Then, as the sun was setting, having returned home, he found eight men waiting for him. Looking upon them with a cheerful and serene expression, he led them into the courtyard. There, he graciously listened to them as they gave thanks for his many kindnesses. He most humanely approved the concessions granted to the city regarding Spanish affairs, legal questions, the establishment of magistrates, and other matters pertaining to the republic, and he commanded them to be of good heart. 

Turning then to jests, he recounted most calmly what he had done at Lorenzo's villa <note>Likely referring to the villa of a member of the prominent Cybo or Lomellini families who hosted the king.</note>, how he had played, and everything else that had occurred. He further added that he would never seek to visit Italy in the future without also coming to Genoa. Thus, being joyful himself, he dismissed the eight happy citizens. 

When, however, the King was about to depart on the following day—which was the 2nd of September <note>original: "iiij.nonas septembris." In the Roman calendar, the 4th day before the Nones of September is September 2nd.</note>—the Senate proclaimed that all magistrates and citizens should be ready in the palace courtyard at the first light of dawn, so that they might accompany him as he departed in the same order with which they had received him upon his arrival. But the King, setting out before daybreak, had already left the city before either the Senate or the citizens could assemble at the palace. Nevertheless, some, hurriedly mounting their horses, followed him without any formal order, blaming themselves for their own negligence and that of the others. 

It is truly a wonder how much the King himself and all the rest were delighted by the sight of the city and the service of the citizens. It is said that they spoke of this most pleasantly among themselves during the entire journey back to France. The most serene Queen <note>Anne of Brittany (1477–1514), Queen of France.</note>, having then been informed of our services toward the King, is said to have been so grateful for it that she did not hesitate to give thanks to our merchants who are in Lyon <note>original: "lugduni." Lyon was a major financial and silk-trading hub for Genoese merchants.</note>. For this reason alone, she extended the time of the passing trade fairs. 

Indeed, the entire city remained so joyful and content with this arrival of the King that he left behind a most pleasant memory and a great longing for himself among everyone. There is now no one at all who does not extol the royal name to the heavens, and who does not hope with all their prayers for the King's safety and the increase of his empire. For my part, I believe that this most happy arrival ought to be forever consecrated by our city and the entire Genoese name, since from the moment they witnessed in person the admirable and divine virtue of their King—both of body and mind—everyone was inspired with greater hope for the affairs of the city.

<column-break/>

->**Bartolomeo Giustiniani to the respected and distinguished Benedetto Portuense, Chancellor of the Genoese Republic.**<-

---

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'V' depicting a seated figure, likely a king or scholar, in an architectural interior with a window view.</image-desc>

When first the booklet was offered to me, which you wrote to me concerning the arrival of Louis XII, King of the Franks, into this city—with no less elegance than faithfulness—I snatched it from the hands of your modest young son Girolamo and immediately ran through it with immense greed. Then, when I had examined every single detail more attentively, I could not help but greatly praise your zeal, diligence, and your vivid and ornate style of speaking, as well as the dignity of the subject matter. I am so delighted by the daily reading of it that I keep the booklet itself as a companion at my table. 

For the sequence of the events, the consultations, the enthusiasm of the citizens, the preparations of the city, and the decorations of the houses have been so aptly expressed by you that I—who was absent while serving in the governorship of Corsica <note>Genoa ruled Corsica at this time; Giustiniani was likely serving as a "prefect" or governor there.</note>—seem to have inspected every single thing with my own eyes and touched them with my hand. But it pleased me above all to know that affection and kindness which our most excellent King showed so greatly toward his Genoese, and the immense devotion and veneration of our entire city, of every rank, and of all the people toward the King. 

While I consider these things in my mind (and I consider them daily), I cannot help but leap with the greatest joy. The best and greatest God must have sent my King to us from heaven—a man who is distinguished no less by his most illustrious virtues than by his most noble kingdoms, many provinces, maritime cities, and peoples; one who both wishes and is able to lift up the Genoese, long afflicted by various calamities, and restore them to their former glory. Rightly, therefore, we ought to rejoice in such a great good, for which, by the testimony of philosophers, nothing more blessed can happen to mortals among human affairs. 

Furthermore, everyone owes a debt to you because you have committed such a noble and memorable matter to writing. And I give no small thanks to your kindness, for you have filled my mind with great pleasure—which I am accustomed to take from repeated reading—and you have decorated it with a distinguished title and praise. Continue, therefore, in writing as you have begun, whereby you will acquire glory for the fatherland and praise for yourself. Farewell. 

Genoa, November 15, 1502.

# Oration of the Genoese.

¶ A decree of Genoa to be observed annually, enacted in the year of our Lord 1502, on the 17th day of November.

The illustrious and exalted Lord Philip of Cleves, Lord of Ravenstein, Royal Admiral, and Governor of the Genoese; and the magnificent council of the Lords <term>Antiani</term> <note>The "Elders" or primary governing magistrates of the Genoese Republic.</note> of the commune of Genoa, assembled in full number, whose names are these: Bernardo Fieschi, Prior; Cristoforo Cattaneo; Battista Vivaldi; Gerolamo Loggia; Ambrogio de' Zerbi; Quilico Di Negro; Stefano Spinola, son of the late Ambrogio; Battista Lomellini; Edoardo Scalia; Paolo Fausti; Niccolò de' Ghirardi; Antonio Canali. Considering how much it becomes all Genoese to constantly offer true evidence of their faith, devotion, and observance toward our sovereign, the <term>Most Christian King</term> <note>The traditional title for the Kings of France.</note>; and to be grateful and mindful of the singular affection and benefits bestowed by him upon this city—among which that which truly deserves to be remembered with perennial memory is that his Most Sacred Majesty deigned to happily visit this city in person this year. His arrival was not only pleasing and joyful to all, but also most wholesome for the entire Genoese Republic. Therefore, by this solemn decree intended to be valid for all time, they have sanctioned and decreed that the day of the arrival of the Most Christian King himself into this city—which was the twenty-third of the month of August last past—shall be observed as a holiday and celebrated as a feast day every year by the entire city; and furthermore, it shall be celebrated with the ringing of bells, with <term>falodi</term> <note>Original: "falodijs." These were large ceremonial bonfires or torchlight displays common in Italian victory celebrations.</note>, and other signs of joy. Thus, the memory of his arrival shall appear most pleasant to all. They command that the present decree be published from this moment throughout the whole city, and that its observance be announced every year by the voice of a herald.

¶ Oration delivered at Genoa before the King of the French by Nicolaus Bignalis, a Genoese citizen, on the day before the Kalends of September <note>August 31st.</note> in the year of salvation 1502.

We receive you, most glorious and invincible of kings, with both reverence and congratulation, as if you were sent down to us from heaven by the favor of the Almighty God, all the celestial beings, the most favorable stars, and the happiest omens. We do so with such alacrity of mind and such great and incredible joy 

<column-break/>

that if it were possible to unlock and see into the depths of our hearts, we would see our souls leaping for joy within our breasts. For when we look upon such a great king as our guest by his own clemency, and contemplate your most distinguished majesty, we fail in the consideration of your magnitude, and our speech falters—which otherwise, in such a great abundance of material, would have found a most rich opportunity for speaking. Your Highness, therefore, is the reason that it is permitted to say little or almost nothing of many things, O most excellent of all kings; for we cannot bear the radiance of your celestial serenity. To me personally, to whom the Senate delegated this task of expressing the public joy, there is such eagerness in my soul that the more I strive to speak well, the more I hesitate. Nor can my mind supply the speech, for joy hinders it; although, even if the speech flowed and all things were ready according to my will, I could not equal even the smallest part of this common joy with words. You will therefore grant pardon, most clement Prince, even if you now see us as less prompt or ready in speaking due to the solemnity of this place and time; for you shall find the city and the entire people so much the prompter in obeying and bravely executing matters for the glory of your highness. Truly, no duties, no services, and finally no servitude of ours can be so great that they could closely approach your magnitude and charity toward us, let alone be sufficient. We confess that your benevolence and the inclination of your most lofty soul toward us surpass the strength of all the Genoese; and we pray that it may long surpass them—which (if I may say so with your kind permission) were neither small nor to be despised. But, illustrious King, your true greatness lies in this: both being able and willing to obligate your peoples through your merits. Conversely, there is no service of the people, however great, that can be equaled to your merits. Nor is that the true method of reigning. This is your law of commanding: that peoples should be won over and held by benefit and charity rather than by impiety. Indeed, that security, directed by the greatest counsel, has brought it about that you decided to leave the Kingdom of the French without anxiety or agitation of mind, and to cross into Italy secure; so that, with your empire in Italy confirmed by these same laws, you might again return to France without care. No further armies, most powerful King, no leaders, so to speak, are necessary for you. If it pleases you, you can protect and preserve such a wide empire—won in great part by your counsel and strength—without taxes or stipends. For even if some external force should attack, the citizens themselves, bound by your benefit, will defend the cities by themselves.

and they will not hesitate to place their own bodies and those of their children before the enemy for your glory. From this comes that most valiant strength of the kings of the Franks, your ancestors. From this come such great and opulent kingdoms, and the borders of an empire extended into the immense. Yet, though you received it at its most ample, you especially—indeed, the very first of all—have added another most powerful kingdom and the wealthiest part of Italy, the most fertile of all, to the **empire of the Gauls** <note>original: "imperio galliarum"; the speaker refers to the French Kingdom using the classical Roman term for France.</note>. And now you embrace such vast spaces of land that more people hear your commands than ever receive them from your physical presence. For someone departing from the farthest **Morini** <note>A people of northern Gaul, near modern-day Boulogne; used here to denote the northernmost edge of the King's territory.</note> and the ultimate ocean, whenever it pleases, one can travel all the way to Apulia and **Magna Graecia** <note>Southern Italy, historically settled by Greeks.</note> at the Adriatic Sea, passing almost entirely through your cities, through your fields, and through your borders in a solid and continuous empire. No Christian kings, no emperors—if you set aside that ancient Roman Empire, to which it is right to yield out of reverence—have ever ruled so widely.

Others boast of the most remote lands sought across the whole ocean, of the discovery of vast islands crowded with throngs of people, of seas frozen thick elsewhere, of frozen lands, of the gradual descent even to the **antipodes** <note>The inhabitants of the opposite side of the world.</note>, and that India has been made accessible from the **Pillars of Hercules** <note>The Strait of Gibraltar.</note> and Gades. They boast of spices brought by sea, which in all ancient centuries were blocked by the continent and vast Arabia, preventing them from penetrating into the Mediterranean Sea by ship. These things are great—indeed, they are of the greatest admiration—nor are they unworthy; yet they were produced by nature from the first beginning of the world, and sought and found by the ingenuity of a few men.

But we admire our King more: since we do not think his rise occurred in the same manner as that of other men, if we contemplate so many and such great things achieved by his own nearly private counsel and in such a short time. Rather, he was sent down to us from heaven (as we have said) and established by the highest counsel of the Greatest God to rule the lands, protect the peoples, and preserve perpetual peace in such a great empire. This is true admiration, and these are the causes of true wonder; they were not (as we said) born of nature, so that it is now well-proven that much divinity dwells within his soul. These causes bring it about (I turn now to those of us standing here) that the most invincible **King of the Gauls** is extolled to the heavens with the highest praises everywhere, and is honored with the highest veneration in the duties and services of nearly all princes. I am pleased to mention, when he was planning the journey into Italy, how many princes and how many most famous embassies went to meet him for the sake of duty when he had scarcely entered his journey, in the middle of the realm of the Gauls.

<column-break/>

Indeed, now that he has crossed the Alps, not only princes and legates, but all the leading men of the provinces and all the Italian nobility have come forward to venerate such a great king in a massive and most great company, so that neither the cities, nor the towns, nor the fields could contain such a multitude. Now, as he travels through Italy and enters even our narrow passes, he is followed not only by dukes but by kings—or those worthy of a kingdom—and the greatest leaders of wars, and especially that celebrated and conspicuous assembly of **Cardinals**, such as could decorate and illustrate Rome itself. So much admiration and so much authority has he acquired, that he no longer wages wars with generals or armies as before, but by his command and his nod. For at his order, arms are set down, armies are dismissed, cities are abandoned, and gates are opened to **heralds** <term>caduceatoribus</term> <note>original: "caduceatoribus"; messengers of peace traditionally carrying a staff (caduceus) to signify immunity.</note> and royal ministers without any weapons. All are stunned by the name of the King; they venerate and obey it as a divinity.

In such great glory, then, as such a great King comes to us, visiting his Genoese, with what thanks shall we follow him? Especially since it appears he wishes to embrace not only everyone together with his kindness and clemency, but even each individual. And indeed, as you see, he would embrace them were he not turned away from such a desired duty by the packed multitude of those rushing together and the acclamations of those congratulating him. I hesitate here; and certainly my life-breath would be shut off, did I not know that the most clement King wants nothing else from his Genoese, nor expects anything more, than incorruptible faith toward him and sincere love. To wish to say anything regarding these would be the mark of one who doubts. Our faith and love are sufficiently witnessed, most clement King (to omit the rest), by the prayers of the multitude for the safety of their King. They are witnessed by the faces of those watching, and the applause and acclamations of those meeting you. Finally, the very walls of the houses seem to wish to express our most burning affection.

Relying on this faith and love, therefore, the Genoese receive you with the greatest possible veneration, most invincible King. The Senate and the people receive you. Every rank receives you. And they receive you in such a way that they dare to promise themselves quieter times through you, and the desired blessings of peace and tranquility. For we desire peace above all things, being always intent upon **commerce** <note>original: "negociationi"; the speaker emphasizes that Genoa's prosperity depends on trade, which is destroyed by war.</note>, to which war is always a baneful enemy at all times. Therefore, for the confirming and stabilizing of that peace which we have already obtained through you, we implore your authority, your strength, and finally your greatest love toward us. And at the last, by which the greater...
