# Trophies of the Gauls <note>original: "Trophei gallorum"; here "Gauls" refers to the French.</note>

with all the affection we are able: the city of Genoa, which is yours: its towns, citadels, villas, fields, its noble islands, its ships and galleys, all things public and private, and finally the whole Genoese name and its entire domain, we commend again and again, most earnestly, to your clemency and kindness.

¶ The description of the royal arrival into the city of Genoa, and of the same Genoese orations delivered to the King himself, edited by Benedictus of Portovenere <note>Benedictus Portuensis was a contemporary chronicler and notary from Portovenere who recorded these events.</note>: **The End.**

<column-break/>

¶ There follows a brief summary, in the form of an epitome, of the expedition against the Genoese, compiled by Master Symphorien Champier <note>A famous French humanist, physician, and historian who accompanied Louis XII on his Italian campaigns.</note>.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' with interlaced foliage and strapwork designs.</image-desc>In the year of our Lord 1506 <note>The text reads M.cccc.vj (1406), but the context of Louis XII’s 10th year and the historical rebellion confirms the date is 1506-1507.</note>, while Louis XII was wielding the Gallic scepter—in the tenth year of his reign, if I am not mistaken—a significant discord occurred among the Genoese. These people had previously surrendered themselves and all their territory to the King. However, a conflict arose: the nobles favored the Royal Majesty to whom they had devoted themselves, while the commoners and the <term>ignoble rabble</term> <note>original: "ignobile vulgus"; a disparaging term for the non-aristocratic classes.</note> strove to withdraw themselves from his rule. Because of these disagreements, a great <term>sedition</term> <note>A revolt or uprising against established authority.</note> followed. Therefore, the nobles, led by a more sensible plan so that the city itself would not suffer greater misfortune, or perhaps lest the Royal Majesty be offended in any way, chose to leave the city of their own accord. They diligently held the fortifications and small forts in favor of the King.

Observing this, the commoners were struck with fear. They dispatched their envoys to the most Christian Royal Majesty to "offer excuses for their sins" <note>original: "excusandas excusationes in peccatis"; a Latin phrasing derived from the Psalms, suggesting they were making flimsy or hypocritical justifications.</note> and to try and earn back the King’s goodwill. Acting in their roles as ambassadors, they set forth their business with the most ornate words and speeches they could muster. They attempted to "cloak their impiety with hands and feet" <note>original: "manibus et pedibus... palliare"; a Latin idiom meaning to try something with all one's might.</note>, being well aware that nothing is so incredible that it cannot be made to seem probable through speaking, and nothing so horrid that it cannot be made to shine and be refined by an oration. But as they say, the matter was "left unfinished" <note>original: "re infecta"; meaning they failed in their mission.</note>, because their petition seemed less than honest. They returned home. 

In the meantime, they heavily fortified that most powerful city and the surrounding fortresses with forces drawn from every side. The nobles also sent their own ambassadors to the Royal Majesty as if to a "most safe asylum," as they were fostering a just and legitimate cause. These noble envoys delivered an oration in the presence of the King at the "first audience" (as they call it). Because this speech is worthy of being read and re-read, we have chosen to insert it here.

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the Genoese rebellion against the French crown. <header>Speech of the Genoese.</header>

### The speech of Lord Stephanus Vinaldus to the 
### King on behalf of the Genoese nobility in the first 
### public audience.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'C' containing a portrait of a man in profile wearing a Renaissance-style soft cap, likely representing the orator Stephanus Vinaldus or the King.</image-desc>Most Christian King <note>original: "Christianissime rex"; a formal title specifically reserved for the Kings of France.</note>, live forever. I know it is the established custom of most distinguished orators performing the duty of an embassy when they approach your Most Christian Majesty: that they strive to extol you with the most exquisite praises they can muster. It is thought that any speech—however elegant and ornate—is maimed, barren, and without grace unless the praises of the man himself precede it. Therefore, I too had intended to do the same; but after I began the work and, as they say, "tested the depths," recognizing that I was entering a vast and deep sea, I immediately drew back my foot. I have imitated those who, when about to speak of Sulla or Carthage, thought it better to remain silent than to say too little. For although it was to be feared that someone might think I undertook this for the sake of flattery—especially with you listening, and perhaps our speech causing you to blush on account of your singular modesty—nevertheless, it was not that reasoning that moved me (for if someone speaks the truth, no one can rightly call him a flatterer). Rather, I am deterred by the immense mountain of your virtues, by whose brilliance the mind is so dazzled that I do not even dare to think of them, let alone hope to describe them. Therefore, with your kind permission and acknowledging my own weakness, I shall omit all those things, as they are well known throughout the whole world on their own. I shall also not dwell on recounting the praises of your most faithful Genoese nobility, as a certain orator of the <term>seditious commoners</term> <note>original: "sediciose plebis"; referring to the leaders of the popular faction who had seized power in Genoa.</note> is said to have done. He, unable to excuse their most grievous crimes in any other way, began with their praises; for praise in one’s own mouth is offensive. And the nobility excels the commoners as much "as cypresses are wont to do among the pliant shrubs" <note>A quote from Virgil’s Eclogues (1.25), comparing the grand nobility to tall trees and the commoners to low bushes.</note>. For if we consider our ancestors, their images and true monuments are present, standing openly before the <term>rostra</term> <note>original: "pro rostris"; the public speaking platforms, modeled after the Roman forum.</note>, and their faces are rendered living in marble. There are the temples, the hospitals, and countless other public buildings constructed at their expense. There are the annual alms established by them. And finally, to compress many things into a few words: whatever fortunate or happy thing the city of Genoa possesses, it has from the nobles. Indeed, she has been enriched and adorned by our resources. Even the common people themselves, or the greater part of them, draw their origin from the camps and villas of the nobles. If, however, we wish to speak of the nobility now living, how can the lazy rabble be compared with them? For there are

<column-break/>

barons, lords, and counts known to your Most Christian Majesty. And unless we had been forbidden three and four times by those acting on behalf of your Majesty, the commoners—so eager for revolution—would have undoubtedly felt what we were prepared to do for your Most Christian Majesty and for the preservation of your Genoese state. It also seems that I should dwell less on recounting the fires, rapes, and robberies—or rather, the murders and injuries—perpetrated against us by the commoners at the instigation of certain seditious men. They had no respect for the honor and state of your Most Christian Majesty, under whose triumphant and most glorious banner we were sleeping securely. These things are notorious. If I wished to recount even the smallest part of them, "evening would close the heavens before the day is done" <note>An allusion to Virgil's Aeneid (1.374), meaning the list of crimes is too long to finish in a single day.</note>. I shall fill in the details, if it pleases your Majesty, when you have more leisure. Nevertheless, though these things are most grave and intolerable, we endure them with a brave spirit—not out of fear of them (since we did not lack the strength to resist), but lest your Serenity be offended in any way. We have never thought to do anything without your nod; and for this reason, leaving our own homes and sweet hearths, we willingly suffer exile. Therefore, we four have come as their envoys to your Most Christian Majesty, to whom it belongs to render to each what is his own and to punish wrongdoers. We ask that a fitting remedy be applied in these matters for our protection and the preservation of your state, firmly believing that this will not be lacking, since nothing else can come from a most wise and just King of kings. This is so that the criminals themselves are not enriched by our loss, but may serve as an example to others and as a consolation to those who have been killed. We have delayed asking for this until now. For when, at the beginning of their rebellion, we had destined two of our leading men to your Majesty, they happened by chance to meet the most illustrious Lord of Ravestein <note>Philip of Cleves, Lord of Ravenstein (1459–1528), who served as the French governor of Genoa.</note>, our governor under your Most Christian Majesty. By his order they returned, as he asserted that he held a fitting remedy from your Majesty. May the Lord make you happy for ages of ages.

-> I have spoken. <-

-># Trophies of the French<-

Therefore, the Most Christian King, having heard both sides—for he who decides anything after hearing only one side is seen to have decided nothing <note>original: "qui pre audita tm altera aliqd statuit: nihil statuisse videtur"; a variation on a legal maxim from Seneca's Medea: "He who decides a case without hearing the other side, though he decide justly, is himself unjust."</note>—and having recognized the truth, was most grieved, as becomes a noble king. Bearing the fact that Genoa was being afflicted by so many and such great injuries and troubles, and that its nobility were being harmed, and seeing them fleeing to him as to the safest asylum of the afflicted (as we have already said), he conducted himself most humanely toward them. He judged it to be the duty of his royal dignity to apply a fitting remedy to such a great evil.

The King, therefore, imitating the most brave Julius Caesar—who was highly trained in military discipline—put aside all hesitation and in a short interval of time quickly summoned a significant multitude of soldiers, both infantry and cavalry, whom he sent ahead. But the King himself, performing the duty of a good shepherd, courageously crossed the harsh Pennine mountains <note>The Pennine Alps, a specific range in the Western Alps.</note>. But who is endowed with such eloquence that they could follow with words the prudence of mind and the bravery he used in this so difficult expedition? Many writers of history commend various leaders and emperors distinguished in military discipline who deserved well of their country either by defending or expanding it; compared to these, our King is not only to be equaled but, not undeservedly, is to be preferred. 

First, Mago, the son of Hamilcar and brother of Hannibal, is commended because he captured Genoa itself—which extended its dominion so far and wide that it was antonomastically <term>antonomastically: the use of an epithet or title in place of a proper name</term> called "The Proud"—by an unexpected arrival when it was fortified by no defenses. Regarding this, Titus Livius <note>Livy, the Roman historian.</note> says in book eight of the Punic War: "In that same summer, Mago, son of Hamilcar, having chosen a select youth from the smaller Balearic island where he had wintered, put them on a fleet and crossed into Italy with thirty beaked ships and many transport vessels, twelve thousand infantry, and nearly two thousand cavalry; and he captured Genoa on the maritime coast by a sudden arrival, as it was protected by no defenses." But greater praise must be ascribed to our King, because he did not shrink from attacking it when it was fortified with the strongest defenses. Nor did he use the cruelty that Mago used—who utterly overturned the city—but rather showed the greatest humanity and clemency.

<margin>Miltiades of Athens</margin>
Miltiades is praised because he liberated Athens and all of Greece. But our King not only liberated his own kingdom but wonderfully expanded it. The Athenians under the leadership of Miltiades prevailed more by valor, so that they routed a ten-fold number of Persians who were under Darius.

<margin>Themistocles</margin>
Xerxes was conquered more by the counsel of Themistocles than by the arms of Greece.

<margin>Pausanias</margin>
Pausanias the Lacedaemonian <note>A Spartan.</note> was a great man. His most illustrious battle was at Plataea. For under his leadership, Mardonius—a royal sa-

<column-break/>

-trap, a Mede by nation and son-in-law of the King, foremost among all the Persians, brave of hand and full of counsel—was put to flight from Greece with two hundred thousand infantry, whom he had hand-picked, and twenty thousand cavalry, by a hand of Greeks that was not so large; and in that battle, the leader himself fell.

<margin>Alcibiades</margin>
Alcibiades the Athenian had a great victory over the Lacedaemonians. He recovered Ionia and the Hellespont. Moreover, he took many Greek cities situated on the coast of Asia, of which he captured several by force, including Byzantium.

<margin>Thrasybulus</margin>
Thrasybulus, son of Lycus, an Athenian: if virtue is to be weighed by itself without fortune, I doubt whether the Greeks would place anyone before him. To him they certainly prefer no one in loyalty, constancy, greatness of soul, and love for his country. For what many wished for, few were able to do: to liberate their country from a single tyrant. From this it happened that he claimed it back into liberty from the slavery imposed by thirty tyrants. To him, for such great merits, a crown of honor was given by the people, made of two olive branches. 

If one should choose to compare our King to these most brave emperors in any kind of virtue—whether in gifts of the mind or in skill in military matters—our King comes not only to be equaled to them but (let there be no offense in the word) far preferred.

<margin>Agesilaus</margin>
Agesilaus, King of the Lacedaemonians, led his troops across the Hellespont and used such great speed that he traversed in thirty days the journey which Xerxes had completed in a turning year. Our King used no less speed in this Genoese expedition. The same man also had victory over barbarians and forbade the temples of the gods to be violated. And our King, having conquered the Genoese people—otherwise untamable and most powerful—as a supreme worshiper of religion and justice, does not allow the sacred buildings to be harmed in any way.

<margin>Carthage</margin>
In Africa there was once Carthage, built by Dido. It was once, after the city of Rome, the other glory of the lands, which was overturned by Scipio Africanus seven hundred and thirty-seven years after it had been built (as Solinus records). Genoa, for a long interval of time the head of many regions and islands, and even cities, and the leader of provinces, was subdued by our King; and she who was the mistress of nations was made subject to tribute. 

The war was fought at Troy for ten years <note>The Trojan War</note>. Genoa, no less noble than Troy, was possessed by the King by force and victory, and he subdued it—despite it trusting in its own strength—within the space of thirty days. Semiramis of the Babylonians and Alexander, surnamed the Great, only tamed the Indians. Likewise Hannibal (though others ascribe this to Mago the Carthaginian, son of Hamilcar and brother of Alexander the Great <note>The text here seems to confuse or conflate Hamilcar's son with the Macedonian lineage, or is referencing a specific classical source's comparison.</note>) and Louis XII, King of the French, alone tamed the Genoese. In the army of Alexander the Great, there were thirty thousand infantry...

<meta>This page continues the narrative following the introduction of King Louis XII’s intervention in Genoa. Genoese Speech.

<column-break/>

# The Speech of Master Stefano Vivaldi to the
# King on behalf of the Genoese nobility in the first
# public audience.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'C' at the start of the text, featuring a figure seated amidst stylized foliage within a square border.</image-desc>

**C**hristianissime King, live forever. I know that it is the custom of the most distinguished orators who, performing the duty of an embassy, approach your Most Christian Majesty, to attempt to extol you with the most exquisite praises using every word they can muster. They think any speech—no matter how elegant or ornate—is crippled, sterile, and without grace unless it is preceded by the praises of the man himself. For this reason, I also intended to do the same; but after I began the task and, as they say, "tested the waters" <note>original: "vadum tentaui"</note>, I realized what a vast and deep sea I was entering. I immediately pulled back my foot, imitating the habit of those who, about to speak of Sulla or Carthage, thought it better to remain silent than to say too little. For although it was to be feared that someone might think I undertook this for the sake of flattery—especially with you listening and our speech perhaps making you blush because of your singular modesty—nevertheless, it was not that reasoning that moved me (for if one speaks the truth, no one can rightly call him a flatterer). Rather, I was deterred by the immense mountain of your virtues, by whose brilliance my mind is so obscured that I do not even dare to think of them, let alone hope to describe them. Therefore, with your kind permission and acknowledging my own weakness, I shall omit all those things, as they are well known through the whole world on their own. I will also not linger in recounting the praises of your most faithful Genoese nobility, as a certain seditious orator of the common people <note>The "plebs" or "popolari"—the common citizens of Genoa who had revolted against the ruling noble class.</note> is said to have done; who, being otherwise unable to excuse their most heavy crimes, began with their praises. For indeed, "praise in one's own mouth becomes foul" <note>A common Latin proverb: "Laus in proprio ore sordescit."</note>. And nobility excels the commoners as much as "the cypresses are wont to do among the bending shrubs" <note>A quote from Virgil’s Eclogues, comparing something grand to something humble.</note>. For if an account of our ancestors is required, their images and true monuments are present, which stand before the rostra <note>The public speaking platforms</note> and render their faces living from the marble. There are temples, hospitals, and countless other public buildings built at their expense. There are annual charities established by them. And finally, to encompass many things in few words: whatever Genoa has that is auspicious and happy, it has from the nobles. Indeed, the city has been increased and adorned by our wealth. The common people themselves, or the greater part of them, draw their origin from the camps and villas of the nobles. But if we wish to speak of the nobility living today, how can the idle common crowd be compared with them? There are

<column-break/>

indeed barons, lords, and counts known to your Most Christian Majesty. And if we had not been forbidden three or four times by those acting on behalf of your Majesty, the common people themselves—greedy for revolution—would have undoubtedly felt how prepared we were to act for your Most Christian Majesty and for the preservation of your state of Genoa. It also seems I should dwell less on recounting the fires, rapes, and robberies—indeed, even the muggings, wounds, murders, and other most serious injuries—perpetrated against us by the common people at the instigation of certain seditious men. This was done with no respect for the honor and status of your Most Christian Majesty, under whose triumphant and most glorious banner we were sleeping securely. These things are notorious. And if I wished to recount even the smallest part of them, "evening would close Olympus before the day was done" <note>A poetic reference to Virgil’s Aeneid, meaning the story is too long to finish in one day.</note>. For who could explain the disaster of that night? Who could recount the deaths? Or who could match our labors with tears? <note>Another reference to Virgil (Aeneid II), lamenting the fall of Troy.</note> I shall fill in the rest, if it pleases your Majesty, when you have more leisure. Nevertheless, we endure all these things, though they are most heavy and intolerable, with a brave heart—not out of fear of them, for we would not have lacked the strength to resist, but lest your Serenity be offended in any way. Without your nod, we never intended to do anything; for this reason, leaving our own homes and sweet hearths, we willingly suffer exile. Therefore, we four orators have come to your Most Christian Majesty, to whom it belongs to give to each what is his own and to punish the delinquent. We ask that a fitting remedy be applied in these matters for our protection and the preservation of your state, firmly persuaded that it will not be lacking, since nothing else can come from a most prudent and just King of kings. This is so that the criminals themselves may not be enriched by our loss, but may be an example to others, and a solace to those who were killed. We have delayed asking for this until now, for when we had destined two of our leading men to your Majesty at the beginning of their rebellion, they by chance encountered our Governor acting for your Most Christian Majesty. By his order they returned, as he asserted that he had a fitting remedy from your Majesty. May the Lord make you happy forever and ever.

->I have spoken.<-

### Trophies of the French.

<image-desc>A decorative drop cap 'C' begins the text in the first column, featuring an eagle with spread wings inside a circular frame, surrounded by floral and leaf motifs.</image-desc>

The most Christian King, therefore, having heard both sides—for he who decides anything having heard only one side seems to have decided nothing <note>original: "nam qui prae audita tantum altera aliquid statuit: nihil statuisse videtur"</note>—and having recognized the truth, was greatly troubled, as was fitting for a noble king. He bore it heavily that the Genoese nobility were being afflicted and harmed by so many injuries and troubles, and as they were fleeing to him as the safest refuge for the afflicted (as we have already said), he behaved toward them with great humanity. He judged it to be the duty of royal dignity to apply a suitable remedy to this great evil. The King, therefore, imitating the most brave Julius Caesar, who was highly trained in military discipline, set aside all hesitation. Within a short interval of time, he quickly called together a significant multitude of soldiers, both infantry and cavalry, whom he sent ahead. The King himself, performing the office of a good shepherd, courageously crossed the rugged Pennine mountains <note>The Pennine Alps, the range between Switzerland and Italy.</note>. But who, even if endowed with great eloquence, could follow with words the prudence of mind and the fortitude he used in this difficult expedition? Many writers of history commend various leaders and emperors distinguished in military discipline who deserved well of their country by either defending or expanding it; compared to these, our King is not only to be equaled but deservedly preferred. First, Mago is commended—the son of Hamilcar and brother of Hannibal—who captured Genoa itself (which spreads its power so far and wide that it is antonomastically <note>A rhetorical term meaning to use an epithet or title instead of a proper name.</note> called "The Proud") by an unexpected arrival when it was fortified by no guards. As Titus Livy says of him in book eight of the Punic War: "In the same summer, Mago, son of Hamilcar, having crossed from the smaller of the Balearic Islands where he had wintered, with a chosen youth placed on a fleet, crossed into Italy with thirty beaked ships and many transport vessels, twelve thousand infantry, and about two thousand cavalry; he captured Genoa by a sudden arrival, as no guards were protecting the maritime coast." <note>original: "Eadem estate Mago almicaris filius... Genuamque nullis praesidiis maritima oram tutantibus repetino adventu cepit."</note> But greater praise should be ascribed to our King, because he did not fear to attack it when it was fortified with the strongest garrisons. Nor did he use the cruelty that Mago used—who utterly overturned the city—but rather the highest humanity and clemency.

<margin>

Miltiades is praised for liberating Athens and all of Greece. Yet our King did not merely liberate his own kingdom but wonderfully expanded it. The Athenians under the leadership of Miltiades prevailed more by valor, so that they defeated a tenfold number of Persians who were under Darius. Xerxes was defeated more by the wisdom of Themistocles than by the arms of Greece. Pausanias the Spartan was a great man; his most illustrious battle was at Plataea. For with him as leader, Mardonius, a royal

<column-break/>

satrap of the Median nation and son-in-law of the King—foremost among all the Persians, brave of hand and full of counsel—was put to flight from Greece with two hundred thousand infantry, whom he had hand-picked man by man, and twenty thousand cavalry, by a not very large force; in that battle, the leader himself fell.

<margin>
Alcibiades.
</margin>
Alcibiades the Athenian had a great victory over the Spartans. He recovered Ionia and the Hellespont. Besides many Greek cities situated on the coast of Asia, he captured several, including Byzantium.

Thrasybulus.
</margin>
Thrasybulus, son of Lycus, the Athenian: if virtue is to be weighed by itself without fortune, I doubt whether the Greeks would place anyone before him. Without doubt, they prefer no one to Thrasybulus in loyalty, constancy, greatness of soul, and love for his country. For what many desired, few were able to do: to liberate the fatherland from a single tyrant. From this it happened that he claimed back the city, oppressed by thirty tyrants, from slavery into liberty. For such great merits, a crown of honor was given to him by the people, made of two olive branches. To these most brave generals—if one chooses to compare our King in any kind of virtue, whether in gifts of the mind or skill in military affairs—not only does he come to be equaled by them, but (may envy be absent from the word) he is to be far preferred.

<margin>
Agesilaus.
</margin>
Agesilaus, King of the Spartans, led his forces across the Hellespont; he used such speed that the journey Xerxes had completed in a full year, he crossed in thirty days. Our King used no less speed in this Genoese expedition. The same man [Agesilaus] also had a victory over the barbarians and forbade the temples of the gods to be violated. And our King, over the Genoese people, otherwise untamable and most powerful, [showed such care] that he did not allow the sacred buildings to be harmed, being himself a supreme observer of religion and justice.

<margin>
Carthage.
</margin>
In Africa there was once Carthage, built by Dido. It was once the second glory of the lands after the city of Rome, which was overturned by Scipio Africanus seven hundred and thirty-seven years after it had been built (as Solinus records). Genoa—for a long interval of time the head of many regions and islands, not to mention cities, and the chief of provinces—was subdued by our King; and she who was a mistress was made subject to tribute.

<margin>
Troy.
</margin>
The Trojan War. The battle at Troy was fought for ten years, six months, and twelve days <note>original: "annis. x. mē. vj. diebus. xij."</note>, until it was finally conquered. No less noble was the King's mastery over Genoa; he subdued Genoa, which was confident in its own strength, in the space of thirty days.

<margin>

Thus Hannibal (others ascribe this to Mago the Carthaginian, son of Hamilcar) and King Louis XII of the French <note>original: "Ludovicus. xij. francorum rex"</note> alone subdued the Genoese. ### The End of the Trophies of the French.

Then, there were four thousand five hundred cavalry. With such a small force he conquered the entire world; it is uncertain which is more admirable: that he conquered it, or that he even dared to attack it. For such a dangerous war, he did not choose robust young men in the first flower of their youth, but mostly veterans—some even retired—who had previously served with his father. He chose them so that you would think them not so much soldiers as elected masters of warfare.

<margin>King Louis is compared to Alexander the Great.</margin>

Therefore, no one in battle thought of flight, but only of victory; hope did not lie in anyone’s feet, but in their arms. In a similar fashion, our most Christian King seems to have acted in this so difficult and laborious Genoese expedition. For he chose not only robust young men or those in the first flower of their youth, but also many veterans most highly instructed in military discipline and experienced in the affairs of war, so that you would think them not so much soldiers as masters of warfare who led the rest of the multitude, both infantry and cavalry, of his army. Among these, the principal leaders are said to be: the Lord of Chaumont, called "The Great" <note>Charles II d'Amboise, Lord of Chaumont, a powerful French commander and Grand Master of France.</note> (as they say in the common tongue), Master of the Royal Household and the King’s Lieutenant General; Lord N. de Molardt, representing the person of the King in the Dauphiné; Lord N. de la Palisse; Lord N., the General of Normandy, whom the aforementioned Lord Grand Master created a Golden Knight; the Duke of Albany; the Count of Roussillon; the Lord of La Roche, called Maugeron; and the spirited man Pierre Terrail, Lord of Bayard <note>Known to history as "the knight without fear and beyond reproach" (le chevalier sans peur et sans reproche).</note>; and many other nobles. All these most strenuous soldiers, along with the others, were prepared not only to courageously withstand the insults of the adversaries, but they feared very little to invade and attack them. Thus, having stormed certain fortifications, they attempted to attack and defeat that strongest fortress situated on the peak of a certain intractable mountain, in which the Genoese placed no small trust. The spirited soldiers climbed like four-legged animals, relying almost

<column-break/>

on hands and feet (as they say), prepared that day either to achieve victory or to die fighting strenuously in arms. (In this place, before the attack, the General of Normandy was decorated with military honors). The adversaries resisted without success; the Lord of La Palisse was wounded. But nonetheless, they proceeded more strenuously, and the French continued the fight. Many of the adversaries were cut down; the rest fled shamefully. The fortress was consumed by fire. At the following light of day, the King arrived, and not long after, behold: those Genoese whom flight had saved, having emerged from the city with others, appeared on the mountain. The French, attacking them, forced them to turn their backs in disgrace. The citizens, indeed noticing the destruction of their soldiers and the less-than-prosperous success of fortune, sent their legates to the Royal Majesty, seeking pardon for their offenses and to be received into grace. The most merciful King humanely received them into grace on this condition: that they submit themselves to the royal mercy and will; which they did. These things having been settled, the King entered Genoa. They exhibited the highest honors to him as a most victorious conqueror, which the other cities subject to the royal jurisdiction, both on this side and that side of the mountains, also performed with all diligence. Someone has most elegantly embraced this royal expedition against the Genoese in these few verses, saying:

-> Cease to marvel, France, at Naples <note>original: "Parthenope," a poetic name for Naples.</note> swiftly conquered, <-
-> and the labors at Parma; you have something greater. <-
-> Louis commands the untamed Ligurians <note>original: "Ligures," the ancient name for the people of the region around Genoa.</note> and the city of Genoa <-
-> to hand over their broken reins in a single day. <-
-> Learn now, nations, what it is to offend Louis: <-
-> He knows how to conquer, and he teaches how to retain the conquered. <-

¶ And let these few things regarding the present business suffice for the reader, given the brevity of this summary.

<meta>This page transitions from the specific account of King Louis XII’s Italian wars to a broader historical supplement (Additamentum) detailing the heroic deeds of various French monarchs throughout history, starting from the early Frankish rulers to the Hundred Years' War.</meta>

# Supplement.

¶ There follow several of the illustrious deeds of the kings of the Franks, collected by way of a supplement to those things which were said of them above.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'L' depicting a male figure (likely a king or noble) standing in a landscape with floral elements.</image-desc>
Lothar II, king of the Gauls <note>original: *gallorum rex*; though the text uses "Gauls," it refers to the Franks and the French throughout</note>, penetrated as far as the Saxons, where he carried out a memorable slaughter, sparing no one of the male sex who exceeded the length of his sword <note>original: *qui gladii sui longitudine excederet*. A traditional medieval trope for a total massacre of all but small children.</note>. Then, having devastated the fields and burned the villages, he returned to France as a glorious victor.

¶ Did not the Basques <note>original: *vascones*; the Gascons/Basques of southwestern France</note> defect from Dagobert, king of the Gauls, after the death of Aubert? At the first encounter with the Franks, they took it poorly, and with many killed and put to flight, some hid themselves in the mountains and others in the woods. But when they had recovered from their flight, they sent messengers to the lord where the war was being waged, promising that they would do as commanded. Thus, the army returned safe to France.

¶ Pope Stephen II blessed Pippin <note>Pippin the Short, father of Charlemagne</note> and his posterity, and he interdicted from the Christian communion any who would rashly move war against the Franks. Pippin, king of the Gauls, led an army against the Lombards. Aistulf <note>original: *Alstulphus*, king of the Lombards</note>, meeting him at the narrow passes of the Alps, contended to prohibit the Franks from crossing. But, unable to withstand the force of the Franks rushing upon him, he retreated to Pavia <note>original: *Papia*</note>. There, surrounded by the Frankish soldiers, he gave forty hostages to Pippin. He swore to the Roman Pontiff that he would restore whatever he had taken. And so, with a very strong force of soldiers assigned to Stephen, Pippin restored the Pope to his seat. Once Pippin's departure for France was known, Aistulf, having no care for either the hostages or his oath, released himself from none of his promises. For that reason, Pippin, having crossed the Alps again, besieged Aistulf in Pavia. Pressed by the siege, Aistulf restored Ravenna to Pippin, along with other cities he had taken from the Pope which belonged to the Exarchate <note>The Exarchate of Ravenna, a Byzantine administrative center in Italy</note>. Having received them, Pippin assigned them to Stephen. Aistulf himself, not much later, happened to fall from his horse and broke his neck. The Saxons, to whom the name of the Franks had always been hateful, attempted to block the way of Pippin as he set out into Saxony <note>original: *saxonianam*</note>. But having made a breakthrough, Pippin compelled the enemy to retreat. Finally, Pippin punished the defeated with an annual tribute <note>original: *pensione*</note> of three hundred of the strongest horses, which they were to bring to him every year in France at the time of the <term>parliament</term> <note>original: *parlamenti tempore*. The translator notes: "For so the Franks call a public assembly for the administration of justice."</note>.

<column-break/>

¶ Louis <note>Louis the German</note>, the son of Louis the Pious, held a victory over the Vandals, having captured their leader.

¶ Louis the Younger <note>Louis VII</note>, the son of Louis the Fat, king of the Gauls, after Conrad the Emperor of the Germans suffered a heavy slaughter of his men by the Sultan of Iconium <note>The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum</note>, and having learned of the matter, Louis passed from there and pitched camp at the river Maeander <note>original: *venandri*</note>, eager to join battle with the Turks. While he held his station in that place, the Frankish soldiers from the other bank of the river prohibited our enemies from gathering water with javelins and slings. But having found a ford, the Franks crossed the river and advanced against the Turks. Having partly routed, partly killed, or captured them, they plundered their camp and carried away immense wealth from there.

¶ In the times of Philip Augustus, king of the Franks, the Albigensian heretics reigned in the province of Narbonne. The obscene foulness of the Albigensians had defenders, namely: the King of Aragon, the Count of Saint-Gilles <note>Raymond VI of Toulouse, often associated with the Saint-Gilles lineage</note>, and the Prince of Foix. Having led out immense forces, they besieged Simon <note>Simon de Montfort, leader of the Albigensian Crusade</note>, the leader of the army for the king of the Gauls, at the fortress of Muret <note>original: *murellum*</note>. Although Simon had few armed men with him in the garrison, despairing of nothing after a divine service was performed by a priest, and after he and his men had first purified themselves by the sacrament of confession, he made a sudden sally and killed the King of Aragon and eighteen thousand of the enemy, while he himself had lost only eight from his garrison. It may rightly be believed that God helped the Count, who was fighting correctly for his religion.

¶ Philip, king of the Gauls, called Augustus, defeated the Emperor Otto IV <note>original: *othonem quintum*, but historically Otto IV</note> eighteen miles distant from Tournai <note>The Battle of Bouvines, 1214</note>; and at the same time his son Louis <note>later Louis VIII</note> obtained a victory over the Poitevins.

¶ Saint Louis <note>Louis IX</note> at Carthage turned the Saracens to flight, with many being killed. And after the victory was held, the king entered Carthage.

¶ In the year of salvation 1382 <note>The text says 1301 (*millesimo trecentesimo vno*), but the event and King Charles VI identify it as the Battle of Roosebeke in 1382</note>, the Flemings were overcome at Roosebeke by Charles VI and the Franks. Of these, forty thousand met their death.

¶ In the times of Charles VII, king of the Gauls, about three thousand of the English fell in battle. Many from the nobility of the English were captured along with Talbot <note>John Talbot, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury, a famous English commander</note>. Then Janville <note>original: *ienuilla*</note> and certain other places throughout Beauce <note>original: *belsia*</note> came into Charles's power. At Châlons <note>original: *cathalanuenses*</note>, a great slaughter of the English was made and the English enemy was overcome.

¶ There was during these days near Argentan <note>original: *argentonum*</note> in the territory of Auge <note>original: *agri fagiensis*</note> a persistent battle; and an admirable fight of thirty Franks against as many English...

# Of the Kings of the Franks

...reigned. For no one left the battle without being wounded. Finally, nine of the enemy's number were slain along with the Marshal of Argenton <note>original: *argentoni marescallo*; likely referring to Jean de Brosse, Marshal of France and Lord of Boussac and Sainte-Sévère, though "Argenton" was a significant title in the French court</note>, and the remaining English committed themselves to flight.

¶ During these same days, de Loré <note>original: *Delorus*; refers to Ambroise de Loré (1395–1446), a prominent French commander and comrade of Joan of Arc</note> contended in battle with the English. Indeed, the infantry, who stood at about seven thousand, positioned themselves between the fortresses and the English; by this means, they routed the intercepted enemy, killing many and taking several prisoners. William de Loré enjoyed the same kindness of fortune at Sillé-le-Guillaume. For when the English were moving from the fortress of Sainte-Suzanne toward Sillé-le-Guillaume with their plunder, de Loré arrived unexpectedly and slew two hundred of the English, carrying off the spoils and recovering the captives. Nor did he experience worse fortune against the Earl of Arundel <note>original: *comitem darouellum*</note> in the meadows of the Varenne river <note>original: *amnis fatrensis*</note> near the village which the inhabitants call Gravelle. For with one hundred and sixty horsemen, he dared to do battle against three thousand English, and he carried off the spoils from the enemy.

¶ Around these days, four hundred English perished at the stone bridge which reaches across the Seine not far from Saint-Denis; many were captured along with Thomas Beaumont, the commander of the soldiers.

¶ At Castillon, eight hundred English of obscure name fell in battle along with forty illustrious men, among whom was the son of Talbot <note>John Talbot, 1st Earl of Shrewsbury, and his son John, Viscount Lisle, both died at the Battle of Castillon in 1453, the final battle of the Hundred Years' War</note>. It is reported that the number of those fleeing and those who committed themselves to the Dordogne river was equal. And when the English saw that Talbot himself had been killed by a French archer, they turned to flight.

¶ In the times of Louis XI, at Tournai, the Duke of Guelders, equipped with one thousand five hundred Germans <note>original: *alemanis*</note> and intending to burn the suburbs of Tournai, was killed in the first conflict by the people of Tournai and carried into the city. In a second encounter, with the French cavalry bursting out against the Germans, they committed a slaughter of two thousand along with some of the city's inhabitants, while seven hundred were taken alive. And when the Flemish had their camp in great numbers at the White Ditch <note>original: *blancā fossam*</note>, they were routed by forces sent against them and about two thousand fell; of the rest caught in flight, about another two thousand also perished.

->**The End.**<-

<column-break/>

¶ Since mention has occurred in the preceding sections regarding the most Christian kings of the Franks, I thought I would be doing something not unwelcome to the studious reader if I added to these accounts their genealogy, reduced into an epitome from both ancient and more recent writers of history.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'G' featuring scrolling floral motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc>
Gaul (according to the witness of Solinus) extends between the Rhine and the Pyrenees, and likewise between the Ocean and the Cevennes mountains and the Jura <note>original: *lirem*; likely referring to the Jura mountains</note>. They are happy with very rich soil and conveniently productive in fruit-bearing plants, most of them planted with vines and shrubs. Everything is most blessed for the use of living creatures. It is watered by the waters of rivers and springs, but sometimes by sacred and steaming springs. 

Furthermore, one Gaul is Cisalpine and the other is Transalpine. Transalpine Gaul—which is called Cisalpine by the Italians—is named "Togata" <note>term: *Togata* (Toga-wearing Gaul); the part of Gaul south of the Alps that adopted Roman dress</note> from the use of the toga. It is divided into Transpadane and Cispadane. Cisalpine—which the Italians call Transalpine—is called by the single name "Comata" <note>term: *Comata* (Long-haired Gaul); referring to the unconquered, "barbarian" Gauls who kept their hair long</note> and is cut into three kinds of peoples, most distinct in their spirits. From the Scheldt to the Seine is Belgica, from which come the Belgians; from there to the Garonne is Celtica, from which come the Celts (and those on their borders with the Spaniards are the Celtiberians). This same area is also called Lugdunensis from Lyon <note>original: *lugduno*</note>, the most noble and distinguished city of the Gauls. From there to the extent of the Pyrenees mountains is Aquitaine, which was formerly called Aremotica, from which come the Aquitanians and the region of Aquitaine.

Gaul is called a "milky" region and "white," for the Gauls are white beyond all others. Wherefore by the Greeks, on account of this kind of color, they are called Galatians <note>original: *galate*</note> from that which is *gala* <note>gloss: milk</note>. From Gaul itself, the region of Galatia bordering Phrygia in Asia Minor is named, which the Gauls coming from Europe once inhabited; from this they were called Galatians, and this region is called Gallo-Graecia, from which the Gallo-Greeks come. For when both Gauls and Greeks had come, having been called to help by the King of Bithynia, they held a part of the kingdom and were called Gallo-Greeks by the Greeks and Gauls. 

And as Pomponius Mela—though an enemy of the Gauls—writes in his third book: The Gauls have their own eloquence and the Druids as masters of wisdom. These men profess to know the magnitude and form of the earth and the world, the motions of the heaven and the stars, and what the gods wish. One of the things they teach has flowed out into the common people, namely, so that they might be better in wars: that souls are eternal and there is another life among the spirits of the dead. Parthenius of Phocis, in the first book of his histories, says: "The Franks, a Gallic race, dwell near the Alpine mountains," and nothing else besides. Some think the cause of their name is their "immunity" from taxes <note>note: play on *Franci* (Franks) and *franchise* (freedom/exemption)</note>, from which they were relieved for ten years by the Emperor Valentinian. Some interpret "Franks" as being "fierce" <note>original: *feroces*</note> after they tamed the Alans; these people were later called Sicambria...

<meta>This page continues the historical chronicle of the French monarchy. While the previous page detailed military engagements involving the Earl of Arundel and French commanders like Ambroise de Loré during the 15th century, this page provides a retrospective genealogical account of the origins of the Frankish people, beginning with their legendary roots and tracing the Merovingian dynasty from the 5th and 6th centuries.</meta>

# Genealogy

Driven by Caesar himself, they <note>The Franks</note> had for a long time claimed an immunity from tribute that was never truly granted; they eventually refused it altogether. Having chosen Marcomir, Sunno, and Genebauld from among their own nobility as dukes, they settled along the Rhine. There, they founded a town and gave it the name Frankfurt. They first gained possession in Gaul of the city of Trier, which the Roman prefect Lucius surrendered to them. However, as their current fortune did not seem sufficient for them, they set out to seek new homes. Wandering, they reached the banks of the Seine; there, captivated by the beauty of the place, they all settled. The administration of their affairs was entrusted to Marcomir, whom they greatly celebrated and revered, for it was the common opinion that he was descended from the blood of Priam <note>original: *Priami sanguine*; this refers to the popular medieval myth that the Franks were descendants of the Trojans who fled the fall of Troy</note>.

¶ Afterward, they promoted his son, named Pharamund, to the royal height, making him the first among them to hold this rank. He ruled for eleven years. Upon his death, his son Chlodio succeeded him; he was nicknamed "the Long-Haired" <note>original: *capillatus*; the Merovingian kings were famously known as the "long-haired kings," as their uncut hair was a symbol of their royal authority and vitality</note> because of his long locks. Through successful battles, he subdued the first nations: the Thuringians, the people of Tournai, and those of Cambrai. Leaving no offspring of his own, he ended his days in the twentieth year of his reign.

¶ In his place succeeded Meroveus, who was of the closest lineage to Chlodio. Constant report has it that he fell fighting for the Romans against the Huns and Visigoths on the Catalaunian Plains <note>The Battle of the Catalaunian Plains (451 AD) was a pivotal moment where a coalition led by the Roman general Aetius stopped Attila the Hun</note>.

¶ Childeric received the paternal honor. He fell into pride and luxury through his good fortune, and because of his inability to rule, he was driven out. However, he was recalled through the wealth and faction of Ginomadus, a prince of his people to whose protection he had fled. Childeric defeated the Roman Aegidius <note>original: *Gillonem*; referring to Aegidius, the Roman commander in Gaul</note>, who had presided over the Suebi, in an equal battle. He brought the people of Orléans and Angers under his rule. In the twenty-fourth year of his reign, he departed from among men.

¶ Clovis, born to his father Childeric, took up the empire. He brought Reims and Soissons under his power. He took Clotilde as his wife, whose uncle was Gondebald, King of the Burgundians. He allowed the children he had by her to be taught the Christian doctrine, with which their mother had imbued them, although he himself persisted in the ceremonies of his ancestors. He enviously complained to Clotilde that her gods were angry because their worship had been neglected; one of her sons had been taken from the living, and another was afflicted with sickness, his life in doubt. But when the boy recovered because of a vow made by his mother, and Clovis himself defeated the Germans in a perilous battle, he converted to his wife's religion. He was cleansed with water by Remigius, the Bishop of Reims, and anointed with oil which, according to rumor, was brought from heaven by a dove <note>This refers to the Holy Ampulla, used for centuries to anoint the Kings of France</note>. From this, the custom remains that the kings of the Franks are anointed with it when they receive the crown and the insignias of honor. Thus, Clovis, having accepted the true worship of God, subdued the Burgundians, the Aquitanians, and the Goths in war. And having placed a garrison in Toulouse,

<column-break/>

he kept it under his power. He granted Burgundy to Gondebald, his wife's uncle and the biological brother of his father-in-law, after first receiving from him a large sum of money as they had agreed.

¶ Upon his death, the kingdom was divided into four parts among his sons. Of these, Theodoric received Metz; Clodomir, Orléans; Chlothar, Soissons; and Childebert was allotted Paris. At the instigation of Clotilde, Clodomir undertook a war against the Burgundians and Gondebald, who had removed Clotilde’s parents from their midst—killing her maternal grandfather and grandmother—and had seized the kingdom that belonged to Clotilde by the law of nations. Burning with a womanly desire for revenge and a lust for ruling, she incited her son against Gondebald. It cost Clodomir dearly to have obeyed his mother; for after leading his army into Burgundy, he fell while fighting bravely in the battle line. He left the victory to his men, along with three sons: Theobald, Gunther, and Clodoard.

¶ Childebert, King of the Parisians and one of the sons of Clovis, undertook a war against Amalaric, King of Spain, for a pious cause. Childebert's sister was married to Amalaric; she was of unpolluted religion and most observant of the worship of the true God. Since she could be turned by neither prayers nor threats to the deceits of the Arian sect <note>Arianism was a Christian belief deemed heretical by the Catholic Church because it denied the full divinity of Christ</note>, in which her husband was steeped, she was treated shamefully by him. Moved by these injuries, her brother entered into battle and was victorious; he forced the Spaniards to obey his commands as far as the borders of Toledo. He died without offspring in the forty-ninth year of his reign.

¶ Theodoric, who ruled the people of Metz, and Chlothar, who ruled Soissons, were the survivors of the brothers I have mentioned. Panting for the kingdom of Clodomir, they dared a deed of barbaric cruelty. They summoned their brother's sons from their grandmother Clotilde, who was educating them in Paris. Two of them, Theobald and Gunther, they foully murdered at Orléans. Clodoard, having escaped the slaughter, fled to the altar of an unplundered temple, which they call a Sanctuary <note>original: *Asylum*</note>. There, for as long as he lived, he worshipped the divinity of that most holy place with exceptional zeal. For this reason, after his death, he was consecrated and numbered among the saints <note>Saint Cloud</note>. Theodoric (his fate thus punishing his immense greed and ambition) was snatched away childless to the shades of the Underworld. From this, the kingdom—which they had torn apart into four members, as it were—was restored to its original form and a single body. Chlothar took possession of it, and when he had reigned for fifty-one years, he met his death and was buried at Soissons. However, the example of their father drove his sons toward every kind of crime. And so, while each of them strove to occupy the paternal throne for himself by means of both good and evil arts...

[Of the Frankish Kings]

...their plans did not succeed: they themselves divided the kingdom into four parts, according to their number, just as they had gathered. To **Charibert**, the eldest, fell Paris; to **Guntram**, Orleans; to **Sigebert**, Metz; and to **Chilperic**, Soissons. **Charibert** <note>original: *Theobertus*; though the text uses *Theobertus*, this refers to Charibert I (r. 561–567)</note>, or as others call him, **Antibert**, was more corrupt than any woman: being most abandoned to lust, he died prematurely in the embrace of concubines. From those multiple marriages, he left no more than one son, who followed his father to the grave immediately after. **Sigebert**, having attempted to overwhelm his unwary brother **Chilperic** with a sudden war, was killed by assassins sent against him. For when **Chilperic**, besieged by his brother at Tournai (where he had retreated in flight), had little faith in his own resources, his wife **Fredegund**—whom he had married after setting aside his previous wife, **Galswintha** <note>original: *Balsonda*</note>, the daughter of Athanagild, King of Spain—shared her husband's fortune and conceived a plan not fitting for a woman. She prepared two young men of daring spirit for any deed; burdened with the hope of rewards and present payment, she sent them into the enemy’s camp. These men attacked and slew **Sigebert** while he was acting without caution. He died in the fourteenth year of his reign, survived by his son **Childebert** <note>Childebert II</note>, whom he had fathered by **Brunhilda**, the daughter of Athanagild, King of Spain (of whom we have shown **Fredegund** was also born) <note>This reflects a common medieval genealogical confusion; Fredegund was actually a low-born servant, while Brunhilda was the Visigothic princess</note>.
¶ Upon the loss of his father, **Childebert** was despoiled of a good part of the kingdom by **Chilperic**. **Guntram**, King of Orleans, his other uncle, adopted him in hope of succession since he lacked children of his own.
¶ However, a grave dissension soon arose between them over the case of **Theodore, Bishop of Marseille**, and **Guntram** revoked the adoption. Thence **Childebert** returned into favor with **Chilperic**, and both led an army against **Guntram** under shared auspices. At last, after matters were settled on equal terms, **Chilperic**, falling into a snare while returning from hunting at night, was struck down by **Landric** in a certain forest. This was by the abominable crime of his wife **Fredegund**, who had committed adultery with **Landric** and preferred her lover to her husband. **Chlothar** <note>Chlothar II</note> survived his father **Chilperic**. **Guntram**, having again reconciled with **Childebert**, died after reigning thirty years and named him his heir.
¶ And so **Childebert**, surnamed "the Younger," died not long after from a draft of poison along with his wife. He was survived by his sons: **Theodebert**, the elder, who ruled the people of Metz (called **Austrasia**), and **Theoderic**, King of the Burgundians, as well as **Childebert’s** own mother, **Brunhilda**. Therefore, **Childebert** held the eighth station of the kingdom along with his cousin **Chlothar**. After his death, the supreme power rested with the one **Chlothar**; however, he took the sons of **Childebert** into a part of the

<column-break/>

government.
¶ But when the brothers **Theodebert** and **Theoderic** were urged by the deceitful schemes of their grandmother **Brunhilda** to sever their shared kinship with the sword, a war broke out between them at the town of **Toul**, which was then being built. As fortune inclined toward **Theoderic** in the struggle, **Theodebert** sought safety in flight. When this was announced, **Theoderic** populated everything with fire and sword like an enemy. He did not make an end until the followers and paid allies of **Theodebert**, having accepted terms, brought the severed head of their king to **Theoderic**. In this manner, the people of Metz passed into the dominion of **Theoderic**. From there, the children of **Theodebert** were led away, among whom was a girl of overflowing beauty; but the males were led into the sight of their great-grandmother **Brunhilda**, who, with a savage womanly spirit, cut their throats. When **Theoderic** intended to take that same girl for himself in marriage, **Brunhilda** intervened, contending it was a sin and not permitted by law to marry a brother’s daughter. **Theoderic**, moved by rage and unable to bear the woman's inconsistency—since she had authorized the war against his brother by affirming he was not from the same father but conceived in adultery, yet now asserted he was the very same biological brother to prevent the marriage—rejected her with sharp insults and barely restrained himself from her destruction. Therefore, the fierce woman, returning to a crime she had long before pre-meditated, mixed poison; and with **Theoderic** extinguished, she piled parricide upon parricide.
¶ By this outcome, the empire of all France was reduced to the one **Chlothar**, the son of **Chilperic**, King of Soissons, and **Fredegund**. **Brunhilda** strove equally against him, earnestly caring that **Sigebert**, **Theodebert**, and a son of a concubine (as was said) should succeed to the paternal place. But the king, the princes, and all the best men, loathing her, opened the gates to **Chlothar**. **Chlothar** overcame **Sigebert** when he marched into battle and captured him alive along with **Brunhilda**. Having now established the kingdom, he exacted punishment from **Brunhilda** for so many impious slaughters—a woman worthy of more than a single and simple death. After many famous deeds performed at such a height of royal power, and after forty-four years had passed, he departed from human affairs. He appointed his son **Dagobert** as sole heir, whom his first wife **Engeltrude** had borne him, except for **Aquitaine**, which he left to **Charibert** <note>Charibert II</note>, born of another wife.
¶ **Charibert**, having obtained **Aquitaine**, died not long after at Toulouse, with an only son surviving who followed his father to the grave prematurely; thus **Aquitaine** also returned to **Dagobert** himself.
¶ This is that **Dagobert** who [founded the church of] Saint Deny[s]...

<meta>This page continues the history of the Frankish kings, specifically the transition from the Merovingian dynasty to the rise of the Carolingian Mayors of the Palace. # Genealogy.

...built a temple <note>The Abbey of St. Denis</note>; in it, he placed the ashes of Saint Denis and his companions, Rusticus and Eleutherius, with great religious devotion and ornament. At last, having died, he wished to be buried there.

After **Dagobert**, affairs passed to **Clovis** <note>original: *Ludovicus*; refers to Clovis II (r. 639–657)</note>, his son by **Balthild** <note>original: *Mathilde*</note>, whom **Dagobert** had married after losing his previous wife. He, born of a lawful mother, obtained the whole kingdom, except for Normandy or (as others call it) **Neustria**, which **Sigebert**—born of **Ragnertruda**, his father’s mistress—obtained with his permission.

**Clovis**, however, performed nothing memorable during the sixteen years in which he commanded; he departed from human affairs without glory. He left behind children by his wife **Balthild**, of the Saxon nation: **Chlothar**, **Childeric**, and **Theuderic**.

**Chlothar**, who had succeeded his father by right of age, departed this life four years later. The Franks received **Theuderic**, the youngest by birth, into the kingship because he seemed more capable of holding it, while sending **Childeric** away into **Austrasia**. Because **Theuderic** was given over to laziness, he did not grant the common people the opportunity of approaching or greeting him, except only on the first of May <note>original: *kal. tantum maijs*; the "Mayfield" assembly</note>. At that time, he was occupied with sending gifts back and forth and administered the kingdom through others. The nobles by no means endured this indignity. Therefore, they forced **Theuderic** and **Ebroin**, the Prefect of the Guard <note>term: *præfectum prætoziu*; the Mayor of the Palace</note>, into the confines of a monastery.

**Childeric**, summoned from Austrasia, came to the throne. When he began to rage barbarously against his own people, and had ordered a man of noble birth to be bound to a stake and beaten with clubs, the atrocity of the deed so moved the minds of all that the man whom **Childeric** had punished found many others to conspire with him against the life of the tyrant. Thus, they ambushed him as he was returning from hunting and slaughtered him along with his pregnant wife, **Bilichild** <note>original: *Alcide*</note>. This made it necessary to flee back to **Theuderic**, whom we said had been driven into the enclosures of a monastery.

Around the same time, due to the inactivity of the kings <note>term: *inertia regum*; refers to the "Do-Nothing Kings" (*Rois fainéants*)</note>, the Prefect of the Palace <note>Mayor of the Palace</note> held the primary dignity from the king. All the most powerful of the Franks strove for this with the greatest contention. **Pepin** of Austrasia was the Prefect—the one to whom the nickname "the Short" <note>original: *pusilli*; refers to Pepin of Herstal here, though the nickname is usually associated with his grandson, Pepin the Short</note> was given due to his small stature—and he rose through various fortunes. Then **Theuderic** departed from life in the nineteenth year after he began to reign. **Clovis** [IV] was substituted in his father's place; three years later he yielded to nature, leaving the kingdom to his brother **Childebert**.

**Childebert**, the third of this name, was on the throne for fifteen years but was not long among human affairs. He died leaving behind a son, **Dagobert**.

During the reign of **Dagobert** [III], various movements of war

<column-break/>

arose among the nobles of the kingdom, as each person aimed for the Prefecture <note>the Mayoralty of the Palace</note> for himself. The favor of men varied toward this one or that one. For as long as **Dagobert** held the rudder of the realm, he did everything according to the judgment of his wife **Plectrude**, and of **Pepin** and **Theudoald**, the Prefects, under whose guardianship the king remained. However, **Theudoald** was cast down from his honor by a victory that was neither bloodless nor easy; **Raganfrid** <note>original: *Rangnefredo*</note> was substituted in his place. Not long after, **Dagobert** exited the human race without offspring, and now the royal line had failed from the stock. Therefore, the nobles first placed a certain priest named **Daniel**—in whom they had great confidence—over the guards and the palace. They waited until he could grow his hair and beard in the secular fashion <note>The Merovingian kings were known as the "Long-Haired Kings," a symbol of their right to rule</note>. Having been consecrated to the sacred rites, and according to the custom handed down by either the Egyptians or the Jews, they had their heads half-shaved even at that age, and did not nourish a beard for the sake of divine freedom, contrary to the custom of the secular world. Therefore, with his tonsure and habit changed, he was promoted from the Prefecture to the royal pinnacle, and instead of **Daniel**, he was called **Chilperic**.

During those same days, **Charles Martel**, the son of **Pepin**, broke out of prison and loosened the chains in which he had been cast by his stepmother **Plectrude**. Having seized arms, he flew to assert his claim to the Prefecture of the palace which his father had held. King **Chilperic** and **Raganfrid** (who was then the Prefect) came out to meet him. They fought for a long time with victory being uncertain, until **Martel** was turned to flight. But having soon increased his army, he returned and drove both of them from the borders of the kingdom. **Chilperic** himself fled to the protection of **Ludo**, prince and ally of the Basques. **Raganfrid** withdrew to Angers; **Martel**, having brought him under his power, released him. He further granted him a certain town to hold where he might rule, and having taken up the Prefecture due to him by hereditary right, he restored **Chilperic** to the kingdom.

Then a new king was created by the vote of the princes, with the support of **Martel**, the Prefect of the Palace: a certain **Childeric** or (as I have found him called by others) **Theuderic** [IV], the son of **Dagobert**, the last of that name. They made a great show of saying he had been educated among the holy virgins of the town of **Chelles** <note>original: *Calensis*</note>. Nevertheless, the sum of power remained entirely with **Martel**. He overcame the King of Spain <note>The Umayyad commander</note>, whose name was **Abdul Rahman** <note>original: *Abdimaro*</note>, in a just battle. He recovered the cities of **Bordeaux** and **Poitiers**, which had been occupied by **Abdul Rahman**. And when he had successfully administered the affairs of the Franks for thirty-five years, upon his death, he was gathered to the house of **Denis** <note>St. Denis</note>.

### Of the Frankish Kings.

...he was laid in a tomb which is still seen today made of alabaster. Before his death, he distributed his lands among his children. To the impious **Carloman**, he granted **Austrasia**, **Swabia**, **Alemannia**, and **Lorraine**. He placed **Pippin** over the **Gauls** <note>original: *Ballis*; referring to the Western Frankish lands</note> who were under his jurisdiction. He passed over **Grifo**, the youngest by birth, in his will. **Carloman**, after many great deeds performed bravely and famously, grew weary of glory and retired to a monastery he had founded at **Mount Soracte**. There, devoted to religion and divine worship, he lived for some time. Finally, desiring a quieter life, he moved to **Monte Cassino**, leaving all care of affairs to his brother **Pippin**.

<margin>He instituted senators.</margin>
**Pippin**, the second of this house, was created king from the rank of **Mayor of the Palace** <note>original: *prefecto pretorij*; a Romanized term used here to describe the high administrative office that preceded the kingship</note> by the decree of **Zachary**, the Roman Pope, on account of the laziness of **Childeric**. The same **Childeric**, forced to return to his former low status, again took up the habit of a monk. Meanwhile, **Pippin**, having crossed the Alps again, brought aid to the struggling Pope **Stephen** against the **Lombards**. Having defeated them in battle, he restored **Stephen** himself to the papal heights. He was also the first to institute the councils of **Senators** <note>This refers to the early foundations of the French Parlements or Royal Councils</note>, though they did not have the same form then as they do now. For he ordained by law that once a year the princes should assemble there, where he would issue decrees partly for judging disputes and partly for ordering the kingdom. The princes also chose "senators" from the senate to preside over the court, who always accompanied the king. Finally, they received a permanent home in **Paris**. When **Pippin** ended his life, he was buried at the **Church of Saint Denis** next to his father, though in another tomb which he had cared to have made for himself while living.

<margin>He instituted the twelve peers of France.</margin>
**Charles**—who was later called **the Great** <note>Charlemagne</note> on account of the magnitude of his deeds—and **Carloman** succeeded their father **Pippin**. Both were designated kings by the decree of the nobles, but a few days later, after **Carloman** was removed from human affairs, the supreme kingship was transferred to his brother **Charles**. At the request of Pope **Hadrian** through his legates, **Charles** led troops into Italy against **Desiderius**, the last king of the **Lombards**. Having overcome him, he restored the Church's property. Then, gifted with special privileges by the Pope, he departed. After a war lasting thirty years, he conquered the **Saxons** and compelled them to the true worship of God. In preparation for an expedition against the **Saracens** <note>Islamic forces in the Iberian Peninsula</note> who then held **Spain**, he instituted twelve whom they call **Peers**. Six of these were from the college of priests, including three leaders: the **Archbishop of Reims**, and the **Bishops of Laon and Langres**. Also three counts who were bishops: of **Beauvais**, **Noyon**, and **Châlons**. The rest were to be from that class of men who are 

<column-break/>

not ordained, whom they commonly call **Laymen** <note>original: *Laicos*; from the Greek *laikos* meaning "of the people"</note>. These were three dukes: of **Burgundy**, **Normandy**, and **Aquitaine**; and three counts: of **Champagne**, **Flanders**, and **Toulouse**. He also subdued the **Huns**, and received the crown and insignia of empire from Pope **Leo**. He established schools for the best arts and a gathering of studies in **Paris** which they call the **University** <note>It was a common historical tradition to credit Charlemagne with founding the University of Paris</note>. From his marriage to **Hildegard**, who was of a Swabian family, he had sons: **Charles**, **Pippin**, and **Louis**, to whom he distributed the empires during his life. To **Pippin**, **Italy**; to **Charles**, **Hither Gaul**. He took **Louis** into a partnership of the principality. Soon, in the forty-seventh year of his reign, the fourteenth of his empire, and the eight-hundred-and-fifteenth year of salvation, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February <note>January 28th, 814 AD; the text says 815</note>, he died at the age of seventy-two and was buried at **Aachen** <note>original: *aquisgrani*</note>.

**Louis**, son of **Charles**, the first of this name, called **the Pious** <note>original: *pius*</note> because of the mildness of his character, although he performed many famous deeds generously and holily, could not, however, lead his sons to the same way of life. They were **Lothair**, **Pippin**, and **Louis** (named after his father). At the instigation of certain treacherous men who accused their father of indulging too much in **Bernard**—who was said to be having an affair with the Empress **Judith**—they took up unpious arms against their father **Louis**. Such madness had invaded them that they could not be brought to a sound mind even by the authority of Pope **Gregory**, who had traveled from Rome to the lands of the Gauls for this one reason. As their madness grew daily, they threw their father and their youngest brother **Charles** <note>Charles the Bald</note> into prison at the **Church of Saint Medard** in **Soissons**. They banished **Judith** to Italy, to the town of **Tortona** <note>original: *Dertonen*</note> in Liguria. Earlier, after tearing her away from her marriage to the father, they had seen to it that she was taken to **Aquitaine** to be guarded in the **Nunnery of Saint Radegund**, even though **Louis**, after the crime of adultery had been conspired and cleared, had joined her to himself in lawful marriage. Having divided their father's empire among themselves, they handed over the father and the brother **Charles** to **Lothair**, who was older, to be kept. Thus, **Louis** set out for **Bavaria** and **Pippin** for **Aquitaine**. They forced the father himself to set aside his insignia, abdicate the empire, and put on the habit of a monk. But as certain of the nobles—whose power **Lothair** feared—were indignant at the situation, **Louis** himself regained both his freedom and the empire. Immediately, he recalled **Judith** from Italy. Around the same time, **Hiero** <note>Likely referring to a Viking leader or early Norman prince</note>, prince of **Normandy**, was converted to the true religion of Christ. **Louis** departed from humanity in the sixty-eighth year of his age, with his children surviving him, except for **Pippin**.
