->### Genealogy.<-

**Charles**, the youngest by birth, ruled over the **Franks**; **Lothair** over **Germany**; **Louis** obtained **Bavaria**; and **Pippin**, the son of the **Pippin** whom we mentioned had died before his father, held **Aquitania**. 
To **Charles**, who was surnamed **the Bald**, fell the empire of the **Franks** upon the death of his father **Louis**. **Lothair** and **Louis**, his brothers, took up arms against him, but having been defeated by him, they finally laid down their weapons under certain conditions. Eventually, **Lothair** himself, having devoted himself to a religious life, surrendered the kingdom to his sons **Lothair** and **Louis**. Of these, **Lothair** obtained **Italy**; having been designated Emperor, he died. 
**Charles**, therefore, the one we have shown was called **the Bald**, was the paternal uncle of this **Lothair**. Hurrying into **Italy** by great and uninterrupted marches through the narrow passes of the **Alps**—which the others had blocked and fortified with a garrison—he drove out the sons of his brother **Louis**. Having been called Emperor by the Roman Pope **John**, he returned from **Italy** to **France**, and from there back to **Italy** again. While he was frequently leading his army back and forth to protect the dignity of the Church and the borders of the Empire from the **Moors** <note>original: *mauritanis*; referring to Saracen raiders</note> who were devastating everything with frequent incursions, he is believed to have been removed from this world by a draught of poison through the work of **Sedechias**, a **Jew** by nation, whom he used as his physician. His body was carried as far as **Vercelli**, and from there across the **Alps** into **Gaul**, where it was buried according to custom at **Paris** in the Church of **Saint Denis**.
After **the Bald**, his son **Louis** held the reins of the Empire; he was the one called **the Stammerer** <note>original: *balbus*</note> because of a speech impediment. Having been declared Emperor by the same Roman Pope, he passed away at **Compiègne**. 
Succession to the kingdom fell to his son, also named **Louis** after his father, and his younger brother **Carloman** (as the **Gauls** call him in their native tongue), who was allotted **Aquitania** and **Burgundy**. **The Stammerer** had fathered both by a noble girl, but not from a lawful marriage. Therefore, when **Louis** was taken early from human affairs after receiving the paternal honor, and upon the death of **Carloman**, **Charles** was accepted into the kingdom. This **Charles** was the son of **Louis the Bavarian** or (as others prefer to call him) **the German**. He was born to the one whom **Louis**, surnamed **the Pious**, had begotten. This **Charles** was called **the Idle** <note>original: *maleferiatus*; literally "badly holidaying" or "unemployed"</note> on account of his laziness, as he did nothing of importance. Thus, he wasted away from leisure and, having quickly met his fate, left the royal palace vacant for his son.
**Charles**, who also bore his father's name, was a man without deceit or trickery, for which reason he was called **the Simple**. To **Rollo**, a worshiper of the Roman gods <note>A common medieval way of describing Norse paganism</note> and skilled in war, he offered the marriage of his daughter **Gisela** <note>original: *Stillie*</note>, provided that he would lay down his arms and accept the Christian dogma. He accepted these 

<column-break/>

conditions of peace, and received as a dowry **Neustria**, which was soon called **Normandy** by the **Norman** settlers. For himself, **Rollo** took the name of **Robert**, from **Robert, Count of Poitou**, who supported him at the baptismal font on his day of purification. **Charles the Simple**, moreover, took as his wife **Eadgifu** <note>original: *Algivaz*</note>, the daughter of the King of the **English**, who bore him **Louis**. He overcame his rebellious son-in-law **Rollo** in battle. When he had come to the town of **Péronne**, he was thrown into custody by **Herbert**, the petty king of **Vermandois**, into whose favor he had turned. Meanwhile, the **Franks** created for themselves a king in **Rudolph**, the son of **Carloman**, Duke of **Burgundy**; for which reason **Louis**, the son of **Charles the Simple** and his mother **Eadgifu**, sought **England** in flight.
In the meantime, **Rudolph** had held the kingdom thus acquired for two decades, and **Charles the Simple** had passed from life in prison, when the **Franks** recalled **Louis** and his mother **Eadgifu** from **England**. Having gained control of affairs, he experienced varied fortune. For it is said he was committed to prison on a certain day by the **Normans**, and having been led out from there to **Bamberg** <note>original: *Embergam*</note>, he joined to himself in marriage the daughter of **Otto**, King of **Germany**, and fathered by her two children, **Lothair** and **Charles**. He closed his final day at **Reims**, and was brought into the Church of **Saint Remigius** in the year of Christian salvation nine hundred and sixty, with the sons I mentioned surviving him. Of these, **Charles** led a private life. The kingdom passed to **Lothair**, who did nothing worthy of that role, except that he led an army against the **Normans** and **Otto**, his grandfather, with little honor. He died without offspring and was buried at **Reims** in the same church as his father.
And when **Lothair's** brother **Charles** aspired to the kingdom—his previous contempt for which he had displayed—he was captured by **Abbot Hugh**. This man, the son of a prelate named **Syrus** <note>The text here attempts to explain the name 'Capet'</note>—otherwise called **Capet**—was born, as they say, from the family of the Counts of **Paris**. Through the treachery of Bishop **Ascelin** <note>original: *Ezellini*</note>, **Charles** was captured at the town of **Laon**, the seat of his home, and placed in the custody of the **Orléanais**. In that state of affairs, however, he had two children: **Louis** and **Charles**, named after his father.
**Hugh**, however, applied himself more to the arts of the occupied royalty, and conducted himself as a lawful king until, upon his death, he was brought to the tombs of the Frankish kings at the Church of **Saint Denis** in the year of the Lord’s birth 998.
**Robert** succeeded **Hugh**, being born of him; he was most skilled in ecclesiastical knowledge. In the solemnities of the Mass, he instituted the rhythmic measures which are called "responsories," the beginning of which is: *May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us* <note>original: *Sancti spũs adsit nobis gratia*</note>. Masses...

->## Of the Kings of the Franks.<-

The mention of the "Mass" <note>original: *missa*; the text here digresses into the etymology of the liturgical term</note> reminds us to investigate the origin of its name, lest anyone reject it as something lowly. In ancient times, amidst that vain superstition of the gods, when the priest had turned to the people during a sacred rite, he would say: **"It is the dismissal of the people"** <note>original: *populis missio*</note>; just as is found in Apuleius <note>a 2nd-century Roman author</note>, by which word he granted the power of departing to those who wished. This same custom has also been preserved by our people, so that when the sacrifice is now finished, it is announced by the minister: **"Go, it is the dismissal"** <note>original: *Ite missa est*</note>. This has the same force as the word *ilicet*—that is, "it is permitted to go." For Cyprian <note>an early Christian bishop and martyr</note> is a witness that the authors of our religion used "sending" <note>original: *missionem*</note> and "Mass" <note>original: *missam*</note> interchangeably, as he often writes of the "remission of sins" <note>original: *remissam peccatorum*</note> and many other things of that kind. Therefore, the whole sacrifice was named "Mass" from a single part of it, as if it were a "sending forth." But the custom of responding in choirs existed even then, as Ausonius <note>a 4th-century poet</note> shows: "From this, songs echo back more greatly in the grove." Though "Responsory" <note>original: *Responsorium*</note> is a relatively new word, let it be permitted for those treating ecclesiastical matters hereafter to use the specific words of the Church. 

When **Henry**, King of Burgundy, was dying, he named **Robert** as his heir in his will, though **Landry**, Count of Nevers <note>original: *Lauderico anniuersensi comite*</note>, opposed this, contending that Burgundy was under his own jurisdiction. From this a war arose, but victory and Burgundy remained in the hands of **Robert**. Having built many magnificent houses in honor of the saints, he departed this life. He was buried at the Church of **Saint Denis** <note>the traditional burial place of French kings</note> in the 14th year after beginning his reign, with his children surviving him: namely **Henry** and **Robert**. **Constance**, the daughter of the Count of Arles, had given birth to them; he had married her after losing his first wife and her son **Hugh**. Likewise **Simon** and **Amalric**, who were born from his marriage to the daughter of the petty king of Noyon.

**Henry** received the paternal honor, while **Robert** held Burgundy. Relying on the support of his mother **Constance**, who had yielded to Henry’s rights, Robert began to make a claim. A war having been incited from this, Henry, being unequal to Robert’s forces and the opposing faction, was driven from the kingdom. He fled to the **Normans**, by whose aid he recovered his possessions. Finally, having claimed the kingdom with such a din of arms, he voluntarily yielded it while still living to his son **Philip**. He died in the year of salvation 1060 and was carried to the burial place of the kings at the Church of **Saint Denis**. 

**Philip**, therefore, the son of **Henry**, having received the kingdom from his father, joined to himself in marriage **Bertha**, the daughter of **Baldwin**, Count of Flanders. By her he had children: **Louis** and **Constance**. Having dismissed her, he took **Bertrade** in her place. For this reason, it is said he was barred from the sacred rites by the high priest <term>Pope Urban II</term> <note>Urban II excommunicated Philip I for his bigamous marriage to Bertrade de Montfort</note>. He also extended the borders of the kingdom by adding the people of Bourges <note>original: *Biuricensibus*</note>, bought from their leader **Arpinus**. The latter, about to go as a companion on the expedition with **Godfrey of Bouillon** to the aid of the land which they call "Holy," lacked the money necessary for the uses of war, and so sold the Duchy to **Philip** himself. Thus, after this addition to his dominion was made, **Philip** received his son **Louis** into a partnership of the principate. Louis succeeded his father in the year of salvation 1108. Philip, having died at Melun <note>original: *Welduni*</note>, was buried at the Church of **Saint Benedict** on the Loire.

<column-break/>

**Louis**, the son of **Philip**, carried out many things prosperously against the English and the **Emperor Henry** <note>Henry V, Holy Roman Emperor</note>. When the high priest **Gelasius** <note>Pope Gelasius II</note>, holding the power of **Henry** in suspicion, had fled to his protection, he perished from a disease at Mâcon. In his place was substituted the Bishop of Vienne, **Guy**, surnamed **Calixtus** <note>Pope Calixtus II</note>. With Louis supporting him with great force, he came to Rome, and having been received by all orders with auspicious acclamations, he held the honor. **Louis** also had a son named **Philip**, after his grandfather; while he was riding for pleasure in the suburbs of **Paris** <note>original: *Lutecie parisiorum*</note>, his horse was startled by the sight of a little pig thrown in its path; he was thrown from the horse and died <note>Philip of France, co-king, died in 1131 when a black pig ran into his horse's legs</note>. 

Indeed, I fear I may seem to have forgotten the work I have undertaken if I dispute like a grammarian about the nomenclature of the city. But even writers of history do this occasionally, and in passing. One must beware of the "scourges of Homer" <note>original: *Homeromastiges*; a term for hyper-critical or malicious scholars</note>, as Pliny says. You may find those who affirm that **Paris** must be spoken of in an indeclinable form through all cases, and thus the usage of many has been preserved. Others, on the testimony of I-know-not-what versifier **Architrenius** <note>a satirical poem by John of Hauville</note> (for the authority of **Boethius** is in doubt), wish it to have been founded by **Julius Caesar**, and called **Par-Siva** <note>the text explores a folk etymology relating the city to Caesar or Isis</note> in the singular and feminine. **Caesar** himself is the primary reason we do not agree with them; he was certainly not one to disparage his own praises, yet in that work (as those people like it) he never mentions **Paris**, though he several times mentions the **Parisii** tribe. **Strabo**, **Pomponius Mela**, **Pliny**, and **Ptolemy** place **Lutetia** in that region in nearly the same way it is now. Therefore, relying on these authors, I have not hesitated to call this city sometimes **Lutetia** and sometimes **Paris**.

**Louis**, being attacked in war by the **Emperor Henry** (of whom we have already spoken) and another **Henry**, the King of the English <note>Henry I of England</note>, who was the son-in-law of the former Henry, brought the bones of **Saint Denis** and his companions—untouched until that time—from their tombs into the battle line. Emerging as victor, he carried the same bones back into their small shrines upon his own shoulders with the greatest veneration. He summoned his son **Louis** into a partnership of the principate; called "the Younger," he was anointed with oil and received the insignia of the royal head with his father’s permission. A little later, he took up the administration when his father was languishing from disease. The elder died in his sixties, having reigned for about 30 years. As he was breathing his last, he ordered himself to be laid on a carpet spread on the ground, upon which a cross had been marked out from ash. He was buried...

<meta>This page continues the genealogy of the French kings, moving from the later reign of Louis VI into the lives and reigns of Louis VII, Philip II Augustus, Louis VIII, and the early years of Louis IX (Saint Louis). It emphasizes their marriages, crusades, and religious foundations.</meta>

# Genealogy.

He himself was buried at the Church of St. Denis <note>original: *edem Dionysij*; the traditional burial site of French royalty</note>, leaving behind (besides Louis) four sons: Henry, Bishop of Beauvais; Philip, Archdeacon of Paris; Peter, who died after his father-in-law, having taken the daughter of Count Reginald as his wife; and another whose name I do not find among the authors, though they record him as the father of Count Robert of Perche and Dreux.

**Louis the Younger** <note>Louis VII</note>, while his father was still alive, was betrothed to Eleanor, the only daughter of the Duke of Aquitaine. After two girls were born of her and their mother had been dismissed <note>their marriage was annulled in 1152</note>, he married Constance, daughter of the King of Castile. When she died following her second childbirth, he joined himself to Adela, born of the Count of Blois. When her child-bearing years were nearly passed, after wearying God with many prayers, he raised up Philip. Because of this, Philip was nicknamed **"God-given"** <note>original: *Adeodatus*</note>. When he was scarcely a youth of fourteen, his father raised him to royal dignity, ensuring he was anointed with oil and crowned with the diadem, first at Reims and again at Paris.

During those same days, a certain **John of the Times** <note>original: *Iohannes de temporibus*; a legendary figure said to have lived over 300 years</note> is said to have died. The length of his life confirms the accounts of the ancients and does not allow them to seem mythical: such as Arganthonius, King of the Tartessians, who lived 150 years; Cinyras, ten more; Aegimius, 200; or certain people of the Epirote nation in Aetolia. The Kings of the Arcadians are said to have lived 300 years, and Dando in Illyria 500. For John is believed to have remained among human affairs for about 361 years, since the reign of Charlemagne.

Furthermore, Louis undertook an expedition to the **Holy Land** with Emperor Conrad under equal leadership <note>the Second Crusade</note>. When his final day arrived, he was buried in the church of the monastery of Barbeau, which he himself had built while living.

**Philip "God-given"** <note>Philip II Augustus</note>, having received the royal insignia from his father while still a youth, made an example of all those Jews convicted by judgment who were said to sacrifice a Christian boy every year <note>this refers to the medieval "blood libel" myths used to justify persecution</note>. He also established an edict of punishments against those who commit blasphemy against God. After his father’s death, he expelled the Jews from the borders of his kingdom. He performed many outstanding deeds against the English and those who laid hands upon the churches. He married Isabella, daughter of Baldwin, Count of Hainaut. He led forces to reclaim the Holy Land, with **Richard, King of the English** <note>Richard the Lionheart</note>, as his companion in the expedition in the year 1189 of the Christian era. He visited the basilicas of the apostles Peter and Paul in the City [Rome] and saw Pope Celestine.

And when, during his reign, they had fixed to the gallows of a cross a man of the Christian race, crowned with thorns, at Bray—the woman who then held the town having been bribed with gifts to conceal the matter—

<column-break/>

Philip, having rapidly led a troop there, burned eighty Jews alive on a pyre—as many as came into his power—while others were put to flight. Isabella having died, he married Ingeborg, sister of Canute <note>original: *Laym*; likely a transcription error for the King of Denmark</note>, King of the Danes <note>original: *Dalmatarum*; likely a confusion with Danorum</note>. After she was quickly dismissed, he celebrated a marriage with Agnes <note>original: *Maria*</note>, daughter of the Duke of Merania. He later granted the Jews a return and residence in Paris after receiving a large sum of money from them. For his son **Louis**, whom he had by Isabella, he betrothed **Blanche**, born of the King of Castile and niece of John Lackland <note>original: *ioannisque sine terra*; King John of England</note>, the brother of the one who had succeeded Richard in the kingdom of England. He ended his days in the year of salvation 1223, having held power for 46 years, and was entombed at the Church of St. Denis.

The helm of the kingdom was taken up by **Louis**, the eighth of that name and son of Philip the God-given, at the age of 32. Through his maternal lineage, he claimed a right to the kingdom of Charlemagne. For Charles, son of Louis IV <note>Charles of Lower Lorraine</note>—the one we showed was handed over to custody at Laon by Hugh Capet—fathered Ermengarde. From her as mother, Baldwin, Count of Hainaut, was born, who was the father of Isabella, who bore Louis to Philip. 

When he could not pull the conquered people of Avignon from the snares of the heretics <note>the Cathars</note> into which they had fallen, finally in the seventh year, attacking those who persisted in their error of opinion despite the edict, he leveled their walls to the ground and overturned 300 houses. From there, having immediately set out against the **Albigensians** of the same sect, while he was leading his army back, he was seized by a sudden violent illness and died at Montpensier. The body of the deceased was brought to Paris and entombed at the Church of St. Denis next to the tomb of his father Philip.

Four children of Blanche survived him: **Louis**, sharing his father's name, Robert, Alphonse, and Charles. Therefore Louis, the eldest—the one who was later canonized by Pope Boniface VIII <note>Saint Louis IX</note>—received the paternal honor at the age of twelve. To his brother Robert, he granted Artois and later bestowed Arras. He crushed a faction of princes rising against him by defeating the English, whom the rebels had incited to cross into Gaul with the hope of rewards and plunder. He had as his wife Margaret, daughter of the Count of Provence (which is called Narbonensis, a part of Gaul washed by the Mediterranean Sea, formerly called **"Trousered Gaul"** <note>original: *bracata*; a Roman term for the region based on the local dress</note>, separated from Italy by the Var river and the ridges of the Alps). A daughter of the Duke of Brabant married his brother Robert. Louis also built the chapel which they call **"Holy"** <note>the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris</note>. There he placed the lance and the sponge, instruments of the Lord's Passion, which Baldwin, the Emperor of Constantinople, gave to him.

# Of the Kings of the Franks.

...had sent: he arranged them most elegantly. For Alfonso, also the brother of the Count of Toulouse, and for Charles, he took care to place Beatrice, the sister of his own wife and born of the same father, with the hope of succession to the county. To Alfonso himself, he granted the counties of Auvergne and Poitiers; to Charles, he gave Maine. This is 그 Charles who, having gained possession of the kingdom of Sicily, is today called **Charles I**. Louis himself, bound by a vow <note>original: *voti reus*</note> because of a sickness from which he suffered to the point of the physicians' despair, was about to set out for the Holy Land. He committed the care of the kingdom to his mother Blanche and his brother Alfonso. Having begun his journey, he met **Innocent IV**, the Supreme Pontiff, at Lyon, who was humbly seeking help against the overbearing rule of **Frederick II**, by whom he said he had been driven from Rome. From there, Louis crossed the sea to Asia and took Damietta, a city of Egypt, by force. In that expedition, however, having suffered many hardships, he was finally captured with his brother Charles and came into the power of the Saladin <note>Though the historical Saladin died in 1193, the text uses "Saladin" here as a general title for the Saracen ruler who captured Louis IX in 1250</note>. After a certain weight of gold was agreed upon, they were released by right of return <note>original: *postliminio*</note> and returned to Gaul <note>France</note>, where Louis founded many monasteries for monks and shelters consecrated to mercy <note>hospitals or almshouses</note>, which still exist even now. Finally, at the instigation of the Pope, in the year of salvation 1269, he led a fleet into Africa, accompanied by his three sons, Philip, John, and Peter. As a victor over the Saracens, he died near the city called **Tunis**. His body, having been kept upright and dried for a year, was brought to Gaul and buried according to custom at the Church of St. Denis. The entrails of the eviscerated corpse <note>original: *extis exenterati cadaueris*</note> were buried in Sicily, in the temple of Monreale (as the inhabitants call it).

**Philip** <note>Philip III, "the Bold"</note> took up the empire. He was married to Isabella, daughter of King James of Aragon; Carcassonne was handed over as her dowry. However, since he had previously yielded any right he might have had in Celtiberia (which is now Catalonia) and Roussillon, and having set up camp in Libya with his father, he did not break the siege until he forced the supplicant king to accept unfavorable peace conditions. Returning to Gaul, he convened a council at Lyon on the appointed day in the year of salvation 1272, at which Pope **Gregory X** was present and presided. After Isabella had already given birth to three sons by him—Louis, Philip, and Charles—she yielded to nature <note>died</note>. Her husband took another wife, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon <note>Philip III actually married Marie of Brabant; the text identifies her as the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon</note>, who saw to it that her stepson Louis was removed by poison. Meanwhile, Philip moved against King Peter of Aragon regarding Sicily, which had been occupied by him but had rightfully passed to Philip's uncle (whom I have shown was **Charles I**);

this he used as a pretext for war. Having gained possession of several towns on the island, he was released by a sudden force of disease <note>he died of illness</note>. And so **Philip the Fair** <note>Philip IV</note>, so named from the excellence of his beauty, initially had disagreements with Pope **Boniface VIII**. Finally, through the betrayal of **Sciarra Colonna**, who was serving under him for pay, the Pope was seized at Anagni (the town from which the Pontiff drew his origin) and led into the city, where a little later, having fallen into illness from grief of mind, he died shortly thereafter. The order of those called **Templars**, a sect already long established, was condemned by Clement himself at Vienne, in the seventh year after he moved to Gaul. Philip had three children: Louis, who was called **Hutin** <note>the Quarreler</note> and took up the scepter upon his father's death, being also King of Navarre; Philip, Count of Poitiers; and likewise Charles, Count of Marche. Philip <note>the Fair</note> departed from life in the year of salvation 1313, in the month of November, and was brought into the Church of St. Denis, having reigned for twenty-eight years.

Immediately upon beginning his rule, he turned his attention to certain friends of his father with capital punishment, and he permitted the **Jews** to have a place of residence within the borders of his kingdom. He took as his wife Clementia, sister of King Robert of Sicily, who was quite close to him by some bond of kinship. From another degree of kinship, Charles, the brother of Louis, for his merits was consecrated King of Sicily and raised another Charles, whom we call the Second. He produced a numerous progeny, and among them Martel, Robert, and **Clementia**, who married Louis and, upon his early death, survived him while pregnant. # Genealogy.

...his name was John <note>John I, known as "the Posthumous," who lived for only five days in 1316</note>: he inherited his father's empire. He administered the state through his paternal uncle, Philip, the Count of Poitou. Not long afterward, John’s death gave Philip the opportunity to transfer the kingdom—which he had previously governed as regent—to himself.

$\P$ Philip of Poitou, the fifth of that name <note>Philip V, "the Tall"</note>, had three daughters: he gave one in marriage to the Duke of Burgundy, another to the Count of Nevers, and the third to the Dauphin of Vienne. When he died without male offspring, a dispute arose over his remains; the priests <note>original: *flaminibus*, used here to mean friars</note> of the Minorite <note>Franciscan</note> and Preacher <note>Dominican</note> orders contended for him, and so his internal organs were buried in two separate places among them, while his body was brought to the Church of Saint Denis. After him, his brother Charles, the Count of March and himself surnamed "the Fair" <note>Charles IV</note>, received the kingdom. He died prematurely, leaving his wife pregnant in the hope of a successor. While the child was still being carried in the womb in the hope of a kingdom, a great debate began as to who should be entrusted with the care of the realm. Two great competitors claimed the province for themselves with the highest level of contention: Charles of Valois <note>The text likely refers to the Valois faction; historically, the competition was between Philip of Valois (son of Charles) and Edward III</note>, the paternal uncle of the other Charles (the Count of March) and the King who had most recently died; and Edward III, the King of the English, born of Isabella <note>original: *maria*, though historically Isabella</note>, the sister of that same Charles. The eager favor of the princes preferred the Valois. In the meantime, the elder Valois died. Thus, after a child of the "weaker sex" <note>original: *deterioris sexus*, referring to a daughter, Joan</note> was born to the queen and excluded from the helm of power, Philip—son of the deceased Charles of Valois and Catherine, whose father was Baldwin, the Emperor of Constantinople—gained the royal power.

$\P$ Philip of Valois, the sixth of this name, took up war against Edward, King of the English. This was because Edward contended that the kingdom belonged to him by right of nations <note>original: *iure gentium*</note> as the closest relative by blood, since his maternal uncle Charles had died without male offspring. After many battles, Philip finally defeated the English in a naval fight at Sluys <note>original: *Elusas*</note>. Furthermore, he obtained from Humbert, the Dauphin of Vienne—who was the grandson of King Philip V through his daughter, and a cousin of this Philip of Valois now under discussion—that since Humbert lacked children, he should designate Philip’s grandson, Charles, as his successor. This Charles was the son of John, Duke of Normandy, the eldest of Philip's sons. Soon after, having received money from Philip, Humbert took vows in the order of the Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note> and yielded his princedom to Philip. From that time on, the Dauphiné has belonged to the French

<column-break/>

kings, or to their eldest sons <note>This is the origin of the title "Dauphin" for the heir to the French throne</note>. Philip departed this life in the 57th year of his age and the 13th of his reign. He was buried at the Church of Saint Denis.

$\P$ After him, his son John <note>John II, "the Good"</note> received the command. While he was fighting with little success against Richard <note>The text says "Richard, son of Edward," but John II was famously captured by Edward the Black Prince, son of Edward III</note>, King of the English and son of Edward, he suffered a defeat and fell alive into the power of the enemy. With him were about 170 knights. He was led away to Bordeaux, and after terms were accepted and a great sum of money promised, he was released four years later. From him were born those who succeeded their father: Charles <note>Charles V</note>, Philip the Count of Touraine, and Louis, the Duke of Anjou and Duke of Berry. In the year of salvation 1364, John passed from this life in London and was buried at the Church of Saint Denis.

$\P$ Charles <note>Charles V, "the Wise"</note> took up the reigns of empire in his father’s place; he is the one called "the Wise." According to custom, he was anointed with oil at Reims, and having received the insignia of the royal head, he returned to Paris. Immediately, he declared his brother Philip to be the Duke of Burgundy, though only after receiving the County of Touraine back from him. Philip, moreover, joined himself in marriage to Margaret of Louis of Flanders; when his father-in-law died, he obtained the County of Flanders through his wife, who succeeded her father. Charles himself, possessing a great capacity for wealth, was somewhat harsh in imposing taxes. Furthermore, he passed laws among the Franks stating that the eldest son of a king, upon the loss of his father, should immediately govern the kingdom by himself once he entered his fourteenth year. During his reign, Gregory XI moved the Apostolic See, which he then led, from Avignon back to Rome. Charles ended his days at Vincennes <note>original: *Viennas agri parisiensis*</note> in the Parisian territory; he was brought to the Church of Saint Denis in the year of salvation 1380, leaving behind two children still in their boyhood: the eldest, Charles, and Louis, who was later the Duke of Orleans. The dying father provided in his will that Louis of Anjou should direct the upbringing of his son Charles and manage affairs as long as the boy was a ward. Charles himself, bearing his father's name but not yet of full age, conducted all things by the counsel of his uncle Louis, as his dying father had commanded. While he was hunting in the forest named Senlis <note>original: *Syluanecto*</note>, he captured a stag with a bronze collar around its neck bearing this inscription: *Caesar gave this to me.* Therefore, from that event, he established that he and his posterity should have the image of a stag with a golden collar in a field of lilies as their emblem. # Philip took up the Empire.

He was married to Isabella, daughter of King James of Aragon, with Carcassonne handed over as a dowry. However, he had previously yielded any right he might have had in Celtiberia (which is now Catalonia <note>original: *Gotalania*</note>) and Roussillon. While encamped with his father in Libya <note>meaning North Africa</note>, he did not lift the siege until he forced the suppliant king to accept harsh peace conditions. Returning to France, he convened a council at Lyon on a set day in the year of salvation 1272, at which Pope Gregory presided. 

After Isabella had already borne him three sons—Louis, Philip, and Charles—she yielded to nature <note>died</note>. Her husband took another wife, the daughter of the Duke of Brabant, who arranged for her stepson Louis to be removed by poison. Meanwhile, Philip moved against King Peter of Aragon because of the occupation of Sicily, which had fallen to his uncle’s right (whom I have shown to be Charles I).

<column-break/>

This served as the pretext for the war. Having already gained several towns on the island, he was released from life by a sudden onset of disease. He was survived by Philip (who succeeded his father) and Charles, Count of Valois, from Isabella; and from Mary [of Brabant], Louis, Count of Evreux, and daughters Margaret and Blanche, of whom one married the King of the English and the other the Duke of Austria.

Thus, **Philip the Fair**, so named for his excellence of form, initially had disagreements with Pope Boniface [VIII]. Then he engaged in open hostilities and prohibited by edict any gold or silver, worked or unworked, from being carried from the borders of his kingdom to Rome. Finally, through the betrayal of Sciarra Colonna, who was in his service, the Pope was seized at Anagni (the town from which he drew his origin) and led into the city, where shortly afterward, having fallen into illness from grief of spirit, he died in a short time. 

During the reign of this same Philip, Clement V moved from Rome to Avignon and transferred the seat of the papacy there in the year of salvation 1305. The Popes who followed remained there for 74 years. The order of those called **Templars**, a sect established long ago, was condemned by the same Clement at Vienne, seven years after he crossed into France. 

Philip had three sons: Louis, who was called **Hutin** <note>Meaning "The Quarrelsome" or "The Obstinate"</note>, who received the scepter upon his father's death and was also King of Navarre; Philip, Count of Poitou; and Charles, Count of Marche. It is well established that the wives of these two latter sons were accused of adultery before their father-in-law and cast into prison. Philip then died in the year of salvation 1314, in the month of November, and was brought to the Church of Saint Denis, having reigned for twenty-eight years.

# OF THE KINGS OF FRANCE

...had sent: he arranged their marriages most elegantly. For Alfonso, the brother of the Count of Toulouse, and for Charles, he arranged for Beatrice—the sister of his own wife and born of the same father—to be placed in marriage, with the hope of succession to the county. Having begun the journey, he met Pope Innocent IV at Lyon, who was humbly seeking aid against the uncontrollable rule of Frederick II, by whom he said he had been driven from Rome. From there, Louis sought Asia across the sea and took the Egyptian city of Damietta by force. In that expedition, however, having suffered many hardships, he was finally captured with his brother Charles and fell into the power of the Sultan <note>original: *Saladini*; though Saladin died in 1193, the name was often used by later chroniclers as a general title for the Saracen ruler</note>. After a certain weight of gold was agreed upon as a ransom, they were released and returned to France. There, Louis founded several monasteries for monks and consecrated asylums of mercy, which still exist today. Finally, at the instigation of the Pope, in the year of salvation 1269, he led a fleet to Africa. Accompanied by his three sons—Philip, John, and Peter—he died, a victor over the Saracens, at the city named Tunis. His body, having been raised and dried for a year, was brought back to France and buried according to custom at the Church of St. Denis. The entrails of his disemboweled corpse were buried in Sicily, in the temple of Monreale <note>original: *Montis regalis*</note>, as the inhabitants call it.

Philip [III] took up the empire. He was the one who was previously married to Isabella, daughter of King James of Aragon, with Carcassonne given as a dowry—though he had previously surrendered any right he might have had in Catalonia <note>original: *Celtiberia*, which is now *Gotalania*</note> and Roussillon. Together with his father in the camps pitched in Africa <note>original: *Libia*</note>, he did not lift the siege until he forced the supplicant king to accept unfavorable peace conditions. Returning to France, he convened a council at Lyon in the year of salvation 1272, which Pope Gregory X attended and presided over. After Isabella had already given birth to three sons—Louis, Philip, and Charles—she passed away. Her husband took another wife, the daughter of the Duke of Brabant <note>original: *ducis borbonij* (Bourbon); historical records identify her as Marie of Brabant</note>, who arranged for her stepson Louis to be removed by poison. Meanwhile, Philip moved against King Peter of Aragon and seized Sicily from him, which had passed to the right of his uncle, whom I have shown was Charles I;

<column-break/>

using the cause of war as a pretext. Having gained several towns on the island, he was taken by a sudden onset of disease. He left behind Philip (who succeeded his father) and Charles, Count of Valois, by Isabella; and by Mary, he left Louis, Count of Evreux, and daughters Margaret and Blanche—one of whom married the King of the English, and the other the Duke of Austria. Thus Philip [IV], surnamed "the Fair" <note>original: *Pulcher*</note> for the excellence of his form, initially had disagreements with Pope Boniface VIII, and later engaged in open hostilities. By edict, he prohibited the carrying of sacred gold or silver, or anything imported, from the borders of his kingdom to Rome. Finally, through the betrayal of Sciarra Colonna—who was in his service—at Anagni (the town from which the Pope drew his origin), the Pope was seized and led into the city. Shortly thereafter, falling into illness from grief of spirit, he died. During the reign of this Philip, Clement V moved from the city [Rome] to Avignon and transferred the seat of the papacy there in the year of salvation 1305. The Popes who followed remained there for seventy-three years. The order of those called Templars, a sect established long ago, was condemned by Clement himself at Vienne in the seventh year after he moved to France. Philip had three sons: Louis, who was called "the Quarreler" <note>original: *Vtinus* (Hutin)</note> and took up the scepter upon his father's death, being also King of Navarre; Philip, Count of Poitou; and likewise Charles, Count of Marche. It is well established that the wives of these two <note>The wives of Philip and Charles; the text omits the wife of Louis X here, though she was also involved</note> were caught in adultery and cast into prison by their father-in-law. Then Philip died in the year of salvation 1314, in the month of November, and was buried in the Church of St. Denis, having reigned for twenty-eight years.

Louis [X], who was surnamed "the Quarreler" and King of Navarre, succeeded his father Philip. At the very start of his rule, he turned his attention to certain friends of his father with capital punishment. He also permitted the Jews <note>original: *inde: os* (likely *Iudeos*)</note> to have a place of residence within the borders of his kingdom. He married Clementia, the sister of King Robert of Sicily, who was quite close to him by some bond of kinship. For there is no doubt that Lord Louis [IX] had a son named Philip [III], by which father Philip surnamed "the Fair" was born, who in turn fathered the Louis we are now discussing. From another branch of the family, Charles, the brother of Louis [IX], was consecrated King of Sicily for his merits and raised another Charles, whom we call Charles II. He fathered a numerous offspring, and among them Charles Martel, Robert, and Clementia, who married Louis [X] and survived him, pregnant, after his early death. ...his name was John <note>John I, known as "the Posthumous," who lived for only five days in 1316</note>; he took up his father’s empire and managed affairs through his paternal uncle Philip, the Count of Poitou. ¶ Philip of Poitou, the fifth of that name <note>Philip V, "the Tall"</note>, since he had three daughters, placed one in marriage to the Duke of Burgundy, another to the Count of Nevers, and the third to the Dauphin of Vienne. From him, his brother Charles, the Count of La Marche, received the kingdom; he was surnamed "the Fair" <note>Charles IV</note>. He died prematurely, leaving his pregnant wife with the hope of a successor. While the child in the mother's womb was carried in hope of the kingdom, a debate began as to who should most especially be entrusted with the care of affairs. Two great competitors sought the highest office for themselves with great contention: Charles of Valois <note>The text likely refers here to the house of Valois, specifically Philip of Valois, son of the elder Charles of Valois</note>, the uncle of the other Charles (the Count of La Marche whom we just mentioned and the King who most recently died); and Edward III, King of the English, born of Isabella <note>original: *Maria*; the text contains an error, as Edward’s mother was Isabella of France</note>, the sister of that same Charles. The eager favor of the princes preferred the Valois. Meanwhile, the elder Valois died. Thus, when a child of the inferior sex <note>a girl</note> was born to the Queen, she was excluded from the government. ...he had sent: he arranged [the marriages] most elegantly. For Alphonse, the brother of the Count of Toulouse, he arranged a marriage with the Count’s daughter; and for Charles, he arranged a marriage with Beatrice, the sister of his own wife and born of the same father <note>Beatrice of Provence, sister to Queen Margaret; this marriage eventually brought the County of Provence under French influence</note>, with the hope of succession to the county. To Alphonse himself, he granted the counties of Auvergne and Poitou; to Charles, he gave the county of Maine. This is that Charles who gained possession of the Kingdom of Sicily and is called "Charles the First" even today. Louis himself, bound by a vow because of a sickness from which he labored to the point of the physicians’ despair, prepared to set out for the Holy Land. He entrusted the care of the kingdom to his mother Blanche <note>Blanche of Castile, who served as a powerful regent</note> and his brother Alphonse. Having begun his journey, he met Pope Innocent IV at Lyon, who was humbly seeking help against the unbridled power of Frederick II, by whom he said he had been driven from Rome. From there, Louis crossed the sea to Asia and took the Egyptian city of Damietta by force. In that expedition, however, having suffered many hardships, he was finally captured along with his brother Charles and fell into the power of the "Saladin" <note>The text uses "Saladin" as a general title for the Saracen ruler, though the historical Saladin had been dead for decades; Louis was actually captured by the Ayyubid/Mamluk forces</note>. After a certain weight of gold was agreed upon for their ransom, they were released and returned to Gaul <note>France</note>. There, Louis founded many monasteries and asylums consecrated to mercy, which still exist today. Finally, at the prompting of the Pope in the year of salvation 1269, he led a fleet to Africa. Surrounded by his three sons—Philip, John, and Peter—the victor over the Saracens died at the city named Tunis. His body, having been raised and dried for a year, was brought back to Gaul and buried according to custom at the Church of Saint-Denis. The internal organs of the disemboweled corpse were buried in Sicily, in the temple of "The Royal Mountain" <note>Monreale, near Palermo</note>, as the inhabitants call it.

¶ Philip <note>Philip III, "the Bold"</note> took up the empire. His wife was Isabella, daughter of King James of Aragon, and Carcassonne was handed over as her dowry. Nevertheless, he had previously yielded any right he might have had in Celtiberia (which is now Catalonia) and Roussillon. While stationed with his father in the camps in Libya, he did not end the siege until he compelled the suppliant king to accept unfair conditions of peace. Returning to Gaul, he called a council at Lyon in the year of salvation 1272, which Pope Gregory X attended and presided over. After Isabella had already given birth to three sons—Louis, Philip, and Charles—she yielded to nature <note>She died</note>. Her husband took another wife, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon <note>Marie of Brabant; the text identifies her father as the Duke of Bourbon, though he was the Duke of Brabant</note>, who saw to it that her stepson Louis was removed by poison. Meanwhile, Philip moved against King Peter of Aragon because Peter had occupied Sicily, which had fallen to the right of Philip’s uncle (whom I have shown was Charles I).

<column-break/>

This served as the pretext for the war. Having already gained possession of several towns on the island, Philip was undone by the sudden force of a disease. Surviving from Isabella were Philip, who succeeded his father, and Charles, the Count of Valois; from Marie were Louis, the Count of Évreux, and daughters Margaret and Blanche, one of whom married the King of the English and the other the Duke of Austria. Thus, Philip "the Fair," so named from the excellence of his beauty, initially had disputes with Pope Boniface VIII. Later, he engaged in open hostilities and issued an edict prohibiting gold or silver, whether minted or raw, from being carried to Rome from the borders of his kingdom. Finally, through the betrayal of Sciarra Colonna—who was a mercenary under him—at Anagni (the town from which the Pope’s family originated), the Pope was seized and led into the city. Shortly afterward, having fallen into a sickness from grief of mind, he died. During the reign of this very Philip, Clement V moved from the City <note>Rome</note> to Avignon and transferred the seat of the papacy there in the year of salvation 1305. The Popes who followed remained there for seventy-three years. The order of those called the Templars, a sect established long ago, was condemned by this same Clement at Vienne in the seventh year after he crossed into Gaul. Philip had three children: Louis, who was called *Hutin* <note>Louis X, "the Quarreler" or "the Stubborn"</note>, took up the scepter upon his father's death, as well as the title of King of Navarre; Philip, the Count of Poitou; and likewise Charles, the Count of La Marche. It is well established that the wives of these two <note>Philip and Charles</note> were accused of adultery before their father-in-law and cast into prison, where they died. Philip then died in the year of salvation 1313 <note>historically 1314</note>, in the month of November, and was carried into the Church of Saint-Denis after he had reigned for twelve—or rather thirty—years.

¶ This Louis, whose surname was *Hutin*, King of Navarre, succeeded his father Philip. Immediately upon entering his reign, he punished certain friends of his father with capital punishment and permitted the Jews to have a place of residence within the borders of his kingdom. He took as his wife Clementia, the sister of King Robert of Sicily, who was quite close to him by a certain bond of kinship. For there is no doubt that Lord Louis <note>Louis IX</note> had a son Philip <note>Philip III</note>, from whom was born Philip surnamed "the Fair," who in turn fathered the Louis of whom we now treat. From another branch of the lineage, Charles <note>Charles of Anjou</note>, the brother of Louis <note>Louis IX</note>, was made King of Sicily for his merits; he raised another Charles, whom we call "the Second"; he fathered a numerous offspring, including Marcellus, Robert, and Clementia, who married Louis and survived him while pregnant, as he died early. His name was John <note>John I, known as "the Posthumous," who lived for only five days in 1316</note>: he inherited his father’s empire. Not long after, John’s death gave Philip the opportunity to transfer the kingdom—which he had previously managed as regent—to himself.

¶ Philip of Poitou, therefore, the fifth of that name <note>Philip V, "the Tall"</note>, since he had three daughters, arranged marriages for them: one to the Duke of Burgundy, another to the Count of Nevers, and the third to the Dauphin of Vienne. When he died without male offspring, the internal organs of his upright corpse <note>A common medieval practice of "division of remains" for multiple burial sites</note> were divided in two by the contending friars of the Minorite and Preacher orders <note>The Franciscans and Dominicans</note> and buried with both; his body was brought to the Church of Saint-Denis. From him, his brother Charles took the kingdom, the Count of Marche, himself surnamed "the Fair" <note>Charles IV</note>. In the hope of succession, he died prematurely, leaving his wife’s womb heavy with child. Two great rivals dragged the province into a high-stakes contention: Charles of Valois, the uncle of the other Charles (the Count of Marche whom I just mentioned and the King who had most recently died); and Edward III, King of the English, born of Mary <note>The text likely means Isabella, the sister of Charles IV</note>, the sister of the same Charles. The widespread support of the princes preferred the Valois. Meanwhile, the interrex <note>regent</note> Valois died. Therefore, when the infant the queen had given birth to—being of the lesser sex <note>a girl, Blanche of France</note>—was excluded from the helm of power, Philip <note>Philip VI</note>, the son of the deceased Charles of Valois and Catherine (born of her father Baldwin, Emperor of Constantinople), gained possession of the royal power.

¶ Philip of Valois, the sixth of this name, took up war against Edward, King of the English. This was because Edward contended that the kingdom belonged to him by the law of nations, as he was closer in lineage to his uncle Charles, who had died without male offspring. ->## OF THE KINGS OF THE FRANKS ##<-

...granted to his brother <note>Louis I, Duke of Orléans</note>: although he had received assurances from the people of Orléans that he would not tear them away from the body of the kingdom. During this same time, Clement VII <note>The Antipope based in Avignon</note>, the Roman pontiff and author of the ecclesiastical schism, passed a law concerning "expectant graces" and "annates." <note>Annates were payments to the Pope consisting of the first year's revenue from a church office.</note> To this, Jean de Monteson <note>original: "Johannes montesonus"</note>, a professor of sacred theology of the order called the Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, dared to affirm in a sermon at Paris that the Mother of the Lord was not conceived without the stain of original sin. He pleaded his case before Pope Innocent VII, by whom he was forced to sing a palinode <note>term: palinode — a formal recantation or retraction of a previous statement</note>. Furthermore, Louis, Duke of Anjou, the King's paternal uncle, was called the King of Naples; he ended his days there. This same Charles <note>Charles VI, "the Well-Beloved"</note>, having defeated the Flemish in a great battle—in which rumor says four thousand of the enemy fell—broke the defiance of the Parisians, which they had shown toward both his father and himself. For he restored the taxes that had been removed by the common people during a riot. He also ordered the removal of the iron chains which since ancient times were used to block the streets, and he destroyed the city gates; he acted no less mercifully toward the people of Rouen, whom he considered accomplices in the same fault. Although all the other children he had received had died, he left one survivor and successor, Charles. He suffered from intermittent madness <note>original: "interpolato furore"</note> throughout his life, and occasionally gave signs of a disturbed mind. His brother Louis, Duke of Orléans, was also assassinated at night in Paris by killers sent by John, Duke of Burgundy, his cousin. A similar end and the same fate of death befell John himself, who was stabbed by a member of Louis’s household <note>John the Fearless was assassinated in 1419 at the Bridge of Montereau</note>. King Charles ended his life in the year of salvation 1422.

¶ From him, another reigned by his father’s name, Charles, whom the common people remember as "the Seventh" <note>Charles VII, "the Victorious"</note>, though it is clear from historical record that he was the eighth. For Charles the Great <note>Charlemagne</note>, Charles the Bald, Charles the Fat <note>original: "iners & malefetiatus"</note>, Charles the Simple, Charles the Count of Marche <note>Charles IV</note>, and that Charles whom we showed was prone to bouts of madness <note>Charles VI</note>, all held power before him. This Charles, however, was attacked in a war by the English and the Burgundians; having lost almost all the territories of his kingdom except for Bourges, he retreated there, which is why he was mockingly called the "King of Bourges" by his enemies. For Henry <note>Henry VI</note>, son of Henry, King of the English, signed himself "King of England and France" among his titles. He boastfully claimed that he had not occupied foreign lands by force of arms, but had, so to speak, laid his hand upon the kingdom of France which he asserted belonged to him by the best right. Firstly, because of his ancestors: Edward <note>Edward III</note>, the grandson of Philip the Fair through his daughter Mary <note>The text likely refers to Isabella</note>, claimed that since Charles, Duke of Marche, had died without male 

<column-break/>

offspring, Philip of Valois should not have been preferred as successor. Secondly, and most importantly, because when his father Henry <note>Henry V</note> led the Charles of whom we now speak <note>Charles VI</note> to a thirty-year peace established between the English and the French, he wished it to be seen as a condition added to the treaty and marriage: namely, that if Henry survived his spouse, the kingdom of France would look to him; if not, any children born of the same marriage would succeed upon the death of Charles VII. Therefore, while Charles’s affairs were in a state of ruin, a maiden of about twenty years from the town of Vaucouleurs <note>Joan of Arc, the Maid of Orléans</note> came to the King, and equipped with manly armor, she performed the duties of a soldier. Under her auspices and leadership, the city of Orléans was relieved from the English siege, and battle was successfully joined in several places. Many cities in Belgian Gaul <note>The northeastern regions of France</note> were also recovered, and among them most notably Reims, where Charles, anointed with oil according to the custom of his ancestors, received the royal crown upon his head. Meanwhile, the maiden of whom I spoke, while she had come to the aid of the besieged French at Compiègne and was retreating into the town after a sally was made, was caught in an ambush and fell into the power of the enemy; Jean de Luxembourg <note>original: "Johannes lumburgus"</note>, an ally of the English, sold her like a slave. Those who brought her to Rouen subjected her to the ultimate punishment <note>Execution by burning</note>, the reason being added that the woman, forgetting her sex, had assumed the dress of a man. Charles had a son named Louis, the Dauphin of Vienne, to whom he betrothed Margaret, daughter of the King of the Scots; he himself took Charlotte, sister of the Duke of the Savoyards <note>original: "Allobrogum vel Sabaudiensium"</note>, in marriage. When Paris was recovered, a severe famine set in, and the slaughter of men by wolves was recorded. This same Louis the Dauphin, having cast off the discipline of his father's kingdom, began to infest the borders with raids and solicit cities to defect. Nevertheless, in the sixth month after he had revolted, he returned into favor with his father.

¶ Around the same time, Charles, Duke of Orléans—son of that Louis whom we said was killed in Paris—having been among the captives of the English for twenty-five years, returned to his own lands after being released upon the payment of four hundred thousand gold pieces. King Charles, with Jean, Count of Dunois <note>The "Bastard of Orléans"</note> and illegitimate son of Louis of Orléans, acting as general, recovered Normandy from the English within a year and six days from when he moved for war. In that land, there are ninety-four very well-fortified towns. He recovered six episcopal cities and one metropolitan city; he also recovered Aquitaine, which the English had held for 140 years.

# GENEALOGY #

...had been. Once the people of Bordeaux were defeated again and Aquitaine was finally at peace, Louis <note>The future King Louis XI</note>, having obtained permission from his father to leave, returned to the Dauphiné <note>The traditional territory of the heir to the French throne</note>. From there, when he began to seize everything as plunder, his father moved against him. Louis then retreated to Philip, the Duke of Burgundy <note>Philip the Good</note>, with whom he remained for ten years until his father’s death. Charles VII also had a daughter named Magdalena, whom he betrothed to Ladislaus <note>Ladislaus the Posthumous</note>, the son of Emperor Sigismund, who held power among the Hungarians; however, she was never wed to the man, as he was taken by an untimely death. Afterward, the King <note>Charles VII</note> perished from starvation, which was forced upon him by his doctors to counter the effects of a poison they claimed had been given to him.

¶ Louis XI took up the reins of government. Immediately upon the start of his reign, the high nobles, believing he would be unjust toward them, incited his brother Charles, the Duke of Berry, against Louis. Charles first betook himself to the Bretons. Meanwhile, after Louis was routed at Montlhéry by Charles, the Duke of Burgundy <note>Charles the Bold</note>, the nobles joined their forces and besieged the city of Paris, where Louis had fled. Negotiations for peace began, and it was granted on these conditions: that Charles, Louis’s brother, would yield the Duchy of Berry and receive Normandy instead, and that a certain sum of money or specific cities should be given to each of the men who had sided with Charles. Thus, by the voice of a herald on the third day before the Kalends of November <note>October 30</note> in the year of salvation 1465, the peace was proclaimed. In the following year, a plague broke out in Paris which is said to have killed some forty thousand people. Louis held a <term>lustrum</term> <note>original: "lustrum" — a Roman term for a census and purification, here used for a military review</note> and twice surveyed the armed men of Paris: once when he declared war on the Burgundians in the year of Christ’s birth 1467, and again when ambassadors from the King of Aragon sought peace from him during the war of Perpignan. In the first census, seven hundred thousand men were counted; in the latter, one hundred and four thousand. Charles the Bold renewed the war and moved against Louis because Louis had driven him out of Normandy in violation of their treaty. The Duke of Brittany brought aid to Charles, making it necessary for Louis to settle the matter. He granted Aquitaine to his brother as a portion of his paternal inheritance. But not long after, his brother was removed by a draft of poison, and Louis reclaimed Aquitaine. He also forced the Duke of Nemours to stand trial, as well as Louis of Luxembourg, the commander of the troops—whom the French call the "Constable"—and punishment followed their condemnation, both being struck by the executioner's axe. Meanwhile, Charles, Duke of Burgundy, had made Edward IV, King of England, an enemy to Louis, and Edward had crossed over into Gaul <note>France</note> with an entire army of twenty thousand men. Distrusting his own resources, Louis entered into a conference with Edward at

<column-break/>

Picquigny. With a great sum of money, he purchased not only immediate peace but also a truce for seven years, including a fixed tribute for peace to be paid every single year. Later, in the battle of the war waged by the Swiss under the leadership of René of Lorraine, Charles the Duke of Burgundy was slain. Louis, finding Upper Burgundy stripped of its protection, recovered it. He betrothed Margaret, the granddaughter of Charles of Burgundy, to his eldest son <note>The future Charles VIII</note>. Margaret was the daughter of Mary of Burgundy and Maximilian of Austria <note>The future Holy Roman Emperor</note>, and through this, he maintained peace with the Flemish. Falling into ill health in the year of salvation 1484 <note>Historical records usually cite August 1483</note>, Louis died at Tours and was buried in the Church of Our Lady at Cléry.

¶ Charles the Dauphin <note>Charles VIII</note> succeeded him. He was the son Louis had by Charlotte of Savoy, who had previously borne two girls. One of these the father had married to Peter of Beaujeu, now the Duke of Bourbon; the other to Louis, Duke of Orléans, who later succeeded Charles when he died without offspring. There is a rumor that on the day of Charles’s birth, a swarm of bees flew into the chamber where he was born. Both his father Louis and those present interpreted this as an omen. Charles was already thirteen years old when he entered into his kingdom; everything was managed by the counsel of his sister Anne and Peter of Beaujeu, to whom Anne was married. Louis of Orléans, taking it poorly that he was excluded and the kingdom was being administered by others, moved for war with the help of the Bretons, for the sake of "the public good" (as he claimed), supported by certain allied princes who agreed with him. The movement began in the territory of Orléans; when Charles had retreated to Orléans, the rebels held Beaugency. Coming out to meet them with an army, Charles forced Louis to retreat. Louis fled to the protection of the Duke of Alençon. Meanwhile, while enjoying his hospitality, he did not cease to negotiate for peace through ambassadors and intermediaries. Having obtained a return on honorable conditions, he came to Charles; but fearing for himself, as he later alleged, he did not stay with him long. He first slipped away to Blois, and from there, by a single day's journey, he sought the nearest borders of Brittany. In the meantime, the movements of civil wars stirred up by John, Duke of Bourbon, and the Count of Angoulême, forced Charles—still a youth—to approach the people of Bourges with his troops; but they withdrew from arms on honorable conditions for both sides.

¶ While Louis XI was still among the living, he had betrothed the young Charles to Margaret, the daughter of Maximilian, King of the Romans, and Mary of Burgundy...

# OF THE KINGS OF THE FRANKS #

...[his] daughter <note>Likely referring to Margaret of Austria, daughter of Maximilian I, who was betrothed to Charles VIII before he broke the engagement</note>. Unwelcome news arrived from Brittany for Charles: that the Bretons were in arms and were about to pour the full force of war into Gaul <note>France</note>. Therefore, thinking he must act quickly, he attacked the city of Nantes <note>Latin: Nematensem; the capital of the Duchy of Brittany</note> and brought it, along with the entire county, under his power. This move stirred Maximilian <note>Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I</note> against Charles, for he considered it an outrage that Brittany—which he hoped would be a thorn in Charles's side—was being seized almost before his eyes. Indeed, Maximilian, having lost his wife Mary <note>Mary of Burgundy</note>, who was Charles's mother-in-law, was seeking a new marriage with the daughter of the Duke of the Bretons <note>Anne of Brittany</note>. Consequently, he began to pressure the borders of Picardy with raids and a regular army. However, although Charles conducted the war through his lieutenants, he easily repressed these attempts after the Germans <note>Latin: Alemanis</note> were routed. 

Proceeding with the expedition organized against the Bretons, he forced Anne—the daughter of Francis, Duke of the Bretons, who had taken charge of affairs after her father's death and had been promised in marriage to Maximilian through ambassadors and certain agents—to submit to his commands. This followed a massive battle at Saint-Aubin <note>The Battle of Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier, 1488</note> where the Bretons were defeated; in this battle, Louis of Orléans <note>The future King Louis XII</note> was captured and brought to Charles. Charles, having dismissed Margaret <note>Margaret of Austria</note>, joined Anne to himself in marriage. From her, he soon became the father of two children, though he outlived them both. 

With Brittany now pacified, he decided to pursue by war the Angevin right to the Kingdom of Naples, which fell to him through his family lineage. Setting out with a very large force in the month of August, he gained possession of Naples the following February. Regarding the fortune and outcome of that kingdom, we have demonstrated it more extensively and distinctly elsewhere. As he was leading his army back to France, the Venetians and Lombards attempted to block his path at the River Taro with their combined forces. But he, having engaged in a fierce battle, opened a way for his arms through a massive slaughter of the enemy. Meanwhile, Naples had revolted from its allegiance to Charles and opened its gates to the returning Aragonese. Having returned to France, Charles was contemplating the recovery of the kingdom, but death interrupted his plans. For on the seventh night of April, followed by the most celebrated Christian day of Palms <note>Palm Sunday</note>, he died of apoplexy without children. He was carried to the Church of Saint Denis near Paris.

¶ In his place, by the competing zeal of all and the highest consensus of the princes, the Duke of Orléans was chosen—the same Louis whom I mentioned a little earlier. He considered nothing more important than to immediately notify Pope Alexander VI and the neighboring powers through a relay of horses and letters that he had been declared King. And as he was receiving the crown at Reims according to custom and was being anointed with the celestial oil <note>The Holy Ampulla, believed to have been brought by a dove for the baptism of Clovis</note>, behold, a messenger arrived from Maximilian,

<column-break/>

the King of the Romans, stating that Burgundy was being attacked in war. Louis, having sent commanders to meet the threat, where he thought enough provision had been made for the present, continued his inauguration. He departed from there and, after surveying several cities of his kingdom along the way, came to Paris. The entire city poured out to meet him with wives and children; the priests, with their regalia as is the custom when receiving kings for the first time, welcomed him. 

Ambassadors sent by the Kings of the Spaniards returned after peace was renewed and strengthened. The treaty with the King of the English was preserved under the same conditions struck with previous kings, with this addition: that it would last only as long as either of their lives. An embassy was also heard from Philip, Duke of Austria and Count of Flanders <note>Philip the Handsome</note>, with whom it was agreed that insofar as Philip ruled within the borders of the Franks, he would swear an oath to the King. Louis restored all the towns to him that were then to be returned according to the treaty struck with Charles VIII. A treaty was also struck with the Venetian and Florentine ambassadors in the name of both nations.

¶ With matters thus settled, he undertook an expedition against Ludovico Sforza, the usurper <note>Latin: incubatorem, literally "squatter"</note> of the Duchy of Milan, which belonged to Louis through the succession of his grandmother Valentina. She was the daughter of Giovanni Galeazzo, the first Duke of the Milanese. In the marriage contract, it had been provided that if the male line should fail, the rule would devolve to Valentina and her children. This agreement had even been confirmed by a decree of the Pope, since at that time the Imperial throne was vacant during an interregnum. 

Therefore, at his first arrival, having put Ludovico Sforza to flight, he took possession of the Insubrians <note>The region around Milan</note>, except for Cremona, which he granted to the Venetians according to their treaty. The King himself also came to Milan, where as soon as the Insubrians and the Ligurians who inhabit Genoa swore their oaths to him, he returned to France. Before he departed for France, he sent part of his troops and artillery to what they call Romagna <note>Latin: Logatam ... Romandiolam</note> to capture Imola <note>Latin: Forum Cornelij</note> and Forlì <note>Latin: Forum Livij</note>, which still retains that name, and certain cities on the high Flaminian Way. 

Once these were brought under the power of Cesare Borgia, Duke of Valentinois and son of Pope Alexander VI, they began their march toward Pesaro. But behold, the Milanese defected to Ascanio Maria Sforza, the Cardinal and brother of Ludovico, and received Ascanio first within the walls. Soon after, they also received Ludovico himself with a hired force of Swiss and Germans. Accordingly, having recalled the troops from the Flaminian Way and sent a new supplement from France, [they moved against] Ludovico...

# Genealogy. #

The French captured Sforza <note>Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan, also known as "Il Moro"</note> alive without a struggle while he was besieging the citadel of Novara with engines and siege machines. Although he had taken possession of the city shortly before by surrender, he fell into the power of his enemies when he was abandoned by the Germans <note>Refers to the Swiss and German mercenaries who refused to fight their fellow countrymen in the French service</note>. They eagerly returned home after being promised immunity and a safe return by the French. Not long after, Ascanio <note>Ascanio Sforza, Ludovico’s brother and a powerful Cardinal</note> was forced into flight and fell into a Venetian garrison; he was led to Venice and, within a few days, was sent to the King by the Venetians, who were allies in the war. Louis <note>King Louis XII of France</note> then turned his mind toward recovering the Kingdom of Naples. He entered into a treaty with Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Spain <note>Latin: "Elizabeth"; Isabella I of Castile</note> on these conditions: that they would divide the Kingdom of Naples, won by war, equally between them. Pope Alexander VI <note>Rodrigo Borgia</note> granted to both parties whatever rights the Church held over the territory. As soon as spring began, Louis sent his forces there. The promontory of Gargano supports a town of the same name, which was attributed to the Apulians known as the Daunians. The Spanish contended that this belonged to them according to the specific terms of the alliance and the formula of the treaties. The French, however, protested that it was left in the middle and should be shared equally; thus, the dispute began legally at first. Soon, as tempers heated and the quarrel spread, they turned to arms. The French were the first to strike, driving the Spanish from the field and forcing them into Barletta <note>Latin: "Barolum"</note>. Having gained the opportunity to roam more freely through all the borders of the kingdom, the French neglected to besiege the Spanish who held Barletta with a garrison along with several other citadels. The enemies, watchful for every opportunity, departed Barletta in the silence of the night and reached Ruvo <note>Latin: "Rubum"</note>. After storming the town, they overwhelmed the French garrison. At almost that same time, German infantry brought in by Spanish pay arrived. From this, such confidence grew in the enemy that on the ninth day before the Kalends of May <note>April 23</note>, in the year of Christ’s birth 1503, they led out all their forces to the bridge of Cannae <note>Site of the famous ancient battle between Hannibal and Rome</note>

<column-break/>

and pitched camp. This was not far from the French camp, which was situated along the banks of the river Ofanto <note>Latin: "Aufidus"</note> near Canosa <note>Latin: "Canusium"</note>. The next day, when the Spanish attempted to take the town of Cerignola <note>Latin: "Cydoniole"</note> by force, the French came to its aid, and a fierce battle was fought on both sides. Eventually, the French cavalry withdrew from the rear of the line even though no one was pressing them. Noticing this, the Italian auxiliary cavalry of the Spanish attacked the flanks of the French who were fighting at the front and threw them into confusion. With the French thus routed, the victory belonged to the Spanish. In that battle fell Louis, Duke of Nemours, of the family of the Counts of Armagnac, who held the person and office of the King’s lieutenant. The Spanish, elated by their success, not long after captured the city of Naples and the citadels commonly called the "New" <note>Castel Nuovo</note> and the "Lucullan" <note>Castel dell’Ovo, named for the Roman Lucullus</note>—so called because of its shape—and took possession of the kingdom. The remaining remnants of the French who survived the war first gathered in their flight on the banks of the Garigliano <note>Latin: "Liris"</note> near Sinuessa; from there they retreated to Gaeta, where they were destitute of all help. Then, due to the wickedness of the questors—or treasurers, if you prefer—who (though they did not escape unpunished) were led by damnable greed and provided neither the wages due to them nor necessary travel funds, the soldiers bravely and spiritedly endured the insults of their adversaries while fighting. They were comforted in no small measure by that line of Virgil: *It comes to mind that it is beautiful to die in arms.* <note>Original Latin: "Pulchrumque mori succurrit in armis," from the Aeneid, 2.317</note>. The rest who survived, whose leader was the high-minded man Louis d'Ars <note>Latin: "Ludouicus dast"</note>, having despaired of all things, cast aside all weakness of spirit. Resuming their strength, with an armed hand and an outstretched arm, and with no one contradicting them, they arrived safely all the way back to France.

->of the kings of the Franks.<-
