# Prefatory Letter #

->¶ To the most excellent man, Lord Jacques de Amoncourt <note>original: "Jacobo de amuncuria"</note>, well-deserving professor of both laws <note>Referring to Civil and Canon law, a standard of high legal education</note>, most worthy Count and teacher in the Church of Saint John the Baptist in Lyon, and Vicar General of the Lord of Lyon: Symphorien Champier, physician <note>original: "physicus"</note> of Lyon, sends many greetings.<-

The divine Plato and Marcus Cicero, the prince of Latin eloquence, have recorded in literary monuments that seats in heaven are prepared for the rulers of cities and for other wise men. Antiquity also counted many famous men among the gods, and Hesiod ranks the ancient kings alongside the divine. Virgil <note>original: "Maro Virgilius"</note> seems to agree sufficiently with these opinions in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*. There, after describing the punishments of the wicked, he recounts the rewards of the good who served others and their country well; among other things, he speaks thus:

*Behold, he sees others to the right and left upon the grass feasting, and joyfully singing the paean <note>A song of praise or triumph</note> in chorus amid the fragrant laurel grove; from where, above, the mighty river Eridanus <note>A mythical river often identified with the Po or the Rhône</note> rolls through the forest. Here is the band of those who suffered wounds fighting for their fatherland. And those who were chaste priests while life remained, and those who were pious poets and spoke things worthy of Apollo, or those who improved life through discovered arts, and those who made others remember them through their merit. All these have their temples bound with a snow-white ribbon <note>original: "vitta"; a headband symbolizing purity and religious consecration</note>.*

Therefore, I shall perhaps not seem to be failing in my duty as a man grateful to my country if I collect briefly into one volume some of those many who, having served the country and the Christian republic well, spared no labors (since they nurtured noble spirits well-formed by nature). For who could recount them all with the elegance of words that the subject itself seems to demand? Indeed, I have attempted to undertake this, not because I judge myself to be of such great talent that I could provide it sufficiently, but partly to stir others—those who are naturally learned and supported by varied and manifold teaching—to be sufficient for such a great province, and partly so that some monument might remain to testify that I once lived. For he truly lives who is useful to others and makes use of himself; nothing is more shameful than a man who has no proof that he has lived long except for the years in which he did not truly live, but lost his life by being a slave to his belly. For, as Seneca bears witness, it does not matter how long someone lives, but how well.

I ask, therefore, that you receive with the same favor you usually show me this brief compendium regarding the antiquity and praise of the city of Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunensis"</note> and its illustrious men. I wished to dedicate this to you because I know that you embrace good literature—the true ornament of a churchman—and that you do not wish to be ignorant of the origin and progress of your country (which is the duty of a diligent man) or whatever has happened to it in former times. History, the knowledge of which brings the greatest pleasure to the mind and no small utility, will teach you these things.

Farewell, lover of letters, and do not be unmindful of your Symphorien. Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507, on the 13th day before the Kalends of August <note>July 20, 1507</note>.

<summary>A formal dedication from the physician Symphorien Champier to Jacques de Amoncourt, justifying the historical study of Lyon through classical philosophy and Virgil’s poetry. Champier argues that recording the lives of great men is a civic duty and a means of achieving a meaningful legacy.</summary>

# On the antiquity of Lyon #

->By the same master Symphorien Champier, physician <note>original: "physici"; here referring to a doctor of medicine and natural philosophy</note>, on the origin and praise of the city of Lyon.
Also: a small book on the illustrious men of the same city.<-

### ¶ On the origin and antiquity of the city of Lyon. Chapter One. ###

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' featuring intertwining floral and vine motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
The people of Lyon, or the Celts, were a people of the Gauls; from them, the third part of Gaul was named. These people, coming to the Ebro <note>original: "Iberum"</note> river of Spain and settling there, were called Celtiberians. Hence, 
<margin>A</margin>
Lucan <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD)</note> says in his fourth book: *And the Celts, refugees from the ancient race of Gauls, mixing their name with the Iberians.* Lyon, therefore, is a royal and most flourishing city. Indeed, the city is most worthy of admiration, both for the convenience of its site and for other great matters; among the Celts, it shines and radiates like the sun among the stars. For it is a city 
<margin>Praise of Lyon</margin>
that can compete in every kind of praise and virtue—not only with any of those cities which in this time are considered famous and celebrated, but also with all the memory of antiquity. For this reason, I would not be wrong to say that the lands adjacent to the territory of Lyon are especially cherished and cultivated by "Nourishing Ceres" <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture and grain</note>. Nor is the city only famous for its multitude of inhabitants; it seems, not without reason, to be sacred to Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine</note> himself. Why should I speak of the diverse kinds of fruits, or the forests and other groves? For those things are not only most useful for food, but even those that seem unfruitful bring infinite benefits to human use. There is the beauty of the gardens and their spacious pleasantness. Lyon, I say, is a city watered by rivers and springs; for it is distinguished by two great rivers made famous in the songs of poets and the books of historians: namely, the Saône <note>original: "Arar"</note> and the Rhône. 
<margin>B</margin>
The Saône, I say—or as we commonly call it now, the *Sagonna*—flows between the city with a wonderful tranquility. The Rhône, however, washes the walls of the city from the eastern side with a swift motion. There, all things are most blessed in their yield for the use of living creatures. The city is a neighbor to Vienne. In the times of Octavian Augustus, as Eusebius <note>A 4th-century historian and bishop</note> testifies, it was founded by Plancus <note>Lucius Munatius Plancus, a Roman senator</note>, a disciple of Cicero and a most famous orator, in a level place near a certain hill where it had been founded previously, where the Saône mixes with the Rhône. Nor did it shine for long only among the other cities of Gaul because of its order of most famous men; for it was always of great use to them, just as it is at present, as a great trading center <note>original: "emporium"</note>. Likewise, just as this city was once preferred to the other cities of all Gaul because of a 

<column-break/>

certain singular excellence of all the virtues found within it, so too now the Church of Lyon exists, not without merit, as the head of the rest of the churches of all Gaul, and holds the primacy <note>The Archbishop of Lyon still holds the title "Primate of the Gauls"</note>. In this church, the Arch-prelate <note>The Archbishop</note>, the Dean, the Official, the Archpriest, and the other counts <note>The canons of the Cathedral of Saint-Jean held the noble title of "Count of Lyon"</note> shine forth with a refined nobility of birth, excellence of learning, integrity of character, and the whole assembly of clerics. Likewise, I cannot easily express in words how festively and beautifully the divine office is performed daily with the observation of ceremonies and harmony. Thus it happens that I more quickly induce my mind to believe, without doubt, that the famous Altar of Lyon <note>The Sanctuary of the Three Gauls</note>—which in previous centuries was decorated with such honor and was famous throughout almost the entire world—was a certain omen and augury of this present church. And lest I seem to anyone to be flattering our people rather than telling the pure truth, I say nothing of its wealth; I say nothing of the innumerable and almost infinite gifts that are placed there daily at the sacred altars. Finally, I pass over in silence many things that greatly adorn this city. Moreover, many other temples occur, both at home and abroad, dedicated to divine worship and the Christian religion, such as the most sumptuously built basilicas of the most blessed Apostle Paul, Saint Justus, and Saint Nizier <note>original: "Nicetij"</note>; the decoration and the lavishness of these buildings could be the ornaments of any of the most celebrated cities. Furthermore, wherever you turn, so many and such magnificent houses and royal palaces offer themselves to your sight, whose number and magnificence render the city itself spectacular and admirable. Both historians and poets also commend this city, as has been said. Regarding this, Strabo <note>An ancient Greek geographer (64 BC–24 AD)</note> says among the first: 
<margin>Strabo</margin>
*Lyon, therefore, founded on a hill where the river Saône mixes with the Rhône, is held by the Roman Empire. It flourishes more than the rest of the cities, except for Narbonne, in its order of men. For it is also a great trading center for them. The Roman leaders mint silver and gold coins in that place. Also, a temple designated by all the Gauls at common expense and dedicated to Augustus Caesar was built before this city where the meeting of the rivers is. There is also an altar of exceptional dignity having a title inscribed with the number of sixty nations, and a huge statue for each of them was placed near the altar.* It is established that this city is situated in the territory of the Sequani people, which lies in the middle of the Rhône and the Doubs <note>original: "Dubidis"</note> rivers. From here, the remaining peoples verging toward the Rhine are separated partly by the Doubs and partly by the Saône. For these rivers, as was said above, are carried down from the Alps, then flowing together into one channel, they fall into the Rhône. There is another river similarly having its origin in the Alps called the Seine <note>original: "Sequana"</note>; however, it flows out into the ocean, separated by a parallel line.

<summary>This page describes the ancient origins and geographical splendor of Lyon, highlighting its founding by the Romans and its natural beauty at the confluence of the Saône and Rhône rivers. It also emphasizes Lyon's ecclesiastical importance as the "Primacy of the Gauls" and its historical role as a Roman administrative and economic hub.</summary>

<meta>The previous page introduced the historical and geographical origins of Lyon, focusing on its Celtic and Roman roots. # Introductory Epistle #

¶ To the most excellent man, Lord Jacobus de Amuncuria <note>Jacques d'Amboise, a prominent church official and patron of the arts in Lyon</note>, well-deserving professor of both laws <note>Referring to Canon and Civil law</note>, most worthy count and precentor in the church of the divine John the Baptist in Lyon, and Vicar General of the Lord of Lyon: Symphorien Champier of Lyon, physician, sends his greatest greetings.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'L' featuring foliate and floral patterns.</image-desc>
The divine Plato and the prince of Latin eloquence, Marcus Cicero, have entrusted to literary monuments that seats in heaven are prepared for the rulers of cities and other wise men. Antiquity also elevated many famous men to the rank of gods, and Hesiod numbers ancient kings among the deities. Maro Virgil seems to agree sufficiently with their opinions; in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, where he describes the punishments of the wicked and the rewards of the good who have served others and their country well, he says among other things:

*Behold, he sees others to the right and left upon the grass*
*Feasting, and singing a joyful paean <note>A song of praise or triumph</note> in chorus*
*Amid a fragrant grove of laurel; from where the great river*
*Eridanus <note>A mythical river often identified with the Po river</note> rolls through the forest.*
*Here is the band of those who suffered wounds fighting for their country;*
*Those who were chaste priests while life remained,*
*Those who were pious poets and spoke things worthy of Apollo;*
*Or those who improved life through discovered arts,*
*And those who made others mindful of them by their merit.*
*The temples of all these are bound with snow-white ribbons.*
<note>original Latin: "Conspicit ecce alios dextra leuaq̄ per herbam... Omnib’ his niuea cingūtur tpa vitta." Virgil, Aeneid VI.656–665</note>

Therefore, I will perhaps be seen as performing the duty of a man not ungrateful toward his country if I collect into one volume, in summary form, some of the many who have served their country and the Christian republic well. These men (since nature nourished their noble and well-disposed minds) spared no labors. For who could recount them all, or with such elegance of words as the matter itself seems to demand? I have indeed attempted to approach this task, not because I judge myself so great that I could sufficiently provide it, but so that I might rouse others—who are nobly learned and supported by varied and manifold teaching—to be sufficient for such a great <term>province</term> <note>original: "provinciae"; used here in the Roman sense to mean a specific duty or field of responsibility</note>. Furthermore, I do this so that some monument remains which may testify that I once lived. For he truly lives who is of use to others and employs his own talents; nothing is more shameful than a man who has no proof that he has lived long except for the years in which he did not truly live, but lost his life being obedient to his belly. For, as Seneca bears witness, it does not matter how long someone lives, but how well. 

I ask, therefore, that you receive this brief compendium on the antiquity and praise of the city of Lyon and its illustrious men with the same kind face you usually show me. I wished it to be dedicated to you because I know you embrace "good letters" <note>The humanities and classical literature</note>, which are the true ornament of a man of the Church. I also know that you do not wish to be ignorant of the origin and progress of your homeland (which is the duty of a diligent man) and whatever has happened to it through former times. History, the knowledge of which brings the greatest pleasure of the mind and no small utility, will teach you this. Farewell, lover of literature; not unmindful of your Symphorien. 

At Lyon. In the year of our Lord 1507, on the 20th of July <note>original: "xiij. kal. Augusti"</note>.

# ¶ On the origin and antiquity of the city of Ly-
# on. Chapter One.

<sig>A</sig> <image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'L' depicting a seated figure in robes, likely a king or scholar, within a square border decorated with leafy vines.</image-desc> The people of Lyon, or the Celts, were a people of Gaul; from them, the third part of Gaul <note>Gallia Celtica, one of the three divisions of Gaul described by Julius Caesar</note> was named. These people, coming to the Ebro <term>Iberus: The Ebro river in Spain</term>, a river of Spain, and settling there, were called Celtiberians. Hence Lucan <note>A Roman poet, 39–65 AD</note> says in book 4: *And refugees from the ancient race of Gauls, the Celts mixing their name with the Iberians.* Therefore, Lyon is a royal and most flourishing city. This city, by its own nature and the opportuneness of its site, and by the admiration of other great things, is most worthy; among the Celts it shines and radiates like the sun among the stars. For it is a city <margin>Praise of Lyon</margin> which, in every kind of praise and virtue, can contend not only with those that are held famous and celebrated in this time, but even with all the memory of antiquity. For which reason I might not unjustly say that the lands adjacent to the territory of Lyon are especially beloved and cultivated by nourishing Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture and grain</note>. This city is famous for the multitude of its inhabitants, and it seems sacred to Bacchus <note>The Roman god of wine and festivity</note> himself, not without reason. Why should I speak of the different kinds of fruits, the forests, and the other orchards? For those things which are not only most useful for food, but even those which seem fruitless, bring infinite conveniences for the uses of men. The beauty of the gardens is a spacious delight. Lyon, I say, is a city watered by rivers and fountains. Indeed, it is distinguished by two great rivers made famous in the songs of poets and the books <sig>B</sig> of historians: namely, the Arar and the Rhone. The Arar, I say, or as we now commonly call it, the Saône, flows through the middle of the city with wondrous tranquility. But the Rhone, with a headlong motion, washes the walls of the city from the eastern part. There, everything is most blessed for the use of living creatures. The city is neighboring to Vienne. In the times of Octavian Augustus, according to the testimony of Eusebius <note>A 4th-century Christian historian and chronicler</note>, it was founded by Plancus <note>Lucius Munatius Plancus, a Roman general and associate of Julius Caesar</note>, a most famous orator and disciple of Cicero, in a level place near a certain hill where it had previously been established, where the Arar joins the Rhone. This city has long shone above the other cities of Gaul by its order of most famous men; for it was always a great emporium <term>Emporium: A major center of commerce and trade</term> for them, just as it is at present. Also, just as this city was once preferred to the other cities of all Gaul because of a certain

<column-break/>

singular excellence of all the virtues found in it, so also now the church of Lyon stands, not without merit, as the head of all the other churches of Gaul and holds the primacy. For in this church, the arch-prelate <note>The Archbishop</note>, the dean himself, the official, the archpriest, and the other counts shine with such nobility of birth, excellence of doctrine, and uprightness of character, as does the whole assembly of the clergy. Likewise, how festively and with what observation of ceremonies and harmony the divine office is performed daily, I could not easily express in words. Whence it happens that I am more quickly led to believe that the altar of Lyon <note>Referring to the Altar of the Three Gauls, a monument of the imperial cult</note>, which in former centuries was adorned with such beauty and was famous throughout almost the whole world, was a certain omen and augury for this church. And lest I seem to anyone to flatter our own people rather than to narrate the pure truth, I say nothing of its wealth, I say nothing of the countless and almost infinite gifts which are daily placed there at the sacred altars. Finally, I pass over in silence many things which greatly adorn it. Furthermore, many other temples occur, both at home and abroad, dedicated to divine worship and the Christian religion, such as the most sumptuously built basilicas of the most blessed Apostle Paul, Saint Justus, and Saint Nicetius <note>Saint Nizier, a 6th-century Bishop of Lyon</note>, whose ornamentation and lavishness of construction could be the ornaments of even the most celebrated city. Moreover, wherever you turn, so many and such magnificent houses and royal palaces offer themselves to the view, that their number and magnificence make the city itself spectacular and admirable. This city also, as has been said, is commended by <margin>Strabo</margin> historians and poets. Whence Strabo <note>A Greek geographer of the 1st century BC/AD</note> primarily says of it: Lyon, therefore, <margin>The river Arar mixing with the Rhone</margin> is built on a hill where the river Arar mixes with the Rhone; it is held by the Roman empire. It flourishes also above the other cities, except Narbonne, in its order of men. For it is also a great emporium for them. In that place, the Roman leaders mint silver and gold coinage. A temple also, designated by the common expense of all the Gauls and dedicated to Augustus Caesar, was built before this city where the confluence of the rivers is. There is also an altar of exceptional dignity, having a title inscribed with the number of sixty tribes; and an immense altar was placed there with a statue of each of them. It is established that this city is the seat of the Sequani people, which lies in the middle of the Rhone and the Doubs <term>Dubis: The Doubs river</term> rivers. From here, the remaining peoples turning toward the Rhine are separated partly by the Doubs and partly by the Arar. For these rivers, as was said above, are brought down from the Alps, then flowing together into one channel, they descend into the Rhone. There is another river similarly having its origin in the Alps, the Seine by name, which flows out or is separated from the ocean in a parallel...

<meta>This page is the dedicatory preface of Symphorien Champier’s work on Lyon. It follows the previous section's introduction to the city's antiquity, serving as a formal address to his patron, Jacobus de Amuncuria, justifying the historical project through classical and moral philosophy.</meta>

# Introductory Letter

¶ To the most excellent man, Lord Jacobus de Amuncuria, a well-deserving professor of both laws <note>Referring to Canon Law and Civil Law</note>, a most worthy count in the church of Saint John the Baptist of Lyon, and teacher; vicar general to the Lord [Archbishop] of Lyon: Symphorien Champier, physician of Lyon, sends many greetings.

---

<image-desc>Large woodcut decorative initial 'L' containing floral and foliate scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>

The divine Plato and the prince of Latin eloquence, Marcus Cicero, have committed to literary monuments that seats in heaven are prepared for the rulers of cities and other wise men. Antiquity also regarded many famous men as gods, and Hesiod numbers ancient kings among the gods. Maro Virgil <note>The Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro</note> seems to agree sufficiently with their opinions; in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*, where, after describing the punishments of the wicked, he recounts the rewards of the good who have deserved well of others and their country, he says thus among other things: *Behold, he sees others to the right and left upon the grass, feasting and singing a joyful paean <note>A song of praise or triumph</note> in a choir within a fragrant laurel grove, from where the mighty river Eridanus rolls through the forest from above. Here is the band of those who suffered wounds fighting for their country; and those who were chaste priests while life remained; and pious bards who spoke things worthy of Phoebus <note>The god Apollo, patron of poetry</note>; or those who refined life through discovered arts; and those who made others remember them by their merit. For all these, the temples of the head are bound with a snow-white fillet.* <note>Original Latin: "Conspicit ecce alios... Omnib⁹ his niuea cingūtur tpa vitta."</note>

Therefore, I shall perhaps be seen to have performed the duty of a man not ungrateful toward his country if I collect briefly into one volume some from among the many who, having deserved well of their country and the Christian republic, spared no labors (since they nourished noble and naturally well-disposed souls). For who could recount them all, or do so with that elegance of words which the matter itself seems to demand? This I have indeed attempted to approach—not because I judge myself to be of such great stature that I could sufficiently provide it, but both to rouse others who, being nobly learned and supported by varied and manifold doctrine, are sufficient for such a task, and so that some monument may remain which may testify that I once lived. For he truly lives who benefits others and makes use of himself; since nothing is more base than a man who has no argument by which to prove he has lived long except for the years in which he did not live, but lost his life being obedient to his belly. For according to the witness of Seneca <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher</note>, it does not matter how long someone lives, but how well. 

I ask, therefore, that you receive with that countenance you usually show me this brief compendium on the antiquity and commendation of the city of Lyon and its illustrious men, which I wished to be dedicated to you. For I know that you embrace good literature—the true ornament of a churchman—and that you (as is the duty of a diligent man) do not wish to be ignorant of the origin and progress of your country and whatever has happened to it through former times. History, the knowledge of which holds the greatest pleasure of the mind and no small utility, will teach you this. Farewell, lover of the learned, and be not unmindful of your Symphorien. 

At Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507, the 14th Kalends of August <note>July 19th</note>.

### On the origin and antiquity of the city of Lyon. Chapter One.

The people of Lyon, or the Celts, were a people of Gaul; from them the third part of Gaul was named. Those who traveled to the Ebro river in Spain and settled there were called Celtiberians.
<sig>A</sig>
Hence Lucan writes in his fourth book: "And the Celts, fugitives from the ancient race of the Gauls, mixing their name with the Iberians." <note>original: "Profugiqz a gente vetusta Gallorū celte miscentes nomē hiberis." This refers to the migration of tribes and the mixing of cultures.</note> Lyon, therefore, is a royal and most flourishing city. Indeed, this city, by the advantage of its location and the wonder of its other great qualities, is most worthy of admiration; among the Celts, it shines and radiates like the sun among the stars. For it is a city that, in every kind of praise and virtue, can compete not only with those that are considered famous and celebrated in this age, but even with every memory of antiquity.

<margin>Praise of Lyon</margin> For this reason, I would not be wrong to say that the lands adjacent to the territory of Lyon are especially beloved and cultivated by nourishing Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture and grain.</note>. This city is famous for its multitude of merchants <note>The original "netorū" is likely a shorthand for *negotiatorum* (merchants), as Lyon was a major trade hub.</note> and it seems, not without reason, sacred to Bacchus <note>The god of wine, reflecting the region's viticulture.</note> himself. Why should I speak of the various kinds of fruits, the woods, and the other orchards? For those things which are not only most useful for food, but even those which seem fruitless, bring infinite conveniences for the use of men. There is the beauty of the gardens and a spacious delight. Lyon, I say, is a city watered by rivers and springs; for it is distinguished by two great rivers made famous in the songs of poets and the books of historians.
<sig>B</sig>
It is marked by the Arar <note>The Saône river.</note> and the Rhone. The Arar, or as we now commonly call it, the Saône, glides between the city with wonderful tranquility. The Rhone, however, washes the city walls on the eastern side with a swift motion. There, everything is most blessed for the offspring of living creatures. The city is a neighbor to Vienne. This city has long outshone the other cities of Gaul in its rank of most illustrious men; for it has always been of great use to them, just as it is in these present times. Likewise, just as this city was once preferred to the other cities of all Gaul because of a 

<column-break/>

certain singular excellence of all the virtues found within it, so too now the Church of Lyon, not without merit, stands as the head of the rest of the churches of all Gaul and holds the primacy. For in this church, the archprelate <note>The Archbishop.</note> himself, the dean, the official, the archpriest, and the other counts shine forth with such nobility of birth, excellence of doctrine, integrity of character, and the entire assembly of clerics. And lest I seem to anyone to be flattering our own people rather than telling the pure truth, I say nothing of its wealth, I say nothing of the immune honors and the almost infinite gifts which are placed there daily at the sacred altars. Finally, I pass over in silence many things which greatly adorn it. Furthermore, wherever you turn, so many and such magnificent houses and royal palaces offer themselves to your sight, that both their number and magnificence render the city itself spectacular and admirable. Both historians and poets also commend this city, as has been said.

A temple, designated by all the Gauls in common and dedicated to Augustus Caesar at their expense, was built before this city where the rivers join. There is also an altar of great dignity, having an inscribed title with the names of sixty nations, and a separate statue of each of them was placed there, and a huge altar was established. For these rivers, as was said above, are carried down from the Alps, then flowing together into one channel, they descend into the Rhone. Suetonius, in his life of Caligula, and Pliny the Second, mention a village of the Treveri called Ambiatarinus, otherwise Biatino, above the confluence. The verse: "Born in the camp, nurtured in his father's arms, he was already an omen of the designated Prince." Eusebius, in his *Chronicon*, says: Munatius Plancus, a disciple of Cicero and a distinguished orator, founded Lyon while he was governor of "Long-haired Gaul" <note>original: "galliam comatā." Cornelius Tacitus in his *Histories* <note>original: "libzo. xvij historie auguste." This likely refers to Book 1 or 2 of Tacitus' *Histories*, though the text cites "17".</note>: A cause for war was sought against the Aedui in vain; ordered to bring money and arms, they furthermore provided free provisions. What the Aedui did out of fear, the people of Lyon did with joy. But when the Italian legion and the Taurine wing were led away, it was decided that the seventeen cohorts should be left in their usual winter quarters at Lyon. Manlius Valens, legate of the Italian legion, though he had deserved well of the fathers, was held in no honor by Vitellius. Fabius had defamed him with secret accusations, praising him openly while he was unaware, so that he might be more easily deceived. An ancient discord between the people of Lyon and Vienne had first ignited the war. There were many mutual slaughters, more frequent and fiercer than could be explained by merely fighting for Nero or Galba. And Galba, using the occasion of the Lyon people’s anger, had turned their revenues into the treasury. Great was the honor given to those of Vienne; hence came emulation and envy, and a hatred bound together between those separated by only a single river. Therefore, the people of Lyon incited individual soldiers and urged them toward the destruction of the people of Vienne, claiming their colony had been besieged by them and that they had aided Vindex's

<column-break/>

attempts, and that they were not raising legions for the protection of Galba. And where he had pretended causes for hatred, he showed the magnitude of the prey. It was no longer a secret exhortation, but public prayers that the avengers should go and destroy the seat of the Gallic war. Everything there was foreign and hostile, they said, while they themselves were a Roman colony, a part of the army, and companions in both prosperous and adverse times—praying they would not be left to their enemies if fortune turned. By these and more arguments in the same vein, they so persuaded the soldiers that even the legates and leaders of the factions did not think the anger of the army could be restrained. The people of Vienne, not unaware of their danger, held out veils and sacred fillets <note>original: "velamēta et infulas." Symbols of supplication and religious sanctuary.</note> as the column approached; by prostrating themselves and embracing the soldiers' knees and feet, they began to turn their minds. Valens added three hundred sesterces for each soldier. The antiquity and dignity of the colony prevailed, and the words of Fabius, commending the safety and welfare of the people of Vienne, were received with favorable ears. Nevertheless, they were publicly fined of their arms and provided the soldiers with various supplies. But the rumor remained constant that Valens himself had been bought with a large sum of money; he, who had long been impoverished, suddenly became rich and poorly concealed his change of fortune.

->¶ On the preeminence or hierarchy of the<-
->Church of Lyon. Chapter Two.<-

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'E' with floral/vine patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>
The Church of Lyon was founded long ago by the holy fathers to be as similar as possible to the Church Triumphant <note>The "Church Triumphant" refers to the assembly of the blessed in Heaven.</note>. For just as the Trinity of Persons in the unity of essence is venerated and worshipped by the citizens of the Church Triumphant, so in the Church of Lyon there are three contiguous churches, as if representing the Trinity, in which there is an identity of college and office, and they are summoned by a single sound of the bells to represent the divine unity. In each of these, the entire Bible is read through every year in a uniform manner. These churches are: Saint John the Baptist, Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, and the third is Holy Cross. In this same church, there were from the beginning nine dignities <note>original: "psonat?" for *personatus*, referring to high-ranking ecclesiastical offices.</note> established to represent the nine orders of angels in the Church Triumphant. One of these dignities is called the Abbey of Saint Justus of Lyon, which dignity is held by whoever is Archbishop of Lyon. Their names and descriptions can be found in another writing. Likewise, there are thirteen perpetual chaplains established there, among whom one is the principal Archbishop of Lyon; and this is to represent our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the head of the church, and the venerable college of the twelve apostles. Similarly, the status of these may be found in another writing. Furthermore, in the said church there are four keepers at the high altar celebrating the feasts of Blessed John and Blessed Stephen like canons, and these four represent the Evangelists. Also there are...

<header>On the famous people of Lyon.</header>

In the same church, there are seven knights learned in the law who defend the interior of the church, so that the others might be more freely and devoutly intent on those things which pertain to the divine office. These seven represent the seven lampstands that John saw in the Apocalypse <note>A reference to the Book of Revelation 1:12.</note>. All the other canons, who number fifty-eight or more—some of whom are at times non-resident—signify the disciples of the Lord who were substituted in the place of the Apostles. Truly, the manner of life to be observed by the holy fathers in the said church during the divine office was as follows: All canons holding personages <term>personatus: high-ranking ecclesiastical offices with specific duties</term> or other priestly roles, and all other prebendary clerics in the said church, or those in the service of the canons, are bound by necessity to rise for Matins on alternate nights according to the custom and statutes of the church. They must enter the choir before the end of the third verse of the first psalm after the Invitatory. No one may leave until the seventh lesson has begun on feasts of nine lessons, or the third lesson on feasts of three lessons. Transgressors receive nothing at all from the daily distributions; in such cases, the distribution is turned into alms, and neither the one who is absent that day nor any other may profit from it.

¶ The dignities of this same sacred house: Archbishop, Dean, Archdeacon, Precentor, Cantor, Chamberlain, Sacristan, Custos, and the Provost of Fourvière <note>original: "foruerij," referring to the historic district of Fourvière in Lyon.</note>. Following these is the Master of the Choir, the first canon after those canons holding personages. He is followed by one of the seven perpetual chaplains, the Vice-Master, whom they call the Master of the Boys. Likewise, the holy fathers decreed for the preservation of the church’s dignity that no canon should dare to go through the city outside the boundaries of the said church unless on horseback, and then not alone but with decent company and in respectable habit; nor should he dare to enter any dishonest lodging. They are bound to observe these rules by oath. Likewise, Brother Hugh of Saint-Cher <note>original: "hugo de scto Theodozo," referring to the Dominican cardinal Hugh of Saint-Cher (c. 1200–1263).</note> of the Order of Preachers—the first Master of Theology of that order, a Cardinal, and a Legate in Germany—reformed and organized the Church of Liège according to the rite, manner, and ordinances of the Church of Lyon; and so it is observed there today. This temple shines with such eminent dignity that I would not even compare the Temple of Diana at Ephesus, built with such extravagance, to it. For they say that the Ephesian temple was built over two hundred and twenty years by all of Asia on marshy ground so that it would not feel earthquakes. In that temple, there were 127 columns, each sixty feet high, constructed by individual kings, thirty-six of which were carved with wondrous skill. Nor would I compare it to the richest temple of Delphic Apollo where oracles were given, nor finally to that most famous temple in the city of Paphos sacred to Venus, of which Virgil writes in the first book of the *Aeneid*: "She herself departs to Paphos on high and joyfully revisits her own seats, where she has a temple and a hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense and exhale the scent of fresh garlands." <note>original: "Ipsa paphū sublimis abit sedesqz reuisit Leta suas: vbi tēplū illi: cetū qƷ sabeo Thure calent are: sertisqƷ recētibus halant." Virgil, Aeneid 1.415-417.</note>

<column-break/>

¶ On the famous people of Lyon. Chapter 58.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial E featuring white vine-work and floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
It is recorded in memory that from this city, famous among the others of Gaul, there have arisen very many men distinguished both in various human sciences and in the perfection of the Christian religion. 
<margin>Lucius Plotius</margin> 
From their flock, it is said, was Lucius Plotius Gallus, who was the first to teach Latin rhetoric to the Romans and who, as they say, drew his origin from Lyon. Regarding him, Suetonius, in his book *On Famous Rhetoricians*, records that Cicero spoke of him thus: "Indeed, I remember that when we were boys, a certain Plotius first began to teach in Latin. When a great crowd flocked to him—since all the most studious students practiced with him—I grieved that I was not allowed to do so. I was restrained, however, by the authority of the most learned men, who thought that minds could be better nourished by Greek exercises." This Lucius, according to the same witness, lived a long life. Likewise, I have read elsewhere that Cicero himself asserted that he and his brother Quintus received the rudiments of the Latin language from this same man in the first years of their adolescence.

<margin>E</margin> ¶ The names of the forty-eight martyrs who suffered at Lyon are these: Pothinus, Bishop of Lyon; Zacharias the priest; Epagathus; Macarius; Alcibiades; Silvius; Primus; Ulpius; Vitalis; Cominus; October; Geminus; Pitminicius; Geminus; Julia; Albina; Grata; Rogata; Emilia; Potamia; Pompeya; Rodana; Biblis; Quarta; Materna; Helpes and her daughters. Those, however, who were delivered to the beasts were: Saint Maturus, Attalus, Alexander, Ponticus, and Blandina. Those who gave up their spirit in prison were: Aristens, Cornelius, Iofimus, Titus, Julius, Toticus, Apollonius, Geminianus, Julia, Ausoma, Emimilia, Jannica, Pompeya, Dona, Justa, Trophimia, and Antonia. All these servants of God were crowned together under Antoninus Verus <note>Referring to the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, often called Antoninus.</note>. The place in which they suffered is now commonly called Athanacus <note>The Abbey of Saint-Martin d'Ainay.</note>, a place familiar and very dear to me, where I also perform a respectable office. In that place, a very famous basilica was built in honor of Almighty God and the blessed confessor Martin, as well as a monastery of monks of the Order of Saint Benedict, where very many relics rest. They are commonly called by the people of Lyon the "Athanatian Martyrs."

<margin>F</margin> ¶ Saint Blandina of Lyon is numbered among the forty-eight recent martyrs. The executioners, who from first light until evening were constantly renewing her torments, finally confessed that they were defeated. Though she was struck a second time with tortures, she was not overcome. On the third day, tied to a stake and stretched out in the manner of a cross, she was prepared as food for the beasts. When none of the beasts dared to touch her, she was led back again to prison.

¶ Saint Baldomerus <note>Saint Galmier</note> of Lyon: whose tomb is illustrated by frequent miracles: and he was and is worshipped with fitting honor by the people of Lyon.

¶ Saint Stephen, Bishop of Lyon, is famous among them for many miracles.

¶ Saint Desiderius <note>Saint Didier</note>, Bishop and martyr of the church of Lyon: he shines forth through very many miracles.

¶ Saint Nicetius <note>Saint Nizier</note>, a most worthy prelate of the church of Lyon: although his life was made illustrious by many miracles, his death is nonetheless commended by precious miracles: as a testimony to his holiness, a very celebrated parochial church was built for him among the people of Lyon, of which he is also the patron son: which the parishioners are at present enlarging and making more sumptuous.

¶ Saint Epipodius, who, during the persecution of Antoninus Verus after the glorious struggles of the forty-eight martyrs who suffered in that same city: was seized with his dearest colleague Alexander: while the latter was cast into prison, Epipodius was first beaten with cruel blows of fists: then tortured by the stretching of the rack <term>eculeus: a wooden torture device used to stretch the body</term>: and finally completed his martyrdom by the cutting off of his head.

¶ Saint Alexander, led out from prison on the third day after the passion of the blessed Epipodius, was first

<column-break/>

so mangled by the cruelty of those beating him: that as the cage of his ribs was broken and his internal organs laid bare, the secrets of his soul were revealed. Then, fixed to the frame of a cross, he gave up his blessed spirit. Thirty-four others suffered with him. They were both buried on either side of the altar in a crypt which was built with beautiful and ancient workmanship on the hill situated above the city.

¶ Saint Agobard, Bishop of Lyon, is famous among the same people for many miracles.

¶ Saint Peregrine, a priest of Lyon: the glory of whose miracles bears witness to the holiness of his life and the blessedness of his soul.

¶ Saint Justus, Bishop of Lyon, a man of wondrous holiness and prophetic spirit: who indeed died in Egypt: but his body, along with the bones of the blessed Viator his servant, was brought back to Lyon by religious citizens and interred with fitting worship in the basilica.

¶ Saint Elpidius, Bishop and confessor of the city of Lyon, flourishes with many miracles.

¶ Saint Lupus <note>Saint Loup</note>, a most worthy prelate and hermit of the church of Lyon, is famous among his people for not a few miracles.

¶ Saint Annemundus <note>Saint Chamond</note>, Bishop and martyr of Lyon, taking his origin from an illustrious lineage, was raised among the courtiers of Dagobert, King of the Franks: but avoiding their wicked company, he ran the way of God’s commandments: because of the sanctity of his life, he was substituted as the Archbishop of the city of Lyon by the [former] Archbishop of the same city. Thus, decorated with the pontifical mitre <term>infula: a headband or mitre signifying high religious office</term>, he stood out as very pleasing to all, both the inhabitants of the kingdom and foreigners: which some of the nobles took poorly, and accusing him before the king of the crime of treason <term>lese-majeste: an offense against the dignity of a reigning sovereign</term> as if he were a subverter of the kingdom: for which cause he went into exile from his episcopal see. But the man of God, bearing all things with an equal mind: was always instant with the clergy in alms, fasts, vigils, and prayers, and other works of piety. Thus enduring many labors and hardships: at last, as envy against him grew daily, he was seized by ministers sent to him: and perished by the sword in the dead of night. Thus the holy confessor suffered in the territory of Chalon on the 4th day before the Kalends of October <note>September 28th</note>. When his martyrdom was completed, his holy little body was carried to a ship by the servants of God: and they returned to their city on a vessel of the altars. On the second day of the journey, the little boat having turned toward the "Insula Barbara" <note>Île Barbe, "the Barbarian Island" in the Saône river</note>, where a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict was founded: they landed. ...was most dutifully received by the brothers: and there, as is the custom, having been washed and wrapped in worthy garments, they placed him upon a bier. So they led him all the way to the city; there, he was surrounded by the clergy of Lyon with due honor and by a very great multitude of the entire populace, with tears watering their faces. Having taken up the holy little body from there, they delivered it to a most decent burial in the basilica of the blessed apostles: that is, Saint Nicetius <note>Saint Nizier, bishop of Lyon in the 6th century</note>, as is asserted by many. This church was originally founded in honor of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, as the insignia of that same basilica testify. Others, however, believe he was buried in the basilica of the 48 martyrs: that is, in the monastery of Athanacum <note>The Abbey of Saint-Martin d'Ainay</note>, where there is the confluence of the Rhône and Saône <note>original: "rhodani & araris"</note> rivers. For his tomb is seen daily in the temple of Saint Nicetius, before the high altar, with an inscription of his name on a leaden tomb; this has been approved by the testimony of many trustworthy people. It is also confirmed by the frequent miracles performed there and the devotion of the people offering their vows in that place.

<margin>R</margin>
¶ Saint Benedicta, virgin and martyr, took her origin from the territory of Lyon; she is adorned with many miracles.

¶ Saint Eucherius, most deserving prelate of the church of Lyon, was a man most learned in human as well as divine letters. He was prompt in genius and composed in speech; in his life and conduct, he was pleasing to God and men, for indeed he turned many away from their iniquity and led them back to the path of truth. He drew his origin from the senatorial order, having a wife born of noble lineage named Galla, by whom he had two daughters. At length, with his wife’s consent, he deserted worldly life to lead a solitary existence in a certain cave in the territory of Aix near the river Durance <note>The Durance river in Provence</note>, with his wife supplying him with necessities. Then, after the Bishop of Lyon was removed from this life, Eucherius was elected bishop of that same city by divine revelation. He was pulled by force from his cave and raised up to the episcopal chair, which he ruled most decently for the duration of his life. This most holy prelate wrote many volumes of exquisite doctrine, but few have yet reached our hands. However, those listed below are circulated:

He flourished under Theodosius the Younger in the year of Christ 440.

¶ Galla, the wife of the aforementioned Saint Eucherius, after he was appointed to the episcopal honor in the church of Lyon, entered his cave and spent the remainder of her religious life there. Their two daughters also lived holy lives: one of them, named Consortia, provided daily food to her mother in the cave and finally ended her days in virginity. The other, named Tullia, also persevering in virginity, happily migrated from this world to the Lord. Both were illustrious by the merit of their virginity, shown through grace and miracles.

¶ Saint Antiochus, a priest of Lyon and a contemporary of Saint Justus, the bishop of Lyon (as was said), was raised to the height of that same bishopric after some time had passed because of the holiness of his life.

¶ Saint Sacerdos <note>Bishop of Lyon, 544–552 AD</note>, who from his tender years was remarkable for both integrity of character and perfection of knowledge, was elevated to the dignity of the bishopric of the church of Lyon with great applause from the whole people. He lived there holily and laudably, devoting himself to alms, prayers, and other works of piety; it would be a great task to narrate every deed. But among other things in the city of Lyon, he founded a sumptuous temple in honor of the blessed Paul, his patron, endowed with many services and (as is piously believed) consecrated by a divine mouth.

¶ Saint Augendus <note>Saint Oyand</note> of Lyon is much commended for his distinguished life and his power in obtaining miracles.

¶ Romanus the Abbot, who first led a hermit's life at Lyon and stood as the father of many monks there.

¶ Saint Aurelianus of Lyon, on account of the perfection of his life, deserved to be chosen as the bishop of the church of Arles.

¶ Domitianus the abbot and Antiochus the bishop, both possessing the fame of a good life, rest at Lyon.

<margin>L Z</margin>
¶ Faustus, a Gaul by nation—though some believe he was a native of Lyon—was a contemporary of Boethius, Claudianus Mamertus, and Cassiodorus, all most learned men. The venerable Cassiodorus and many others testify that he was of upright character. He excelled in poetry, writing epigrams for the instruction of the Christian profession and hymns on sacred matters, as is gathered from the letters of Ennodius. He is said to have been active in Lyon, where he obtained the greatest praise for his learning. He flourished in the time of the Emperor Theodoric, whose secretary <note>original: "asecreatis," likely *a secretis*</note> (as they say) he was.

# On the famous people of Lyon

Amulo <note>original: "Amulus"</note>, Bishop of Lyon, was a man deeply devoted to the divine scriptures, learned in the reading of the ancients, and moderately skilled in secular literature. He was knowledgeable in both the Hebrew and Latin languages, possessing a sharp intellect, forceful eloquence, and a scholarly, composed manner. He wrote short works of significant value, among which I have read these: A distinguished work addressed to Charles <note>Charles the Bald, 9th-century King of West Francia</note> against the Jews, in one volume. Of his other works, I have seen nothing yet. He flourished under Louis <note>Louis the Pious</note>, the son of Charlemagne, in the year of Christ 845.

William of Lyon <note>original: "Guilhelmus lugduneñ."</note>, of the Order of Preachers <note>the Dominicans</note> and, as they say, Bishop of that same church. He was a man much learned in the divine scriptures and not ignorant of secular letters; in wit he was sweet and subtle, in speech not overly ornate but nevertheless composed, and quite outstanding in delivering sermons to the people. He wrote:
*On the Sentences* <note>A standard medieval theological textbook by Peter Lombard</note>
*A Summary of Virtues*
*A Summary of Vices*
*Sermones to the People*

These, most fair reader, are but a few things out of many that have come to us in literary monuments concerning the illustrious men of the city of Lyon and their deeds worthy of admiration. For if I presumed to attempt to put into writing the memorable deeds of each and every one of the most famous men of this city, an immense labor would arise, which perhaps the strength of our capacity (which is small) would refuse to bear. I also deliberately pass over many most worthy of eternal memory who took their origin from this territory of Lyon, out of a desire for the brevity which modern people enjoy. Among these was the most reverend lord of blessed memory, Lord Peter Gerard <note>Pierre Gérard</note>, formerly a Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and Bishop of Le Puy <note>original: "antistes anicien̄."</note>. He originated from Saint-Symphorien <note>Saint-Symphorien-le-Château</note>, which is also where my own origin lies, as I descend from the lineage of the said Cardinal. He also founded four excellent prebends there, where he wished to be buried; his most sumptuous marble tomb is visited daily. And Brother Symphorien Champier <note>The author of this work</note>, who is either my biological brother or the one who received me from the sacred font of rebirth <note>my godfather</note>; he is a professor of the sacred Order of Saint John of Jerusalem <note>the Knights Hospitaller</note>, as well as a most deserving interpreter of both laws <note>Civil and Canon law</note>, and was 

<column-break/>

designated as the vicar and protector of the Lords of Rhodes <note>the Hospitallers</note> in France because of his integrity. The author himself could have included himself in this assembly of most famous men by a just title; however, caring nothing for human favor—and lest he seem to some to be seeking popular applause more than is right—he took very little care to do so. Nevertheless, I, Nicolas de Chêne <note>original: "Nicolaus de quercu"</note>, who oversaw the editing of this little work so that it might come to light more cleanly from the printer's workshop, have spent no little effort (according to the strength of my intellect, which I frankly confess is quite weak). I did not want such a man, who has undoubtedly deserved the very best from me, to be deprived of worthy honor. For he too is from Lyon, although his ancestors drew their origin from a noble family in the Dauphiné. He displays not only the coats of arms of temporal nobility (with which his family is distinguished), but also that of the soul, which is far more excellent. Indeed, anyone may observe that his soul—the better part of a man—is adorned with good disciplines, the best character, and every kind of virtue. He wrote several short works of no small value, among which these noted below are cited:

# Prefatory Epistle
E iij

# To the highly learned man: Master André Briell, royal counselor and physician: Symphorien Champier, likewise a physician, sends his most distinguished greetings.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'Q' featuring a scholar or physician seated at a lectern with an open book, framed by stylized floral and leaf motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
Because I value your exceptional love toward me and your singular learning, most learned of men, I have yet to reveal the extent of my esteem for you through any proof. To remain silent thus far is like carrying a sword hidden in its sheath, or possessing a lyre that stays silent, or a bow that is never strung. Therefore, when I had turned over in my mind for a long time—even quite a long time—what service I might perform for your kindness, so that you might recognize my mutual love toward you, I decided I would be doing something not entirely outside the scope of our professional duty if I were to dedicate to your name this present work. It is a work concerning the famous writers of the Gauls (from whom both you and I draw our origin) which I have labored over during these past days—I will not say years—that have slipped by. 

Now, if some curious investigator should perhaps ask by what reasoning I mingle the study of the <term>Paeonian art<note>The art of medicine or healing, named after Paeon, the physician of the Greek gods.</note></term> with theology—for the material handled here concerns the theological faculty rather than any other—since it stands outside our usual professional duties, I shall very easily respond that it is because nature has joined the soul to the body within us by means of the spirit. 

The body, indeed, is cured by the remedies of medicine; for as the Ecclesiastic witness says: *The Most High created medicine from the earth, and a prudent man will not abhor it.* <note>original: "Altissimus de terra creauit medicinã: et vir prudens non abhorrebit eam." Reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:4.</note> Likewise, as Cornelius Celsus <note>A Roman medical encyclopedist from the 1st century AD.</note> affirms when he says: *As agriculture provides food for healthy bodies, so medicine promises health to the sick.* 

The spirit, however, which is the airy vapor of the blood and a kind of knot between the mind and the body, is also tempered and nourished by the scents of the air and by sounds and songs. For as the sacred history of the Kings <note>1 Samuel 16:23.</note> bears witness, when David played upon the lyre, Saul was refreshed and felt better. <margin>1 Samuel 16</margin> 

Finally, the soul, being divine, is purified by the divine mysteries of theology. Therefore, according to the authority of Plato, diseases arise no less from a vice of the soul than from a vice of the body. For this reason, the physician promises the health of the body, while the theologian promises the health of the soul. Farewell, and continue to love me as you do; and if you believe yourself to be loved, love me in return.

At Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507, on the 20th of July. <note>original: "xiij. kalẽdas Augusti" — literally the 13th day before the Kalends of August.</note>

<summary>In this prefatory letter, the physician Symphorien Champier dedicates his work on Gallic writers to André Briell, defending his foray into theology by arguing that a physician must understand the soul-body connection.</summary>
<keywords>Symphorien Champier, André Briell, medical humanism, theology and medicine, Lyon, Gallic writers, Cornelius Celsus, Plato</keywords>

->Introductory Letter<-

# To the exceptionally learned man: Lord Andreas Baiellus, royal counselor and physician: Symphorianus Champerius, also a physician, sends many greetings. <note>original: "S. P. D." (Salutem Plurimam Dicit), a standard Latin greeting meaning "sends many greetings."</note>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'Q' decorated with vines, leaves, and a bird.</image-desc>
Most learned of men, I truly hold your exceptional love for me and your singular learning in high regard. Yet, I have not yet revealed by any proof how much I value you yourself; to do so would be like always carrying a sword hidden in its scabbard, or like a lyre that remains silent, or a bow that is never strung. Therefore, since I have turned over in my mind for a long time—and even longer—what service I might offer to your kindness so that you might recognize my mutual love for you, I decided I would be doing something not entirely foreign to our professional duty if I dedicated to your name this present work. It concerns the illustrious writers of the Gauls <note>referring to French authors; Champier was a key figure in early French humanism</note> (from whom both you and I have our origin), which has been labored over during these past—I will not say years—but days. 

Wherefore, if some curious investigator should perhaps ask by what reasoning I mix the study of the <term>Paeonian art<note>A classical poetic term for medicine, named after Paeon, the physician of the Greek gods.</note></term> with theology—for the matter handled in these pages concerns the theological faculty rather than any other—since it seems to stand outside our professional duty, I will answer most easily: it is because nature has joined the soul to the body within us by means of a middle spirit. The body indeed is cured by the remedies of medicine; for as the Ecclesiastic witness says: *The Most High created medicine from the earth, and a prudent man will not abhor it.* <note>A quote from the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:4.</note> Likewise, as Cornelius Celsus <note>A Roman encyclopedist known for his medical treatise *De Medicina*.</note> approves when he says: *As agriculture promises food to healthy bodies, so medicine promises health to the sick.* 

But the spirit, which is an airy vapor of the blood and acts as a kind of knot between the soul and the body, is also tempered and nourished by the scents of the air, and by sounds and songs. For, as sacred history attests, when David played the lyre, Saul was refreshed and felt better. <note>A reference to 1 Samuel 16:23, where David’s music soothes King Saul's troubled spirit.</note> Finally, the soul, being divine, is purified by the divine mysteries of theology. And so, on the authority of Plato, diseases arise no less from a vice of the soul than from a vice of the body. Therefore, the physician promises health of the body, but the theologian promises health of the soul. Farewell, and love me as you do; and if you think you are loved, love me in return.

At Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507, on the 13th day before the Kalends of August. <note>July 20, 1507.</note>

<header>On the Illustrious Men of Gaul.</header>

<margin>A</margin>
### Concerning the illustrious and distinguished writers of all Gaul.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' featuring intertwined floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
Many writers of various nations and peoples commend their kings and princes not only for their skill in the administration of the state, but also for their excellence in diverse learning, doctrine, and character; we are permitted to do the same for the kings of the Gauls. For Gaul has possessed many men perfected both in the skill of military discipline and in the excellence of multifaceted learning. Among these, Robert <note>Robert II, known as Robert the Pious (reigned 996–1031), noted for his musical compositions and deep personal piety.</note>, a man most worthy of royal honor, rightly claims the primary place for us. 
<margin>King Robert</margin> 
He was strong, just, learned, and religious. Indeed, he composed songs and responsories <note>A "responsory" is a type of chant in western Christian liturgy.</note> with sweet and regular melody for the honor of the Catholic church. In the humanities, and especially in music, he was most learned. He was of such great religious devotion that he would sing the <term>canonical hours<note>The fixed cycle of daily prayers performed by clergy and monks at specific times.</note></term> in the church with the clerics, and read them privately at home with his own household. He showed such piety and mercy toward the poor that, stripping himself of his own garments, he would many times cover their nakedness. A book never left his hands; so much so that, while sitting on the judgment seat, amidst the noise of judgments and legal cases, he would have an open <term>psalter<note>The Book of Psalms.</note></term> in his lap. Hence, it is read that he shone with miracles after his death. There is that well-known <term>sequence<note>A liturgical hymn sung after the Alleluia.</note></term> concerning the Holy Spirit: *Let the grace of the Holy Spirit be with us* <note>original: "Sancti spiritus assit nobis gratia"</note> or *Come Holy Spirit and send forth*, etc. <note>original: "Ueni scē spūs z emitte"</note>

A responsory for the Nativity of the Lord: namely, *Judea and Jerusalem*.

Also that Alleluia: namely, *Deliver me from my enemies*.

Also that one concerning the triumph of the holy martyrs: *O constancy of martyrs*.

Also that one concerning Saint Peter: *Cornelius the Centurion*. He offered this with great devotion at the altar in Rome during the time of the offertory while the Supreme Pontiff was celebrating Mass for Saint Peter. The ministers of the altar, hurrying forward, thought the wealthy king had offered gold of great weight. But finding a small sheet written and noted with music, they were filled with admiration, praising the talent and devotion of the prince. Hence the Pope decreed, at the request of the clerics and in memory of the most holy king, that this responsory should henceforth be sung in honor of Saint Peter. He is said to have written many other things which have not come to our knowledge.

¶ **Jean Gerson**, formerly the disciple of Pierre d'Ailly and Chancellor of Paris. He took part in the Council of Constance, in which he labored gloriously for the uprooting of heresies. Sermons at the Council of Constance.

¶ **John Noblet**, a Carmelite of the Parisian convent and study; before entering the religious life he was a most celebrated physician; he wrote:

¶ **Nicholas de Orbellis** of Angers, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis <note>The Franciscans.</note>; he wrote:

¶ **Peter de Orbellis**, of the same nation and religious order, still living and formerly a close friend of mine; he wrote:
Lenten Sermons.

¶ **John Soreth**, a Norman Carmelite and formerly Prior General of the same order; he wrote:
On the Sentences.
Various Sermons.

He also organized the Constitutions.

¶ **Henry, surnamed "the Prudent"**, of the Carthusian Order, a Fleming by birth; prior of the house in the Valley near Bruges in Flanders; he wrote a most celebrated work highly suited for devotion, arranged as a dialogue, which he divided into three parts and titled:
The *Tetralogue of Devotion*.

¶ **Laurent Bureau** of Dijon, of the Order of Carmelites, confessor to King Louis XI of France, and Bishop of Sisteron. I once shared a great friendship with him; he was a man most learned in the divine scriptures and extraordinarily taught in secular literature, possessing excellent talent and clear eloquence; he wrote certain distinguished works in both verse and prose, of which these are circulated:
A most celebrated work in praise of Elijah, the patriarch of the Carmelites, which he titled the *Heliad*.
On the Illustrious Men of His Order.

¶ **Robert Gaguin**, Minister General of the Order of the Holy Trinity <note>The Trinitarians.</note>; a distinguished Doctor of Decrees <note>A doctor of Canon Law.</note>, and most learned in both the divine scriptures and secular literature; a famous poet and most eloquent orator, who often left the Italians stunned by his eloquence; excellent in talent, and devout in life and conduct. He wrote distinguished short works in verse and prose. Of these, the following are extant:
A notable work in verse addressed to Arnold Bostius, a Carmelite living in Ghent, Flanders, against Vincent de Castronovo of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>.
On the Conception of the Blessed Mary.
On the same subject, in prose.
On the Wretched Condition of Man.
On the Art of Versification.
Many most elegant Orations.
Very many Letters.
Innumerable Epigrams.

¶ **Arnold Bostius**, a Fleming by birth, of the Order of Carmelites in the Ghent convent; a man highly learned in both human and divine literature...

### ->On the Illustrious Men of Gaul<-

He wrote the books:
On the Patronage of Mary.
On the Illustrious Men of the Carthusians.
On the Illustrious Men of His Order.
Against Vincent of Newcastle. <note>original: "Contra vincentium de nouocastro"</note>

Various Poems.

¶ **Charles Fernand**, born in the town of Bruges in Flanders: blind from his early years, and for that reason completely ignorant even of the basic elements of reading. Yet he presents such a miracle of himself that he emerged as a most celebrated poet, musician, philosopher, and orator, like a second Homer. He is a most wise interpreter of the divine scriptures, excelling in both verse and prose; he is subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, and most upright in his life and conduct. Granted a public and permanent pension by the King of France, he taught the humanities for a long time in the most famous university of Paris and most learnedly explained many authors. Finally, despising all worldly things, he left the world and its pensions and entered the Order of Saint Benedict in a well-reformed monastery <note>This refers to the Abbey of Saint-Sulpice in Bourges, a center of monastic reform.</note> not far from the city of Bourges, where he remains to this day. He burns with such great zeal for souls that, having been ordained as a deacon <note>original: "leuita"; literally a 'Levite,' a common term for a deacon in this period.</note> by apostolic dispensation, he publicly preaches the word of God with the greatest success and the admiration of all. He wrote:
One book of Commentaries.
Praises of the Carmelite Order.
Four books of Odes in Praise of Christ.
On the Conception [of Mary], against Vincent.
An Iambic Poem on the same subject.
An Oration on the Conception addressed to the Carthusians.
An Oration on Saint Catherine.
Several Letters.
Almost countless Poems.
Elegies on the Contempt of the World.

¶ **John Fernand**, brother of the aforementioned Charles and a fellow student of the same city: a man most learned in every respect, a most celebrated philosopher, orator, and poet, and not ignorant of the divine scriptures. He is subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. The King, granting him a permanent pension, chose him as his musician. But finally, setting all things aside, he renounced the world and, imitating his brothers, professed the same rule in the same monastery. He wrote many useful short works in meter and prose, among which are these:
On Saint John the Baptist.
Many and various Orations.
Letters to Various People.
Many Poems and Epigrams.

<column-break/>

He also wrote the *Hours of the Holy Cross* and of the *Compassion of the Blessed Virgin Mary* in elegant verse.

¶ **Guy Jouvenneaux**, <note>original: "Guido iuuenalis"</note> a native of Maine: a man most learned in every respect, a student of sacred letters, and most highly skilled in the study of the humanities, practiced in both verse and prose. For a long time, he taught literature for free in the university of Paris. But afterward, casting aside all worldly things, he took the monastic habit with the aforementioned Fernands in the same monastery, where after only a few days had passed, he was elected abbot because of his integrity of life. He wrote:
A Grammar very useful for beginners in literature.
Also most learned commentaries on Terence.
He fervently and publicly preached the word of God, but an untimely death took him from us.

¶ **Josse Badius**, <note>original: "Judocus badius"</note> a native of Flanders: a man most erudite in secular letters and not ignorant of divine letters; a most famous philosopher, rhetorician, and poet. He is excellent in intellect and eloquent in speech; he is skilled in Greek letters and proficient in both verse and prose. He wrote:
Moral "Forests." <note>original: "Siluas morales"; 'Sylvae' or 'Forests' was a common title for a collection of miscellaneous poems or essays.</note>
Also a work against Vincent.
A Psalter of Mary in Sapphic stanzas.
Small works on grammar.
Many Epigrams.
Many Letters.
Also commentaries on Virgil.
On Persius.
On Juvenal.
On Baptista Mantuanus.
On Cicero’s *On Duties*, *On Friendship*, *On Old Age*, and *Paradoxes*.
He lives still in Paris, teaching literature there publicly and forging various commentaries on different authors.

¶ **Gilles Nettelet**, Dean of the Church of Cambrai: a man studious in both divine and human sciences. He excerpted a most famous work, necessary for people of every status, from the letters of Saint Jerome the priest, divided into four books. His other works have not yet come to our knowledge.

¶ **Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples**, <note>original: "Jacobus fabri stapulensis"</note> a man most learned in every respect: a most celebrated dialectician, philosopher, and mathematician (if I may say so with everyone's permission) and by no means ignorant of sacred letters. He is worthy of being preferred not only to those of the present, but even to those whom antiquity counted among the gods. Subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, and most upright in life and conduct, he wrote:
Introductions to the Logic of Aristotle.
Also works on Logic, Physics, and Metaphysics.

### ->On the Illustrious Men of Gaul<-

He restored the works of **Aristotle**, which had been mutilated and corrupted by various commentators, to their original truth and, in a sense, renewed them.
He published dialogues on physics and metaphysics.
Also commentaries on moral philosophy.
On arithmetic.
On geometry.
On the music of **Boethius**.
On the treatise *The Sphere of the World*. <note>original: "de sphera mundi"; a standard medieval astronomical text by Johannes de Sacrobosco.</note>
Also short commentaries on **Hermes Trismegistus**. <note>original: "mercuriū trismegistū"; a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with hermetic philosophy.</note>
Also, he oversaw the printing of the works of **Dionysius the Areopagite**, which he searched for most diligently across various regions; he also added scholarly notes <term>scholia: brief explanatory notes or comments</term> to these in several places. He translated **John of Damascus** *On the Orthodox Faith*. He commissioned to the craftsmen <note>meaning the printers</note>: *The Paradise of Heraclides* and the *Recognitions of Peter* by **Clement**.
**Cyril** on the Gospel of John.
He published commentaries on the *Politics* and *Economics* of **Aristotle**.
He added the *Hecatonomiae* <note>original: "hecatonomias"; from the Greek for "a hundred laws," referring to his collection of legal principles</note> of Socratic and Platonic laws, along with the *Public Economics* of **Aristotle**.
He still lives today in Paris, teaching there, explaining various works, and having them printed for the benefit of the public good. Among his countless most learned disciples, he had **Josse Clichtove** the Fleming, a theologian and most faithful commentator on his works; and **Charles de Bovelles**, who is most devoted to mathematics and wrote: *On the Constitution and Utility of the Human Arts* (1 book) and *Introductory to Metaphysics* (1 book).

<column-break/>

Also **Gregory of Livonia**, a most deserving professor of the healing arts <note>original: "peonie artis"; referring to Paean, the physician of the gods in Greek mythology</note>; all of whom are still surviving at this time except for Lord **Gregory of Livonia**, who died of the plague among the people of Toulouse the year before these things were printed.

¶ **Jean de Pins** of Toulouse, formerly a student of **Filippo Beroaldo** at the University of Bologna; most learned in both laws <note>Referring to Civil and Canon (Church) law.</note>; a great lover of humanistic letters; practiced in both poetry and prose. He still survives and "breathes the air" <note>an idiomatic expression for being alive</note> in Bologna, producing various works. He wrote in prose <term>prose: "soluta oratione," literally "untied speech," as opposed to the constraints of verse</term> certain small works of no negligible reading, of which the following titles are known:
*The Life of Saint Catherine of Siena* of the Order of Saint Dominic (1 book).
*The Life of Filippo Beroaldo*, his teacher (1 book).
A book of *Various Orations*.
He is said to have composed certain other things which have not yet come into our hands.

¶ We have collected these from the many famous writers of the Gauls; for it was impossible for our frailty to attain a knowledge of all of them. For we candidly confess that many others, well-deserving of the world of letters, have written much and are writing at present, works which have not yet come into public view.
