# ->Introductory Letter<-

¶ To the most respected lord: Lord Francisco de Stagno, well-deserving doctor of decrees <note>original: "decretorum doctori"; a scholar of Canon Law</note>, and most worthy Bishop of Rodez <note>original: "Ruthenē. presuli"</note>; acting lieutenant general and governor of Avignon for the most reverend Lord Georges d’Amboise, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and Legate of Avignon: Symphorien Champier of Lyon, physician, sends fondest greetings.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' featuring a stylized floral pattern with curling vines and foliage within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

If writers of history so greatly commend the region of Italy—the most famous of all nations—because of the residence of the High Pontiff <note>the Pope</note>, among other things which (in my opinion) not undeservedly make it commendable, then perhaps our own Gaul—which they call "Transalpine" and "Long-haired" <note>original: "gallia... comatamqz"; a Roman term for the regions of Gaul that retained their traditional customs and long hair before full Romanization</note>—will come to be commended no less, provided that the truth itself is allowed into the light. For Gaul itself was also graced by the presence of High Pontiffs and universal councils. ¶ I pass over how many councils, both general and particular, concerning the republic of the orthodox faith and untainted Christianity, were celebrated in various places and times within it. And since men eager for letters claim it is one’s duty not to be ignorant of the origin and progress of one's fatherland, and whatever has happened to it in times past, the desire came upon me to briefly touch upon the lives of the High Pontiffs who resided in our country—that is, in Celtic Gaul, or if you prefer, Lyonnaise Gaul—and at Lyon, the most noble marketplace of all Gaul, and at Avignon for a space of about seventy years. <note>This refers to the "Avignon Papacy" (1309–1376), a period when the Popes resided in France rather than Rome.</note> Then, I shall also touch upon those who, before the dignity of the High Priesthood was transferred to the Gauls, were raised from among the Gauls to the pinnacle of the High Pontificate. 

But because, as the poet says: *The envious man grows thin when his neighbor prospers* <note>original: "Invidus alterius rebus marcessit opimis"; a quote from the Roman poet Horace</note>, someone suffering from envy and begrudging Gaul such great happiness—having no regard for his own dignity—dared to burst out in insulting words after the High Pontiff returned to Rome. In a public speech held at Rome before the High Pontiff, he attacked the fertile region of Gaul with a slanderous tongue, shamefully tearing it apart, though it was undeserving. Gaul is a land which his palate could not taste because it was infected with the poison of envy, even though it has brought to light so many men distinguished by piety who have served the Christian republic most excellently. 

But there was no lack of a faithful son of the fatherland who, knowing that our birthplace claims a great part of us, and bearing most heavily (as he ought) such a great injury to his country, responded to that slander with a defense <term>apologia: a formal written defense of one's opinions or conduct</term> fortified by authentic authorities and most effective reasons. I wished to insert that defense into these small nightly labors <note>original: "lucubracinsculis"; works produced by candlelight or late-night study</note> of ours, dedicated to you, a man most loving of letters and most deserving of your fatherland, so that anyone may understand that one ought to be as devoted to one's country as to one's parents. 

Farewell, most upright patron of the learned, and be mindful of your Champier. Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1507, on the 12th day before the Kalends of August <note>July 21st</note>.

# On the French High Pontiffs.

### A small book by the same Lord Symphorien Champier regarding the French high pontiffs: those who resided both in Italy and in France.

<sig>A</sig>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'C' depicting a figure in prayer or study.</image-desc> **Pope Clement**, the fifth of this name, was a Gascon by birth. <note>Gascony is a region of Aquitanian Gaul.</note> Previously known as Bernard of Bordeaux, he was elected in absentia at Perugia. <note>The Roman Court had been moved there by Benedict XI to more freely deliberate on peace while Italy was shaken by various long-standing turmoils; it was there that Benedict passed away.</note> After long disputes, in the year of our Lord 1305, he was created High Pontiff. He sat for 7 years, 10 months, and 15 days. While living in France and consenting to his election, he traveled from Bordeaux to Lyon, the most celebrated city in all of Gaul. The Cardinals, summoned to him, set out without delay. The Roman Court then resided in Lyon, France, with the highest unity of the Church and the greatest honor for 74 years. Countless crowds of French people attended his coronation, along with King Philip, <note>Philip IV, known as Philip the Fair.</note> his brother Charles, and John, Duke of Brittany. By his command, the Dulcinian heresy was suppressed, and the religious order of the Templars was utterly extinguished; their property was granted to the Knights of Rhodes. <note>The Knights Hospitaller.</note> When he turned his mind to organizing the state of the Church, he held three councils at different times and places, where he acted with great wisdom and maturity. He most accurately ordained many constitutions concerning the state of religious orders, in which he also clarified the rule of Saint Francis. From these very constitutions, the book of "Clementines" <note>original: "Clementinarum liber"; a primary source of Canon Law.</note> was later compiled. During this time, he also enrolled Pope Celestine—under the name Peter of Morrone—into the catalog of saintly confessors. Finally, afflicted by various ailments, he died in the eighth year and tenth month of his papacy. His body was carried to his homeland in Gascony, where he was honorably buried in the Church of the Blessed Mary of Uzeste in the diocese of Gascony. The seat then remained vacant for 2 years, 4 months, and 17 days.

<sig>B</sig>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' depicting a clerical figure.</image-desc> **Pope John**, the twenty-second of this name, previously called James of Cahors <note>Jacobus Caturcensis</note> and Bishop of Porto, was unanimously elected in the year of our Lord 1316 after a long dispute among twenty-two cardinals at Lyon in the monastery of the Preaching Friars. <note>The Dominicans.</note> He sat for 19 years, 4 months, and 27 days. He was a man of great learning, distinguished by much wisdom,

<column-break/>

and a great lover of the most learned men. Created Pontiff on the seventh of September, he received the crown of the papacy in the cathedral basilica. From there, having set out for Avignon, he soon created seven cardinals. He canonized two deceased men: namely, Thomas of Hereford, a bishop, and Thomas Aquinas, a doctor of the Order of Preachers. He then raised the church of Toulouse to the dignity of an archbishopric and assigned certain dioceses to it. He elevated the church of Zaragoza, which was dear to him, to a metropolitan see, assigning five cathedral churches to it. He restored the Order of Montesa <note>original: "Bratidimonensem," likely referring to the Order of Santa Maria de Montesa</note>—which had been weakened by the factions of certain wicked men—to a better form. He condemned many heretics, especially a certain commentary <note>original: "glossulam"</note> by Brother Peter of the Order of Friars Minor, <note>Peter John Olivi, a leader of the "Spiritual" Franciscans.</note> who had encouraged a certain gathering of the Third Order to imitate the poverty of Christ; many of their number were condemned and burned. In the eleventh year of his papacy, having held an assembly, he declared Louis the Bavarian a rebel and schismatic against the Church. He also stripped Guido Tarlati of Pietramala of his priesthood and bishopric after he occupied the city of Castello. He separated Cortona from the diocese of Arezzo and raised it to the status of a city. Finally, in the ninetieth year of his age, he died at Avignon, leaving such a great force of gold and silver in his treasury as no pontiff before him had ever left. When he was once asked who might be most removed from the truth, he replied: "The opinion of the common people. For whatever they praise is worthy of reproach; whatever they think is vain; whatever they speak is false; what they reject is good, and what they approve is evil, and whatever they extol is infamous."

<margin>e</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'B' depicting a seated figure, likely a pope or scholar.</image-desc> **Pope Benedict**, the twelfth of this name, a native of Toulouse and a professed member of the Cistercian Order, was previously called James. In the year of our Lord 1336, having been a Cardinal Priest, he was created Pontiff. He sat for 7 years, 3 months, and 17 days. Having entered the papacy, he ratified the censures thundered against the Bavarian <note>Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor.</note> as an usurper of the Empire; however, fearing later that the Empire might be occupied by some external enemy while vacant, he appointed Azzone and Luchino Visconti as his vicars in Milan and the other cities they possessed. He granted the same power to other rulers. He persuaded the Senate and the Roman people through a legate that they should finally administer the senatorial dignity—which they had long held in the King's name—under his own auspices and those of the Church. This Pontiff, since he was distinguished in theology and many other doctrines as well as upright character, was of such constancy that he never turned from the right path, whether by force, promises, or prayers...

<meta>This page continues the history of the French Popes during the Avignon Papacy. # On the French High Pontiffs.

...could be moved from his purpose. And therefore, although he celebrated sacred orders only once in the entire time of his pontificate—where he created six cardinal priests, most distinguished men, not from among his own relatives as is often the case, but summoned to him from everywhere—he built famous palatial buildings here in Avignon, complete with towers and orchards <note>original: "pomerijs"</note>, and he caused the roof of the Basilica of Saint Peter in Rome to be restored. Moreover, these were his maxims: Be the kind of son you would wish your own relatives to be. An evil man fears death, but a good man fears vice more. Keep what you have acquired by reading; learn what you do not know by reading. It is equally shameful to lack friends and to change them often. Friends are best preserved if they consider each other’s requests. It is more shameful for a king to be conquered by kindness than by arms. Finally, upon his death, he left a great sum of gold not to his relatives, but to the Church, as becomes a good pontiff. For this reason, almost everyone, both those present and those absent, wept together at his death.

<margin>D</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'C' containing a portrait of Pope Clement VI in profile, wearing a papal tiara.</image-desc>
**Pope Clement**, the sixth of that name, was from the region of Limoges and was a monk. Previously called Peter <note>Pierre Roger (1291–1352).</note>, he was chosen to succeed Pope Benedict in the year of our Lord 1342, moving from the position of Archbishop of Rouen. He sat for ten years, six months, and eight days. He was indeed a very humane and liberal man, possessed of much learning and refined eloquence. In the first year of his pontificate, when he had created ten cardinals, he made one of his brothers a monk-cardinal and another, his nephew by his sister, a cardinal. Later, he reduced the Jubilee—which Boniface VIII had celebrated in the 1300th year of our Lord and had declared should be observed from century to century—to every fiftieth year, which is properly the Jubilee number. Then, following the deposition of "the Bavarian" <note>Louis IV, Holy Roman Emperor, whom the Church opposed.</note> from the Empire, while all of Italy was in turmoil, he confirmed Luchino and his brother John, the Archbishop, of the Visconti family, as his vicars in Milan; however, he restrained the others. When the Bavarian, seeking Trento, seemed ready to enter Italy, he also appointed vicars by imperial authority in the titles of the Church's lands and many other places in like manner. Pope Clement sent certain cardinals from Avignon to Rome. These men, organizing the state of the city and removing seditions, declared Peter Sarra Colonna and John, son of Use, as senators. And Nicholas, a public scribe and Roman citizen <note>The famous revolutionary Cola di Rienzo.</note> who had brought the state of the city under his own power and appointed himself Tribune, they captured and threw into chains.

<column-break/>

For this reason, the pontiff, fearing lest all of Italy be wasted by fire and sword, immediately granted Bologna to the Visconti under this law: that they should pay twelve thousand gold coins to the Church every year and establish peace among all. Finally, when barbarians and infidel Moors were tearing apart both Spain and Germany, this Pope Clement compelled the Christian princes to wage war against them; they fought often and successfully against the enemies, and having slain many of them, they led innumerable triumphs. Then, although he attempted to arrange a treaty between Philip, King of the French, and Edward, King of the English, he labored in vain. At last, having performed the office of a good shepherd in all things, he died in Avignon in the year of our Lord 1352, and was buried there with a noble funeral procession conducted by the cardinals. Because this excellent pontiff was most highly learned in the sacred scriptures and not ignorant of secular literature—as well as being a distinguished doctor of pontifical law <note>Canon Law.</note> and a most famous preacher of the Divine Word—he published several learned works in which he showed the liveliness of his intellect. Among those works, these are circulated:

| Title of Work | Volume |
| :--- | :--- |
| Of Various Sermons | 1 book |
| On the Approval of King Charles | 1 book |
| Of Many Collations <note>Theological or legal discussions.</note> | 2 books |
| Of Letters to Various People | 1 book |
| On the Canonization of Saint Ivo the Confessor | 1 book |

Which begins: "Rejoice and praise, O inhabitant."

<margin>E</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'I' containing a portrait of Pope Innocent VI in profile, wearing a papal tiara.</image-desc>
**Pope Innocent**, the sixth of this name, was from the region of Limoges and was previously called Stephen <note>Étienne Aubert (1282–1362).</note>. He was a doctor of both laws <note>Civil Law and Canon Law.</note>. In the year of Christ 1352, on the first of December, he was chosen to succeed Pope Clement. He sat for ten years, a man of most upright life and great constancy and severity; he never wished to grant ecclesiastical benefits except to the most religious and indeed learned men. Upon taking up the pontificate, he immediately commanded all bishops and other prelates, under penalty of excommunication <note>original: "anathematis pena"</note>, to depart for their own benefices <note>Meaning they must live in their assigned dioceses rather than at the papal court.</note>. He himself, so that he might be an example to others, immediately reduced his domestic expenses and brought his household—namely, of the most proven men—down to an honorable number. Furthermore, he established salaries for the Judges of the Sacred Palace <note>The Roman Rota.</note> so that they might not be corrupted by gifts due to poverty. He was frugal in his own diet, but was considered most generous in military expenses. By his persuasion and prudence, a treaty was finally entered into between the Genoese and the Venetians...

**Pope Urban**, the fifth of this name, was also from the region of Limoges and was a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict. Previously called William <note>Guillaume de Grimoard (1310–1370).</note>, he was the abbot of Saint-Victor at Marseille. Having taken up the pontificate, he applied his mind to defending the liberty of the Church and sent Giles the Spaniard <note>Egidio Albornoz</note> back to Italy as a legate with the greatest authority. Giles defeated Bernabò Visconti and brought all things back to union and concord. After these achievements, the Pope himself came to Rome in the fifth year of his pontificate, where he built many buildings both at Viterbo and Montefiascone. **Pope Gregory**, the eleventh of this name, was of the Limoges nation. Previously called Pierre de Beaufort, he was a Cardinal Deacon of Santa Maria Nuova. In the year of our Lord 1371, he was chosen to succeed Pope Urban and sat for eight years. He was the nephew of Clement [VI] through his brother. He was certainly a man of great innocence and gentleness, and because of these virtues, he was greatly beloved by everyone. Having undertaken the office of the pontificate, he immediately sent a legate to Italy to review the affairs of the Church. However, at the beginning, because of a treaty with Bernabò Visconti, everything was in turmoil. For all except the Venetians were hostile to the Visconti; therefore, many evils arose. But when the Pope attributed those evils occurring in Italy to his own absence, he began to think about his return to Italy. He was also moved (as they say) by the words of a certain bishop. When Gregory said to him with a kind of familiar confidence, "Why, Bishop, do you not go to your church?" the man intrepidly replied, "And why do you, the High Pontiff who should set an example for others, not return to your own bishopric and your Roman Church?" Stirred by these words, the Pope immediately prepared twenty-one galleys on the Rhône River. Pretending to be doing something else, he began the journey: first to Genoa, then to Lerici, and finally he arrived at Rome by a land journey in the month of January. This was in the year of our Lord 1376, the sixth of his pontificate, and the seventieth year since the Roman Church moved to France. With what preparation, with what joy of all souls, and how festively he was received by the Roman people, would be a long and very difficult thing to describe. Indeed, everything in the city was in need of the Pope's arrival. For the walls of the city and the churches, and even private buildings everywhere, were threatening to ruin; all of these the Pope himself repaired in large part. I say nothing of good morals, honorable institutions, and civil refinements, which were falling apart almost everywhere. For the city which once, by its fame, had lured nearly the entire world to civilization <note>original: "urbanitatem"</note>, had declined during the Pope's absence to the greatest rusticity of manners. **Pope Martin**, the second of this name <note>Historically known as Marinus I (r. 882–884). Due to medieval confusion between the names Marinus and Martinus, he was often listed as Martin II.</note>, was French by nation. In the year of our Lord 887, having succeeded Pope John IX <note>Actually succeeded John VIII.</note>, he sat in the chair of Peter for one year and five months. Because of the brevity of his life in the papacy, few of his deeds are recorded by historians.

<margin>3</margin>
**Pope Sylvester**, the second of this name, was also French by nation and previously called Gilbert <note>Gerbert of Aurillac (c. 946–1003), a prolific scholar and teacher who introduced Arabic numerals and the abacus to Europe.</note>. In the year of our Lord 995, substituted for Gregory V, he sat for four years, one month, and eight days. He first reached the Archbishopric of the church of Rheims, then of Ravenna, and finally the dignity of the High Pontificate. They assert that his body was buried in the Lateran church.

<margin>R</margin>
**Pope Stephen**, the ninth of this name, was a native of Lorraine (for Lorraine is a region of France). He was the Abbot of Monte Cassino and was previously called Frederick. In the year of Christ 1055, he was elected High Pontiff at Florence and sat for four months. Immediately when he had accepted the pontificate, he took care that the church of Milan—which had withdrawn itself from Rome for nearly two hundred years—should recognize Rome as the first among others, and as its greater and superior. This obedience continues even now. In the first year of his pontificate, dying at Florence, he was buried there in the cathedral church.

<margin>2</margin>
**Pope Nicholas**, the second of this name, was of the Savoyard nation. Previously called Gerard, he was the Bishop of Florence. After the deposition of Benedict X, who was not legitimately created, Gerard was canonically elected at Siena by the cardinals and bishops due to his reputation for a good life. He sat for three years, six months, and twenty-six days. Having undertaken the pontificate, he immediately went to Sutri, and there, having held a council, he compelled the aforementioned Benedict to abdicate the pontificate. Moving from there to Rome, he held another council at the Lateran, in which he instituted the form for electing the Roman Pontiffs by the Cardinals <term>Papal Election Decree: The 1059 decree that transitioned the power to elect the Pope exclusively to the College of Cardinals.</term>. In that same council, they say he admitted Berengarius <note>Berengar of Tours, whose views on the Eucharist were deemed heretical.</note>, who had been recalled from error, back into the unity of the Church. There he also declared Henry III <note>Likely referring to Henry IV, though the text names the father.</note> as Emperor and Augustus, and distinguished him with the imperial crown. Upon his death, the papacy was vacant for twelve days.

<margin>B</margin>
**Pope Urban II**, previously named Odo <note>Also known as Eudes of Châtillon</note>, was the Abbot of Cluny <note>A powerful and influential Benedictine monastery in France</note>. In the year of our Lord 1086, he was elected High Pontiff and sat for thirteen years and four months. He was a man of exceptional learning and holiness, who wonderfully strengthened the Church of God against heretics through his words, deeds, examples, and most elegant writings. His letters to Matilda <note>Matilda of Canossa, a powerful Italian noblewoman and key ally of the papacy</note> are still extant. At the urging of this Countess Matilda, after he had held a council at Melfi and found no place of peace, he came to Piacenza. There he held another synod in which he confirmed the excommunication <note>original: "execrationem"</note> against Emperor Henry IV and the antipope Guibert <note>Clement III</note> that had been issued by Gregory VII. In the same meeting, he restrained the insolence of certain churchmen. He also decreed that the ordination of a bishop performed "without a title" <note>original: "sine titulo"; referring to a priest ordained without being assigned to a specific church or ministry</note> would be void. This Urban then traveled into Gaul <note>France</note> where, again concerned for the safety of the faith, he called a council at Clermont, a city in Auvergne. There he persuaded the people to undertake an expedition against the Saracens to recover Jerusalem, and he marked 300,000 men for that expedition with the sign of the cross <note>The First Crusade</note>. Many statutes were made in that council, including one that the Hours of the Blessed Virgin <note>A set of daily prayers</note> should be recited daily by the clergy, and her office should be solemnly celebrated on Saturdays. Having done this, he immediately returned to Rome so that, once affairs in Italy were settled, he might also encourage the Italian princes to join the same expedition. However, he began to be harassed by the great seditions of John the Pagan, a most rebellious man; seized with fear, he hid for two years in the house of a certain Roman citizen. Once that John had died, being made more free, he again applied his mind to organizing the state of the Church. He received back into favor the Archbishop of Milan, who had been expelled because he had been consecrated by only one person against all law and right; the Pope restored the pallium <note>A circular band of white wool worn by archbishops, symbolizing their authority and bond with the papacy</note> to him when he humbly requested it with full power. He did the same for the Bishop of Toledo. Finally, after many persecutions and labors, this holy man died on the 29th of July <note>original: "iiij. kal. Augusti"</note> and was buried in the Basilica of Saint Peter in Rome. The Apostolic See remained vacant for sixteen days.

---

<margin>C</margin>
**Pope Calixtus II**, Archbishop of Vienne and a Burgundian by birth, was the brother of the Count of Burgundy. In the year of our Lord 1120, he was elected High Pontiff at Cluny by the cardinals who had followed Pope Gelasius II when he fled into Gaul while being pursued by Emperor Henry.

<column-break/>

He was descended from the royal lineages of France, England, and Germany. Previously called Guy <note>Guido of Burgundy</note>, he was a Doctor of Civil Law and Sacred Theology. He refused to accept the papacy until he had the consent of the clergy and the Roman people through the Roman cardinals. Once this was obtained, he came to Rome and was received with great longing and great honor. He immediately moved to Benevento, and there he met with many Italian princes and nobles, who promised by oath that they would always remain faithful to the Roman Pontiff. Returning from there to Rome, he sent legates to Emperor Henry to establish peace with him, and then returned again to Benevento. The reason for that journey was that William, Duke of Apulia and Calabria, was about to marry the daughter of the Greek Emperor Alexios; since he had to sail to Constantinople, he committed the care of his duchy to the Pope. When the Pope had lost many of his followers there to fevers, and he himself was finally returned to Rome in poor health, he recovered his strength and celebrated a council of nine hundred fathers at the Lateran <note>The First Council of the Lateran, 1123</note>. In this council, it was decreed that reinforcements and aid be sent so that the Christians in Asia would not be overwhelmed, as Baldwin <note>King Baldwin II of Jerusalem</note> had been captured. For this reason, he roused the Genoese, Venetians, and Pisans to move against the enemies with a great fleet. In that fleet, the Genoese are said to have sent seventy transport ships. Having managed these things successfully according to his wishes, the Pontiff found some peace and repaired many basilicas in the city, restored the city walls, fortified all the citadels, and brought a certain water supply <note>likely an aqueduct repair</note> into the city. He also offered many gifts to churches here and there. Finally, having deserved well of God and men, he rested in peace in the fifth year of his pontificate.

---

**Pope Urban IV**, a Frenchman by birth, was exalted to the summit of the high priesthood in the year of our Lord 1262. He sat for four years, one month, and four days. Although born of humble status, he possessed an outstanding and elegant tongue. When he was once taunted for being born of a lowly father, he replied: "It is a matter of virtue and nobility for a man not to be born noble, but to become so." Upon taking up the papacy, he immediately summoned soldiers from Gaul who defended the Church's territory from an unjust oppressor. He instituted the solemnity of Corpus Christi <note>The Feast of the Body of Christ</note> to be celebrated by all the faithful with processions and octaves <note>An eight-day period of celebration following a feast</note>, for which he also granted "Martinan" indulgences <note>original: "martinas"; likely referring to specific grants of spiritual merit</note>. He decreed that the liturgy <note>original: "officium"</note> for this feast, based on figures from the Old Testament, should be composed by Saint Thomas Aquinas. Likewise, he aided the mendicant orders <note>Religious orders like the Franciscans and Dominicans who survived on alms</note> with many favors and privileges.

**Pope Clement IV**, of the Narbonne region <note>In southern France</note>, previously called Guy Foulques <note>original: "Guido fulcadij"</note>, was distinguished with the honor of the high priesthood in the year of our Lord 1264. He administered the pontifical office excellently. Finally, dying while leaving a great longing for himself among all people, he was buried at Viterbo. After his death, since no successor worthy of him could be found among the cardinals, a very great contention arose among them; for this reason, the see remained vacant for two years.

**Pope Felix V**, from the nation of Savoy, previously called Amadeus the Hermit, was elected High Pontiff during the schism <note>A split within the Church</note> in the Council of Basel on November 17, 1439, after Eugenius IV had been deposed. There were also others who were called "neutrals" because they obeyed neither. This man was the first Duke of Savoy, whereas they were previously called Counts. Having obtained the title of a Dukedom from the Emperor Sigismund, and having held the government of the province for nearly forty years after his father's death, he increased his paternal dominion and secured peace everywhere. Finally, leaving behind the glorious heights of his princedom, he withdrew into a hermitage with six men of the knightly order who were advanced in age. While he was leading a celibate life in that state, he was elected High Pontiff by the Council of Basel. He shaved the beard which he had previously grown. He handed over the Dukedom to his firstborn son. He learned the ecclesiastical ceremonies. Surrounded by a large crowd of nobles, he proceeded to Basel, where he was crowned prelate of the Church between his two sons, youths of elegant form. He often celebrated divine rites, blessed the people, and organized the offices of the court. He appointed cardinals who were outstanding in learning and authority...

...profited. Truly, since he was a lover of peace and humility, after the death of Pope Eugenius <note>Pope Eugenius IV, died 1447</note> and the election of Nicholas V <note>Tommaso Parentucelli</note> to his place by the votes of all—a man most learned in every respect and most respectful of learned men, whom he also wonderfully assisted with money and benefices. Because of this concord and ecclesiastical unity, not only the Roman people but indeed the whole world was liberated from such great discord and rejoiced greatly. Moreover, lest Pope Nicholas should seem ungrateful to God for such a great benefit, he held very celebrated supplications with the people and clergy. All the peoples of Italy did the same. Therefore, moved by that grace and the authority of the pontiff, the people and princes rested from discords and seditions.

### ¶ A Defense against the slanderer of Gaul regarding the state of the Church at Avignon, and containing its tranquility.

<margin>
Luke 10
Psalm 8
</margin>
<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial 'H' decorated with classical foliate motifs and scrolling vines.</image-desc>
A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among thieves. These words can be quite appropriately adapted to our lord the Pope, the highest and most sacred pontiff of the Church. For he is the man whom, according to the prophet’s sentiment, the Lord has crowned with glory and honor, and under whose feet He has subjected all things. This man, therefore, "descends from Jerusalem to Jericho" when he transferred himself from the regions of Gaul <note>France</note> to the regions of the Romans. For "Jerusalem" is understood as the "vision of peace" <note>A traditional medieval etymology for the name Jerusalem</note>. Now, having experienced it, the Church feels and remembers how much peace it found in the regions of Gaul, how much humility in the great, how much readiness in the small, and how much obedience in all.

But the Church herself descends into "Jericho," which is interpreted as the "Moon" <note>Another traditional etymology; Jericho was linked to the Hebrew word for moon, 'Yareah'</note>, whose changeability is more clearly evident to everyone than any other thing in the world. For what in human affairs is more inconstant or more changeable than the Romans? Indeed, certainly Rome herself has been changed more often and more many times than any other city. For if one considers the beginning she had, as they say, in the time of Romulus; the height of honor she had in the time of Augustus; and also her misery in the present time—one can truly and realistically compare the changing of Rome to the changing of the moon. For from the beginning, her light—that is, her power—appeared somewhat like the moon when it is called *monoides* <note>original Greek: "monoides" - the crescent moon</note>. Afterward, she grew notably strong like the moon when it is called *amphiarchos* <note>original Greek: "amphiarchos" - the waxing moon</note>. Then she reached full perfection like the moon when it is called *pampilenos* <note>original Greek: "pampilenos" - the full moon</note>. But afterward, just as she had grown, so she decreased, and was reduced almost to nothing. 

For she is, as Orosius <note>Paulus Orosius, a 5th-century Christian historian</note> says, like an insatiable belly, consuming all things, always hungry, leaving nothing for others. Having nothing, she is left not only more miserable than all the nations and cities she made wretched, but more unhappy. I certainly could not believe her misery unless I had seen it. And then the verses of a certain poet occurred to me, saying: "Rome's scepters lie low; the high palaces are in the mud. Caesar's high house now becomes a vile hut for the needy. Rome is now nothing; Rome is nothing but a sign. Caesar sees nothing in his city worthy of Caesar." <note>A common medieval lament for the ruins of Rome</note> Why, then, does that man reproach us for the poverty of Gaul?

<meta>This page continues the "Apologia" (Defense) begun at the end of the previous section. Having established the transition of the papacy back to Rome, the author now shifts to a fierce intellectual defense of France against an Italian critic (likely Petrarch), who had characterized the Church’s time in Avignon as a period of "Babylonian Captivity" or "Egyptian exile."</meta>

# An Apology against the Slanderer of France:

It is well-established that the part of France from which the Church departed is more fertile—or at least as fertile as Rome—or that part of Italy where he <note>Referring to the critic/slanderer</note> currently resides. What does it matter to the argument if the Gauls <note>The people of France, referred to by their Roman name, Galli</note> learned the use of wine and oil while Rome was still in its youth? This only proves his own lack of refinement; indeed, he ought to be ashamed of this, because the Gauls now surpass them in this very wisdom.

<margin>Lucan, Claudian, Horace</margin>
The Gauls also certainly accept a scarcity of food and wine as a minor loss, following that saying of Lucan <note>A Roman poet (39–65 AD) known for his epic on the civil war</note> in his fifth book: "The human race lives on a little." <note>original: "Humanum paucis viuit genus"</note> And again, that saying of Claudian <note>A late Roman court poet</note> against Rufinus: "One lives better on a small amount; nature has granted all men the ability to be happy, if only one knows how to use what they have." And again, that saying of Horace <note>A leading Roman lyric poet</note> in his letter to Bullatus: "If it is well with your belly, your side, and your feet, the riches of kings can add nothing more." Therefore, although they are not poor through a lack of things, they are nonetheless wealthier through having enough—according to that saying of Maximianus <note>An elegiac poet of the 6th century</note>: "I became master of things by desiring nothing." But the Italians are not like this, and especially the Romans, who are always gasping after worldly profit. They think of nothing else and dream of nothing else except gain, following the word of the Apostle.

<margin>1 Timothy 6</margin>
"Supposing that gain is godliness." <note>original: "Questum estimantes pietatem." 1 Timothy 6:5</note> There is no jest there, no game; indeed, generally there is no action in which virtue is placed before utility. Let him speak, therefore, not of France, but of the poverty of his own Italy, where almost no one has power over their own goods—or what is worse, over their own body. For through the cowardice of their souls, they have been reduced to the misery of Tantalus <note>A Greek mythological figure punished by eternal hunger and thirst</note> and the greatest wretchedness under the rule of tyrants. It follows: "And he fell among thieves." <note>A reference to the Parable of the Good Samaritan</note> For even if what is commonly said is not entirely false—and according to Aristotle, a rumor that many people cry out is not entirely false—I would have turned my pen away from such words, had not the injury of the words of that literate and skilled man (who, I believe, is poorly observant) led me there. This man, about to speak of the Church's departure from the regions of France, shamefully borrowed a biblical harmony, and being wrapped in unskilled words, began his sentence even more shamefully with these words: "When Israel went out of Egypt, the house of Jacob from a barbarous people." <note>original: "In exitu israel de egypto domus Jacob de populo barbaro." Psalm 114:1</note> You have heard the blasphemy! For although he understands the Church well enough through "Israel" and the "house of Jacob," he undoubtedly raved by naming France "Egypt" and the French "barbarous." For if he understands that France from which the Church exited to be "Egypt" truly, realistically, and by its own nature—with all due respect, this is false.

<column-break/>

If, however, he means it by way of a comparison, then it is as if he were calling white "black." For "Egypt" is interpreted as "darkness," while "Gaul" <note>France</note> means "bright" or "white." For in Greek, Gaul is called "whiteness," <note>The author incorrectly links the name "Galli" to the Greek word "gala" (milk/white)</note> whence the Gauls are, as it were, white of body. What agreement, then, has light with darkness?

<margin>Isaiah 5</margin>
Truly, he should have shuddered at the curse of the prophet saying: "Woe to you who call evil good and good evil, putting darkness for light and light for darkness." <note>Isaiah 5:20</note> Egypt is also understood by another interpretation as "anguish" or "tribulation." Whence the commentary <term>glosa</term> <note>A standard medieval marginal explanation of the Bible</note> says on that passage: "When Israel went out of Egypt," that is, the Church went out from "anguish." But what anguish the Church suffered in France, I certainly have not heard. For I saw her there quiet and tranquil in all things: not harassed by the injury of tyrants, not disturbed by the ignorance of the people, nor oppressed by the power of the great, but equally venerated and loved by the benevolence and obedience of all. Therefore, he should not have called the Church’s departure from France a departure "from Egypt." But I ask you to notice what follows: "The house of Jacob," he says, "from a barbarous people." Oh, what a truly admirable and inept improper word—and not to be brought forth by such a man, or at least not so recklessly. For as he himself says, a lie that breaks out into the injury of another is abominable. Behold, he calls the French people a "barbarous people." But what does it mean to be "barbarous"? Is it not to be a stranger and unknown, unregulated by laws, undisciplined in character, rude, and dishonest? If he understands it thus, as he should, he should not seek barbarism among the Gauls, because it is not and does not remain among them. For who of sound mind, healthy head, and true judgment of reason would say the French people are barbarous? In them, there is temperance in food, cleanliness in dress, the pleasantness of mercy, the sweetness of eloquence, truth in words, honesty in deeds, happiness in heart, vigor in work, and agility of body.

<margin>Julius Celsus</margin>
This is according to what Julius Celsus <note>A name often attributed to Julius Caesar's writings in this period</note> says in the fifth book of "Caesar’s Wars," even though he was an enemy of this people: "The Gauls," he says, "are open men and not at all treacherous, who are accustomed to fight by virtue rather than by ambush." Where then, I ask, is the barbarism of such a noble people? But surely, Saint Bernard describes the very real barbarism of the Romans, writing thus to Pope Eugenius:

<margin>Bernard</margin>
"What is so well known to the ages as the insolence of the Romans? A race unaccustomed to peace, accustomed to riot; a race cruel and untamable, knowing not how to be subject, except when it lacks the strength to resist." And it follows: "I know where you dwell; the unbelieving and subverters are with you in Rome..." <note>A quote from Bernard of Clairvaux’s "De Consideratione," a book of advice to the Pope</note>

<meta>This page continues the "Apologia" (Defense) of France against a detractor who advocated for the Pope's return to Rome. Having previously argued for the physical and cultural superiority of France, the author now turns to a moral critique of the Roman people using classical Roman authorities to prove that the environment the Pope has returned to is one of vice and danger. # In Defense against the Slanderers of France.

...they are: impious toward God; reckless toward holy things and the saints; seditious among themselves; envious toward their neighbors; inhumane toward strangers—since they love no one, no one loves them; unfaithful to their superiors; implacable toward their inferiors; shameless in asking; brazen in denying; ungrateful when they have received. They speak grandly though they perform meagerly; they are the most flattering of fawners, the most biting of detractors, and the most learned of traitors.

Are these, then, the manners and character of barbarians? But someone here will perhaps say: "This author was a foreigner and could judge poorly of things unknown to him." I answer for certain: it is not likely, indeed it is not even credible, that so great a man would have spoken thus without knowledge and experience. But so that every occasion for suspicion may be uprooted, let him <note>Referring to the opponent/critic</note> heed Juvenal the Italian.

<margin>Juvenal</margin>
In the third satire of his first book, Juvenal commemoratively laments the words of his companion Umbricius, who had departed from Rome because of the multitude of vices there. Among other things, he says: "For what do we believe is so miserable, or so cruel, that you would not believe it worse to dread fires, the constant collapse of roofs, and the thousand perils of the cruel city?" <note>original: "Nam quid tam miserum... et mille pericula seue vrbis."</note>

It follows: "Ambition had no place then," he says, "where there is no room for honest arts, and no rewards for labor."

It follows: "Let us leave our fatherland; let Arturius and Catulus live there; let those remain who turn black into white." Now, these men, Arturius and Catulus, were two pimps and deceivers of men.

It follows: "What should I do at Rome? I do not know how to lie. If a book is bad, I cannot praise it; I am ignorant of the motions of the stars; I neither wish nor am able to promise the funeral of a father; I have never inspected the entrails of frogs; others know how to carry what an adulterer sends to a bride. Others know those commands; no one will be a thief with me as their teacher." <note>original: "Quid rhome faciam. mentiri nescio..."</note>

See, therefore, how Juvenal the Italian, like a good satirist, stripped bare the vices of the Romans. For when he says, "What should I do at Rome? I do not know how to lie," he denotes that they are liars. When he says, "If a book, etc.," he demonstrates that they are flatterers. When he says, "I am ignorant of the motions of stars," he reprimands them for their glory in superstition and vain opinion. When he says, "To carry to a bride, etc.," he reprimands them for the foul infamy of procurement. When he says, "No one will be a thief with me as teacher," he reprimands them for their base and thieving malice—so that it might rightly be said that our lord the Pope, descending (as has been said) from Jerusalem to Jericho, fell among thieves. I am silent on what follows: namely, those who stripped him and, having inflicted blows, went away leaving him half-dead. <note>A reference to the Parable of the Good Samaritan, suggesting the Pope is the victim and the Romans are the thieves.</note>

<column-break/>

Far be this, good Jesus! Far be it that from the Romans themselves or other inhabitants of the city's borders, the most holy father, together with the most sacred college of reverend cardinals, should be similarly attacked or even despoiled. Far be it that, with a large part of the venerable cardinals removed from their midst—who together with the supreme pontiff make up one body—the Pope himself should be left half-dead with his limbs lost.

These and many other things I do not pursue for the sake of brevity. And because I neither wish nor need to pick apart all of his <note>The critic's</note> sayings one by one, it will be enough for me to run through only four among his other statements. 

First, he wonderfully congratulates our lord the Pope on that wretched approach to Italy, or Rome. 
Second, he exhorts and preaches virtue to him and the lord cardinals. 
Third, he terribly vilifies the people of Belue <note>Likely referring to the region around Avignon/the Rhone</note>, the Rhone, and the neighboring parts. 
Fourth, by depressing France, he glorifies and exalts Italy and Rome. 

First, then, as to the happiness of our lord the Pope: I say that if he understands "happiness" <term>felicitas (happiness/felicity)</term> to mean "operating according to virtue," as 

<gloss>Aristotle</gloss>
Aristotle seems to feel in the tenth book of the *Ethics*, saying: "Life will be happy according to the one operating in virtue as one living well and operating virtuously," then I do not doubt the Pope is happy. But I do not concede that this is so, as he says, because of his "approach" [to Rome]. On the contrary, I firmly believe that path was a great impediment and obstacle to many operations, both speculative and practical, both contemplative and active. For according to Aristotle (cited above), "accidents trouble and disturb the blessed man," for they bring sadness and hinder him.

If, however, he understands "happiness" according to the sentiment of 

<gloss>Boethius</gloss>
Boethius in the third book of *The Consolation of Philosophy* as "a state made perfect by the aggregation of all goods," then according to the deduction of the same Boethius in that same work, it is necessary that true happiness exists in God himself. Because of this, such a state is not possessed "on the way" <note>During the mortal journey of life</note> but is reserved for the blessed in the "homeland" <note>Heaven</note>. 

Whence, also according to the sentiment of Solomon: "No one is called happy in this life." For the mutability of mortal fortune annihilates the name of happiness. Even if this were to happen to anyone, it would not—according to the opinion of many wise men—be for the powerful, the wealthy, and those raised to great honors. As the old man 

<gloss>The same [Boethius]</gloss>
Boethius also said in the first book of *The Consolation*: "Why, friends, have you so often boasted that I was happy? He who has fallen was not in a stable position." <note>original: "Quid me felicem totiens iactastis amici..."</note> 

<gloss>Aristotle</gloss>
Whence also Aristotle, [quoting] the sentiment of Anaxagoras in the tenth book of the *Ethics*...

# Defense Against the Slanderer of France

Repeating, he says: "It seems, moreover, that Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who famously prioritized the pursuit of mind and truth over wealth.</note> did not consider the rich or the powerful to be happy; for he said that it would certainly not be surprising if this appeared unsuitable to the many. For these people judge only those things which are perceived from the outside." Whence the same Anaxagoras, when someone asked him who might be truly blessed, replied: "None of those whom you consider happy; rather, you will find him in the number of those believed by you to be miserable." He will not be a man abounding in riches or honors, but either the faithful and persistent cultivator of a small farm, or of an unpretentious learning; a man more blessed in his private retreat than in his public appearance. Aristotle sufficiently touches upon the reasons why the rich and powerful are not called happy in the first and tenth books of the

<margin>The same Seneca.</margin>
*Ethics*. Seneca also touches upon these things in the tragedy *Hercules Oetaeus*, beautifully saying: "Golden roofs break one’s peace, and purple robes bring sleepless nights. O, if the hearts of the wealthy were laid open, what sublime fears Fortune drives within them! The heart of the poor man remains secure; he holds his cups made of wide-spreading beechwood, but he does not hold them with a trembling hand. He enjoys easy and cheap food, but he does not look back in fear at drawn swords." <note>original: "Aurea rumpūt tecta quietem... sed nō strictos respicit enses."</note> And Lucan in his fifth

<margin>Lucan.</margin>
book: "O, the safe opportunity of the poor man’s life, and his narrow hearth! O, pure gifts of the gods, now understood!" <note>original: "o vite tuta facultas pauperis angustoq; lares."</note> 

<margin>Virgil.</margin>
Virgil also, in his poem *The Gnat* <note>The *Culex*, a poem traditionally attributed to Virgil in the Middle Ages.</note>, says among other things regarding this matter: "Who could be more blessed in a well-ordered age than he who, with a pure mind and proven judgment, stays far away? He knows no greedy riches, nor does he fear grim wars or the deadly struggles of a mighty fleet," etc. It follows: "To him comes sweet rest and pure pleasure." 

<margin>Valerius Maximus</margin>
Valerius Maximus, in his fifth book, tells a notable example of this sentiment regarding Gyges, the King of the Lydians. Gyges had risen from the lowest status to a most wealthy kingdom; inflated by this pride, when he asked Apollo if any mortal was happier than himself, Apollo replied that Aglaus of Psophis was happier. This man was the poorest of the Arcadians, but already old in age, he had never crossed the boundaries of his tiny field, content with the fruits and pleasures of his small farm. From this, Valerius concludes that he more approves of a "smiling hut" than a "palace sad with cares and anxieties," and a few clods of earth free from fear rather than the most fertile fields of Lydia filled with dread; and one or two yokes of oxen easy to maintain rather than an army and weapons and cavalry burdened by voracious expenses; and a small granary serving necessary use, which no one would overly covet, rather than treasures

<column-break/>

exposed to the traps and greed of all. f. 5.
If, therefore, cares and anxieties impede worldly happiness, why then does that man <note>The "slanderer" or opponent who argued for the Pope's return to Rome.</note> congratulate our lord the Pope for his return to Italy, where not only he himself, but all his followers are filled with cares and anxieties, and are troubled by manifold fears? And he who has seen it bears witness: I saw weapons being ordered for everyone, and fortresses being prepared and walled. I saw flight in the fields, gatherings in the villages—indeed, dread almost everywhere. And who is there who has not seen or heard of the furious conflict of the Viterbans, the injurious commotion of the Romans, the spirited rebellion and obstinacy of the Perugians, and generally the hateful opposition of tyrants? Where, then, there is no tranquility of mind or

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
security of body, what kind of human happiness, I ask, can there be? Aristotle also says in the first book of the *Ethics* that he is not happy who has bad children. But what kind of spiritual children our lord the Pope has there, God knows. Nor is it necessary to say more than what Moses wrote in his song: "This generation is perverse, and they are faithless children." <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 32:5 and 32:20.</note> And again: if the arrival in Italy so "gladdens" the lord Pope, and the spirit by which he was led into the wilderness moves him toward a return, will not his departure, if it happens, make him unhappy? Heaven forbid! For all things are permitted to him. For it was permitted to him to go; it is also permitted to him to return. I do not know, however, if the power to do so will remain when he wishes it. I know, however, according to

<margin>Seneca.</margin>
Seneca in the tragedy *Agamemnon*: the way to acting well is never closed. And he who repents of having sinned is almost innocent. I do not say that he has sinned—far from it! For a good spirit told him, as I believe; nor will I say he is bad, but he would be much better if he returned. Now, therefore, I return to that man’s preaching and exhortation. It is a truly marvelous and unheard-of novelty for a blind man to show the way and the right path to those who see sharply. For who in this high College <note>The College of Cardinals.</note> is ignorant that he is mortal? Who does not also think at some time of eternal life? Which of them does not know that everything lived or possessed here is unstable—indeed, transitory and falling? For to believe that such great men are ignorant of such things, or do not notice them, is a sacrilege. For none of them, as far as this is concerned, is either ignorant of where he is, nor did he stand in need of such words. Hence, one could certainly doubt with probability whether that man...

<meta>This page continues the "Apologia" (Defense) of France, specifically responding to the arguments made by an Italian critic (likely Petrarch) who mocked the Papal court's stay in Avignon. The previous page discussed the nature of true happiness and retreat; here, the author turns to a sharp rebuttal of the critic's hypocrisy and his specific insults against French wine and the city of Avignon.</meta>

# Defense Against the Slanderer of France

### Column 1

They might object, as in John 9: "You were born entirely in sin, and do you teach us?" <note>John 9:34. The author suggests his opponent is acting like the Pharisees who rejected the man born blind.</note> And again: "Physician, heal yourself." <note>Luke 4:23.</note> And again: "Rabbi, where do you live?" If he were truly to consider the reason for his exhortation, he would find plenty of material very close to home. Let him look and consider how injustice flourishes in the land where he lives, where the oppression of subjects is found instead of justice. <margin>Ovid's *Metamorphoses*</margin> There, true faith is cast aside by the wicked as if by inheritance, and wickedness stands in the place of piety. There is such violence there, <margin>Ovid</margin> as Ovid said: "Men live by plunder; the guest is not safe from his host, nor the father-in-law from his son-in-law; even the affection of brothers is rare." <note>original: "Vivitur ex rapto non hospes ab hospite tutus..." from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, Book I.</note> Let him therefore consider the manner of living and ruling there, and the infinite ways—which he himself knows—by which money is shamefully extorted. Let him speak and preach to such people!

But what is more: Have I not seen in Milan an abominable idol upon the altar of God? I mean the image of an armed man sitting upon a horse made of white marble, <note>This refers to the equestrian tomb of Bernabò Visconti, which was provocatively placed behind the high altar in the church of San Giovanni in Conca, Milan.</note> placed right where the body of Christ is usually consecrated or kept. Is that something to be passed over in silence? <margin>Psalms</margin> Is it not to be feared that God will avenge the insult to Himself? For the Psalmist says: "I saw the wicked man highly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon. And I passed by, and behold, he was not." <note>Psalm 37:35-36.</note> <margin>Seneca</margin> For according to Seneca in the tragedy *Thyestes*: "Where there is no shame, no care for law, holiness, piety, or faith, the kingdom is unstable." And in the tragedy *Oedipus*: "Hated empires are never held for long." And in the eighth book on prosperous fortune, the same says: "Believe me, follow [Fortune] sparingly; the goddess is fickle."

If, therefore, God is patient for a time, one must not be at all confident, for the Lord is clothed in the garments of vengeance; for vengeance belongs to Him, and He will abundantly repay those who act in pride. Let this "excellent preacher" consider how much his preaching or exhortation could benefit many with God’s help, and that he has people at his very doors whom he might soothe with the gentleness of his eloquence and direct with the depth of his knowledge. Let him leave the speck in a distant eye, while removing the great beam from his own eyes. <note>A reference to the "Sermon on the Mount" in Matthew 7:3-5.</note>

<column-break/>

### Column 2

Now I come to the blasphemy against the wine of Beaune <note>original: "vini bennensis". Beaune is the center of Burgundy wine, which the Popes in Avignon famously preferred.</note> which I heard gladly, though it was certainly undeserved—an insult to the Rhone region. For what person in their right mind would not shudder at the cursing of such a wine, or rather, of such a great good? For he says: "Would that those vines had never been! I would almost say any vines at all, if they were to produce a harvest so poisonous to the Church of Christ." <note>The critic argued that the Cardinals refused to return to Rome only because they couldn't bear to leave their French wine.</note> O noble vintage! O precious wine, sweet above all other wines, health-giving and pleasant! How wretched and inept is the reason for this curse. For this reason, may it never enter his mouth, and may your sweet flavor never pass through his throat! <margin>Ovid</margin> He has almost earned the curse Ovid wretchedly cast upon an old woman: "May you be unable to drink wine unless it be thick or sour."

Does he believe that such great men are so devoted to their bellies and so affected that they flee and dread Italy because of a lack of this wine? Far be it! Especially since they could have that wine easily if they wished. But what is the cause of this? Without a doubt, I believe it is because the malice of the Romans and the treachery of many Italians has been heard and experienced; indeed, the morals of almost everyone there are bad. They once believed in this malice through hearsay; now, in fact, they contemplate it face-to-face. Therefore, they do not flee Italy or Rome because of wine, but because of cruelty and treachery, fearing for their own lives, <margin>Matthew 10</margin> and heeding that Gospel command: "When they persecute you in one city, flee to another."

But also, what did the Rhone deserve, as he himself says? "If," he says, "it was to give the Church of God cause for exile." But why, I ask, when the Church was in Avignon, did it suffer "exile"? There, it flourished in power, rested in security, and was held in great veneration. Is not even the Vicar of the most high Lord—to whom belongs all the earth and its fullness—in "exile" in any part of the earth? Is he a debtor to the Romans alone? Far be it! For wherever he decides to reside for the benefit of the Catholic faith, there is his seat. Nor was it said without cause: "Where the Pope is, there is Rome." <note>original: "Ubi papa ibi rhoma". A famous legal maxim justifying the Papacy's stay in Avignon.</note>

But he says that in Avignon there is nothing good unless it is brought from elsewhere. But where, I ask, is there a good city that does not need foreign goods? Unless perhaps he means Rome, <margin>Psalms</margin> where the squares are so large that they are believed to suffice for all its citizens for grain and wine—which proves not abundance, but a manifest emptiness. And again, that noble city of the Venetians, which he extols so highly: what does it have except what is brought from elsewhere? Let the discerning man, therefore, cease his wordy and empty arguments, which even the young boys in our Street of Straw <note>The *Rue du Fouarre* in Paris, the center of the university district where students sat on straw during lectures.</note>—which he mockingly calls "clattery"—would tear to pieces. I dare to say...

Having previously addressed the critic's hypocrisy regarding Italian corruption, the author now specifically defends the city of Avignon and the historical prestige of the Gallic people, using classical Roman historians like Justin and Solinus to prove that Gaul is not a "barbaric" wasteland but a fertile, heroic land that even once saved Rome itself.</meta>

# Apology Against the Slanderer of France

### Column 1

...an injury to the name, yet you should not transcend the boundary of truth; for a similar uproar is not heard in any other place. In Avignon, truly, there is and has been an abundance of all good things, as is evident and has been shown by the result. This is why Lord Anselm, <note>Lord Anselm likely refers to Anselm Choquart, a French jurist and diplomat who defended the French cause before the Pope.</note> who was sent by the Lord King, clearly showed these and many other things that could have called our Lord Pope back from his undertaking; yet he was wrongly refuted by that man <note>The "slanderer," likely Petrarch, who advocated for the Papacy to return to Rome.</note>—saving all reverence. Certainly, if Anselm had lived, he would have shown this with living reasons. He did not believe he was speaking to a master of the kitchen or a prince of cooks, but to the Lord of the Church and the Supreme Pontiff, whom it befits and behooves as a good father to care for everyone. But what does Terence say? "Truth begets hatred." <note>original: "Veritas odium parit" from Terence's play *Andria*.</note>

<margin>
Justin
</margin>

Because of this, it happened that he became his enemy for speaking the truth. Why does he also disparage the Rhone and the neighboring places so without reason? Let him remember Justin <note>Marcus Junianus Justinus, a 2nd or 3rd-century historian whose "Epitome" was a standard history textbook in the Middle Ages.</note> in Book 43, reporting that in the time of King Tarquin, a youth of Phocaeans from Asia set out in ships to the furthest reaches of Gaul and founded Marseille among the Ligurians and the wild tribes of the Gauls. For the Phocaeans, forced by the smallness and thinness of their soil, practiced the sea more studiously than the land. And so, daring to proceed to the furthest shore of the ocean, they came into the Gallic gulf at the mouth of the Rhone river. Captivated by the pleasantness of the place, they returned home and reported what they had seen, enticing more people; bringing these with them, they founded Marseille. Why, then, does that man speak of "bad houses" on the Rhone and marshy places, when the ancients, wandering the seas, were so captivated by the beauty of the place that they founded a powerful city there? I say powerful indeed: as even Rome herself was ransomed from the hands of the Gauls with its gold. For it is written there that the ambassadors of Marseille, returning from Delphi where they had brought gifts to Apollo, heard from the Gauls that the city of Rome had been captured and burned. When this news reached home, the people of Marseille contributed gold and silver, both public and private, to fill the weight [of the ransom] for the Gauls, from whom they knew peace had been purchased. Let not that man, or even the Romans, disdain the places around the Rhone or their inhabitants, by whose benefit they were ransomed, and by whose help it was brought about that the young Rome—then poor and wretched—did not suffer ultimate destruction. Now, however, I return unwillingly and forced to a defense of Gaul, knowing that comparisons between these regions are hateful. I neither wish nor need to recite every kind of praise for Gaul and the virtue of the Gauls celebrated by many illustrious authors; nor should I be entirely silent about them. For concerning the Gauls

<column-break/>

Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a Roman geographer noted for his "Collection of Remarkable Facts."</note> says this: "The Gauls stretch between the Rhine and the Pyrenees. Likewise, they extend between the ocean and Mount Cevennes with very fertile soil and convenient fruit-bearing yields; mostly planted with vines and shrubs, most blessed with every offspring for the use of animals, and watered by the waters of rivers and springs." Thus says he. And what more can be said of the goodness of the land? Regarding the virtue of the Gauls, celebrated by many writers, I could fill many books. One, however, may suffice for many: and to be brief, let him take notice of Justin, the abridger of Pompeius Trogus, speaking thus in Book 24.

<margin>
Justin
</margin>

"The Gauls, in an abundant multitude, since the lands that had birthed them could not contain them, sent out three hundred thousand men like a swarm to seek new seats. A portion settled in Italy, which also captured and burned the city of Rome. And a portion penetrated the Illyrian gulfs through the slaughter of barbarians and settled in Pannonia. <note>An ancient province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note> A harsh, bold, and warlike race, which first after Hercules—to whom that feat gave admiration for his virtue and faith in his immortality—crossed the unconquered peaks of the Alps and the intractable cold. There, having subdued the Pannonians, they waged various wars with their neighbors for many years. Encouraged then by success, different columns sought, some Greece, others Macedonia, laying everything low with the sword. And so great was the terror of the Gallic name that even kings, not provoked, would voluntarily buy peace with a huge amount of money." Likewise in Book 25, he says the same: "The youth of the Gauls at that time was of such fertility that they filled all of Asia like a certain swarm. Finally, neither the kings of the East waged any wars without a mercenary army of Gauls, nor when driven from their kingdoms did they flee to any others but the Gauls. So great was the terror of the Gallic name and the unconquered success of their arms, that they thought they could neither keep their majesty safe nor recover what was lost without Gallic virtue." Thus says he. Why then does that man disparage the Gauls and Gaul? For I confess and it is true that Italy is a great and good part of the world. Neither is it anyone's intention, nor was it, I believe, to so depress her as to contradict this truth. But because speeches must be understood according to the subject matter, when Lord Anselm spoke about Italy, he was thinking of Italy or that part of Italy to which the Curia <note>The administrative apparatus and court of the Holy See.</note> itself was migrating. Comparing, therefore, the parts he was leaving with the parts he was approaching. If he spoke the truth, God knows. It was not necessary, therefore, because of these things, to [praise] the riches and greatness of the cities of Italy as if up to the heavens...

<summary>The author defends the wealth of Avignon and the historical prestige of Gaul, citing classical historians to remind the reader that the Gauls once saved Rome and were a globally respected military power. He argues that praising France does not require hating Italy, but rather understanding the context of the Papal court's location.</summary>

# Apology Against the Slanderer of France

### Column 1

...to elevate them with greatness: especially since the Gauls founded a large part of them after driving out the Italians. For the aforementioned Justin says in Book 19 that when the Gauls had come to Italy, they expelled the Tuscans from their seats, 

<margin>
The same [Justin]
</margin>

and they founded Milan, Como, Brescia, Verona, Bergamo, Trento, and Vicenza. And he himself also testifies in Book 20 that many other cities of Italy—indeed, without doubt, almost all—were founded by other nations. For according to what he himself writes there somewhat more extensively: the Tuscans came from Lydia. After the capture of Troy, Antenor led the Venetians there. Adria is a Greek city. Diomedes founded Arpi. Pisa among the Ligurians has Greek authors. And among the Tuscans, Tarquinia was founded by the Thessalians and Spina by the Umbrians. <note>original: "Spinambis." The author is likely referring to the ancient city of Spina, which was often associated with Greek or Pelasgian origins in classical texts.</note> The people of Perugia derive their origin from the Achaeans. The Latin people seem to have been founded by Aeneas. The Phalisci, Iapigians, Nolans, and Abellans are colonists of the Chalcidians. The Sabines, Samnites, and Tarentines set out from Lacedaemon and were called "spurious." They say that Philoctetes founded the city of the Thurians; and they say his monument and the arrows of Hercules, which were the fate of Troy, can still be seen there. Epeus founded Metapontum; and they say the iron tools with which he fabricated the Trojan horse are there. Because of this, that whole part of Italy was called Greater Greece. <note>original: "maior grecia," more commonly known as Magna Graecia.</note> Why, therefore, does that man glory so much in his cities, which those foreigners found as miserable, or non-existent, or deserted by the Italian race? Why does he also so extol the gravity and knowledge of the Italians? Indeed, he even broke out into such an insult as to say: "No one learned is in Gaul." <note>original: "Nullus doctus in gallia." A stinging critique from the Italian side, suggesting France was an intellectual wasteland.</note> Certainly, there are many in Gaul, and many more have been—with all due respect—truly learned. I believe he did not remember Hilary of Poitiers, Pothinus the Bishop of Lyon, Eucherius of Lyon, Vincent of Lérins, Salvian of Marseille, nor Prosper of Aquitaine, and many other very learned men. Nor did he have before his eyes others who are quite recent, namely Hugh and Richard of Saint Victor, Peter Comestor, Alexander of Hales, Henry of Ghent, Peter Auriol, William of Auxerre, and John Duns Scotus, who is called the "Subtle Doctor," and many other great men. And if perhaps he says that he means that none of the Four Doctors <note>The Four Doctors of the Western Church: Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory the Great.</note> learned their science in Gaul, yet the words themselves at first glance sound foul, especially since in that passage, while praising Italy, he disparages Gaul as much as possible. Even if that were perhaps true, I could also name many subtle and ingenious Gallic men most famous in every science—as I have already said—and truly conclude: "No one learned is in Italy." Who

<column-break/>

indeed among the Italians, as a natural philosopher, has so penetrated secrets and revealed hidden things that a certain person—or rather many non-Italians—did not do so much better? Where, I ask, are Tully’s <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> *Physics* or Varro’s *Metaphysics* read, or the natural philosophy of any of them? I frankly confess that many of them certainly composed some good books beneficial to human life; however, God is my witness, they are to be placed far behind the *Ethics* of Aristotle. But why does he even speak of "Latinity" for the praise of the Romans, since between the Romans and the Latins there is, or has been, as much difference and discord as between the French and the English? Why then do the Romans, just like us, glory in Latin letters? But he says that orators and poets should not be sought outside of Italy. And what of it? Are not the excellent poets Statius and Claudian Italians? Of whom Statius is from Toulouse <note>A common medieval error; the poet P. Papinius Statius was from Naples, but was confused with a rhetorician from Toulouse.</note>—or as many others say, from Toulouse—and Claudian is said to be from Vienne. I do not name many others for the sake of brevity. Only in ancient times did Rome itself prevail in these matters, and especially in poets, which John the Englishman <note>referring to John of Hauville, author of the satirical poem *Architrenius*.</note>—who is almost naturally our enemy—touches upon somewhat in his *Architrenius*. When he was speaking among other things about our city of Paris, compelled by the truth, he speaks of it among other magnificent cities thus: "Paris, a land [rich in] harvest, burning with metals, <note>original: "esa a metallis" / "aesa a metallis."</note> industrious with books, Greek in its studies; Rome for poets, Attica for philosophers; the rose of the world, the balsam of the globe; Sidonian in its adornment; and its own in food and drink; fertile in the reaping, not covered by brambles; wooded with clusters of grapes; full of wild beasts; fish-filled in its lake; bird-filled in its waters; rich in fields; favorable in its wine; mild to its settlers; pure for God; strong in gifts; pious to its kings; sweet in its air; pleasant in its site; good in every way; all-beautiful; all-good—if only fortune would favor the good." This John, therefore, being experienced in many languages and in every most excellent word, attributing true things as I believe (since praise from an enemy is more than true), noted that the most excellent poets were of the city of Rome. Yet Plato judged that poets, as being contrary to the truth, should be expelled from a well-ordered city, as Augustine recounts in *The City of God*, Book 10, Chapter 14; because of which he pronounces that the palm should be given to the Greek Plato, as is clear in the same place. But [the critic] says: "You have a city that is shattered, I confess, but holy." I do not know what he means by "the city." If he understands "the city" to mean the holy places and the relics of the saints themselves, I certainly grant that it is holy; but then he has spoken willfully and most improperly. But if he calls the very streets and houses "the city," which he calls shattered, I find no holiness there. Nor should he have called it a holy city, but rather, as Juvenal says, a "cruel city." <note>original: "vrbem seuā" (urbem saevam).</note>
