# Apology Against the Slanderer of France

<margin>
Africanus, a Roman expelled
</margin>

And certainly, I preserve well the memory of that city which, by its own cruelty, killed so many capable men, slaughtered so many innocent heroes, and cruelly destroyed and murdered so many holy and just people. A city that, as if by its own greed, despoiled the whole world: not only pursuing its enemies, but always standing out as unjust and ungrateful toward those who served it well. Was not Africanus the Elder <note>original: "Aphricanus superior." This refers to Scipio Africanus, the general who defeated Hannibal.</note> a prime example? He had restored the Roman Republic when it was not only bruised and broken by the arms of the Punic War, but almost bloodless and dying, making it the mistress of Carthage. Yet, by weighing his most glorious works against injuries, he was driven from his fatherland and died in exile. He ordered to be inscribed on his tomb: *Ungrateful fatherland, you shall not even have my bones.* <note>original: "Ingrata patria nec ossa quidem mea habebis."</note> For, as Valerius says, he denied his ashes to the city which he had not allowed to fall into ash itself. 

<margin>
Africanus the Younger and Scipio Nasica.
</margin>

Africanus the Younger <note>Scipio Aemilianus, who finally destroyed Carthage in 146 BC.</note>—after the two cities that threatened the Roman Empire, Numantia and Carthage, were removed from the nature of things—found a thief of his life within his own home, but found no punisher of his death in the forum. Then there is Scipio Nasica, who did not allow the Republic, which was being choked by the pestilential hand of Tiberius Gracchus, to be strangled. Because of a most unfair estimation of his virtues among the citizens, he withdrew to Pergamum under the title of an embassy; there he spent what remained of his life without any longing for his ungrateful fatherland. For the sake of brevity, I pass over other endless ingratitudes of the Romans. Is it right, therefore, to call "sacred" a city stained with such great vices and ingratitudes? A city whose ingratitude was shown not only toward its ancient leaders and princes, but even toward the ministers of the Church and the High Pontiffs <note>The Popes.</note>, some of whom they drove away, some of whom they killed, and almost all of whom they troubled in some way. But he says: "They praise Romulus for founding it, Brutus for liberating it, and Camillus for restoring it." Whatever may be the case or whatever he may write, many authentic authors have felt differently about the founding of the city of Rome and the cause of its name.

<margin>
The origin of Rome
</margin>

For according to Solinus, some say the name of Rome was first given by Evander; before that, it was called *Valentia* <note>Meaning "Strength" or "Valor" in Latin.</note>. They say the meaning of the name was preserved when it was named *Rhome* in Greek (which also means Strength). Because the Arcadians had lived on the high part of the mountain, it was derived from there that the most secure parts of cities should be called "citadels" <note>original: "arces."</note>. It pleases Heraclides to say that after the capture of Troy, certain Greeks reached the place where Rome is now by way of the Tiber. Then, at the persuasion of Rhome, the most noble of the captive women who was their companion, they burned their ships, established their seats, built walls, and called the town *Rhome* after her. Agatocles writes 

<column-break/>

that Rhome was not a captive, but rather the daughter of Ascanius and granddaughter of Aeneas, and was the cause of this name. It is also handed down that Rome has a "proper" name, which was forbidden to be published; indeed, they decreed it should not be announced as a sacred secret, so that the faith of silent quietude would abolish knowledge of it. Finally, they killed Valerius Soranus because he even dared to speak it aloud. Others say that the name was meant to conceal a "fever" <note>original: "febris."</note> where it was so imposed in honor of Februa, the mother of Mars. Whether this is true I do not assert; however, I know that the blessed Augustine, in Book 4 of *The City of God*, chapter 12, called Fever itself a "Roman citizen." I believe this was said because fever inhabits Rome almost naturally and hereditarily <note>A reference to the prevalence of malaria in the Roman marshlands.</note>. Whatever the truth of Rome's founding and name, even if—as is more commonly said—it was founded by Romulus, it is no great thing. Wherefore

<margin>
Juvenal.
</margin>

Juvenal, at the end of his third satire, says this to a certain Roman citizen boasting of his origin: *However far back you go, and however much you unroll your lineage, your first ancestor, whoever he was, was either a shepherd or—that which I do not wish to say.* <note>Juvenal, Satire 3.312-314. The "unspeakable" thing is a criminal.</note> That is, a thief and a murderer, as the commentary says in that same place. It is therefore not a great thing, since even according to their own opinion, their founder was shamefully born and raised. For as they say themselves, a she-wolf nourished the exposed Remus and Romulus with her breasts. Because of this, it is no wonder if Roman manners are wolf-like. Regarding these men, Romulus and Brutus, whom he brings forward here for the glory of Rome,

<margin>
Orosius.
</margin>

Orosius speaks in his second book, saying: *Romulus endowed the abducted Sabine women, joined in wicked marriages, with the blood of their husbands and parents. After first killing his grandfather Numitor, he seized power from his brother Remus. He dedicated his kingdom, his brother's walls, and his father-in-law's temple with blood.* Regarding Brutus, he follows: *Brutus, the first consul among the Romans, strove not only to equal the first king of Rome in parricide, but to surpass him. Indeed, he struck with an axe his two adolescent sons and likewise the two brothers of his wife, who were accused of a plot to recall the kings to the city.* Is it therefore a great thing to name such criminal men as founders and patrons for the praise of this city? As for Furius Camillus, whom

<margin>
Furius Camillus.
</margin>

he says restored Rome: his most ungrateful citizens drove him out of that very city of Rome. Yet I do not deny that many capable men have existed in the city of Rome; but the present Romans, by not following them, have degenerated from the strong integrity of their predecessors. Where and in whom,

<margin>
Upright Romans.
</margin>

I ask, is there now in Rome the bravery of Horatius Cocles? The mildness of Quinctius Crispinus? The [wisdom of] Fabius...?

He argues that modern Romans have lost the virtues of their ancestors, making their claims of superiority hollow.</summary>

# Apology Against the Slanderer of France

...the moderation of [Fabius] Maximus. The confidence of Cato. The constancy of Quintus Mucius Scaevola. The adequacy of Valerius Publicola. The military skill and self-restraint of the Scipios. The abstinence of Lucius Paulus. The modesty of Varro. The daring of Curtius. The clemency of Julius Caesar. The patience of Pompey. The justice of Fabricius. The fidelity of Regulus. The generosity of Quintus Considius.

<margin>
Roman vices
</margin>
For leaving behind the footsteps of all those great men, they follow the footsteps of the worst. For they well retain the greed of Septimilius <note>likely referring to Septimius, who betrayed and murdered Pompey the Great</note>. The treachery of Catiline. The pride of the Marsic leader. The cruelty of Servius Galba. The luxury of Clodius Pulcher. The voracity of Caius Sergius. The greed of Crassus. The cruelty of Sulla and Marius. 

<margin>
Question
</margin>
For the Romans, stained by these vices, boast only in the names of those aforementioned men of worth, as if they themselves were such people; they are foolishly and vainly proud. For Horace says this would be a great thing: *I speak not of a famous father, but of a life and a beautiful body.* <note>original: "dico non patre preclaro: sed vita et corpore pulchro." This emphasizes personal merit over lineage.</note>

<margin>
Juvenal
</margin>
And Juvenal asks: *Who would call this man noble who is unworthy of his race, distinguished only by a famous name?* <note>Quoting Juvenal’s eighth Satire on true nobility.</note> Because of this, toward the end of his third book, he said: *I would rather your father be Thersites* <note>the lowliest and ugliest Greek at Troy</note> *provided you are like the grandson of Aeacus* <note>Achilles</note> *and can take up the arms of Vulcan, than that Achilles should produce you as someone like Thersites.* Therefore, it is foolish to believe oneself adorned by the goods of others while one's own virtues are abandoned. Nor should they boast in the oppression of nations and the power of ancient arms; for the virtue of the majority of them was cruelty, cloaked in a sophistical virtue, born of greed, and nourished by pride—

<column-break/>

—and widowed of all true honor. This is also testified by the blessed Augustine in the third book of *The City of God*, chapter 13, saying: *Rome, conquered by the lust for dominating, triumphs that she has conquered Alba; and she called the praise of her crime 'glory.'* <note>original: "Libidine dominandi Rhoma victa albam se vicisse triumphat." Augustine argues that Roman expansion was often fueled by sinful ambition rather than justice.</note> For, as our Scripture says: *The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who acts unjustly is blessed.* <note>Psalm 10:3.</note> Let false coverings and deceptive whitewashings be stripped from things, he says, so they may be inspected by a sincere examination. He follows: *Cruelty itself has the rewards of praise.* But I think it is better to pay the penalties of any sort of inactivity than to seek the glory of such arms. 

Here, therefore, I stay my hand and do not permit my pen to run further, lest the satiety of an insipid style bring boredom to the listener. May every good Italian or Roman citizen spare me, if they please; for although I wrote being struck by injury, I have not written things more grave than Sallust and his authors <note>The Roman historian Sallust was famous for his scathing critiques of Roman corruption.</note>. 

Truly, because it is not fitting for my smallness to touch upon such sublimity by giving counsel, I neither advise our most holy father and Supreme Pontiff <note>This refers to the Pope, likely during the period when the Papacy was in Avignon, France.</note> toward a return to Rome, nor do I exhort him to remain here; but let him, as a spiritual man judging all things, always act according to the good pleasure of his Holiness for the praise of God himself, and for the benefit and solace of the people subject to him: so that by meriting the grace of God and men, he may attain eternal glory.

<meta>This page transitions from a general defense of French culture to a specific dedication and praise of the French polymath Symphorien Champier. It moves from a critique of Roman vanity to an exaltation of intellectual and medical pursuit as the highest form of human endeavor, establishing Champier as the pinnacle of this ideal.</meta>

### Friar Angelus de Duccis

### ¶ To the Lord Symphorien Champier
### of Lyon, most worthy professor of the liberal arts
### and the faculty of medicine <note>original: "apollinaris," referring to Apollo, the god of healing</note>,
### Friar Angelus de Duccis of the Carmelite
### Order of Brescia <note>a city in Northern Italy</note>, a defense.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring elaborate foliage and floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
Since the activities of mortals are various and—if I may say so—nearly infinite, my most learned Symphorien, by which the minds of men (which can in no way be idle) and their talents are driven: some are entirely devoted to learning and the studies of others; others, indeed, are enslaved to fragile earthly goods or the accumulation of family wealth, not only for themselves but also for their children and others whom they hold dear and must protect. It is likewise found that many apply themselves to the military art (which is most worthy and most suited to human peace and society, since wars are to be undertaken for the purpose of living in peace without injury). Yet we see some who cling to lust and idleness (than which nothing is worse or more foul in human nature), as Horace says: *There are those whom it pleases to have gathered Olympic dust in the chariot race, and the goal-post cleared by glowing wheels.* <note>original: "Sunt quos curriculo pulucre olympicum collegisse iuvat: metaqz feruidis evitata rotis." From Horace, Odes 1.1.</note> I, however, agreeing with the opinion of many other men of great reputation, have always judged the first class of men—those devoted to the most pleasant study of letters—to be preferred above all others. This is because I notice that those laboring in physical studies, which pertain only to the care and adornment of the body, are least able to enjoy peace of soul or tranquility of mind (than which nothing is more divine). Furthermore, because those very exercises which tend to weary the mind and the bodily mass, and to depress the spirit (which is said to be divine within us) to the depths where death lurks, can be easily discovered by anyone who is rightly wise and desires to be called a wise man: they should neither be cultivated nor held in high price. Finally, because we see men tormented by various desires of this sort, panting for greater things day by day. For riches are sought by them, partly for the necessary uses of human life, and partly for enjoying pleasures. In those whose spirit is greater, the desire for money looks toward power and the ability to grant favors; but in others, the smallness of the soul is easily recognized. For nothing is so characteristic of a narrow and small mind as to love riches. Nothing is more honorable and magnificent than to despise money if you do not have it, or if you do have it, to apply it to beneficence and liberality.

<column-break/>

From this it follows that riches cannot be desired by any philosopher or person of sound heart. For wisdom alone, knowledge alone, and the inquiry and investigation of truth alone—which is thought by illustrious and studious men to be necessary for living well and happily—is most suited to the nature of man. It is this which makes a man brave, rich, free, sincere, free from cares, and more excellent and noble than all other living creatures. Nor is it wisdom alone (since there is no other animal that has any knowledge of God) that distinguishes man from the beasts; it is through wisdom that man discerns consequences, sees the causes of things and their motions and progress, and joins the past to the present and connects it to the future. Since this capacity belongs to man alone, it certainly testifies that we both affect and desire that which can make us blessed and happy. For this reason, we cannot but pursue the generosity of your spirit, your magnificent deliberation, and your most prudent arrangement with the highest proclamations, special praises, and immortal honor. For although you were born of the most famous lineage, you do not lead a degenerate life (as many do) from the integrity of their character. Moreover, your homeland is Lyon, than which no better or more opulent city can be found among the provinces of Gaul, made noble by the celebrated rivers of the Saône and the Rhône <note>original: "arare et rhodano"</note>. Furthermore, though you were elegantly and splendidly educated from the cradle, as nobles usually are, you spared no vigils, no late-night studies, no pursuit of letters (whether human or divine), and finally no "toil that conquers all" <note>original: "labori improbo (qui omnia vincit)," a reference to Virgil's Georgics</note>. On the contrary, you have sailed through a vast heap and a most rich treasury of the Muses, the art of Apollo <term>medicine</term>, the vast chaos of philosophical knowledge, and the immense sea of theological wisdom. From these you have brought back such a great merchandise of all sciences that, in these times of ours in Gaul (if I may say so without offense to anyone), I would judge that there is either no one or only the rarest of men to be placed before you. I myself experienced this in reality during these past Lenten days while staying in Lyon, when—at times free from my public lectures—I read through your "golden" works (if I may call them that) with great desire. In these works, you have treated with an elegant style and with great depth and precision: the famous writers of medicine, the founders of divine laws, the refutation of the sect of Muhammad <note>original: "secte machometice"</note>, the diseases of bodies and souls and their remedies, introductions to the practice of medicine, the approval of the Gospel religion from the writings of the Gentiles, and many other matters.

It argues that the pursuit of wisdom and science is the only noble human path, contrasting it with the pursuit of wealth or war, and praises Champier's extensive publications across medicine, theology, and philosophy.</summary>

<meta>The previous page established the dedication to Symphorien Champier, a renowned French physician and humanist. ### Apologeticon

...you have excited the youth to the love of knowledge <note>original: "scientiarum"</note>, and invited the elders to perform similar deeds. Recently, however, it happened that after the Easter solemnity, having been invited by your generosity to a sufficiently sumptious banquet, I entered your library, which is adorned with various and indeed not common books, but such as befit a most learned man. As I was investigating everything more diligently, enticed by the novelty of the place, there fell into my hands certain small works <term>opuscula|small or minor literary works</term> composed by you a few days earlier, but not yet polished, entitled *On the Fourfold Life* and *On the Fourfold History of the Gauls*. I earnestly requested that you commit these to the printers <note>original: "chalcographis," literally "brass-writers," a common humanist term for printers</note> once they were more exactly corrected; and I have no doubt that other lovers of good literature, joined to you by friendship and necessity, would advise the same. For it is not easy to say how much utility and delight they would bring to learned men and sound minds if they were to be printed and brought to light. In these small works, as if in certain little gardens or pleasant groves, you have wandered through almost all the volumes of authentic authors—as if through fragrant meadows and fields wreathed with every kind of sweet-smelling flower—and picking all the most choice specimens, you have transplanted them for the common utility of all, watering them with the fertility of your own talent. In these works, you have left nothing untouched that is required for a healthy or long life, or for attaining a heavenly or super-heavenly life, or if you prefer, a spiritual and divine one. Thus, although in the three preceding parts you have omitted nothing pertaining to the matter from the opinions of philosophers, physicians, and sometimes theologians, in the fourth and most recent of these, you discuss so graphically and ingeniously the principles of physical things, the fabric of the world, separate substances <note>refers to angels or purely intellectual beings in Scholastic philosophy</note>, fate, happiness, God and the First Being, and other things of that ancient kind. You bring forth testimonies from both philosophers and theologians that are not entirely dissonant from Christian truth, such that (if I may say so with the peace of all) I have not easily found many like you among the ancients who have surveyed such wisdom. You have adorned Asclepius <note>an ancient figure associated with medicine and the Hermetic tradition</note>, that most ancient theologian and disciple of Hermes Trismegistus—known to very few except the most learned—with such faithful and clear commentaries that he seems to need the help of no other. Certainly, in these works of yours, the most learned have that which delights them, the average have that in which they may profit, and the lowest are also encouraged toward the study of knowledge. If any, indeed, are captured by the pleasure of histories,

<column-break/>

they have the small work on the *Fourfold History of the Gauls* <note>original: "Gallorum," referring to the people of France</note> divided into four small books. In the first of these, the deeds of the ancient Gauls are related succinctly and in a brief text from Justin, the faithful historian, as well as the illustrious deeds of recent times and our own day. In the second, he treats the praise and antiquity of the city of Lyon <note>original: "Lugdunum"</note> and the illustrious men of that same city. In the third, he treats the famous writers who flourished among the Gauls. In the fourth, the tranquility of the ecclesiastical state at Lyon and Avignon <note>original: "Auinionem"</note> is discussed. You compress a vast material into a few small books, mindful of that precept of Horace: *Whatever you teach, be brief* <note>original: "Quicquid precipias esto breuis," from Horace's Ars Poetica</note>, etc., and you bring this into the public for the propagation of your humanity and discipline, and for the common utility of students. That noble saying of your Plato <note>referring to Champier’s devotion to Neoplatonism</note> does not escape you, of which you are a most worthy follower: *We are not born for ourselves alone; for our country claims a part of our birth, and our friends another part.* <note>original: "Non solum nobis nati sumus..." A famous sentiment found in Plato and Cicero</note> And as it pleases the Stoics: all things produced on earth are created for the use of man, but men are born for the sake of men, so that they may be able to benefit one another. In this, we ought to follow nature as our leader and bring common utilities into the midst, so that we may meditate on being good and beneficent as much as we can; since whatever knowledge or doctrine is in us—which is a gift of God, from whom every best and perfect gift descends—it should be imparted not only for our own pleasure, but for the salvation of many. For all our thought and the movement of our soul will be occupied either in taking counsel concerning honest things pertaining to living well and blessedly, or in the studies of science and knowledge, or in the instruction and beneficence of men. That you have done this until now is testified by many published works of widespread erudition throughout the world, and there is a most certain expectation of all that you will do the same hereafter. For I hope that you will shortly commit your small works, which are still in your hands, to the press, whereby you may be able to benefit many and deserve good fame among God and men (which is considered the best good of fortune). But you seem to me to be somewhat angry with Italian writers and to rail against them; who (even though very many among other nations have emerged as most learned in every kind of discipline) nevertheless [claim to excel] in poetry, the art of speaking, invention, memory, gestures of the body, pronunciation, theology, and finally in subtlety of talent, industry, prudence, wisdom, and other things of that kind.

<sig>B 4</sig>

<meta>This page continues the "Apologeticon," or formal defense, written by Angelo de Duccis to the French humanist and physician Symphorien Champier. Following the praise of Champier's personal library and recent writings, the author moves into a comparative defense of the intellectual and military merits of the Gauls (the French) in relation to the Italians, a common theme in Renaissance "cultural wars."</meta>

# From Father Angelo de Duccis.

They seem to yield to no nation (let there be no ill will in the word <note>original: "absit verbo inuidia"</note>). I freely confess that the Gauls <note>The "Gauls" refers to the French, as humanists preferred using ancient Roman tribal names for modern nations.</note> have had quite strenuous soldiers, famous throughout almost the entire world; the Italians have had them too. The Gauls had professors of wisdom whom they called **Druids**; the Italians also had students of wisdom. The Gauls have had and still have learned writers of history; the Italians have had, and still have, far more. The Gauls had most eloquent rhetoricians who taught rhetoric in Italy; for they contend that Cicero’s first teacher, and the very celebrated poet **Statius**, were Gauls. The Italians have and have had those who adorned the Latin language with their eloquence and the beauty of their speech, and who rendered it neat and splendid from a foul state, and raised it up even to the stars. If one attempted to number them all and review their writings, the "voice would stick in the throat," as the poet **Maro** <note>original: "Maro," referring to Publius Vergilius Maro, the poet Vergil.</note> says, and "the evening star would close Olympus before the day was done." What shall I say of the most worthy professors of the **Paeonian art** <term>Paeonian art|The art of medicine, named after Paeon, the physician of the Greek gods</term>? What of the most accurate interpreters of **both laws** <term>both laws|The study of both Civil (Roman) Law and Canon (Church) Law</term> and the most diligent expositors of other disciplines who illuminated all of Christendom with their writings? But why do I commemorate ancient writers, when even in our own time, among the rest, nature has brought into this light an extraordinary poet, a most consummate philosopher, a most profound theologian, and a man perfect in the **three languages**—namely Latin, Hebrew, and Greek—Brother **Baptista Mantuanus**, a Carmelite? God gave him to us as a singular gift, and his many works display not only human but rather divine doctrine. Indeed, because of his singular virtues and his most studiously labored works, he is illustrated more and more every day in authority, glory, and dignity—to say nothing of the admirable fame and greatest honor he brings as an ornament to the most excellent city of Mantua. What should I say of **Antonio Sabellico**, that most elegant historiographer, who attributed much to the city of Venice, and who extols that city with the highest praises for every kind of well-deserved virtue? And he does this with good reason. For what sort of rulers the city of Venice has always had, and what justice, faith, counsel, constancy, prudence, and wisdom it has always used in conducting its affairs, can easily be recognized by the administration, customs, and power of that republic. Does it then seem to you worthy

<column-break/>

that Sabellicus himself should extol such a city with the highest praises? I know you will respond that it was a **Pythagorean precept** <note>A rule attributed to the Greek philosopher Pythagoras.</note> that, after God, truth is to be cultivated in all things, which alone makes men closest to God. Truth separates the persona of the free man and the slave; a lie mixes the slave and the free man together. Great is the force of truth, which easily defends itself by its own power against the ingenuity, craftiness, and skill of all men, and against the deceitful snares of all. For a just man will judge it not his way to lie, not only to a friend and familiar associate, but even to an enemy and a stranger. Nor will he ever allow his tongue—the interpreter of his soul—to discord from his senses, experience, and true judgment. Therefore Sabellicus (if he be a just man) ought not to have lied in this matter, even though the Venetians deserve well of him, just so he might praise them. But in that matter in which the whole reason of life most turns, one ought rather, on the testimony of **Lactantius** <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) known as the "Christian Cicero."</note>, to trust oneself and rely on one's own judgment and proper senses to investigate and weigh the truth, rather than being shamefully deceived by believing the words and reasons of others, as if one were himself devoid of reason. For God gave wisdom to everyone in a manly portion, so that they might both investigate unheard-of things and weigh those things already heard; so that they might search out unknown and hidden things and judge what is found with prudence. Therefore, since to be wise—that is, to seek the truth—is innate to all, they deprive themselves of wisdom who approve what they have heard without any judgment and are led by others (in the manner of cattle <note>original: "pecudum more"</note>). For they think it impossible that they themselves could be wiser or know the truth more truly than the reporters of wars. I confess indeed that truth is to be preferred above all things; Sacred Scripture affirms it is great and stronger than all. "All the earth calls upon truth, even heaven blesses it, and all works move and tremble before it, and there is nothing iniquitous with it." Therefore **Paul**, the teacher of the Gentiles, says: "Putting away all lying, speak the truth every man with his neighbor, for we are members one of another." Nor is it right to boast and be liars against the truth; for this is not the wisdom of God descending from above, but earthly and animal malice. But have not Italian writers followed the truth? Have we not read the most excellent historian **Titus Livy** reporting that his own Italians were killed and routed by **Hannibal** in the battle at Lake Trasimene and at Cannae, and writing that Rome was captured by the Senonian Gauls? And have we not...

<meta>This page continues Angelo de Duccis's "Apologeticon" addressed to the scholar Symphorien Champier. Having previously compared the cultural and military achievements of the French (Gauls) and Italians, the author now addresses the reliability of historians and the tension between national loyalty and objective truth.</meta>

->Apologeticon.<-

Valerius Maximus, a distinguished Roman citizen and historian, recounted many misfortunes of the Italians. What wonder is it, then, if Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506), a prominent Venetian historian.</note> and other Italian writers assert that many very brave leaders from the Venetian army fell at Parma—or rather Fornovo <note>The Battle of Fornovo (1495) was a bloody encounter between the French army of Charles VIII and the League of Venice. Both sides claimed victory.</note>—and that the Italians fought most bravely but unsuccessfully that day? For I think there is almost no one who doubts that this is true. It is worthwhile not to attack the truth, but to protect it—though sometimes it is also worthwhile to remain silent about it. You might say that they have not only been silent regarding many things that add to the glory of the Gauls, but have even fabricated a great many lies, especially where they have committed to written records that the defeated emerged as victors.

If they wished to describe anything to the praise of their own princes, I confess that an account of the truth should have been maintained; first, the affections of the human mind and the passions of the soul must be driven away, according to the sentiment of the divine Severinus Boethius, who said:
> Drive away joys; drive away fear; put hope to flight; and let no grief be present. The mind is clouded and bound with chains where these hold sway. <note>original: "Gaudia pelle: pelle timorem spemque fugato: nec dolor adsit. Nubila mens est vinctaque frenis hic ubi regnant." A famous stoic passage from Boethius's *Consolation of Philosophy*.</note>

Nor is it easy to have a sound and upright judgment, or to perceive the truth, where these passions dominate. What should we think of those who, even when they feel themselves to be erring, willingly throw themselves against the stones so that the rest of the people might follow them? They dig out their own eyes so that all may become dim-sighted, or rather blind. They deserve well neither of others, whom they lead into error, nor of themselves, who assent to the errors of others. They do not use the gift of their wisdom to fulfill in deed or writing what they have truly perceived in their minds; instead, though wise and knowing, they strike their foot into a snare so that they, along with the others whom they ought to have freed as the more prudent ones, are themselves ensnared. 

For if those who feel themselves to be erring do so willingly, how much more so the unlearned and inconstant common folk, who rejoice in empty things and are delighted by childish fables? But for the learned and those who wish to be called and held as such, there is a very great journey, I confess: lest they drive others headlong into the Scyllan rocks and the abyss of Charybdis <note>References to the famous sea monsters of Greek mythology representing a choice between two evils.</note>, so that they may finally deserve well of themselves as well as others. But as I see it, Brother Baptista Mantuanus <note>Battista Spagnoli (1447–1516), a famous Carmelite poet and philosopher known as the "Christian Virgil."</note>, an excellent philosopher, most learned poet, and most profound theologian, and Antonius Sabellicus, a most eloquent orator, have followed the truth as far as was possible—

<column-break/>

understanding that the distinction between humans and mute beasts lies solely, or certainly mostly, in the truth. Indeed, they understood how shameful a lie is, being alien to every principle of immortality. They have praised their own princes worthily and deservedly, yet they have not yet reached the summit of praise. On the contrary, since they excel in many virtues, they are compelled with "hands and feet" (as they say) <note>A Latin idiom meaning "with all one's might."</note> not to lead the unrefined people into an inextricable labyrinth of errors, but to make them wise and understanding of the truth. 

For it was fitting that, just as these two surpass all Italians in both eloquence and knowledge, they should likewise describe the illustrious deeds of the Italians. Nor should it be thought that their speech was lacking in this matter, for they have also often, copiously and eloquently, illustrated and defended the glory of others. Indeed, you have from Brother Baptista Mantuanus that illustrious and divine work on the life of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, the Apostle of the Gauls <note>Saint Denis, the patron saint of France.</note>, recently published, which illustrates not only all of Gaul but a good part of all Christendom. For he wished to satisfy both the Gauls and the Italians by singing of their brave deeds. 

But to what end is all this? If they have strayed a little from the path of truth (as is charged against them), I should say it must be granted to the love of their fatherland (to which we owe much), whom (as the Bard of Mantua <note>Referring to the Roman poet Virgil.</note> says): 
> Love of country conquered, and the immense desire for praise. <note>original: "Vicit amor patriae laudumque immensa cupido." From Virgil's *Aeneid*.</note>

Even though these things ought not to fall upon a steadfast and wise man, they nevertheless follow nature and incline the mind. But however the matter stands, I ask you again and again (if you will allow it) to bring your works into the light, so that from their collation and comparison with others, the truth itself may shine upon dim-sighted eyes, and the mists of error may be removed from our midst. 

I have no doubt that you will win for yourself a good name (which is better than <margin>Proverbs 22.</margin> great riches) <note>original: "Prouuerb. xxij." Referring to Proverbs 22:1: "A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches."</note> and perpetual fame among posterity—you who have followed the truth, distracted by no passion of the mind, and who will bring much honor to the Gauls (of which they are worthy). Finally, if I consider all your exceptional virtues, by which you are rightly compared with all those who are held in the highest regard: in greatness of soul, wisdom of counsel, liberality of nature, excellence of doctrine, knowledge of things, integrity of life, observance of religion, constancy of faith, and the breadth of your love toward the learned...

<sig>B ij</sig>

<summary>In this passage, De Duccis discusses the difficulty of historical objectivity, arguing that while Italian historians like Sabellicus may be biased by patriotism, scholars must strive for truth over national glory. He praises the works of Baptista Mantuanus and encourages Champier to publish his own writings to help clear the "mists of error" regarding French and Italian history.</summary>

->### Father Angelo de’ Bucci’s Defense.<-

<margin>Virgil, *Aeneid* Book 6.</margin>
...and by your goodwill, the beauty of your body, the eloquence of your speech, the kindness of your voice, the nobility of your lineage, the abundance of your riches, and the honor, modesty, and charm of your noble wife. Indeed, in every kind of praise—whether of the mind, the body, or of fortune—you seem capable of being numbered among the greatest and compared to them. If, I say, I wished to recount all these things, my speech today would not be enough to close the matter; rather, a decade-long history would have to be written. And to use the words of the ancient poet: "Not if I had a hundred tongues, and a hundred mouths, and a voice of iron, could I encompass all the forms of praise," <note>original: "Non mihi si lingue centum sint: oraque centum: Ferrea vox omnes laudes compendere formas." A famous excerpt from Virgil’s *Aeneid* (6.625–627), often used by Renaissance writers to signal that their subject is beyond description.</note> nor

<column-break/>

could I run through the names of your divine virtues. O, I would proclaim you a happy man, who is so strong in the hallmarks of so many and such great virtues! O blessed is not only the city in which you live, but also all of France, which is adorned by such a man. One last thing I most earnestly ask of you, my most beloved Symphorien: that from now on, as you have so eloquently begun, you deign to illuminate with your most careful scholarly works <term>lucubrationibus</term> <note>This term refers to "lucubrations," literally works produced by candlelight or late-night study, signaling intense intellectual labor.</note> not only the regions of France, but the whole world of Christendom. Farewell, and continue to love me as you do. Lyon, <note>original: "Lugd." or *Lugdunum*, the Latin name for Lyon, a major center for Renaissance printing.</note> in the year of our Lord 1508, on the day before the Nones of April. <note>April 4th, 1508.</note>

# Letter
<sig>B iij</sig>

¶ Sebastian Coppin sends many greetings to Symphorien Champier: both a most wise interpreter of the medical arts <note>original: "apollinee artis," referring to Apollo, the god of healing and medicine.</note> and a distinguished theologian.

Your letter has reached me, most honorable man, and it was indeed very pleasant. Although you use iambic meter <note>A rhythmic pattern in poetry</note> more than is usual (if I may say so of a prose speech), your words seemed full of kindness, as I have always found you to act with the moderation of a guide toward me. I give you immense thanks—though my strength is not enough to repay them—because you urge me toward that distinguished fortitude, or rather, magnanimity <term>magnanimitatem</term> <note>Literally "greatness of soul," a key virtue in Renaissance ethics involving the pursuit of great honors and the endurance of hardship.</note>. Imbued with this, no one will succumb to difficult tasks in arduous affairs, but will instead rage against them with a Herculean spirit, just as Hercules did against untamable monsters. No one can easily deny that you are practiced in this, not to mention being distinguished by the gifts of sacred Minerva <note>The goddess of wisdom.</note>; indeed, your words correspond to the opinions of the experts.

<margin>
Aristotle,
*Ethics*,
Book 3.
</margin>
First, consider the Olympic games, celebrated every five years and distinguished among the four kinds of games. If we trust Aristotle, the leader of the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note>, it was not just any strong men who were crowned, but those who fought manfully. I pass over what the monuments of literature have left written concerning fortitude. For it is not enough for one wishing to climb to the peak of the highest good to be imbued with bright talents, unless, having utterly driven away discord, he exercises them intrepidly and, patient in labor, struggles against adversity.

<margin>Virgil, *Georgics* Book 1.</margin>
Does not that poet from the Andes, Virgil <note>original: "andinus ille maro." Virgil was born in the village of Andes, near Mantua.</note>, say:
> Relentless labor conquers all things, and poverty pressing in harsh circumstances. <note>original: "Labor improbus oia vincit: & duris vrgēs in rebus egestas."</note>

<margin>Faustus on the Virtues, Book 2, on the Intellect.</margin>
Our friend Faustus <note>Likely Faustus Andrelinus, a contemporary humanist poet.</note> imitated this: "Nor do all harsh things yield to unconquered labor."

<margin>Baptista Mantuanus</margin>
Does not Baptista Mantuanus <note>A famous Carmelite poet known as the "Christian Virgil."</note> introduce Labor as having hairy, nervous, and marble-like limbs? What of Saint Peter, crying out that we must resist the devil’s impulse not with a sluggish mind, but with a strong one? For this reason, for one who desires the Good itself,

of the

</margin>

<margin>Horace, *The Art of Poetry*.</margin>
> You who write, take up a subject equal to your strength; and ponder long what your shoulders refuse to bear, and what they are capable of. For when a matter is chosen according to one's power, neither order nor clear eloquence will fail him.

What else do the attempts of Icarus mean, who, flying higher than was right, fell into the sea below when his wings melted? What thing led the Fabian family of Rome to their death, except that,

<margin>1 Peter, Chapter 5.</margin>
Furthermore, you say it should be noted that we seek out pagan places and very humble towns, having left behind the most grand cities. You know

that much greater work is needed in swimming across the sea than in a small river. You are surely delirious to want us to enter the seas when we lack the ships and oars fit to accomplish it. You understand the metaphor. You exclaim that we should be rebuked because things have not succeeded according to our wish; I respond immediately that we cannot hold Fortune in our hands. Truly, I would wish you to turn this over in your mind: it is not in the power of one who sails the Black Sea <note>original: "euxinū"</note> to go often where he wishes, but where the winds draw him. The sentiment of Terence’s character Mysis to Glycerium <note>original: "Eritonē andriū," referring to characters in Terence's play *Andria*.</note> is not hidden from you:
> We live as we can, since we may not live as we wish. <note>original: "Uiuimꝛ vt qmus qñ vt volumꝛ nō lʒ."</note>

# Letter
<sig>B iij</sig>

...the Phrygian <note>original: "phrygia," referring to Aeneas, the legendary hero of Troy (which was in Phrygia) who fled to Italy.</note> who, about to migrate to Italy, stayed for a short time at Carthage after being received by Dido. I confess: I am indeed not a hired man as before, but one whose mind is set on interpreting the art of Palaemon <note>original: "palemoniã artẽ." This refers to the art of grammar and rhetoric, named after the Roman grammarian Remmius Palaemon.</note>. Truly, I shrink from the continuous exercise of this duty as much as a sailor shrinks from the dogs of Scylla <note>A legendary sea monster.</note> or from the deep, devouring jaws of the marine Charybdis. Yet it is sometimes pleasing to follow the footsteps of certain Romans who, when they had exhausted themselves in public business or in conducting legal cases in the forum, took joy in humble agriculture and simple things. I hope to be released from here shortly; for this 
<margin>do[mini?] manoq[ue?] psuetu[m?]</margin> 
shore of Tellene <note>A reference to a specific local region or an obscure classical site.</note> is not only subject to Saturn or Scorpio, as you say, but to Mercury, who is considered the god of thieves, merchants, and the crafty. One thing noted in your letter caused me some irritation: you assert that my love for you is as unsteady as a small boat <note>original: "cumbe instar," literally "like a skiff."</note>, as befits a fickle man who is moved by any impulse. I would have you know that I am not like the sea-god Proteus, whom they say changes into various forms. For I truly know the conditions of true love, and I shall observe them toward you in the future for as long as life is my companion. If the famous painter Apelles were to depict love, he would paint both winter and summer upon its brow. This signifies that love, without pretense, ought to remain the same in both favorable and adverse fortune. There are many who smile when things succeed with "favorable winds," as they say; but when things turn against them, they turn their faces away. These people perform the duty of flatterers rather than true lovers. Furthermore, true love has these two words carved into its heart: *near* and *far*. By this it is marked that we must pursue with love not only those who are present, but also those who are absent and removed from us by a great distance of space. Therefore, those seem to me to be far removed from true love who promise mountains and seas to those present, but mock them when they are absent. The satirical poet Persius warns us to beware of such people: "O you of patrician blood, who must live with a blind back of the head, beware the mockery that happens behind you." <note>A reference to Persius, *Satire 1*, suggesting that since humans cannot see behind their own heads, they are vulnerable to people making faces or mocking them from behind.</note> Furthermore, love has "death" and "life" depicted on the hem of its garment; by which we are reminded that we should pursue with love not only those enjoying the breath of life, but also those who have been taken from our midst and who deserved well of us while life was our companion. Memory records that among the ancients, only four pairs of friends were most highly celebrated for this kind of love: Theseus and Pirithous; Achilles and Patroclus; Orestes and Pylades; Pythias and Damon. 
<margin>Four pairs of friends.</margin> 
He also adds among the younger Greeks Epaminondas and Pelopidas; but believe me, none of their love was ever truer or firmer than ours. These are the things which my Minerva <note>His own intellect or inspiration.</note> thought should be noted on these pages; if they seem to you to be etched with a very rough style, attribute it to my sorrow; for I wrote these things with a troubled mind and weeping eyes, because I am deprived of your presence and that of my brother, and of that pleasing conversation we once enjoyed. I ask that you give my warmest regards to your Andreas, my most skilled doctor; I value him as much as those of lesser rank value either Aesculapius or Podalirius <note>Famous healers of Greek mythology.</note>. He is certainly close to my heart, although the human will does not incline toward the unknown—to use the words of our theologians—yet he is known to me through your eloquence regarding his excellent gifts. If the opportunity were given to me to speak with you both in person, I would seem to have obtained no small part of the happiness of this age. Farewell, our protection and glory, and be always mindful of us.

->¶ Jacques Robertet <note>A French humanist and diplomat (c. 1460–1519).</note> sends many greetings to Master Symphorien Champier, most worthy professor of the Apolline art <note>The art of Apollo, meaning medicine.</note>.<-

Because of that singular and long-standing close friendship we share—or rather, out of necessity—and because of your many kindnesses toward me, my dear and most deserving Symphorien: I now at last give you immortal thanks. These are not the thanks I truly owe, but those I am able to give according to the smallness of my strength. Though my powers are confined within a very narrow channel <note>original: "angustissimo euripo," referring to the Strait of Euripus, known for its strong currents.</note>, they nevertheless pour forth whatever gratitude they can. And would that Jupiter <note>A common humanist substitution for God.</note> might grant—to use a phrase from Plautus—that I might one day be able to repay you most abundantly. If ever so bright a day shines upon me, that my ability might match my most fervent desire, I do not know if I could ever consider myself happier. I have wished to be so persuaded since the moment your character was first seen by me: the uprightness of your ways, the kindness of your companionship, and finally a certain open and serene cheerfulness of your countenance. To this is added your literary condition. Who, by Hercules, knows all the "topics" of <term>dialectic</term> <note>The art of logical argument.</note> better than you? Who navigates those winding bends of the logicians and the inexplicable tangles of the sophists more swiftly or smoothly—or more cleverly entangles and traps others in them? I say nothing of both branches of philosophy <note>Natural and moral philosophy.</note>. I gladly pass over theological precepts and the most abstruse decrees. I do not mention the disciplines which our ancestors called the <term>mathematics</term> <note>In the Renaissance, this included the Quadrivium: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy/astrology.</note>: Geometry and Astrology, in which you are unceasingly engaged. As for your strength and value in Medicine—since it is your own proper and peculiar profession—I would prefer the judgment of others to stand, were it not for the fact that recently my left hand, mangled by a most unlucky wound, was saved by your help—or more truly, by your Apolline or Aesculapian gift <note>Aesculapius was the god of medicine and son of Apollo.</note>. Indeed, we know what sort of ointments and what "basilica" <note>original: "basilica," perhaps referring to a royal remedy or a specific medical preparation mentioned by Pliny the Elder.</note> you prepare when you choose to relax; we know because we have put them to the test. What more? That most subtle art by which you extract the soul, or if you prefer, a certain spirit of diverse materials <note>A reference to distillation or early chemical medicine (alchemy/spagyrics).</note>, provides the most immediate remedies for the many and various illnesses of mortals. It has even seemed that you once held back the spirit of a half-dead and clearly bloodless body—a spirit that was barely clinging on and just about to vanish into the air—using your healing waters <note>original: "salutarib' lymphis," referring to distilled medicinal essences.</note>, and having applied your poultices, you have preserved it to this very day. When I consider all these gifts of your genius within myself, I am accustomed to congratulate not only you, but also myself. For in this barbarian region of ours and in such an uncultivated climate, I have found a man—a true man, I say. For as Cicero says, some are "men" in name only, not in reality. With you, I am permitted to make noise regarding the <term>humanities</term> <note>The *studia humanitatis*, including grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history, and moral philosophy.</note>, in which you hold the laurel as a priest and high official. Though I am only initiated into the sacred rites, I am a most fervent follower of the Muses—or to use the Greek word, a <term>philomuso</term> <note>A lover of the Muses.</note>. It has been worthwhile whenever we were permitted to spend not just hours, but entire days, in conversation regarding these same liberal studies. You, most generous Symphorien, have wished to make me a participant in all these things, as if by a perpetual right of use <note>original: "usufructuariū ppetuū," a legal term for the right to use and enjoy the profits of another's property.</note>. Thus, unless I wished to appear the most ungrateful of all ungrateful men, I realized I must return thanks...

# Letter
<sig>B iij</sig>

...let us judge. We do so as willingly as we do dutifully, and would do even more if the shoulders (if I may speak so) of our ability could bear the weight. Therefore, you will be content with this alone in exchange for all our mutual services, since we can do no other. Yet what greater or even more pleasing thing can be provided than the sincere goodwill of a well-wishing mind? We have heard that even the immortal gods themselves are accustomed to rejoice in such a thing. But now let us sound the retreat and conclude our letter with verses, where that well-known saying of Naso <note>original: "nasonianuz," referring to the Roman poet Publius Ovidius Naso, known as Ovid.</note> occurs in passing:

> Though strength is lacking, yet the will is to be praised;
> By this, I divine that the gods are content.
> Nor does it happen that a poor man comes unpleasing to the altars;
> A lamb pleases no less than a slaughtered ox.
> Nor does the incense which the poor man offers to the gods
> From a small censer have less value than that given from a great platter.

Thus he sang. It remains only for you to fare well, and to love me so that I may have the strength to fare well. From our library, in the year of our Lord 1496, on the Ides of May <note>May 15th.</note>.

->Jacques Robertet <note>A member of the influential Robertet family, prominent officials in the French court.</note> to Symphorien Champier, interpreter of philosophy and medicine. Great Greetings.<-

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'N' depicting two figures, likely scholars or saints, in an interior setting with books.</image-desc>
I am not unaware, most learned man, that as soon as you see the face of this letter, you will immediately be angry with me because I did not come to you yesterday. This is especially true since that day had been set for starting our work together, that hour appointed, and that time designated for the beginning. It was a matter indeed as pleasant to you as it would have been most convenient for me. But if you will grant my excuses and receive my reasons with a kind mind—as is your custom in all things—there will be no reason for you to think we have fallen into fault. I would have you be so persuaded.

For I do not scorn those studies which I am about to undertake—not just because of your encouragements but because of my own almost daily demands. Indeed, I approach them with such a cheerful, vigorous, and persevering mind that no difficulty of the matter nor weight of cares can deter me from starting. Perhaps the same thing will happen to me as usually happens to those of the dullest intellect: for it often happens that through an immoderate fervor for learning, great labors, and diligent late-night studies, they achieve everything. And we therefore (let it be said without boasting) will not deny having "withdrawn our hand from the rod" <note>original: "manum ferule subduxisse," a Latin idiom meaning to have completed one's basic education or rhetorical schooling.</note>.

But that is beside the point. Truly, the reason I did not come to you as I promised was that it was not possible for me yesterday evening, nor is there even a place to approach today. For I am overflowing right now with many and varied affairs, partly domestic and partly legal <note>original: "forensibus," relating to the forum or public legal business.</note>, which have long distracted me. Tomorrow occupies me; I have a very serious lawsuit which we are forced to renew now that the holidays are over; my adversary compels it. For my part, I am girding myself for the fight, equipped as it were with the arms of Vulcan <note>The god of fire and smithing; implies being "heavily armed" or well-prepared.</note>. I will come myself the day after tomorrow, wearing boots, greaves, breastplate, and gauntlets—what more can I say? I shall be so equipped that it seems nothing could be added to a most perfect man-at-arms.

But enough joking. I wish you to take all this in good part so that you may understand that, although my mind is most burning for all the disciplines of good letters—and especially Philosophy, the queen of the rest—the time does not correspond to my desires. Farewell meanwhile, most studious Symphorien; embrace me as you do, and farewell again. From our house, the 12th day before the Kalends of November <note>October 21st.</note>, in the year of our Lord 1496.

# Letter
### Page 137

<margin>Virgil</margin>
...before the evening star should settle the day in closed Olympus. <note>original: "ante diem clauſo componeret veſper olimpo." A reference to Virgil’s *Aeneid*, meaning "before the day ends."</note> Furthermore, you have sent me a most pleasant and long-desired gift: your most accurate sleepless labors <note>term: "lucubrationibus" — literally "works produced by lamplight," referring to late-night scholarly study.</note> which you have gathered regarding the medical writers worthy of eternity. I read this so greedily that (in the manner of Virgil’s Bitias, <note>original: "vittæ" (likely a typo for Bitiae). In the *Aeneid*, Bitias is a Carthaginian noble who boldly drinks from a golden bowl at Dido's feast.</note> who undaunted drained the foaming bowl and drenched himself with the full gold) I swallowed it all down at once on the very first day, almost without pausing for breath. Therefore, I first of all owe and give you immortal thanks, and I shall continue to do so as long as "this breath rules these limbs." <note>A common Virgilian expression for "as long as I live."</note> I thank you because, setting all other things aside, you wished me to be a participant in your scholarly labors, in which one enjoys an honorable pleasure. For there is an old proverb: "Among friends, all things are held in common." I see verified in you that saying of Horace: "The jar will long preserve the odor with which it was once imbued when new." <note>original: "Quo ſemel eſt imbuta recens ſeruabit odorem teſta diu." This suggests that lessons learned in youth stay with a person forever.</note> For in your tender years—or "from your tender fingernails" as the Greeks say—you drank in that which you not only preserve in your mature age, but indeed pour forth in abundance. You were never less idle than when you were at leisure, like that famous Roman, Cato. You never allowed your soul, which has a heavenly origin, to languish in sluggish laziness. You did not spare yourself from constant labor, which brings worthy rewards. You never permitted the times, which slip away with constant motion, to depart in vain. Nor did you receive the grace of God to no purpose. Studies make you more noble, even if you are of a lineage that is not ignoble. For without study, the mind is sick. Studies most excellently elevate happiness and most easily diminish calamities. Many exercise their bodies; few exercise their wits. Leisure without letters is death, and the burial of a living man. Thus, life without learning is like an image of death. Likewise, as Quintilian witnesses, "nature is blind without discipline." You, indeed—whom that saying of the divine Plato (found in Cicero's *On Duties*) does not escape—namely, that none of us is born for himself alone; and as the Stoics believe, humans were created for the sake of humans so that they might be able to be useful to one another; you have studied for the utility of mortals. You have applied all that time, which Theophrastus asserted was the most precious thing to spend, to writing and teaching. And so, lest the illustrious talents of young men should grow filthy with base idleness, and lest the refinement of your excellent genius and learning—and that facility for writing which you obtained from the gods—should seem to have been granted in vain: You have written a *Manual of Logic*, a *Summary of Physics*, *On the Heaven and the World*, *On Generation and Corruption*, *On the Soul and its Immortality*, and *Against Mages and Enchanters*. You have added to the works of Guy de Chauliac, the surgeon. <note>term: "Guidonem Chirurgū" — Guy de Chauliac (c. 1300–1368) was one of the most influential surgeons of the Middle Ages.</note> Also, in the previous year, a little book *On Curing Diseases of the Body and Soul*, *On the Inventors of Divine Laws*, and a *Dialogue on the Errors of Muhammad*. Also, in these days, a work *On the Fourfold Life*, and the *Trophy of the Gauls*, with several other small works added, as the work itself can show to the reader. Likewise, following these in the vernacular language: the *Ship of Princes*, and *On the Sibyls and their Prophecies*. Also, that which must not be passed over in silence: the book entitled the *Ship of Ladies*, <note>original: "nauis dominarum" (Nef des Dames). This was one of Champier's most famous works, defending the virtues of women.</note> which at last, after it had remained with you for many days, you committed to the printers at Lyon. Having left the workshop of the bookseller filled with the praises of honorable women, it was honorably received by them. From this matter (though you deserved it not a little before), you have earned the favor of the minds of ladies much more. So much so, that they have joined a maiden of excellent body and most beautiful form to you in "stable marriage and declared her your own." <note>Another reference to Virgil's *Aeneid* (Book 1), where Juno promises a nymph to Aeolus.</note> So that she "may spend all her years with you for such merits, and make you a parent with beautiful offspring." This was a most high and early reward. Behold what utility learning brings! Theophrastus used to say that this is better than trusting in money. For the learned man alone among all is neither a stranger in foreign lands, nor—having lost his family and relatives—is he destitute of friends; rather, in every city, he is a citizen. 

But to return to the matter of the excellent medical writers, from which I have digressed: Let the malevolent disparage it, into whose souls wisdom shall not enter. Let them waste away with envy, than which the Sicilian tyrants found no greater torment. Whoever does not refuse to read through this book of yours will certainly find—provided he lends a patient ear—that not only humble philosophers, but even divine heroes, the highest priests, kings, and princes of medicine have spent much time on the art and have practiced the same. But the prudent reader or listener hears all with an equal mind and reads everything; he is not moved by the authority of the speaker, but notices what is being said. He despises no one's learning. He inquires indifferently from all concerning what he sees he lacks. He considers in his mind not how much he knows, but how much he is ignorant of. Since, as Themistius says, those things we know are the smallest part of those things of which we are ignorant. It is right to turn over a bushel of beans to find one small pearl, as that Cordoban, Averroes, <note>term: "Averroes" — Ibn Rushd, a 12th-century Andalusian polymath. Known here as "the Cordoban."</note> wrote in the fourth book of his *Colliget*. Nor is it the duty of a good man to praise or blame anything unless the truth of the matter is first known. This is what Pliny the Younger is read to have practiced regarding the Christians; not condemning them, but studiously weighing their ceremonies and rites. But enough of these things. And lest you lose the "oil" <note>An idiom for "wasting one's efforts" or "burning the midnight oil."</note> of your sleepless labor, it would be worthwhile for your kindness, in exchange for so great a gift with which you have honored me...

# Letter

...you have deigned in this matter: to give thanks: for I cannot repay you. This I would perform with a willing heart <margin>Persius</margin> <note>Persius was a Roman satirist known for his Stoic themes.</note> were it not that the magnitude of the matter exceeds my ability to speak. Therefore, I thought it better to make use of silence, and to restrain my lip with a finger <note>A gesture of humble silence or awe.</note> since it is not within our power <margin>Virgil</margin> to pay worthy thanks. Nor should I attempt what I could not fulfill after attempting in vain. I would rather diminish the matter with ineffective words than extol it according to its proper dignity. Yet, lest I incur the mark of wicked ingratitude, I beseech you that you might wish to accept this confession of my powerlessness to give the thanks owed, in place of a worthy return of gratitude. Farewell, and see that you love me in return.
->Lyon, in the Year of our Lord 1507.<-

### Henry Valuphin sends his greatest
### greetings to Symphorien Champier,
### most illustrious in much learning and
### most adorned with the precepts of the medical art.
<note>original: "physice artis." In this period, "physic" referred to the art of medicine and natural philosophy.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter E featuring foliate and floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>

Although in these past days, O most kind Symphorien, little or no leisure was left to me, involved as I was in both secular and ecclesiastical business, to give any thanks to you and many others who have deserved well of me by your sole munificence—I will not say in deed, but at least in words or writings, or at least to signify that I hold you in my heart. However, as soon as it was possible for me, I took care to perform this in whatever way I could according to my strength, lest I seem unmindful of benefits and ungrateful; for there might perhaps be more trouble in delay than there is error in excessive haste. Indeed, I do not seek to offer such thanks as are expected by so great a man, filled with every discipline, but rather those which I could offer with all my effort, relying perhaps more on boldness than wisdom. I do this especially trusting in your no small benevolence, which is sometimes extended even to the unworthy. If I have erred in anything through this boldness, I know for certain I shall easily obtain your pardon. 

Therefore, my Symphorien, most distinguished in both learning and virtue, I both hold and give immortal thanks to you with these unsalted, meager, and dry little letters for your gifts abundantly bestowed upon me, though I do not deserve them. I speak of those books, sweet as nectar, and your speech, circumspect with no small erudition, so much so that no one ever departs from you without being first taught something. Nor do I satisfy my debt to you with these words, for the magnitude of your merits toward me is so great. Indeed, to return a favor in deed and in words is a matter of great importance, as you know best. But I know you are accustomed to enjoy such kindness that you think thanks are sufficiently returned by me if you perceive they are truly held in my heart. The joyful expression of your Henry must be noticed first; for by a happy countenance, a small gift is often made huge and pleasing. Meanwhile, if you recognize any strength in me—whatever of mind or body or external goods (which belong to Fortune herself) may be mine—all of that will be deservedly given and dedicated to you, by whom I have been moved by so many and such great various gifts. Farewell at last, my Symphorien, to be numbered among my most faithful friends, and greetings; I pray, and would that I might prevail by prayer, that you wish to remember your Henry thus far.

You have gifted us these things, though we are surely undeserving.

->¶ Henry Valuphin sends his warmest greetings to Master Symphorien Champier, a man most especially devoted to the liberal arts and to all virtue.<-

<image-desc>historiated initial 'H' containing a scene with two figures in robes, possibly scholars, conversing in a vaulted classical room with pillars.</image-desc>
Indeed, O most skillfully learned of men, Symphorien: with your singular learning and modesty, as well as your probity, you are most outstanding among others in your talent to act in such a way that you may consult most abundantly not only for yourself, but for others. For, as Cicero, the prince of orators, bears witness: we are not born for ourselves alone <note>original: "nobis solis nati sumus." A famous Stoic sentiment from Cicero’s *De Officiis* emphasizing social duty.</note>. Therefore, noticing that the life of the human race is short and filled with various and many miseries, it seemed honorable and fitting to you to bring to light—with dedicated effort—certain things quickly and briefly approved by the learned, faithfully observed, and most accurately excerpted from the books of scholars and philosophers, so that you might more and more be of service. This work is especially necessary, concerning the *Fourfold Life* <note>original: "de quadruplici vita." This refers to Champier's book *De quadruplici vita* (1507), which combined medicine, Neoplatonic philosophy, and local history.</note>, interspersed with certain errors of the victorious Gallic nation, the antiquity and origin of the city of Lyon <note>original: "lugdunensis."</note>, the famous citizens of Lyon, Gallic writers, and several other things as the title of the work proclaims. You have established these as mirrors and examples for future generations, by which you might properly care not only for the body but also for the soul, which is of first importance. Truly, this is the one provision <term>viaticum: originally money or supplies for a journey, here used metaphorically for spiritual and intellectual nourishment</term> most desired by all mortals, which, if anyone is ever supported by it, they will be safe and sound wherever they go. What more, then, O traveler, if you are wise, would you wish to seek beyond this? For it is sufficient for you to live well and blessedly: that there be a sound mind in a sound body <note>original: "mens sana... in corpore sano." A famous quote from the Roman poet Juvenal.</note> during this turbulent life. Hence it is, my Symphorien, most devoted to all liberal disciplines, that not only the noble homes <note>original: "patritii lares." In Roman religion, the Lares were household gods; here the term refers to the households of the elite.</note> but indeed all mortals owe much to you, and desire the highest happiness for you, and will always hold immortal thanks, since they cannot repay them. Live long and farewell; and greetings, my protector. At Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1506.

# Letter

...is to Samson Cottard, a Doctor of Arts of Paris; he is my intimate friend and companion. He is now heading to Montpellier for the sake of medical studies. You will find him to be a man of exceptional literacy and devoted to the liberal arts. And because I know your kindness especially favors those talents which are imbued with learning and, in turn, aspire to greater things: for that reason, I would greatly wish to entreat you to deign to write to your friends in Montpellier—of whom I know there are many—in his favor, and indeed with your usual affection. For it was by your auspices <note>Under your guidance or influence.</note> that I persuaded him to undertake this province <note>This specific task or journey.</note>. I also gave him the book recently composed by you, which he values as a great gift, and not without reason. Furthermore, you will first see the Lord Elect Gondisalvus; I ask that you deign to greet him in my words. Concerning the copperplate engravers <note>original: "chalcographis"—referring to printers or illustrators using metal plates.</note>, if you have done anything with them, let me know. Meanwhile, farewell. From the town <note>Likely Bourg-en-Bresse.</note>, the eleventh day of October, in the year of our Lord 1506.

---

->Humbert Fournier sends heartiest greetings to Master Symphorien<-
->Champier, the most skillful interpreter of the Peonian art <note>The "Peonian art" refers to medicine, named after Paean, the physician to the Greek gods.</note>.<-

---

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' featuring floral and foliage motifs within a square border.</image-desc>
You wish to know what we are primarily doing now in this once-famous market of Venus, on the sacred mount of the Virgin Mother of God <note>Fournier is likely punning on the name of Montpellier (Mons Pessulanus), which humanists sometimes associated with "Mons Puellarum" (Mount of Maidens/Venus) or religious devotion.</note>. Behold, we live in celibacy and literary leisure: embracing humane letters with "arms drawn tight" (as they say) by day and by night. We strive to repair the loss of wasted time—if such a thing is possible—by the expense of the "midnight oil" <note>original: "olei impensa"—a classical metaphor for late-night study.</note>, grieving that we spent so many sluggish hours and so many years in prodigal luxury; we pay the cruel penalty for such an unfortunate waste. Here, all labor is noble. 

First, conversation is held concerning religion, death, and the establishing of morals and disciplines of the soul with my "Socrates," Andreas Victorius—a man of such virtue that if I wished to relate his merits one by one, I would be forced to compress into the narrowness of a letter things that would require a solid volume; that is not my purpose here. You would marvel to the point of stupor at his rare gifts of mind and talent, his piety, the brilliance of his character, and the pure flower of a theological life, if you knew him more intimately. 

Guests also flow here, who, though they are few, are nevertheless conspicuous for their virtue. There is present no small relief for our cares: Master Gondisalvus, the "other eye" of our academy; he is at once our Apollo and our Praxiteles <note>Praxiteles was a famous ancient Greek sculptor; Fournier is praising Gondisalvus's artistic or intellectual refinement.</note>. Since he is most brilliantly distinguished in the disciplines of the liberal arts and welcomed into the good graces of all noble craftsmen, he exists not so much as a studious lover of these things as a diligent imitator of them. 

After we have indulged the Muses <note>original: "camenis"—the Roman goddesses of poetry and song.</note>, and a truce has been given to our sedentary readings, our studies are relaxed and witty conversation, "toothless" jests <note>original: "sales sine dente"—harmless, gentle humor that does not "bite" or offend.</note>, and a pleasing urbanity pass back and forth between us. Here, one man weaves a subtle commentary; another describes the wild rage of the Turks against our people; and I, not idle among such works, play the Etruscan bard <note>Likely referring to Petrarch or Dante, the great poets of Tuscany/Etruria.</note> surrounded by an appreciative circle. Another, acting out various roles of eloquence and character according to the occasion—faces, ridiculous stories, magical tricks—portrays the slips of those falling headlong. Expressing the ferocity of a beast, the atrocity of a fratricide, or the "Medusan error" regarding metamorphosis and old wives' tales to frighten children, he holds the mouths of those standing around suspended in gaps of wonder. 

To these things, my "Socrates" [Andreas Victorius] argues most weightily that one must not trade in the gems and gold of Midas, nor the strength of Milo, nor the grandiloquence of Maro <note>Virgil</note>, or the merchandise of such fleeting household goods; nor should time be risked in the leisure of the lazy. Instead, one must think most intensely on the impending destruction of death—which is the true philosophy of the soul. He discourses most gravely on the pearls of theological maxims, seeking not so much to spurn pleasure and luxury as to banish them into an exile from which there is no return. 

Then, for the great pleasure of our ears, let "Orpheus" <note>Referring to a musician.</note> separate the hollow lute with a learned thumb and tuneful strings. To these, the little birds chirp in harmony with alternating measures of distinct little voices. Now the wandering weeping of the hollow and multi-holed reed <note>A flute or pipe.</note>, stirred by a fervent finger, with a swift-moving tongue and a shrill tinkling, Musaeus—your sister's son <note>Or "your kindred Muse."</note>—sweetly soothes the ear with a Siren-like song. 

Now we care for mind and body with harmless wrestling <note>original: "palestritatide"—referring to the palaestra or gymnasium.</note>. Now, breathed upon by a soft breeze, we look upon the Arar <note>The Saône river in Lyons.</note> gliding past the houses of the city. We hear the high-sounding crashes of machines; we see fiery globes of sparks scrape the liquid air. Echo responds. The valleys ring out to the stars. And what is delightful to see from a high vantage point is a sort of mirror of the most beautiful things for those reclining: the grassy circuit of the region, the twin vines most beautifully hoed in the open, the meadows variegated with flowers...
