# Letter

Namely: smiling meadows; happy fates; lush crops; grassy fields; lofty mountains, turning green far and wide on every side. But enough of joking now; and abundantly, as I believe, we depict the successes of our studies and our fates and fortunes on this present paper. Furthermore, since my virtues, talent, and character are so very meager and small, the blind charity of your love for me could not have been ignorant of how little substance they have. In that place, and among strangers, you have praised me abundantly. That is your great kindness toward me and toward all—for which I thank you with all my might—which allows none of your friends to go unpraised, provided they are supported by even a tiny spark of virtue. Thus it happens that everyone wishes to owe everything to you alone. Add to this that while you carry the virtues of others so dearly in your heart, you show those virtues by which you yourself shine forth. 

Indeed, what expectation can these leading men have of me? For as you clearly know, I have been breathless from so many hardships exhaled from the bitter breast of my adversary in lawsuits; my paternal coffers have been exhausted; and this notable insult—more unhappy than any other irreparable loss—has affected us so that, by the longest legal delays <note>original: "postliminiis"—a legal term regarding the restoration of rights, here used for the delay in returning to his studies.</note>, it has at last banished us from the threshold of the Muses <note>The "threshold of the Muses" refers to his academic and literary pursuits.</note>. Regarding the recent victory of our little mountain <note>Likely a reference to a specific local dispute or a place name like Mont-Luel.</note>, I think enough punishment was taken for vengeance, which defrauded those of us who were emptied out of the better part of a richer harvest of learning. 

Therefore, you shall keep fixed and engraved upon the tablets of your mind that memorable saying of Stilpo <note>Stilpo (c. 360–280 BCE) was a philosopher of the Megarian school.</note>, which I cannot recall to mind with dry cheeks: when others were carrying away his worldly goods and he was asked by Demetrius whether the hands of the soldiers had snatched any of his things, Stilpo replied: "Not at all"; for he asserted that he saw no one carrying away his knowledge. You understand the point. However it may turn out, my dear Symphorien, I am one from whom you can, by a certain special right, promise yourself everything that can be provided by a grateful man. Farewell, and be happy for a long time. At Lyon, in the year of our Lord 1506.

->¶ Humbert Fournier sends heartiest greetings to Master Symphorien<- 
->Champier, a physician most learned in every respect.<-

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'V' depicting a scholar or cleric in academic robes seated at a desk or lectern with an open book, situated within an architectural interior.</image-desc>

I was wonderfully delighted by the delightful feast of your letters. Indeed, my dear Symphorien, I ran joyfully to meet your letters (which had conveniently reached the shelves of our library) speaking thus: "From what shores, at last, have you come, O most charming letters, you who have worn us down with long expectation while we were so anxiously suspended? Truly, we were worthy of such honor that your arrival among us should be skillful. We give you the greatest thanks; and we pray for the desired successes for your master." 

Those letters, as they return the favor of love with the words of a noble education, say: "We have come so that we might compensate you for the delay with a gift of doubled pleasure." You have done a thing most pleasing to me—no light pledge of friendship—and one worthy of you. For since I have been filled up from the reading of these letters by the succulence of your erudition, sweetened by the healthiness of your counsel, and abundantly satisfied, how much profit do you think I have made? What joy do you think is in me? You have humored me, my dearest friend, beyond what I had dared to hope. From this, melting for you in my innermost marrow, I take up the burden untiringly, and I obey your wishes, which no one could resist unless they were of unsound mind. Indeed, to distrust you even a little in this is as far from me as you are remote from vice. 

Furthermore, I have learned through a messenger that you have experienced the insolent impudence of a hooded, slandering rival <note>The "hooded" rival likely refers to a member of a monastic order who opposed the humanist medical reforms of Champier.</note>, and that you have narrowly escaped the rabid barking of a Molossian dog <note>A Molossian dog was a large ancient breed of guard dog; the term was a common humanist metaphor for a fierce critic.</note> and teeth sharpened on the whetstone of envy. This should not be so much a trouble to you as a joy: that you have someone who, by your easy victory, may spread your fame more brightly. For it usually happens to railers and such envious types as it does to those who stir glowing embers: when they try to extinguish them with their breath, they only make them shine more strongly. But more on these things with you another time. 

I proceed to the other point. You have freed me from a great trouble, unraveling the doubt of a hesitant mind; with the true cauteries <note>In a medical context, a "cautery" is a hot iron used for healing; here it refers to Champier's sharp but curative wisdom.</note> of your wisdom, you alone, my dear Symphorien, have driven out the weapon of sorrow which had been sitting deep within the marrow of my soul, as I had recently complained to you. By the antidote of your counsel, this so prominent an evil was met quite opportunely; for previously it was not permitted for anyone to try to reach my soul with prayers, so hedged in was I by so many errors of old. Truly, I do not know with what great duties of humanity I may respond to you, except by loving and honoring you in return—since my resources will never be sufficient—which I shall do as long as spirit rules these limbs. I will, moreover, take care that you realize that you did not give counsel, nor did I obey your advice, in vain. Farewell.

# Letter

<image-desc>A decorative historiated woodcut initial 'W' <note>The Latin text begins with a decorative 'C' for 'Cum,' but the English translation begins with 'W' for 'While.'</note> depicting a scholar or cleric seated at a desk within a vaulted architectural setting, engaged in writing or study.</image-desc>

**W**hile I was at the bookseller's workshop, moving with a sharper eye to select a book—as is my habit—by some favorable omen, your brilliant book, which is titled *On Curing the Ailments of the Soul and Body*, came into my hands. It had just begun to be printed <note>original: "formulis ereis excudi"—literally "to be struck from bronze molds," referring to the relatively new technology of the printing press.</note> from the metal types, and it affected me with a sudden and twofold joy. For attached to the back of your original manuscript <note>original: "archetypi"</note> followed a companion letter by **Jean Lemaire**. This is a surname <note>original: "Lognomentum," likely a variant of "Cognomentum."</note> truly consistent with his virtues, as one who, by a certain greatness of his excellent talent, surpasses other men of his station in the narrow field of eloquence. 

Indeed, last summer—while the fates and God allowed me to enjoy the wonderful companionship of my "Socrates" at the Autumn of Venus <note>original: "olum veneris," likely a classical or local seasonal reference</note>, inhabiting what is now the shrine of the Virgin—I experienced the man's talent, his timely eloquence, his strategies, his well-rounded rhythms, and his multi-faceted knowledge of history and heroes. And I experienced it in such a way that I felt a shiver of shame for my own idleness and weariness of studies. For indeed, with his ready speech in both the French and Italian <note>original: "ausonia"—literally Ausonian, a poetic term for Latin or Italian.</note> tongues, a firm friendship was suddenly forged between us. It left me so stunned and astonished that his image entered my mind and remained for many days—just as happened to **Dido** regarding **Aeneas**, whose living face and words remained fixed in her heart—and it caused me to scarcely remember myself. 

Truly, my mind was once set ablaze with a youthful love by his reputation, and I longed to address the man and join right hand to right hand. In his company, I seemed to be in the "Fortunate Isles"; for he, having used little or no teacher, but occupying his spare time and royal business with a wealth of words and the clearest streams of thought—with a friendly and overflowing nature—seemed to gush forth entirely.

From these things, indeed, it has happened, my **Symphorianus**, that I have been so charmed by a "double symphony": by his brilliance and by the rhythms with which he, weaving flowers among sweet words, courteously cultivates the **"Little Garden of Champier"** <note>original: "Champerianū hortulum"—a play on Symphorien Champier's name, suggesting his works are a cultivated garden of knowledge.</note> and waters it with a honeyed coating of praise. In this lush field of your erudition, you have left nothing to be desired for solid pleasure. I shall never speak so magnificently of you that your virtue does not surpass it.

But now I return to you, best of philosophers, who look after both the diseases of the soul and the body for the human race. That which can neither be ransomed by wealth, nor healed by gold, nor avoided by gems, you nevertheless rescue from destruction with the restorative portions of your philosophy. You explode the enticing marshes <note>original: "lernas"—referring to the Lernaean Hydra, symbolizing a multifaceted evil or swamp.</note> of pleasures; you thrust away every kind of dire disease; and once thrust away, you cherish the patient with healthy medicines. This you have done with the manifold talent of your genius, with which you have enriched us abundantly. This was not done without the will of the gods—or rather, not without great labor and a distinguished devotion toward your homeland. Although you had already earned enough merit from the labors of your youth, you now show not just a natural love but your noble work; you wished to declare by this manifest proof and this extraordinary offspring of yours how much the future will be indebted to you.

What gifts, therefore, shall we repay in worthy exchange? With what civic or laurel crown shall we deserve such an excellent citizen? With what thanks shall we fulfill our duty? What praises worthy of you shall I bring forth for this late-night labor <note>original: "lucubratione"—work produced by lamplight, signifying intense study.</note>? These works need neither my heraldry nor anyone else's, since they shine sufficiently with their own brightness. Come now, if there were a need for recommendation or patronage, it would be superfluous to "teach Minerva" <note>An idiom meaning to teach someone something they already know better than you.</note> when the work is supported by such a firm pillar of protection that it seems to cut off all handle for slanderers. This support comes from that most noble prelate, a famous trumpet of eloquence and a man learned in every respect: **Laurent Bureau**. 

But alas! A dark day took him away and plunged him into a bitter death. Wicked death has snatched away this man, another element of nature, whose talent was to be admired rather than imitated, and who alone could withstand the rotations of Fortune. Posterity can never mourn his funeral rites enough. We are afflicted by such a great hardship; we are damaged by such a great and calamitous loss in his passing, that by this cruel death, the **Muses**, the **Graces**, the **Venuses**, the **Wits**, and whatever else is desirable have all perished together. Add to this that the light which he poured out upon the blind ignorance of men through the rays of his doctrine, he has taken away with him as well.

This archetype of wit, having deserved well of God, of virtue, and of men, before he breathed out his happy soul, used to be very humorous and witty in his kindness. He would often mingle jokes with his speech, as was his clever custom, when rubbing elbows with crowds of guests at the table. Not only did he deem this "golden monument" of your talent worthy of being a handbook <note>original: "enchiridio"</note>, but he also illuminated it with heaped praises and his own signature before our Suffragan <note>An assistant bishop.</note>—a man of no less virtue—and other nobles who were present. 

Indeed, it must not be passed over in silence that with a richer thread of his eloquence and a sweet-sounding Pierian <note>A poetic reference to the Muses.</note> song (I drank in the voice with these very ears), he voluntarily added himself as a sponsor, like the most precious pearls, with a very firm pledge of faith. For I remember while he still drew the vital air, he wished to be called to you quite often, being delighted by your company both for the sake of his health and social life, and so that he might frequently use your services in serious matters. Nor is it a wonder, since he was well aware of your virtues...

<summary>This preface praises the physician and philosopher Symphorien Champier, noting the author's discovery of his new book at a printer's. It highlights Champier's connection to the poet Jean Lemaire de Belges and mourns the recent death of their patron, the learned Bishop Laurent Bureau.</summary>
<keywords>Symphorien Champier, Jean Lemaire de Belges, Laurent Bureau, printing history, humanist correspondence, medicine and philosophy, mourning, Muses</keywords>

# Letter

[The author continues praising Champier’s virtues] ...the wealth of your talent: your constant study, the incredible tenacity of your memory, the elegance of your manners, the integrity of your life, your tall stature, the dignity of your countenance, and your expertise as a storehouse <note>original: "promptuarium"</note> of the history and deeds of all nations everywhere. These qualities did not escape that most keen-eyed man <note>referring to Jean Lemaire de Belges mentioned on the previous page</note>, who, having observed them sharply, was drawn to you by no common friendship. Since this is so, why do you hesitate to set sail? I, like the Sirens, shall rouse men—not monsters <note>original: "martas," likely a corruption of "monstra"</note>—but I shall set your ship ablaze with song. Receive it then with happy minds, O venerable cohort of the lettered, if any of your flock are about to board our vessel, so that you may more graciously pay the fare <note>original: "naulum," the fee paid to a ferryman like Charon.</note>.

Know that this ship is not Alexandrian <note>The "Alexandrian ships" were the massive grain freighters of the Roman Empire; here, the author contrasts material cargo with intellectual cargo.</note>, but **Symphorian**; it does not sweat with perishable goods, nor painted curls, nor seductive trappings, nor is it decaying with foul odors or cracking with adulterated parts. Instead, it is filled with pearls, bright with gems, radiating with gold, girded with the maxims of teachings, and loaded with such merchandise that will calmly carry you to the field of erudition, the summit of virtue, and the health of the "twofold man" <note>original: "vtriusq; hominis salutem," referring to the health of both the soul and the body, the subject of Champier’s book.</note>, provided you fix your mind’s eye toward the port of Wisdom.

Why do you fear? All is safe. The fleet is solid, not shaken by ruins or gaping with cracks, and these things are available as a useful provision for the journey. Our founder <note>Champier</note> is carried along by skillful rowing, supported by the strong mast of prudence, armed with the poles of energy, girt with the anchor of doctrine, and secured by the ropes of mature counsel and similar strengths. 

Run here, all of you, with a swift course! Why do you stand there yawning? Listen again in a few words: if any fear clings to your hearts, if you dread an unfaithful harbor for the keel or the threats of the trident and the sea: be of good heart; "the matter is in the shallows" <note>original: "res e in vado," a Latin idiom meaning a situation is safe or the danger is past.</note>. Already, shake off the cloud of terror! Behold, the Zephyrs blow gently. Daedalean companions are present who sweep the blue seas, steering with the tiller of Ulysses; they will be able to safely wear down the sharp rocks of teeth, put to flight the stormy tempests of the ghastly, restrain Scylla <note>A legendary sea monster from Greek mythology.</note>, and plow through the storm-bearing waves of the envious.

But I have already gone on half as long again as I intended. I will make an end, lest I seem to flatter you longer with this "trash of words" <note>original: "quisquilijs," literally sweepings or dregs</note>, from which, in your modesty, you are far removed, and which I also greatly abhor. It remains, my **Symphorian**, that I kindle you with these torches and incite you with these goads—though you are already running of your own accord—so that you might use the spur of your talent to surpass others. This is through this meritorious glory and dutiful labor, and—as befits great souls—the excellence of eternal fame, by whose sweetness the minds of the ancients were ignited, leaving us a most fertile harvest. With this fame, I hope you will enrich us equally, both now and in the future, for the common utility of all, for the great increase of your virtues and praises, and for the perpetual glory of your name.

Farewell. 

At Lyons, in the year of our salvation 1506.

***

->¶ This present work was printed at Lyons at the expense of the most honest booksellers **Stephanus Gueynard** and **Jacobus Huguetan**; indeed, by the art and industry of **Jannot de Campis**. In the year of our Lord 1507. Finished on the day before the Kalends of August <note>July 31, 1507.</note><-
